When you validate an ISP-3505, ISP-3506 or ISP-3507 form, and you suspect that a false or misleading statement has been made, refer to Referral Process for Administrative Investigations—CPP (Scenario) or Referral Process for Administrative Investigations—OAS (Scenario) . The individual making the statement can be subject to an administrative penalty and interest or can be charged with an offence. The individual must repay any benefits they received to which they were not entitled. Referral Process for Administrative Investigations—CPP (Scenario) Referral Process for Administrative Investigations—OAS (Scenario) By signing the ISP-3506 or the ISP-3507 form, the person or agency agrees to: act on the client's behalf by accounting for all benefits received from the Department and indicating how this money was spent; notify the Department if they feel that they are no longer in a position to administer the benefits effectively; notify the Department of any changes regarding the client's condition; return the payment for any month during which the client is no longer in their care; and return any benefits paid for the month following the month of a beneficiary's death. Senior who is incapable and homeless Additional sections must be completed on the ISP-3507 form when the senior is incapable, is homeless or at risk of being homeless and is approaching 65 years of age or older. An organization can be appointed to administer benefits on behalf of a senior who is incapable and homeless if the following requirements are met: the organization has entered into an agreement with the Minister; and there is no existing third-party agreement on file with the Department. This requirement is satisfied when the designated representative completes the ISP-3507 form. The ISP-3507 form also specifies the roles and responsibilities of the administrating organization. If a charitable organization completed the form, refer to the CRA's List of charities and certain other qualified donees - basic search Internal link to verify that the organization is tax exempt and is registered. List of charities and certain other qualified donees - basic search To administer benefits on behalf of a senior who is incapable and homeless, non-profit organizations must also have a tax exempt status and must demonstrate that they are valid and reputable. The validity of a non-profit organization is determined through: their constitution or by-laws; their letters of incorporation; or other information provided to support their reputation (e.g. documentation indicating a history and recognizing their excellence in delivering services to seniors who are homeless or at risk of being homeless). The applicant or organization will attest that it is a non-profit organization with tax exempt status on the ISP-3507 form. Municipalities must be incorporated under a provincial and or territorial statute and must provide the name of the statute when they complete the ISP-3507 form. You must verify if the municipality is incorporated in the relevant jurisdiction. You can access information regarding statutes through provincial or territorial websites. Liability insurance All organizations must have the ability to fund liabilities. To be appointed to administer the benefits of a senior who is incapable and homeless or at risk of being homeless, non-profit organizations and registered charities must have liability insurance of one million dollars. Municipalities without this insurance will generally be able to cover such a liability. If either of these requirements is not met, you must refuse the application. If an organization or municipality does not provide their liability coverage with the application package, you can find this information in publicly available budgets, audits, financial statements or annual reports. If there is a risk that the organization or municipality does not have the required ability or insurance (e.g. small municipal units or unknown organizations), you must contact the organization for further information or written confirmation. The person certifying the incapability of the senior who is homeless must affirm on the ISP-3505 form (Section 12) that they are a member in good standing of the relevant professional association or organization. They must be a designated non-medical professional (social worker, lawyer or member of the clergy) or medical professional (physician, registered nurse, nurse practitioner, psychologist or psychiatrist). If the person completing the ISP-3505 form has not indicated that they are a member of the professional association or organization, you cannot accept the ISP-3505 form. To accept the certification, you must verify the name of the association or organization and the membership by using publicly available information. You must verify the following: the name of the association or organization and the province indicated is correct; and the person is listed as a member on their website (only applicable to some professions, provinces or territories). If the information provided is questionable or unclear, request further information or verification from the applicable third-party organization or individual.

This procedure demonstrates how to review the Client Status screen to verify the benefits a client has applied for or is receiving. It also demonstrates how to determine which processing centre is responsible for the client's file.

Office of Control Numbers, Region Codes and Processing Centres

You must review the Client Status screen every time you receive a work item. This review will determine which benefits a client has applied for or is currently receiving. The information on the Client Status screen is separated into 5 columns: Benefit Type ; Benefit Status ; Reason ; Region / OCON ; and OCON Client Identifier . The columns can be sorted in ascending and descending alphabetical order. The Region / OCON information displayed in the Client Status screen is automatically determined by the system when it saves an initial application. This is done regardless of the status of the application or when a client's home address is changed where a Region / OCON already exists. For CPP, the Region / OCON displays the name of the region where the client lives, the regional office or specialized centre maintaining the client's account and the associated 4-digit Office of Control (OCON), e.g. Alberta Duals (0819). For OAS, the Region / OCON displays the name of the regional office responsible for maintaining the client‘s account (e.g. Alberta Regional). An individual's CPP benefits can have more than one OCON attached to them, where their Identifier is displayed for each OCON. For example, a child can receive one Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit payment from each disabled parent. The Identifier of each parent must be displayed with the associated OCON. An NRT withhold may be applied to a client’s account if they reside in a country other than Canada. This withhold is automatically added by ITRDS but can be manually modified, if required. NRT rate reasons The NRT rate reasons are the following : Rate Selection Reason Result Deemed The client is deemed a Canadian resident by Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for tax purposes. ITRDS automatically sets the rate to 0%. Federal voluntary tax withhold (FVTW) is allowed on the account. Default The client’s home address or the rate reason selected sets a system-generated rate. The rate is set according to the beneficiary's country of residence in the Non-Resident Tax table . No FVTW is allowed on the client’s account. Non-Resident Tax table NR5 Reduction CRA has advised the reduction of the NRT rate. No FVTW is allowed on the client’s account. Retroactive CRA has advised the increase of the rate by up to 50%, i.e. higher than the default rate, so that NRT can be withheld retroactively. No FVTW is allowed on the client’s account. NRT exception rate reasons When a client has a payee or non-payee contact and both the client and their contact live in different countries, you must use a tax withhold exception. The exception rate reasons are the following : Exception rate selection Reasons Client Exception The client resides in Canada. The client's contact resides outside of Canada. Deemed Exception The client is a deemed resident. The client's contact resides in Canada or in a different foreign country than the client. Default Exception The client is foreign. The client’s contact resides in Canada or in a different foreign country than the client. The default rate is applied. NR5 Exception The client is foreign. The client's contact resides in Canada or in a different foreign country than the client. An approved NR5 Reduction rate is applied. Retro Exception The client is foreign. The client’s contact resides in Canada or in a different foreign country than the client. There is retroactive non-resident tax to be collected.

When you need to communicate with a client or their authorized representative, you must first make a reasonable effort to contact them by phone, if applicable, before sending any correspondence by mail, except in the following situations: when the client has indicated that they do not wish to be or cannot be contacted by phone; or The information requested must be received in writing. Contacting a client or their authorized representative by phone minimizes processing timeframes. Ensure that you consider time zones before calling. When speaking with the client or their authorized representative, use neutral and plain language. Use only the first and last name provided on the application or documentation unless a preferred title (e.g. Mr., Mrs., Ms.) is requested during the call, specified on their application, or recorded in the system. Ensure that you are speaking with the client or their authorized representative before you discuss any personal information on file. To do this you must authenticate the individual's identity. For specific direction, Authenticate a Client or an Authorized Representative During a Phone Call (Action) Once the call is complete, you must document the details of your conversation using ITRDS Notes and the Telephone Call (ISP-0112) form or the appropriate CPPD form.

Letters are the most common way of communicating with a client or their authorized representative. When requesting information, a letter to the client or their authorized representative must be all-inclusive. Where possible, one letter must request all required information or documents needed for adjudication or clarification of a client's file. For information on using the departmental letter systems, including signature requirements, Correspondence (Knowledge) Clients can request to have any of the Department's correspondence be sent in an alternate format. All CPP and OAS forms, publications and letters are available in the following alternate formats: audio CD (MP3 or WAV format); braille; Digital Accessible Information System (DAISY), an audio alternate format for written materials that allows the user to: go to specific chapters or pages; place a bookmark; and use an index. e-text CD, an easy-read text using word-processing software (MS Word format); or large print. When a client's file contains an Important Note in ITRDS indicating their request for an alternate format, you must ensure all communication adheres to the client's request. For more information, Requesting or Receiving Forms, Publications or Letters in Alternate Formats (Action)

text: When a client provides their consent for a third party to communicate with the Department, an authorizing document must be on the client's file. Information about the authorized representative and contact details are found: on the client's Contact / Applicant screen in ITRDS ; on the ITRDS Notes screen; and by clicking on Third Party Contact on the Evidence tab in Cúram. If a third party asks for or gives information about a client, review ITRDS , Cúram and the client's file to make sure appropriate documentation has been received to authorize the Department to communicate with the third party. If there is documentation to support communication with the third party, you may communicate only the information they are authorized to receive. For more information, Privacy and Personal Information (Scenario) You can also send correspondence to a third party's address if it is authorized in the client's file. text: If you are calling the client or their authorized representative, you must leave a message on a voicemail service when there is no answer. You are not required to confirm that the voicemail includes the client's or their authorized representative's name before leaving a voicemail requesting a call back. If an unauthorized third party answers the client's or the authorized representative's phone, you can leave a message with that individual. Leave a message on the voicemail or with the third party with the following details. For script examples, refer to Call Scripts for Client Engagement : Identify yourself including your name and that you are calling from Service Canada; Indicate who the message is for; Ask for the client or their authorized representative to call you back; Provide one of the following numbers: your direct phone number including the area code if it is necessary to speak with the client or their authorized representative regarding the client's file. one of the following Service Canada Call Centre numbers if the call is general in nature: 1-800-277-9914 (English) 1-800-277-9915 (French) 1-800-255-4786—Teletype users 1-800-454-8731—International Operations 1-613-957-1954 (collect calls will be accepted) 1-800-255-4786—Teletype users Call Scripts for Client Engagement Update ITRDS notes and complete the Telephone Call (ISP-0112) form or the applicable CPPD form to record: the date and time of the call; the reason for the call; that a message was left requesting a call-back; and your name and direct phone number for call centre staff to redirect the client's call, if applicable.

If you are calling the client or their authorized representative and there is no answer or a voice message cannot be left, update ITRDS notes to record that you could not reach the client or their authorized representative by phone and a voice message could not be left. Take the appropriate actions to process the work item (e.g. send a letter, BF or close the work item). The bankruptcy trustee sends a consumer proposal , creditor's voting form and expense report to all the creditors identified by the debtor. All debts incurred up to and including the date of filing a consumer proposal are included in the proposal. Any debts after the date of filing are collectible. The creditors have 45 days to vote on the proposal. If a creditor fails to vote within 45 days, it is viewed as accepting the proposal. For information on Consumer Proposal policy, refer to the Insolvency section of the policy Overpayments—Recovery and Collection . If the proposal is accepted UPDATED! When the Department receives formal notification that a consumer proposal has been filed, all recovery actions on the account are deferred (where recovery has not yet been initiated) or suspended (where recovery has been initiated) until a decision is rendered. UPDATED! You must place any CPP receivables on the debtor's CPMS account on Hold when a proposal is filed. Refer to Change a Departmental Receivable Status . The consumer proposal includes the amount that the debtor must reimburse along with a payment schedule of up to 5 years. The debtor must make these monthly payments to the bankruptcy trustee until the full proposed amount is collected. The bankruptcy trustee informs the creditors when the monies are sent to the creditor. This can be yearly or semi-annually, depending on the case. The bankruptcy trustee attaches a dividend sheet with each payment. The dividend sheet provides the creditors with a breakdown of how the monies were disbursed to each creditor. During the repayment period, the dividend sheets are marked “interim dividend”. When the last payment is made, the dividend sheet is marked “final dividend.” UPDATED! When the final payment is received, the outstanding balance of the debt incurred up to the date of filing is permanently written off. consumer proposal Change a Departmental Receivable Status Write-Offs—Overpayment If the proposal is rejected or annulled UPDATED! If the consumer proposal is rejected by the court or by creditors or if a debtor fails to make 3 consecutive monthly payments to the bankruptcy trustee and the proposal is annulled, the bankruptcy trustee will inform the Department by letter. UPDATED! In such cases, when you receive this letter or are informed by the CRA that the proposal is rejected or annulled, you must change the departmental receivable status to Active . This reinstates the collection recovery rate and the full amount of the initial debt is collected. If any monies are received from the bankruptcy trustee before an annulment, these amounts are kept. consumer proposal change the departmental receivable status

text: CPP and OAS receivables are higher on the priority of withholds than a CRA debt. In cases where CRA requests to withhold 100% of a client's benefit but there is already an amount being recovered for a CPP or OAS receivable, only the remaining can be withheld for the CRA Statutory set-off. For example, you receive a Statutory Set-Off form from CRA indicating that a client has a significant income tax debt and they are requesting the Department withhold 100% of the client’s CPP and OAS benefits. After a review of the file, you determine that there is already a recovery rate of 25% on the client’s CPP and OAS benefits applied to a CPP debt. The Department will continue to recover 25% of the client’s benefits for the CPP debt and the remaining 75% of their benefits will be withheld for CRA.

The Department will honour requests for a set-off from Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) or another federal department against active CPP and/or OAS accounts when the request has been made in the appropriate manner. A third party receivable is recovered from benefits currently payable to a client (i.e. debtor). You can deduct from a monthly or supplementary payment, in whole or in part, and apply it to the third party receivable debt. For active accounts, the recovery will begin as soon as possible upon receipt of the completed form. If it is too late to process the recovery in the current accounting month, the action should be done in the next accounting month. Cheques should not be pulled. When the account is not yet in pay and a notice is received, the application should be processed, if approved, and the recovery action should be applied retroactively against the arrears entitlement. If a balance is still owing, a recovery rate must be established. CRA If CRA is requesting a set-off against an active CPP and/or an OAS benefit, they must provide a properly completed CRA Statutory Set-Off form. Refer to Information Sharing . CRA can request to recover a tax debt from a client’s CPP or OAS benefit payments without their authorization. Information Sharing Veterans Affairs Canada To deduct a third party receivable from CPP or OAS benefit payments, Veterans Affairs Canada must submit a written request that includes the client's authorization. Other departments Requests from other federal departments will be accepted when such requests are made in writing and are approved at the ministerial level. Once the Minister has authorized the request, a third party receivable can be processed. Family Orders Enforcement Family Orders and Agreements allows for garnishment orders to recover against federal monies. This is an automated process and requires no action by the processing staff. Full remission The Department considers a full remission to be the request to remit an entire initial overpayment amount. topic_title: Remissions due to Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error
text: If it is determined that a debt is a result of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) made by the Department, the debt can be considered for a full or partial remission. The amount of the debt that you will recommend remitting will be determined on a case-by-case basis. It will also depend on the circumstances and sequences of events that occurred. When a debt is increased because of the Department's actions or inactions, depending on the circumstances of the case, there is flexibility to consider remitting all or portions of the debt. You must use your judgment and discretion to review each individual file to determine: who is responsible for the error (i.e. the Department or the client); if the other party (the Department or client, as applicable) knew about the error; and any events that occurred after the error was made, such as: the timeline of events; attempts made to correct the error; and any action that increased the overpayment amount. The following table provides direction on whether to recommend a full or partial remission. This is not an exhaustive list of situations and can vary based on each case's specific circumstances. Table 1. Remitting Erroneous Advice or Administrative Error Cases Responsible for the error Awareness of error Direction The client is responsible for the error. The Department could not have been aware of the error. Fully recover the overpayment from the client as this is not a case of EA/AE. The client is responsible for the error. The Department should have noticed the error (e.g. evidence is on file or in the system). If the information was on file to allow the Department to correct the error but it was overlooked, then a portion of the responsibility lies with the Department. Recommend remitting 50% of the debt. The Department is responsible for the error. The client could not have been aware of the error. Recommend fully remitting the debt. The Department is responsible for the error. The client was aware of the error but did not contact the Department to correct it. Both the Department and the client are partially responsible for the overpayment when: the Department is initially responsible for the error; the Department informs the client about the error (e.g. incorrect date of birth on an award letter); and the client fails to contact the Department to correct the error. Recommend remitting 50% of the debt as we cannot attribute specific portions of the debt to each party. The Department is responsible for the error. The client was aware of the error and contacted the Department to have it corrected. If you determined the Department should be held accountable for a portion of the overpayment, you can recommend a partial remission for that portion. Once you determine the portion of the Department's responsibility in relation to the EA/AE case, you must do the following: provide a rationale to explain your recommendation for the proposed percentage rates; provide what period of time or portion it covers; and recover any remaining balance of the debt, if applicable. For more information on how to determine a partial remission, refer to Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) and Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) Examples of Partial Remission (Work Tool)

topic_title: Should you write-off the debt instead of remitting it?
text: A write-off is an accounting action that removes, in whole or in part, a legally enforceable debt from the accounts receivable records. A write-off does not mean that the debt is forgiven. The debt continues to exist but the recovery is deferred so that the debt can be collected in the future. After you review the file, you may determine that the debt should be recommended for a write-off. The following situations are examples where a write-off should be recommended: The debtor is deceased and there is no known estate or person responsible for the deceased debtor's affairs (e.g. there is no response to the Department's request for repayment when sent to the deceased's last known address); The debtor is a non-resident and there is no apparent means of collecting the debt at this time; The debtor cannot be located; The debtor is experiencing long term hardship with the possibility of future recovery; A balance of a debt remains after a compromised settlement is accepted; A balance of a debt remains after a discharged bankruptcy; A balance of a debt remains after an undischarged bankruptcy; A balance of a debt remains after the closure of a consumer proposal; The Department determined the debt was the result of misrepresentation and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts. The debtor has a debt arising from a conviction of fraud and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts. For more information, refer to Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) and Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) Write-Off an Overpayment (Scenario)

There is no time limit on the certification of a document as long as there is no reason to doubt the document's authenticity. An individual certifying a copied document is attesting to the fact that they have compared it to the original document and found it to be a true copy of the original and unaltered in any way. For a complete list of officials who can certify a photocopy of a document, Documentary Evidence—Treatment and Use (Policy)

A certified true copy means that a copy bears a stamp or written statement attesting to the fact that it is exactly the same as the original document. There is no set formal or standardized legal wording to use when certifying documents. When certifying documents, you must do so in writing using phrases or stamps such as the following: Certified copy of the original; This copy conforms to the original; or I certify this to be a true copy of the original. The Department uses the following standard statement: “This photocopy conforms to the original document which has not been altered in any way.” There are a number of other conditions that must be met before you can accept a certified copy. For more information, Documentary Evidence—Treatment and Use (Policy)

When you receive an original document: Copy each page of the document, excluding blank pages. Ensure the entire page has been copied. If a document is double-sided, ensure both sides are copied. If a document has multiple pages, copy all pages containing information. Complete the certification of the document. Certify the first page of the copy with the certification stamp. If the document contains multiple pages: stamp the first page only; indicate beside the certification the total number of pages and which pages are blank (e.g. “30 pages, 18-30 are blank”). Sign and date the stamp in the appropriate space. Add the certified true copy to the file. Return the original documentation to the client with the applicable letter: For CPP, send the Supply: Sending applications and information (ISS-6191) letter. For OAS, send the OAS - CPP, Return of original documents (ISS-0385) letter. Indicate in ITRDS notes the type of original documentation that you returned to the client. See details Update the client's notes in ITRDS to record details of your actions or decisions made on the account. Refer to ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) . topic_title: Copy of a certified true copy
text: Sometimes a document or form is received as a stamped certified copy of a certified true copy. Copies of certified true copies are unacceptable as certified true copies because an individual cannot certify an already certified copy of a document. It is impossible to accurately make a proper attestation when the certifier does not have access to the original document. There is one exception to this rule: in the past, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) issued immigration documents that were a certified copy of a certified copy. For more information, Documentary Evidence—Treatment and Use (Policy)

A certified document with multiple pages (e.g. passport) is acceptable if all the pages containing information are copied. Blank pages are excluded, but are noted in the certification that they are blank along with the total number of pages.

text: When you receive a certified true copy of a document: Review the copy of the document to ensure it is acceptable. The copy must: be legible and copied in full; not be altered in any way; have all pages of the document copied, excluding blank pages. topic_title: OAS Time Bar Provision and Common-Law Adjustments
text: OAS Time Bar Provision When an overpayment for an OAS pension, the Guaranteed Income Sup plement (GIS), the Allowance (ALW) or th e Allowance f or the Survivor (ALWS) ben efits covers a period before April 1, 1994, the full amount of the overpayment—including the time bar portion—must be set up as an overpayment. The time bar portion must be remitted before the debtor is advised of the outstanding debt due. For more information on actioning a remission, Remit an Overpayment If there is an outstanding OAS overpayment balance after the time bar portion has been remitted, follow standard recovery proced ures to collect the overpayment. Refer t o Departmental Receivable (Overpayments) The following are examples of common recovery situations involving the time bar provision: Common-law adjustments on income-tested benefits Updated Bill C-23 came into force in July 2000 and its purpose was to: recognize same-sex relationships; extend CPP and OAS benefits and obligations to all individuals in common-law relationships; and establish a common definition of spouse and common-law partner in the CPP and OAS programs. If you are informed or become aware of an existing common-law relationship that impacts entitlement to an income-tested benefit (e.g., GIS, ALW or ALWS), the affected accounts must be recalculated back to the effective date of the common-law relationship, but no earlier than July 2000. If the recalculation results in an overpayment, follow standard recovery procedures to collect the overpayment. Refe r to Departmental Receivable (Overpayments)

The debtor was overpaid from June 1990 to September 1995 for a total amount of $25,000. The overpayment was not discovered and set up until September 1995; The overpayment for the period from June 1990 to March 1994 of $15,000 is not recoverable, because it was not established and set up before the removal of the time bar provisions of April 1, 1994. The total overpayment amount that is owing is from April 1, 1994, to September 1995 and is $10,000. The full $25,000 amount must be set up in the system. The $15,000 for the period of June 1990 to March 1994 must be remitted. The $10,000 for the period of April 1994 to September 1995 must be recovered in full.

Bankruptcy is a legal process undertaken by a debtor who is unable to repay their debts. When a debtor files for bankruptcy, a bankruptcy trustee submits a bankruptcy notice and proof of claim to the debtor’s creditors. Insolvency occurs when a debtor is unable to repay their debts at the time they are due. Under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act , an offer to repay under modified repayment terms is made through a consumer proposal. Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has been delegated to handle matters related to bankruptcy and insolvency. When CRA receives a bankruptcy or insolvency notice, they email the Department requesting to defer or suspend recovery action. Upon receipt of a formal written notification, the Department must defer or suspend recovery action on a debtor’s CPP receivable by placing it on Hold until the bankruptcy court makes a decision. A charge back to the financial institution is requested when the Department must recover a redeemed payment from a deceased client's account. A charge back is only possible when the payment attempt status is Redeemed in the Standard Payment System (SPS). When a monthly payment has been issued after the month of death, you must also attempt to recover any redeemed payments from the estate at the same time. Overpayment on a Deceased's Account (Scenario) For domestic payments (cheques and direct deposit), the Payment Status and Authorization to Charge Back to Financial Institution (ISP0111) form must be completed and sent to the Imaging and Receiver General Operations Directorate (IRGOD) within Public Services and Procurement Canada to initiate a charge back to the financial institution that negotiated the payment. For foreign direct deposit payments, a trace request must be initiated in SPS. If the charge back request includes payments for both OAS and CPP, you must initiate a trace request for each program. You only need to initiate a trace for one Payment Reference Number per program. These requests are sent to Business Operations, who will contact the IRGOD to request a reimbursement from the Bank of America. The IRGOD will complete the investigation and carry out the charge back, if possible. Once the investigation is completed, the IRGOD will advise the Department of the results. If the charge back is successful and the Department receives monies back from both the financial institution and the estate, the estate will be refunded any amount that is over-recovered. A charge back request will be refused by the financial institution if they determine the client's estate has benefited from the monies deposited into the account.

Some specific situations that may cause an OAS overpayment include: a change in the marital status, income information or Canadian residence periods; when a client is outside the country for more than 6 months and is in receipt of a non-portable OAS pension or benefit, or an income-tested benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit); or a change to foreign pension rates for income-tested benefits.

topic_title: CPMS functionality and interaction with the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system
text: CPMS automatically sends all departmental receivable information to the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements (PSCD) system. For an active account, CPMS will automatically set a recovery rate and start recovery against the debtor's CPP payments after a departmental receivable is created in CPMS . For inactive accounts, the CRA is responsible for the collection of overpayments. The CRA will start their collection activities 90 days after you have created a departmental receivable in CPMS . They will use PSCD to view the departmental receivable information. If you must suspend recovery actions on an overpayment (e.g. reconsideration, Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error), you must place the departmental receivable on Hold . If the account is inactive, you must also request for a lock to be placed on the account in PSCD.

Overpayments are normally recovered from monthly OAS or CPP payments, or from other eligible payments received from the same program from which the benefit was initially paid. However, if the overpayment cannot be recovered from the same program, it can be recovered from the other program. This process is known as the cross-program recovery . Cross Program Recovery (Scenario)

A cross-program recovery can be initiated when: a change results in an overpayment and the debtor is no longer eligible or entitled to an OAS pension or benefit, but the debtor is receiving benefits under the CPP program, including in the International Agreements (IA) system; a recovery rate of 100% against the debtor's OAS pension or benefit is insufficient to permit the Department to recover the overpayment within the 5- or 10-year period as per the and the debtor is receiving benefits under CPP, including in the IA system. For more information, refer to Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) ; or Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) a client dies with an overpayment owing on their OAS account and the debtor's estate applies for a DTH benefit, including in the IA system, unless the initial overpayment amount is $100 or less. To calculate the overpayment amount, you need to determine the overpayment period (i.e. when it begins and when it ends). An overpayment period begins the month: the first duplicate payment was received; following the month of death; following the month the entitlement ends; or the amended benefit amount becomes effective. An overpayment period ends the month: that the last duplicate payment was received; before the month the benefit amount is changed on the applicable system; before the month in which the payments are no longer issued; or before the month the account is suspended, cancelled or terminated (includes ceased after reassessment), as applicable.

topic_title: Notifying the debtor or legal representative Updated
text: When you establish an overpayment on a client's account, including cases of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE), you must promptly send an initial overpayment letter to the debtor or their legal representative. This letter is to inform the debtor about the amount of the overpayment and any changes to their entitlement amount. You must also request full repayment of the overpayment, except in cases of EA/AE. However, if the overpayment is $100 or less on an active account, you must notify the debtor of the amount and advise them that it will be automatically recovered from their next monthly payment. When sending an overpayment letter for an EA/AE case that you are investigating, you must ensure you: inform the debtor or legal representative that their file is under review and that information regarding recovery will be provided later; and do not request repayment or inform them that the overpayment may be remitted. When the investigation of the EA/AE is complete and if it is determined that the overpayment was due to EA/AE, you must obtain necessary approval to remit the overpayment either fully or partially before requesting any repayment, if applicable. If the overpayment: is fully remitted, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them that the overpayment was remitted; is partially remitted, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them about the remitted amount and request repayment of the remaining balance; is determined not to be due to EA/AE, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them that the review of the file is complete and to request repayment. Refer to the applicable tab within this procedure for instructions on recovery. For more information, Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) In cases of a sensitive nature (e.g. a large overpayment, recovery may cause undue hardship), it is recommended that you call the debtor or their legal representative before initiating recovery to inform them that they will receive a letter about their overpayment. For information regarding calling the debtor or legal representative, Authenticate a Client or an Authorized Representative During a Phone Call (Action) You must give a debtor or legal representative a minimum of 30 days to reply to the letter, except when recovering from arrears or overpayments of $100 or less on active accounts. The deadline to reply varies based on each situation (e.g. the debtor lives outside Canada or is ill). If the debtor or legal representative does not respond within 30 days: for an active account with overpayments over $100, you can initiate recovery from the debtor's monthly benefit payments. for an inactive account: with a CPP or CPPD receivable in CPMS , the CRA Collections Unit will be responsible for collecting the overpayment. A monthly Statement of Account will be sent to the debtor until the overpayment it is fully recovered. Reconsiderations and appeals The letter informing the client about the overpayment and the reason for the overpayment must include the debtor's reconsideration or appeal rights. If the debtor or their legal representative is not satisfied with the CPP or OAS decision: they have the right to request a reconsideration or appeal regarding the reason for the overpayment; and they cannot request a reconsideration or appeal regarding the amount of the overpayment or the recovery rate. Reconsideration or appeal rights are not provided for CPP or CPPD overpayments, for an account dependent on another beneficiary's eligibility and the beneficiary is no longer eligible. Reconsideration or appeal rights for OAS overpayments are provided for all benefits. This includes when an ALW beneficiary loses eligibility due to the OAS pensioner no longer being eligible for OAS and GIS. For more information, Reconsideration (Scenario)

topic_title: Recovery of an overpayment on an active account
text: When the overpayment is $100.00 or less and there is a monthly benefit in pay in ITRDS , CPMS recovers the full overpayment from the debtor's next monthly benefit payment. If the monthly entitlement amount is insufficient to recover the full amount of the overpayment, the outstanding balance will be recovered from the subsequent payments. When the overpayment is more than $100.00 and there is a monthly benefit in pay in ITRDS , CPMS automatically sets the recovery rate at 25% against the debtor's monthly CPP entitlement. You must adjust the recovery rate if the debtor is also in receipt of an OAS pension or benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit), including in the International Agreements system. If the CPP debtor is also in receipt of: an OAS pension only (i.e. no GIS), you must calculate the recovery rate at 25% of the total CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts; or an OAS pension and a GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit, you must calculate the recovery rate at 10% of the total CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. If the OAS program is currently recovering their own overpayment, you must: set the applicable recovery rate (e.g. 25% or 10%) in CPMS based only on the CPP monthly entitlement amount; and notify the OAS program to adjust their recovery rate based only on the OAS monthly entitlement amount if OAS is currently recovering based on the CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. Based on the amount of the overpayment, you must ensure the recovery rate guarantees the overpayment is collected within specified timelines (i.e. 5 years or 10 years). Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) Your rationale and decision regarding the recovery rate must be documented on the Undue Hardship, Deferral, Recovery Rates and Set-Offs Decision Rationale Worksheet (ISP-0119) form and placed on the debtor's file.

topic_title: Recovery of an overpayment on an active account
text: You do not have to set a recovery rate on a debtor's account in OAS Online when you initially discover an overpayment. The process automation of the Monthly OAS/GIS Overpayment Report will perform this task in most cases. When you add the overpayment amount to the Deductions (DED) screen on a debtor's account in OAS Online, the debtor's account will appear on the Monthly OAS/GIS Overpayment Report at the end of the accounting month (i.e. after monthly cut-off). The automated process will take action on active accounts found on this report when the overpayment is less than $25,000 and when there is no recovery rate set on the account. The automated process will set the recovery rate against the account as long as it does not identify an exception. It will also send a notification letter to the debtor informing them of the amount of recovery and the date when the recovery will start. However, you will be required to send the applicable letter (e.g. Entitlement Change, Overpayment letter, etc.) to the debtor explaining the cause of the overpayment and the amount of the overpayment. The letter may need adjusting, as there are specific paragraphs that need to be included due to process automation. To view these paragraphs and the exceptions, Process Automation—OAS/GIS Monthly Overpayment Report (Knowledge) Process automation exceptions When the automated process identifies an exception, the reason for the exception is recorded in the PWS notes of the work item and the work item status is set to Unassigned . Processing staff will be responsible to review and manually set the recovery rate on process automation exceptions. If you establish an overpayment on a client's account that you know is a process automation exception (e.g. overpayment of $25,000 or more), you can choose to manually set the recovery rate, and this will stop the account from going through the process automation. Setting a recovery rate To set a recovery rate in OAS Online, you must manually add the percentage or dollar value on the Deductions (DED) screen of the debtor's account. When an overpayment is $100 or less on an active account, you can set the recovery rate to 100% so that the full amount of the overpayment will be recovered from the debtor's next monthly benefit payment. If the monthly entitlement is not sufficient, the balance will be recovered from subsequent payments. When an overpayment is more than $100 on an active account, you must: use the Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) to determine the applicable recovery rate to set on the debtor's account; and Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) record the dollar value or percentage on the Deductions (DED) screen of the debtor's account. When determining the recovery rate, you must verify if the debtor is also receiving a CPP program benefit and if a CPP overpayment is already being recovered, including in the International Agreements system. If a CPP overpayment is not being recovered, you must take the CPP program benefit amount into consideration when calculating the recovery rate. If the debtor receives: an OAS pension only (i.e. no GIS), you must calculate the rate at 25% of the total CPP and OAS entitlement amounts; or an OAS pension and a GIS or an ALW benefit or ALWS benefit, you must calculate the rate at 10% of the total CPP and OAS entitlement amounts. If the CPP program is currently recovering their own overpayment, you must: set the applicable rate (i.e. 25% or 10%) in OAS Online only against the debtor's OAS monthly entitlement amount; and notify the CPP program to adjust their recovery rate based only on the CPP monthly entitlement amount, if CPP is currently recovering based on the CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. Based on the amount of the overpayment, you must also determine if the percentage allows the Department to recover the overpayment within a 5- or 10-year period, as applicable. For more information, refer to the Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) Your decision and rationale for setting the recovery rate must be documented on the Undue Hardship, Deferral, Recovery Rates and Set-Offs Decision Rationale Worksheet (ISP-0119) form and retained on the debtor's file for audit purposes. OAS Online will start recovery from the debtor's benefits in the accounting month when the recovery rate is set in the system. For example, if you set the recovery rate on September 26, 2023, which is during the October 2023 accounting month, the recovery will be deducted from the debtor's October 2023 payment. When you set a recovery rate on the debtor's account, you must ensure that the debtor receives 30 days notice before the recovery starts. Do not set a recovery rate on a debtor's account during the last week of an accounting month, as this does not provide the debtor with the required 30 days notice. Wait for the new accounting month to start in the following week (i.e. after cut-off).

topic_title: Recovery of an overpayment on an inactive account
text: When there is a departmental receivable established on an account and there are no CPP benefits in pay in ITRDS , you must notify the debtor and attempt to recover the overpayment. After 90 days, the CRA will take over the collection of overpayments on all CPP accounts in CPMS where there are no benefits in pay in ITRDS . However, if the debtor is in pay for an OAS pension or benefit, this would not be considered an inactive account. You must request a cross program recovery and for a lock on the overpayment in the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system. This will prevent the CRA from starting their collection.

topic_title: Recovery of an overpayment on inactive accounts
text: When an account is inactive, this means there are no benefits in pay in any system, under any program (i.e. CPP or OAS). Any outstanding issues or work items that could result in monies owing to a debtor should be reviewed before an account is considered inactive. An initial overpayment refers to the overpayment amount when it is discovered. An initial overpayment on an inactive account can be recovered if: the overpayment amount is more than $100 per program; or the overpayment amount is $100 or less, and is a result of misrepresentation, fraud or cashed duplicate payments. In all other cases, if an initial overpayment on an inactive account is $100.00 or less per benefit payment under each program, the full amount of the overpayment is remitted. The overpayment is remitted as the overall cost of recovery exceeds the amount of the overpayment. Remit an Overpayment (Scenario)

topic_title: Was the Death benefit top-up amount overpaid?
text: As of January 1, 2025 the Death ( DTH ) benefit includes a top-up amount when a deceased contributor meets the Minimum Qualifying Period. To be eligible for the DTH benefit flat-rate amount, the deceased contributor: must not have received a CPP or QPP RTR pension or DSB ; and there is no SVR pension payable as a result of their death. If the DTH benefit top-up amount is paid and a post-mortem RTR pension or an SVR pension is subsequently received and approved, the top-up amount is a valid and collectible overpayment. Refer to the CPMS tab of this procedure for the steps to recover the overpayment.

topic_title: Was the departmental receivable created as a result of processing a credit split application?
text: If yes, you must determine if the departmental receivable is collectible or not. If a separated legal spouse is receiving an SVR pension and the Department receives a credit split application on or after January 1, 2025, for the same deceased separated legal spouse, the SVR pension ceases as of the effective date of approval of the credit split. The effective date of the approval of a credit split is the last day of the month in which the Department received the request for the credit split (i.e. the last day of the month of the date stamp of the application or request) and not the date it is data captured and approved in ITRDS . Due to this, an SVR pension left in pay awaiting processing of the credit split application could result in an overpayment. The SVR pension overpayment is valid and collectible. Refer to the CPMS tab of this procedure for the steps to recover the overpayment. In all other cases, the departmental receivable that is created as a result of processing a credit split application is not collectible and needs to be adjusted in the CPMS . For more information, Credit Split Application (Scenario)

An overpayment refers to any CPP or OAS payment that an individual has received to which they are not entitled. It is considered a debt owed to the Crown and generally must be recovered. Before taking any action on an overpayment, ensure that you review the following overpayment policies: Overpayments—Key Principles (Policy) ; and Overpayments—Key Principles (Policy) Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) . Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) Overpayments can occur for a variety of reasons. Most commonly, an overpayment is caused by a change made to a client's account after the approval of their CPP or OAS pension or benefit. Typically, an overpayment is created when the change affects their benefit entitlement or causes them to no longer meet the eligibility requirements.

If you change information on a client's account in ITRDS , it automatically readjudicates the client's benefit entitlement. This can result in the creation of a departmental receivable in CPMS . You must always verify and validate the results in CPMS . Departmental receivables that are created for each benefit type (e.g. RTR1 , 1st RTR1 ) will be displayed individually in their own receivable block in CPMS . If an action in ITRDS results in an incorrect departmental receivable amount in CPMS , you must make any necessary changes to the account information in ITRDS to correct the results in CPMS . If you determine the appropriate actions were taken in ITRDS , but the departmental receivable amount is still not calculated correctly, contact your regional Business Expertise for guidance via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Internal link . National Business Expertise Tool If the departmental receivable is invalid (e.g. due to a keying error or a system issue), you must adjust the receivable amount. If you identify a situation (e.g. duplicate payment, Death ( DTH ) benefit top-up amount) where an overpayment should be calculated in CPMS , but you cannot enter a transaction in ITRDS to create it, you must manually add the departmental receivable in CPMS . If it is a combined benefit payment, you must create a separate departmental receivable for each benefit type. CPMS does not contain information on which benefits should be present on the account. This means that all the benefits will be available for selection when adding the departmental receivable. You must ensure you select the correct benefit type (e.g. RTR1, 1st RTR1, DSB2, 1st DSB2, 2nd DSB2 ) when adding the departmental receivable. The status of a departmental receivable in CPMS is based on: the receivable balance; the recovery start date; and the benefit status. For more information on a status of a departmental receivable, Change a Departmental Receivable Status in CPMS (Action)

Once you update and/or correct a client's account, you must determine if the change results in an overpayment. The OAS Online system does not automatically calculate an overpayment, except where: a date of birth is amended to a later date and entitlement was paid before the new eligibility date (i.e. age 60 for ALW or ALWS and age 65 for OAS and GIS); or a date of death is recorded on the T4A screen. When a change is effective before the current accounting month, you must manually calculate the overpayment amount using one of the following screens: For a change that occurs from January 1998 to present, access the Recalculation Input (CAL) screen in OAS Online. For a change that occurred before January 1998, access the Retroactive Calculation and Recalculation of OAS/GIS/SPA (1I4) screen in the International Agreements (IA) system. If you determine an overpayment exists, the amount must be recorded on the deductions (DED) screen of the debtor's account in OAS Online. If you used the 1I4 screen to calculate an overpayment amount for an account in OAS Online, the action of recording the overpayment on the DED screen will put the account out-of-balance. To put the account in-balance, you must also record the overpayment amount in the Recalculation Adjustment (ADJ) screen. If the overpayment exceeds $99,999.99, refer to OAS Online and International Agreements System—Overpayment Exceeds $99,999.99 (Scenario) for guidance on how to record it. An informant lead (also known as a third-party complaint) is a notification from an individual that, in their opinion, an investigation should be made into a client's eligibility or entitlement to a CPP pension or benefit. An informant lead can be received by letter, telephone or any other means to CPP. All informant leads must be sent to Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for a potential administrative investigation. It is the Department's obligation to review each lead received to determine if it is valid or has an impact on an applicant or a beneficiary's eligibility or entitlement. You must never indicate receipt of an informant lead on an individual's file or in ITRDS notes, as this could reveal an informant's identity. You must protect the informant, even if they do not indicate they want to remain anonymous. Information that might reveal the identity of an informant must not be divulged or disclosed. A verbal or written disclosure is when an individual or third party voluntarily admits to knowingly making a misrepresentation to the CPP program. If you receive a verbal or written disclosure where the individual comes forward to correct inaccurate or incomplete information, or to provide information they did not divulge during previous dealings with the Department, you must refer it to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB). An administrative investigation is an impartial process conducted by ISB when there is a concern, suspected fraud or potential misrepresentation regarding eligibility or entitlement to the CPP pensions and benefits. A file can be sent for an administrative investigation for a number of reasons, including: anomalies, discrepancies or suspected fraud discovered by departmental officials; informant leads (third party complaints); or verbal or written disclosures. While reviewing a file or processing an application, you may discover an anomaly or discrepancy that warrants further review. You should thoroughly review the client's OAS and CPP files, ITRDS and notes, Cúram and PWS for historical data. If you cannot determine a reasonable explanation, before making a decision on the account, the file and all relevant documentation must be referred to ISB immediately. When a debtor owes an overpayment, it can be recovered from any pension or benefit payable under any Act or program administered by the Minister. Recovery from another program is known as a cross program recovery. For more information, Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) For the purpose of this procedure, an underpayment includes an arrears payment, retroactive payment or an amount payable to a debtor after a recalculation of their benefits. A cross program recovery: can be: a lump sum recovery from a monthly benefit payment or an underpayment; an ongoing recovery from monthly benefits; or both. is only possible when dealing with benefits for the same debtor; cannot include a child's benefit; and must not cause the debtor undue hardship. A cross program recovery does not require the debtor's consent; however, they must be notified about the recovery in writing. For a monthly cross program recovery, the debtor must receive 30 days notice before the recovery starts. The 30 days notice does not apply when the cross program recovery is from: an underpayment payable to the debtor or their legal representative; or a DTH benefit payable to the estate of the deceased debtor.

topic_title: When to ask the program with the overpayment for a cross program recovery request
text: You must verify if the other program has an overpayment when you: approve a new monthly pension or benefit; reinstate a monthly pension or benefit; approve a DTH benefit payable to the deceased debtor's estate; or determine that there is an underpayment owing to the debtor, their legal representative or another appropriate payee. If any of the above situations apply, the other program will not necessarily be aware of the available funds under your program. Therefore, before releasing any payments to the debtor, their legal representative or the appropriate payee, you must inform the other program that funds are available and ask them to submit a cross program recovery request. In cases where the other program has not been informed about the debtor's death and is continuing to issue payments, you must communicate with the other program to: inform them of the debtor's date of death so that they can calculate their overpayment; inform them of the funds available under your program (e.g. DTH benefit, funds owing after death or a post-mortem application), if applicable; and ask them to submit a cross program recovery request. The table below provides situations when to ask the other program for a cross program recovery request: Table 2. Funds available—When to ask the other program for a cross program recovery request Situation under your program Situation under the other program The debtor is entitled to an underpayment under your program. The same debtor has an overpayment under the other program, regardless of whether they are recovering it or not. The debtor is: approved for a new monthly pension or benefit; or put back into pay for a monthly pension or benefit. The same debtor has an overpayment under the other program that is not being recovered as they have no benefits in pay. The CPP program receives a DTH benefit application and the benefit will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate. The same deceased debtor has an OAS overpayment. A post-mortem application is received under your program and the benefit will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate or another appropriate payee. Or There are benefits owed to the deceased debtor that were unpaid at the time of their death under your program and they will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate or another appropriate payee. The same deceased debtor has an overpayment under the other program. Once you have asked the other program for a cross program recovery request: release the monthly pension or benefit into pay, if applicable; and do not release the underpayment, if any, until the other program responds; or if you are approving a DTH benefit payable to the deceased debtor's estate, do not release it until the other program responds.

topic_title: When to submit a cross program recovery request
text: When an overpayment is established or exists on a debtor's account under your program, you must always verify if the debtor has applied for benefits or is receiving benefits under the other program. This is not only to determine a recovery rate, if applicable, but also to identify situations when a cross program recovery request can be submitted. The table below provides situations when you can submit a request for a cross program recovery to the other program: Table 1. Program with an overpayment—When to submit a cross program recovery request Situation under your program Situation under the other program The debtor has an overpayment on their account and is: no longer eligible or entitled to receive a benefit under your program; or in pay for a benefit and a recovery rate of 100% against their benefits under your program is insufficient to allow you to recover their debt within the 5- or 10-year period. The same debtor is or will be receiving any one of the following benefit payments under the other program: a monthly benefit; or an underpayment. The debtor has an overpayment on their account and is in pay for a benefit under your program. A recovery rate is being withheld from the debtor's monthly benefit payments under your program. The same debtor will be receiving an underpayment under the other program. A deceased debtor has an OAS overpayment (i.e. existing or established after their death) on their account. The CPP program receives a DTH benefit application and the benefit will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate. A deceased debtor has an overpayment (i.e. existing or established after death) on their account under your program. A post-mortem application is received by the other program and the benefit will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate or another appropriate payee. Or Any benefits owed to the deceased debtor that were unpaid at the time of their death under the other program will be paid to the deceased debtor's estate or another appropriate payee.

Specific program debt should be recovered from their own program according to the priority of withholds policy. You must contact the applicable OAS regional office (e.g. OAS or OAS International Operations) and request that they reduce the recovery rate to 25% of the debtor's OAS benefits ($613.53 × 25% = $153.38) before the CPP monthly recovery starts. Multiple receivables in CPMS The debtor has the following overpayments: A RTR1 of $393.24; and A SVR1 of $201.02. The debtor is not in pay for OAS. The debtor's total entitlement to CPP benefits is $753.40 per month that consists of: RTR pension: $438.93 SVR pension: $249.45 PRB 2018: $21.98 PRB 2019: $16.98 PRB 2020: $14.76 PRB 2021: $11.30 As the debtor's RTR1 receivable and SVR1 receivable are both over $100.00, CPMS will automatically set each receivable with a recovery rate of 25%. 25% of the debtor's total monthly payment is $188.35 ($753.40 × 25% = $188.35). As 25% of the debtor's total monthly amount is less than the RTR1 overpayment amount ($393.24), CPMS will collect $188.35 on this receivable. As 25% of the debtor's total monthly amount is less than the SVR1 overpayment amount ($201.02), CPMS will also collect $188.35 against this receivable. The recovery rates must be modified before the recovery begins so that no more than 25% of the debtor's monthly entitlement is withheld. Without manual intervention, CPMS will automatically collect $376.70 from the debtor's payment, which is 50% of the debtor's entitlement.

When calculating a recovery rate, you must: consider the debtor's total monthly amount of their CPP and OAS benefit entitlements. ensure that a rate is set to allow the Department to collect the debt within specific time frames (e.g. within 5 years or within 10 years for debts greater than $10,000.00). exclude the monthly amount of a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit and Surviving Child's benefit if the overpayment is not directly related to these benefits. determine if the debtor is receiving income-tested benefits (i.e. GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit); and ensure the recovery rate is not less than $10.00 per month unless their monthly entitlement is less than $10.00. The Department must follow nationally established BF standards and guidelines to ensure: consistent delivery of the CPP and OAS programs, as well as foreign benefit applications and liaison requests under international social security agreements; timely and equitable outcomes for all applicants and beneficiaries; effective national workload management for the Department. You can use the BF system to recall a file, work item or task on a given future date to take follow-up action or to review a case. You must use one of the following systems: In PWS , you will place a work item On Hold . For more information, refer to Pensions Workload System Guide External link . Pensions Workload System Guide In Cúram, Defer and Bring Forward are the system actions used to put an item on hold for review at a later date: Defer a task in Cúram Deferring a task is the system action used when you want a task to remain assigned to you for follow-up. When you defer a task, it is moved to your Deferred Tasks page. On the specified date, the task will move back to your My Open Tasks page for review, unless you restart the task beforehand. Bring Forward a task in Cúram Bringing forward a task is the system action used when follow up is required on an item but it can be done by other staff members. When you bring forward a task, you will assign it to a Work Queue. On the specified date, the task will be automatically allocated to another staff member.

You must use your judgment to determine if an apparent name mismatch is acceptable according to the tolerances listed below. The following list of acceptable tolerances is exhaustive. However, the examples provided are not exhaustive. You cannot accept any type of mismatch other than the 6 tolerance types listed below, and you must request documentary evidence to correct a discrepancy.

When an applicant’s name does not exactly match with information in the Social Insurance Registry (SIR), but is considered an abbreviated name (i.e. a familiar or shortened form of the applicant’s [usual] first name). Examples of abbreviated names are: Name Abbreviated name Andrew Andy Christine Chris Mohammed Mo

When an applicant’s name on the application differs from SIR, but is substantially similar, with minor typographical differences. Examples of spelling mistakes are: Name Acceptable variation Donald Donold Sébastien Sebasten Ashley Ashely

topic_title: Tolerance 3—Middle name used as first name
text: When there would be a match with SIR if the applicant’s first and middle names were reversed. Sometimes, the first name provided on an application does not match the first name in SIR because the client’s middle name is used as the first name in SIR. Examples of name reversal are: First and middle names provided by the applicant First name in SIR Kelly Anne Anne Roger James James John Richard Richard

Many names contain non-alphabetic characters (e.g. hyphenated names). SIR does not accept non-alphabetic characters as a valid value. Names in these cases are considered a match when you remove all non-alphabetic characters from the name on the application and obtain a match in SIR. Examples of the removal of non-alphabetic characters are: Name provided by the applicant Name in SIR Jean-Guy Jeanguy O’Brien Obrien François Francois

When the first and last names shown in one data source (the application or SIR) match the first and last names shown in the other data source when reversed. Examples of name reversal are: Name provided by the applicant Name in SIR Carol Gale Gale Carol Fisher James James Fisher John Henry Henry John

topic_title: Tolerance 6—Surname at birth vs. surname on the application
text: When individuals change their surname (e.g. through marriage), but do not inform SIR, we can consider the names identical if the surname at birth matches the surname in SIR.

When entering multiple incarceration periods, ensure the following: An incarceration period end date can be equal to, but not before, the next incarceration period start date. topic_title: Authenticating a client or their authorized representative Updated
text: During a security check, do not tell the individual what information they got wrong. You can say: "The information you provided does not match the information available in our systems." Do not provide any information regarding the client, the existence of a CPP or OAS file or an application in progress. Only provide general information. If the individual is hesitant or refuses to provide personal information required to validate their identify, go to the Individual refuses to provide personal information section below. For examples of scripts that can be used during a phone call to identify yourself and to complete the security check, Script Examples—Authenticating a Client or Their Authorized Representative Complete one of the following: If you call or receive a call from a client , go to Step 2 . Step 2 If you call or receive a call from a third party , verify the Contact / Applicant screen in ITRDS for the third party's Name and Role . If the third party's information is valid, review the ITRDS Notes to ensure that the authorization has not been revoked. Go to Step 2 . ITRDS Notes Step 2 If the individual is not an authorized representative, inform them that you cannot provide the client's information. If the individual requires further assistance, go to the Unauthorized third party section below. Review the important notes in ITRDS to verify if there are additional security measures on the client's account (e.g. a password). If a security measure is present on the account, note it to request the required information during Part I of the security check. Conduct the following security check before discussing client-specific information. Security check—Part I Part I Direction Requirements All information in this part of the security check is mandatory. The answers provided must be correct and complete as there is no room for error or incomplete information. Client If you are speaking with the client, ask them to provide the following: their account number (e.g. their SIN or Client Identifier number). Proceed as follows: If you called the client, ask for the last 3 digits of their account number. Do not request the client's full SIN unless it is not available on file and is required for the call. If the client called you, ask them to provide their full account number. their full name; any security measure (e.g. a password) indicated in the important notes in ITRDS . If the caller cannot provide a password previously added to the account, do not continue with the security check. Inform them that you cannot continue the call as you cannot authenticate their identity. You can say: “The information you provided does not match the information available in our systems.” Go to the Failed security check section below. Authorized representative If you are speaking with the client's authorized representative, ask them to provide the following: the full name of the client that they are representing; the client's account number (e.g. SIN or Client Identifier number). Proceed as follows: If you called the authorized representative, ask for the last 3 digits of the client's account number. Do not request the client's full SIN unless it is not available on file and is required for the call. If the authorized representative called you, ask for the client's full account number. any security measure (e.g. password) indicated in the important notes in ITRDS . If the caller cannot provide a password previously added to the account, do not continue with the security check. Inform them that you cannot continue the call as you cannot authenticate their identity. You can say: “The information you provided does not match the information available in our systems.” Go to the Failed security check section below. Results If the client or their authorized representative correctly provides all information, go to Security check—Part II to continue the authentication process. If the individual's answers are incorrect, incomplete or they are unable to answer, inform them that you cannot continue the call as you cannot authenticate their identity. You can say: “The information you provided does not match the information available in our systems.” Go to the Failed security check section below. Security check—Part II Security check—Part II Part II Direction Requirements The client or their authorized representative must correctly provide 2 additional pieces of information about the client's account. If your call is with the authorized representative, the answers provided must be the information belonging to the client that they are representing (i.e. do not ask for the name or address of a contact or authorized representative on the account). The authorized representative's identity was already confirmed in Security Check—Part I . If an incorrect answer is provided during the check, one additional piece of information is required for each error made. Client or authorized representative Ask for 2 of the following pieces of client-specific information: the client's date of birth (day, month and year); the start date or end date of a CPP or OAS pension or benefit (month and year); a source or amount of income reported for GIS purposes; a source, amount or date (month and year) of income reduction for options; the amount showing on a CPP or OAS tax slip; the name of a contact or authorized representative on the account (this can only be used when authenticating the client); the address of a contact or authorized representative on the account (this can only be used when authenticating the client); the first or last year of CPP contributions; the amount of CPP earnings or contributions; the date of or reason for the last verbal or written communication with the CPP / OAS call centre, in-person centre or processing centre, if this can be confirmed in the ITRDS Notes or PWS ; any recent My Service Canada Account activity; the date of or reason for correspondence from Service Canada recently received by the client; the source of any deductions from payments (tax withholds, Family Orders Enforcement, statutory set-off, etc.); the names and dates of birth of any interrelated children on the account; the amount that appears on line 11400 ( CPP or QPP benefits) or 11500 (Other pensions or superannuation) of the client's latest income tax return; the name of the spouse or common-law partner linked to the account; a previous address appearing on file (the postal code is not required); current or previous pension sharing information (start and/or end date, provision application date, years of cohabitation, documentation received); or current or previous credit splitting information (start and end date of cohabitation period, provision application date, years of cohabitation, documentation received). In certain situations when there is no application, benefit or CPP or QPP contribution information available, the following information may be provided by the client or their authorized representative: the client's complete address; the client's mother's surname at birth; or the confirmation of CPP or QPP contributions (for clients who are automatically enrolled). Results If the client or their authorized representative correctly provides the additional 2 pieces of information, you have successfully authenticated their identity. Go to Step 4 If the client or their authorized representative cannot provide 2 additional pieces of information, they have failed the security check. Inform them that you cannot continue the call as you cannot authenticate their identity. You can say: “The information you provided does not match the information available in our systems.” Go to the Failed security check section below. Step 4 Proceed with the call. The client or their authorized representative can receive information regarding the CPP or OAS account, file or application. Update any outdated client information, if applicable. Complete the Telephone Call (ISP0112) form or relevant CPPD form to record the details of your conversation with the client or their authorized representative. Include the following details: the date and time of the call; the name of the person with whom you spoke; the results of the authentication process; and the information provided or gathered during the call. Take the appropriate actions on the account (e.g. send a letter). Update the client's notes in ITRDS to record details of your actions or decisions made on the account. Refer to ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) . ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) Update the work item in PWS or the task in Cúram. For more information, refer to: PWS—Guidelines for Pensions Internal link ; or PWS—Guidelines for Pensions Manage Tasks in Cúram (Action) . text: If, for any reason (such as a language or medical barrier), a client asks that you speak with an unauthorized third party (e.g. a friend, relative or translator) who is with them at the time of the call, you can conduct the security check with the assistance of this unauthorized third party. However, the client must be partially authenticated and must consent to the disclosure of their personal information to the other party on the call before any client-specific details are discussed. When the client gives verbal consent to disclose personal information to an unauthorized third party, indicate this consent in the Telephone Call (ISP0112) form and in the ITRDS notes. CPPD staff can record the information on the appropriate template. CPPD Templates and Updated Naming and Saving Conventions This verbal consent is only valid for the duration of the phone call. If the client would like to give consent to communicate with this third party on an ongoing basis, refer them to their My Service Canada Account to provide this consent or send a Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP1603) form to the client to complete and return.
