topic_title: Funding from a federal or provincial program to attend school or a training program
text: CPP child's benefits are not income tested. As a result, a dependent child can receive funding from a federal or provincial program to attend an institution and still be entitled to the child's benefit.

topic_title: How can a +18 child or third party apply or renew their child's benefit? Updated
text: The +18 child or third party can apply, renew or re-apply for their child's benefit in writing by submitting: a completed ISP-1402 form signed by both the child and school official. The school official's signature must be dated after the first day of class. a written statement or declaration containing all mandatory information, including a statement confirming the child's full-time or part-time attendance. The statement must be signed by both the child and a school official. The school official's signature must be dated after the first day of class; or a completed ISP-1402 form signed by the child, along with proof of enrolment that is obtained from the student's online portal after the first day of class. The proof of enrolment must contain the following information: Student's name; Student identification number or date of birth; Degree and program of study; Name and address of school or university; Start and end dates for the semester, term or school year they are enrolled in; and Enrolment status (full-time or part-time) for the semester, term, or school year. If a +18 child who qualified for a child's benefit using an International Social Security Agreement submits a XXX/Canada Agreement - Application for CPP Child's Benefits (ISP-5055-XXX) form and an Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP-1401-IO-XXX) form, the ISP-1401-IO-XXX form must be signed by the child. The child can submit either the ISP-1401-IO-XXX form signed by a school official or proof of enrolment obtained from the school's online portal to support their attestation of attendance at school or university. The school official's signature or proof of enrolment must be obtained after the first day of class. In addition, any proof of enrolment submitted must meet the criteria outlined above. A child in full-time attendance can also renew their benefit by using the online Declaration of Attendance at School or University service on their My Service Canada Account. The child will be prompted to answer mandatory questions where their responses will populate the corresponding data fields in ITRDS . If they meet the eligibility criteria, the benefit will automatically adjudicate without any processor intervention. If the child is in receipt of 2 benefits, both benefits will be adjudicated using the same declaration. The information received will be displayed under the School Declaration section in ITRDS . If the child is unable to complete the declaration online due to an error message, the child can complete their declaration using the paper ISP-1402 form. For more information on the online renewal, Online Applications for CPP (Knowledge) ISP-1402 forms are automatically sent to eligible children one month before the end of each school period. For children under the age of 18, the forms are sent to the payee three months before the child's 18th birthday to assist in the renewal process.

topic_title: Internships, articling and practical working experience Updated
text: A child's benefit is not payable during internships that occur after the completion of a diploma, degree or certificate (post-graduate internships). Individuals are not eligible for a child's benefit when an internship takes place after a diploma, degree, or certificate is awarded. This includes internships required to become a full member of a profession, such as when an individual must: write an examination and complete a residency in a hospital (e.g. doctors); complete articling in a law firm (e.g.lawyers); or obtain practical work experience in an accounting firm (e.g. chartered professional accountants). If a child is attending school or university full-time or part-time and obtains their diploma, degree, or certificate right before a school vacation period, they are still entitled to a benefit for the school vacation period. However, a postgraduate internship that continues or begins after the end of the school vacation period is not considered attendance at school or university.

topic_title: Is an application for the CPP child's benefit required?
text: Each time a disabled contributor's child over 18 years of age or a surviving child over 18 years of age makes an initial application for a child's benefit or applies to renew an existing benefit, a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form is required. When a child's benefit status in ITRDS is In Pay , only the declaration of attendance at school or university and required supporting documentation of attendance are needed to renew the child's benefit, provided there is no break in eligibility between the last school period and the newly submitted period of attendance. The child's school or university attendance information is entered on the School Declaration screen and benefit payments continue uninterrupted. When the child's benefit status in ITRDS is Terminated , a new ISP-1402 form is required. When the form is received within 12 months from the end date of the last period of school attendance, the following applies: If there is no break in the child's attendance at school or university, the attendance information is entered on the School Declaration screen for the child's subsequent school period. If there is a break in the child's attendance at school or university, the attendance information is entered on the School Declaration screen to pay the child for the new period of school attendance. If the child's benefit status in ITRDS is Terminated for more than 12 months , a new ISP-1402 form must be submitted. The child is only entitled to 11 months of retroactive child's benefits payments from the receipt date of the new application. For more information, refer to Surviving Child's Benefit Application (Scenario) or to Surviving Child's Benefit Application (Scenario) Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit Application (Scenario)

Standard vacation period A standard vacation period may begin as early as April 1 and end as late as September 30. Students who have been in full-time or part-time attendance at school or university immediately prior to a vacation period falling within these dates are entitled to receive the CPP child's benefit for the entire vacation period. Although international schools or universities schedule vacation periods other than April to September, the vacation period is acceptable for CPP purposes. Non-standard vacation period A student whose vacation period does not fall within the April to September time frame may be deemed to be in full-time or part-time attendance during their chosen 4-month vacation period. For this to occur, they must attend school or university on a full-time or part-time basis for 8 consecutive months in the 12 months ending with the vacation period. Most universities and colleges offer students the opportunity to take courses during all three semesters (fall, winter and summer). This allows students to go to school and complete their program earlier or to choose their own vacation period. In addition, some universities can offer Co-op programs that are set up to allow for a schedule that alternates between a semester of school and a semester of work experience. During these schedules, students are considered to be in full-time or part-time attendance. This enables students to acquire work experience in their field of study as part of the requirements of the program. Some technical or trade schools have courses that begin at any time during the year. Eligibility to a child's benefit for a +18 child begins during a school vacation period The following are events that make a +18 child eligible to a child's benefit: The contributor dies; The contributor becomes disabled; or The child reaches age 18. When any of these events occur during a school vacation period, the child must complete and submit a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form and provide proof of attendance from the school or university for the previous academic year. The current school vacation period is connected to the academic year that just ended. Therefore, the +18 child must have been in attendance in the past academic year to be paid the child's benefit for the school vacation period following the event. For subsequent school years, school vacation period entitlement depends on meeting full-time or part-time attendance requirements and the completion of another ISP-1402 form. Vacation periods when the year or semester has not been completed If a child did not complete a school year or semester for reasons other than illness, the child is not entitled to receive benefits for the vacation period or any month after the month the child last attended school. topic_title: What is considered full-time or part-time attendance? Updated
text: Use the information provided by the child and the educational institution on the Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form to determine if the child is in full-time or part-time attendance. A child is considered to be in full-time attendance if they are deemed full-time by an acceptable educational institution, regardless of the number of courses in which they are enrolled. A child is considered to be in part-time attendance if they are not considered full-time by the educational institution. In addition, they must be enrolled in courses that make up at least 20% of a full course load as recognized by the educational institution. For more information, CPP Children's Benefits—Attendance at School or University (Policy)

For spouses or common-law partners to qualify for a single PNSH or a double PNSH, they must: submit an application in writing; be at least 60 years of age; be living together or cohabiting in a common-law relationship for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the PNSH approval date; have made valid contributions from at least one applicant to CPP or QPP and have applied for or is currently receiving an RTR pension or a QPP RTR pension; not be voluntarily separated at the time of application; and not have a spousal agreement that is binding on the Minister indicating their intention of not sharing their RTR pension under CPP. As of January 1, 2019, the Department phased in enhanced components of the CPP. The first additional and second additional components are not separate benefits, but top-ups to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. If the RTR pension amount is calculated using the base, first additional and second additional earnings, then the amount redistributed through PNSH will also include the base, first additional and second additional components. CPP enhancement will not affect the eligibility criteria and calculation of the cohabitation period for the base component of the PNSH amount. As the cohabitation and joint contributory period for the first additional component began on January 1, 2019, and the second additional component began on January 1, 2024, the pension share factor may be different between the base, the first additional and the second additional components. Each component of the pension share will be calculated separately; a couple may have a double base pension share and a single first additional pension share, and a single second additional pension share if only one spouse or common-law partner made enhanced contributions. Similarly, a base pension share may include both CPP and QPP portions, while the first additional and second components may be 100% CPP or 100% QPP, depending on the individual's contributions. For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge)

A spouse or common-law partner can request in writing or by submitting a Pension Sharing (PNSH) application to have their PNSH reinstated. If only one spouse or common-law partner requests a reinstatement, the other spouse or common-law partner must be notified. Before reinstating the PNSH, review the file to ensure there is continued eligibility. Request any information necessary from the applicants to verify that eligibility continues or resumes (i.e. the spouses or common-law partners may have been separated during the period the PNSH was cancelled). Reinstate a single PNSH Reinstating a single PNSH can result in a different ratio if, at the time of approval of the first PNSH, the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner had not yet reached age 70. The joint contributory period and period of cohabitation will be extended to the month in which they reach 70 or the month in which the request for reinstatement is approved, whichever is earliest. Reinstate a double PNSH When reinstating a double PNSH, the ratio is the same ratio that was calculated at the time the first PNSH was approved. If the reinstatement is approved, the effective date is the month following the month of approval, i.e. the accounting month in which the PNSH is accepted by the system.

The goal of sharing a pension is to redistribute RTR pension payments between spouses or common-law partners when one individual has a higher entitlement amount than the other. The redistribution of the couple's pension amount does not change the total dollar amount payable. Spouses or common-law partners can share a portion of each other's RTR pension based on the period they lived together and their joint CPP contributory period. For spouses who lived together before they were married, their periods of cohabitation before marriage are included in the cohabitation period. Any periods where the couple was separated are not included in the cohabitation period, except for periods when they lived apart for reasons beyond their control. For more information, Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond their Control—CPP (Policy) There are 2 types of PNSH, single PNSH and double PNSH. A single PNSH is when only one spouse or common-law partner has contributed to the CPP and is in pay for an RTR pension. They may share their RTR with their spouse or common-law partner who: does not have any contributions; and is 60 years or older. You must verify the non-contributor's Record of Earnings to ensure there are no valid CPP contributions. If at any point the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner starts working and contributing to CPP, ITRDS will automatically cancel the single PNSH when earnings are added to the non-contributor's account. If this occurs, either common-law partner or spouse can then apply for double PNSH when both partners or spouses have applied and been approved for their own RTR pensions. A double PNSH is when both spouses or common-law partners are in pay for an RTR pension. This also applies if: one spouse or common-law partner is in pay for an RTR pension; and the other is in pay for a QPP pension.

topic_title: When can an individual or a third party apply?
text: PNSH applications must be received no earlier than 12 months before the earliest date when the PNSH can start. PNSH starts the month after the month in which the application is approved. There is no retroactivity. Third party representatives are not authorized to use online services on behalf of the applicant. A third party can only apply in writing and submit documentation to prove they are authorized to act on the client's behalf. For more information, refer to Third Party Requests (Scenario) and Third Party Requests (Scenario) Legal Representation (Policy) Effective date The sharing of an RTR pension starts the month after the PNSH application is approved. However, for processing purposes, the effective date of the PNSH is the accounting month in which the application is processed and approved in ITRDS . PNSH can start the same month as the RTR pension only if the RTR pension is effective immediately and the PNSH request was received in the current accounting month. For more information on PNSH with a future or pending RTR pension, refer to the Exceptions and special cases—Pension Sharing with future/pending RTR pension section in the Step by Step tab.

topic_title: Contacting the CRA with Child Rearing Provision Enquiries
text: Information received from the CRA may be used to support a Child Rearing Provision determination, but the CRA records cannot replace documentation or evidence where required. In cases where you are not able to confirm that an individual was eligible to receive the Canada Child Benefit (CCB) or obtain the required supporting documentation, the CRA may be able to confirm periods where an individual was eligible to receive CCB (and in some cases, the Family Allowance). Requests to the CRA must include the individual's name, SIN and the name or names of the children with their dates of birth and must be submitted through your designated CRA Regional Contact. Refer to the CRA Contact List in the Benefits Toolbox for a list of regional contacts. Benefits Toolbox

The CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation of a CPP benefit or pension. The drop-in adds UPE to the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhanced components of a benefit or provision. The CRDI is applied for any contributor who, at the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child, is eligible to receive the CCB and acts as the primary caregiver. An eligible contributor will receive UPE dropped into the calculation of the enhanced portion of their CPP benefit beginning the month after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility for the child and ending the month of the child's 7th birthday. After January 1, 2019, the CPP enhancement will drop in an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average first additional earnings during the 5 years before the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child for each year the child is under the age of 7. After January 1, 2024, the CPP enhancement will drop in an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average second additional earnings (i.e. earnings between the year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (MPE) amount and the year's additional MPE amount) during the 5 years before the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child for each year the child is under the age of 7. The drop-in provisions are only applied to the first additional and second additional contributory periods if: the drop-in amount is higher than the contributor's actual earnings during that period; and the child is under the age of 7. When a contributor loses decision-making responsibility and parenting time for a child but regains it later, separate CRDI calculations are required for each period the contributor had decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child. Therefore, some contributors may have multiple first additional CRDI and second additional CRDI periods per child. When first additional or second additional CRDI periods are attributed for the year of the child's birth, the child's adoption, or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child, the attributed amount covers the whole year regardless of when the date of birth, adoption or assumption of decision-making responsibility falls within the year. However, when a contributor's first additional and second additional contributory periods end within 7 years after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date on which the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child (e.g. the contributor starts receiving their CPP RTR pension, reaches age 70 or dies), the calculated amount of the CRDI must be prorated over 12 months. The CRDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility requirements or Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for CPP benefits, as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. It is only the base earnings and contributions that are considered in determining eligibility and MQP. UPE's dropped in as a result of the CRDI are eligible for a Credit Split provision (division of pensionable earnings). When a client is in pay for a DSB and has UPE attributed from the CRDI for any year during which they are in pay, it will trigger a recalculation of the additional components of their DSB every year following the attribution of the CRDI UPE. Recalculations will occur in January, coinciding with the indexation of the DSB . For more information on how the CRDI is calculated and its impact on the calculation of benefits, refer to Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation and Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) For more information about the CRDI and CPP enhancement, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge)

The CRDO only applies to the base calculation of a CPP pension or benefit. The CRDO removes contributory months with low or zero earnings from the base calculation, starting with the month after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility for the child, and ending with the month of the child's 7th birthday. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average of monthly pensionable earnings. The CRDO applies only to the time period when the individual was the primary caregiver for children under the age of 7. The CRDO can help individuals meet the eligibility requirements for CPPD benefits. In the event of an individual's death, the CRDO can also help their estate and survivors qualify for benefits.

The following are situations when all or a portion of the CRP period cannot be applied to an individual's account. When a child named on the form was: born before January 1, 1959; born outside of Canada and did not arrive in Canada until after their 7th birthday; or over the age of 7 when the contributory period began. When the child was under the age of 7 and: the Family Allowance was not paid to the individual requesting the CRP or to their spouse or common-law partner. An exception to this would be if a contributor or their spouse or common-law partner were in the Canadian Armed Forces and was posted outside of Canada between 1966 and 1973; the Family Allowance was paid to someone other than the individual requesting or their spouse or common-law partner; or the individual requesting CRP was not eligible for the CCB. The CRP will have no impact on an individual's eligibility or entitlement to a benefit when the individual: is in receipt of a CPP benefit that is already being paid at the maximum rate or, after processing the CRP, there is no change in the benefit rate; was in receipt of a CPP benefit that was cancelled before January 1978, or whose CPP Death benefit was paid before January 1978; still does not meet the MQP requirements for a CPP benefit after the CRP is processed and there are no other CPP benefits in pay; is the spouse or common-law partner of the Family Allowance recipient; however, the Family Allowance recipient does not waive their rights to the CRP in favour of the individual requesting the CRP; is the spouse or common-law partner of the Family Allowance recipient who waived their right to the CRP in favour of the individual requesting the CRP, but did not remain at home and was not the primary caregiver for the child while the child was under the age of 7; is a contributor and has not submitted an application for a CPP benefit. In this case, the individual requesting for the CRP must be contacted to verify if they applied or plan to apply for a benefit before denying the CRP; does not submit the additional information or documents that were requested to process the CRP request (after a reasonable period of time); received children's special allowances payments from the CRA for a child they fostered, the period for that child cannot be considered as part of the CRP period; or received, or their spouse or common-law partner received, children's special allowances payments from the CRA while acting as temporary primary caregivers for minor children and neither were eligible for Family Allowance or CCB payments, the period for that child cannot be considered as part of the CRP period.

topic_title: Did the individual requesting the Child Rearing Provision or any children named on the declaration live outside of Canada before the child's 7th birthday?
text: Individuals were not eligible to be paid Family Allowance during periods when they or their children lived outside of Canada. These periods cannot be included in the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) date range. In these cases, the following documents should be requested to prove the date of entry into Canada: Canadian immigration records (e.g. the IMM1000); a complete passport; a customs declaration; an airline ticket; a bus ticket; or a ship ticket. Send the Development—Child-rearing provision (ISS-4550) letter to the individual requesting the CRP to request proof of entry. If an individual is unable to provide documentation to support the child's entry date into Canada, the Department may accept other evidence that would be satisfactory on a case-by-case basis. If you encounter such a scenario, please submit an enquiry in the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) Internal link to be escalated to Operational Policy at National Headquarters for further review. topic_title: How is the CRP applied to benefit calculations
text: The CRP became effective in January 1978 and has the following impact: Benefits which began before January 1978 may be recalculated retroactive to, but not before, January 1978. Benefits which began after January 1978 may be recalculated retroactive to the effective date of the benefit. Individuals who were not previously eligible for SVR pension and/or DSB may be eligible after the CRP is applied to their account. In the case of an individual who had previously been denied a CPP benefit and who now qualifies with the CRP, benefit payment can be made retroactively back to January 1978, or back to the effective date of the benefit, whichever is later. A benefit amount should not be reduced because of the CRP. In this case, the CRP will not be applied if it causes a reduction in entitlement amount. If an individual was previously denied a CPP benefit, and they did not make a request for the CRP, provide the individual with the appropriate CRP request form, and advise them that they must reapply for the CPP benefit or request a reconsideration of the denial decision if they are within the prescribed reconsideration time frame. The CRDO is applied in 3 distinct ways to the base calculation to: drop certain months with no pensionable earnings from the contributory period for calculation purposes; drop certain months of low adjusted pensionable earnings from the calculation used in determining the average monthly pensionable earnings; or establish the Minimum Qualifying Period by dropping months from the contributory period with no pensionable earnings . Additionally, effective January 1998, for disability benefit purposes, the CRDO allows the exclusion of certain months that are either below or above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) but below the Disability Basic Exemption. The CRDI is applied to the enhanced portion: The CRDI is applied to child rearing periods that include January 2019 or later. The CRDI will drop in UPE in the first and second additional contributory periods. The CRDI will drop in UPE in the first and second additional contributory periods when the primary caregiver has low or no earnings. For the first additional contributory period, which began January 2019, the UPE will be equal to the average percentage of earnings the contributor has made in relation to the Year's Maximum Contributory Earnings (YMPE) for the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date they came under the decision-making responsibility of the contributor. For the second additional contributory period, beginning in January 2024, the UPE are based on earnings between the YMPE and the year's additional maximum pensionable earnings, which equals 107% of the YMPE in 2024 and 114% of the YMPE in 2025 and after. Only higher earners who make more than the YMPE will contribute to the second additional contributory period. If there are less than 5 years in the first additional or second additional contributory periods, the average is determined by the actual number of available months in the contributory period, down to a lower limit of 36 months (3 years). If there are less than 3 years in the first additional contributory period, the client is awarded 40% of the YMPE for each month outside of the contributory period, up to a maximum of 36 months for the CRDI. However, this is not applicable to the second additional benefit. When overlapping drop-in periods exist due to the birth of more than one child, the highest of the two or more drop-in amounts will be used. For more information on CRDI, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) For more information on how CRDI impacts the calculation of a CPP benefit, refer to Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) and Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation

topic_title: Periods used for the CRP Updated
text: A CRP period refers to the 7-year eligibility period for a child. All CRP periods beginning in January 1966 or later will have the CRDO considered when calculating the base component of a CPP pension or benefit. If the 7-year period includes periods starting: January 2019 or later, the CRDI will also be considered when calculating the first additional component; or January 2024 or later, the CRDI will be considered when calculating the second additional component. ITRDS usually establishes eligibility to the CRDO and CRDI after data capture. However, in cases where the individual requesting the CRP did not receive the Family Allowance or CCB for the whole of the 7-year eligibility period for a child, you must manually enter the CRP start date and end date for that particular child. The CRP period begins with the later of: January 1966; the month following the month of the child's birth; the month in which Family Allowance payments began (for a child born before December 1, 1992); or the month in which eligibility to the CCB began (for a child born on or after December 1, 1992). If you cannot confirm the month of the first Family Allowance payment, you must use the month following the month of arrival in Canada or the month following the month in which decision-making responsibility of the child began. The CRP period ends the earliest of: the child's 7th birthday; the last Family Allowance payment (only in cases where the Family Allowance was not converted to CCB on January 1, 1993); the month in which the individual requesting the CRP ceased to be a Family Allowance recipient as defined by legislation; or the month in which the individual requesting the CRP ceased to be an individual eligible for the CCB. If you cannot confirm the month of the last Family Allowance payment, use the month: of departure from Canada; in which decision-making responsibility of the child was lost; of the child's death; or in which the common-law relationship ended (if the child is the child of the individual's common-law partner).

An individual or a third party can request the CRP by submitting any of the following: the Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP-1640) form; the Application for a Canada Pension Plan Retirement Pension (ISP-1000) form; the Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151) form; the Terminal Illness Application Kit for Disability Benefits Under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530A) form; a signed letter saying they want to request the CRP; or a request via their My Service Canada Account (MSCA). Individuals requesting the CRP should provide each child's SIN with their CRP request. If the individual does not provide the SIN, you must search ITRDS to locate the SIN record of the child. If you locate the child's account in ITRDS and are satisfied that you have found the correct child by validating the child's information, you can use the SIN profile to process the CRP without requesting proof of birth. If there are discrepancies and you cannot validate the child's information, the individual requesting the CRP must submit proof of birth for the child. If a child was not born in Canada, the individual requesting the CRP must provide proof of the child's date of entry into Canada along with that child's SIN or proof of birth. A letter of explanation must be obtained from the individual requesting the CRP if: the child's surname is different from the surname of the individual named on the CRP request; the child is adopted; there are any changes in the decision-making responsibility of the child; or information on the individual's file shows that they are not the natural or adoptive parent of the child (the individual is the child's grandparent, aunt, etc.). In addition to the items listed above, a legal representative must also submit documentation showing that they are authorized to act on behalf of the individual named on the CRP request. For more information, Legal Representation (Policy) There is no time limit to apply for the CRP. However, the individual must meet the eligibility criteria.

Communicating with clients Individuals must be advised of the possible consequences of waiving their rights to the CRP. The individual requesting the CRP must be advised that the individual who received the Family Allowance and who agrees to waive their rights to the CRP will not be able to use the CRP. The Department cannot advise that individual to change their CRP eligibility. It is the responsibility of the individual requesting the CRP to advise the individual who received the Family Allowance that waiving their rights to the CRP could affect their future eligibility for CPPD benefits and the family's eligibility for the Death benefit, SVR pension, and children's benefits (Surviving Child's benefit and Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit). In addition, if the individual who received the Family Allowance waives their rights in favour of the individual requesting the CRP, it may affect the dollar amount of the Family Allowance recipient's future CPP benefits. However, the CRP may increase the dollar amount of the benefits for the individual requesting it. The Department can only contact the Family Allowance recipient to explain the consequences of waiving their rights if we receive written authorization from the person requesting the CRP. Family Allowance recipient If the individual requesting the CRP remained at home to care for a child under the age of 7, but their spouse or common-law partner received a Family Allowance benefit for a period between January 1959 to December 1992, the individual requesting CRP must provide the Department with the periods during which they remained at home and were the primary caregiver for the child(ren). The individual requesting the CRP will only benefit from the CRP for those periods if the Family Allowance recipient: confirms the periods claimed by the individual who submitted the request; and waives their rights to the CRP in favour of the individual requesting the CRP for those same periods. To waive their rights to the CRP, the individual who received Family Allowance must complete, sign and date: Section D on the Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP-1640) form; Section B4—F on the Application for a Canada Pension Plan Retirement Pension (ISP-1000) form; or Section B3—E on the Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151). If the individual who received Family Allowance is deceased, the deceased's estate cannot sign the Family Allowance waiver on their behalf. If there is conflicting or insufficient information on the form or waiver, send the Development – Child-rearing provision (ISS-4550) letter seeking more information to the individual requesting the CRP. Individual eligible for CCB In the CCB Program, only the CCB-eligible individual can benefit from the CRP. There are cases where an individual who stayed at home to raise the child(ren) could not benefit from the CRP because the other parent received the CCB. The CRA has agreed to provide a letter confirming the fact that if the individual had applied for the CCB at the time when they were at home, caring for the children, they would have been determined to have been the eligible individual for the dates indicated. That individual will not receive retroactive CCB payments for this period. Before the CRA issues this letter, they must receive a signed declaration from the parent who had been identified as the "eligible" recipient of the CCB, attesting to the fact that the individual requesting the CRP was, in fact, the primary caregiver of the child(ren). The CCB-eligible parent must specify the period of time the individual requesting the CRP was the primary caregiver of the child(ren). All other periods would remain with the parent who had originally been identified as the CCB-eligible recipient. Individuals requesting the CRP will be advised of their options for qualifying as the eligible CCB individual and contributors will be advised to contact officials at the appropriate CRA regional tax centre to obtain the CRA letter noted above. Eligibility for the CRP is proven by the CRA letter. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Policy)

text: If the children listed on the request are already interrelated to the contributor, do not modify the existing interrelationship. Continue to process the Child Rearing Provision request with the existing interrelationship intact, as changes to the interrelationship may affect eligibility and entitlement to already existing benefits (e.g. an SVR pension rate for periods prior to January 2019 or a child's benefit). Interrelationships in ITRDS (Scenario)

When an individual requests the CRP, the request is applied to both the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) and Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) provisions. The CRP prevents the financial penalization of individuals who stopped working or reduced their paid employment or self-employment to raise children under the age of 7. Periods of time with low or no contributions result in lower payment amounts for CPP benefits. The purpose of the CRP is to help eligible individuals qualify or receive a higher entitlement amount for CPP benefits. The CRP is only applied if it is to an individual's advantage. If it reduces eligibility or entitlement, it is not applied. The CRP applies only to the time period when the individual had little to no earnings and was eligible for the Family Allowance or Canada Child Benefit (CCB). The primary caregiver is the person who was most responsible for the day-to-day needs of a child or children. An individual who worked at home while taking care of a child or children also meets this requirement. The CRP can only be applied to one individual's account for a given time period and particular child, even if there were multiple primary caregivers for the same child. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Individuals are urged to request the CRP when they first apply for a CPP benefit or pension. However, the individual or their authorized representative can request the CRP even after the initial benefit amount has been calculated. The CRDO allows for the removal of months or years of low or no earnings from an individual's contributory period when calculating a CPP benefit. This can help an individual meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for CPP pensions or benefits. The CRDO can also improve the MQP for CPPD benefits. The CRDI adds Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhanced component of a benefit.

Attach a related receivable (overpayment) to a supplementary payable (underpayment) in CPMS.

A related receivable is created in CPMS when the benefit payments of a client (e.g. spouse, parent or child) is applied to a receivable of another client. Attaching a related receivable to a supplementary payable does not change the recovery account of the related receivable. It is a one-time process, and the monthly recovery will be removed from the set recovery account. You can attach a related receivable to a supplementary payable when a supplementary payable is generated and the client wants to have a related receivable deducted only from this payable. The attached receivable must be in active status—if not, you must use the Updated Recovery Account procedure. Refer to Update a Departmental Receivable's Recovery Account in CPMS . topic_title: An applicant withdraws their consent to exchange information with IRCC
text: An applicant or their legal representative can withdraw their consent authorizing Service Canada to contact IRCC at any time by providing such a withdrawal request in writing. If Service Canada receives the withdraw consent request from an applicant before receiving a response from IRCC, you must notify IRCC that the consent has been revoked. Complete the ISP3222 form and send it in PDF format by email to the MSFT delegate for transmission to IRCC.

When sending the completed ISP3210 form to IRCC, you must indicate which type of request is required based on a review of the applicant's file. Basic or complex request Request type Description Basic Provides confirmation of the applicant's permanent residence information which includes their legal status and date of original entry. Complex Provides confirmation of the applicant's entire residence history. A complex request includes a search for the applicant's: permanent residence information; legal status; Updated sponsorship status ( it will only be provided if Yes is selected in the sponsorship checkbox); date of entry; and immigration documents (e.g. study permits, work permits, visitor records). It also provides requested information in the remarks section on the IMM5716 form. Noted gaps in residence status are provided, if available. If the type of request is not selected, IRCC treats the consent form as a Basic Request and only searches the applicant’s permanent resident history. If both sections are checked, IRCC treats the consent form as a Complex Request .

Updated When the applicant initiates a request from IRCC to obtain verification of their legal status, Service Canada cannot cancel it nor ask questions on the applicant's behalf of IRCC. If the applicant sends the required immigration documentation to Service Canada before sending it to IRCC, you must complete the Follow-up Communication with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (ISP3222) form and send it to IRCC. topic_title: Determine the level of misrepresentation and associated penalty amount
text: The level of misrepresentation is important for the overall penalty determination process because it helps to determine the maximum penalty amount that can be applied. First misrepresentation A first misrepresentation occurs when there are no records of a previous penalty or conviction under the same program, CPP or OAS, within the last ten years. The maximum penalty amount for the first level of misrepresentation is: 10% of the gross overpayment amount (resulting from the misrepresentation); or 10% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation if there was no overpayment. Subsequent misrepresentation A subsequent misrepresentation occurs when: the individual makes another misrepresentation under the same program (e.g. CPP or OAS); and the penalty imposition date for that misrepresentation is within ten years from the date of imposition of a prior OAS or CPP penalty or conviction. The maximum penalty amount for a subsequent misrepresentation is: 20% of the gross overpayment amount (resulting from the misrepresentation); or 20% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation if there was no overpayment. Multiple misrepresentations discovered at the same time When there is a false statement or declaration made under both the CPP and OAS program, each program can impose its own penalty. If there are multiple misrepresentations detected under the same program during the same investigation, only one penalty will be imposed.

To determine the penalty amount, you must verify: any overpayment amounts, if applicable; that there are no limitations on the imposition of a penalty; the level of misrepresentation; the maximum penalty percentage; and any potential mitigating circumstances.

topic_title: Limitations on the imposition of a penalty
text: Do not impose a penalty if: the case is with the RCMP; the individual or individuals involved have been convicted of the offence; the individual makes a valid voluntary disclosure of the misrepresentation; the individual who committed the misrepresentation is now deceased; or five years have passed since the day on which the Department became aware of the misrepresentation.

Once it is determined that an individual has knowingly misrepresented, mitigating circumstances must be considered. Mitigating circumstances are situations, facts or actions that can offer some explanation of the individual's actions and lead to a possible reduction of the penalty amount. Although these circumstances offer some explanation, they do not excuse the misrepresentation. The Integrity Services Branch (ISB) will investigate the information surrounding these mitigating circumstances and will clearly document them in their Report of Investigation (ROI). The ISB will not take mitigating circumstances into consideration when making a recommendation to impose a penalty. However, you must consider the mitigating circumstances when determining the penalty amount. For more information, refer to Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) and Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) Assessing Mitigating Circumstances (Action)

This procedure provides guidance on how to: impose an administrative penalty; and perform the necessary actions on an individual's file when Integrity Services Branch (ISB) completes an administrative investigation recommending a penalty.

If you are imposing a penalty on a third party debtor, the details of the overpayment must be recorded in ITRDS notes on both accounts. This would involve recording the following details in ITRDS notes: The debtor's name and SIN under the beneficiary's SIN (the SIN under which the monies were paid out); and The beneficiary's name and SIN on the debtor's account. The overpayment remains on the beneficiary's account, but a receivable for the penalty must be manually created on the debtor's account in CPMS . Cross-referencing both the beneficiary's and debtor's account is currently the only way to track third-party involvement on a beneficiary's account. This also allows the recovery of any outstanding debts still owed by the third party at a later date (i.e. when RTR pension or OAS begins). Under the Privacy Act , individuals have a right to access their personal information held by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC). However, any personal information contained in the file relating to an individual other than the requester may be exempt under the Privacy Act .

An administrative penalty is an amount that is charged to a beneficiary or third party who knowingly misrepresented information in relation to CPP or OAS benefits or pensions. The intention of an administrative penalty is: to be a deterrent to discourage individuals from committing further misrepresentations; and to protect the integrity of the programs. The imposition of administrative penalties was implemented on July 21, 2011. Misrepresentations that occurred before that date are not subject to an administrative penalty. The ISB determines that an individual knowingly misrepresented. They are responsible for making a recommendation to Benefits Delivery Services (BDS) to impose an administrative penalty. Once complete, the ISB Report of Investigation (ROI) will be returned to BDS where it will be added to the individual's file for action. The report will include Prior Offences/Misrepresentation, Facts, Contributing Circumstances and Recommendation sections. Contact the ISB immediately if you have any questions or clarifications needed regarding the investigation or the recommendation of an administrative penalty before taking any action on the account. Under no circumstances are you to contact the individual during the assessment phase of a penalty. For more information, refer to Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) and Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) Administrative penalties (Policy)

The effective date of a common-law relationship is the month after the common-law requirement of one year is met. Clients are considered single until this requirement is met. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a client's marital status changes to "common-law": Program Benefits CPP The SVR pension is not affected if the client begins a common-law relationship. The Pension Sharing provision can be effective as early as the month following the month the one-year requirement of living together is met, if all other requirements are met. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on combined income the month following the month the one-year requirement of living together is met. Until that time, the members of the couple will continue to be paid the GIS based on single income. The ALWS benefit ceases the month following the month the one-year requirement of living together is met (i.e. the final payment is issued in the 12th month of living together). The client will remain a survivor until this time. The ALW benefit can be effective as early as the month following the month the one-year requirement of living together is met, if all other requirements are met. For more information, Validate a Common-Law Relationship (Action)

text: Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control refers to specific situations where a married couple or common-law partners are unable to reside together, and it does not reflect a breakdown in the marriage or common-law relationship. The couple is still considered married or common-law. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on single income the month following the month the couple began living apart, if it is to their advantage. The ALW benefit is calculated based on single income the month following the month the couple began living apart but not before January 1, 2017, if it is to their advantage. topic_title: Legal marriage dissolution (divorced or legal annulment)
text: The effective date of a divorce is the month after the divorce is finalized (i.e. after the 30-day period has elapsed). Clients are considered married, common-law or separated until the 30-day requirement is met. The death of one spouse during this 30-day period effectively ends the marriage. For CPP and OAS purposes, the surviving party is then considered to be the surviving spouse. However, if a common-law partner exists, they may be considered the surviving spouse. The effective date of an annulment is the month after the legal annulment is finalized. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a client's marital status changes to “divorced” or their “marriage is annulled”: Program Benefits CPP Pension Sharing ceases the month following the month the divorce or annulment is finalized (i.e. the final payment is issued in the month the divorce or annulment is finalized). The division of credits for a Credit Split can take place as early as the month following the month the divorce or annulment is finalized if all other requirements are met. However, if the client had a period of separation before the divorce, the division of credits may take place earlier. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on single income the month following the month the divorce or annulment is finalized. The ALW benefit ceases the month following the month the divorce or annulment is finalized (i.e. the final payment is issued in the month the divorce or annulment is finalized). For more information, Validate a Legal Marriage Dissolution (Action)

When a couple reconciles and the separation was for a period less than the required time period to be considered separated, the marital status will not change, meaning that the couple will continue to be considered married or common-law. When a married couple reconciles after the required time has elapsed to be considered separated, they are considered married again effective the month following the month of reconciliation. When a common-law couple reconciles after the required time has elapsed to be considered separated, they are required to live together for one year before they are considered common-law again. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a couple reconciles: Program Benefits CPP A new Pension Sharing application is required to resume the provision after a separation of more than 12 months. A Credit Split application can be withdrawn if the criteria to withdraw are met. Refer to Withdraw an Application (Scenario) . Withdraw an Application (Scenario) A separated spouse with a credit split approved on or after January 1, 2025 is not eligible for an SVR pension after the death of their same separated spouse. However, if the couple reconciled for at least one year immediately before the death of their spouse, they may be eligible for the SVR pension if all other requirements are met. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on combined income the month following the month: the one-year requirement of living together is met if the couple resumes a common-law relationship; or the couple resumes living together if they are married. A new ALW benefit application is required after a separation of more than 3 months as the lifetime renewal designation (i.e. GIS for Life) is lost.

The effective date of a separation is either the month after 3 full months of separation or the 12th month following the month of separation, depending on the program. Clients are considered married or common-law until the requirement is met. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a client's marital status changes to "separated": Program Benefits CPP Pension Sharing (PNSH) continues for the first 11 consecutive months of separation following the month in which the separation occurred. PNSH ceases in the 12th month after the month of separation (i.e. the final payment is issued in the 11th month after the separation). The division of credits for a Credit Split can take place after the couple have been separated for one year if all other requirements are met. An SVR pension will be denied if the applicant: selects common-law as their marital status; and indicates they were living apart by choice from the deceased contributor at the time of death. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on combined income for the first 3 consecutive months of separation following the month in which the separation occurred. Effective the 4th month, the GIS is calculated based on single income. The ALW benefit continues for the first 3 consecutive months of separation following the month in which the separation occurred. The ALW benefit ceases effective the 4th month after the separation (i.e. the final payment is issued in the 3rd month after the month of the separation). For more information, Validate a Separation (Action)

To be considered a survivor, the client's marriage must not have been terminated by divorce or annulment before the death of the spouse. If the clients have recently divorced, ensure that the 30-day appeal period after the granting of the judgement of divorce has not passed. A client is considered a survivor the month following the month of death. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a client's marital status changes to "survivor": Program Benefits CPP The SVR pension can be effective as early as the month following the month of death of their spouse or common-law partner if all other requirements are met. Pension Sharing ceases the month following the month of death of their spouse or common-law partner. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is recalculated based on single income the month following the death of their spouse or common-law partner. The ALW benefit ceases the month following the month of death (i.e. the final payment is issued in the month of death). The ALWS benefit can be effective as early as the month following the month of death of their spouse or common-law partner if all other requirements are met. For more information, Validate a Survivor (Action)

topic_title: Withdrawals from a Registered Retirement Savings Plan and the effects on the Registered Retirement Income Fund
text: Effective in 2007, there was an increase in the Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) and Registered Retirement Plan conversion age from 69 to 71 years of age. This measure benefits individuals who turned 69 years of age in 2007 or in a subsequent year. The measure also benefits individuals who turned 70 or 71 years of age in 2007. If contribution room was available, 70-year-old individuals were permitted to make RRSP contributions in 2007 and 2008, and 71-year-old individuals, in 2007. Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) owners must normally withdraw a specified minimum amount each year following the year in which the RRIF is established. This requirement was waived for 2007 for RRIF owners who turned 71 years of age in 2007, and waived for 2007 and 2008 for RRIF owners who turned 70 years of age in 2007. A RRIF annuitant who was 71 years of age or younger at the end of 2007 can reconvert the RRIF to a RRSP as long as the re-established RRSP is converted to a RRIF before the end of the taxation year in which the individual turned 71 years of age. Registered plan annuities can be amended, without adverse tax consequences, to reflect the later conversion age. Employers are also allowed to amend their Registered Retirement Plans to allow benefits to accrue, and contributions to be made, for employed members who were 71 years of age or younger at the end of 2007, subject to any otherwise applicable adjustments to pensions in pay. Annuity payments from an RRSP and RRIF income (including transfers from an RRSP) are considered pension income and an option can be granted if they cease or reduce. RRSP withdrawals are not considered pension income and therefore, are not eligible for an option.

text: If you receive notification of a change of decision-making responsibility and parenting time without the supporting documentation, you must suspend the child's benefit. For more information, Suspend Pensions or Benefits (Scenario)

Payees must inform the Department when a change of decision-making responsibility and parenting time occurs. When the periods of decision-making responsibility and parenting time are confirmed, payments are made to each payee for the months they had decision-making responsibility and parenting time for each eligible dependent child. To change the payee of a -18 child's benefit, the individual or agency requesting the change must submit documentation proving they have decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child. When there is a request for a change in the payee of a -18 child, you must always confirm there is: an approved application for a children's benefit for the child on the file; and evidence that supports a continuous child-contributor relationship from the application date to the present. The person who has more decision-making responsibility and parenting time is not the determining factor of who will be paid the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit or Surviving Child's benefit under the CPP. The disabled contributor or surviving spouse with decision-making responsibility of a -18 child who has at least 20% of parenting time is the eligible payee and will be paid the full amount of the child's benefit. For more information on determining the payee of a -18 child, Children's Benefits—Change in Decision-Making Responsibility and Parenting Time (Policy)

topic_title: Can a foreign benefit be reconsidered?
text: Information provided to foreign social security agencies (e.g. certification of periods of Canadian residence) for adjudicating a foreign benefit cannot be reconsidered by the Department. If the client has requested a reconsideration or additional information regarding their foreign benefit decision, you should advise them to contact the foreign social security agency directly. The Department is not involved in determining the client's eligibility for a foreign benefit.

The most common reasons to request a reconsideration are listed below: CPP and CPPD amount of the benefit; contributory requirements; date of birth (age); effective date; marital status; medical determination or date of onset in a CPPD case; more than one person claiming to be eligible for a benefit ( DTH benefit, SVR pension); and range of division after a credit split. text: Verbal requests for reconsideration are not accepted. topic_title: How can a client or third party request a reconsideration?
text: Requests for reconsideration can be made by: using the online services through My Service Canada Account (MSCA); submitting a signed written request; or submitting one of the following forms: Request for Reconsideration of a Canada Pension Plan Disability Decision and/or Post-Retirement Disability Decision (ISP-1145); Request for reconsideration of a Canada Pension Plan decision (ISP-1238); or Request for reconsideration of an Old Age Security decision (ISP-3134). A request for reconsideration can be submitted as an original, certified true copy, photocopy, fax, or scanned email. If the written request or form is unsigned, you must request that the client or authorized third party to sign it. If the third party is not authorized, send it to the client. The Department will protect the reconsideration request receipt date using the unsigned written request or form if the signed request is received within the Bring Forward (BF) period. When the client or third party submits a reconsideration request, they can indicate they want the Department to review the decision using: information already submitted; information already submitted and new information provided with the request; or information already submitted and new information that will be provided later. When a client or third party indicates they will provide new information later, they must provide the date they will send the new information. If no date is provided or the date provided goes beyond the National BF Guidelines, call the client to obtain the date or the reason the stated timeframe is required. National Bring Forward Guidelines (Work Tool) A BF period can be extended in some circumstances. Refer to Bring Forward (BF) (Action) . For CPPD, use discretion when increasing the time limit when clients are awaiting medical appointments or tests that may impact eligibility. When establishing residence for an OAS pension or benefit, any absences interrupting residence in Canada are excluded from the Canadian residence calculation. An applicant is considered absent from Canada when they are not physically present in Canada. However, not all absences interrupt residence and they must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. When evaluating an absence, consider the following: Length of the absence Temporary absences lasting less than one year do not necessarily interrupt residence and may not need to be investigated unless they are part of a larger pattern of absences. An absence lasting more than one year, depending on its nature, can interrupt residence. Reason for the absence The applicant may need to clarify whether the absence was temporary in nature for it to be considered as residence in Canada. Frequency of absences Absences that are a part of a larger pattern of absences may indicate residential ties to another country. When reviewing the length, nature or frequency of an absence, consider the applicant's residential ties to Canada when they are outside of the country. The applicant may need to demonstrate that they maintained significant ties to Canada during the period(s) that they were absent. If residential ties cannot be verified, the period of absence is excluded from the Canadian residence calculation. For factors to consider when reviewing an applicant’s residential ties, refer to the Residential Ties work tool. The most common types of absences are: Table 1. Absence Type and Description Absence Type Description Absences under specified circumstances An applicant may be deemed to have been residing in Canada during periods of time when they were: physically absent from Canada; or physically present in Canada but their primary residence was in another country. Refer to the Absences from Canada under specified circumstances section below. Absences for the purpose of attending school or university Absences for the purpose of attending school or university do not interrupt the applicant's residence in Canada. If the applicant was outside of Canada to attend school or university, they are deemed to be resident in Canada for that period. Applicants must provide official documentation to support the absence; however, they are not required to return to Canada within 6 months of completing their education abroad for the period to be considered residence in Canada. If the applicant did not return to Canada, or there is a period of absence after the final school term ended, residence is calculated up to and including the last day of the final school term. Refer to Example—Absences for the purpose of attending school or university . Example—Absences for the purpose of attending school or university Absences less than one year, a pattern of short-term absences, and frequent absences of 6 months or more Absences from Canada of less than one year generally do not interrupt residence. However, a pattern of short-term absences or frequent absences of 6 months or more over a period of several years, requires review to determine if the applicant maintained residential ties to Canada during these absences and can be considered a Canadian resident for these periods. Although applicants do not need to provide information regarding absences of less than 6 months in length on their residence statement, a pattern of absences is often discovered when: reviewing a passport; receiving an informant lead (third party complaint); or the Integrity Services Branch conducts an investigation. Refer to: Example—Absences less than one year ; Example—Absences less than one year Example—Pattern of short-term absences ; and Example—Pattern of short-term absences Example—Frequent absences of 6 months or more . Example—Frequent absences of 6 months or more Example—Absences less than one year Example—Pattern of short-term absences Example—Frequent absences of 6 months or more Absences greater than one year Absences greater than one year may be determined to have interrupted residence in Canada; however, this cannot be assumed and requires review. There are circumstances in which a longer period of absence from Canada can be determined to be temporary and not interrupt residence. All absences over one year require review to determine if the applicant maintained residential ties with Canada and can be considered a Canadian resident for these periods of absence. Refer to Example—Absences greater than one year . Example—Absences greater than one year For more information on absences from Canada, Defining Residence (Policy)

topic_title: Absences from Canada under specified circumstances
text: Applicants may indicate that they lived outside of Canada, unaware that the period abroad could be deemed as Canadian residence. Although a complete residence statement may not require further review, it is important to consider whether absences of more than one year could be deemed as Canadian residence. Review the application and the residence statement for indications that the stated absences can be deemed as Canadian residence and do not interrupt residence. The following are some of the factors that could indicate that an absence can be deemed as Canadian residence: the applicant made CPP contributions during periods of absence; the applicant or their current or ex-spouse or common-law partner is or was a member of the Canadian Forces; or the applicant is or was a missionary or member of an international charitable organization (e.g. the applicant states their name is Reverend John Smith and has multiple absences from Canada). For more information, Defining Residence (Policy) Documentary evidence for specified circumstances Specific documents must be provided as documentary evidence depending on the type of absence. Applicants must provide official documentation to support that they were employed or engaged outside of Canada by one of the specified occupations or organizations. For example, a Record of Employment or Military Personnel Records Resumé can be used to support the applicant's employment or engagement outside of Canada. If the applicant declares that they returned to Canada within 6 months of completing their employment or activity, or if they reached the age of 65 while still engaged abroad, no further documents are required. Family members and specified circumstances A family member refers to the applicant's: spouse or common-law partner; mother; father; mother-in-law; father-in-law; brother; sister; and any natural, adoptive or foster children. Similar documentary requirements apply to family members living abroad with the applicant who is absent under specified circumstances. Family members who lived abroad with the applicant must provide documentary evidence to support that they accompanied the applicant who was employed or engaged outside of Canada under a specified circumstance. The supporting documentary evidence must be on an official letterhead and signed by an official. The date of return to Canada indicated on the family member’s residence statement must be within 6 months after the return or death of their family member upon whom they are or were dependent. Unless there is a discrepancy or inconsistency on file, documents to prove the date of return are not required. Changes in marital status while absent from Canada under a specified circumstance An applicant who is absent under one of the specified circumstances and exceptions who enters into a marriage or a common-law union, needs to provide documentary evidence to support their marriage or common-law union. For more information, Defining Residence (Policy)

For a residence statement to be considered complete, it must include all periods of residence in Canada and absence from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement. Documentary Evidence—Residence (Policy) This includes all periods of Canadian residence and all absences from Canada greater than 6 months: from the latest of: the applicant’s 18th birthday; or the date of initial arrival into Canada; and up to and including the date the applicant submits their application. If an applicant selects Yes in response to the question about having lived continuously in Canada since birth or age 18 on an OAS pension or benefit application, this is considered a complete residence statement. While the residence history is considered complete if it includes only the years of residence, clarification is required if months are missing. If an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) is needed for the applicant to be eligible for an OAS pension or benefit, all residence periods, including those outside of Canada, from age 18 to the date the applicant submits their application are required in writing. When an application is submitted early, confirmation of the applicant's continued residence up to their pension or benefit effective date is required if the additional time affects the residence calculation.

topic_title: Establishing the applicant's intent to reside in Canada at their original date of entry
text: Where an applicant indicates on their residence statement, an original date of entry that is before their landed or permanent resident date, clarification may be required to determine if this period is considered residence or presence. Clarification of an applicant's intent to reside in Canada from their original date of entry to their landed or permanent resident date is not required if: there are no discrepancies or inconsistencies between the residence statement and the documentation on file; there are no absences declared between the original date of entry and the permanent resident status or landed date; and the applicant’s current legal status is permanent in nature (e.g. permanent resident or Canadian citizen); or the applicant had a permanent legal status on the date of departure from Canada, if they are applying from outside of Canada. In these cases, the period of Canadian residence begins with the applicant's stated original date of entry. You must contact the applicant to clarify their intent to reside in Canada from their original date of entry to their landed or permanent resident date when: there are inconsistencies between the residence statement and the documentation on file; the applicant was absent between the original date of entry and the permanent resident status or landed date; the applicant's current legal status is temporary in nature (e.g. visitor visa); the applicant did not have a permanent legal status on the date of departure from Canada, if they are applying from outside of Canada; or the applicant is using a 900-series SIN . Although an individual may be physically present in Canada, this does not always mean that these periods can be considered as Canadian residence for OAS purposes. In these situations, an applicant's intention to reside in Canada permanently cannot be assumed.
