topic_title: Did the survivor marry the deceased contributor within one year of their death?
text: The general rule is to accept that a one-year life expectancy existed at the time of the contributor's marriage, unless the applicant voluntarily provided that the deceased contributor knew that death would occur within one year. If there is no reason to question the information provided, you may process the application using normal procedures. If a contributor dies within one year from the date of their marriage, no SVR pension is payable if the Department is satisfied that the contributor believed, at the time of the marriage that they had a life expectancy of less than one year. This situation is commonly known as a deathbed marriage. When the information indicates that the life expectancy of the contributor might have been less than one year at the time of marriage, you must investigate the issue. An example of this situation is when the date of death of a person receiving a Disability ( DSB ) benefit is less than one year after the date of their marriage. You must investigate when: information on file indicates that the life expectancy of the contributor might have been less than one year at the time of marriage (e.g. there was a diagnosis of a terminal or grave illness); or the date of death of an individual receiving a DSB benefit is less than one year after the date of their marriage. It is possible the contributor had a terminal illness. Review the disability file to determine if it contains a possible deathbed marriage situation. Contact the CPP disability unit for assistance, if applicable. If you review the file and have reason to believe that you might be dealing with a deathbed marriage, follow these steps: Review the application for the possibility that you can approve the surviving spouse based on a common-law relationship existing before the marriage. Pursue information in connection with a possible deathbed marriage only if you cannot establish the common-law union. Ask the applicant discreetly to answer the following questions as specifically as possible: How did the contributor die? The cause of the contributor's death might be an indicator. If it was an automobile accident, this is not a deathbed marriage. However, you must investigate a medical cause of death, such as cancer. To the best of the applicant's knowledge, did the deceased contributor believe, at the time of the marriage, that their life expectancy was less than one year? What was the basis of the contributor's expectations? Assess the contributor's expectation at the time of marriage. You can only deny an SVR pension application if you can clearly establish that the contributor believed, at the time of marriage, that they had a life expectancy of less than one year.

As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in the CPP enhancement. This component increases the amount of CPP retirement, disability and survivor's pensions, and the post-retirement benefit of people who work and contribute in 2019 or later. The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but a "top-up" to the original, now referred to as the base CPP. This means working Canadians will receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. The eligibility criteria for CPP benefits are not affected by the enhancement as only the base portion is used to determine eligibility and the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. The increase that individuals receive on their SVR pension will depend on how much and for how long their deceased spouse or common-law partner made enhanced contributions. The current formula used to calculate CPP combined benefits continues to apply, and the maximum payable for a combined benefit cannot exceed the maximum RTR pension or DSB rate. If there is a first additional or second additional SVR pension, RTR pension or DSB component, the additional components will be added to the amount of the base component of the combined benefit. A combined first additional amount cannot be more than the maximum payable amount of a first additional RTR pension or first additional DSB . Similarly, a combined second additional amount cannot be more than the maximum payable amount of a second additional RTR pension or second additional DSB . For more information, refer to CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) and to CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge)

topic_title: Is the applicant separated from the contributor at the time of death? Updated
text: When the applicant indicates the separation was for reasons beyond their control (e.g. illness or employment), a written statement with the date and reasons for the separation is acceptable. A written statement can include a notation on the application or file by the applicant. If the applicant claims common-law as their marital status and indicates that they were living apart from the deceased at the time of death by choice (i.e. voluntary) or for a reason beyond their control that is not due to illness or employment, you must deny the application. If the applicant requests a reconsideration, use the normal business process to escalate an enquiry to CPP Operational Policy for guidance. For additional information, Defining Marital Status (Policy) If the separation of the legal spouses was by choice (i.e. voluntary) and less than one year at the time of the contributor's death, there is no possibility of any eligible common-law partner. If no one else claims to be the survivor and the applicant meets all eligibility requirements, you can process the application. If the separation of the legal spouses was by choice and for a period of more than one year at the time of the contributor's death, it is possible that the legal spouse is not the eligible survivor if there was a common-law partner. You must obtain a completed Statutory Declaration - Separation of Legal Spouses and Common-law Partners (ISP-1811) form from the applicant if the information was not provided on the Application for CPP Survivor's pension and Child(ren's) Benefits (ISP-1300) form. If there is indication of an existing common-law partner on the file, or the separated legal spouse indicates on the SVR pension application or the ISP-1811 form that the deceased contributor lived in a common-law relationship, you must make a reasonable attempt to locate the potential common-law partner. If the separated legal spouse provided a name and an address, you must mail an SVR pension application to the potential common-law partner and follow the bring forward procedures to allow the potential common-law partner up to 60 days to apply. Bring Forward (BF) (Action) If the potential common-law partner: applies and meets the definition of surviving spouse, deny the separated legal spouse applicant; or applies and does not meet the definition of surviving spouse, deny the common-law applicant. The separated legal spouse may now be considered the survivor. If the potential common-law partner does not respond, you may only consider approving the separated legal spouse's application after you have determined with greatest certainty there is no common-law partner that meets the definition of surviving spouse. If there is evidence on file that the deceased contributor was living in a common-law relationship for at least one year at the time of death, the legal spouse cannot be the eligible survivor. The common-law partner is considered to be the surviving spouse even if they do not apply for the SVR pension or they apply and their application is denied based on a greater of 2 SVR pensions. For more information, Defining Marital Status (Policy) If you determine there are anomalies or discrepancies in either applicant's information, refer the file to the Integrity Services Branch. text: When an SVR pension is in pay under one deceased contributor and a second SVR pension application for another deceased contributor is data captured, ITRDS correctly calculates the greater of the 2 SVR pensions. text: A survivor is only entitled to receive one SVR pension. However, they are entitled to receive whichever SVR pension provides the highest payment between their previous and current deceased contributor spouses or common-law partners. You must process the new SVR pension application, and ITRDS will always determine which SVR pension to pay. ITRDS will terminate the lesser SVR pension with the reason Pay Greater SVR . You must advise the applicant of the results in writing, with either the Award - Survivor's Pension Award (ISS-4525) letter or the Denial - Survivor's pension (ISS-4520) letter to advise the applicant that they are already receiving a larger SVR pension from their former spouse or former common-law partner. If the survivor requests to receive the lesser of the 2 SVR pensions, refer to The applicant wants to receive the lesser of the 2 SVR pensions in the Exceptions and Special Cases section below.

topic_title: Was the applicant the legal spouse of the deceased contributor, and has a credit split with the contributor?
text: If the SVR pension applicant is the separated legal spouse of the deceased contributor and was approved for a credit split submitted on or after January 1, 2025 during their separation from the same contributor, they are not eligible to a CPP SVR pension. The separated legal spouse who applied for the credit split (or their executor, if it was the estate who applied on behalf of a deceased legal spouse) has up to 60 days after they receive their credit split Notice of Canada Pension Plan Credit Split Approval (ISP-1900C) form to request to withdraw the credit split. If a request to withdraw the credit split is received and approved, the SVR pension applicant may be eligible to the SVR pension, if they meet all of the other eligibility requirements. You must determine when the ISP-1900C form was sent. If you are within or at 60 days of the date, verify PWS for a request to withdraw the credit split received from the credit split applicant. If there is one, a decision must be made on the request to withdraw the credit split before data capturing the SVR pension application. If there is no request to withdraw the credit split, proceed with processing the SVR pension application. Additionally, the SVR pension applicant may be eligible to the SVR pension if, after the credit split was submitted and approved, they reconciled and resumed their spousal relationship with their separated legal spouse for a period of one year or more immediately before the contributor died. If this is a possibility, given the date the credit split was submitted, you must determine the status of the relationship between the applicant and the deceased contributor at the time of death and the length of time during which they were reconciled, if applicable. If this information already provided to the Department is on file or has been provided on the SVR pension application itself and there are no discrepancies, you do not need to request additional information from the applicant. If you require information from the applicant to determine if they resumed their spousal relationship with the deceased contributor for a period of one year or more immediately before the contributor's death, send the Development - Marital Status (ISS-6182) letter to the applicant. Follow the bring forward procedures to allow the applicant to reply. Bring Forward (BF) (Action) For more information about the impact of a credit split on a separated legal spouse's eligibility to an SVR pension, Survivor's Pension—Eligibility Requirements and Disqualifying Conditions (Policy)

topic_title: Was the top-up amount included in the deceased contributor's payment for the DTH benefit?
text: When you receive an SVR pension application, you must verify the deceased contributor's account to determine if the DTH benefit has already been paid. If the DTH benefit was paid with the top-up amount included, and the SVR pension is approved, there is no longer entitlement to the DTH benefit top-up amount. This becomes an overpayment and must be collected. For more information, Departmental Receivables (Overpayments) (Scenario)

topic_title: When a readjudication causes a change to the effective date of an SVR pension and overrides the SVR DSB Periods workaround
text: As of January 1, 2019, when a second SVR pension application was received but a previous application for the same deceased spouse was processed before January 1, 2019 with a status of Eligible but no Entitlement, to put the SVR1 application In Pay you had to use the SVR DSB Periods triennial reform workaround in ITRDS by entering the latest of: the month following the date of death; 11 months before the receipt date of the second application; or January 2019. The second survivor's application was data captured and denied with the reason Benefit already exists . Effective May 21, 2022, any previous SVR pension that was adjudicated using the SVR DSB Periods triennial workaround is subject to a change in effective date if the account is re-adjudicated regardless of the date that was used in the SVR DSB Periods triennial reform workaround. In cases where the SVR DSB Periods triennial reform workaround was used, ITRDS will re-adjudicate the account using January 2019 as the effective date, which may be earlier than what the client is entitled to. The correct effective date of the SVR pension is 11 months retroactive to the receipt date of the second application, or January 2019, whichever is later. In cases where an incorrect January 2019 effective date was created when a re-adjudication was done on an account, you must: Terminate the SVR1 benefit with the status of In Pay in ITRDS . Refer to Cancel, Reinstate, Release, Suspend or Terminate a Benefit in ITRDS (Action) . In order to terminate the SVR1, click Modify under SVR1 to open the Modify Benefits screen, and: enter the current date as the Receipt Date ; for Type of Action , select Terminate ; for the End Date , enter the 1st of the month and year equal to the initial start date of the benefit; for Reason(s) , select No Eligibility ; for Outstanding Payments Returned select Yes ; and click Submit . A survivor is defined as a person whose spouse or common-law partner has died. For the ALWS benefit, the person has not become the spouse or common-law partner of another person since the spouse or common-law partner's death. For more information, Defining Marital Status (Policy) Documentary evidence may be required to support a client's marital status when: the marital status impacts the eligibility or entitlement to a CPP or OAS pension, benefit or provision for an initial benefit; there is a marital status change on an existing benefit; there is a difference in the information recorded for different programs (i.e. CPP, OAS, International Operations (IO)); or there is a difference between the documentation on file and the documentation in the systems. When a client submits the appropriate documentation to establish the marital status and the spouse or common-law partner's death in one program area (CPP, OAS or IO), it is also accepted for the other program areas. Applicants with a My Service Canada Account (MSCA) have the option to upload documents online in certain situations. For CPP, applicants can upload documents using the Document Upload Solution service in MSCA to support their: applications for CPPD benefits, DTH benefit, SVR pension and Child(ren)'s benefits; and reconsideration requests (CPPD only). For OAS, applicants can upload documents using the Client Portal accessed through MSCA to support their: applications; reconsideration requests; and changes to life events (e.g. marital relationship, income). For more information about uploading documents, refer to : Document Upload Solution (Scenario) Document Upload Solution (Scenario) Introduction to the Client Portal (Knowledge) Introduction to the Client Portal (Knowledge) For an individual to be considered a survivor, you must receive evidence of the marriage or common-law relationship and the spouse or common-law partner's death. If the spouse or common-law partner is missing and certain criteria are met, the date of death can be presumed and a presumption of death certificate issued. For information regarding documentation required to support being a survivor, refer to Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) and Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) Documentary Evidence—Death (Policy) Validating documentary evidence When validating the documentary evidence received, ensure that: it is acceptable proof that the applicant is a surviving spouse or common-law partner. Refer to Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) and Documentary Evidence—Death (Policy) ; Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) Documentary Evidence—Death (Policy) the document is legible; the document does not appear to be altered in any way; and the details of the document support the information provided by the client, such as the: names of the married or common-law individuals; date of the marriage or date that the common-law relationship began; name of the deceased individual; and date of death of the deceased individual. Documentary evidence in a foreign language For the purpose of administering CPP and OAS benefits, you may need to have foreign documents translated. However, translation is not required when the documents received are: translated by a Canadian, provincial or territorial government; or translated by foreign missions (e.g. embassies, consulates, High Commissions), Government departments and certified translators. You do not have to translate documents provided in a foreign language if : the material is not relevant to the consideration of the application or the ongoing receipt of benefits; or the relevant details are provided by the foreign agency. For more information, Translation (Action)

You can cancel or reissue a returned payment; however, cancelling the payment renders it void without the possibility of being negotiated or redeemed. Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) cancels returned cheques for the following reasons: Original Returned/Duplicate Issued Duplicate Returned/Original Cashed PSPC stamps these cheques as Spoiled . You can reissue a returned payment: as a direct deposit payment; or as a cheque mailed to the appropriate person or address (e.g. the payee's home address or the beneficiary's estate). PSPC automatically resends cheques by mail that have been returned as mutilated . ITRDS notes sometimes indicate why a payment was returned or cancelled. Such payments can often be redirected with new address, direct deposit or other information from the client's file. ITRDS notes also indicate if any actions are already underway when there are issues with the payment.

Payments are commonly returned for one of the following reasons: The payee's entitlement ceases (e.g. a beneficiary dies, a survivor receiving OAS benefits remarries, a surviving child receiving CPP benefits who is over the age of 18 and leaves school). The payee died, and the estate cannot cash the payment as it was originally issued to the client. There is a change of payee (e.g. a trustee dies). The payee's address changed or the payee cannot be located. The payee's name changed (e.g. the payee marries or remarries). The payee's name is incorrect. The payee's bank account number changed. The payee's bank account is closed, frozen or transferred to another financial institution. The payee receives an original payment and its duplicate one and returns one of the two payments; The bank deems a cheque to be stale-dated. The Department stops or recalls a payment. The client requests to have their benefit cancelled. The Imaging and Receiver General Operations Directorate records all returned payments in SPS. The Payment Information Status indicates Outstanding and the Payment Attempt Status indicates Returned with a return Reason Code .

A stale-dated cheque is a cheque that is non-negotiable because of its age. Some financial institutions will not negotiate cheques that are over 6 months old. If a cheque is returned to the Department with a claim that it is stale-dated, the Imaging and Receiver General Operations Directorate resends the cheque to the payee by mail and includes a letter explaining that payments drawn on the account of the Receiver General for Canada do not become stale dated. This only applies to cheques printed by the Receiver General for Canada as these cheques never expire. However, according to Public Services and Procurement Canada, foreign Government of Canada cheques issued by the foreign service provider are considered ordinary cheques and become stale-dated after 6 months. This procedure provides instructions on how to process a request from a client or third party who wants to send a payment by international wire transfer. International wire transfers are an alternative method for debtors or third parties who live outside of Canada, to reimburse an overpayment under the CPP or OAS programs.

An international wire transfer is an electronic, real-time transfer of funds from a debtor or a third party. A wire transfer sends the funds individually at the time of the request instead of joining them to other payments. A debtor or a third party can use an international wire transfer service to send funds electronically from a foreign country to the Department to repay a debt. International wire transfers are part of the Electronic Funds Transfer service provided by Public Services and Procurement Canada on behalf of the Receiver General for Canada. Effective immediately, the Department can only accept cheques, money orders or international wire transfers for CPP and OAS repayments in Canadian currency and issued by a Canadian bank. The Department will not accept any repayments in any other currency and will return them to the client. To mitigate the risk of late repayments, you must advise clients that live outside of Canada to make their payments by international wire transfer in Canadian currency. If this is not possible, advise the client that the Department can only accept cheques or money orders in Canadian currency issued by a Canadian bank. When a debtor or a third party requests to send an international wire transfer to repay an outstanding debt, you must immediately inform the Chief Financial Officer Branch's National Receipt and Deposit unit in the Atlantic region. The debtor or third party must be provided with the Scotiabank Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) – Payment Instructions (783 KB, PDF) Download link sheet. The instruction sheet provides the debtor's or third party's financial institution with the information required to complete a transfer of money to the Department. topic_title: Block 2—Other pension income, (superannuation, Registered Retirement Income Fund, foreign pensions, etc.) from Canadian and foreign sources
text: The gross amount of the following Canadian and foreign sources of pension income must be reported in Block 2, with no allowable deductions. If the amount reported is less than $500, contact the client to verify that it is an annual amount and not a monthly amount, unless this is what is normally reported for this income in other years. Pension income from Canadian sources The following Canadian sources of pension income are considered income for OAS purposes: Annuity payments (persons aged 65 or older may declare these payments as pension income or as interest); Disability pensions (excluding CPP and QPP); Other payments received as a result of former employment or contributions to a retirement plan; Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF); Although this income should be reported in this block ( CRA Line 11500), clients may also report this income as Other Income in block 9 ( CRA Line 13000). RTR pensions (excluding CPP and QPP); Superannuation benefits; and Survivor's pension (excluding CPP and QPP). Pension income from foreign sources The following foreign pensions are generally considered income for OAS purposes: Disability pensions Retirement pensions; Private pensions; Survivor's pension; United States Veterans Administration Disability Benefit that is non-service connected. There are 2 types of disability pensions and a client may receive both of these pensions at the same time so you may need to confirm the type before including it as income: Non-service connected (generally called Disability) is treated as the equivalent of a superannuation pension. Service-connected (generally called Compensation) is a disability pension given because of serious injuries sustained while on duty. Always review ITRDS and Cúram to determine if the client has applied for a foreign benefit through International Operations (IO). Foreign Benefit Application—Add, View, Modify, and Delete in Cúram (Action) Review ITRDS notes to determine if foreign pension rates for the client have been documented. Because Canadian benefits are administered according to Canadian laws, the client's income must be calculated based on the Canadian definition of income. All amounts reported in a foreign currency must be converted into Canadian dollars. If there is no indication that the amount reported is in a foreign currency, assume that the client has converted the amount into Canadian dollars. Go to the Foreign Income conversion section below for information and the tools available to convert the income, if required. Pension Income Splitting Bill C-52 came into force on June 22, 2007, allowing for Pension Income Splitting. This allows couples to split private pension income for the purpose of reducing their joint tax liability. When the income for the year is received from the CRA , the pension split can be identified by a deduction in Block 9 for the person transferring the amount and income of the same amount in Block 2 for the transferee. If there is a change in marital status in the current year, a lower income spouse or common-law partner may be disadvantaged if the income from the pension split is included in their income. If this happens, they may make a written request to have any pension income split that was declared to CRA excluded from the income on which their income tested benefit is calculated. This written request may be waived if certain conditions are met. topic_title: Block 3—Employment Insurance and Workers' Compensation Benefits
text: Employment Insurance (EI) EI provides income benefits to individuals who are currently unemployed through no fault of their own. The gross amount of EI benefits must be reported in Block 3, with no allowable deductions. Repayment of EI benefits Sometimes the client must repay some of their EI benefits because they were overpaid. If the repayment occurs while the client is still in receipt of benefits, the net amount will be reported on line 11900 of the CRA income and will appear in block 3. If the repayment happens after the benefits have ended, the repayment will be reported as a deduction on Line 23200 of the CRA income and will appear in block 9. Provincial Workers' Compensation benefits Provincial Workers' Compensation benefits provide income benefits to individuals who have suffered work-related injuries or occupational diseases. Provincial Workers' Compensation benefits are not taxable. However, they do get reported on the client's income tax return. The gross amount of provincial worker's compensation benefits must be reported in Block 3, with no allowable deductions. If the amount reported is less than $500, contact the client to verify that it is an annual amount, not a monthly amount. Quebec Parental Insurance Plan The Quebec Parental Insurance Plan provides financial benefits to all eligible workers residing in Quebec – salaried and self-employed taking maternity leave, paternity leave, parental leave or adoption leave. It replaces the maternity, parental or adoption benefits previously provided to Quebec parents under the federal employment insurance plan. Quebec Parental Insurance Plan benefits are taxable. The gross amount of benefits must be reported in Block 3. Contributions paid to the Quebec Parental Insurance Plan by employers are allowable deductions under Block 9—Other Income . Table 6. topic_title: Block 4—Interest and other investment income, including foreign dividends
text: The interest received on deposits in a bank, caisse populaire or credit union, and on savings bonds or mortgage receivables must be reported in Block 4. Carrying charges are an allowable deduction for this income source. They are reported on Block 9 and include the following: accounting fees paid for the recording of the investment income; fees paid for the management or safe custody of such investments (not including brokerage or transfer charges in buying or selling securities); interest paid on money borrowed to purchase the investment that produced the income; investment counsel fees; and safety deposit box charges. Interest on mortgage receivables cannot be offset by interest on mortgage payables. The interest part of the mortgage receivables is considered income. Interest earned on prepaid funeral expenses is not considered income for the person who made the payment. Interest earned in a joint bank account is considered income for the person who owns the money on deposit. If more than one person has contributed to the account, divide the interest income based on how much each person contributed to the account. If a negative amount is reported for this type of income, you must enter the amount in Block 9—Other Income . Foreign dividends are considered income. If the amount of interest or foreign dividend income is reported in foreign currency, convert the amount into Canadian dollars. If there is no indication that the amount reported is in a foreign currency, assume that the client has converted the amount into Canadian dollars. Go to the Foreign Income conversion section below for information and the tools available to convert the income, if required. Table 7. topic_title: Block 5—Taxable Canadian dividends (eligible and other than eligible) and capital gains
text: Dividends Dividends are money paid by a corporation to shareholders from its profits. A dividend is income for the year in which it is received. It is considered received on the day it is paid. All taxable dividend income must be reported. A federal dividend tax credit may be applied to the reported amount. For the dividend tax credit to be applied, a federal Income Tax and Benefit Return must be filed. Clients receiving income tested benefits with reported dividend income have their adjustments calculated automatically through the CRA . Refer to Calculating Income (Policy) for more information. Calculating Income (Policy) If the CRA income is not available, you may have to calculate the deduction manually or contact the client for further information. Refer to Functional Guidance and Procedures Interim Update Calculating Canadian Dividends and Capital Gains (PDF, 173 KB) Download link . Functional Guidance and Procedures Interim Update Calculating Canadian Dividends and Capital Gains Capital Gains Capital gains are profits made from the sale of assets and possessions. The taxable portion of capital gains must be reported in Block 5. The only allowable deduction against capital gains is a capital loss. If the loss is greater than the gains, zero must be declared for that year. This income source cannot be negative. If there is a variance between the income reported by the client and the income reported by the CRA , accept the amount of Capital Gains from the CRA feed as correct. Table 8. Net rental income is the total amount received from renting rooms, dwellings, land or any other property, less allowable deductions. If the rental income is considered business income, it will be reported in Block 8. Earnings received from family members in the form of rent or board that is reported as income for income tax purposes must also be reported as income for OAS purposes. The net amount of employment income includes the following income: salary; wages; tips and gratuities; commissions; bonuses; directors' fees; adult training allowances; net research grants; and taxable employee benefits (e.g. contributions by an employer to a medical care plan on behalf of an employee). If the client has not indicated the amount of employment income they reported is gross or net and the CRA income is not available to confirm, assume that all allowable deductions have been made and accept the amount as net. If the client has retired and an option has been processed for the retirement event, any subsequent employment income related to the retirement that is received in the payment period immediately following the previous year option, must be removed. The employment income can include the following: severance pay; vacation pay; sick leave benefits; retroactive salary adjustments; bonuses and commissions; and disposition of business assets. If you are excluding employment income as an option has been processed for this event, first confirm with the client that this income is related to the employment from which they retired. If the subsequent income is received more than a year after the last option ending, it cannot be removed from the base calendar year income and you must include it as income in the calculation of income-tested benefits. topic_title: Variances in income and tolerance levels
text: When validating income, you must check for variances and ensure that they do not exceed the nationally set levels of tolerance. A tolerance is the threshold amount of an acceptable difference in income. There are two types of variances that require further review: Accounts with a difference between the amount of income reported to the Department and the amount of the same type of income reported to the CRA for the same year. The nationally set level of tolerance for this type of variance is $101; or Accounts with a decrease in the amount of income reported in one year and the amount of income for the same type of income reported in the next consecutive year. The nationally set level of tolerance for this type of variance is $501. When a variance exceeds the level of tolerance, you must ask the client to provide an explanation if the variance cannot be resolved by reviewing the systems and information on the client's file. Some common reasons for a variance include, the client forgot to report some of their income information, or an event occurred causing a decrease in their income (e.g. an optionable event).

Entitlement to income-tested benefits (GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits) is based on income. All reconsideration requests must have an appeal record file added to the ADMS-P. For CPP accounts in ITRDS, when you activate the appeal indicator, the client’s tombstone data transfers to the ADMS-P, which automatically creates the appeal record file for reconsiderations. For CPPD, a request for reconsideration of a PRDB decision must be entered manually into the ADMS-P. For OAS accounts, you must manually create the appeal record file for an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal in the ADMS-P. You must manually add subsequent levels of appeal following reconsideration, if applicable. The ADMS-P tracks the progress of all CPP requests for reconsideration and appeal. Tracking the progress of the reconsideration or appeal ensures that a decision is made in the shortest time possible and that resources are adequately allocated to the appropriate regional offices. It also provides statistics supporting program development, resource management and forecasting. Statistics provide a reference tool for legislative amendments. Your user profile dictates which actions you can perform in the ADMS-P. If the client’s record was created using an OAS account number, IA system account number or Client ID, and a SIN is now available, do not create a new record using the client’s SIN. Instead, modify the existing record by selecting SIN at Identifier Type and enter the SIN in the Identifier Number field.

For the automatic reinstatement of a DSB or PRDB , the DOO is set as the date: the applicant stopped work if the date of recurrence of the same or a related disability is simultaneous; or of recurrence of the same or a related disability, if the recurrence took place after the date the applicant stopped work. For fast-track applications, the DOO: cannot be greater than 12 months before the Date of Application; and is set as the date the applicant stopped work, which must be the same date as the recurrence of the same or a related disability.

When setting the DOO, review the available information and consider: the reported date the applicant stopped work; whether the date the applicant stopped work was due to a medical condition; the claimed date of disability; and the date the medical information supports the medical condition became severe and prolonged.

topic_title: Criteria to use when setting a DOO Updated
text: Use the criteria below to set the correct DOO. The DOO: must be supported by the available evidence; must be on or before the Latest Possible Date of Onset; may need to be adjusted when a possible prorate date is used; cannot be before the Earliest Possible Date of Onset, which is the maximum retroactive period, and is: 15 months before the Date of Application (DOA); or 12 months before the DOA if the applicant previously received CPPD benefits within the last 5 years; must be tied to the specific CPPD benefits application in which the severe and prolonged criteria are met; cannot be set based on the receipt dates of Employment Insurance benefits only ; and can never be earlier than a previous cease decision date.

topic_title: DOO after the date of application
text: An applicant may meet the severe and prolonged criteria after the Date of Application (DOA). CPP does not prohibit granting CPPD benefits after the DOA when all other eligibility criteria are met.

topic_title: DOO results in Earnings and Contributions denial
text: If the selected DOO results in the system dropping year(s) needed for Earnings and Contributions (E & C) purposes, the SCBO will provide: an explanation that the DOO results in insufficient E & C; the years needed to calculate the latest possible date of onset; and the earliest month and year that can be used to establish the DOO to meet the E & C requirement. If you are uncertain how to proceed, submit an enquiry through the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) Internal link to obtain guidance from a Medical Adjudicator Consultant. Write a rationale for an initial decision, a reconsideration or a reassessment decision.

A rationale to support the decision must be provided once a determination is made on whether or not the applicant or beneficiary meets the definition of disabled in accordance with the legislation. The rationale may include several aspects of the adjudication process and must be persuasive, convincing and form the basis on which the decision is made. You must action the following best practices: Provide clear reasons for your decision supported by relevant evidence (e.g. applicant or beneficiary statements, medical information and employment information). At the initial and the reconsideration stage, explain how the impact was considered and factored in your decision, if applicable: medical conditions; functional limitations; work capacity ; and personal characteristics. Address conflicting information, explain and support your analysis. Ensure your reasons align with the CPP legislation, jurisprudence and relevant policy direction. Provide a logical and concise explanation of whether or not the applicant or beneficiary meets the criteria for a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit. Complete your rationale with a brief concluding statement as to whether or not the applicant or beneficiary meets the severe and prolonged criteria. Table 1. Complete the rationale using the following factors: Factors To grant, reverse and grant or continue a benefit To deny, maintain a deny decision, or cease a benefit Other actions Multiple medical conditions Explain how the combined effect of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical conditions assessed to determine if they are more likely than not regularly incapable of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation (SGO). If the determination is satisfied based on a single medical condition, state that all medical conditions were considered. Explain how the combined effect of the medical conditions does not meet the definition of disabled in accordance with the CPP legislation. N/A Personal characteristics Explain how the combined impact of the medical conditions and the personal characteristics result in the applicant or beneficiary meeting the standard of review on the balance of probabilities. Explain how the combined impact of the medical conditions and personal characteristics do not meet the definition of severe and prolonged. Personal characteristics are not sufficient on their own to entitle a person for disability. Consider the following in addition to the medical condition: age; education; work experience; and language proficiency. Severe criterion—in the absence of work activity For more information, refer to Severe Criterion—Impact of Medical Condition(s) and Functional Limitations on Work Capacity Severe Criterion—Impact of Medical Condition(s) and Functional Limitations on Work Capacity Explain how the severe criterion is met and how the functional limitations from the medical conditions are regularly preventing all types of SGO work . Explain how the severe criterion is not met and how the functional limitations from the medical conditions are not regularly preventing all types of SGO work . You must show that all aspects of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical conditions and treatments, along with resulting functional limitations, were considered and that all pertinent facts related to work capacity were included. The rationale must specify whether or not all of the information on file supports that the applicant or beneficiary has severe functional limitations associated with their medical condition(s) that prevents them from regularly pursuing all types of SGO work. Severe criterion—in the presence of work activity For more information, refer to Work capacity (regular employment, self-employment, seasonal and accommodated) . Work capacity (regular employment, self-employment, seasonal and accommodated) Explain how the severe criterion is met in the presence of work activity. The rationale must include the hours, predictability of attendance and earnings from the work activity in addition to the functional limitations from the medical conditions and personal characteristics. The Medical Adjudicator (MA) must explain how the severe criterion is not met in the presence of work activity. When work capacity is established include: work activity hours and predictability; or earnings to the rationale. When work activity is present (current and at the last possible date of onset), work capacity is measured by assessing the following in relation to the work activity: hours predictability of attendance; and earnings from the work activity. The rationale must explain the above factors of work capacity even though work capacity can be demonstrated with either work activity or earnings alone. If work capacity is established with hours, predictability of attendance and earnings, this is all that is required in the rationale. If work capacity cannot be determined with the above, further explanation of the functional limitations related to the medical conditions and personal characteristics need to be included. Prolonged criterion If there is a favourable prognosis, explain all factors that support granting or continuing of the benefit. If a determination is made that the applicant or beneficiary's medical conditions are not severe, it is not necessary to make a finding on the prolonged criterion. However, the MA must indicate in the rationale their decision to deny the benefit is based on whether or not the applicant or beneficiary meets both the severe and prolonged criterion (e.g. recognizing that the applicant or beneficiary’s medical condition may prevent them from doing any type of work at present but that they are expected to recover following treatment and, therefore, they do not satisfy the definition of severe and prolonged). N/A Late applicant provision Explain how the applicant or beneficiary: is considered disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements (i.e. the Latest Possible Date Of Onset (LPDOO)); continues to meet the "severe and prolonged" criteria since the LPDOO; is disabled at the date of adjudication; will likely be disabled in the future; and is considered incapable of pursuing any SGO. Explain why they are not considered disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements for their LPDOO. Explain whether or not the applicant or beneficiary meets the definition of "severe and prolonged" when they last met their LPDOO. Multiple applications If you are establishing a date of onset within the time period of the previous application, you must explain any significant changes supported by medical, employment or other information. If there is no change to the LPDOO, you must show that there is new significant medical and employment information in the current active application that differs from the previous application and relates to the LPDOO. If there are no changes to the LPDOO, you must submit a Business Expertise Request Tool enquiry. Business Expertise Request Tool N/A N/A Res Judicata. For more information, refer to the New Facts and Determining Jurisdiction and Res Judicata for an Application or Multiple Applications for the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability . New Facts and Determining Jurisdiction and Res Judicata for an Application or Multiple Applications for the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability N/A N/A In this case, a rationale is not written. On the Decision Summary, enter the: hearing date; current LPDOO; previous LPDOO; last decision maker; date the last decision was made; and application date. Terminally Ill Application State "The applicant's personal characteristics were not considered given the grant on the medical condition only", if applicable. For more information, refer to Terminally Ill . Terminally Ill N/A Only include the relevant medical evidence and indicate why the applicant or beneficiary was confirmed to have a terminal illness.

When the Program Support Clerk (PSC) or SCBO submits the data capture for adjudication, the system provides a complete or incomplete data capture session response. If you see the Incomplete Data Capture indicator displayed on the Client Profile screen, you will be unable to open the MQP Results or the Medical Determination fields. In these cases, you will be unable to data capture the medical determination. topic_title: Is there possible eligibility to other CPP and OAS benefits, pensions or provisions?
text: Sometimes you may determine that the deceased client was eligible for other CPP and OAS benefits, pensions or provisions, but never applied for them. If the benefit, pension or provision can be processed post-mortem, send the appropriate application or information sheets to the estate or legal representative to inform them: of possible eligibility; and of the requirement to apply within 12 months from the date of death. Qualifying benefits, pensions and provisions include the following: CPP RTR pension (the deceased contributor must have been over 70 years of age at the time of their death); CPP SVR 's pension, Children's benefits, Credit Split and Child Rearing Provision; OAS pension (the deceased individual must have been over 65 years of age at the time of their death).

An application received by the Department on or before the applicant's date of death is not considered a post-mortem application even if it is processed after the death of the applicant. An application is considered post-mortem when the Department receives it after the applicant's date of death, even if the application is signed by the individual before their death. The Department, however, deems the post-mortem application to be received on the individual's date of death. Additional information is information from an applicant, beneficiary or third party that the Department receives after a CPPD benefits eligibility decision. This information may affect an applicant's eligibility or a beneficiary's ongoing eligibility for a CPPD benefit.
When additional information is received, review the systems and the account status. CPPD Benefits Application (Scenario)

Solicited and unsolicited information are types of additional information that can be received after a decision has been made. Solicited information is information that was requested by the Department during the adjudication. This type of information can include: applicant or beneficiary statements; and medical, employer or educational reports. Unsolicited information is information that was not requested by the Department. This type of information can be submitted by the applicant, beneficiary or a third party and can include: letters from the applicant or beneficiary; letters from representatives, family members, lawyers, employers, insurance programs and other third parties; unsolicited medical documentation sent by the applicant or beneficiary, their physician or their representative; or earnings information posted to or amended on the Record of Earnings. Only in exceptional circumstances, if the additional information meets certain conditions, it may be considered as “New Facts”. For more information, Review Under New Facts (Scenario)

topic_title: Obtaining consent to request CRA information
text: The client and their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable, must provide their consent for the Department to obtain their income information from the CRA by signing one of the following forms or letters: Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP-3025) form; Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement with Statement of Income (ISP-3025B) form; Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form; Application for the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP-3550) form; Spousal Consent and Declaration GIS (ISS-0954A) letter; Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor - Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form; Application for Allowance Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3033) form; or Spousal Consent and Declaration ALW (ISS-0954B) letter.

A one-way income feed occurs when the CRA sends an income feed on its own during the renewal period. Once a client or their spouse or common-law partner is added to the CRA Lifetime List, the CRA will begin to automatically send the income data to the Department once the tax return has been assessed or reassessed by the CRA . One-way income feeds are received in the system on Wednesdays each week. If the income data is not available at the time the account is added to the CRA Lifetime List, the CRA will send the information via the one-way income feed process once it becomes available. When the CRA income data is received through the one-way income feed process, any new income data (i.e. reassessed income by the CRA ) will be sent to the Department by the CRA .
This procedure provides guidance on the CRA Lifetime List.

In February of each year, CRA switches to providing the next year's income information. As a result, the Department must also make system enhancements in advance of the upcoming renewal period so that it can start receiving income information based on the next taxation year. During this period, the receipt and processing of the electronic files and manual requests received from the CRA are temporarily delayed. For more information regarding this process, GIS—Taxation Year Change Coordination (Cyclical)

Once an income request has been submitted, the CRA will match the request based on the client's and spouse or common-law partner's personal information and perform the following two-step validation: Match the SIN sent by the Department to an account on the CRA database. Match 2 out of the following 3 data elements: surname; given name; and date of birth. If there is a match, the account is added to the CRA Lifetime List and the current year income will be provided to the Department by the CRA . Once the client or their spouse or common-law partner is on the CRA Lifetime List, the Department will receive the income information on an annual basis from the CRA as long as the client files an Income Tax and Benefit Return. When income information is received electronically from the CRA , it can be viewed in Cúram: by clicking CRA Income in the Evidence tab; or by accessing the CRA Income Data section of the CRA Interface screen. CRA Income—View and Request New Income in Cúram (Action) If the account does not pass the two-step validation criteria, the account is not added to the CRA Lifetime List. The Department will not receive any income information from the CRA and the client will need to submit a statement of income each year to renew their income-tested benefit. A CRA - Income Validation task is generated for accounts that initially do not get matched on the CRA Lifetime List. These tasks must be reviewed to perform the necessary actions to resolve any income variances or discrepancies.

A two-way income feed occurs when the Department makes a request for income and a feed is generated. Once an account is added to the CRA Lifetime List, the Department can initiate an income request at any time in Cúram for the current income year and up to 3 previous consecutive income years. Two-way income feeds are received in the system each week, generally on Thursday. A manual request for income can also be submitted to the CRA using the Request for Information for Guaranteed Income Supplement purposes (ISP-3090) form. If the income is available, the CRA will send it to the Department within one to two weeks.

The CRA Lifetime List was created to enable income information to be received annually from the CRA . In Cúram, a client is added to the CRA Lifetime List when: the GIS, ALW or ALWS Application Case is created; you send a manual request to add them to the CRA Lifetime List. topic_title: Criterion 1—There is a reasonable explanation for the delay
text: A reasonable explanation for the delay may include an exceptional or extenuating circumstance. The applicant or beneficiary had an exceptional circumstance if they experienced a medical condition that prevented them from requesting a reconsideration within the 90-day time limit. Examples may include: a physical, mental or learning limitation that prevented them from filing a reconsideration request on time; an inability to manage their own affairs during the 90-day time limit to request a reconsideration; or a serious illness. The applicant or beneficiary had an extenuating circumstance if they had an experience that was unusual, unexpected, unavoidable or beyond their control and led to the delay. Examples may include: a sudden death or serious illness in the immediate family; an important record that was destroyed or damaged by a fire or another accidental cause; a delay in obtaining information; a serious personal or family-related situation where they were away from home for an extended period of time; a mistake where they submitted the reconsideration request to another government agency; a postal service disruption; or a natural disaster. Some explanations that are generally not accepted as a reasonable explanation for the delay may include: the applicant or beneficiary had been busy with their regular everyday life (e.g. raising a family) and therefore, missed the 90-day reconsideration time limit; or the applicant or beneficiary needed the time to obtain a lawyer or was delayed because of the lawyer, advocate or representative.

topic_title: Criterion 2—There is continuing intent to request a reconsideration
text: The applicant or beneficiary demonstrates continuing intent to request a reconsideration when they communicate with the Department following a decision. Examples may include: the applicant or beneficiary maintained contact with the Department either in person, in writing or by telephone within the 90-day time limit, indicating their intent to request a reconsideration; the applicant or beneficiary called the Department seeking clarification of the decision or asking questions about the reconsideration process within the 90-day time limit; the applicant or beneficiary did not understand the process for requesting a reconsideration and obtained further evidence before requesting a reconsideration; the applicant or beneficiary sought assistance from a lawyer, advocate or representative; a third party contacted the Department on behalf of the applicant or beneficiary; or the beneficiary continued to disagree about an overpayment rather than requesting a reconsideration of the cessation or a reduction of a CPP or OAS pension, benefit or provision.

topic_title: Criterion 3—The reconsideration request has a reasonable chance of success
text: A reasonable chance of success exists when the decision to deny or cease a pension, benefit or provision is disputable, debatable or open to question. The applicant or beneficiary must provide evidence to support their reconsideration request that was not presented before the previous decision-maker. There is no reasonable chance of success if they do not provide new information to explain why the decision was incorrect.

topic_title: Criterion 4—The Minister or another party would not experience prejudice caused by allowing a longer period to make the request
text: Normally, it is unlikely that prejudice to the Minister or another party will be significant in determining whether to allow an extension. If there has been a time lapse of months or years, there may be prejudice to the Minister or another party, as the relevant evidence to reconsider the decision could no longer be available.

topic_title: If the applicant or beneficiary requests an appeal to the SST
text: If the applicant or beneficiary submits additional information to the Social Security Tribunal—General Division ( SST —GD) that allows the Minister to extend the 90-day reconsideration time limit, an Agreement Offer can be made. If the applicant and the SST —GD accept the Agreement Offer, forward the file for a reconsideration. If the applicant or beneficiary or the SST —GD do not accept the Agreement Offer, the appeal continues. Prepare a change of position submission. If the SST —GD maintains the decision to not allow the extension of the 90-day time limit to request a reconsideration, the applicant or beneficiary may request an appeal for this decision to the Social Security Tribunal—Appeal Division ( SST —AD). If the SST —GD allows the extension of the 90-day time limit to request a reconsideration, the Minister can request an appeal of the decision to the SST —AD. If the Minister does not request an appeal for the decision, forward the file to reconsideration. This document is used to present the Minister's case if the applicant or beneficiary requests an appeal regarding the extension decision to the Social Security Tribunal—General Division ( SST —GD). Appeals If the 90-day reconsideration time limit extension is not allowed, the applicant or beneficiary can request an appeal to the SST —GD. If the SST —GD determines that the Minister fairly assessed the criteria for an extension, the appeal will be dismissed and the file will not proceed to reconsideration. If the applicant or beneficiary does not request an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal—Appeal Division ( SST —AD), the decision on eligibility becomes final. If the SST —GD determines the Minister did not fairly assess the criteria for an extension of the reconsideration time limit and allows the extension, the Minister must reconsider the eligibility decision or request an appeal regarding the SST —GD decision to the SST —AD.

These procedures provide guidance on assessing and processing a request to extend the 90-day reconsideration time limit after a decision on eligibility or entitlement for any pension, benefit and provision under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act .

An applicant or beneficiary, or a third party acting on their behalf, has the right to request a reconsideration of a decision and must do so within 90 days of being notified of the decision. The reconsideration request must be made in writing or via the individual's My Service Canada Account. To allow for mailing delays, the 90-day time limit for requesting a reconsideration begins 10 calendar days after the date of the decision letter or the Notice of Entitlement letter. The Department has the discretionary authority to accept reconsideration requests that are received beyond the 90-day time limit. The CPP and OAS regulations set out the criteria that are used for assessing a request to extend the 90-day time limit. If a reconsideration request is received beyond the 90-day time limit without a request for an extension or an explanation for the delay, a letter is sent to the applicant or beneficiary. This letter asks them to provide information supporting the assessment criteria for extending the 90-day time limit to request a reconsideration. It also informs them that their file will remain closed until further information is received. For more information, refer to: Reconsideration (Policy) ; or Reconsideration (Policy) Reconsideration (Scenario) . Reconsideration (Scenario) Criteria for accepting a reconsideration request after the 90-day time limit If the reconsideration request is received after the 90-day time limit but within 365 days following the decision, criteria 1 and 2 must be met for the request to be accepted. If a late reconsideration request is received more than 365 days after the decision, criteria 3 and 4 must be met in addition to criteria 1 and 2. If a late reconsideration request is received with a subsequent application or a request for a New Facts review, all 4 criteria must be met regardless of when it is received.

Appropriate file development is a principle of effective adjudication and demonstrates careful and diligent effort to obtain information. When required, file development helps make the best decision at the earliest level of adjudication. When an outstanding information gap impedes a reasonable medical decision on eligibility, it is important to identify what specific information is needed and who is the best information source. Equal attention must also be given to the time period in which the outstanding information gap exists. For complex applications, creating a timeline is recommended to organize and summarize available information. This includes documenting the order and significance of events. Determine the right information It is important to request the right information to resolve outstanding information gaps that are relevant to the decision. This likely involves details regarding the medical conditions, work capacity and personal characteristics and whether the impairments are likely to be prolonged. Only request information that is not present on the application. Unless an update is required, do not send a duplicate request for information that is present on the application. Consider the following topics to focus the file development request: Topic: Medical conditions Topic: Medical conditions Topic: Work capacity and personal characteristics Topic: Work capacity and personal characteristics Topic: Prolonged Topic: Prolonged Topic Considerations Medical conditions. Staging Symptoms Prognosis Diagnostic evidence Limitations on functional capacity Treatment outcomes and side effects Medical statements Trajectory (e.g. episodic, recurrent) Duration since onset of symptoms Types of medical providers Combined effect of multiple medical conditions Topic Considerations Work capacity and personal characteristics. Previous and current work experience including hours worked and responsibilities Hours, predictability and income Self-employment Skills Gaps in employment Work trials and results Type of work Work accommodations Education and training Participation in school or retraining Participation in volunteer activities Language proficiency Age Topic Considerations Prolonged. Staging Progressive nature of medical conditions Expected treatment outcomes Unsuccessful treatments Prognosis Determine the best information source It is important to carefully consider the available sources of information in relation to the facts of the case. This will help determine which source or sources are most likely to provide strong and relevant evidence to fill any outstanding information gaps or clarify conflicting information. For more information, refer to Consent to collect personal information section of the Consent for Service Canada to Collect Personal Information (ISP-2502) form. Determine the right time period When seeking additional information to resolve outstanding information gaps, consider the time period in which the information gap exists. Assess the following: Is the medical information current or relevant to the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO), valid earnings after the LPDOO or incapacity provision? Is the date the applicant stopped working aligned with the applicant's statements and medical information? Is information needed in relation to a potential date of onset, date the applicant stopped working, claim date, LPDOO or date of application? Are there unexplained earnings after the date the applicant stopped working or the disability claim date?

text: Contact that does not involve requesting additional information to address outstanding information gaps or inconsistencies relevant to the decision is not considered file development. If the definition for file development is not met, any information gathered will be recorded as appropriate. Contact that is not considered file development includes the following: Requests by PSCs for missing forms or instances where the application is filled out incorrectly or is incomplete and therefore does not meet the service standards. Calls to: improve the client experience; provide general program information; discuss application processing timeframes; inform the applicant about expectations and explain eligibility requirements; discuss the rationale behind decisions made regarding their application; or explain expectations for the applicant's next steps when a decision has been made. These calls are not considered file development on their own. However, these calls may lead to file development if the applicant reveals additional information that is relevant to the decision.

Documenting file development is an essential step in the adjudication process. Consistent documentation at all levels of an application provides the Department with reliable, complete and timely data. When requesting additional information by phone, the documentation is completed following the call. When requesting additional information by letter, the documentation is completed when the letter is prepared. topic_title: Factors to consider when determining the need for medical file development
text: When determining the issues during medical adjudication, the following factors can assist you in weighing and determining the strength of evidence on file and identifying if there are outstanding information gaps that need file development. What is the applicant's primary medical condition? Additional information may be required if: the applicant has a condition with ill-defined functional impairment; the prognosis lacks objective evidence to quantify the applicant's capacity to work; and subjective evidence dominates. Gathering more information may provide a clearer measure of the applicant's capacity to work (e.g. dates and reasons for clinic visits). If the applicant has a condition where the clinical course and degree of functional impairment are typically well defined, additional information is likely not required to address this factor. For example, a late-stage progressive disease where the medical information clearly supports the determination of work capacity or the degree of impairment. Does the applicant have multiple medical conditions? Often, the main medical condition alone is not disabling, but when combined with multiple medical conditions, may result in disability. When additional medical conditions are identified with limited information provided in the medical report, in the enclosures or by the applicant, file development may be required to clarify the cumulative impact of all the medical conditions. Did the applicant and medical provider present consistent evidence regarding functional limitations and capacity for work? Consistent evidence from the applicant and licensed medical provider describing functional abilities or limitations provides strong support for the applicant's capacity to work. Additional information is likely not required to address this factor as they are part of the application for CPPD benefits. Are the treatment outcomes unknown? The ongoing status may be unknown when treatments are pending, such as when: the applicant is undergoing medication trials; the medical report is completed early in the treatment plan; the applicant is undergoing procedures (e.g. surgery); the applicant is hospitalized at the time of adjudication; or ongoing medical follow-up is required. File development may provide current evidence regarding the applicant's capacity to work in response to treatment and can address the temporary versus indefinite nature of functional impairment. Does the applicant have a pending appointment, follow up or outstanding referral? Additional reports resulting from medical follow-ups and consultations can provide evidence regarding the diagnosis, prognosis, treatment outcomes and functional limitations. These reports can help fill outstanding information gaps if they are available to request at the time of adjudication. Is there conflicting medical evidence? Conflicting medical evidence refers to inconsistencies between medical professionals regarding the same time period. In this context, the evidence is not simply an omission but rather an obvious inconsistency. If conflicting medical evidence is present and relevant to the decision, file development may provide a clearer understanding of the applicant's situation. Do evidence-based prognostic statements align with the medical information on file? Evidence-based means that the medical information in the file supports the prognosis. The prognosis aligns with the medical information. The prognosis should not be solely based on a medical provider's assertion that the disability is severe and prolonged without corresponding medical documentation recorded on the medical report, narrative report or enclosures. Statements of disability without supporting evidence of what findings led to that conclusion do not constitute evidence of disability. If this occurs, file development is likely needed to address outstanding information gaps or reconcile conflicting information. For example, a specialist may provide a second opinion in cases where there are conflicting medical statements. A recent report may provide an accurate picture of the applicant's abilities. What is the applicant's job? Job requirements are different for each position. Jobs with more flexibility are more likely to require additional information from the employer to fill any gaps in employment. If the applicant is self-employed, Assess the Client's Self-Employment Work Capacity (Action) If the applicant's employment is seasonal, additional information may be needed to determine patterns, timelines and potential return to work plans. This may include whether there is a job waiting or to show a decline in earnings over the years. Assess Self-Reported Seasonal Employment at Reassessment (Action) Is the applicant working or is there a return to work plan? Information about work activity is required to establish work capacity. You may consider developing a file for clear information regarding return to work plans. These plans provide strong evidence for decision making. Severe Criterion—Work Capacity (Regular Employment, Self-Employment, Seasonal and Accommodated) (Scenario) Are earnings present since the date the applicant stopped working or the disability claim date? When earnings are present and not explained on the application, file development is likely needed to help determine whether the earnings provide evidence of capacity to work. What is the reason the applicant stopped working? If the applicant stopped working for a non-medical reason, additional information may be required to clarify whether there is a medical reason for a continuing inability to work. What is the timeframe between the reported last date worked, the disability claim date and the date of application? If information is missing or conflicting, combined with the length of time since the applicant felt they could no longer work because of their medical condition or last day worked, the more likely file development will be required. Clear information allows the MA to consider the facts of the case and contributes to fair decision making. Has the applicant attended school or participated in volunteer activity since stopping work? Information may be needed to determine if the applicant's attendance at school or if volunteer activity demonstrates work capacity. For more information, Severe Criterion—Assess Educational and Volunteer Activities (Action) Is there information missing regarding the applicant's personal characteristics? File development may be required if there are outstanding questions which prevent appropriate consideration of the personal characteristics. Assess the Impact of Personal Characteristics (Action) Is the Late Applicant Provision applied? When the Late Applicant Provision is applied, it is more likely that file development will be required to determine eligibility for a CPPD benefit because of the retrospective assessment. However, if the information on file supports that the applicant is not disabled at any point between their Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) to the present, file development is likely not needed and a decision can be made. Closing outstanding information gaps can lead to the best decision for the applicant at the earliest possible time. Valid earnings after the LPDOO must be considered to determine work capacity. What is the adjudication level? The need for file development may increase with the level of adjudication as the issues may change during the lifecycle of the application. File development is completed for the current decision and is not intended to address potential future issues. Reconsideration, appeal and reassessment decisions may not need file development if the information is current or if sufficient relevant evidence is present to address the issues and support a decision or an agreement offer. Collection and Use of Personal Information (Policy) What is the age of the application? The longer the time between the application receipt date and adjudication, the greater the need for file development.

Eligibility for CPPD benefits involves both non-medical and medical factors. Through the adjudication process, outstanding information gaps may be identified. Once resolved, the information supports a reasonable determination of eligibility for CPPD benefits. File development is the method for attempting to resolve these outstanding information gaps. There may be situations when file development occurs, but additional information is not obtained within the allotted timeframes. If the requested information is not received, make a decision based on the information available without additional file development. Only develop a file for information necessary for the decision. Developing a file when it is not necessary will delay service to applicants and require time that would otherwise be directed to serving another applicant. File development for information that is beyond what is necessary for the decision can place an additional burden on third parties who respond to the file development request. Non-medical file development During the non-medical assessment of the earnings and contributions criteria, the SCBO applies CPPD guidance to obtain the best latest possible date of onset for the applicant. This involves considering all available provisions and seeking all relevant earnings information. CPPD Earnings and Contributions Criteria (Scenario) Medical file development Medical adjudication involves a review of the information and weighing all relevant factors of the case before making a decision on an application. The MA applies their medical knowledge and CPPD guidance to determine: if there is evidence on file to allow for a reasonable eligibility determination; or if file development is needed to address the relevant issues. There is no single factor that leads to file development. To determine when file development is appropriate, consider all relevant factors. Individual pieces of information may not be sufficient to predict the need for file development when taken in isolation. The interaction of all the relevant information on file must be considered concurrently. [[ARTICLE-KA-05073]] (Snippet 26.0 content. Do not modify or delete. File development by phone call or by letter are 2 methods of requesting information. The type of information needed impacts the method of file development. The phone call can be regarding: functional limitations; medical conditions; treatment and outcomes; medical providers seen; hospital admissions; or work activity, including participation in education or volunteer activities. Letter Letters provide written documentation of the reason for the request and the type of information requested. File development by letter should be reserved for, but is not limited to, the following situations: The applicant indicated on the application not to contact them by phone. You are unable to reach the applicant by phone. Documentary evidence is required.
