Roles and responsibilities After the Program Support Clerk (PSC) prepares the complete application, the CPPD adjudication process requires SCBO s and Medical Adjudicators (MAs) to assess and determine the following: The SCBO assesses and determines whether an applicant meets or continues to meet the earnings and contributions criteria necessary to qualify for benefits. The MA assesses and determines whether an applicant meets or continues to meet the medical criteria necessary to qualify for benefits. Definition of file development File development is defined as the process of requesting information or documentation that is not included on the application forms. File development can be requested to resolve outstanding information gaps or when inconsistencies are identified before a decision can be made. Outstanding information gaps are areas where missing information could affect the decision on the applicant's eligibility for CPPD benefits. This includes information needed to select a date of onset or to explore applicable provisions. The decision to develop a file is made individually for each case based on the specific details and missing information. File development must also be relevant to the application to ensure fair and accurate judgment. If you require assistance after following this guidance, send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) Internal link . Business Expertise Request Tool Evidence for review and standard of proof for medical adjudication CPPD benefits application forms request specific information from both the applicant and the medical provider. This information should supply enough evidence to support an assessment and determination of eligibility. However, there may be situations when the information supplied by the applicant or medical provider is insufficient. To determine an applicant's eligibility, the civil standard of proof is applied. Based on the balance of probabilities, this standard is satisfied when it is established that the applicant is either more likely than not disabled or is not disabled. At Step 2 of the 5-step medical adjudication process, a decision is made regarding the need for additional information based on the documentation submitted by the applicant and their medical provider. When outstanding information gaps are present, file development occurs at Step 2. It is important to note that the satisfied on the balance of probabilities standard is not applied at this step but rather applied later at Step 4. For more information, refer to Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) and the Step 2—Determine the issues and Step 4—Make a medical decision sections of Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) Medical Adjudication (Scenario)

text: The invoice is processed according to its service date. topic_title: Licensed professionals who can provide medical documentation
text: The Department pays invoices for medical reports and medical developments completed by a licensed physician or nurse practitioner (NP) in support of an applicant's application or claim of incapacity, or to determine continued eligibility for a beneficiary. Medical evidence can be accepted from a registered nurse (RN) when the applicant or beneficiary resides in a geographically isolated area. Medical Evidence Completed by Nurse Practitioners and Registered Nurses (Policy) Chiropractors, psychologists, physiotherapists, and optometrists can also be compensated (this is not an exhaustive list). The medical documentation may not be sufficient when received from these allied healthcare professionals. Medical documentation from a licensed physician, NP, or RN, may still be required when the applicant or beneficiary resides in a geographically isolated area. The physician's registration and licensing status can be verified by searching their name on the registrant directory in their province of employment. The NP or RN registration and licensing status can be verified by searching their name on the website of their respective provincial regulatory body.

Age is considered in terms of how it can impact an applicant's ability to recover from an injury or illness, sustain work or retrain for alternate employment. Consider the following elements: the applicant's age when the medical condition began; the applicant's age at which the medical condition began to significantly deteriorate; if there has been a pattern of an increasing number of medical conditions over time; if there has been a pattern of increasing inability to function related to age, disability and work; the length of time the applicant has been in the workforce; and whether the combination of the present age and medical condition result in a significant decrease in their residual capacity for any substantially gainful work. For the Impact of Age on Employability table, Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy)

The analysis of this factor helps determine the potential impact of the applicant's education on their employability, including the ability to retrain. Formal education completed in the distant past may not be relevant in terms of current employability. More weight should be given to education, training and knowledge used in the applicant's more recent work. Consideration must also be given to the medical conditions, treatment and any cognitive or functional limitations and their impact on the applicant's ability to retrain. Consider the following elements: the applicant's level of education; any physical and cognitive functional limitations related to the medical condition that may affect the ability to retrain; any other work-related skills that have been acquired; if their skills would support the capacity for any work now; and if upgrading their skills would result in the ability to pursue regular gainful work. For the Impact of Education on Employability table, Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy)

A greater proficiency in English, French or both increases the employment opportunities available to individuals. However, limited language proficiency cannot be the only personal characteristic used to grant a disability benefit. The medical adjudicator considers whether the applicant's language proficiency has impacted their ability to work in the past and whether it could affect their ability to obtain alternate work or participate in retraining. For the Language Proficiency Guide, Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy)

Although socio-economic factors affect groups or populations living in regions or provinces or the country as a whole and may constitute a barrier to work, they are not to be considered in the determination of disability eligibility. These are conditions that exist in society that are outside the context of the individual with the disability: regional unemployment rates; local access to specific jobs; types of occupations offered by regional industries; and occupational skills needed for those industries.
Assess the impact of personal characteristics in the determination of the severe and prolonged criterion for CPPD benefits.

If a holistic assessment is required, you will include how the personal characteristics were considered in the assessment of severe and prolonged disability in the context of the whole person. For more information Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy) For applicants who are engaged in paid work and found to be demonstrating work capacity, a holistic assessment may not need to occur. For the rationale requirements, Severe Criterion—Work Capacity (Regular Employment, Self-Employment, Seasonal and Accommodated) (Scenario) Additionally, a holistic assessment does not occur for those applicants with a terminal illness that are granted solely on their medical condition. In this case, you may include the following statement in place of the assessment described below: "The applicant's personal characteristics were not considered as they were granted on medical condition only." When conducting a holistic assessment, your documentation must include how the applicant's personal characteristics do or do not impact their capacity for regular gainful work. You will document your assessment on the appropriate template. Personal characteristics, factors unique to a particular applicant that directly affect their ability to pursue any substantially gainful occupation, are considered when making a disability eligibility decision. Personal characteristics including age, education, work experience and language proficiency, on their own, are not sufficient to entitle an applicant or beneficiary to a disability pension. These personal characteristics are considered in combination with the medical condition and evaluated for impact on the applicant in the same way a medical condition is evaluated.

An applicant's work history and life experience is relevant as it provides information regarding transferable skills that could enhance their ability to pursue regular gainful work. Variation in work experience indicates a capability of adjusting to other work. In addition, persons with transferable skills generally have an advantage over low skilled workers in the labour market. Consider the following elements: the reason the applicant stopped working: e.g. medical condition, illness, care of a family member, shortage of work or contract end, maternity or paternity, dismissed or quit, lay off, company closure, etc.; whether the applicant has always worked for the same employer or had multiple employers; duration working with the employer or employers(s); the nature of the previous occupation; what the physical and cognitive demands were of the last job held; the applicant's past pattern regarding the type of work (regular or seasonal, contract, casual, etc.); whether the medical condition limited the applicant to part-time work; if the applicant was working in an accommodated workplace that provided specialized equipment, access for persons with disability, etc.; if there are gaps in the record of earnings or work history; whether there has been a decline in earnings that can be related to the medical condition; whether or not the evidence supports that the applicant can do their current job or a job they have done in the past; whether the evidence supports the capacity for regular gainful work suited to their education and work experience; and any attempts to return to work and the outcome. For the Work Experience Guide, Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy)

A compromise settlement offer is an agreement between a debtor and Service Canada to finalize a debt by accepting a partial payment of the debt as full repayment. A debtor or their representative must request a compromise settlement offer in writing. They must give the reason for the request and details of the proposal. All requests for a compromise settlement are forwarded to the Collections Litigations and Advisory Services section of Canada Revenue Agency. The Collections Litigations and Advisory Services is the delegated authority to negotiate and accept such requests. After a compromise settlement offer is accepted, the balance owing on the debt is permanently written off from the accounts receivable records, and the debtor is released from any obligation to pay the remaining balance. For more information, refer to the policy Overpayments—Recovery and Collection

A Federal Court certificate is a legal document registered with the Federal Court of Canada to enforce the recovery of an outstanding debt. This certificate allows for the: seizure and sale of goods and possessions; placement of a lien; sale of real property. Recovery of an overpayment by a Federal Court certificate is only initiated on inactive accounts after the debtor has been notified. If the debtor claims undue hardship during the process of debt recovery, the recovery action continues. The recovery action does not, on its own, constitute an undue hardship. A Federal Court certificate is not commonly used. It is considered an exception to normal recovery methods for overpayments over $250. Any decision to proceed with a Federal Court certificate must be referred to CRA Collection Services, who are the delegated authority to request Federal Court certificates. CRA Collection Services only consider using a certificate if normal recovery methods are unsuccessful and they have obtained information to show that: the debtor is capable of repaying—in which case, a certificate can be used for the immediate recovery of the overpayment; or the debtor is currently incapable of repaying—in which case, a certificate can be used to protect the overpayment for future recovery. For more information, refer to the policy Overpayments—Recovery and Collection

A garnishment is a legal process where the debtor's property, credit or salary is taken to reimburse a debt. Example A garnishment can occur when person A has a CPP or OAS overpayment and person B owes money to person A. If Service Canada is notified that person A will receive money from person B, the Minister can garnishee the money in whole or partially from person B to apply against person A's overpayment. Garnishment is only considered for overpayments on inactive accounts when the usual recovery methods are unsuccessful. Service Canada can suggest a garnishment for an overpayment on an inactive account. However, only CRA Collection Services are authorized to decide to proceed with a garnishment or not. The debtor must be notified before a garnishment begins. If the debtor claims undue hardship during the garnishment process, the action must be suspended until the debtor's claim is assessed. A garnishment action is only withdrawn when the debtor's undue hardship claim has been substantiated. For more information, refer to the policy Overpayments—Recovery and Collection

This procedure provides guidance on how to validate a client's marital status when they indicate their legal marriage ended in divorce or legal annulment.

Determine if documentary evidence of the divorce or annulment is required. Refer to Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) . If yes , go to Step 2 . Step 2 If no , continue processing the application or correspondence using divorced or single as the client's marital status, as applicable. Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) Review the client's account in the systems to determine if evidence was provided to confirm the divorce or annulment. Refer to ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) . If yes and the evidence was previously validated, continue processing the application or correspondence using divorced or single as the client's marital status, as applicable. If new documentary evidence was received to support the divorce or annulment, go to Step 7 . Step 7 If no or there is a discrepancy, go to Step 3 . Step 3 ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) If the client does not provided evidence of a divorce or of an annulment, or if there is insufficient proof or a discrepancy between the declared marital status and the evidence, send the following letters. For CPP, send one of the following letters: Development - Request for more information - General (ISS-6203) letter; or Development - Marital Status (ISS-6182) letter. For OAS, send the OAS, More information/docs needed, send questionnaires, lists of documents, etc (ISS-8583) letter. Refer to Correspondence—Create, Update, and Check Status in Cúram (Action) . Step 6 If no , proceed as follows: Refer to the procedure related to the application or correspondence you are processing for the appropriate next steps (e.g. deny the application, suspend benefits, refer to the Integrity Services Branch). The term "Legal marriage dissolution" refers to the termination of a legal marriage between 2 people by either divorce or annulment. For more information, Defining Marital Status (Policy) Documentary evidence may be required to support a client's marital status when: the marital status impacts the eligibility or entitlement to a CPP or OAS pension, benefit or provision for an initial benefit; there is a marital status change on an existing benefit; there is a difference in the information recorded for different programs (i.e. CPP, OAS, International Operations (IO)); or there is a difference between the documentation on file and the documentation in the systems. When a client submits the appropriate documentation to establish the marital status in one program area (CPP, OAS or IO), it is also accepted for the other program areas. Applicants with a My Service Canada Account (MSCA) have the option to upload documents online in certain situations. For CPP, applicants can upload documents using the Document Upload Solution service in MSCA to support their: applications for CPPD benefits, DTH benefit, SVR pension and Child(ren)'s benefits; and reconsideration requests (CPPD only). For OAS, applicants can upload documents using the Client Portal accessed through MSCA to support their: applications; reconsideration requests; and changes to life events (e.g. marital relationship, income). For more information about uploading documents, refer to: Document Upload Solution (Scenario) Document Upload Solution (Scenario) Introduction to the Client Portal (Knowledge) Introduction to the Client Portal (Knowledge) If a divorce has been initiated and one party dies before the divorce is finalized, the marriage is effectively ended by the death. The client may be considered a surviving spouse or common-law partner. For information regarding documentation required to support a legal marriage dissolution, Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) Validating Documentary Evidence When validating the documentary evidence received, ensure that: it is acceptable proof of the divorce or annulment. Refer to Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) ; Documentary Evidence—Marital Status (Policy) the document is legible; the document does not appear to be altered in any way; and the details of the document support the information provided by the client, such as the: names of the individuals; and date of the divorce or annulment. Documentary evidence in a foreign language For the purpose of administering CPP and OAS benefits, you may need to have foreign documents translated. However, translation is not required when the documents received are: translated by a Canadian, provincial or territorial government; or translated by foreign missions (e.g. embassies, consulates, High Commissions), Government departments and certified translators. You do not have to translate documents provided in a foreign language if: the material is not relevant to the consideration of the application or the ongoing receipt of benefits; or the relevant details are provided by the foreign agency. For more information, Translation (Action)

topic_title: Recovery of the Death benefit top-up amount
text: Some situations can occur after the Death ( DTH ) benefit is paid that can result in an overpayment. As of January 1, 2019, the DTH benefit includes a flat-rate amount for all deceased contributors who meet the Minimum Qualifying Period. In addition, as of January 1, 2025 some deceased contributors may meet the criteria for a top-up amount. When the DTH benefit payment includes both the flat rate and top-up amounts, and a subsequent SVR pension application or post-mortem RTR pension is received and approved, the deceased contributor no longer meets the eligibility criteria for the top-up amount. The top-up amount is considered an overpayment on the DTH benefit amount, but the deceased contributor is not the debtor. The overpayment must be recovered from the DTH benefit payee, regardless of whether the payee is an estate, administrator, or third party (e.g. an individual or institution responsible for funeral expenses, a survivor or next of kin). When the Department receives a notification of the death of a debtor, you must make every effort to collect any debt owing on their account from the estate by: contacting the deceased debtor's representative to obtain details of the estate administration; informing them the Department has a claim against the estate and request repayment; and recovering from any CPP or OAS benefit entitlement owing to the deceased debtor, including the Death ( DTH ) benefit when it is payable to the estate. If the representative is unknown , you must send the appropriate letter to the estate of the deceased debtor at their last known address. You must make every effort to collect the debt from the estate. If payments were issued after death, you must attempt to reduce the amount owing on the account by: initiating a charge back to the financial institution; and/or intercepting payments in the Standard Payment System. You cannot intercept outstanding benefit payments for the month of death and apply them to the overpayment. However, if the estate returns the payment for the month of death, it can be applied towards the overpayment. You cannot solicit recovery of a deceased debtor's overpayment from benefits paid to a survivor (e.g. ALWS benefit or SVR pension). However, if the survivor (e.g. surviving spouse or child) voluntarily offers to pay back the overpayment, you can accept it. For more information, Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) Recovery from a Death benefit You can only recover an overpayment from a DTH benefit if: an application for a DTH benefit has been received from the deceased's estate; and the payment is owed to the deceased's estate. You cannot recover a deceased debtor's overpayment from a DTH benefit when it is payable to a third party (e.g. an individual or institution responsible for funeral expenses, a survivor or next of kin). You must immediately notify the estate of any overpayment on the deceased's account. The Department cannot collect the overpayment after the assets of the estate have been dispersed and the estate account is closed, except in cases of fraud or misrepresentation. The overpayment on a deceased debtor's account can be partially or fully remitted in the following situations when all conditions listed in each situation are met: Situation 1 No estate exists; The individual responsible for the deceased's financial affairs submits a written statement stating that the individual died without a will and indicates there are insufficient funds to repay the debt; and There are no other means to recover the debt. Situation 2 An estate exists and is not closed; The executor provides a written statement indicating: the deceased debtor's assets have been dispersed according to the terms of the will and that there are no funds available to repay the debt; whether or not the estate is probated; a description of the assets and claims against the assets, if not probated; and There are no other means to recover the debt. This procedure provides guidance on how to determine when to send a foreign benefit application to an individual.

Foreign benefits Individuals may be eligible for benefits from another country if they have lived or worked in that country. They may also be eligible if they are the surviving spouse or common-law partner of someone who lived or worked in another country. A foreign benefit is any benefit paid by the social security administration of a country other than Canada. Benefits from other countries are comparable to Canada's social security benefits and include: retirement old age disability death survivor Many countries have minimum requirements regarding contributions or residence for an individual to qualify for benefits. If the minimum requirements are not met, an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) may help an individual qualify for a foreign benefit. If an individual resides in Canada and wants to apply for a benefit from another country where they lived or worked, they must complete a foreign benefits application form. Most countries with an agreement with Canada have their own unique foreign benefits application form. These forms are available in English, French and in the language of the particular country, if applicable. The applicant completes the form and sends it to International Operations (IO) where it is reviewed for completeness. IO then forwards the form to the other country, along with all supporting documentation and information. When to send a foreign benefit application to an applicant A foreign benefits application form must be sent to an individual that has requested an application, an applicant or the surviving spouse or common-law partner of an individual who has indicated on their Canadian benefits application that they have lived or worked in a country with which Canada has an ISSA. The applicant can indicate periods of residence and employment in foreign countries on Canadian applications for: ALW benefit ALWS benefit CPP Death benefit CPPD benefits CPP RTR pension CPP SVR pension OAS pension New versions of paper and online applications can provide applicants with information and a website link to investigate their eligibility or possible entitlement to benefits from another country. You no longer need to send a foreign benefit application to the client when they apply using the following forms: Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151) form; and Terminal Illness Application Kit for Disability Benefits under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530A) form. If the client submits any other versions of the form, you must determine the correct foreign benefits application form and send it to them. If the client has indicated that they lived or worked in the United States and has not already requested or applied for United States benefits, you must notify the IO-Atlantic (ATL) region. The IO-ATL region will communicate with the client and send a foreign benefit application to the United States, if applicable. Interim Application form You must only send the applicant a Foreign Benefits under an Agreement on Social Security, Interim Application for (ISP-5005) form when the foreign benefit application form for their country is not available online.

topic_title: Applying for a benefit and claiming incapacity
text: You must obtain a Declaration of Incapacity - Physician’s Report (ISP1800) form when an applicant or their representative claims they filed an application late because of incapacity. You must also obtain a declaration form if you become aware of potential incapacity at any point during the adjudication process. If the applicant indicates financial hardship during the processing of the application, you must process the benefit or provision and, if necessary, adjust the effective date after a determination of incapacity. A Medical Adjudicator (MA) has the delegated authority to determine if they can apply the incapacity provision to the application for benefits. You must know the conditions for consideration under the incapacity provision when applicants or their representatives are unaware of them. To identify applications that warrant consideration under the incapacity provision, ask the following questions: Is there any indication of a medical condition or information related to a claim of incapacity (e.g. advanced dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, severe brain decease or head injury, severe psychiatric illnesses or a comatose state)? Was the applicant unable to participate in the process of their application? Is there a completed ISP1800 form? Has the applicant or their representative specifically requested a review under the incapacity provision? If you answer no to all of the questions above, you cannot consider a medical determination of incapacity. If you answer yes to any of the questions above, you must action a medical determination of incapacity.

topic_title: Deemed date of receipt for an application due to incapacity
text: An MA must provide a deemed date of receipt for the application after they establish incapacity. You can then process the application by using the deemed date of receipt instead of the actual received date of the application. For more information, refer to the appropriate policy under the Program Fundamentals menu. (KA-02834 Snippet 17.0 content. Do not modify or delete.) When an individual files their application late due to incapacity, the incapacity provision allows for the application to be deemed to have been received earlier. The deemed date of an application is the later of: the month before the earliest month when the benefit could have begun; or the month when the latest period of continuous incapacity began. Consult the following examples: Examples Deemed data of receipt Situation Example 1 The deemed date of receipt is earlier than the earliest eligibility date. Mr. Bernard became totally incapacitated in May 2014 as a result of a car accident. He turned 65 in January 2016. An application for an OAS pension is completed on his behalf in May 2017 and includes an ISP1800 form . The file is forwarded to an MA for review. The MA determines that Mr. Bernard was indeed incapacitated in May 2014 and returns the file for processing. Because the date of incapacity is earlier than Mr. Bernard's 65th birthday, the deemed date of receipt is January 2016. As a result, you must use this date, and not May 2017 , to calculate the entitlement. In addition, if all legislative requirements are met, the effective date can be as early as February 2016, the month following Mr. Bernard's 65th birthday. Example 2 The deemed date of receipt is more than 11 months after the earliest eligibility date. Mrs. Chartrand turned 65 in April 2014. In October 2015, she suffered a severe stroke that le ft her totally incapacitated as of that month. An application for an RTR pension i s filed on her behalf in March 2016 and includes an ISP1800 form . The file is forwarded to an MA for review. The MA determines that Mrs. Chartrand was indeed incapacitated in October 2015 and returns the file for processing. As a result, you must use October 2015, and not March 2016, to calculate the entitlement. In addition, i f all legislative requirements are met, the effective date for benefits can be as early as November 2014. This effective date is based on 11 months retroactively from the deemed date of receipt of October 2015.

Incapacity means that a person who is or was incapable of forming or expressing an intention to complete an application. The incapacity provision, as prescribed under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act , protects people who are incapable of forming or expressing an intention to apply for benefits or provisions. Incapacity is often associated with severe psychiatric illnesses, brain disease or physical injury, which can result in a long-term stay in an institution. You must consider an application under the incapacity provision i f: the applicant has regained capacity after indicating on their application that they were incapacitated; and the applicant has submitted their application within the required timeframe: one month of regaining capacity, if the period of incapacity was less than 30 days; the number of days equal to the number of days the person was incapacitated, if the period was less than one year; or one year, if the period of incapacity was greater than one year. The MA must deem the application to be received the later of: the start of the period of incapacity; or the month before the benefit could have started. Example Mr. Brown became incapacitated as a result of a severe head injury in November 2015, 4 months after his 65th birthday in July 2015. After extensive treatment, he has recovered to the point of having regained capacity by December 2017. He submits an application for an OAS pension in March 2018, with a note explaining his prior incapacity. An ISP1800 form is sent to Mr. Brown for completion. When it is returned to Service Canada, the complete file is sent to an MA for review. The MA determines that Mr. Brown was indeed incapacitated from November 2015 to December 2017 and returns the file for processing. Because Service Canada received the application within the prescribed timeframe for consideration under the incapacity provision, the deemed date of receipt is November 2015. You must use November 2015, and not March 2018, to calculate the entitlement. In addition, if all legislative requirements are met, the effective date can be as early as August 2015, the month following Mr. Brown's 65th birthday.

text: If an incarcerated client submits a request to cancel their OAS pension and/or GIS , or to withdraw their OAS pension application, process the request as usual. If granted, the cancellation or withdrawal may affect benefits payable to the spouse or common-law partner, if applicable. For more information, refer to: Withdraw an Application (Scenario) ; and Withdraw an Application (Scenario) KA-05344 Cancellation—OAS Benefits (Scenario) (article not available).

The Correctional Service of Canada will provide the release date information to the Department on the monthly Correctional Service of Canada report. Before the Incarceration team can reinstate the benefit to the incarcerated client, the client must advise the Department in writing of their release. Adjustments must be made immediately to their spouse or common-law partner’s income-tested benefit, if applicable, even if the incarcerated client has not provided written notification. If the client submits written notification of their release to the regional processing office, advise the Incarceration team in Timmins using the OAS Incarceration Enquiry (ISP-5014) form. The Incarceration team will confirm that the date matches the Correctional Service of Canada’s record on the report. If there is a discrepancy, the Incarceration team will verify the date with the Correctional Service of Canada. The Correctional Service of Canada's release date is the authoritative source. If the client insists the wrong release date is being used, they may contact the Correctional Service of Canada to clarify the information. The applicant can notify the Department in advance if they know their release date. Payments can be reinstated by the Incarceration team the month the individual is released if they are still eligible and entitled. If an application is received after the client has been released, the regional or International Operations (IO) processing office must confirm the incarceration details with the applicant or their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable. These dates must then be confirmed with the Incarceration team who will compare the details with the dates on the Correctional Service of Canada report. Once the dates have been confirmed, the regional or IO processing office will process the application and perform all required actions on the account as usual, including: systems actions; issuing retroactive payments; sending award letters; and updating ITRDS notes. The applicant is entitled to receive up to 11 months of retroactivity for any months in which they were not incarcerated (including the 1st month of incarceration and the month of their release). If the entitlement is affected by the period of incarceration, it must be reflected in the award letter.

topic_title: Impact on the OAS pension and income-tested benefits when a notification of incarceration or release is received
text: OAS benefits are in pay prior to incarceration If the incarcerated individual is receiving OAS benefits when the notice of incarceration is received, the initial suspension of benefits is effective the month following the transfer of information from the Correctional Service of Canada or from the province or territory. Once the information regarding the incarceration is reviewed, the OAS account will need to be suspended effective the month following the month of incarceration. If the suspension is retroactive, an overpayment may be incurred. For more information on the impact of the incarceration on the spouse or common-law partner’s OAS benefits, refer to the OAS benefits for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual section below. OAS benefit applications processed during incarceration If an incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner submits an application for an OAS pension or benefit, the application is processed in the regional or International Operations (IO) processing office as usual, along with any related work items (e.g. a Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form) to determine eligibility and entitlement. Application is approved If the application is approved, payments are not released by the regional or IO processing office. The regional or IO processing office will advise the Incarceration team of the outcome using the OAS Incarceration Enquiry (ISP-5014) form and the Incarceration team will perform the necessary actions to issue payments, release the account and notify the client and their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable. The Incarceration team cannot perform the required actions in the International Agreements systems. Therefore, the Incarceration team will advise the applicable IO processing office of any system actions required. These actions must be performed as a priority. If they are eligible and entitled, the incarcerated client's benefit payments will begin the month they are released. The incarcerated client is entitled to receive up to 11 months of retroactive payments for any months in which they were not incarcerated (including the 1st month of incarceration and the month of their release). If the application is approved for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the Incarceration team will review the account to determine which entitlement rate is more advantageous to them. Individuals incarcerated in a federal penitentiary or in a provincial correctional facility are not eligible to accrue an actuarial adjustment for the months they are incarcerated (i.e. the month after the month of incarceration up to the month before release). Entitlement—Voluntary Deferral and Pension Choices (Policy) Individuals will be able to accumulate residence while incarcerated up until their OAS pension or benefit application has been approved. After the approval of an application, individuals will be able to accumulate residence while incarcerated for the purpose of portability, but they may not accumulate residence for a higher payment rate. For more information on the impact of the incarceration on the spouse or common-law partner’s OAS benefits, refer to the OAS benefits for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual section below. Application is denied If the application is denied, the regional or IO processing office will perform all required actions on the account as usual, including: systems actions; sending denial letters; and updating ITRDS notes. If the Incarceration team in Timmins requested that the application be processed, notify them of the type of application processed and the pension or benefit that was denied using the ISP-5014 form.

text: On a monthly basis, the Correctional Service of Canada or the province or territory will provide a report to the Department that lists newly incarcerated and released individuals over the age of 60. topic_title: OAS benefits for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual
text: If the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated individual is in pay for the GIS or the ALW benefit, their account may require an adjustment by the Incarceration team to calculate their entitlement based on their individual income if it is to their advantage. Calculating the spouse or common-law partner’s entitlement based on their individual income Once eligibility and entitlement have been established, the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated individual may be entitled to have their entitlement to the GIS or the ALW benefit calculated based on their own income if it is to their advantage. If it is not advantageous, the benefit will be based on the combined income of the couple as usual. For more information on marital status and rate tables, Marital Status and Rate Tables for Income-Tested Benefits Payment based on individual income will begin the later of: the month following the month the spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated; or at the effective date of the benefit (normal retroactivity applies) if the spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated on this date. Entitlement at this rate continues to be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual is released. The spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing when their payment rate has been adjusted due to this provision. If the spouse or common-law partner is paid based on their own income, they must notify the Department in writing of: a change in marital status; and the date of release of their incarcerated spouse or common-law partner. The release date they provide must match the release date of their spouse or common-law partner from the Correctional Service of Canada transfer of information.

Any OAS payment that a client or their spouse or common-law partner receives where there is no entitlement due to their incarceration or the incarceration of their spouse or common-law partner will be set up as an overpayment and will be recovered. To ensure that the lower income spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated individual is not disadvantaged by a pension income split when recalculating the GIS or the ALW benefit based on their individual income, the spouse or common-law partner may ask to exclude the amount of split pension income they received from their spouse or common-law partner. Before the income is removed, the spouse or common-law partner who has the income on Line 116/11600 of their tax return must submit a new statement of income or a GIS or ALWS (Pension Income Splitting - Change in Marital Status situation - Consent to remove a transferred amount) (ISP-3032) form to consent to the removal of the pension income split amount.

An appeal is a legal proceeding where the SST reviews the Minister's decisions using the principles of procedural fairness and a person's right to be heard. CPP and OAS applicants and beneficiaries have the right of appeal.

The SST —AD will be limited to whether the Social Security Tribunal—General Division ( SST —GD): failed to observe the principles of natural justice; acted beyond or refused to exercise its jurisdiction; made an error of law; in fact or in mixed law and fact; or was not presented with evidence included in the application for leave to appeal. The appellant or the Minister may request Leave to Appeal within 90 days of the SST —GD decision. If Leave to Appeal is granted, the SST will send the parties the deadlines to file: evidence, arguments or any other documents; and readiness to proceed.

Before an applicant or beneficiary can file an appeal to the SST , they must request a reconsideration of the decision on their CPP or OAS application. For more information, Reconsideration (Scenario)

The Social Security Tribunal—General Division ( SST —GD) hears appeals de novo, where: the matter under appeal is considered and heard completely afresh; and the previous administrative decision is not taken into account. Parties may present new information on: issues considered by previous decision makers; or new evidence on issues not previously raised. The appellant must provide a statement of the new facts or new material facts that would allow the SST to rescind or amend a decision. Within 30 days after the day the request is filed, the parties may: file documents or submissions; or file a notice indicating there are no new documents or submissions (Notice of Readiness). CPP and OAS applicants and beneficiaries who disagree with the SST —GD decision may request leave to appeal to the next level.

The appellant must complete the Notice of Appeal — Income Security — General Division form from the SST and include the reconsideration decision letter to file an appeal. The SST can initiate conferences for discussion of: the steps in the appeal process; the issues under appeal; The SST ’s authority; or the deadlines for filing documents. The Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act serve to make government more open and transparent and allow Canadians to fully participate in the democratic process. Under these Acts, individuals have the legal right to: obtain information, in any form, that is contained in government records; and the protection of their privacy and personal information held by the government.

The Access to Information Act gives Canadian citizens, permanent residents and any person or corporation present in Canada a right to access records of government institutions that are subject to the Act. The Privacy Act gives Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and individuals present in Canada the right to access their personal information held by government institutions that are subject to the Act. The Act also protects that information against unauthorized collection, use, retention and disclosure. Individuals present in Canada can access their government-held personal information by making an Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) request through the ATIP website. For more information on the collection, use, disclosure and retention of personal information, refer to Privacy and Personal Information . Refer to Employment and Social Development Canada’s Corporate Secretariat Branch ’s website for more information on the Department’s ATIP Division and its units, as well as these ATIP-related details: ATIP Privacy and Personal Information Corporate Secretariat Branch Steps required to access records held by federal government departments; and Forms to fill out. topic_title: Administrative investigations and client file reviews
text: To ensure the integrity of the department and our clients and ensure appropriate payments are made, the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) conducts a number of administrative investigations annually. An administrative investigation is an impartial investigative process conducted by ISB on files referred from the Department's employees due to: anomalies and discrepancies identified in the files; or third party complaints and disclosures received by the department. There are a number of triggers that may elicit a case specific review that may lead to an administrative investigation on a client's file. Additionally, ISB initiates annual projects to review client files that ensure: client files are up to date, accurate and complete; appropriate payments are received; and national processes are followed.

The Integrity Services Branch (ISB) protects the integrity of the department, ensuring compliance by both staff and clients. The ISB Services Branch aims to ensure that: error, fraud and misuse are prevented, detected and addressed; essential services are managed; and employees work in a safe and secure environment.

topic_title: The purpose of the Integrity Services Branch
text: The Integrity Services Branch (ISB) is responsible for completing investigations where fraud or discrepancies have been identified. An investigation may result in a recommendation for an overpayment, underpayment, change to benefit entitlement, to impose a penalty or to send a file to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The Service Canada Benefit Officer (SCBO) responsible for the client's file uses the recommendation provided by ISB to make a decision to agree or disagree with their findings. All CPP and OAS applications, files and accounts may be subject to random audits and reviews to: monitor the compliance of the guiding principles and procedures outlined by ISB; and improve transparency of the administration of CPP and OAS benefits while reducing perception of conflict of interest.

Staff observations are one of the most important triggers to identify accounts that require an investigation by the Integrity Services Branch. These observations are be made by staff in the normal course of their duties and may involve many conditions. The following is a list of triggers or sources which may identify CPP and OAS cases that warrant a referral for an administrative investigation: the display of a warning on ITRDS; age; contradicting death information; CPP/QPP contribution contradictions; data matches, including foreign pension income discrepancies; disclosure; discrepancies/anomalies relating to the Social Insurance Number; duplicate accounts; identity; income; informant leads (also known as Third Party Complaints); late applicants; maintenance/custody issues; marital status; medical condition; multiple accounts; P.O. box addresses in urban areas; payments after the death of a beneficiary; residence; review of the provincial vital statistics death listings; suspicious or questionable documents; undeliverable mail/returned payments; unreported return to work; etc.

Pensions and benefits payable under the CPP and the OAS Act are adjusted to reflect increases in the cost of living as measured by the Consumer Price Index. This document provides procedures for the escalation of CPP and OAS pensions and benefits.

CPP amount CPP rate increases are calculated once per year to reflect increases in the cost of living as measured by the Consumer Price Index All-Items Index. CPP escalation factors CPP amounts are adjusted once a year in January. The rate increase is the percentage change from one 12-month period to the previous 12-month period. Refer to All Benefit Rates in the CPP Benefit Rates section of the Benefits Toolbox in the KMT. The information in the following table explains the various CPP benefits rate tables found in the CPP Maximum Benefit Amounts publication which is updated annually. Title of table Table Maximum monthly amounts for new benefits Table 1 Maximum monthly amounts at the beginning of pension and value in 20XX Table 2 Data related to calculations of contributions and benefits Table 3 Contributions calculation for 20XX Table 4 Consumer price index average and pension index for use in benefit calculations Table 5 Pension index factors to be used in accordance with Section 58(3) Table 6.A and 6.B Escalation factors Table 7 Actuarial adjustment factors and maximum retirement pension, 20XX Table 8 The following table shows how the Consumer Price Index was used to calculate the annual increase of CPP benefit amounts for January 1, 2018: Average Consumer Price Index (November 2016 to October 2017) ÷ Average Consumer Price Index (November 2015 to October 2016) = Rate Increase Example The following example illustrates the concept explained above. To determine the 2018 Pension Index, calculate the average of the Consumer Price Index figures for the 12-month period from November 2016 to October 2017 as shown in the following table: Month Consumer Price Index Figure November 2016 128.6 December 2016 128.4 January 2017 129.5 February 2017 129.7 March 2017 129.9 April 2017 130.4 May 2017 130.5 June 2017 130.4 July 2017 130.4 August 2017 130.5 September 2017 130.8 October 2017 130.9 Total 1560 ÷ 12 = 130.00 To determine the 2017 Pension Index, calculate the average of the Consumer Price Index figures for the 12-month period from November 2015 to October 2016. Month Consumer Price Index Figure November 2015 127.1 December 2015 126.5 January 2016 126.8 February 2016 127.1 March 2016 127.9 April 2016 128.3 May 2016 128.8 June 2016 129.1 July 2016 128.9 August 2016 128.7 September 2016 128.8 October 2016 129.1 Total 1537.1 ÷ 12 = 128.09 (rounded to 128.10) Determine the Pension Index ratio (escalation factor). Pension Index 2018 ÷ Pension Index 2017, therefore: 130.00 ÷ 128.10 = 1.0148 (rounded to 1.015) The escalation factor for CPP benefits in January 2018 was 1.015, which resulted in a 1.5% increase applied to CPP pension and benefit payments. OAS amount OAS amounts are adjusted quarterly each year in January, April, July and October. For more information, refer to Table: 1 2 3 4 5 in the OAS Benefit Rates section in the Benefits Toolbox in the KMT. The OAS pension and benefits amounts increase every 3 months by a factor based on the Consumer Price Index. For example, the factor used for increasing OAS benefits in January is equal to the ratio of the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous July to the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous October. Example To determine the OAS escalation factor for January 2018 : Calculate the average for the 3-month period from August to October 2017 as follows: (130.5 + 130.8 + 130.9) ÷ 3 = 130.73 Calculate the average for the 3-month period from May to July 2017 as follows: (130.5 + 130.4 + 130.4) ÷ 3 = 130.43 Calculate the OAS escalation factor as follows: 130.73 ÷ 130.43 = 1.0023 (rounded to 1.002 ) To calculate the OAS pension increase for January 2018: Take the maximum OAS pension monthly payment amount in effect for the period from October to December 2017 and multiply it by the calculated OAS escalation factor. The product is the maximum OAS pension amount for the period from January to March 2018: $585.49 x 1.002 = $586.66 The increase to the OAS pension amount in January 2018 was $1.17; $586.66 - $585.49 = $1.17.

Employment and Social Development Canada currently has 61 Information Sharing Agreements (ISA) with federal, provincial and territorial partners under the CPP and OAS programs. These agreements (irrespective of them being identified as an agreement, arrangement, memorandum of understanding, letter of agreement, letter of concurrence, etc.) are considered written records of understanding between government parties that outline the terms and conditions, including the specific data elements, under which personal information is shared between the parties.

The Department has developed ISA regional and federal tools to ensure standards related to the disclosure of personal information are in place for federal, provincial and territorial agreements. These documents provide guidance on information sharing practices with federal, provincial and territorial partners. For more information, Information Sharing Agreements Regional and Federal Tools Service Canada employees must protect the personal information of clients and are responsible for ensuring that the collection, retention, use and disclosure of client information comply with all standards and directives as they pertain to the protection of sensitive information. Employees must review the tools before responding to enquiries from federal, provincial or territorial partners under an ISA. Information shared outside the scope of an ISA is considered a privacy breach.

topic_title: Contributor lived or worked in another country
text: If a contributor lived or worked in Canada and in another country and does not meet the contributory or residence requirements for CPP benefits, a social security agreement may help them qualify. It may also provide benefits for their surviving spouse, common-law partner or children.

Canadians contribute to CPP if they meet the following criteria: are over the age of 18; work in Canada (outside of Quebec); and earn more than $3,500 a year. The employer pays half of the required contributions and the employee pays the other half. A self-employed individual pays both the employee and employer contribution.

The contributory period is the period during which the individual is eligible to contribute a portion of their earnings to CPP. With CPP enhancement, there are up to three components to an individual's contributory period: the Base contributory period (as of January 1, 1966); the First additional contributory period (as of January 1, 2019); and the Second additional contributory period (as of January 1, 2024). The base contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 1966; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. The first additional contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 2019; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. The second additional contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 2024; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. All three contributory periods end with the earliest of the following: the month before the start of the contributor's RTR pension; the month of the contributor's 70th birthday; or the month of their death. For more information, CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy)

A contribution is an amount paid to CPP by individuals with pensionable employment or income between the Year's Basic Exemption and the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) amount, multiplied by the contribution rate from that year. As of January 1, 2019, the Department began the enhancement phase of the CPP components. The first additional and second additional components are not separate benefits, but top-ups to the original base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. Gradual increases to CPP contribution rates took place over a 7-year period (2019 to 2025). For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) CPP consists of: a base or original component (since January 1, 1966) that is calculated on earnings between the year's minimum and maximum amounts of pensionable earnings. The current base contribution rate is 9.9% (4.95% from the employer and 4.95% from the employee). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts; and additional or enhanced components (since January 1, 2019) that provides a top-up to the base and that is broken down in first and second additional components. The first additional component is calculated on the same range of earnings as the base and has a total contribution rate of 2% (1% from the employer and 1% from the employee). This additional rate was introduced gradually between 2019 and 2023. Table 1—Increase to total contribution rates for years 2019-2023 with the phase-in of the First Additional component Year First Additional Contribution Rate Total Contribution Rate (Base + First Additional) for Employer/Employee Total Employer and Employee Contribution Rate (Base + First Additional), or for Self-Employed 2019 Was 0.30% (0.15% employer / 0.15% employee) (4.95% + 0.15%) = 5.10% (9.9% + 0.30%) = 10.2% 2020 Increased to 0.60% (0.30% employer / 0.30% employee) (4.95% + 0.30%) = 5.25% (9.9% + 0.60%) = 10.5% 2021 Increased to 1.0% (0.50% employer / 0.50% employee) (4.95% + 0.50%) = 5.45% (9.9% + 1.0%) = 10.9% 2022 Increased to 1.5% (0.75% employer / 0.75% employee) (4.95% + 0.75%) = 5.70% (9.9% + 1.5%) = 11.4% 2023 Reached the full value of 2% (1.0% employer / 1.0 % employee) (4.95% + 1.0%) = 5.95% (9.9% + 2.0%) = 11.9% The second additional component introduced a new range of pensionable earnings from the year's maximum to 14% above that maximum between 2024 and 2025. This range started at the original annual earnings limit (the YMPE amount) and stopped at the additional earnings limit (the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) amount). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts. This contribution rate only applies to individuals with earnings above the YMPE amount. With the implementation of CPP enhancement, First Nations employees on reserves will still be able to choose whether to contribute to the CPP. The PRB is a monthly CPP benefit that is payable for the lifetime of the beneficiary.

The PRB is only payable to a CPP or QPP RTR pension recipient who works and makes valid contributions on earnings above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE). It is payable even if the recipient is already receiving the maximum CPP RTR pension. Since it is a taxable benefit, it may affect eligibility for other benefits. Payment of the first PRB was made effective January 1, 2013. Individuals will make compulsory contributions to the plan if they are: between the ages of 60 and 65 (including the month of their 65th birthday); receiving a CPP RTR pension; and still working. Individuals may opt out or stop contributing if they are: at least 65 years of age but under 70; receiving a CPP RTR pension; and still working. For more information, Eligibility Requirements—Post-Retirement Benefit (Policy) Enhancement to the CPP As of January 1, 2019, the department began phasing in the CPP enhancement, a new component of the CPP. The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but rather a top-up to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians will receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. The base component of the PRB and the additional components of the PRB are calculated using the same formula. The total amount of the PRB is the sum of the base and additional components . To understand how the PRB is calculated, Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) Manual adjudication Although the PRB is an automatically adjudicated benefit and staff are not required to manually make calculations, there may be exceptional cases that require manual intervention in order to complete the adjudication process. In these cases, there will be enquiries that require subject matter expertise for responses. Some examples of the situations requiring PRB subject matter expertise are: QPP RTR pension-only clients entitled to a PRB ; QPP and CPP (dual) contributors entitled to a PRB ; PRB adjudication exception report processing; and complex enquiries regarding entitlement amounts and/or the calculation of the PRB .

Certain provincial legislative laws require the appointment of a committee. A committee can consist of one or more persons. If a client is found to be incapable of managing their own affairs, the public trustee may be automatically appointed as the committee. This only happens if there is no existing valid legal representative (e.g. enduring POA). If the public trustee becomes the committee of an incapable client, that client's POA (other than an enduring POA) is void. A third party can be appointed as the committee in place of the public trustee when the third party applies to the provincial court. Since a committee may be given authority over the client's financial affairs, their personal affairs, or both, it is very important to read the authorizing document carefully. The Department only pays benefits to committees managing the financial affairs of incapable clients. The committee is responsible for managing the client's affairs, such as: the administration of the client's income. This includes: conducting banking; paying expenses; budgeting for the client and their family; preparing income tax returns. the client's real estate and personal assets. This includes: selling if it is in the client's best interest; entering into contracts; operating all existing businesses; bringing or defending any lawsuits on the client's behalf. the preparation of a complete inventory of the client's assets and liabilities. This includes: expenses; assets; debts; a detailed accounting when required. A committee remains in effect until one of the following occurs: the court makes an order appointing another committee to replace the existing committee; the client's capability to make decisions is restored; the client or committee applies to the court for an order terminating the committee; or the client or committee dies. Before amending the client's account, you must verify the committee has been terminated by requesting the court order declaring the termination of the committee.

A change in payee will only occur when the Department receives: another court order revoking the first one; or a certificate or official letter from the public trustee naming a private citizen responsible for administering the client's benefits.

The trustee who is appointed by the court to manage the care of an incapable client or minor is called a "guardian of the person". A statutory guardian is issued a certificate from the applicable provincial court. This certificate is proof of the guardian's authority and can contain conditions. The guardian also manages all of the incapable client's or minor's property that is not otherwise held in trust, unless the guardian is limited by the terms of appointment. In most cases, a statutory guardianship of property for a client who is incapable of managing their personal affairs remains in effect until one of the following happens: the court appoints another guardian; the guardian resigns; the guardian is notified that the certificate of incapability is cancelled; the incapable client is discharged (from a medical care facility) unless a certificate of continuance is issued; or the client or guardian dies. In most cases, a statutory guardianship of property for a minor remains in effect until one of the following happens: it is terminated by a court order; a private guardianship order is made; an adoption order is made; the minor reaches the age of majority; or the minor marries.

topic_title: Complex and discretionary disclosure of personal information
text: Complex and discretionary requests are made by individuals and third parties and may require removal of personal information before disclosure. Examples include: all privacy requests submitted on a Personal Information Request Form (TBC/CTC 350-58) or Access to Information Request form (TBC/CTC 350-57) ; requests for medical reports; requests made by a third party; requests for a copy of the application; requests for a copy of the entire file; requests for documents related to an Integrity Investigation. Complex and discretionary requests are administered and processed by Regional Privacy Coordinators. Complex and discretionary requests for personal information must be in writing and sent to the Regional Privacy Unit. To protect personal information, the Regional Privacy Unit ensures that the Department obtains consent in writing and removes third party personal information unrelated to the client.

For criminal proceedings related to CPP and OAS, the RCMP is the investigative body authorized to conduct investigations. You may submit original documents only when requested to do so. For criminal proceedings not related to OAS or CPP, forward all requests to Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP). You are not required to give evidence or produce documents that are not related to OAS or CPP unless the Minister considers it appropriate. Information can only be released when charges are laid or legal instruments are issued. For example, the RCMP contacts Service Canada for the address of one of our clients in a matter unrelated to CPP or OAS. Because Service Canada did not initiate the investigation, it notifies the RCMP that we cannot comply with their request for information without a "legal instrument." The RCMP responds that they only need a letter from Service Canada confirming that the person who is under investigation is our client. We must respond to the RCMP that without a "legal instrument" we cannot confirm or deny if the person is a client of CPP or OAS. For civil proceedings related to CPP or OAS, you can release personal information in the following situations: When the SST—General Division hears a case, only release information that is relevant for making a decision. Charter Challenges: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees all Canadians equality under the law. If a client claims that a piece of legislation violates their rights, they can challenge the validity of the legislation. Contact Legal Services for advice in these cases. Only information that has been used in the ISP decision will be released. Civil Proceedings Related to but not Initiated by ISP: only release information when you receive a valid "legal instrument" for a civil proceeding that is not initiated by Service Canada. Forward all requests to National Headquarters (NHQ) ISP ATIP. Civil Proceedings Initiated by ISP: a "legal instrument" is not required because the Minister is normally named as party to the proceedings. Forward all requests to Program Integrity. Civil Proceedings not related to CPP or OAS: we do not release information that does not relate to the administration of the CPP or OAS. Forward all requests to ATIP. When you receive a subpoena or summons, contact your manager immediately. The manager locates the file and determines whether it is for a case initiated by Service Canada or by another party. If Service Canada initiated the proceedings, they must forward the legal instrument to the regional Program Integrity Officer. If someone else issued the subpoena or summons, the manager forwards it to the regional ATIP Coordinator. Appearing in court When you receive a subpoena or summons in your name, you must appear. If you do not appear, the court can issue an arrest warrant and lay a charge of contempt of court. If you are not the individual best qualified to give evidence or are not available on the particular date, have the NHQ ISP ATIP Coordinator or a delegated authority negotiate with the party or lawyer who initiated the subpoena to ask if someone else may appear. If the party or lawyer agrees, a letter must be sent or the subpoena or summons reissued to confirm the agreement and give the name and phone number of the new witness. If the party or lawyer does not agree, the person named in the subpoena must attend court. If you receive a subpoena to appear in court: be prepared; familiarize yourself with all aspects of the case; listen to the questions, make sure you understand them, and speak loudly and clearly. Releasing or not releasing information to the court When releasing the requested information: Obtain written consent from the party issuing the subpoena confirming that certified copies are acceptable. If they are not acceptable, bring both the original and a certified copy to court so that the copies may be authenticated. Keep copies of any original documents taken to court. Attend court at the date and time set out in the subpoena. At the conclusion of the court appearance, submit a report on the service and disposition of the subpoena to the designated NHQ ISP ATIP official words removed. When an employee is authorized to release information as noted on the "legal instrument", the following information is required in a letter and signed by the Director of ATIP Employment and Social Development Canada: "This is confirmation that (name of individual) is authorized to release the following documents in response to (identify type of "legal instrument"), dated (date), concerning the case involving (name legal case) as per section (104.08/33.08) of the (Canada Pension Plan/Old Age Security) Act." (In addition, list the information provided). When not releasing the requested information: The subpoenaed employee must bring a copy of the specified file documents in a sealed envelope, a copy of the Act (CPP or OAS) and photocopies of the relevant sections of the Act . The employee must state that the program cannot release information due to legislative constraints (CPP, Section 104.08 and OAS Act, Section 33.08 ) and that the information is in a sealed envelope and the Administration seeks the court's ruling on the disclosure. Provide a written request to have the documents returned to the Department, especially if they are the originals. If the judge orders the envelope unsealed, request an adjournment to consult Legal Services. topic_title: Did you receive a request for medical information?
text: Send all requests for medical information to your Regional Privacy Coordinator. Be cautious when releasing medical information. Requests for medical information must be made in writing. You cannot release medical information on the basis of a verbal request—the Regional Privacy Coordinator may want to consult with the Medical Adjudicator (MA) before releasing the information. Do not release medical information unless the participating program authorizes its release. This includes the disclosure of medical information to other program areas of the Department. Based on the MA's advice, the Regional Privacy Coordinator can exempt the report if the disclosure of part of a medical report may have an adverse effect on the physical, mental or emotional health of the client or may not be in the best interests of the client. In some instances, the physician indicates “Not to be released” on the medical report. The medical report is the property of the CPP Program. As such, the decision to release or not rests with the Regional Privacy Coordinator, based on the best interests of the client or third party. Before releasing medical information, ensure that: you clearly identify the need for the requested information; the doctor's report does not specify that the information must not be released because it could cause harm to the client or to someone else; you release only information that is relevant for the administration of the program; you apply due diligence when disclosing medical information. Example Employment Insurance (EI) requests a copy of a letter contained in the DSB benefit file. The client references work activity in the letter. However, the letter also contains information on the client's medical condition.Because substantiating work activity is relevant to the administration of the EI Act, you can release the specific information about the work activity. Do not release the medical information, because it is not relevant to the administration of the EI Act.

topic_title: Did you receive a request from a federal institution?
text: You must not disclose income information to CRA. Make it available to CRA only if they request it for the purpose of administering the Income Tax Act (ITA) and Part I of the Energy Costs Assistance Measures Act (ECAMA). Any discrepancies with income must be resolved with the beneficiary or with the beneficiary’s spouse or common-law partner, as appropriate. Any request for information (including income) from CRA must: include the purpose of the request; identify the Act (ITA or ECAMA); include the name and title of the CRA requestor. Keep a record of the request for information on the beneficiary’s file (in notes or on file). The above procedure is effective immediately to protect information obtained under the OAS Act and to deny requests from CRA for purposes other than the administration of the ITA or the ECAMA. Example The Department receives a letter from an employee of CRA requesting the name, address and phone number of a CPP or OAS client’s executor, as well as a copy of the death certificate and will. The letter is signed by a CRA Collection Contact Officer. CRA informs the Department that the client died while in the process of declaring bankruptcy.The letter does not state under which CRA legislation the information is required. When the Department employee contacts CRA, it is confirmed that the information is needed to expedite bankruptcy proceedings. Because the information requested is needed to administer the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act , and not the ITA, the Department cannot release the information.

topic_title: Did you receive a request from an individual for their own personal information?
text: The Privacy Act gives individuals a right to access information about themselves and to request the correction of their personal information held by federal government organizations. The request can also come from the individual’s legal representative for personal information or an authorized person. You can make corrections to personal information in the case of errors or omissions. You can also change or amend information on a client file, such as an application or a worksheet, for different reasons. An individual can request the disclosure of their personal information verbally (in person or by telephone) or by submitting an original and dated letter. You cannot release hard copies (i.e. photocopied documentation from the client’s file), other than non-complex and non-discretionary, based on a phone call, email or faxed request. Advise the client that they must submit an original written request for hard copies. The process to release the information can begin, but you cannot release the information until you receive written authorization. The ATIP Division must respond to some requests. As a result, you must send requests to your Regional Privacy Coordinator immediately.

Use and disclosure Send all requests for the document types listed below to the Regional Privacy Coordinator. These document types cannot be released. Cabinet documents, record of Cabinet decisions and draft legislation; client-solicitor privileged information; documents related to War Crimes and Crimes against Humanity; informant lead (third party complaint, e.g. an anonymous phone call stating that an individual is receiving a DSB benefit while doing undeclared work).
