Enquire about the location of the recipient’s fax to assess the risk of who has access to the fax. Contact the recipient by telephone before transmitting the fax to ensure the person is there to receive the document personally. Ensure the fax number entered is correct before transmission. Ask the recipient to confirm receipt of the information.

topic_title: Non-complex and non-discretionary disclosure of personal information
text: Non-complex and non-discretionary disclosure includes routine informal requests from individuals or a third party for copies of documentation on file or other records. Examples include: benefit letters ; effective date of benefit; benefit status; statements of contributions. Non-complex and non-discretionary requests are actioned by CPP and OAS Pensions staff.

Personal information includes any recorded detail about an identifiable individual, including: race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age or marital status of the individual; education, the medical, criminal or employment history of the individual; financial transactions in which the individual has been involved; any identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, such as a social insurance number (SIN); the address, fingerprints or blood type of the individual; the personal opinions or views of the individual, except where they are about another individual; correspondence sent to a government institution by the individual that is implicitly or explicitly of a private or confidential nature, and replies to such correspondence that would reveal the contents of the original correspondence; the views or opinions of another individual about the individual; the name of the individual where it appears with other personal information relating to the individual or where the disclosure of the name itself would reveal information about the individual. For a description of what Protected A, B and C information is and how to safeguard it when transmitting it by hand, mail, fax and email, refer to the Information Classification Tool

topic_title: Protection of employee personal information—Signing correspondence standards
text: Employees are no longer required to include their name on correspondence to the client. An employee’s name and signature must be excluded in situations where there has been a documented incident or threat representing a real danger to an employee (e.g. clients uttering threats, clients with a known history of substantial verbal abuse, clients with a known history of violence).

topic_title: Request for disclosure of personal information
text: If you receive a formal request for personal or medical information on a TBC/CTC 350-58 form or a TBC/CTC 350-57 form, forward the request to your Regional Privacy Coordinator immediately. A response must be sent within 30 calendar days. The Regional Privacy Coordinator sends formal requests to the ATIP Division, which is responsible for gathering the requested documents and determining if the request satisfies privacy requirements before they release information to the individual. Only the Director of the ATIP Division, the Department and the NHQ ATIP Coordinator have the authority to deny formal requests for access to personal information. Before the release of any personal information, documentation must be on file authorizing the individual. Refer to Non-Payee Contact or to Non-Payee Contact Payee Contact

topic_title: Requesting Protected B information from CRA for the administration of CPP and OAS
text: Contact your regional representative on the Service Canada/CRA contact list who will contact CRA on your behalf. Service Canada/CRA contact list The regional representative must submit the request via email using encryption software (Entrust).
The Department is obligated to protect a client's personal information in its collection, use, disclosure and retention.

topic_title: The client agrees to usage and disclosure at the time of application
text: Personal information cannot be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected, unless the individual provides consent or where there is legal authority. Each application for CPP or OAS benefits contains a privacy statement. The privacy statement informs the client that personal information may be shared under certain circumstances without any additional consent and may be shared with: any federal institution; provincial authority or public bodies created under provincial law; foreign countries based on Social Security Agreements; non-government third parties. For guidance on information sharing practices with provincial and federal partners, Information Sharing You can also share certain personal information with Members of Parliament if the release of personal information is in the public interest. Before releasing any personal information, you must consult with the Regional Privacy Coordinator. See your manager for the name of your privacy coordinator. Personal information can also be shared for the purposes of policy analysis, research and evaluation. Before collecting personal information from sources other than the individual, you must inform the individual of the following: the nature of the information being sought and the purpose of the collection; the source of the information collection; the consequences of a refusal to consent to the collection if the information is essential to making a decision directly affecting them; refusal to consent to the collection does not result in any adverse decision about them if the information is not essential to making a decision directly affecting them; the registration number of the personal information bank in which the information is to be contained; their right of access and protection under the Canada Pension Plan , the OAS Act, the Department of Employment and Social Development Act and the Privacy Act , where the information is collected directly from them; the information requested may be accessible to them, when the information is collected from another individual.

topic_title: Unacceptable collection of publicly available information
text: You cannot access social networking sites to search for information on individuals, their families or their businesses for any administrative purposes. This includes searching for information by: signing into any social networking site using a personal profile; requesting that another employee sign into a personal profile for a social networking site on their behalf; requesting the social networking profile information about an individual or about their business, from the individual or from others; creating any profile using an alias; creating a social networking profile using the Department or Service Canada.

topic_title: Use of email and fax to disclose personal information
text: As long as no personal information is disclosed, you can email blank forms and Protected A information to clients, if requested. You can only email Protected B information to another federal department if the other de partment is using approved encryption software (Entrust). When Protected B information is transmitted, either from a secured or unsecured fax machine, the following paragraph is to be included: Sensitive/Confidential Information “The attached information is sensitive in nature and confidential to its recipient. It is intended only for the addressee(s) identified above. If you are not the addressee(s), or an employee or agent of the addressee(s), please note that any dissemination, distribution or copying of this communication is strictly prohibited. If you have received this fax in error, please destroy the document and notify the sender of the error." In all cases, you must consult with your Manager prior to faxing, and create a note in ITRDS that lists the Manager consulted, what was faxed and the time and date. When a document or an application for benefits is received by fax and that document is necessary to establish entitlement to a CPP or OAS benefit, the original or a certified true copy of the document or the application must be received before benefits can be approved for payment. In the case of an application for benefits, the faxed application can be used to protect the effective date of the benefit but it cannot be used to approve payment of the benefit. Protected C information, such as investigations into threats of individuals, is information that is extremely sensitive and can cause extremely serious injury to individuals. Protected C information can only be transmitted via a secure fax machine. You can use a non-secure fax machine in urgent situations when information is required immediately or when no other practical method is available to communicate the information (e.g. when a secure fax is temporarily inoperable due to technical difficulties). You can fax medical information to a non-secure fax machine when processing a Disability (DSB) benefit application that involves a terminal illness. Example In order to meet timelines for terminal illness applications, a decision on eligibility must be made within 5 business days of receipt of the application. In such cases, the Department can accept medical documentation from a non-secure fax.

A client's SIN can be used as the client identifier on correspondence sent to third parties if: the client has given authorization to obtain personal information from a third party; or a signed document is available to confirm that this person is the client’s representative. For information on which document is required, refer to Non-Payee Contact or to Payee Contact . Non-Payee Contact Payee Contact If no authorizing documentation is on file, you must use other identifiers on the correspondence, such as the Client Identification Number. topic_title: Was any unacceptable public information obtained?
text: If publicly available personal information was used to make an administrative decision on an OAS or CPP file, it must be retained on the file. While the publicly available personal information does not have any inherent value in determining eligibility, it is necessary for the individual and all future evaluators to understand the rationale behind any previously rendered decisions, as well as the findings on which they were based. Do not destroy or remove this information from the file.

A privacy breach occurs when there is improper or unauthorized collection, use, disclosure, retention or disposal of personal information. A breach can be the result of inadvertent errors or malicious actions by employees, third parties, partners in information-sharing agreements or intruders. In the event of improper or accidental use, disclosure or loss of personal information, you must report the incident to an immediate supervisor. Proactively identify privacy risks to the supervisor and seek advice on how to improve the secure handling of personal information. In the event of a possible security incident involving the compromise of personal information, you must advise your manager or delegate as soon as possible so that the appropriate reporting and follow-up can be undertaken. If you become aware of a security incident that may involve a compromise of personal information, immediately follow these steps: Contain and stop the incident to the extent possible. Inform your manager or delegate immediately or, in their absence, the Regional Security Officer. Preserve any relevant documentation. Unauthorized disclosures or privacy breaches of personal information are handled in accordance with the Departmental direction Directives on the Management of Privacy Breaches at ESDC Example An employee receives a telephone call from an individual who informs the employee that they were the recipient of misdirected documents. The employee must request that the documents be returned to the Department. The employee must also document the conversation and contact their manager. If you experience problems recovering the documents, consult with the Regional Security Officer. For more information, Reporting Security Incidents

topic_title: Determine if the provision is advantageous to the couple
text: Once it has been established that a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control, manual calculations are required to determine if applying the provision results in an advantage or disadvantage to either member of the couple. The provision should only be applied if it is advantageous to the couple. This means that they would receive a higher amount as a couple based on their individual incomes than they would receive as a couple based on their combined income. There may be situations where the entitlement based on individual income is advantageous for the couple but results in a higher monthly benefit amount for one member of the couple and a lower monthly benefit amount for the other member. When this occurs, you must obtain authorization from the disadvantaged client or their legal representative to receive a lower entitlement before the provision can be applied. For examples on how to determine if the provision is advantageous to the couple or not, Examples—Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Work Tool)

The CRA and Revenu Québec are responsible for collecting Earnings and Contributions (E & C) data from copies of T4 and Relevé 1 forms by employers or T1 and TP1 general forms submitted by the self-employed. The agency responsible for administering a client's income tax is based on the client's province of residence on December 31st of the tax year. For dual contributors, Revenu Québec collects E & C, but QPP electronically transfers the information from Relevé 1 and TP1 to the Department. The Department receives regularly scheduled Record of Earnings (ROE) updates from the CRA . The CPP ROE is a record of the yearly earnings and contributions of a contributor. A person's CPP ROE is used to: determine eligibility for a CPP benefit; update client information; calculate CPP benefits; calculate any financial adjustment with QPP, in the case of a dual contributor; calculate RTR and post-retirement pensionable earnings by year; and prepare and issue a CPP Statement of Contributions. When a CPP benefit application is processed and approved for payment, the monthly entitlement is calculated based on the information contained in the contributor's CPP ROE at the time the decision is released in ITRDS (interim earnings). When the ROE is updated, ITRDS recalculates the benefit on the finalized earnings.

Contributors can receive a copy of their Statement of Contributions (SOC) through their My Service Canada Account or by requesting it from the Department by telephone, in person or by mail. If the contributor is not in pay for a benefit, the SOC will be sent to the address on their ITRDS account which is the last address they reported to the Canada Revenue Agency. For more information, Explaining the Statement of Contributions (Work Tool)

You can request an Earnings and Contributions investigation for any of the following reasons: the CPP Record of Earnings (ROE) indicates a pensionable earnings amount which is different from the documentary evidence of earnings submitted by the applicant; the CPP ROE appears to be incomplete for one or more years in the contributory period; a contributor's refunded year(s) of valid contributions that could help establish a Minimum Qualifying Period; a CPPD applicant is granted a benefit with a Date of Onset (DOO) or Established DOO in a prorated year; a contributor has indicated that there are discrepancies in the CPP Statement of Contributions; there are 2 identical postings for the same calendar year with the same employer code; evidence submitted for one year is recorded under a different year; there is an incorrect SIN or no SIN on the earnings evidence; there is Earnings and Contributions evidence on file, but no record of it in the ROE; a differentiation between self-employment gross and net amounts; a history of self-employment; a contributor who is unwilling or unable to supply information; pattern of earnings needed, pre- or post-disability; earnings information to support a CPPD cease decision; an informant lead claiming employment; or any other unusual circumstances.

text: When the CRA updates the deemed earnings information on the contributor's Record of Earnings (ROE), all benefits associated with those earnings (current or previous) must be re-adjudicated. This is done to ensure that all Earnings and Contributions on the contributor's ROE have been applied to all benefit calculations. This procedure provides guidance on: providing the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) with a breakdown of the total CPP or QPP taxable income issued in a calendar year for notional tax purposes; and applying the notional tax provision to OAS income-tested benefits.

Refer to the applicable procedure according to the work item you are processing: If you have received a request from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for a lump sum breakdown, refer to Provide Breakdown Information to the CRA for Notional Tax Purposes (Action) . Provide Breakdown Information to the CRA for Notional Tax Purposes (Action) If you are reviewing an OAS income-tested benefit account and need to determine if you must apply the notional tax provision, refer to Apply the Notional Tax Provision to Income-Tested Benefits (Action) . Apply the Notional Tax Provision to Income-Tested Benefits (Action)

Under the Income Tax Act , when a client receives a CPP or QPP retroactive payment of which $300.00 or more relates to previous years, they can choose to exclude the previous year(s) retroactive amounts from their current tax year. The CRA can apply the notional tax provision to exclude any previous year’s portion from the current tax year if it reduces the client’s tax liability. When the notional tax provision is applied, the portion of the retroactive payment that relates to previous years can be attributed to the corresponding tax assessments for income tax purposes. Every year in mid-January, the Department transfers 2 files to the CRA. The first file has last year's T4 information for all clients who received a lump sum payment of which $300.00 or more is for a previous year. This file also includes a breakdown of the lump sum payment by year, for up to 10 years. The CRA then uses this information to apply the notional tax provision automatically if this action reduces the client's tax liability. However, if the provision does not benefit the client for taxation purposes, the CRA does not subtract the previous year's arrears payments when calculating the client's total amount for the current taxation year. The second file has a list of rejected accounts where ITRDS could not automatically break down the lump-sum payme nt by year. CRA uploads these 2 files to their system, which will compare the T4 information with the clients’ accounts. For any rejected accounts, the CRA will request breakdowns of the lump-sum payments from the Department by email. For clients who are eligible for an income-tested benefit, if the notional tax provision is applied to their CPP or QPP income, their benefits are based on this adjusted income and not the gross amount. If the CRA has not applied the notional tax provision automatically but the client meets the criteria to have it applied, staff will manually calculate the CPP or QPP with the notional tax provision and adjust the income as required.

topic_title: Transfer a client's file to International Operations Updated
text: International Operations (IO) coordinates the administration of Canada's International Social Security Agreements (ISSA) with other countries. IO processing in the Atlantic (ATL) region and the Western Canada and Territories (W-T) region is based on the country of agreement. You must send the client's file to IO when: a Canadian pension or benefit requires an ISSA to help the applicant or contributor meet the minimum eligibility requirements (i.e. contributions or residence); a work item is related to foreign benefits; a work item is related to a pension or benefit in pay with IO; or a work item is related to an application under review with IO.

topic_title: Transfer a file or work item from International Operations to a regional or a specialized processing unit Updated
text: When International Operations (IO) receives Canadian pension or benefit applications that do not require International Social Security Agreement provisions to meet eligibility requirements at the earliest effective date, the applications can be processed by the regional processing units. If an application is forwarded to IO in error or IO is not required to administer the account for eligibility, entitlement or administrative reasons, the file is transferred to the regional or specialized processing unit for review.

For more information, Timeline of the Development of the Old Age Security Act (Policy) Table 2. Historical marital status update requirements Situation Before July 1, 1999 July 1, 1999, to December 31, 2016 Marriage The marital status changed the month following the marriage. The couple had the choice to continue as single or married until the end of the payment period, whichever was to their advantage. The ALWS benefit was ceased the month following the marriage. The couple was changed to "married" the month following the marriage. The ALWS benefit was ceased the month following the marriage. Common-Law To be considered common-law, couples had to indicate that they publicly represented themselves as a couple. The marital status changed the month following the requirement of living together for one year was met. After the one-year requirement was met, common-law partners had the choice to continue as common-law or single until the end of the current payment period, whichever was to their advantage. The requirement to publicly represent themselves as a couple ended effective July 2000. The marital status changed to "common-law" the month after the requirement of living together for one year was met. The ALWS benefit was ceased the month after the common-law requirement of living together for 1 year was met. Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control The marital status changed the month following the month the couple began living apart, only if it was advantageous to the couple. The recalculation of benefits from "married" or "common-law" to "separated for reasons beyond their control" did not go beyond the current and previous payment period. The marital status changed the month following the month the couple began living apart, only if it was advantageous to the couple. The recalculation of benefits from "married" or "common-law" to "separated for reasons beyond their control" did not go beyond the current and previous payment period. Separation The couple is married or common-law for the first 6 months following the month of separation. After being separated for 6 months, the client had the choice to continue as "single" or "married" or "common-law" until the end of the payment period, whichever was to their advantage. The ALW benefit ceased the month after separation. There was no waiting period. The couple is married or common-law for the first 3 months following the month of separation, then changed to "single". The ALW benefit ceased the month after the 3-month waiting period. Divorce or annulment The marital status changed the month following the month the divorce or annulment was finalized. The client had the choice to continue as "married" or "single" until the end of the payment period. The ALW benefit ceased the month following the divorce or annulment. The client is single the month following the month the divorce or annulment was finalized. The ALW benefit ceased the month following the month the divorce or annulment was finalized. Reconciliation Couples who resumed cohabitation before the end of the 6-month period of separation continued to be married or common-law. In cases where the ALW benefit was involved, if the couple reconciled within the 6-month period, the ALW benefit payments were reinstated the month following the reconciliation. Married couples who separated for more than 6 months then reconciled would be considered "married" the month following the reconciliation. Common-law partners who separated for more than 6 months then reconciled would have to live together and publicly represent themselves as a couple for one year before they could be considered common-law partners again. If the separation is less than 3 months, the marital status will not have changed. For married couples, the marital status changed to "married" the month following the reconciliation, no matter how long they separated. If the separation is more than 3 months, common-law partners would have to live together for one year before they could be considered common-law partners again. Death The survivor has the choice to continue as "single" or as "married" following the death of their spouse or common-law partner until the end of the current payment period, whichever is to their advantage. The survivor is single the month following the death of their spouse or common-law partner.

International social security agreements allow a province or territory of Canada to conclude "Understandings" concerning social security with other countries. Quebec is currently the only province to enter into Understandings under social security agreements with other countries. Quebec has its own provincial pension plan, the QPP, which is Quebec’s counterpart to the CPP. The BESS is the liaison agency between Quebec and other countries when an Understanding is in force. The BESS is responsible for processing foreign benefit applications and providing information to social security agencies of other countries for individuals within the QPP's jurisdiction.

These survivors, between the age of 35 and 45, were in receipt of a full Survivor's (SVR) pension as of the monthly report due to the qualifying conditions. Effective the month following the report, they will receive a reduced SVR pension rate because they no longer have a qualifying condition. These qualifying conditions are: Dependency Ends when the child reaches age 18 and is not attending school; school ends for a child 18-25 years of age; change in custody for a -18 child. Disability Ends when the survivor’s Disability benefit is terminated. Before January 1, 2019, individuals who became survivors between the age of 35 and 45, who were without dependent children and who were not disabled had the amount of their SVR pension reduced by 1/120th for each month they were under age 45. Effective January 1, 2019: A full SVR pension will be paid out to every eligible survivor, regardless of their age, the contributor’s date of death, the existence of dependent children or disability, as long as the deceased contributor had enough CPP contributions to meet the Minimum Qualifying Period. Due to changes made to the legislation as part of the CPP Triennial Review , beneficiaries who are aged 35 to 45, have no dependent children and are not disabled according to the CPP legislation will have the reduction factor removed from the calculation of the SVR pension amount. Beneficiaries who were receiving a reduced SVR pension had their benefit amounts recalculated to the full amount. Before May 21, 2022 due to system limitations, a workaround to override the SVR pension's age restrictions programmed in ITRDS was required. This workaround was used when the survivor was under the age of 45 at the time of the contributor's death. This workaround applied where a SVR pension was ceased due to a loss of qualifier. In order for ITRDS to override the age restrictions, the Start Date on the ITRDS SVR DSB Periods screen must be: the month following the month of death of the contributor; or 11 months before the receipt date of the second application; and no earlier than January 2019. Effective May 21, 2022 this workaround is no longer applicable. For more information, Survivor's Pension Application

topic_title: Is the recovery rate and/or start date correct? Updated
text: When determining the recovery rate and start date for the departmental receivable, refer to Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) . You must also consider the following: Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) CPMS will automatically set a recovery rate of 100% in cases where the receivable is $100.00 or less. Recovery will start with the next monthly payment following the creation of the receivable. CPMS will automatically set a recovery rate of 25% in cases where the receivable is over $100.00. The recovery starts the second month following creation of the receivable. When the client is in receiving of an OAS income-tested benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW and ALWS ), the rate of recovery should be reduced to 10%. If there are two or more receivables on an active account, CPMS will automatically set up the recovery rate of 25% on each receivable. This would result in a 50% or more recovery from the client's payment. To ensure that only 25% is recovered, you must: modify the recovery rate of the receivable(s) to ensure no more than 25% is recovered; or select a future start date for the second receivable that is after the projected end date of the first one, if the first receivable will be fully recovered in the near future. When the client is entitled to an arrears or retroactive payment from CPP or OAS, apply the full amount of the arrears or retroactive payment to the debt, if applicable. A minimum period of 30 days, from the time a client is notified of an overpayment, must pass before starting recovery from their monthly benefit. However, you are not required to give 30 days notice to the client when you are applying an arrears or retroactive payment against the debt. In cases where the debtor has claimed undue hardship and a reduced rate is supported, the new rate should be set for recovery within 5 or 10 years; Bring Forward (BF) and review after 12 months. Refer to Undue Hardship (Scenario) . Undue Hardship (Scenario) In cases where the debtor declares bankruptcy or files an appeal, you must put the recovery of the debt in Hold status until the disposition by bankruptcy Court or the appeal is finalized. Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Benefit with child rearing drop-out pre-1987 The CRP was implemented in 1983. However, it could not be processed in the CPP Legacy System until 1989. It was processed in the Contin uing Supplementary Cheque System. ITRDS processes all CRP declarations. N/A Child Rearing Provision (CRP) with more than 7 ranges The CRP only applies to periods of time when a dependent child was in the care of the contributor and was under the age of 7. In the CPP Legacy System, these drop- out periods were entered as a series of ranges. The CPP Legacy System could not have accepted more than 7 separate ranges. The benefit had to b e processed in the Co ntinuing Supplementary Cheque System. ITRDS processes a maximum of 19 periods. Accounts with many breaks in the CRP period do not require special handling. N/A

Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Disabled contributor’s child if a Disability (DSB) benefit has a period of zero entitlement If you were gra nting a DSB benefit based on divided earnings, there were no entitlement paid until after the date of attribution of those earnings. If a disabled contributor’s child was also associated to that DSB benefit, the Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit (DCCB) should also have had a period of zero entitlement. At R7, ITRDS was incorrectly putting a DCCB into pay at the DSB benefit effective date instead of the DSB benefit entitlement date. Program Exception Process (PEP) was required to pay all of the accounts of these c hildren correctly. ITRDS correctly processes the DCCB with the entitlement beginning after the date of attribution of the disability earnings. If the sole period of eligibility for a DCCB is within the period of zero DSB benefit entitlement, ITRDS denies the application rather than terminating it at the proper end date. Payments for more than 12 children The CPP Legacy System could not have accepted more than 12 children attached to a ben efit. In addition, if the c hildren’s benefits were for a period before 1975, the system incorrectly calculated the benefit rates. ITRDS has no limit to the number of children attached to a benefit or contributor account. No special processing is required for large families. N/A Previous cross-reference child benefit previously in pay in the Continuing Supplementary Cheque System now entitled to their ow n benefits If c hildren’s benefits were paid through the CPP Legacy System and were then transferred to the Continuing Supplementary Che que System, subsequent benefits payable to the child were rejected in the CPP Legacy System (e.g. DSB benefit, Retirement pension or Survivor's pension). ITRDS adjudicates clients’ accounts with a previous PEP child’s benefit without special processing. ITRDS correctly adjudicates subsequent benefits. N/A

Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Combined accounts with c redit split National Information and Benefit Services (NIBS) processed all combined accounts with a division of earnings on at least one of the accounts. The division of earnings can occur before the combined calculation of benefits. However, NIBS processed the new benefit. The division could occur after the effective date of the benefits. In these cases, recalculation of the combined benefits was done before the file transfer to NIBS. You can process DSB/SVR or RTR/SVR accounts with a credit split in ITRDS without additional intervention. You can process credit split applications in cases wh ere a combined benefit is present in the region. N/A Combined accounts with Pension Sharing (PNSH) NIBS processed all account scenarios in which a client with a combined benefit in pay applied for PNSH. You can process RTR/SVR with PNSH in ITRDS without intervention. N/A Combined accounts with credit split and PNSH NIBS processed all account scenarios in which a client with a combined benefit in pay then applied for both a credit split and PNSH. You can process RTR/SVR with both a credit split and a PNSH in ITRDS without intervention. N/A

You must manually calculate the credit splitting, and any CPP benefits. You must create manual Priority Payments. N/A Send a request to QPP via the QPP Request Screen. Monitor the update on the Contributions Screen to determine if the earnings were updated. Once the earnings are updated, the Credit Split will either re-adjudicate systematically and change to "Approved" or the Service Canada Benefits Officer will be required to re-data capture the Credit Split to ensure the status of the Credit Split changes to "Approved" . Benefits with credit split, dual credit split, or both Any credit split with years of QPP contributions could not initially be processed in the CPP Legacy System; it required Continuing Supplementary Cheque System processing. ITRDS processes a credit split with years of QPP contributions. ITRDS correctly splits the CP P contribution years and sends the request for updated earnings to QPP. This does not require PEP processing. If the date of divorce is before July 1989, eligibility for a QPP division requires that the application be received within 36 months of the divorce. ITRDS does not apply this rule correctly and is granting the division for both CPP and QPP. Only CPP years should be divided.

Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Automatic reinstatement of a Disability (DSB) benefit If a client successfully returned to work, their DSB benefit was cancelled. If the client stopped working due to the same medical problem within 2 years of the DSB benefit cancellation, the DSB benefit could be reinstated upon approval of an application for reinstatement. NIBS processed all automatic reinstatement s. Automatic reinstatement of a DSB benefit can be done in the regions. If a payable is created, you must determine if the arrears payment will be issued within 30 days from the date of receip t of the automatic reinstatement request based on the CPP production schedule. If the arrears payment is not issued, you must issue a CPMS priority payment within 30 days of the automatic reinstatement request. Refer to Payable (Underpayments) . Payable (Underpayments) Client dies after the Date of Onset (DOO), but before the disability effective date. A Death (DTH) benefit application is received and approved. If a DSB benefit was approved, there was a 4-month waiting period between the DOO and the disability effective date. The DOO ended the client’s contributory period. If the client passed away during the waiting period, the DSB benefit never became payable. In these cases, if a DTH benefit application was processed, the system did not end the contributory period with the DOO since the DSB benefit was not paid. The calculation of the DTH benefit was done through Program Exception Process. ITRDS correctly calculates the contributory period based on the presence of a DOO. Special handling is not required. N/A Credit split used to qualify for a DSB benefit National Information and Benefit Services (NIBS) processed all accounts in which divided earnings were present and a client qualified for a DSB benefit using the Late Applicant Provision (LAP). ITRDS correctly adjudicates accounts where credit splitting is used to qualify a client for a DSB benefit. No special handling is required. N/A DSB1 with a LAP DSB2 NIBS processed all accounts when a client qualified for a second DSB benefit using the LAP. ITRDS processes LAP DSB accounts based on whether or not a previous DSB benefit was paid. Combined benefits Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Combined accounts with QPP If a client received both an Survivor's (SVR) pension and a Disability (D SB) benefit or a Retirement (RT R) pension, the benefits’ calculation was combined . If one of the 2 benefits was paid through QPP, ITRDS could not have correctly calculated the combined rate where th e individual rate may be incorrect. If the DSB benefit or the RTR pension was paid through CPP, the SVR pension at QPP would have been incorrect and must have been manually adjusted. If the SVR pension was paid through CPP, the calculation in ITRDS could have been incorrect. The SVR pension would have been incorrectly recalculated if a readjudication occurred. If there is a DSB benefit or an RTR pension application that must be paid though QPP, send the application to Timmins Dual Processing Unit for processing when an SVR is processed in ITRDS. Using the CP P Calculation Module , the Tim mins Dual Processing Unit enters the QPP RTR/DSB amounts, then calculates the actual SVR pension entitlement. If the rate is the same as the amount calculated by ITRDS (this occurs if the RTR/DSB amount is not at the max imum rate), the survivor continues to be paid automatically through ITRDS. This must be revalidated with each readjudication. If the SVR pension rate in ITRDS is not the same as the calculated amount from the CPP Calculation Module, special handling is required. PEP cannot be used in these cases. If the SVR pension amount calculated by ITRDS is lower than the actual entitlement, a manual priority payment must be issued for the additional amount owing each month. If the SVR pension amount calculated by ITRDS is higher than the actual entitlement, the SVR pension will be suspended in ITRDS to prevent any payments without review. CPMS payments are intercepted monthly and a manual priority payment is issued in the correct amount. Decimal round up on QPP percentage If the resulting QPP percentage was greater than 0.99995, the CPP Legacy System incorrectly rounded up to 100%. These cases required processing in the Continuing Supplementary Cheque System. ITRDS correctly calculates the QPP percentage. No special handling is required. N/A Credit Splitting Scenario Original process Revised process Workaround Dual accounts with Credit Splitting Any credit split with years of QPP contributions could not be processed in the CPP Legacy System. Continuing Supplementary Cheque System processing was required. ITRDS can process a credit split with years of QPP contributions. If the date of divorce is before July 1989, eligibility for a QPP division requires that the application be received within 36 months of the divorce. ITRDS does not apply this rule correctly and grants the division of both CPP and QPP. Only CPP years should be divided. Dual credit split with a common-law period before 1999 QPP did not recognize common-law periods before 1999. ITRDS was incorrectly including these periods and dividing them. National Information and Benefit Services (NIBS) performed a manual division and an adjustment of earnings. ITRDS excludes common-law periods before 1999. No special handling is required. topic_title: Appeal of the murder or manslaughter conviction
text: The decision to cancel the benefit as a result of the original court conviction remains in effect until the completion of the appeal process or the final outcome of a new trial. If the client is convicted of a lesser charge or acquitted of the charge altogether at the completion of the appeal process or a new trial, Service Canada will reinstate the benefit in full. This means that the client is entitled to full retroactive payment back to the date of cancellation when they receive the court documentation. The client is responsible for providing any supporting court documentation to Service Canada when the appeal process or a new trial is complete.

The CPP DTH is paid to the Estate, as usual, as long as all eligibility requirements are met under the CPP. The DTH is paid to help pay the funeral expenses of the deceased contributor and does not benefit the applicant. Refer to the appropriate policy under the Program Fundamentals menu. (KA-02835 Snippet 18.0 content. Do not modify or delete.) If there is no estate, you can pay the DTH to the individual convicted of murder, but only if that individual is responsible for payment of the funeral expenses. In such cases, no amount in excess of the actual documented funeral expenses will be paid.

This benefit is cancelled when the beneficiary child is convicted of the manslaughter or murder of their (contributor) parent. An overpayment is calculated back to the effective date of the Surviving Child's benefit.

This benefit continues to be paid to the survivor or guardian who has custody and control of the beneficiary child convicted of the manslaughter or murder of their parent until: the month in which the survivor or guardian no longer has custody and control of the child; or the month in which the child turns 18 years of age.

These benefits are denied or cancelled when a person is convicted for the manslaughter or murder of their spouse or common-law partner. An overpayment is calculated on the account back to the effective date of the benefit.

topic_title: Have previous applications been obtained and matched to the file?
text: Notify the Program Support Clerk to request the previous application(s). If previous applications cannot be located and you need to re-create a file, consult with your manager.

To meet the New Facts criteria, the additional information submitted must meet the two-part test of not discoverable with reasonable diligence and materiality . Only once it is determined that the additional information meets the New Facts criteria can the Department determine whether the New Facts will allow the previous decision to be changed. Not discoverable with reasonable diligence The additional information must refer to something that existed when the Department made its decision and the applicant or former beneficiary, could not have found it even if they made reasonable efforts to obtain all the evidence pertinent to their application. The onus is on the individual to prove that the additional information could not have been previously discovered with reasonable diligence and that had it been available would reasonably be expected to affect the outcome. Reasonable diligence is what is expected from an ordinary, prudent person. You must decide whether the applicant or former beneficiary exercised reasonable diligence and made reasonable efforts to provide the information. There may be exceptional circumstances related to their medical condition that prevented them from acting with reasonable diligence. Exceptional circumstances are determined on a case-by-case basis. Exceptional circumstances may include: medical conditions, injuries, procedures or treatments that affected the person's ability to communicate or to manage their own affairs; mental illness or cognitive impairment; or hospitalization or institutionalization. Materiality Materiality means that the evidence: must be pertinent to the issues and facts that were the subject of the application or reassessment and the final decision; and might reasonably be expected to affect the outcome of the previous decision. The standard of proof for determining if additional information meets the test of discoverable with reasonable diligence and materiality is on "a more likely than not” basis or "the balance of probabilities". For more information, refer to Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) . Once both components are met, it must still be determined if the New Facts and all the evidence considered in the previous decision can allow the final decision to be changed. Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) Additional information that is New Facts New Facts may include: physical and mental conditions that were not well understood by medical practitioners at the time of the previous decision, but have become clearer with time; earnings and contributions (E & C) that were not reported because of exceptional circumstances, such as an employer not submitting contributions; or a fact not previously known to the applicant or former beneficiary but in existence at the time of the final decision and could not have been found even with reasonable diligence. The Federal Court has provided direction that a different diagnosis of the medical condition in and of itself would not bring an applicant closer to a disability benefit in the absence of persuasive evidence that they were disabled within the meaning of the CPP. Additional information that is not New Facts New Facts does not include: most new or modified E & C where the applicant had the knowledge and ability to pay contributions to CPP but did not, or where they were aware of previous work activity and did not report the E & C; information about a change in a medical condition or functional limitations related to a time after the final decision; a medical condition that has deteriorated after the final decision; any new medical condition that is unrelated to the situation that existed at the final decision; any opinions or revisions of an opinion based on previously available and known medical information where the medical conditions were reasonably well known to medical practitioners; copies of medical reports that are already on file or that contain information that is a reiteration of facts available in reports received prior to the final decision; rulings by administrative tribunals and the courts; or clarification or change in policy direction.

A CPPD benefits decision is final (functus officio) in the following situations: The 90-day time limit to request a reconsideration ends and there is no request for a reconsideration. An extension of the time limit to request a reconsideration cannot be provided. For more information, refer to Extension of the 90-day Time Limit to Request a Reconsideration (Scenario) . Extension of the 90-day Time Limit to Request a Reconsideration (Scenario) The 90-day time limit to request an appeal to the SST following a reconsideration decision ends and there has been no appeal to the SST . An exception to functus officio is New Facts. New Facts is additional information submitted after a decision that could not have been previously discovered with reasonable diligence at the time of the original decision and is material to the issue to be determined. The New Facts provision is not another level of appeal and can only be applied in exceptional circumstances. A final CPPD benefits decision by the Department can be re-examined if additional information meets the criteria of New Facts, however it should first be determined if a reconsideration can remedy the situation. Extension of the 90-day Time Limit to Request a Reconsideration (Scenario) If the Department determines that the additional information does not meet the criteria for New Facts, or that the additional information meets the criteria for New Facts but the New Facts will not change the previous decision, there is no right to request a reconsideration. The recourse is to request an appeal to the SST . There is no deadline or limit on the number of times that an applicant or former beneficiary can request a New Facts review regarding a CPPD benefits decision made by the department. Requests for a New Facts review must be made in writing. The Department does not have jurisdiction to revisit decisions by the SST . If you require more information about decisions by the SST and New Facts, submit an inquiry to the IS Appeals GD Box Email . IS Appeals GD Box

topic_title: Are there valid earnings present after the Latest Possible Date of Onset?
text: If there are valid earnings present after the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO), you must: determine if the applicant met the definition of “severe and prolonged” when they last met their LPDOO; and investigate the valid earnings after the LPDOO to determine the applicant's work activity and whether the earnings support the capacity for substantially gainful work, as the earnings may be unrelated to work activity. Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy)

The established Date of Onset (DOO) is a term used for late applicants only. The established DOO is the date on which the applicant's disability started. It is a medically determined date that is separate from the DOO and the LPDOO. However, there will be instances where the established DOO may be adjusted for administrative purposes, i.e. setting the established DOO results in dropped years of earnings needed to qualify, or when the applicant is found disabled prior to the year of a possible prorate date. The CPPD benefit can be approved using the LAP only if the established DOO is on or before the LPDOO. Determine and Record the Established Date of Onset (Action)

topic_title: Valid Earnings After Latest Possible Date of Onset
text: As of January 1, 1998, earnings are valid if they are above the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year External link . Earnings below the DBE are not considered to be a valid year of earnings for the purposes of CPPD and do not require investigation. Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year The DBE is 10% of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings. The applicant can have one to three years of valid earnings after they last met the contributory requirements. The SCBO will identify any years of valid earnings after the LPDOO from the Contributions screen as the Benefits screen in ITRDS only identifies the LPDOO. Earnings after the LPDOO may represent earnings from several sources. This may include, but is not limited to: regular work activity; private benefits; pensionable earnings not from work; foreign work activity; credit splitting; or paid out vacation credits or severance pay. For more information, Valid Earnings after the Latest Possible Date of Onset (Policy)

topic_title: Was credit splitting used to calculate the LPDOO?
text: Credit splitting allows Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings or pension credits to be equally divided between 2 former marital or common-law partners. Additional pension credits attributed to a contributor's record of earnings following the approval of a credit split can improve an applicant's qualifying period or establish one when they do not qualify with their own pensionable earnings. Refer to Credit Split Application (Scenario) and the policy on Credit Split Application (Scenario) Medical Adjudication with Credit Splitting (Policy) Earnings as a result of credit splitting do not represent work capacity.

An application for CPPD benefits is considered late if, at the Date of Application (DOA), the EPDOO is after the LPDOO. The EPDOO is 15 months before the DOA or 12 months before the DOA for applicants that stopped receiving a CPPD benefit within the last 5 years. For PRDB , the EPDOO cannot be before the start of the applicant's Early Retirement pension. The DOA cannot be before 2019, the year PRDB came into force. For more information, Process a PRDB (Scenario) Example An individual submitted their application in April 2020. The LPDOO is December 2015, based on their Earnings and Contributions. The EPDOO is January 2019 (15 months before the DOA) which is after the LPDOO. Therefore, since the LPDOO is before the EPDOO, this is a late application.

topic_title: When you can apply the LAP
text: You can apply the LAP when the applicant: is considered disabled within the meaning of the CPP by the LPDOO; continued to meet the severe and prolonged criteria since the LPDOO to the present time; and will likely be disabled into the future.

topic_title: When you can consider the LAP
text: You can consider the LAP when the: Child Rearing Provision, credit splitting, additional earnings, proration of earnings and previous disability periods have been considered and the applicant still does not meet the current contributory requirements; applicant met the contributory requirements at an earlier date; and applicant claims to have been disabled at an earlier date. This procedure provides you with the steps on how to process a fast-track reapplication for an applicant who was previously in receipt of a CPPD benefit and who meets specific criteria.

Fast-track reapplication is an accelerated application process for applicants whose benefits ceased within the last 5 years. This process receives priority attention through all stages of service. To qualify, applicants must meet the severe and prolonged eligibility criteria under the fast-track reapplication process. The fast-track reapplication is available to applicants who meet all the following criteria: They previously received a CPPD benefit. Their CPPD benefit ceased (i.e. not suspended), and they are not: in an active appeal period; or appealing the cease decision, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or Federal Court of Appeal. They worked or participated in work-like activities(e.g. volunteer or educational activities) after their CPPD benefit ceased and have since stopped. They stopped work or stopped work-like activities within: one year of the date of the fast-track reapplication; and five years of the cease date. They stopped work or stopped work-like activities due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were originally approved. They are applying for the same benefit that was previously in pay. They are not receiving a CPP RTR pension at the date of the recurrence (for DSB applicants only). They are under the age of 65. They meet the earnings and contributions requirements. The fast-track reapplication process is not available to applicants whose benefits ceased due to regained capacity or non-compliance, without evidence the past beneficiary returned to work. For more information, refer to Fast Track Reapplication (Policy) and Automatic Reinstatement & Fast Track Reapplication Reference Guide Share Point link . topic_title: How can a past beneficiary or authorized third party request an AR?
text: To request the reinstatement of a CPPD benefit, a past beneficiary or authorized third party must provide information about the recurrence of the same or related disability. They must also provide the date the past beneficiary: stopped working; or was unable to participate in volunteer or educational activities. When a benefit is ceased, the past beneficiary is provided with personalized AR request forms, if applicable. These AR request forms for a CPPD benefit include the: Automatic Reinstatement of CPP Disability Benefits form; and Automatic Reinstatement of CPP Disability Benefits Physician or Nurse Practitioner Confirmation form. The following documents can also be considered as a request for an AR, if received within the appropriate timeframes: A Fast-Track Re-Application for Canada Pension Plan Disability Benefits form; A Terminal Illness Application Kit for Disability Benefits under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530A) form; An Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151) form; or A signed written statement requesting the reinstatement of their CPPD benefits. If any of these documents are received and accepted as a request for an AR, the PWS work type is changed to Disability Auto Reinstate . These documents are accepted as confirmation of entitlement and generally no additional information is required. However, in some circumstances, file development may be required to support the AR of the benefit. A past beneficiary can upload a copy of their AR request forms to My Service Canada Account by selecting Other/correspondence . This information is uploaded into PWS as a Correspondence work type and the work type must be manually changed to Disability Auto Reinstate . Requests for an AR receive priority attention through all stages of service. It is the intent of the legislation to ensure that payments resume within 30 days of receipt of the AR request.

This procedure provides you with the steps on how to process a request for an Automatic Reinstatement (AR).

AR is not a readjudication of CPPD benefits. It is a return-to-work incentive available to past beneficiaries who were previously in receipt of CPPD benefits and who now meet specific eligibility criteria. There is no limit to the number of times a past beneficiary can request an AR.

topic_title: When a past beneficiary dies and a request for an AR is received
text: If a request for an AR is received from either the past beneficiary or an authorized third party on or before the date of death and within one year of the date the same or related disability reoccurred, their DSB or PRDB can be reinstated if all other criteria are met. If a request for an AR is received after the beneficiary's date of death, the request cannot be granted. For more information, refer to Post-Mortem Applications (Policy) and Post-Mortem Applications (Policy) Automatic Reinstatement—CPPD Benefits (Policy)

topic_title: When is AR not available to past beneficiaries?
text: AR is not available to past beneficiaries who meet any of the following criteria: They were laid off, quit work or stopped work-like activities and do not have a recurrence of the same or related disability within two years after the month their CPPD benefit ceased. They cannot continue to work due to a new disability. They are unable to work due to a recurrence of the same or related disability more than two years after the month in which the benefit ceased. They request a reinstatement of benefits more than one year after the month in which the same or related disability reoccurred. They are currently working. They had their benefits stopped due to regained capacity or non-compliance in the absence of work activity. They had a recurrence of the same or related disability (for DSB beneficiaries only) on or after the start date of their Early Retirement (ERTR) pension or their ERTR pension has been in pay for 15 months or more. If a past beneficiary does not meet the AR requirements they can: appeal the decision to deny the AR; reapply for a CPPD benefit as a fast-track reapplication or a new application with possible consideration as a late applicant, if appropriate. The date of the signed AR request will date protect the application.

topic_title: Who is eligible for AR? Updated
text: Past beneficiaries may request AR if they have stopped work or work-like activities (i.e. volunteer or educational activities) due to a recurrence of the same or related medical condition for which they were originally approved. The CPPD benefit that was previously in pay must be the same benefit that is reinstated. For example, a PRDB cannot be reinstated if a DSB was the benefit previously in pay. To be eligible for AR, the past beneficiary must meet all of the following criteria: They are under the age of 65. They had a recurrence of the same or related medical condition prior to the start date of an Early Retirement (ERTR) pension (for DSB beneficiaries only). Their DSB or PRDB ceased due to a: return to work; participation in an educational activity; or participation in a volunteer activity. They had a recurrence of the same or related disability within 2 years of the date their DSB or PRDB ceased. They submitted a request for a reinstatement within one year of the recurrence of the disability that caused them to stop work or work-like activities (e.g. volunteer or educational activities). Their cease decision is not under appeal, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or Federal Court of Appeal. If a past beneficiary requests an appeal of a cease decision and also requests an AR before the appeal decision is finalized, the AR request will be held in abeyance until the outcome of the appeal is determined. A past DSB beneficiary who started to receive their ERTR pension may be eligible for an AR if they: are deemed disabled before the start date of their ERTR pension; and have been receiving their ERTR pension for less than 15 months. If the above criteria is not met, they may be entitled to a PRDB. However, a new application specifically for the PRDB is required. The trustee must maintain records of CPP and OAS benefits received and spent on behalf of the client. If the Department requires an accounting report for a specific period, the trustee must provide the necessary documentation. The Trustee's Accounting Report (ISP-3509) form states the total amount of benefit payments received for a specified period, including any balance unspent from the last report. When the ISP-3509 form is received, you must review the information provided by the trustee to ensure the money was spent for the benefit of the client.

Absences that occur within an academic year Brian submits an ISP1401 form; it is approved. The school year starts in September 2015 and ends in June 2016. In December 2015, Brian becomes ill and provides an Illness Certificate (ISP1403) confirming his inability to resume school attendance until February 2016. Payment of the children's benefit can continue until February 2016. Absences that last until the end of an academic year Cindy submits a completed ISP1401 form. The school year starts September 2015 and ends April 2016. The vacation period runs from May 2016 until the middle of September 2016, when school resumes again. Cindy's ISP1401 form is approved. Cindy later advises CPP that as of December 2015, she stopped attending school due to illness. She submits an ISP1403 form to support her claim that she cannot resume full-time attendance at school during that academic year. Children's benefits payments must not be suspended in this situation. Cindy is deemed to be in full-time attendance until the end of the normal period of school vacation, i.e. until September 2016. Absences that extend into the next academic year Pierre submits an ISP1401 form; it is approved. The school year starts in September 2015 and ends in June 2016. The vacation period starts in July 2016 and ends in September 2016. In December 2015, Pierre stops attending school due to illness. If Pierre submits an ISP1403 form that is approved, his children's benefit payments will continue for the remainder of the 2015-2016 academic year, including the summer vacation period. Pierre does not resume school attendance during the 2015-2016 academic year, but is able to return to school or university on a full-time basis in the next school year (2016-2017). He must submit an ISP1403 form to confirm that illness was the reason for non-attendance for the full period of his absence. Payment of the children's benefit is made for the full period of absence, including the normal vacation period. If Pierre in the above example does not attend school or university in the 2016-2017 academic year, but resumes attendance in the 2017-2018 academic year, he cannot be considered to have been in full-time attendance, even though he may have otherwise been deemed to have been in full-time attendance in the 2015-2016 year.

Off-site attendance A student took one course by physically attending a university classroom and four courses that the university broadcast on television. The combined total of on-site and off-site courses (5 courses) met the course load requirement for full-time attendance at that university and satisfied full-time school attendance criteria for CPP. Correspondence courses—Documentation requirements Jeanne, the 18-year-old child of a disabled CPP beneficiary, submitted an ISP1401 form for a period of 14 months starting in September. She indicated that she was taking an interior decorating course by correspondence and that she expected to complete 2 courses and spend 6 to 8 hours a week doing course work. When contacted, the school stated that they considered Jeanne a part-time student. The interior decorating program requires completion of 13 courses in 24 months. Jeanne's application for a disabled contributor's children's benefit was denied because she was not fulfilling the requirements of full-time school attendance as defined by CPP. Multiple institutions, day and evening During the same university semester, a 20-year-old child of a deceased contributor takes 2 courses at University A and another course at University B. Each university considers him a part-time student. However. CPP considers him to be a full-time student and entitled to children's benefits. The determining factor is the total number of courses the student is taking in a given period of time.

A mechanic's apprentice submitted an application for children's benefits and an ISP1401 form. He works for a car dealership, where he is working on his mechanic's apprenticeship to receive his certification as a Class A Mechanic. To obtain this certification, he must receive on-the-job training combined with 8 weeks a year of classroom instruction. During the period of classroom instruction, he continues to receive his weekly wage. The period of classroom training is the equivalent of an employer-sponsored training program. The person participating in such a program is not considered to be in full-time attendance by the CPP. The period of time spent in the classroom is too short to make him eligible for children's benefits. By policy, the minimum length of time that will be considered as full-time school attendance is a period of 12 weeks' duration within a 15-week timeframe.

topic_title: Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability benefit ceases with dependent child absent from school or university due to Illness
text: Mr. D's CPP disability benefit ended December, 2015. His 20-year-old son, Sammy, submitted an ISP1403 form to confirm that Sammy became ill in July 2015 and could not attend school for the period from October 2015 to December 2015. Sammy resumed attending school in January 2016. As a result, Sammy was entitled to the children's benefit payments for the October 2015 to November 2015 period.

A student submitted an ISP1401 form indicating that they had enrolled at the Canadian Animal Training Academy, a division of the Bowmanville Zoo. The program has the joint sponsorship of the Youth Internship Program and the Zoological Association of Canada. The program consists of 12 weeks of classroom instruction, followed by a 10-month mandatory hands-on training period at the Bowmanville Zoo. During the 12 weeks that the students are in the classroom, they receive $150.00 a week. During the hands-on portion of the program, they receive $6.85 an hour. After successfully completing the program, students receive a certificate. The completion of this training enables the students to find work in zoos or as animal trainers. The application for children's benefits was approved. The program met the 12 weeks of classroom training, and the hands-on training portion of the program is a graduation requirement.

topic_title: Prerequisite courses and the completion of a program
text: Completion of a program An 18-year-old child of a deceased contributor finished school in June, but did not receive her high school diploma. She returned the following September to take one required additional course in order to graduate. She was considered to be in full-time school attendance by CPP and entitled to children's benefits because she was completing the requirements of her program. This exception shows the underlying purpose of CPP children's benefits. The applicant, being at the end of a certificate course of study, must not be required to take unnecessary courses to qualify for a CPP benefit, particularly as she may not be able to take any additional courses even if she wanted to. Not full-time attendance A disabled contributor's 22-year-old child, out of school for 3 years, returns to university to take 2 courses needed to obtain his B.Sc. degree. Although he is taking the courses to finish his degree, he had interrupted his studies and returned on a part-time basis. As a result of the gap in his attendance, the exception allowing CPP to pay children's benefits by considering him a full-time student while he finishes his degree cannot be applied. Full-time attendance An 18-year-old child of a deceased contributor graduated from high school in June. He was granted conditional acceptance at university. When his final high school marks were submitted, the university did not grant him admission, because he had not achieved the required 60% in Mathematics. He returned to high school in September to retake the Mathematics course to improve his mark. Although he is taking only one course, he is considered a full-time student, which allows him to receive children's benefits from CPP. CPP deems him to be in full-time attendance at high school because he was rejected by the university for not satisfying their entrance requirement. Child taking courses from September to January with eligibility for children's benefits for the full school year David, who is over 18 years old, was in school full time from September 2015 to June 2016 at the grade 12 level. David was not permitted to graduate in June 2016 because he did not have the required number of credits. As a result, David returned to school from September 2016 to January 2017 to obtain the remaining credits. He completed the courses and graduated in January 2017. In February 2017, he applied to enter university in September 2017. He began a full-time university program in September 2017. As a result, David is entitled to benefits from June 2016 to January 2017 because he was completing the requirements for his high school diploma. Regulation 66 of the CPP allows for the payment of a children's benefit during normal school vacation periods. However, David is not entitled to benefits from February 2017 to August 2017. In the scenario above, David received his high school diploma in January, but did not attend school from February to August 2017. He only returned to school full time in September 2017. Regulation 66 of the CPP

Normal vacation periods Example Miranda is the 20-year-old child of a CPP contributor who receives disability benefits. Miranda, who had been out of school for some time, attended university during the January to April term as a full-time student. Because she was in full-time attendance, she was paid children's benefits for the January to April (winter) term. After she completed the winter term, Miranda was absent from school for the normal academic vacation period associated with her university program (May-Aug). Because she had attended a university program full-time up to the end of the semester or school year that immediately precedes the school's vacation period, Miranda was entitled to continued children's benefits payments during the summer vacation. When a child successfully completes an academic year before the beginning of the normal period of school vacation, the child is entitled to receive CPP children's benefits up to the end of the scholastic vacation period. Non-standard vacation periods Michael, the 22-year-old child of a deceased CPP contributor, attended university during the January to April term and continued as a full-time student during the May to August term. He was considered to be in full-time attendance and entitled to children's benefits during the period he was attending school. Michael chose to take his vacation period from September to December. His school vacation period was considered to be from September to December, because he had attended school during 8 of the last 12 months. As a result, Michael was entitled to children's benefits from September to December. The next semester began on January 10. Michael did not return to university for the winter semester and lost his entitlement to children's benefits on February 1. He is no longer in full-time school attendance as of January 10, the date his school vacation period ended. As a result, Michael is not entitled to children's benefits as of the month following the month in which he left school. When the event leading to children's benefits eligibility occurs during a school vacation period, i.e. when: the contributor dies; the contributor becomes disabled; or the child reaches age 18, The child must obtain a Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) for the previous academic year to be paid any benefits during the vacation period. This is necessary because the current school vacation is related to the academic year that just ended. If the child attended school during the school year just ended, that child is eligible for children's benefits payments for the school vacation period which follows the event. For subsequent school years, school vacation period entitlement depends on meeting full-time attendance requirements and the completion of another ISP1401 form. Vacations related to internships or articling Heather, the 23-year-old child of a disabled contributor, was attending school on a full-time basis and obtained her law degree in June. She attended university full time up to the end of the spring semester that immediately preceded the school vacation period. As a result, she was entitled to children's benefits during the summer vacation period that followed. Classes at her university resumed on September 10. CPP considers her a full-time student until that date and to be entitled to children's benefits for the month of September. In October, Heather started articling with a medium-sized law firm. Although she is required to article with a law firm in order to practice law in Canada, her entitlement to CPP children's benefits ends after the payment for the month of September. She is not entitled to it because she now has her degree and is no longer attending school on a full-time basis.

topic_title: Non-beneficiary third party debtor starts receiving OAS benefits New
text: A non-beneficiary third party debtor is an individual who has been deemed responsible for a debt but is not receiving any OAS pension or benefits of their own. If a third party debtor is initially categorized as a non-beneficiary debtor but later becomes eligible for benefits, the outstanding balance must be re-established as a manual overpayment. Cúram automatically calculates the recovery rate based on the maximum deduction amount.

One or more third party debtors may be deemed responsible for a debt incurred on a client's account. Once ISB identifies the liable party or parties, you must verify whether each third party debtor exists in Cúram and confirm if they are currently receiving benefits. This information determines how to record the overpayment and initiate the recovery. Once the debt is set up on the third party debtor's account, write-off the overpayment on the client's account using the Reallocation code for the amount deemed payable by the third party debtor or debtors. Applying the Reallocation code triggers a debt adjustment in PSCD, which reduces the outstanding debt accordingly.

Legislation defines a school or university as a "school, college, university or other educational institution that provides training or instruction of an educational, professional, vocational or technical nature." Acceptable institutions include, but are not limited to: Universities Composite High Schools Comprehensive Schools High Schools Colleges (regular) Community Colleges Military Colleges Business Colleges Bible Colleges Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Collegiate Institutes Convents Novitiates Institutes of Technology Music Academies (School) Polytechnic Schools Schools of Applied Arts and Technology Schools of Nursing Technical Schools Vocational Schools The institution can be located in Canada or abroad. Use the following factors to determine if an institution is acceptable for CPP purposes. It is recognized as an educational institution by a province or territory, or its course of study is affiliated with an institution that is so recognized. It offers the student a diploma or certificate upon completion of the course of study. It provides training that will directly prepare the student for further study at a recognized educational institution. It can demonstrate that the student must attend or otherwise participate in courses (e.g. submit papers, make presentations, write tests, pass examinations and other activities that indicate full-time study).
