Once you have reviewed, considered and assessed all of the evidence on the file and determined that the severe criterion is met, you must consider the prolonged criterion. For more information on determining the severe criterion, refer to Severe Criterion—Medical Condition and Functional Limitations (Policy) and Severe Criterion—Medical Condition and Functional Limitations (Policy) Severe Criterion—Impact of Medical Condition(s) and Functional Limitations on Work Capacity (Scenario) If you determine that the client's medical condition(s) is not severe, you do not consider the prolonged criterion. Prolonged Components For a severe disability to be considered prolonged, based on a balance of probabilities, one of the following two components must be met: the disability is likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration, with no reasonable end in sight based on existing or expected treatment(s) and intervention(s); or the disability is likely to result in death. For more information, Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) It is possible for a disability to be long continued but not of indefinite duration and an expectation of improvement, recovery, or a favourable prognosis for recovery may or may not meet the prolonged criterion. For more information, Prolonged Criterion (Policy) What to consider Consider the following factors to determine if the client's medical condition(s) is likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration: the nature of the medical condition(s); the likelihood that existing or expected treatments or interventions will be successful; past treatment failures; the side effects associated with past, present and future treatments ; the long-term medical conditions (with or without a new exacerbation) that are recurrent, episodic or cyclical; any time frames noted for expected improvement or recovery; and the prognosis: A favourable prognosis may not be enough to determine that the medical condition(s) does not meet the prolonged criterion. When there is evidence of a favourable prognosis, you must use your medical knowledge and experience to carefully weigh all the information on file to determine the impacts on the client's ability to work. Holistically assess the client's individual situation, and consider: their medical condition(s); existing or expected treatment(s) and intervention(s); work capacity; and the impact of personal characteristics (age, education, work experience and language proficiency). OR Consider the following factors to determine if the client's medical condition(s) is likely to result in death: the prognosis; and your knowledge of various medical conditions and their progression.

topic_title: Consider the combined impact of multiple medical conditions on functional limitations New
text: When a single medical condition does not support a severe disability, a holistic assessment considers all medical conditions in combination to determine the functional limitations affecting work capacity, even if the medical conditions are not related. When an individual has two or more medical conditions, this holistic assessment must include the consideration of all relevant physical and mental health conditions identified in the file, as well as the cumulative effect on the capacity to work. Each medical condition is not to be considered individually or in isolation when determining whether the individual's medical conditions prevent them from working. For more information, Consideration of Multiple Medical Conditions (Policy) In assessing the cumulative effect of all the medical conditions, consider the impact of the following: progressive nature of chronic conditions; impact on activities of daily living and increased complexity of self-care; response to medication; impacts of various interventions and treatments; barriers to treatment (e.g. wait list times) and impact of delayed treatment; increased likelihood of having multiple medical appointments; and stress and uncertainty from the impact of all of the above.

topic_title: Consider the nature of the medical condition
text: You can get an idea of the severity in the description of the medical condition. A medical condition described as mild may have little impact on the functional limitations whereas a moderate medical condition may have more impact on functional limitations. A medical condition could be acute or chronic with periods of stability or instability. This may result in fluctuating levels of functional abilities and limitations impacting work capacity. The medical condition and related functional limitations could also be described as progressive, which can demonstrate increased functional limitations affecting an individual's ability to pursue work over time. This information may assist when determining eligibility and establishing a date of onset as functional limitations from a medical condition can occur prior to a diagnosis. While functional limitations may progress, the applicant may not have functional limitations preventing them from pursuing all work at the time of application. The medical condition falls within a spectrum based on the following indicators: mild to severe; acute or chronic; and stable or unstable. The following lists contain the criteria which differentiate an acute and a chronic medical condition: An acute medical condition: can be severe; can have a sudden onset but usually has a shorter duration; can also result in long-term functional limitations; and can become a chronic condition. A chronic/progressive medical condition: develops and worsens over an extended period of time; does not resolve; can cause functional limitations that the individual may be able to adapt to over time; and is relapsing, remitting, episodic in nature, or results in exacerbations. The following lists contain the criteria which differentiate a stable and an unstable medical condition: A stable medical condition: does not deteriorate in health; and does not substantially change over time. An unstable medical condition: is prone to change; and is not controlled. Once you establish the nature of the medical condition(s) based on the above indicators, determine where it falls on the spectrum and how it affects their functional abilities. Refer to the What you need to know section.

topic_title: Determine the impact of functional limitations on work capacity
text: Review the cumulative effect of the functional limitations resulting from the medical condition(s) described by the applicant or beneficiary, the treating practitioner and other health professionals. The same medical condition can affect people differently. For CPPD, the focus is on how the medical condition(s) affect one's capacity to pursue work. The medical condition(s), treatments and personal characteristics can cause limitations in the way a person functions in both daily life and their ability to perform tasks required to work. Keep in mind limitations in one functional ability can impact another. Consider the following when determining the impact of functional limitations on work capacity: how the limitations of physical, emotional or psychological abilities interfere with performing routine activities of daily living and impact their ability to pursue work at any substantially gainful occupation, not just their previous work; and if there are conflicts in the reporting of functional limitations, and clarify as necessary. Refer to Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability Medical Adjudication Guide File Development (PDF, 1.0 MB) Download link . Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability Medical Adjudication Guide File Development Determine the impact of functional limitations on work capacity: on or before the latest possible date of onset for applicants with current earnings and contributions; when the late applicant provision is applied, refer to Late Applicant Provision (Scenario) ; or Late Applicant Provision (Scenario) for beneficiaries to establish continuing eligibility. For more information, refer to Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability Medical Adjudication Guide File Development (PDF, 1.0 MB) Download link and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability Medical Adjudication Guide File Development Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) The following table is a guide to assess how factors related to one or more medical conditions may result in functional limitations to their physical, behavioural, emotional and cognitive abilities affecting their capacity to pursue work. Review each case individually. If a factor appears among the Factors likely resulting in functional limitations (right hand lists below), but the individual is not experiencing resulting functional limitations, it does not affect their work capacity. Table 1. Factors of the medical condition Factors not likely resulting in functional limitations (physical, behavioural, emotional and cognitive) affecting work capacity Factors likely resulting in functional limitations (physical, behavioural, emotional and cognitive) affecting work capacity The nature of the medical condition described as: mild; acute—short term with no lasting limitations; chronic/progressive—early stages identified by: date of diagnosis; good prior work history (no indication of functional limitations); and no fluctuations of prior work patterns or earnings (no indication of functional limitations); and stable—not deteriorating in health without changes over time. The nature of the medical condition described as: severe; acute—may become chronic or be left with permanent limitations; chronic/progressive—advance stages identified by: date of diagnosis; prior work history shows long or frequent absences related to the medical condition; fluctuations in prior earnings correspond to episodes or exacerbations of the medical condition; patterns of prior missed work from the medical condition and resulting functional limitations increasing over time; and frequent job changes; stable—a critical or severe medical condition that is stable with no further deterioration or improvement expected; and unstable—medical condition prone to change or is not controlled. Relapsing remitting condition with: short relapses; long remissions; and no or minimal resulting limitations. Relapsing progressive condition or relapsing remitting with: long periods of relapses; short remissions; and functional limitations increasing over time. Episodes or exacerbations that: are occasional; have no change in frequency or intensity; and have a quick recovery time with no residual functional limitations. Episodes or exacerbations that: are frequent; increase in frequency, intensity and recovery time; and lead to functional limitations that increase after remission to prevent work capacity. Treatment, interventions and appointments (current or planned) that: are curative; are occasional, resulting in minimal or no limitations, for example: chiropractor; massage; some medications (e.g. statins); have flexible scheduling; are close in proximity for the individual; have little or no wait time; provide good results; and result in minimal stress. Treatment, interventions and appointments (current or planned) that: are palliative or only provide symptom relief; are occasional or frequent with resulting limitations, for example: pain medications; or chemotherapy; are frequent or time consuming, for example: chiropractic therapy, physiotherapy or massage 3-4 times a week; hemodialysis; or weekly appointments; have no flexible scheduling; are at a distant location or are difficult to access (no or limited transportation); have long or uncertain wait times with resulting functional limitations from the medical condition; cause side effects such as, but not limited to, fatigue, sleep difficulties, physical or mobility limitations, cognitive issues, depression, and anxiety impacting work capacity; provide poor results; have been exhausted; the individual has a reasonable reason to not follow through due to personal situation; and result in stress due to psychological impacts, personal factors, time, intensity or duration. Medical statements identify: a positive outcome; a minimal or no progression; minimal functional limitations; and an inability to do physical or current work but no indication affecting lighter work. Medical statements identify: a poor outcome; progression over time causing an increase in limitations; functional limitations that impact work capacity; and the presence of multiple medical conditions.

The goal of treatment varies depending on the medical condition(s). Some treatments may be to cure a condition, others to prevent progression or for symptom relief. Once you determine the goal of the treatment, evaluate how it impacts a person's ability to pursue work. A goal of symptom relief may only result in allowing the person to cope with their activities of daily living and the intent is not to improve their ability to return to work. The treatment may also create unintended debilitating side effects impacting the individual's ability to pursue work. The treating healthcare provider in consultation with the individual makes the determination of the best treatment options. The individual may choose not to take part in certain treatment options based on their personal situation. For example, the treatment may not be affordable or located near the individual. Another consideration could stem from psychological impacts due to comorbid conditions and previous negative experiences. For example, a person diagnosed with claustrophobia may choose not to have magnetic resonance imaging, or an individual whose family member died in surgery may be reluctant to consent to an invasive procedure. Frequent or lengthy treatments, interventions and appointments may impact a person's ability to attend work. This also includes travel time and accessibility to the destination. Review past, current and planned treatments, interventions and appointments at the date of adjudication, or the latest possible date of onset. Consider the following indicators: type, duration and frequency; response to treatment; side effects; barriers to treatment (e.g. wait list times) and impact of delayed treatment; impact of stress and uncertainty; and functional limitations arising from the impact of all of the above. Once you consider the above indicators, determine how they impact the individual's functional abilities, referring to the What you need to know section. Determine the resulting functional limitations and if they prevent them from pursuing work.

topic_title: Review medical statements and medical evidence
text: Review healthcare providers' statements and professional opinions detailing the individual's medical history and assessment over time. These should be consistent with the information on file and the applicant's description of their functional limitations. Longitudinal evidence can provide insight into the decline in functioning resulting from the medical condition(s). Consider if: the statements or opinions are consistent with CPP's definition of severe and prolonged; there is information to support the statements; conflicting information is present: ensure statements or opinions are from the same period with no gaps; assess the pertinence and reliability of conflicting pieces of evidence as they relate to the disabling medical condition(s); and address relevant gaps through development; and there is a medical statement that the applicant or beneficiary cannot work. If there is, determine if the individual: cannot return to their previous work; or is unable to do any type of work. When the Medical Adjudicator (MA) medically adjudicates a file to determine CPPD eligibility or continuing eligibility, the applicant or beneficiary must meet the Severe criterion. The MA determines how the functional limitations caused by the medical condition, or by the cumulative effect of multiple medical conditions, impact their ability to pursue work.

Review the information Review all the medical information, including statements and opinions expressed by medical practitioners, health professionals, and the client. Use your health sciences knowledge to assist in determining whether the following factors support an inability to pursue work at any substantially gainful occupation: the nature of the medical condition(s); the impact of multiple medical conditions on functional status; and the impact of treatment and interventions. Review the applicant's responses in section C8 of the application or questionnaires from the reassessment kit to determine which functional abilities may be limited. For more information, Severe Criterion—Medical Condition and Functional Limitations (Policy)

When the individual is not working, you will assess their medical condition(s) and determine how their functional limitations impact their ability to pursue work. If the applicant or beneficiary does not demonstrate work capacity, consider the Prolonged Criterion (Policy) Functional limitations occur when a disability interferes with a person's physical, cognitive or psychological ability to perform the routine activities of daily living and their ability to pursue work. All medical conditions that are likely to affect an individual's ability to pursue work must be considered. A medical condition can affect the following functional abilities: physical abilities: stamina, strength, resistance and flexibility; behavioural abilities: interacting with others and the environment; emotional abilities: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and relationship management; and cognitive abilities: learn, remember, concentrate, plan and execute a goal. The focus for CPPD is on the limitations of functional abilities arising from the medical condition or the cumulative effect of multiple medical conditions.

Accommodation allows persons with disabilities to participate in the workplace. Beneficiaries earning above the substantially gainful occupation amount with accommodations are likely demonstrating work capacity. An example of an accommodation can include flexible or less work hours than others are offered. This differs from sheltered employment, which is for therapeutic reasons rather than to provide an income. For additional guidance, send an enquiry. Go to the Enquiries section below. Enquiries

The main goal of the PSRTW assessment is to confirm ongoing eligibility for benefits, which could involve the following actions: Determine readiness or willingness to RTW. Assess any changes in medical diagnosis, prognosis and functional limitations. Review updated earnings (including self-employment and any pre-grant or new self-employment activity). Determine current work activity, educational or volunteer activities. Consider the results of previous reassessments, if applicable. Consider any prior or ongoing participation in vocational rehabilitation programs, in addition to the potential for participation. The following additional goals of the PSRTW assessment: offer guidance and support; remind the beneficiary of their CPPD benefit reporting responsibilities; and explain all work incentives including allowable earnings, 3-month paid work trial, automatic reinstatement and fast-track reapplication. Development may be required during the PSRTW review or when a beneficiary reports an improvement in their medical condition or adaptation to their functional limitations that may increase their overall work capacity. The decision maker must assess whether the reported improvement relates to only the ability to perform basic activities of daily living or whether it demonstrates increased capacity to regularly pursue any substantially gainful occupation. Once the PSRTW assessment is completed, one of the following outcomes occurs: The benefit is continued, and if required, a new PSRTW date is set. A referral is made to the CPP Disability Vocational Rehabilitation Program. The benefit is ceased. topic_title: Is there a claim or allegation of erroneous advice or administrative error?
text: A claim or allegation of Erroneous Advice/ Administrative Error (EA/AE) made by a beneficiary or an authorized third party during the reassessment, at any level, must be fully investigated. The Minister may also initiate remedial action in the process of reviewing an application or file if it is noticed that an EA/AE has occurred in the processing of a pension, benefit or provision. If the EA/AE is likely to result in an overpayment , the investigation must be completed after the decision on the reassessment has been made and appeal rights expired. If the EA/AE is likely to result in an underpayment , the investigation must be initiated immediately, prior to the completion of the reassessment decision. topic_title: Was an incorrect date of onset discovered?
text: If an incorrect date of onset is discovered, it is corrected before processing the final reassessment decision. For more information, refer to Correct a Date of Onset at Reassessment (Action) KA-02310 (article not available).

PSRTW assessment The PSRTW assessment can be set at any level of adjudication (i.e. initial, reconsideration, SST or reassessment). A PSRTW may be set when: a Return to Work (RTW) is considered likely, based on the expected course of the disabling medical condition; there is potential for recovery with treatment; or there is potential for the beneficiary to adapt to ongoing functional limitations. This type of assessment can occur when: a medical adjudicator, medical advisor (in the Medical Expertise Division) or an SST member has scheduled a future review of the file to confirm continued eligibility for a CPPD benefit; the beneficiary informs the Department of an improvement in their medical condition or functional limitations; or the beneficiary reports engaging in work-like activities (i.e. educational or volunteer activities) for 15 hours or more per week for 4 months or more. For more information, refer to Severe Criterion—Assess Educational and Volunteer Activities (Action) . Severe Criterion—Assess Educational and Volunteer Activities (Action) Once the PSRTW assessment date has been set, this date is entered into the beneficiary's accounts in both ITRDS and the Rules Based Reassessment System ( RBRS ). From RBRS , the PSRTW date is loaded into PWS under the Reassessment Triggers work type with the Prescheduled Return to Work Description field. For more information, PWS Disability Reassessment Triggers The PSRTW trigger is actioned, according to the due date, by the reassessment unit.

topic_title: When a PSRTW assessment is not initiated Updated
text: A PSRTW assessment is not initiated in the following circumstances: The beneficiary is not in pay. An assessment or reassessment is already in progress. The beneficiary is participating in the CPP Vocational Rehabilitation program. The beneficiary dies before the scheduled PSRTW date and no other trigger or evidence of work activity exists. The case is at any appeal level, including an appeal to the SST (General Division (GD) or Appeal Division (AD)) or Federal Court of Appeal. For beneficiaries reassessed previously with a continues to be decision based on sheltered or benevolent work, go to the Sheltered or inclusive employment section below. These beneficiaries still require a review to determine if there is a change in employment status, earnings, employer (or business under new management) or medical condition. The following examples of significant change may include: A change of employer. The number of hours worked increases to 5 or more hours per week. A promotion within the same organization (higher level of responsibility and salary). An increase in salary or wages above standard cost of living increases. Minor increments in salary are not significant and do not indicate an increase in work capacity. The medical condition has improved, which means the individual is no longer experiencing functional limitations that regularly prevents them from demonstrating overall work capacity. For these cases, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Share Point link (access is required). (KA-04735 Snippet 35.0 content. Do not modify or delete.) National Business Expertise Tool

Accommodation allows persons with disabilities to participate fully in the workplace. Beneficiaries earning above the substantially gainful occupation amount with accommodations are likely demonstrating work capacity. An example of an accommodation can include flexible or less work hours than offered to others. This differs from sheltered work, which is for therapeutic reasons, rather than to provide an income. Sheltered work is an exception occurring in rare circumstances. topic_title: Are there earnings associated with retraining or rehabilitation?
text: When a beneficiary is in receipt of long-term disability insurance or workers' compensation benefits there may be opportunities for them to participate in rehabilitation or retraining programs. The wages of a CPPD beneficiary are sometimes paid in partnership by their insurance providers. Over time, as the program progresses and the beneficiary's work activity increases, the employer resumes paying the beneficiary's salary. When the allowable earnings amount has been reached, after the employer resumes paying the beneficiary's salary due to completion of the rehabilitation or retraining program and work capacity is demonstrated during the observation month, the 3-month paid work trial can be set at that time. For more information, refer to Severe Criterion—Work Capacity (Regular Employment, Self-Employment, Seasonal and Accommodated) (Scenario) and Severe Criterion—Work Capacity (Regular Employment, Self-Employment, Seasonal and Accommodated) (Scenario) Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy)

topic_title: Factors to consider when a beneficiary has reported an unsuccessful attempt to return to work
text: When a beneficiary has reported an unsuccessful attempt to return to work, consider if the following factors apply: The medical condition or functional limitations continue to be disabling. The beneficiary reported: that they stopped work because they quit or were laid off; the end of seasonal work; a return to a job with minimal or irregular hours of work because that was their preference or it was the only work that was available; or a failed work attempt after working for more than 3 months. In cases where the work trial was not completed or was deemed unsuccessful, for reasons not related to the medical condition or functional limitations, overall work capacity may be demonstrated, and benefits may be ceased. If further guidance is needed, send an enquiry to receive further instructions.Go to the Enquiries section below. Enquiries

topic_title: If you are unable to contact the beneficiary by phone at the end of the 3-month paid work trial
text: When you are unable to contact the beneficiary by phone at the end of the 3-month paid work trial period: Review all systems including PWS , Pensions Trusted Digital Repository and Rules Based Reassessment System ( RBRS ) to verify that a Report on an Unsuccessful Attempt to Return to Work form has not been received by the Department; and Review ITRDS Notes to verify that the beneficiary has not called the Department to report an unsuccessful work trial. topic_title: Is the reported return to work seasonal?
text: Seasonal work is work activity that occurs around the same time each year, for a certain length of time, and generally has prearranged start and end dates. When assessing seasonal work, it is important to identify the time, length of the seasonal work, and determine if the work activity is aligned with that type of work. For example, if a season lasts only a few months and the beneficiary is able to complete the work required for the position, the beneficiary returning for a second consecutive season shows predictability aligned with this type of work. For more information, refer to Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy) and Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy) Assess Self-Reported Seasonal Employment at Reassessment (Action)

text: The letter sent to the beneficiary during their 3-month paid work trial period includes the Report on an Unsuccessful Attempt to Return to Work form. Most CPPD beneficiaries will notify the call centre when they Return to Work (RTW). However, some may report their RTW at the In-Person Centres, via letters, or during phone calls with staff. topic_title: When a self-reported RTW assessment is not initiated Updated
text: A self-reported RTW assessment is not initiated in the following circumstances: an assessment or reassessment is already in progress; the beneficiary is participating in the CPP Vocational Rehabilitation program; or the beneficiary is at any level of appeal including an appeal to the SST (General Division (GD) or Appeal Division (AD)) or Federal Court of Appeal. For beneficiaries reassessed previously with a "continues to be" decision based on sheltered or benevolent work, see the Sheltered or inclusive employment section below. These beneficiaries still require a review to determine if there is a change in employment status, earnings, employer (or business under new management) or medical condition. Examples of significant change may include the following cases: change in employer; increase in number of hours worked per week by 5 or more hours; promotion within the same organization (higher level of responsibility and salary); increase in salary or wages above standard cost of living increases. Minor increments in salary are not significant and do not indicate an increase in work capacity; or Improvement in the medical condition, meaning the individual is no longer experiencing functional limitations that regularly prevents them from demonstrating overall work capacity. For these cases, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Share Point link (access is required). (KA-04735 Snippet 35.0 content. Do not modify or delete.) National Business Expertise Tool

Accommodation allows persons with disabilities to participate fully in the workplace. Beneficiaries earning above the substantially gainful occupation amount with accommodations are likely demonstrating work capacity. An example of an accommodation can include flexible or less work hours than others are offered. This differs from sheltered work, which is for therapeutic reasons rather than to provide an income. Sheltered work is an exception occurring in rare circumstances. Send an enquiry to receive further instructions when assessing accommodated employment. Go to the Enquiries section below. Enquiries

topic_title: Addressing possible misrepresentation, SIN misuse or error
text: During review of the file, if you suspect misrepresentation or SIN misuse, do not contact the beneficiary by phone and do not suspend or cease the benefit. In these cases, you must refer the file to the Integrity Services Branch. Do not use the words "fraud" or "abuse" in your documentation. Instead, use words like "discrepancy" or "anomaly". For more information, refer to CPPD Reassessment Referral to Integrity Services Branch (Action) KA-03422 (article not available).

topic_title: Are the earnings from possible SIN misuse or error?
text: There are situations in which earnings are reported but, following a review of the file, it is determined that they were not from the beneficiary's work activity. These situations can occur when work is done: by someone using the beneficiary's SIN; by someone deliberately impersonating the beneficiary; or as a result of an error (i.e. income is credited to the beneficiary instead of another employee with the same name working at the same company). For more information, refer to CPPD Reassessment Referral to Integrity Services Branch KA-03422 (article not available).

topic_title: Are there earnings with CPP contributions listed as $0? Updated
text: Earnings with CPP contributions listed as $0 in the ITRDS Earnings screen can be from: an honorarium, which is a payment made in the beneficiary's name for services rendered without charge (i.e. a guest speaker or lecturer). These earnings can be from municipal governments, school boards, townships or management fees paid by corporations; or long-term disability benefits, which can come from various sources including insurance companies, government agencies and employers. A reassessment is required to determine the nature of the earnings (i.e. are the earnings indicative of work capacity?).

topic_title: When a CPP/EI RISE reassessment is not to be initiated Updated
text: A CPP/EI RISE reassessment will not be initiated in the following circumstances: The beneficiary is not in pay. However, a reassessment is still conducted in certain circumstances, such as if the beneficiary now receives an RTR pension or if they die before the reassessment is initiated. An assessment or reassessment is already in progress. The beneficiary is participating in CPP Vocational Rehabilitation Services. The beneficiary's case is at any level of appeal, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or Federal Court of Appeal. For beneficiaries who were previously reassessed with a "Continues to be" decision based on sheltered or benevolent work, go to the Sheltered or inclusive employment section. These beneficiaries still require a review to determine if there are changes in the medical condition, employment status, earnings or employer (or business under new management). A few examples of significant change may include one or more of the following: The employer changes. The number of hours worked per week increases by 5 or more hours. There is a promotion within the same organization (higher level of responsibility and salary). There is an increase in salary or wages above the standard cost of living increases. Minor increments in salary are not significant and do not indicate an increase in work capacity. The medical condition has improved, meaning the individual is no longer experiencing functional limitations that regularly prevents them from demonstrating overall work capacity. For these cases, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Share Point link (access is required). If an application has inconsistencies and documentation must be provided, the applicant must provide details of their residence from age 18 to the present and proof of all dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries into Canada, as required. If the applicant was born outside of Canada and was a resident in Canada at age 18, proof of the latest date of entry before age 18 is required. For applicants born outside of Canada who entered into Canada on or before July 1, 1977, and who qualify for a full OAS pension under the 10-year rule or the 40-year rule, the normal documentation used to verify the original date of entry into Canada is not required if Canadian citizenship was obtained before July 1, 1977. If an applicant can provide proof of Canadian citizenship before July 1, 1977, with their application, this is considered acceptable documentation to prove the original date of entry into Canada. However, if the application is approved under the 10-year rule, absences exceeding 6 months within the 10-year period must be documented with proof of each entry, departure and re-entry. If the applicant has not resided in Canada continuously since July 1, 1977, proof of entry is required for the period that includes the last 10 years. If the applicant is not residing in Canada at the time of application, proof of final departure must be provided.

For the residence history to be considered complete, it must state all periods of residence in Canada and absences from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement. For example, if an applicant born outside of Canada qualifies under domestic legislation, only the residence history from the date of initial entry into Canada is required. If an applicant qualifies under an International Social Security Agreement, a complete residence history from age 18 to present is required. In general, absences of less than one year do not necessarily interrupt residence and may not need to be investigated. The application should be processed based on the stated residence history, unless there is a pattern of frequent absences over a period of several years, as it could be indicative of presence rather than residence. Absences from Canada over one year can interrupt residence unless the absence is: of a temporary nature; for the purpose of attending school or university; or deemed as residence in Canada under a specified circumstance. When an individual claims a large number of separate periods as Canadian residence, the decision regarding the periods of residence must be based on a judgment of the particular circumstances of the case. In certain situations, there will be no alternative but to accept the statement of the applicant for at least part of the claimed residence. In dealing with these cases, it is reasonable to require something more than a signed statement from a reference supporting an applicant’s claim. An agent should contact the applicant and the references by telephone and interviewed whenever possible, as interviews can turn up pertinent information. If, after an interview, the applicant's claim still lacks credibility, or that there is concern about potential impropriety, the file should be referred to the Integrity Services Branch. In difficult residence cases, if, after a thorough review, judgment dictates that there is insufficient proof of residence or that there is a lack of credibility in the applicant’s statement, then any decision to deny the application should be made on that basis. Contact the individual when: there is information on the residence history or the application that indicates their residence in Canada can be deemed residence for OAS purposes; there are contradictions on the residence history itself; or the residence history is not complete. After contacting the individual, if the number of 40ths changes, obtain additional information and/or amendments to the residence history in writing.

topic_title: Exact dates of entry, departure and return are unknown
text: When it is not possible for applicants to state the exact day in a month on which they entered or left Canada and the date cannot be confirmed with documentary evidence, the day of entry or day of departure is assumed to have been the 15th of that month. Using the 15th day of the month in calculating residence when the actual day of entry or departure is not certain also requires careful review, especially when the calculation results in non-entitlement to a benefit. Steps must be taken to ensure that all possible measures of obtaining the exact date of entry or departure have been exhausted before resorting to the procedure of using the 15th day of the month. Similarly, when applicants are only able to provide a general statement as to when they entered or left Canada, the following guidelines must be used for residence calculation purposes: Statement provided by the applicant Assumed date for OAS purposes April-May May 1 June, July or August July 15 Spring (March 22-June 21) May 6 Summer (June 22-Sept. 21) August 6 Autumn (Sept. 22-Dec. 21) November 6 Winter (Dec. 22-March 21) February 6
OAS Regulations Section 20—Statement of Residence Required Section 21—Residence, Presence and Absences Section 22.1—Sponsored Immigrants’ Exceptions

The official documents below are required to prove dates of entry into and return to Canada: Immigration records (e.g. Canadian Immigration Identification Card, IMM 1000, IMM 1436, IMM 1097, IMM 5716 or a valid Temporary Resident permit [formerly called a Minister’s Permit]); Stamps in passports; Customs declaration; or airline, ship or bus tickets (including electronic tickets); The official documents below are required to prove dates of departure from Canada: Immigration records; Stamps in passports; United States documents (e.g. Alien Registration Receipt Card [Green Card], Visa, Customs Declaration, Letter from U.S. Department of Justice, Immigration and Naturalization Service). If the date appearing on the immigration record “Permanent Resident Card (Green Card)” is different from the date of the departure claimed by the applicant, obtain an explanation and another document to substantiate the claimed date of departure from the applicant: airline, ship or bus tickets (including electronic tickets); Old unemployment insurance work booklets showing last week contributions were made; Residence certificate or record of contributions from a country with which Canada has an ISSA in force.

When official documents supporting dates of entry into, departure from or return to Canada cannot be obtained (e.g. IRCC does not have a record or the applicant does not have an official document) other documentary evidence such as the following may be used: letters from employers or religious orders; school records; contracts (e.g. public utility, insurance, mortgage, lease); Census of Canada records; letters from band councils or a representative from Aboriginal organizations. All letters submitted by any organization or institution to support dates of entry into or departure from Canada must: be on official letterhead; be signed by an official; be consistent with other information on the applicant’s OAS file; contain detailed information regarding residence; include periods when the individual resided inside and outside of Canada; contain the physical home address of the applicant for periods in Canada.

ITRDS Contributions screen The ITRDS Contributions screen does not contain all the required information to properly evaluate periods of residence. It can only be used to determine whether a contribution was made in a given year. The length of time over which these contributions were made (e.g. 2 months, 6 months, a full year) is difficult to determine from the information provided on this screen. As a result, the ITRDS Contributions screen cannot be used as the sole source of documentary evidence to validate the applicant’s original date of entry into Canada and periods of residence in Canada. It can be used to support residence in addition to other documentary evidence. Third party statements and references When applicants are unable to provide documentary evidence, a third party statement from a reference provided by the applicant may be accepted. When corresponding with a reference, inform them that their name has been given by the applicant as an individual able to confirm the facts of the applicant’s residence request and confirm that the applicant lived in Canada between certain dates or, if not, ask them provide whatever information they can. Statutory declarations As a last resort, it may be necessary to accept a statutory declaration from the applicant.

Residence for OAS purposes is determined by ensuring that the time an individual is physically in Canada is actually residence and not merely presence. Similarly, an individual who may not be physically (i.e. present) in Canada, may be considered as having residence in Canada (deemed). The documentary evidence to support dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries to Canada to establish periods of residence in Canada may not always be required as described below. However, where applicable, the requirement for documentary evidence when determining residence rather than presence, and when deeming periods of absences from Canada under specified circumstances, still applies. The policy Defining Residence describes the circumstances when these residence determinations are required. Section 20 of the OAS Regulations does not specifically require documentary evidence to support the residence history on an OAS application or residence statement. An application or residence statement that has been signed and that provides a statement of all periods of residence and absences from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement fulfills the residence requirement. Defining Residence Since June 5, 2017, provided the eligibility requirements of age and legal status are met, residence for all initial OAS pension applications processed under domestic legislation can be established through a review of the residence history on the application against all available documents currently on file. If there are no inconsistencies between the residence history provided on the application and any documents on file, there is no requirement for proof of all dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries into Canada. On November 20, 2017, the policy was extended to include all initial OAS pension applications processed under an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA). As of July 2019, this policy was extended to situations when confirmation of residence in Canada is required by a foreign institution with which Canada has an ISSA in force. This operational policy applies to both full and partial pensions, including those that may qualify under transitional rules or ISSAs and all OAS applications. This also includes applications for the Allowance or the Allowance for the Survivor benefit and conversion applications. This operational policy must be applied when there are no inconsistencies between the residence history or residence statement and the available documents currently on file, even if proof is missing for some or all of the dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries into Canada. Any requests for reconsideration will require applicants to provide documentary evidence of residence, even if the initial decision on the application was made under this interim process. However, if the beneficiary has requested a reconsideration of an approved benefit under the above policy on the basis that the entitlement is incorrect and a specific period is being disputed, it would be acceptable to request documentation for that period only. Documentary evidence to support residence is waived for individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension. These individuals must meet all the eligibility requirements for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension through a combination of data elements when an individual is in the following situations: was not selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension; submits a paper application to apply for a full OAS pension under the 40 year rule; and meets the data elements to substantiate eligibility for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension. In these cases, an individual may have their eligibility determined for an OAS pension by using the same combination of data elements. In October 2013, the Department was given the authority through a Service Level Agreement to go directly to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada to verify the initial date of entry for residence purposes as long as the Department obtains the written consent from the applicant or their authorized representative.
