There are areas in the CPP and OAS legislation that require broad discretionary decision-making. These areas are characterized by expressions such as "...the Minister is satisfied that...", "...if, in the opinion of the Minister..." or "...the Minister may...". The 2 major areas requiring broad discretionary decision-making are: the authority to take remedial action to grant a benefit on the basis of administrative error or erroneous advice; and the authority to remit an overpayment on the basis of administrative error or erroneous advice.

The responsibility for making discretionary decisions under the CPP and the OAS Act is delegated by the Minister to departmental officials, who must make decisions in the administration of this legislation that affect applicants or beneficiaries. The legislation for the delegation of power can be found in the Interpretation Act . The Interpretation Act is sufficient authority for the kind of sub-delegation scheme that the Department has devised. Program administrators have been given responsibility for making decisions that affect applicants or beneficiaries. Before deciding to sub-delegate any of their powers or duties to a subordinate, the individual who holds the delegated authority must verify that the level of authority of the individual selected to exercise ministerial discretion is appropriate given the nature and importance of the decision or task at hand. The responsibility for the final decision rests with the individual who has the delegated responsibility to make it. It is critical for program administrators to remember they are making a decision on behalf of the Minister when they exercise ministerial discretion.

Canada Pension Plan Section 55—Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings for Divorces and Annulments before the Coming into Force of section 55.1 Section 55.1—Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings—When mandatory division to take place Section 55.2(3)—Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings—Agreement binding on Minister Section 81(1)—Reconsiderations and Appeals—Appeal to Minister Interpretation Act Section 24(2)—Appointment, Retirement and Powers of Officers—Power to act for ministers

In the majority of cases, the decision-maker does not exercise ministerial discretion in determining an applicant or beneficiary’s eligibility for or continuing eligibility to benefits. The legislation has set out explicit eligibility criteria, such as age of eligibility, start date of benefits and minimum contributory requirements so that there is no need to exercise a significant degree of judgment. In such areas, there is no discretion—the legislation and case law combine to stipulate the “rules” to follow. An example where no discretion is allowed can be found in subsection 55.2(3) of the CPP, which states that the Minister shall not make a credit split (legislatively known as a "division of unadjusted pensionable earnings") under section 55 or 55.1 when a spousal agreement is binding on the Minister.

Ministerial discretion is the flexibility provided in the legislation to accommodate an exception to the general rules. It allows decisions to be made on a case-by-case basis. There is an obligation on the part of employees to exercise this delegated authority when necessary. A discretionary decision involves carefully weighing the facts of an individual’s circumstances and applying relevant policy guidelines and applicable legislation to them. Responsible decisions are made based on sound administrative practices. This does not mean always deciding in the applicant’s favour. Decisions made when administering the CPP and OAS programs involve the use of discretion. The exercise of discretion in decision-making is a responsibility set out in both the CPP and the OAS Act. Legislators grant authority for the use of discretion because the legislation itself cannot address all of the circumstances that arise in the administration of programs as complex as the CPP and the OAS. Discretion can also allow—within the limitations of the legislation—for programs to adapt to new situations and changing times. Discretion must be used in a way that maintains the goals of the legislation and cannot be used to circumvent the purposes of the legislation. To the individual, the result of a discretionary decision—as with any decision about their case—has considerable impact (e.g. if they must pay back an overpayment). When the legislation says "the Minister may...", ministerial discretion is implied in that section of the legislation. When the legislation says "the Minister shall...", there is no discretion on the part of the Minister. In some instances, "the Minister may..." can be used to meet individual circumstances when it is to the applicant or beneficiary’s advantage or when the applicant or beneficiary makes a request for ministerial discretion to be applied to their case. For example, section 81 of the CPP provides the means for an individual to request a reconsideration of an earlier decision made by the Minister when they do not agree with that decision. The individual must make their request for reconsideration in writing within 90 days after the day they were notified of any decision. However, the Minister may extend the 90-day period in extenuating circumstances: within 365 days of notification of the initial decision; and beyond 365 days following the notification of the initial decision. It is the use of the word "may" in subsection 81(1) that allows the Minister to exercise discretion regarding the 90-day period when there are exceptional or extenuating circumstances. Only on rare occasions can the Minister’s approval be sought to apply a discretionary decision to a group of cases.

If an individual is dissatisfied with a decision made in accordance with ministerial discretion, that individual cannot request a reconsideration or an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal. The individual must apply to the federal court for judicial review of the Minister’s decision.

After an application and any supporting documentary evidence is received and reviewed, the application is approved as long as the applicant is eligible for a pension or benefit. When approving ensure to: calculate the pension or benefit amount; determine the effective month to begin; determine the payee for the pension or benefit; establish a method of payment where entitlement exists; and advise the applicant in writing of the pension or benefit details as well as of their right to reconsideration or appeal.

When denying an initial application for a pension or benefit, the applicant must be informed of their right to request a reconsideration of the decision. The decision must be communicated to the applicant in writing and provide the applicant with the reason(s) for the denial.

Canada Pension Plan Subsection 60(7)—Consideration of application and approval by Minister Section 81—Reconsiderations and Appeals, Appeal to Minister Old Age Security Act Section 16—Payment of Supplement, Consideration of application or waiver Section 24—Payment of Allowance, Consideration of application or waiver Section 27.1—Reconsiderations and Appeals,:Request for reconsideration by Minister

Paper and online applications A decision to approve or deny a valid application for a pension or benefit must be made as soon as can be reasonably done after its receipt. The applicant must also be notified, in writing, of the decision. Decisions to approve or deny CPP and OAS pension or benefit applications are made after assessing the information and documentation received. Based on the information and documentation the applicant provided, an application can be approved: for a pension or benefit payable at a reduced rate; or for a lesser period of retroactivity (e.g. an OAS pension paid at a reduced number of 40ths, or a CPP Disability benefit paid at a later effective date). Similarly, an application can be denied because the applicant has not provided sufficient information to determine their eligibility to the pension, benefit or provision. OAS automatic enrolment For OAS, if an individual is selected for automatic enrolment, the individual is notified in writing of the Department’s intent to: waive the application form; and provide the individual with the information the Minister intends to use to determine their eligibility. Approval and denial

Old Age Security Act Section 5.1(1)—Withdrawal of an application CPP regulations Subsection 45(1),(3),(5)—Application for benefits, for assignment of a retirement pension and for division of unadjusted pensionable earnings

An application for a CPP benefit or an OAS pension can be withdrawn if: the applicant requests in writing to withdraw their application; and the request is received before the benefit or pension payment is issued. It is not necessary to withdraw an application for a CPP benefit or an OAS pension if the applicant requests a change to the effective date and the new date they request is within one year (before or after) of the date the application was received, the requested change can be made if the Department has not yet: finalized a decision on the application; communicated a decision to the applicant ; and issued any payments. After an application is withdrawn, applicants must be advised in writing that a new application is required if and when they decide to re-apply in the future. Eligibility to a pension or a benefit will be based on the new application and not on the application that was withdrawn. CPP Credit Split (Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings) For the policy and parameters on the withdrawal of a CPP Credit Split, CPP Credit Splitting (Policy) Guaranteed Income Supplement, Allowance and Allowance for the Survivor benefits There is no authority in the OAS Act to withdraw an application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), the Allowance ( ALW ) and the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ). A beneficiary may, however, request in writing that the GIS, ALW or ALWS cease .

topic_title: CPPD benefits—Onus and burden of proof Updated
text: Reassessment Reassessment review is the only area where the burden of proof lies primarily on the Minister. The Department, on behalf of the Minister, must show the beneficiary has ceased to be disabled according to the CPP legislation. When CPPD benefits are ceased, the onus is with the Minister to show the beneficiary is no longer disabled. At the reassessment level, there is also an onus on the Department to periodically review cases of individuals who are receiving a CPPD benefit to ensure continuing eligibility. The beneficiary or their authorized representative is responsible for providing or reporting: a return to work once they have gross earnings at or above the allowable earnings threshold; if they are participating in education or volunteer activities after four months at 15 hours or more per week; if there has been an improvement in their medical condition; and/or all documents and information required to support the beneficiary's continuing eligibility, including information related to: earnings; hours worked or participated in volunteer or educational activities; absences; nature of the activity or tasks; any accommodations; and any changes to the above that occurred since the last decision. all documents and information required to support the beneficiary's continuing eligibility. The Department is responsible for reviewing and investigating any: reported return to work or educational or volunteer activities; triggers related to unreported earnings or work activity; pre-scheduled return to work triggers; reported regained capacity; and/or third party complaints.

Canada Pension Plan Section 52—Earnings for which base contribution deemed to have been made for month Section 69—Disability Pension and Post-retirement Disability Benefit—Commencement of pension Section 70—When pension ceases to be payable CPP regulations Section 69(1)(2)(3)—Determination of disability OAS regulations Section 3—Forms for applications Section 4—Forms for applications Section 5—Approval for an application for a pension Section 19—Evidence of age and identity Section 23—Further information and investigation before or after the approval of an application or after the requirement of an application is waived Section 26—Suspension of payments

The burden of proof regarding determinations of eligibility for benefits at the initial, reconsideration, and other levels of appeal lie with the applicant . This applies even when the Minister is the appellant as well. Regulations state that after an individual has applied for a pension, benefit or provision, they are responsible to provide the information necessary to determine their eligibility or entitlement. Once an individual is in receipt of benefits that contain an ongoing eligibility or entitlement requirement, they are responsible for notifying the Department about any information that could affect the status of their benefit or continuing eligibility or entitlement. This includes and is not limited to a change: of address; in marital status; in medical condition; in custody and control of a dependent. When there is evidence a beneficiary is no longer entitled to a benefit, the legislation places the onus on the beneficiary to return any pension or benefit money received by them, to which they were no longer entitled. Allegations of erroneous advice or administrative error When an individual alleges erroneous advice or administrative error, the onus is on the applicant or beneficiary or their authorized representative to submit evidence to support the allegation by providing: dates of events; documents; and/or names and description of conversations with Departmental employees.

The Department is responsible for making a decision in a timely manner and communicating that decision to the applicant. There are situations when the Department is required and is responsible to provide information to applicants who may be uncertain or unaware of other possible pensions, benefits or provisions to which they may be entitled. The Department has the responsibility to inform applicants of the following provisions: Credit splitting There is an onus on the Department to inform CPP applicants about the Credit splitting provision (division of unadjusted pensionable earnings) if they indicate they are divorced or separated. Child Rearing Provision There is an onus on the Department to inform CPP applicants about the Child Rearing Provision when children are indicated on an application. International benefits File transfer There is an onus on the Department to transfer a file to International Operations (IO) if: the applicant does not qualify for a benefit or pension under domestic legislation at the earliest effective date and indicates residence and/or contributions in a country with which Canada has an international agreement in force that contains benefit provisions; an individual with a partial OAS pension in pay decides to reside permanently outside of Canada, but: does not have the required 20 years of residence in Canada after reaching age 18 to export the pension; and indicates residence and/or contributions in a country with which Canada has an agreement in force that contains benefit provisions; a spouse or common-law partner requires an international agreement to qualify for an OAS pension or an Allowance benefit; an individual applies for a CPP pension or benefit and is or was receiving a CPP pension or benefit and requires an international agreement to qualify for an additional CPP pension or benefit; or an individual applies for a CPP pension or benefit and is or was receiving a CPP pension or benefit from IO. Possible eligibility to foreign benefits The Department must send the applicant a letter advising them of their possible entitlement to foreign benefits along with the appropriate application form if the applicant: applied for a benefit under domestic legislation; indicated residence and/or contributions in a country (except the United States of America) with which Canada has an international agreement in force that contains benefit provisions; and indicated they have not previously requested a benefit from that country. If an applicant is eligible to receive a benefit under domestic legislation and indicates residence and/or contributions in the United States, no action is required if : the applicant indicates on their Canadian pension or benefit application that they have already requested a benefit from the United States; or there is an indication that an application for United States benefits has been received. When a benefit has not been requested from the United States, communicate the applicant's information to IO. Legislative changes Where possible, it is the Department's responsibility to inform individuals of legislative changes that can affect their eligibility or entitlement to for pensions, benefits or provisions. Time frames The Department is responsible for establishing reasonable time frames to allow applicants or beneficiaries to provide documentation in support of an application such as: birth certificates; marriage certificates; death certificates; statutory declarations; or other relevant information. Time frames are established for the efficient administration of the Department's programs and are intended to meet the needs of the majority of applicants and beneficiaries. However, Ministerial discretion can be used when applying time frames to meet an applicant's or beneficiary's particular circumstances. As long as the applicant or beneficiary continues to attempt to satisfy the requirements necessary to establish their eligibility or entitlement to a pension or benefit, the Department will continue to process the application or request. Appeals The Department has the responsibility of submitting to the body hearing the appeal: all relevant information regarding the original decision; and any relevant information received after the initial decision.

Onus is defined as a duty or responsibility. In this document, the terms "onus" and "responsibility" are used interchangeably. While the overall responsibility to complete the process of applying for benefits or provisions and maintaining pensions and benefits eligibility and entitlement is shared by applicants, beneficiaries and the Department, each party assumes different responsibilities.

A birth certificate received from an applicant born in a former "Iron Curtain" country is recognized as Class A evidence. However, it can be difficult and costly to obtain such documents or the applicant may be reluctant to communicate with the authorities of the country concerned. It is not necessary to insist on the submission of a birth certificate for a person born in a country which was under the communist sphere of influence, unless the person possesses such a document. In such situations, a minimum of 2 Class B evidence documents can be requested. In some circumstances, due to weak or conflicting evidence of age, it may be to the applicant's advantage to obtain such a certificate if the applicant does not have strong personal objections against communicating with either the religious or civil authorities in their country of birth. Former "Iron Curtain" countries are: Albania Bulgaria Czechoslovakia (now the Czech Republic and Slovakia) East Germany Hungary Poland Romania Yugoslavia (now Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro) Union of Soviet Socialist Republics or Soviet Union (USSR), including many Soviet Socialist Republics (SSRs) in Europe and Asia such as the: Armenian SSR; Estonian SSR; Karelian SSR (was East Finland); Latvian SSR; Lithuanian SSR; Russian SSR; and Ukrainian SSR

Birth certificates are the most common type of Class A documents. However, there are other documents that can also be considered as Class A, given the applicant's circumstances. To be considered a birth certificate, a document (from all countries, except those listed in the Unacceptable birth and baptismal certificate section below) must meet the following basic standards and: be issued on an official form and be signed by a Vital Statistics authority of the department responsible for issuing birth certificates; have details that can be verified on the certificate by direct request to the issuing authority, if required; show the parent(s) surname or the applicant's surname at birth and it must show the applicant's given name(s); show the applicant's full date of birth (day, month and year); be an unaltered and legible document. Any amendments to the information on the document are acceptable if the change is supported by Vital Statistics or court documentation; not be proven to be incorrect by other acceptable evidence; and be a copy of or an extract from an original entry of birth in the official Vital Statistics records of the province, territory, state, etc. of the country of birth.

topic_title: Birth certificates—Additional requirements and other acceptable Class A birth evidence
text: To be considered a Class A document, birth certificates must meet the basic standards shown above plus additional requirements. The following chart identifies what additional information is required and includes a description of other documents that can be considered as Class A evidence. Table 1. Class A evidence—Additional requirements Country of issue Class A documents Canada The birth certificate issued by a provincial or territorial Vital Statistics authority or by the Department of Justice and the Superior Court in Quebec must show the date of registration. The confirmation letter issued by the Office of the Registrar General of Ontario and signed by the Deputy. Individuals presenting such a letter as birth evidence should be minimal and would normally be applicants for CPP Children's benefits and the Child Rearing Provision. The following Canadian government issued documents if the name (given name and surname) and the date of birth (day, month, year) on these documents match the name and date of birth provided on the application: Record of Landing; Passport; Citizenship certificate; Permanent Resident card. If the name and date of birth are not an exact match, they are considered class B evidence. England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland The date of registration is not required on birth certificates issued by the Registrar General or local registrars. Belgium, Netherlands The date of registration is not required on birth certificates from Belgium and the Netherlands. Italy The date of registration is not required on birth certificates issued by Italy (usually shows the year of registration only). Germany The date of registration is not required on birth certificates from Germany. A German marriage certificate called "Heiratsurkunde" or an extract of the marriage register called the " Heiratsschein" (marriage page/certificate) if the individual's date of birth and marriage registration number are recorded on it. United States of America The date of registration is required on birth certificates issued by any state(can show a delayed registration date). Japan A Japanese "Family Register" is acceptable as Class A evidence. A certified translation of, or extract from such a Japanese Family Record (as translated by the Japanese Embassy in Canada) is also acceptable as Class A evidence. The original register does not have to accompany the translation. Norway An emigration certificate called "Utvandringstillatelse" is acceptable as Class A if: the church seal is on it; it shows the date of the original church record; and the date is within 5 years of the date of birth. Portugal A Portuguese "Cédula Pessoal" is acceptable as Class A evidence. Sweden An emigration certificate called "Flyttningbetyg" is acceptable as Class A if: issued before 1991; the church seal is on it; it shows the date of the original church record; and the date is within 5 years of the date of birth. Effective 1991, the Extract of the Population Register issued by the Swedish Tax Agency is considered a Class A document. All countries (excluding those listed in below) The government or another civil authority in any country may issue a birth certificate. The date of registration must be within 5 years of the date of birth.

topic_title: Lack of or conflicting age evidence
text: In most cases, the applicant can provide a birth certificate that meets Class A criteria. When such a document does not meet the required criteria or is not available, consideration is given to a variety of Class B documents that show the age or date of birth of the applicant. On occasion, the applicant is unable to obtain sufficient evidence to establish age or the evidence obtained is contradictory. In such cases, the following rules must be followed: When the date of birth claimed on an application conflicts with the documentary evidence submitted, the applicant must be questioned about the discrepancy and given the opportunity to amend the claimed date of birth. If it is impossible to verify the month of birth from the evidence of age submitted, a decision can be reached using the following method: Where the evidence gives the age at a certain date, consider that the applicant reached that age on that date. For example, an individual shown to be 18 years old on the census of June 1, 1941 is considered to have been born on June 1, 1923. In rare cases where all evidence states only a year of birth, the month of December is used as the month of birth. An administrative decision regarding the date of birth of the applicant is made by the processing centre based on the evidence submitted. Such decisions are subject to reconsideration and appeal.

Canada Pension Plan Section 87 CPP regulations Subsection 47 (1) Section 49 Section 50 Section 51 Old Age Security Act Section 6 Paragraphs 34 (a) and (f) OAS regulations Section 18 Section 19 Subsection 23.1

In most cases, the applicant can provide a birth certificate that meets Class A criteria. If a satisfactory reason is given for being unable to provide Class A birth evidence, or the document does not meet the required criteria, a minimum of 2 Class B evidence items that show the age or date of birth of the applicant is compulsory. The exception to this rule is in the case of an application for a CPP Death benefit where only one Class B document for the deceased contributor is required. To be considered Class B evidence, a document must meet the following basic standards: the age or date of birth of the applicant is on it; and the record is dated, legible and unaltered. Generally, the older the record, the more value it is deemed to have. When only 2 items are being considered, the following guidelines must be followed: one item must be at least 10 years old; both items must confirm the year of birth; and at least one item must confirm the month of birth. Discrepancies in the date of birth between documents will necessitate obtaining additional evidence. In some cases of conflicting dates, a decision must be made regarding the acceptance of a claimed date of birth. The following is a list of examples of Class B documents. Other types of documents may be acceptable as well. Table 2. Examples of Class B documents Document type Requirements Class B birth certificates A document which meets the basic standards of a Class A birth certificate but does not meet the additional requirements with the exception of certificates issued by a special policy country. Refer to the Unacceptable birth and baptismal certificates section below . Standard baptismal certificates To be considered acceptable (from all countries except from those considered to have unacceptable birth evidence), a baptismal certificate must show the age or date of birth of the applicant and meet the following basic standards: bear the seal (can simply be a seal printed on paper or a form) of the church or be on official church letterhead and must be signed by an official of the church. Church letterhead means not only the letterhead of a particular congregation or parish but includes printed forms and letter paper bearing the name of a denomination, such as "The United Church of Canada"; include a statement that the information on the document was taken from the original record of baptism which is in the custody of the church,and the individual issuing the certificate should be an official of that church, or else it should be judged to have been taken from the record of baptism; show the parent(s) surname or the applicant's surname at birth and the applicant's given name(s); show the applicant's age or full date of birth (day, month and year) at the time of baptism; be an unaltered and legible document. Any amendments to the information on the document are acceptable if the change is supported by church documentation; indicate that the date of baptism is less than 5 years from the date of birth; and not be proven to be incorrect by other acceptable evidence. Care must be taken to ensure that the baptismal certificate meets all of the above requirements. For instance, where the certificate is not on church letterhead or does not bear a church seal, confirmation of the particulars are to be requested from the church before the document can be considered a Class B baptismal certificate. A similar type of confirmation letter should be obtained if there is any doubt as to the authenticity of a document presented by the applicant as a baptismal certificate. Non-standard baptismal record In most cases, a document that does not meet the standards of a baptismal certificate and cannot be confirmed is not considered acceptable evidence. However, depending on the contents of the document and the date of issue, it may be accepted as one piece of Class B evidence, provided the document is legible and unaltered. Examples are: a certificate that does not show the date of baptism but shows the date of birth and appears to be a very old document; a certificate that does not show the age or date of birth but indicates that the date of baptism was within days of the claimed date of birth; a document believed to be a baptismal certificate which was issued 20 years or more before the date on which it is being considered. Affidavits and declarations Affidavits and declarations made at least 10 years before the age of eligibility. Census Canadian census records are held in Ottawa by Statistics Canada. The individual concerned or their legal representative must consent to a search if the individual does not already hold a record of a previous search that may have been carried out. Statistics Canada does not release information in respect of a deceased individual; however, they will release such information is released from the National Registration records. Census records should only be searched in cases where Class A or other older-type of good Class B age evidence is not available. Each census record for any given year is considered as a separate item of Class B evidence. Due to the cost involved in searching records, the number of years to be searched must be kept to a minimum relative to the numbers and weight of other Class B items which have been submitted. United States census records: An applicant can obtain data from the United States census records. In the United States, a census was taken in January 1920 and in April of 1930, 1940, 1950 and 1960. Children's birth registration records Parents' ages have been included for many years in registrations of birth in Canada and other countries. When contacting the Vital Statistics authority for such a document, applicants must stress that they only wish the document if the age of the parent(s) is shown at the time of the child's birth. Church records Church records, such as cradle roll, communion, confirmation, mission bands, records of membership or contributions, etc. Immigration and citizenship documents In most cases, immigration records will show the age of the individual as of their arrival date in Canada. The Request to Amend the Record of Landing (IMM1436) form stamped as amended and signed by an Immigration Officer can also be accepted as evidence of age. An IMM1436 will only be issued if their immigration records were wrong but not at the request of the individual. Citizenship and naturalization papers generally show an individual's date of birth. These papers can be Canadian or those issued by other countries. Effective January 15, 1996, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) amended their policy on how they determine the date of birth of an individual. As of that date, the date of birth appearing on the Record of Landing (IMM 1000), issued to the individual when admitted to Canada, is that individual's date of birth for all IRCC purposes (passport, Canadian Citizenship Certificate and Permanent Resident (PR) Card). Since the date of birth appearing on the individual's passport, Canadian Citizenship Certificate and Permanent Resident Card is directly linked to the Record of Landing (IMM 1000), these documents cannot be used as separate pieces of Class B age evidence if they were issued on January 15, 1996 or later. The following documents, if dated and issued prior to January 15, 1996, are used as separate pieces of Class B evidence: The Record of Landing; The Canadian passport; The Canadian citizenship certificate. If the above documents are dated and issued on January 15, 1996 or later, it is necessary to obtain at least one other piece of Class B evidence such as marriage records, medical records, etc., before the proof of age requirement can be considered to have been met. Educational records A record signed by a competent official, indicating the required particulars. Records of attending school at an early age are the most desirable. Other records include diplomas, graduation awards or certificates. Employment insurance records Employment insurance records, including cards and books that were issued for a period of about 30 years from July 1941 and in which the month and year of birth are indicated in code. Employment records These records can be copies of the employment card or a letter from the employer stating an age or date of birth given by the applicant as of a certain date. Records must be on the company letterhead and signed by an official of the company. Family bibles and other private records Family bibles and other private records showing the date of birth and other private records of the applicant can be considered if it appears the record was made shortly after the individual's birth. The entire record is to be examined to determine the publication date, apparent age of the document, dates of other information recorded, etc. Foreign documents (e.g. travel documents, refugee documents, etc.) Individuals, or their relatives, who came to Canada from foreign countries, may still have useful documents such as passports, border crossing cards, travel documents, identity certificates, refugee documents, etc. Former residents of Hong Kong frequently possess a Hong Kong Certificate of Identity if they were a resident in the former Crown colony. This area must always be explored for all individuals born outside of Canada. Homestead and land patent records Individuals who applied for homestead and land patents in Western Canada many years ago were required to state their age at the time of application. Hospital or medical record of birth A copy of, or extract from, the actual record of birth, certified by a competent official who has custody of the records (hospital, doctor, nurse, midwife). Indian treaty, status card and interest pay lists, Inuit disc numbers and Métis scrip records These historical records are maintained by Indigenous Services Canada. Inuit were issued a disc number until they were asked to choose a surname under the Operation Surname Program, which occurred in the 1960's. In many cases, Inuit remember birth dates by the season, e.g. "when the ice was breaking up" or "when the geese returned". Métis scrip records were issued many years ago to adult male Métis for the purchase of land. The records include age or date of birth. Insurance or government annuities A statement from the insurance company or the annuities branch as to the date of birth admitted is most desirable. However, a document showing a claimed date of birth can be considered. Marriage registration records When writing to a Vital Statistics authority, the individual must stress that only a document that shows age at the time of the marriage is required. A marriage certificate may not provide this information, but such information is generally found on a registration of marriage. Medical and hospital records Records of hospital, doctors, clinics, hospital insurance organizations, vaccination certificates, etc. signed by a physician or an officer of the institution can be considered. Member records Many fraternal, lodge, trade and commercial organizations keep records of members' ages. Extracts from such records can be considered. Mental institution records The institution's record of age that is based on the patient's admission date is acceptable as class B evidence if it was made 2 years prior to the CPP or OAS benefit application date. No subsequent records of the institution can be considered as separate items of age evidence as the age given in any record after the admission date is likely based on the institution's records and not on birth evidence. The authority representing the applicant can authorize a search of census records. In some cases, evidence of age for an individual in a mental institution cannot be obtained from the usual sources. Military service record, Veterans Affairs Canada (VAC) record, etc. An applicant may have a military record from Canada or another country that shows a date of birth. In addition, records of Canadian ex-service members, VAC applicants, Canadian Pension Commission recipients and War Veterans Allowance recipients are available upon request. National Registration records The records of the National Registration taken from August 1940 to 1946 are maintained by Statistics Canada. Newspaper clippings, photos, letters, etc. Old newspaper or magazine clippings, correspondence, letters, photographs or similar records can be given consideration if they directly, or by inference, indicate an applicant's age. Passports, border crossing, etc. Passport (foreign or Canadian issued), border crossing records and other documents of this nature which show age or date of birth can be given consideration. Pension or superannuation records These must be on letterhead and signed by the appropriate authority. A statement from such records showing the date of birth accepted for pension purposes can be accepted as evidence of age. Public records Assessment rolls, court records, driver's license records, jury lists, motor vehicle operator's licenses, transfers of property, voter's lists, etc. can be given consideration as evidence of age. USA Selective Service records Individuals who were registered under the USA Selective Service System can provide age evidence from those records. Vital Statistics A letter from Vital Statistics confirming the birth particulars concerning the individual would only be accepted as a Class B document. Some applicants may present a letter from their provincial Vital Statistics as birth evidence. These letters can also be receipt-type documents for search fees paid to obtain a birth certificate and may also include birth particulars (some may have a notation to the effect that "This is not a certificate of birth". These documents are not acceptable as Class A or as Class B evidence; however, if the letter specifically mentions in the body that it is confirming birth particulars, then it may be accepted as Class B evidence.

The Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act require proof of an applicant's or beneficiary's age to establish eligibility or continued eligibility for pensions, benefits or provisions, with the exception of individuals for whom the requirement for documentation has been waived. After either OAS or CPP has established an individual's date of birth, the other program accepts the date of birth. Should there be a discrepancy noted between what was previously accepted by one program (other than an original or certified true copy of a birth certificate) further proof of age is required. In situations where documentary evidence is required, a copy of a birth certificate to support the applicant's claimed date of birth should be obtained. The minister reserves the right to request documentary evidence at any time, including original or certified copies. If there is sufficient reason to believe that a birth certificate is not available or attainable, age may be determined based on other documentation. Birth evidence is divided into two categories: Class A; and Class B. These terms are used for internal use and reference only. The type of birth evidence establishes the category under which it belongs. In cases related to international social security agreements (ISSAs), certification of an applicant's age provided by foreign liaison agencies are accepted as valid evidence, whether the payment is made in accordance with the ISSA or through domestic legislation. Types of evidence Proof of age for individuals in special categories Applicants are to be encouraged to submit sufficient evidence of age. In some cases, the only evidence of age that applicants submit may present problems due to different calendars that were used for recording dates of birth. This includes Chinese Calendars and documents, Hebrew calendars and Julian calendars. OAS automatic enrolment For individuals selected for automatic enrolment for the OAS pension, documentary evidence to support age is not required if the application is waived on their 65th birthday. The age eligibility requirement is met through a combination of data elements. For individuals not selected for automatic enrolment for the OAS pension who: submit an application to apply for a full OAS pension under the 40 year rule; and meet the data elements to substantiate eligibility for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension may have their eligibility determined for an OAS pension by using the same combination of data elements as those used for individuals selected for automatic enrolment. In these cases, although documentation to support age may not be required, documentary evidence can be requested at any time before or after approval of the OAS pension.

If an individual's age was already established for the administration of another program (CPP or OAS) or the applicant has provided proof of age with the current application, then that birth evidence is the primary source. Following that, the primary source for date of birth validation is the record in the Social Insurance Register (SIR) displayed in ITRDS . The date (day, month and year) of birth, the name (given name and surname) and Social Insurance Number (SIN) indicated on the application must be identical to the date of birth (day, month, and year), name (given name and surname) and SIN found in ITRDS and received through SIR or it must meet the requirements of the policy on name tolerances. Documentary evidence to prove the date of birth must be obtained from the applicant where the applicant has not submitted evidence of birth with their application and: their age has not already been proven for another program pension, benefit or provision (OAS or CPP); there is a discrepancy noted between the date of birth indicated on the application and the date that was previously accepted by another program; the date of birth (day, month and year) on the application does not match the date of birth in the SIR; the sur name on the application does not match the surname at birth or the current surname in ITRDS as derived through the SIR; or the differences in the name don't meet the requirements under the variances of the name tolerance policy. Where individuals change their name (e.g. by marriage) but do not inform the SIR, we may consider the name as identical if the name at birth matches the name in the SIR. in the SIR that do not exactly match abbreviations on the application, or abbreviations included in the policy on name tolerances are not acceptable and documentary birth evidence must be obtained. When there is a discrepancy between the application and the SIR, birth evidence is required to support the applicant's claimed date of birth. If there is sufficient reason to believe that a birth certificate is not available, age may be determined on the basis of other documentation such as, class B documents provided by the applicant. For more information on class B documents,refer to the Other birth evidence (class B)—Basic standards section below.

Birth or baptismal certificates issued from the following countries are not recognized as Class A or Class B evidence: Anatolia Arabia Egypt Greece Islands of the Aegean Sea Iran Iraq Israel Jordan Lebanon Palestine People's Republic of China Syria Turkey Yemen Information obtained from these countries has been limited. Indications are that birth and baptismal certificates issued by these countries are not based on original records. If the applicant provides such a birth or baptismal certificate, it can be accepted but not recognized as Class A or as B evidence. Other evidence must be obtained. In some situations, the foreign document can help in the determination of age as it indicates that the individual was using the same date of birth prior to arriving in Canada. At least 2 pieces of satisfactory Class B documentary evidence based on records made after the person's arrival in Canada should be used.

This procedure provides instructions on how to proceed when a client or applicant provides a PO Box address as their home address on a change of address request or on an application.

When you receive an application or an address change request with only a PO Box provided and no physical address, or you encounter an account that was selected for automatic enrolment with only a PO Box, proceed as follows:

If a client or applicant provides a PO Box address as their home address, you must request confirmation of their home address (e.g. their civic address or physical location). For CPP and CPPD, once you have requested confirmation of the home address, you may continue processing the application or request. For OAS, you may continue processing the application or request once you have requested the home address only if eligibility or entitlement to benefits is not affected. An applicant who did not provide a home address can use a PO Box only if they: reside on a fire road; live in a remote location; or have no other legal means of identifying their property. If they cannot provide a physical home address, clarify the reason why and use the OAS—CPP, Request confirmation of home address and absences in the past year (ISS-0605) letter. Having a PO Box as an address does not exclude the individual from this process. Clients who have been automatically enrolled should not be treated differently from those who apply using a paper application. You must request confirmation of the applicant's home address as well as any absences in the past year if this information has not already been confirmed.

topic_title: Acceptable validation for proof of date of death New
text: Determination of death can be validated and accepted using: another program (i.e. OAS, CPP); third-party government data sources, such as the Social Insurance Registry (SIR); information provided directly from funeral directors; and information provided from a foreign institution with whom the Department has an International Social Security Agreement.

For the CPP, proof of the date of death is required. However, the requirement is considered met when the determination of death matches a validation from a third-party government data source, such as the Social Insurance Registry, information provided directly from funeral directors or from a foreign government with whom the Department has an International Social Security Agreement. Proof of death is required when processing applications in which the month of death is a factor in determining eligibility for the pension or benefit. The date of death can be determined using third-party government data sources or documentary evidence for the following: a CPP Death benefit; a CPP SVR pension; a CPP Surviving Child's benefit; a post-mortem CPP pension or benefit; and any CPP pension or benefit where the applicant dies before the application is processed.

topic_title: Documentary evidence for the date of death is required Updated
text: Proof of death is required in the following situations: information on the application does not match the date of death previously provided to the Department; the death is reported but the date the death occurred is in doubt; the death is reported long after the event and a large overpayment may result; notice is received from the SIR, and following receipt, a discrepancy report is produced; notice is received from the CRA, and following receipt, a discrepancy report is produced; or there is a presumption of death. The following documents are accepted as proof of the date of death: a registration of death under a provincial or territorial authority; an official death certificate or other document confirming the date of death issued under the authority of some level of government (domestic or foreign) where the death occurred (e.g. a Japanese Family Register, a Portuguese Cédula Pessoal); the burial or death certificate issued by a funeral home by either: the funeral director; or any person authorized through the funeral home to issue such documents; a proof provided in accordance with the custom of any religious denomination by an ordained religious leader; a medical certificate of death issued by the attending doctor or coroner; a statement by a doctor last in attendance, or by a coroner or funeral director using stationery with the appropriate identifying letterhead; a certification or notification of death received from the social security office of a country with which the Department has an international social security agreement; a memorandum of notification of death issued by the Chief of National Defence Staff, Department of National Defence Canada, where the death of a member of the Canadian Armed Forces occurs outside of Canada; a statement of verification of death from the Department of Veterans Affairs Canada written on the letterhead of that department; an official notification from the administrator of the estate appointed by a court; an official notification written on the letterhead of a provincial public trustee or administrator of estates; a copy of the letters of probate; or a life or group insurance claim, provided it includes a statement signed by a medical doctor.

Canada Pension Plan Section 60(1)—Payment of Benefits: General Provisions, Application for benefit Section 88—Presumption as to death CPP regulations Section 52—Information and Evidence Required to be Furnished by an Applicant or Beneficiary Section 63—Determination by the Minister Old Age Security Act Subsection 8(3)—Payment of pension, duration Subsection 29(1)—Death, application for pension by estate, etc. Section 31—Death, presumption as to death of applicant or beneficiary OAS regulations Section 23—Further information and investigation before or after the approval of an application or before or after the requirement of an application is waived

The requirement for documentary evidence for proof of death will be waived for the following if the exact date of death is known: an OAS ALWS ; a post-mortem OAS pension; any OAS pension or benefit where the applicant dies before the application is processed; and a cancellation of OAS benefits.

Documentary evidence to prove a date of death may be required to determine initial or continuing eligibility to, and the entitlement amounts of, certain pensions and benefits under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act . The Minister reserves the right to request documentary evidence at any time. Date of death The date of death has an important impact on a deceased CPP contributor's contributory period. This can affect: the benefit effective date for an SVR pension; the termination date of a benefit that the deceased was receiving before their death; and eligibility to certain benefits. When CPP and/or OAS benefits are in pay to an individual, these benefits are payable for the month in which the individual dies, regardless of the day of the month that the death occurs. The individual's benefits end the month following their month of death.

A presumption of death must be considered when an individual disappears and continues to be absent from their customary location or home for an extended period without any apparent reason for this absence. Under these circumstances, when the Department determines that an applicant or beneficiary is dead, it also needs to determine the date of death and issue a presumption of death certificate. The date of death must be established as accurately as possible since it has an impact on entitlement to certain CPP and/or OAS pensions and benefits. For example, the date of death can help determine whether to approve and/or when to end pensions and benefits under both the CPP and the OAS. Both the circumstances surrounding the disappearance of an applicant or beneficiary and the actual length of time of the absence are important factors when determining that an applicant or beneficiary is dead. Individuals with the authority to issue a presumption of death certificate The Department has the authority to issue a presumption of death certificate and to declare the date on which an individual's death is presumed to have occurred. OAS Under the Old Age Security Act , the Department's authority is restricted to issuing presumption of death certificates for applicants and beneficiaries only . For the ALWS because there is nothing in the legislation to allow presumption of death for the applicant's spouse or common-law partner, we accept a statutory declaration. CPP Under the Canada Pension Plan , the Department's authority to declare the date of presumed death and issue the presumption of death certificate extends to the death of: the contributor or beneficiary; the contributor's spouse or common-law partner; or the contributor's former spouse or former common-law partner. Documentation to determine the date of death and to issue a presumption of death certificate Evidence describing the circumstances surrounding the person's disappearance and indicating the date and the source of the information is required before the Department issues a presumption of death certificate. Evidence of death can include: newspaper clippings; police reports; search and rescue reports; eyewitness statements; and private insurance company reports. A detailed report received from a Service Canada Centre and/or a Mail Processing Centre, or, if available, a court order that is issued in provinces or territories that have legislation around presumption of death can also be used as evidence for the date of death when other evidence is not available. The Department is not bound by the issuance or cancelling of a death certificate by any authority other than by the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act . However, the Department reviews these other authorities' documents, which could be used as new evidence in relation to a decision to change a presumed date of death declared by the Department. For example, if a presumption of death for a member of the Canadian Armed Forces issued later than a Department-issued presumption of death indicates a different date of death, the Department, at its discretion, can change its date of death to match that of the Canadian Armed Forces document. Documentation to determine the date of death caused by a natural disaster When an individual has gone missing in a natural disaster, in many cases, applications made immediately after the disaster for CPP or OAS survivor benefits (e.g. CPP Death benefit, SVR pension, Surviving Child's benefit or OAS ALWS benefit) may not have the appropriate documentation for proof of death. Because of the unique circumstances and in order to address the immediate financial needs of the survivors, on a case by case basis, the Department can accept a statutory declaration instead of official documents that confirms the death and pay the survivor benefits. The usual documentation requirements for presumption of death, (a court order, police reports or search and rescue reports, etc.), will be waived. The statutory declaration will be accepted as sufficient evidence to deem the presumed date of death to be the date of the disaster. If the individual applying for survivor's pension or other survivor's benefits has not submitted a statutory declaration, but has provided sufficient information regarding the circumstances, place and date of death of the deceased person or contributor, a statutory declaration will not be required. In addition, a statutory declaration is not required when the applicant has provided a death certificate. When the Department receives an application for an SVR pension or other survivor's benefit and the death is reported long after the natural disaster, the usual proof of death documentation required in a presumption of death situation is required. A statutory declaration could be accepted, but another document showing that the individual died is also required. Examples of such other documents include: a registration of the person's death with the Canadian or a foreign government; a search and rescue report; an insurance claim; and a document issued by the Canadian or a foreign government showing that the applicant is considered widowed, orphaned, etc. New evidence shows that an individual who was presumed dead is alive The authority to change an individual's status from presumed dead to alive is based on new evidence or information received. If the Department is satisfied, based on the new evidence or information, that the individual is alive: all actions taken on the individual's file, and any related files, which were based on the individual's Presumed Dead status must be reviewed; and the appropriate changes must be made. These changes could include: cancelling or terminating some CPP and/or OAS pensions and benefits; or reinstating or initiating payment of other CPP and/or OAS pensions and benefits.

The following are examples of acceptable documentary evidence of proof of Canadian citizenship or legal status: Canadian birth certificate; Canadian passport (issued in 1970 or later); Canadian Permanent Resident card; Certificate of Canadian citizenship; Commemoration of Canadian Citizenship certificate (if N/A is used in the date area, the person is a Canadian citizen by birth or was a Canadian citizen before 1947 under the British Nationality Act); Canadian temporary resident visa; Certificate of Indian Status card; Certificate of naturalization (for British subjects); Certificate of retention of Canadian citizenship; Certificate of registration of birth abroad; Canadian immigration record; Confirmation of permanent residence; Certificate of identity issued by the Department of External Affairs; Minister's permit; Canadian immigration stamp in passport; Letter from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC); Verification of Status (VOS) document from IRCC Other Immigration documents (e.g. IMM 1000, IMM 5292, IMM 5688, IMM 5716, IMM 2740b forms).

topic_title: Documentary evidence required for Canadian-born applicants
text: Canadian-born applicants fall into one of several categories when determining their eligibility for an OAS pension or benefit. The categories are as follows: Applicants with no absences If there have been no absences that would interrupt residence in Canada for OAS purposes, applicants may be considered Canadian citizens when proof of age is established by the CPP program or from the Social Insurance Registry (SIR) records. If information is not confirmed through CPP or SIR, applicants must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth as proof of legal status. Applicants with an absence of less than 5 years An absence of less than 5 years, or any absence that does not interrupt residence in Canada for OAS purposes, may be considered not to have affected citizenship. An applicant must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth as proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or SIR and the applicant indicated on their application that they are a Canadian citizen. Absence of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977 An individual born in Canada who has been absent for a period of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977 may be asked to complete a Statutory Declaration stating that they have not become citizens of another country at any time or by February 15, 1977. An individual who has become a citizen of another country may automatically have their Canadian citizenship reinstated as of April 17, 2009 by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). An applicant must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth as proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or SIR and the applicant indicated on their application that they are a Canadian citizen. Departure to and return from the United Kingdom before 1949 An individual born in Canada who went to the United Kingdom or one of the Commonwealth countries and returned before 1949 may be considered to have continued their Canadian citizenship. An applicant must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth as proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or SIR and the applicant indicated on their application that they are a Canadian citizen. Former Canadian residents applying from abroad Canadian-born applicants abroad may be considered to have been Canadian citizens at the time of departure if they had resided continuously in Canada up to that date. An applicant must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth as proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or SIR and the applicant indicated on their application that they are a Canadian citizen. The OAS application does not differentiate between individuals born in Newfoundland and Labrador before April 1, 1949 (when Newfoundland and Labrador joined Confederation) from those who were born on or after that date. For the purpose of determining legal status, they are considered to be naturalized Canadians.

topic_title: Documentary evidence required for foreign-born applicants
text: Foreign-born applicants fall into one of several categories when determining their legal status. The following individuals must provide proof of legal status: Applicants who were born in the United Kingdom Applicants who were born in the United Kingdom and arrived in Canada before January 1, 1947 may be considered to be legal residents in Canada if they can: produce a Class A birth certificate; and establish that there have been no absences from Canada that would interrupt residence for the purposes of OAS since their date of arrival. Naturalized British subjects Before January 1, 1947, immigrants to Canada could become naturalized as British subjects and receive a naturalization certificate. When the Canadian Citizenship Act became law on January 1, 1947, naturalized British subjects with at least 5 years of residence in Canada automatically became Canadian citizens. Naturalized Canadians who have had no absences from Canada may be considered to have retained their status in the same way as Canadian-born applicants. If the applicant had any absences of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977, they must complete a statutory declaration declaring that they have not become citizens of another country before February 15, 1977. All members of a family were frequently included as British subjects in Canada in certificates of naturalization issued before 1947. Where the applicant is named as a dependant in such a certificate, you may accept it as proof of status, provided there is no indication of a change since that time. Immigrants with permanent resident/legal resident status For applicants, who immigrated to Canada in 1925 and later, the process of confirming their status is simplified because of the central alphabetical index that was established by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) authorities at that time. Immigrants who became Canadian citizens In addition to proving their citizenship, Canadian citizens who have been absent for a period of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977, may be asked to complete a Statutory Declaration stating that they have not become citizens of another country before February 15, 1977. For those individuals who may have automatically had their Canadian citizenship reinstated as of April 17, 2009 by IRCC, a Statutory Declaration is not required.

The requirement for documentation to support legal status will be waived when processing all initial OAS pension, ALW or ALWS benefit applications, provided the applicant: completes the appropriate sections of the application pertaining to their legal status (this will meet the requirement of confirming their legal status in writing); has a Canadian address; indicates one of the following legal statuses on the application: Canadian citizen; Permanent resident (landed immigrant); or Status Indian; is not currently under a sponsorship agreement. This operational policy will be applied only when there are no changes or inconsistencies between the information on the application or any documentation submitted with the application(s) currently on file. If there are changes or inconsistencies, a review will be completed and evidence of legal status is required. OAS automatic enrolment For individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension, documentary evidence to support legal status is waived as these individuals meet the eligibility requirements through a combination of data elements. Although documentation to support legal status may not be required, documentary evidence can be requested at any time before or after approval of the OAS pension.

topic_title: Immigration documents issued by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
text: The Permanent Residence card has replaced the IMM 1000 (Record of Landing) form as a travel document. The card was created to provide secure proof of legal status for permanent residents who are re-entering Canada. It is valid for a period of 5 years, is renewable and shows the original date when permanent residence was granted. The Confirmation of Permanent Residence form is issued to individuals before their entry into Canada.
