topic_title: Requesting the legal status from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
text: In October 2013, the Department was granted the authority to go directly to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)—formerly Citizenship and Immigration Canada—to obtain legal status and/or residence information as long as the Department obtained the written consent from the applicant or their authorized representative. However, in extenuating circumstances, it may be difficult for some applicants to obtain proof of legal status. Examples of extenuating circumstances include: where there are no known relatives and immigration information is limited or unknown; where there has been a history of mental illness and the individual has been institutionalized; where homelessness has been an issue; where the individual is illiterate or was brought into Canada as a child. You must look at each case on an individual basis and contact IRCC to try to retrieve legal status information on behalf of the applicant, as long as the department obtained written consent from the applicant or their authorized representative. If the IRCC search is not successful, ask the applicant or their authorized representative to complete a Statutory Declaration, which may be accepted as proof of legal status.

topic_title: Defining erroneous advice and administrative error
text: Erroneous advice Erroneous advice (EA) is false or misleading oral or written communication containing incorrect or misleading information provided by a departmental employee in the course of administering the CPP or the OAS Act. As a result, the EA affects a beneficiary or applicant’s actions or conduct in relation to the CPP and OAS programs to their detriment. EA includes the omission of crucial information. If a departmental employee does not give an applicant information that could affect them making an informed decision in regard to an application, the omission is considered to be just as erroneous as providing incorrect information. Information provided by anyone outside of the delegated administration of the CPP and the OAS Act (the Canada Revenue Agency or a private sector human resources expert) cannot be remedied under the Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) provisions under any circumstances. Information communicated to the applicant or beneficiary may or may not be indicated on the file or in ITRDS notes. The legislative requirement is that the Minister be satisfied. For the purposes of the EA/AE provisions, the term "satisfied" means "convinced". There is no statutory onus on the Minister to prove that EA/AE occurred. However, all available documents and additional information provided by the applicant or beneficiary must be reviewed. Administrative Error An administrative error (AE) is an action by an official of the Department acting in an official capacity in the administration of the CPP and the OAS Act. This action causes: a benefit; a provision; a portion of a benefit; or a provision to be denied. This includes access to a credit split and pension sharing. The sole purpose of the EA/AE provisions is to enable the Department to take remedial action when an error is made by departmental officials. "Administrative" (from "administration") relates to the management or conduct of business. Administrative actions in the context of the CPP and the OAS Act are necessary to carrying out legislation, policies, procedures and practices. For the purposes of the CPP and the OAS Act, an AE is an incorrect action or a failure to act of a departmental employee while administering the policies, procedures and practices related to the CPP and the OAS Act. Time limit There is no time limit on a request for, or on the approval or non-approval of an allegation of EA/AE, nor is there a time limit to implement the provision. This applies to both minister-initiated reviews of a potential EA/AE or a request from an applicant or beneficiary-initiated allegation. However, the legislation, policies, procedures and practices in place at the time the alleged EA/AE is said to have occurred, must be used to determine if EA/AE occurred. Clerical error For program administration purposes, clerical errors are not considered under the EA/AE provisions. There is no discretion or decision made on clerical errors as is the case with EA/AE. A clerical error (e.g. missing a step in a calculation or process, keying in the wrong date of birth) is an evident error that simply needs to be corrected. While clerical errors are not administrative errors for program administration purposes, federal courts make no such distinctions. From a court and an applicant or beneficiary’s perspective, when an error is found to have occurred, it must be corrected. There may be cases where an error occurred while administering an applicant or beneficiary’s file, but did not cause any loss of benefits to the applicant or beneficiary or prevent access to a credit split or pension sharing. As there was not a loss of benefits or access to a provision, it is not a case of EA/AE as detailed under the legislation. Depending on the situation, the error must be corrected or the individual must be informed although nothing in the file changes. EA/AE and overpayments (remission) The EA/AE provisions (subsection 66(4) of the CPP and section 32 of the OAS Act) do not apply to cases where an overpayment has occurred due to EA/AE. Overpayments resulting from EA/AE are considered under the remission provisions of the CPP and OAS Act. The remission provision for EA/AE provides the Minister with discretion, when satisfied, in cases where an overpayment is caused by EA/AE, to remit all or any portion of that overpayment.

topic_title: Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error submissions do not need to be submitted in the following situation:
text: Reinstatement due to legislative change—CPP Survivor’s pension Rescinded The Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) provision cannot be used to pay more than 11 months of retroactivity to individuals whose benefits were cancelled because of remarriage before January 1, 1987 and reinstated following receipt of a new survivor application. Failure to advise individuals of a legislative amendment is not an administrative error by the Department as per the legislation in these cases. Credit split—Kempling remedy Documentation for cases that are a result of applying the Kempling provisions is not required. Although an EA/AE submission is prepared in these cases, the authority to remedy these situations does not fall under the EA/AE provision but under the provision where a credit split is denied.

topic_title: Investigative criteria of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error
text: Certain criteria must be met before consideration is given to a claim of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE): The error was an EA or AE, and not a clerical error. There was legislative authority to have paid the benefit or to apply the provision that was allegedly denied. There are no other legislative provisions (e.g. incapacity) that can correct the situation. Legislative criteria of EA/AE When making a decision, the following 4 legislative criteria must be considered: The alleged EA/AE was made by a departmental employee acting in an official capacity in the administration of the CPP and the OAS Act. The applicant or beneficiary has been denied in whole or in part a pension, benefit, or denied access to a provision (i.e. Credit Splitting or pension sharing). The individual is entitled to the pension, benefit or provision for which they would have been eligible had the error not occurred. There was legislative authority to pay the pension, benefit or to apply the provision to which the applicant or beneficiary would be eligible if the error had not occurred. The Minister (i.e. the investigating agent) is satisfied, based on the evidence and the balance of probabilities, that the EA/AE has occurred. An individual must have been denied a pension, benefit or provision or portion thereof due to EA/AE by a departmental employee in the administration of the CPP or OAS Act The EA/AE must have been made by someone acting in an official capacity in the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act. There is no authority to apply the legislative provision when: someone other than an employee administering the CPP or the OAS Act provides information; an employee provides information, but not in an official capacity (e.g. at a social function). If allegations of EA/AE are confirmed, the error must be corrected. The individual must be advised in writing that an error has been found, corrected and the pension or benefit paid or provision applied. There must have been legislative authority to pay the benefits that were denied (or denied in part) as a result of the EA/AE To apply the remedial provisions, the applicant or beneficiary must have been denied a pension or benefit to which they would have (otherwise) been entitled. EA/AE provisions cannot be used to pay benefits for which there would not have been any entitlement, regardless of any error that may have occurred. The provisions cannot be used as a compassionate clause in cases where an applicant or beneficiary does not otherwise qualify or in cases where a mistake occurred, but is not considered to be EA/AE. When reviewing a case, it is essential to research legislation and regulations of the CPP or the OAS Act that were in place when the EA/AE is alleged to have taken place. Of equal importance is researching the policies, procedures, practices, brochures, and forms and other historical information in place at the time of the alleged EA/AE. When the collection of the research is complete, review the claim of EA/AE in the context of the facts that existed at the time the EA/AE is alleged to have occurred. EA/AE provisions are not used to: alleviate a potentially embarrassing situation; to circumvent the appeals process; rectify any perceived inadequacies or inequities in the legislation; be used as a compensatory measure to appease someone who was inconvenienced by an error who does not satisfy all other eligibility or entitlement requirement Eligibility cannot be created using the EA/AE provisions. The provisions are a remedy for situations where an individual has been denied a benefit, a part of a benefit, a credit split or pension sharing because of EA/AE in the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act. The Minister must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that EA/AE occurred The CPP and the OAS Act state that the Minister must be satisfied (i.e. the evidence must show, on a balance of probabilities that an error occurred). "Balance of probabilities" means that after having determined all the facts of the case, which may include statements by the applicant or beneficiary, whether corroborated or not, one could logically conclude that there was a reasonable likelihood that an administrative error (AE) was made or erroneous advice (EA) was given. The applicant’s or beneficiaries unsupported evidence cannot be accepted as the only means of determining if EA was provided or AE was made. There must be supporting evidence. A decision not to invoke EA/AE under the EA/AE provisions does not require proof that a situation did not occur. The decision means that there is insufficient information and documentation to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that EA/AE most likely occurred. In some cases, it may have already been determined that a situation occurred affecting an entire group of applicants or beneficiaries. For these cases, the burden of proof is less onerous because it has already been determined that the situation can be corrected by applying the EA/AE provisions. If the Minister is satisfied that EA/AE occurred and that the applicant or beneficiary has been denied part or all of a pension, benefit or provision, the Minister must put the individual in the position that they would have been in had the EA/AE not occurred and pay those benefits that were not paid due to EA/AE or take action to implement the provision. All other entitlement requirements for the period in question must be met.

Canada Pension Plan Subsection 66(4)—Where person denied benefit due to departmental error, etc. Subsection 66(5)—When person denied division Old Age Security Act Section 32—Erroneous Advice or Administrative Error—Where person denied benefit due to departmental error, etc. Federal Courts Act Section 18.1—Jurisdiction of Federal Court—Application for judicial review Section 28—Jurisdiction of Federal Court of Appeal—Judicial review

The CPP and the OAS Act provide authority to re-open decisions made on an application for pensions, benefits or provisions, including the following CPP provisions: credit split, legislatively known as a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings; or pension sharing, legislatively known as an assignment of a Retirement pension. Appropriate remedial action can be taken if an eligible individual was denied in whole or in part a pension, benefit or provision as a result of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) in the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act. EA/AE provisions are not intended to bypass the reconsideration and appeals process, nor are they meant to supersede any other provision contained in the CPP or the OAS Act. EA/AE provisions are to be used exceptionally—they cannot be used if other provisions or recourses remain available. Is the late applicant provision available? If no, then: Is the incapacity provision available? If no, then: Is the "new facts" provision available? If no, then: Have the reconsideration and appeals recourses been exhausted? If yes, then: Consider the EA/AE provisions. The legislation applies to cases where an individual was denied a pension, benefit, a provision or a portion thereof to which they were entitled because of EA/AE. In most cases, an underpayment is created when EA/AE deems an application to have been received earlier than its actual receipt date. An allegation of EA/AE can be put forth by an applicant or beneficiary or someone acting on their behalf. The Minister may also initiate remedial action in the process of reviewing an application or file if it is noticed that an EA/AE has occurred in the processing of a pension, benefit or provision. A written request is not needed to initiate a review of EA/AE. However, a written statement can be submitted to initiate a review.

topic_title: Recourse rights and jurisdiction of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error
text: No right of appeal Ministerial decisions made in relation to the Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) provisions cannot be appealed. These decisions can be reviewed in the Federal Court by way of an application for judicial review. Judicial review The Social Security Tribunal General Division has no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal from the Minister’s decision under the EA/AE provisions. The only recourse available to someone who wants to dispute the Minister’s decision in these situations is to apply to the Federal Court for judicial review. Continued allegations Some applicants or beneficiaries will continue to assert that EA/AE took place after being advised the allegation of EA/AE was unfounded. Each additional claim must be responded to in writing, but not all claims will necessarily warrant a new investigation. The Department can only reverse its previous decision on EA/AE if one of the following circumstances is met: The employee who determined that EA/AE did not occur did not have the delegated authority to perform the review. The Department had not advised the applicant or beneficiary of the outcome of the review (i.e. the applicant or beneficiary was not advised in writing). The applicant or beneficiary had not been given the opportunity to respond to the Minister's decision or had not been given the opportunity to support their allegation of EA/AE.

topic_title: Requests for reconsideration appeals to the Social Security Tribunal
text: Whether an applicant or beneficiary is addressing one issue in a reconsideration letter or appeal or several, it is important to identify, clarify and address each of the issues and what the applicant or beneficiary is specifically alleging or requesting. In cases of CPP Disability benefit applications, the EA/AE process must be done first to provide the required parameters for disability decision-making (e.g. a date of application might be changed as a result of EA/AE; a disability determination cannot be made unless the actual or deemed date of application is known). Allegation of error at the reconsideration stage: When an individual simultaneously makes an allegation of EA/AE and requests a reconsideration of a decision, the processes must be dealt with separately. The outcome of each must be communicated to the individual at the same time, but separately. Allegation of error at the appeals stage: When an individual makes an allegation of EA/AE while the matter is already before the Social Security Tribunal, the Department will resolve the EA/AE allegation first, on the grounds that an error might resolve the appeal.

topic_title: Where there is an allegation of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error, the individual must be contacted and provided with an opportunity to submit more information
text: The best practice in assessing if Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) has occurred is for decision-makers to allow the applicant or beneficiary the opportunity to explain their case or provide additional information before the final decision. Before conducting or concluding an investigation of EA/AE, contact the individual and invite them to provide further information or submissions to support their claim. This is an opportunity for the applicant or beneficiary to describe the circumstances in their own words. Requests for information should not be in the form of questions as the applicant or beneficiary should not be put in a position to be influenced by the questions being asked. Thus, if the case proceeds to the Federal Court, the Minister can substantiate that all possible documentation was reviewed and that the applicant or beneficiary was provided with every opportunity to substantiate the facts of their case. Written submission prepared by employee and approval The individual who reviews and makes the decision on the EA/AE case cannot be the same individual who was originally involved in the decision that resulted in the allegation being made. A submission must be prepared for each case that is reviewed under EA/AE, regardless of whether or not the remedy provisions are provided. Once the submission is prepared, it is submitted to the next level of delegated authority for approval. All submissions have to go through all levels of the "chain of approvals" that are between the investigator and the delegated authority. Approvals are based on the potential monetary value of the entitlement whether EA/AE is invoked or not. If the EA/AE submission is approved, action must be taken to remedy the situation or adjust the account. If the recommendation is for no remedial action, then the applicant or beneficiary must be advised of the decision with a rationale by the individual who investigated the EA/AE.
Old Age Security Act Section 2(e)—Definitions Section 13—Calculation of Income Section 14—Options OAS regulations Section 14—Definition of pension income

When an applicant or beneficiary completes a statement of income, no documentary evidence is generally required to prove income, except in the following situations: A deduction is claimed that cannot be verified by the Canada Revenue Agency income feed; There is a doubt about a source of income; Foreign income or foreign pension is reported on the initial application and there is conflicting information; and/or The beneficiary is claiming foreign income or a foreign pension for the first time after receiving the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit for more than one payment period. It is essential to establish a baseline for the beneficiary that includes the initial year and rate of the pension income.

When incapacity may be assessed The incapacity provision applies to CPP and OAS benefit applications and to the CPP credit split provision (see exceptions in the drop-down titled "When incapacity may NOT be assessed"). The incapacity provision applies to individuals on whose behalf the application for a benefit is made (i.e. the beneficiary), not to the individual making the application on behalf of someone else (e.g. a legal representative). A claim of incapacity may be assessed at the time of application for a benefit or provision, on reconsideration, and before the Social Security Tribunal. The issue of incapacity should be addressed as early as possible in the review process and is to be addressed before a decision on benefit eligibility is made. The incapacity provision is to be used in a precise and focused manner to address exceptional cases. The threshold for establishing incapacity within the meaning of the legislation is high, while the standard of proof remains on a balance of probabilities. A determination of incapacity is when an individual is unable to apply for a benefit due to a medical condition. It should not occur when the applicant (or someone applying on their behalf) states they did not apply earlier for non-medical reasons (e.g. being unaware of the benefit or not wanting to apply earlier). In cases where the application has been made by the individual claiming incapacity, it is important to assess what triggered the benefit application. There may be an indication of change in the applicant's condition such that they now possess the necessary capacity to apply for benefits. Alternatively, they may have applied upon learning of their possible entitlement to benefits, which may be evidence that there was a lack of knowledge about entitlement rather than incapacity. Evidence Declaration of Incapacity - Physician's Report (ISP-1800) form is not required to make an incapacity determination; the form facilitates the provision of evidence to the Department but is not a requirement (i.e. if the medical information on file is sufficient, the Department does not need to have an ISP-1800 form on file to make a determination). During the review of benefit eligibility or entitlement, the Department may initiate an assessment of incapacity at any time there is an indication that an applicant or beneficiary is or has been incapacitated. Evidence of incapacity must be available and received by the Department; however, an explicit claim of incapacity does not need to be made by: the applicant or beneficiary; their representative; or a physician. Criteria Must be continuous To apply the incapacity provision the applicant must have been incapacitated for a continuous period of time. Continuous period means there were no periods of time during which the applicant was capable of forming or expressing an intention to apply for benefits. Time limits for applications In cases where an applicant was incapacitated and is subsequently no longer incapacitated, there are time limits for submitting an application. The application must be submitted within: one month of when the applicant is no longer incapacitated, if the period of incapacity was less than 30 days; the number of days equal to the number of days the applicant was incapacitated, if the period of incapacity was less than one year; and one year, if the period of incapacity was greater than one year. Deeming an application receipt date If an applicant is found to be incapacitated, the deemed date of receipt of the application for CPP and OAS purposes, is the later of: the month preceding the first month in which the relevant benefit could have commenced to be paid; or the month in which the latest continuous period of incapacity commenced.

topic_title: CPP Disability and Post Retirement Disability Benefits
text: Life-long developmental disability In cases where an applicant has a life-long developmental disability and they have made contributions to the CPP, the incapacity provision should be assessed but would only be applied if it is to the advantage of the applicant. In the case where the life-long disability is the incapacitating condition and the application of the incapacity provision would negate the earnings and contributions made, thereby disqualifying the individual from being entitled to a benefit, the incapacity provision should not be applied. For OAS benefits, earnings and contributions are not a factor when determining eligibility, therefore if the applicant has a life-long developmental disability, the incapacity provision can be assessed and could be applied. Determining a medical date of onset for disability For CPP Disability benefits (CPPD benefits) (both DSB and the PRDB ), an applicant cannot be deemed to have become disabled earlier than 15 months before the date of their CPPD benefits application. If the applicant is found to be incapacitated, the 15-month retroactivity begins from the new deemed date of application. For applicants in pay for benefits in the previous 5 years, the maximum retroactivity of 12 months applies to the earlier deemed date of application. Determination using the Late Applicant Provision It is possible to consider the incapacity and the late applicant provisions when reviewing an application for disability benefits. The provisions operate together without any conflict between them. The incapacity provision is applied first, and then, if necessary, the late applicant provision is considered. If as a result of a determination of incapacity, the disability application is deemed to have been received at an earlier date: it must be determined if the person has sufficient contributions to meet the Minimum Qualifying Period at an earlier date; and whether the person met the CPP definition of disability before or at their Latest Possible Date of Onset and continuously thereafter.

topic_title: Interaction with related policies and provisions
text: New facts A determination of incapacity does not meet the test of New Facts. Therefore, incapacity cannot be used to re-open an initial decision in order to deem an earlier effective date. Erroneous Advice/ Administrative Error An applicant or beneficiary cannot claim erroneous advice or administrative error in situations where they were not advised of the possibility of making a claim of incapacity. There is no obligation to inform the individual of the incapacity provision. A failure to make a claim of incapacity until years after an application for benefits has been granted or approved would not be considered under the Erroneous Advice/ Administrative Error provisions. If existing evidence of incapacity is not addressed, there could be possibility of Administrative Error. In this scenario, consultation with National Headquarters via National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Internal link (access is required). National Business Expertise Tool Post-mortem If a CPP or OAS application is received post-mortem, a claim of incapacity cannot be assessed. However, any CPP or OAS application that is accepted post-mortem can still be processed for possible eligibility and entitlement. When an applicant dies at any time after a signed application has been received by the Department, the incapacity claim can be assessed. Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit The incapacity provision applies to the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) when the child is under the age of 18 (-18 child) or would have been a -18 child at the earlier deemed date of application. This earlier deemed date of application is from a determination of the disabled contributor`s incapacity, and is listed on the DSB application or a separate DCCB application submitted with the DSB or PRDB application. For a child who is the age of 18 or over, the incapacity provision can only be applied based on their DCCB application, and not the disabled contributor's incapacity application. Therefore, the DCCB application cannot be deemed to have been made at the earlier date. Child Rearing Provision Where the applicant claims incapacity for the same period as they were the child's primary caregiver, an assessment of relevant activities should be done. This assessment may include reviewing the activities undertaken, or choices made, by the applicant in their role as the child's primary caregiver. It can provide information pertaining to the applicant's ability to form or express the intention to apply for benefits. Relevant activities that might serve as evidence against incapacity include: scheduling and attending medical appointments for the child; consenting to medical tests or treatments for the child; or registering the child in daycare or school.

There may be times when the legal representative does not submit an application for a CPP or OAS pension/benefit on behalf of an applicant in a timely manner. The failure of a legal representative to submit an application promptly does not prevent a determination of incapacity. If the medical evidence supports the applicant or beneficiary is incapacitated, the Minister may deem the application to have been made at an earlier date, despite the failure of the legal representative to submit an application in a timely manner.
Old Age Security Act Section 28.1(1)—Incapacity when application actually made Canada Pension Plan Section 55.3(1)—Incapacity Subsection 60(8) to 60(11)—Application for a benefit

The CPP and the OAS act provide protection to individuals who could not or cannot apply for benefits due to their medical condition. Incapacity refers to an individual's cognitive or physical state preventing the formation or expression of their intention to apply for benefits. Coming into force For CPP benefits, the incapacity provision applies to individuals who were incapacitated on or after January 1, 1991, as this is when the provision came into force. For OAS benefits, the provision came into force on January 1, 1995. An individual's incapacity may have started before the coming into force dates, however, it must have continued through those dates. In cases where there is retroactive payment of a benefit, the start date of the retroactive payment can be before the effective date of the incapacity provision, as long as the applicant was incapacitated on or after the effective date of the incapacity provision.

A claim of incapacity may be submitted at the: initial; reconsideration; or appeal level. However, the incapacity provision itself does not have reconsideration or appeal rights. Review of application at reconsideration Incapacity can be assessed during the review of an accepted reconsideration request. If the time limit for reconsideration has expired and the criteria for extending the 90-day reconsideration period are not met, incapacity cannot be assessed. Review of application at Social Security Tribunal If the applicant did not make a claim of incapacity at the time of application or at reconsideration, and then appeals to the Social Security Tribunal ( SST ) - General Division (GD), the applicant may make a claim of incapacity at this stage of appeal. If a claim of incapacity is made before the SST -GD hearing, the Minister must investigate the claim by obtaining relevant evidence.

topic_title: When incapacity may NOT be assessed
text: The incapacity provision does not apply to: CPP pension sharing; the CPP death benefit; the CPP Surviving Child's benefit (where the child is under the age of 18); and any application received post-mortem.

A certified photocopy is a copy of an original document that is made and certified by an official from the list below. An individual certifying a photocopied document is attesting to the fact that they have compared it to the original document and found it to be a true copy of the original and unaltered in any way. There is no time limit on the certification if there is no reason to doubt the document's authenticity. There is no formal or legal wording that needs to be used with certifying documents. However, the individual performing the certification must do so in writing and use phrases or stamps that say such things as: "Certified copy of the original"; "This copy conforms to the original"; or "I certify this to be a true copy of the original", etc. The following officials can certify a photocopy of a document: Accountant; Chief of First Nations Band; Commissioner for Oaths; Employee of a Service Canada Centre acting in an official capacity; Funeral Director; Justice of the Peace; Lawyer, Magistrate, Notary; Manager of a financial institution; Medical and Health Practitioner: Chiropractor; Dentist; Doctor; Ophthalmologist; Optometrist; Pharmacist; Psychologist; Naturopathic Doctor; Nurse Practitioner; or Registered Nurse; Member of Parliament or their staff; Member of Provincial Legislature or their staff; Minister of Religion; Municipal Clerk; Official of a country with which Canada has a reciprocal social security agreement; Official of a federal or provincial government department or one of its agencies; Official of an Embassy, Consulate or High Commission; Police Officer; Professional Engineer; Social Worker; Teacher; or University Professor. Acceptable certified photocopies To be considered an acceptable certified true copy of an original document, a certified photocopy must: be clear and readable; contain the signature, name and official position or title of the individual who certified the document; contain the date when it was certified; and include a statement attesting to the fact that the document is a true copy of the original and has been compared to the original to ensure it was not amended or altered in any way. (This may be evident in a stamp that has been pre-formatted for this purpose.) The certified photocopy can be certified by a notary public or by a lawyer or solicitor and does not need to be returned to the individual. A government or court-issued document contains an official stamp and/or seal and is signed by the government or court official (domestic or foreign). A certified true copy of a government or court-issued document is accepted as an original document as the original document is retained by the government or court. A notarized copy is a document that is certified as a true copy by a: notary public; or lawyer/solicitor. Notarized copies bear an embossed seal or stamp along with complete certification and a signature. Multiple page documents often have a stapled blue paper corner or the certified documents are enclosed in a special envelope or folder. Unacceptable certified photocopies A photocopied document that does not contain the standard statement attesting to the fact that the document is a true copy that has been compared to the original which was not amended or altered in any way, is not acceptable. A certified photocopy is not acceptable if the document's appearance gives rise to doubts about its authenticity. This includes such items as family bibles and privately held records, where the date when the record was made is not normally given. Regardless of the certification, a certified true copy is not acceptable if it appears that the original has been altered in any way. Sometimes a document or form is received as a stamped certified copy of a certified true copy. Copies of certified true copies are unacceptable as documentary evidence, when a certified or original copy is requested. An individual cannot certify an already certified copy of a document. It is impossible for the individual performing the certification to make a proper attestation when they do not have access to the original document.

A certified true copy or original document does not need to be requested in cases where a copy is received by mail, fax, email with scan or uploaded through their My Service Canada Account, unless the validity of the document is in question. However, the Minister reserves the right to request original or certified documents at any time. When an applicant submits a document that is uploaded or scanned and emailed to the Department, it is an electronic document and subject to the Department of Employment and Social Development Act and the Electronic Documents and Electronic Information Regulations. For it to be accepted, it must: be sufficiently readable to be usable for subsequent reference; be in a format that does not prevent it from being retained; and have the time and date of receipt recorded by the system used to accept the transmitted document.

Should any provincial or federal government department cease to issue original paper or certified true copies of documents, the electronic version is considered as the original and is acceptable. Acceptable evidence presented to a social security authority for a country with which Canada has a reciprocal social security agreement, will be certified by that authority before being sent to Canada.
