Applicants who bring original documents into a Service Canada Centre or send them by mail can have their documents certified as true copies (free of charge) and returned to them.

When documentary evidence is required to establish eligibility for CPP and or OAS pensions and benefits, the Department accepts: a copy received by mail, fax, email with scan or uploaded through their My Service Canada Account; an original; or a certified true copy.

topic_title: Statutory declaration and commissioner for oaths Updated
text: Statutory declaration forms no longer require the applicant to have a Commissioner for Oaths' sign the form unless it has been requested by the department. All statutory declarations have been revised to remove SECTION B- TO BE COMPLETED BY THE COMMISSIONER FOR OATHS. The original forms remain accessible to secure the Commissioner for Oaths' signature for Integrity Services Branch purposes or when required, but have been updated to include "B" at the end of the ISP number and "Commissioner for Oaths" in the title (e.g. Statutory Declaration-Separation of Legal Spouses and Common-law Partners with Commissioner for Oaths (ISP-1811B)). Section 12 of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act provides the authorization of department-wide commissioners for oaths. These persons or "members of a class of persons" must be either departmental employees or other authorized employees. Commissioners for oaths appointed pursuant to the Department of Employment and Social Development Act may for the purposes of or incidental to the performance of duties or functions of the Department: administer oaths; and take and receive: affidavits; declarations; and affirmations. Effective October 1, 2008, employees who occupy specific positions, including on an interim basis, are authorized to act as commissioners for oaths in the course of their duties and for the purpose of, or incidental to, the performance of those duties. In addition, the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security Act permit other federal and provincial government employees to act as commissioners for oaths for the purpose of Service Canada programs. The legislation also enables Service Canada to accept documents authorized by a commissioner for oaths from another government department or agency. For example, a declaration stamped by a commissioner for oaths for the Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ) could be accepted for Service Canada purposes. If the document provided does not meet all of Service Canada's requirements, Service Canada is not obliged to accept it for the purposes of administering the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security Act . Therefore, the applicant may be contacted to obtain additional information or to submit a new statutory declaration.

topic_title: Use of evidence previously established under one program (CPP or OAS) for another program or the same program/benefit
text: When eligibility or entitlement criteria (such as age, marital status, separation, divorce and death) have been established by one program (CPP, OAS or International Agreements), through the submission of the appropriate documentation; another program, or the same program can accept them without the beneficiary or applicant having to resubmit further documentation. Exception Where marital status documentation is waived, for example when automatic enrolment data elements are used to substantiate OAS marital status for eligibility or entitlement to OAS benefits, it cannot be used for CPP benefit determinations.

The Minister can delegate administrative authority to any agent or departmental representative. ISB undertakes various activities including: determining if a case of misrepresentation meets the criterion of “knowingly” and recommending a penalty; conducting authorized fact-finding activities; compiling evidence and all relevant data; conducting eligibility and entitlement reviews; and referring cases to law enforcement (the National Enforcement Committee with a recommendation to refer the case to the RCMP) for criminal investigation when fraud is suspected. When is there misrepresentation? A misrepresentation is made when an applicant, beneficiary or third party makes a statement, a declaration, or a non-disclosure of facts (omission), in an application or otherwise, which they knew was false or misleading. Under CPP and OAS legislation, the Minister (or an individual acting on behalf of the Minister) can impose on an individual a penalty for each of the following acts or omissions if the Minister becomes aware of facts that, in their opinion, establish that the individual has: made a statement or declaration, in an application or otherwise, that they knew was false or misleading; made a statement or declaration, in an application or otherwise, that they knew was false or misleading because of the non-disclosure (omission) of facts; assented to, or participated in, an act or omission mentioned in the above paragraphs. received or obtained, by cheque or otherwise, a benefit payment to which they knew they were not entitled or a benefit payment which they knew was in excess of the amount of the benefit payment to which they were entitled, and did not return the benefit payment, or the excess amount, as the case may be, without delay. In addition, the legislation provides for penalties where an individual: Knowingly failed to declare to the Minister all or some of their earnings for a period for which they received Disability benefits. knowingly failed to declare to the Minister all or some of their income; knowingly failed to correct any inaccuracies in the information provided by the Minister. The criterion of "knowingly" The criterion of “knowingly” is defined as committing a misrepresentation wilfully, consciously and with knowledge. It involves: being aware or understanding; being well informed, deliberate, or conscious, demonstrating a deliberate attempt by an individual to provide false information or to mislead by omitting relevant information at. “Knowingly” must directly link to the time at which the individual made the misrepresentation. “Knowingly” means the Minister can reasonably conclude the individual knew the information provided was untrue when they provided it, or they did not declare that information. There is no need to prove a fraudulent intent in this consideration and it is not necessary for the Integrity Service Investigator (ISI) to determine a degree of fault. The Minister must only establish that it is more likely the individual understood the information provided and did not accurately portray the facts. When imposing an administrative penalty, knowingly means that the individual, at the time of the misrepresentation: was aware of the rules; and had the capacity to understand the rules. The element of “knowingly” is established based on the balance of probabilities and is to be documented by ISB. This can also be established in the case that an individual admits to their actions during the course of the investigation. Assessing “knowingly” “Knowingly” refers to any false statement or omission that: misleads the Minister, resulting in the real or possible payment of benefits to which the individual was not entitled; and at the time of the statement, is known by the individual to not accurately reflect the facts. General guidelines for determining if an individual knowingly makes a misrepresentation: Was the provided information something that the beneficiary or applicant was likely to know (e.g., marital status, income, dependent children, disability)? Does the individual have the ability to understand information? Can it be demonstrated that the individual expected that the misrepresentation would result in a gain?
Canada Pension Plan Section 90(1)(2)—Offences Criminal Code Section 380(1)—Fraud Financial Administration Act Section 92(e)—Exceptions Old Age Security Act Section 44. (1)(2)(3)—Offences

First misrepresentation A first misrepresentation occurs when the Department determines that an individual has knowingly made a misrepresentation for the first time. Even if the statement or declaration contains several falsehoods, it is still considered as one misrepresentation because it all relates to the same event. The initial value of the penalty percentage for a first misrepresentation is 10% of the overpayment amount. If there is no overpayment, then the initial value of the penalty is 10% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation. Subsequent misrepresentation When the Minister becomes aware of a new misrepresentation by the same individual under the OAS or CPP, and the penalty imposition date for that misrepresentation is within 10 years from the date of imposition of a prior OAS or CPP penalty or conviction, this new misrepresentation would be considered as a subsequent misrepresentation. Any misrepresentation identified after an individual has been notified in writing, and beyond the reconsideration and appeal period, is treated as a subsequent misrepresentation. A subsequent misrepresentation is to be penalized at a higher rate than a first misrepresentation. The initial value of the penalty percentage for a subsequent misrepresentation is 20% of the overpayment amount. If there is no overpayment, then the initial value of the penalty is 20% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation.

If multiple misrepresentations under the same Act (either CPP or OAS) are detected during the course of the same investigation, they are treated as either a first misrepresentation or a subsequent misrepresentation. This compounding results in the calculation and implementation of one overall penalty which covers all the misrepresentations discovered at the same time. For example, an individual with no known prior OAS penalty or conviction falsely indicates the length of Canadian residence on their application for OAS benefits, then later, upon request, participates in supplying a Statutory Declaration with the exact same false information. While there are two misrepresentations, this would be treated as a first misrepresentation if the individual has no prior OAS penalty. Another example: an individual, who was imposed an OAS penalty 3 years ago, misrepresents both their age and their marital status on one GIS application. This is considered one misrepresentation, as one statement or declaration whether containing one falsehood or many falsehoods is treated as one misrepresentation. The case would be treated as a subsequent misrepresentation given the individual's previous OAS penalty. Each receipt of a payment shall not be considered a separate misrepresentation. For example: a payment after death, where an individual doesn't report the death of the beneficiary and receives 7 payments of a retirement pension; the misrepresentation is treated as a single one, not 7 misrepresentations. When the Department has determined that multiple misrepresentations have been made, the individual is advised in writing with a detailed breakdown of each misrepresentation and of the imposition of a penalty. Individuals are informed of their reconsideration and appeal rights on the imposition of the penalty and the amount of the penalty. When a false statement, omission or declaration is made under both the CPP and the OAS Act, each program can impose its own penalty.

topic_title: Overpayments when there is wrongdoing (suspected fraud or misrepresentation)
text: When fraud or misrepresentation has been established, is suspected or is under investigation, the results of the administrative investigation determine who is liable for the debt and are used as a basis for recovery. In addition, if a criminal investigation determines that another individual claimed benefits that belonged to someone else, the findings of that investigation must be used as a basis for recovery from the individual involved. If fraud is successfully proven, the overpayment must be recovered.

The Department administers the Old Age Security Act (OAS) and the Canada Pension Plan (CPP). The administration of the payments relating to these programs includes a requirement to prevent overpayments and underpayments of program funds. If initial and continuing eligibility and entitlement conditions are met due to false and misleading information or due to the withholding of information, action is mandatory. In the daily course of a departmental employee's duties, anomalies or discrepancies may be identified in applications or documentation. After going through a standard review process, if reasonable explanations for an anomaly or a discrepancy are not revealed or explained; all relevant documentation and other evidence received must be referred to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for an administrative investigation. Until the nature and extent of the misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, and the entire administrative investigation process is completed, benefits cannot be cancelled. However, benefits can be temporarily suspended.

“Mitigating circumstances” are situations, facts or actions that do not condone the misrepresentation(s) but can provide some explanation to the individual's actions, which could lead to a reduction of up to 100% of the penalty amount. It may also include situations when the individual takes responsibility for their actions or assists in the investigation. Mitigating circumstances are only considered after the criterion of “knowingly” has been established and a penalty has been recommended. Many personal situations, as well as other factors, can be considered as mitigating circumstances. There are two types of mitigating circumstances: Situations present at the time of the misrepresentation To be considered as mitigating circumstances, situations provided or found must: be present at the time of the misrepresentation; be credible; and help explain the individual's actions. The existence of mitigating circumstances must never be assumed. There must be clear indication that such circumstances exist. The following examples attempt to provide an overview of situations or factors that might constitute mitigating circumstances and may justify a lower penalty. The following is not an exhaustive list: Physical or mental illness serious illness of a close relative or immediate family member; medical circumstances or condition of the beneficiary or individual; or compulsive disorders (such as addictions, gambling, drug, or alcohol dependency, etc.). Emotional death of spouse, partner, relative or immediate family member; financial, physical or mental abuse by a spouse, partner, family member, or other; or separation from a spouse or partner (loss of marital income). Other the beneficiary or individual demonstrates an urgent need due to personal or family circumstance(s); personal theft; other debt obligations; or states of emergency such as wildfires, flooding, earthquakes, etc. Other factors or situations present at the time of the investigation or penalty Other factors or situations that are only present at the time of the investigation or penalty may be considered as mitigating circumstances to reduce a penalty to be imposed. The following is not an exhaustive list: individual expresses genuine regret; individual admits to the misrepresentation without resistance or further misrepresentation; and individual cooperates with, or even assists in the investigation, providing documentation, etc. In addition, the following situations may develop after the misrepresentation but are still present by the time the penalty is applied and may further be considered as mitigating circumstances: individual now lacks the ability to understand, or to judge right from wrong (for example, individual is deemed medically incapable or is incapacitated). Deterrent value Administrative penalties have an important deterrent value in discouraging individuals from committing further misrepresentations and protecting the integrity of the programs. When it is determined that an individual has knowingly made a misrepresentation, the delegated departmental representative must review the Report of Investigation and the individual's file for any mitigating circumstances, to determine if the penalty amount should be adjusted accordingly. The responsible BDS official must rely upon written record and documentation in order to identify any “mitigating circumstances”. However, as a rule, individuals do not need to provide proof. All decisions are made on a case-by-case basis, and a record of all decisions made shall be maintained. The records of decision shall help BDS determine which level of mitigating circumstances may be appropriate. Assessing mitigating circumstances A proper assessment of both types of mitigating circumstances constitutes the cornerstone of the Minister's discretionary authority to establish the amount of a penalty. The Minister always has the discretion to determine if mitigating circumstances exist and to consider those circumstances when setting the penalty amount. Subject to the judgement of the delegated authority, agent or department representative, case-related mitigating circumstances shall have the following impact when determining if there are mitigating circumstances and how significant they are in reducing the penalty amount: where the mitigating circumstances are very significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 80, 90 or 100% ; where the mitigating circumstances are significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 50, 60 or 70% ; where the mitigating circumstances are moderately significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 10, 20, 30 or 40% ; or where there are no mitigating circumstances 0% reduction and full penalty. The existence of increments, however, does not imply a "mechanical" approach to the consideration of case-related circumstances. There is no correlation such as "one case-related circumstance equals one increment. Any single case-related circumstance may be more significant, or less so, and be weighted accordingly. Many situations or factors may be considered as mitigating circumstances. Judgement will be required in determining if case-related circumstances exist to a degree warranting consideration. Consideration should be given to the individual's particular situation and severity, from moderately significant to very significant. The number of circumstances should also be considered in the reduction and may help explain the individual's actions at the time of the misrepresentation.

topic_title: The same mitigating circumstances can be used more than once
text: When an individual claims the same mitigating circumstances on a subsequent misrepresentation, the Minister has the discretion to accept or deny them as valid. The determination depends on the circumstances of each case. Discretionary decision A determination of misrepresentation and the resulting penalty is a discretionary decision that is made with fairness in mind and must be reasonable. This means consideration must be given to any information provided and show how it concludes that the misleading statement was made knowingly. The Department must be able to explain why facts are relevant or irrelevant. In the case of a penalty, the record of decision must clearly show how the penalty amount was calculated.

topic_title: When suspected fraud or misrepresentation is not yet established
text: Until the exact nature and extent of the suspected fraud or misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, and the entire administrative investigation process is completed, benefits must not be cancelled. However, they can be suspended: when advised by ISB; when eligibility has ceased due to death; or when the individual does not reside in Canada. Each case must be evaluated to ensure that any action taken will not interfere with, or obstruct, any investigation by the RCMP.

For a disclosure to be considered valid, it must meet all of the following criteria: The disclosure must be authentic (i.e. the Integrity Services Branch does not have an investigation in progress, and the disclosure is not given in response to an operational fact-finding process). The disclosure is freely given and not made for the purpose of gain. The facts on file must confirm that the admission would have led to a penalty or a possible referral to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) if there had been no disclosure. The disclosure must be made by the individual or third party who committed the misrepresentation. The disclosure must be complete and accurate. Strict adherence to these 5 criteria is necessary to ensure consistent application of the CPP and OAS Disclosure Policy. While the information provided must be substantially complete, a disclosure will not be denied simply because it contains minor errors or omissions. However, if a disclosure is found to contain important errors or omissions, it will not qualify as a complete disclosure. Therefore: the disclosed information will be processed; penalties and interest can be applied to the entire amount; a referral may be made to the RCMP.

Whether a disclosure is valid or invalid, it can result in: a reassessment of the individual's application or the beneficiary's entitlement; the establishment of an overpayment. In cases where a disclosure is deemed to be invalid, a penalty can also be imposed, along with corresponding interest, if applicable. In more severe cases, the matter can be referred to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for investigation by Integrity Services Branch.

A disclosure will not be denied simply because it contains minor errors or omissions. If it is discovered that the disclosure was knowingly incomplete, the disclosure cannot be accepted. The Department can then impose a penalty and interest to the entire amount or refer the matter to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for possible prosecution. The Department will not accept a disclosure as valid if it is discovered that the disclosure was made for the purpose of gain (e.g. to qualify for another benefit). In such cases, the disclosure will not be accepted as valid, and the individual can be subject to a penalty, including interest.

Integrity Services Branch (ISB) is responsible for: conducting the fact-finding; completing a written report; accepting or denying the disclosure; passing this information along with a recommendation for any further action. The recommendation must be supported with documented facts so that action may be taken on the decision and any outstanding overpayment calculated. Departmental officials can still perform the standard review functions. The Disclosure Policy is simply a new trigger prompting the referral of files to ISB when an individual comes forward and discloses a misrepresentation knowingly made.

The Minister's refusal to accept a disclosure cannot be reconsidered to the Minister or appealed to the Social Security Tribunal—General Division. However, an applicant or beneficiary can make an application to the Federal Court for a judicial review of the Ministers' decision.

Old Age Security Act Section 44(1)(2)(3)—Offences Section 44.1—Penalties Canada Pension Plan Section 90(1)(2)—Offences Section 90.1—Penalty for misrepresentation, etc. Financial Administration Act Section 92(e)—Exceptions
There is no limit to the number of times an individual can take advantage of the Disclosure Policy.

The CPP and OAS Disclosure Policy encourages individuals to come forward about misrepresentation and to correct inaccurate or incomplete information. The Disclosure Policy also encourages them to disclose information that they did not divulge at the time of their application or during any subsequent dealings with the CPP or OAS programs. The purpose of the Disclosure Policy is to give individuals the opportunity to correct any situation resulting from a misrepresentation knowingly made. They can do so without fear of penalty or of referral by the Minister to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for possible prosecution if the disclosure is accepted as valid. Although these cases will not be referred for prosecution, the Minister has no control over investigations undertaken by other law enforcement agencies or government bodies. When an individual makes a disclosure under the Disclosure Policy: no administrative penalty is applied; no interest is charged on the debt arising from the overpayment; the misrepresentation is not taken into account in determining if a repetitive misrepresentation occurred.

A disclosure must be program-specific. As the CPP and OAS Act are separate pieces of legislation, each program has to be treated individually. Any information that a person discloses to the Department to correct information (e.g. their age on an OAS application) cannot automatically be considered as a disclosure to correct the same information under the CPP program, unless the person specifically tells us they provided the same false information under both programs and wishes to correct the information under both.

Voluntary disclosure is an admission by an applicant, a beneficiary or an informant lead, that they knowingly made a misrepresentation. The Disclosure Policy does not apply if an investigation is under way. When voluntary disclosure is accepted, no penalty is imposed.

Integrity Services Branch (ISB) is responsible for referrals to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) for a criminal investigation. The circumstances of each case determine if the charges to be laid by the RCMP or the Department of Justice will be under the Criminal Code of Canada, the Act(s) administered by the branch, or a combination of both. If warranted by the findings of their investigation, the RCMP makes the decision concerning the laying of charges in all cases referred by ISB.

In situations where an applicant or beneficiary makes a voluntary admission that they knowingly made misrepresentations and give full disclosure of the facts of the misrepresentation, the file must be referred to Integrity Services Branch for review and an administrative investigation. If an administrative investigation has not already started on a particular file, the Department is not to use the individual’s disclosure as a trigger to apply an administrative penalty.
Old Age Security Act Subsection 44(1)—Offences Canada Pension Plan Subsection 90(1)—Offence of punishment

An administrative investigation is an impartial investigative process conducted by Integrity Services Branch (ISB) on files Service Canada Benefit Officers (SCBOs) or other departmental representatives referred to them due to anomalies and discrepancies identified in applications, other documentation or files. ISB staff will determine whether an administrative investigation is warranted. There are a number of triggers that, when discovered by departmental officials, may elicit an administrative investigation on the file of an applicant or beneficiary concerning eligibility or entitlement to the CPP or OAS pensions and benefits. Such triggers include: misrepresentation; informant leads; suspected fraud and disclosures. As there is no legislative authority under the Canada Pension Plan or the Old Age Security Act for any surveillance activities, surveillance materials to determine eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPP and OAS pensions are not to be solicited. In this context, "surveillance" is considered any technique consisting of concealed observation of activities to obtain information or to support facts. It includes, but is not limited to: written reports; videotapes; audiotapes or any other recordings (electronic or otherwise).

Applicants, beneficiaries and other individuals or groups have attempted and will continue to attempt defrauding our programs. It is everyone’s responsibility to report any information which may identify fraudulent situations. Files referred to Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for an administrative investigation may result in the imposition of an administrative monetary penalty when it has been discovered that the applicant or beneficiary knowingly made a misrepresentation (i.e. they knowingly provided false or misleading information or knowingly withheld or omitted relevant information). Until the exact nature and extent of the suspected fraud or misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, do not cancel benefits before the entire administrative investigation process is completed. However, benefits can be suspended when advised by ISB in cases where eligibility or entitlement has ceased due to death, or due to residence outside of Canada. Each case must be evaluated to ensure that any action taken will not interfere or obstruct any investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

The Minister can delegate authority as deemed appropriate to any agent or Departmental representative to: impose an administrative penalty; collect the monetary portion of the penalty imposed; and reduce or rescind the penalty. The decision of whether to impose, reduce or rescind a penalty rests with the delegated authority. No penalty can be imposed until it is endorsed by the National Administrative Penalties Committee. The committee was established to facilitate and ensure a consistent approach to and application of the imposition of administrative penalties for the CPP and OAS programs.
An administrative penalty is comprised of 3 components: the penalty amount; the notification letter; and the Record of Misrepresentation.

When the Integrity Services Branch determines that a misrepresentation was knowingly made and makes a recommendation to apply a penalty, determine the penalty amount to be imposed. To determine the penalty amount, consider the following: The maximum legislated penalty allowed for each misrepresentation is $10,000. In a first misrepresentation, the penalty is based on an amount not more than 10% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 10% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. In a subsequent misrepresentation, the penalty amount is based on an amount not more than 20% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 20% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. To determine whether a misrepresentation should be penalized as a first or subsequent misrepresentation , the Minister must be aware of the subsequent misrepresentation and it must be within 10 years from the date a previous penalty was imposed. The penalty amount may be reduced depending on an individual’s mitigating circumstances, outlined in the Report of Investigation. Mitigating circumstances determined to be valid may allow the penalty amount to be reduced by any percentage up to 100%. The minimum penalty amount is $0.00. A $0.00 amount still counts as a penalty. This is an important consideration when establishing a subsequent misrepresentation.

The Minister can impose an administrative penalty on an applicant, a beneficiary or a third party who knowingly makes a misrepresentation affecting CPP or OAS pensions and benefits, including post-retirement benefits. When 2 or more individuals are involved in committing a misrepresentation, both or all can be subjected to an administrative penalty and required to pay the penalty amount and interest. The individual who receives the pension or benefit is responsible for the reimbursement of any overpayment. The individual who committed the misrepresentation, however, is responsible to pay the penalty amount and any interest or the case may be subject to referral to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for possible criminal investigation. This may be one and the same or different individuals, depending on the circumstances. The penalty does not have to be applied evenly against all individuals. Each individual involved is likely to have unique mitigating circumstances. Each person involved is assessed on an individual basis.

Old Age Security Act Section 44—Offences Section 44.1(1)—Penalties Canada Pension Plan Section 90—Offence and punishment Section 90.1(1)—Penalty for misrepresentation, etc. Financial Administration Act Regulations Debt Write-off Regulations, 1994

The CPP and the OAS Act state that a penalty will not be imposed on an individual in the following circumstances: a prosecution for the act or omission has been initiated against the individual; 5 years have passed since the day on which the Minister became aware of the act or omission; the misrepresentation was made before the penalty provisions in the legislation came into force; or the individual who committed the misrepresentation is now deceased.

An administrative penalty can be imposed even if a misrepresentation does not result in an overpayment. When the Minister becomes aware of a misrepresentation before benefits are paid, there is no overpayment. However, a penalty can still be imposed. When there is a determination of misrepresentation and no overpayment exists, the maximum penalty cannot be more than 10% or 20% (in the event of a subsequent misrepresentation) of the maximum monthly pension amount payable at the time of the misrepresentation.

Once a penalty is imposed, the debtors involved must be notified in writing of any debt (penalty and associated overpayment amount, if any) owed to the Crown. The notification letter is sent to the individual or individuals involved, even when the penalty amount is set at $0.00. The letter or letters must cover the following: the ministerial authority to impose a penalty; the legislated maximum penalty of $10,000; detailed facts about the misrepresentation or misrepresentations; mitigating circumstances, if applicable; the overpayment amount, if applicable; the legislation regarding potential interest accrual; the penalty amount (even if it is $0.00); information about the Record of Misrepresentation, including that records are kept for 10 years; options to recover the overpayment (if applicable) and to collect the penalty and interest, if applicable; a request for a lump-sum repayment of the debt; the potential impact of any future misrepresentation; and the individual's right to appeal. Advise debtors of the importance of specifying how their debt payments are to be distributed or allocated when the debtors have more than one debt (e.g. EI, CPP, OAS).

Legislation provides the authority to impose administrative penalties in cases of misrepresentation that are determined to be knowingly made, to collect monetary penalties imposed and to reduce or rescind penalties, when appropriate. The penalty amount imposed must be proportionate with the size of the overpayment and take into account: whether the misrepresentation is repetitive; the presence of any mitigating circumstances. Administrative penalties imposed under the CPP cannot influence a penalty under the OAS Act, and vice-versa. Penalties are determined based on the facts of each case. The amount of the penalty is considered as a debt owed to the Crown. Therefore, it is subject to the write-off regulations in the Financial Administration Act .

Under the CPP and the OAS Act, all individuals who have had a penalty imposed have the right to ask for a reconsideration or an appeal on: the decision to impose a penalty; and the amount of the penalty. If the Minister receives a request for a reconsideration within 90 days of the date of the letter of imposition of a penalty, and collection of the penalty and recovery of the overpayment has already begun, both the collection of the penalty and the recovery of the overpayment are suspended until the outcome of the reconsideration or subsequent appeal has been communicated to the individual.

Once a penalty is imposed, and even if it is reduced, a Record of Misrepresentation must be completed. The Record of Misrepresentation remains open for a period of 10 years, starting from the date the penalty is imposed. This time period is important when establishing a subsequent misrepresentation under the same program, that can be penalized at a higher percentage rate. When the Minister becomes aware of another misrepresentation after the 10-year period has elapsed, the subsequent misrepresentations are treated as a first misrepresentation. The 10-year time limit on using the individual's record of penalty or conviction is solely for the purpose of determining the penalty amount (10% for a first misrepresentation, 20% for a subsequent misrepresentation).

Under the CPP and the OAS Act, the Minister has the discretionary authority to reduce the penalty amount or rescind penalties where appropriate. When a penalty is reduced in part or in full, the penalty itself remains valid and can be used in the future to potentially establish a subsequent misrepresentation. The rescission of the imposition of a penalty reflects the determination that the penalty should never have been imposed in the first place. In relation to upon whom the penalty was imposed, it will be as if the penalty (and any penalty amount assigned) never existed in the first place. The circumstances surrounding the situation will no longer be considered to be a misrepresentation and cannot be used in the future to establish a subsequent misrepresentation. Because of this, the rescission of the imposition of a penalty or the reduction in the penalty amount must only be considered under the CPP and the OAS Act in the following circumstances: the presentation of new facts; the satisfaction that: the penalty was imposed without knowledge of a material fact or based on a mistake regarding that fact; the penalty cannot be collected within the reasonably foreseeable future; or payment of the penalty would cause undue hardship to the debtor. A penalty is meant to be collected in full or until such time as there is a reason to reduce or rescind the penalty or any outstanding balance. All reasonable efforts to recover the receivable must be attempted.

Overpayment remitted or written-off Interest stops accruing on the day the overpayment portion of the debt is remitted or written-off, whether in whole or in part. In cases where an overpayment has been written-off, there is a possibility that recovery activities with respect to that overpayment could resume in the future. Interest charges could start accruing again as of the 120th day from the date of notification of the resumption of the recovery activities. When an overpayment has been remitted in part, the balance of interest is adjusted accordingly as partial remission of the interest charges. Interest charges can then accrue on the outstanding overpayment as of the 120th day from the letter of notification or until a repayment schedule has been established, whichever is the earliest. When an overpayment has been remitted or written-off, it is possible that the corresponding penalty has been either reduced or rescinded. If the penalty to which the overpayment was attached has been rescinded, the overpayment will not be subject to the charging of interest if it is reinstated in the future. Administrative penalty written-off Interest stops accruing on the day the penalty portion of the debt is written-off, whether in whole or in part. There is a possibility that recovery activities with respect to that penalty could resume or be revisited for recovery at a later date. Interest charges could start accruing again as of the 120th day from the date of notification of the resumption of the recovery activities. Penalty rescinded or reduced Interest stops accruing on the day the penalty is reduced, whether in whole or in part. The reduction of a penalty results from a decision with respect to an account. As with all decisions that establish or adjust a debt, interest charges can start accruing again as of the 120th day from the earliest of the following dates: notification of the decision; or the established due date. Interest charges remitted The remission of interest charges legally releases the debtor from any obligation to repay the accrued interest. Where interest charges have been partially remitted based on one of the conditions listed in the Interest charges can be remitted in whole or in part section below, accrual of additional interest will cease until the adjustment has been communicated to the debtor. It will remain suspended until 120 days from the date of the notification letter or until the established due date, whichever is the earliest. Interest charges are fully remitted The CPP and OAS Act require that any interest charges applied against an account are to be remitted when the corresponding administrative penalty has been rescinded. When a penalty is rescinded, it is as if it was never imposed against the individual in the first place. Therefore, interest never should have been charged against the debt. In such a case, any monies recovered are to be applied against the outstanding overpayment, if any. If there is no associated overpayment owing, any monies recovered are to be reimbursed to the individual. If a penalty has been imposed on a third party but the related overpayment is assigned to a different debtor, any monies collected on interest and penalty charges will not be applied against the outstanding overpayment, if any, upon rescission of the penalty. Instead, the monies would be reimbursed to that third party. Interest charges can be remitted in whole or in part In the Interest Charges are fully remitted section above, the remission of interest is related to the rescission of a penalty. However, there are instances where a penalty will remain. In such cases, interest can start accruing again once 120 days have elapsed from the notification letter or once a new due date has been established, whichever is sooner. Interest charges can be remitted, whether in whole or in part, as per CPP and OAS Act when: the interest has ceased to accrue in accordance with bullet 3; the administrative costs of collecting the interest would exceed the amount of interest; or the interest cannot be collected within the reasonably foreseeable future; or payment of the interest would result in undue financial hardship for the debtor. Interest charges are written-off Under the CPP and the OAS Act, accrued interest is considered as “Debts due to her Majesty”, thereby falling under the Financial Administration Act ’s "Debt Write-Off" regulations. This means that accrued interest can be written-off and subsequently revisited for recovery at a later date. Refunds due to rescissions or remissions There are times where a penalty has been rescinded or the interest has been remitted after payments have already been made against the debt. In such cases, the Department can refund the monies paid depending on the circumstances. If, after rescinding the penalty or remitting the interest, there remains an outstanding balance on the overpayment, any monies paid by the individual that was applied against the penalty portion or the interest portion of the debt will be applied against the overpayment instead. In cases where there is no such outstanding overpayment, the monies are reimbursed to the individual. If a penalty has been imposed on a third party but the related overpayment is assigned to a different debtor, upon rescission of the penalty or remission of interest charges, any monies collected will not be applied against the outstanding overpayment. Instead, the monies would be reimbursed to that third party while the other debtor remains responsible for the outstanding overpayment, if any. Debt adjustments and partial remissions Where the amount of an overpayment to which a penalty is attached has been adjusted, either upwards or downwards, on the basis of a decision under the CPP and the OAS Act (or judicial review thereof), the corresponding accrued interest, if any, will be adjusted accordingly for the entire period in question.

topic_title: Debts under both CPP and OAS programs and minimum payments to stop the accrual of interest
text: The concept of making at least a nominal payment towards a debt to stop the accrual of interest is particularly important when a debtor has a debt under both the CPP and OAS programs. They must direct the Department to apply a particular dollar amount to each of the debts to ensure the ceasing of accrual of interest on all debts. In the same way, if an individual has 2 CPP or OAS debts, one older than the other, they must direct the Department to apply a particular amount against each to ensure that no interest accrues on the more recent debt as payments are applied against the oldest debt first.

Old Age Security Act Subsection 37(2.01)—Recovery of amount of interest Subsection 37(4)—Remission of amount owing OAS regulations Section 48(7)(b)(c)(d)—Interest on Amounts Owing to Her Majesty Canada Pension Plan Subsection 66(2.01)—Recovery of amount of interest Subsection 66(3)—Remission of amount owing CPP regulations Section (87)(7)(b)(c)(d)—Interest on Amounts Owing to Her Majesty

Any dollar amount as payment will stop the accrual of interest even if the payment received is less than the established payment amount. However, debtors are encouraged to respect the established repayment schedule and payment amounts as much as possible.

topic_title: Notifying debtors of the potential for interest
text: The Department is responsible for notifying debtors in writing that interest will be charged if they fail to repay the administrative penalty and the associated overpayment amounts according to a repayment schedule.

When there is a monthly repayment schedule, the due date will be on the same calendar day of each month. The Department would consider the following situation as a tacit agreement to repay: the debtor has failed to establish a repayment schedule within the initial 120-day period from the date of notification of the administrative penalty; and the debtor makes a payment at some time within that period. The schedule will be based on a recurring monthly date that is the same day as the initial payment receipt date.

As of April 1, 2011, the Department has the authority to charge interest on administrative penalties and related overpayments owed under the CPP and the OAS Act. Interest will only be charged on administrative penalties and the associated overpayment amounts when the debtor has failed to make a payment by an established due date. Interest is not charged on owing administrative penalties and related overpayments when the debtor is receiving CPP or OAS benefits. In these cases, the debts are collected via a monthly withhold from the benefits being paid.

The prescribed rate of interest is the Bank of Canada average rate plus 3%. Interest will accrue daily where debtors have missed making a payment by the scheduled due date and is compounded monthly. Where the amount of an overpayment to which a penalty is attached has been adjusted, either upwards or downwards, on the basis of a decision under the CPP and the OAS Act (or judicial review thereof), the corresponding accrued interest, if any, will be adjusted accordingly for the entire period in question.
When a repayment schedule is being established, a monthly schedule will be strongly encouraged. Payment frequencies will only be considered under exceptional circumstances.

Interest is charged on owing administrative penalties and related overpayments when the debtor is not receiving CPP or OAS benefits. Interest starts being charged on owing CPP and OAS penalties and related overpayments: on the 120th day after the debtor was informed of a decision linked to the penalty (including reconsideration, appeal, judicial review and debt adjustment) when no repayment schedule has been established or no payment has been received; or on the due date established by the debtor when the debtor chooses to start repayment before the 120th day but fails to provide payment on that date; or on the next payment due date when the debtor fails to adhere to a repayment schedule. Interest stops being charged on owing penalties and related overpayments: on the day before the date on which any payment towards the debt is received, no matter the amount; when the decision that resulted in the debt is under reconsideration or appeal; the day after the debtor dies; and the day the debt is adjusted, meaning: the day the related overpayments are remitted or written-off; or the day the penalty is written-off, reduced or rescinded; or the day the interest charges are written-off or remitted.
Depending on the country, payments made on behalf of deceased individuals can be subject to non-resident tax (the country's default non-resident tax rate).

topic_title: Effective date of non-resident tax withhold
text: The non-resident tax withhold is effective the month the individual starts living in another country. In cases of retroactive payment, the individual's place of residence at the time of payment determines whether the non-resident tax is applied.
Income Tax Act Section 217—Part XIII, Tax on Income from Canada of Non-resident Persons, Alternative re Canadian benefits

topic_title: Pensions and benefits impacted by this policy
text: The following pensions and benefits are impacted by the Non-resident tax withhold policy: OAS pension; Retirement pension; Post-Retirement benefit; Disability benefit; Post-Retirement Disability benefit; Survivor's pension; Death benefit; and Children's benefits.

Since January 1996, the Income Tax Act permits the taxation of Canadian social security benefits paid to non-residents. This tax is applicable to: the OAS pension; and all benefits and pensions paid under the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. The Department is responsible for: withholding the prescribed amount of tax at source from benefits paid to non-residents; and remitting the withheld amounts to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

Individuals who are not Canadian residents can contact the Canada Revenue Agency's (CRA) International Tax Services Office to apply for a reduction in their tax withhold rate. To benefit from a non-resident tax withhold rate reduction, non-residents must complete a Canadian income tax return. Section 217 of the Income Tax Act provides that an individual can apply for a reduction in their non-resident tax rate by filing an Application by a Non-Resident of Canada for a Reduction in the Amount of Non-Resident Tax Required to be Withheld (NR5) form with CRA. After the return is assessed, CRA refunds any excess non-resident tax withheld, if applicable. Non-residents must re-apply annually to CRA to continue to receive a reduction of their non-resident tax withhold. For this reason, the non-resident tax rates are reset to the default rates after the December payment period until a new NR5 form is received and processed. CRA administers the legislation, therefore consideration for reduction of the non-resident tax withhold falls within CRA's jurisdiction. In September each year, the Department conducts a mail-out of NR5 applications. Non-residents must return their completed NR5 forms to CRA by October 31 so that CRA can assess and notify the Department to process a reduction in the withholding rate in time for the January payment of the following year, if applicable. CRA sends a notice of assessment to advise individuals whether or not they qualify for a reduction in their non-resident tax rate. If a decrease in the tax withhold is approved , CRA completes and sends a reduction letter to the Department for processing. Separate reduction letters are issued for both CPP and OAS accounts to indicate the revised percentage of non-resident tax to be withheld. Reduction letters include the expiry date of the approved reduction (usually the current taxation year). Reduction letters must reach the Department by mid-December to be processed in time for the January payment. The reduced withhold rate is based on an estimate of the individual's previous year's income. The precise amount of taxes payable is determined when the individual files an income tax return the following year. CRA has a system in place to identify any accounts where a discrepancy exists between: the amount that an individual reports on the NR5 form; and the amount indicated on the database. It is CRA's responsibility to advise the individual of any discrepancies related to the yearly benefit income amount. If there are any discrepancies, the non-resident tax rate reduction request is reassessed by CRA and an amendment letter issued to the individual. In most situations, an amendment letter reflects a decrease in the withhold rate from the rate specified in the reduction letter. There can be instances where the revised withhold rate indicated in the amendment letter is higher than the rate specified in the reduction letter. If the effective date of the increased rate is before the current accounting month, retroactive recovery of non-resident tax must take place. If CRA does not provide an effective date for a tax withholding reduction, the withhold rate for the current accounting month is reduced. Any arrears owing are refunded to the individual by CRA when the individual's tax return is assessed the next year. Individuals are to be reimbursed for excess monies withheld from January of the current year to the month before the accounting month in which the reduction is accepted in the system. For example, if the reduction notice received in April 2019 indicates that the individual's non-resident tax rate should have been reduced effective January 2019, and the reduction notice is processed in the May 2019 accounting month, the refund due to the individual would be for the months of January to April 2019.

According to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), an individual is generally considered a non-resident of Canada during the period they do not normally, regularly or customarily live in Canada. That is: the individual does not maintain significant residential ties in Canada while living outside of Canada; the individual's absence from Canada has a degree of permanence ; and the individual has established significant residential ties outside of Canada. Where doubt exists regarding residence status, individuals must contact CRA's International Tax Services Office or local tax services office, where a residency determination can be made following completion of either: a Determination of Residency Status (Leaving Canada) (NR73) form; or a Determination of Residency Status (Entering Canada) (NR74) form. A deemed resident is not subject to non-resident tax. CRA identifies deemed residents each year and sends a list of these individuals to Business Operations. These lists are then distributed to the regions by mid-December to enable them to reset the non-resident tax rate to zero on these accounts starting in the month of January.

Recovery of non-resident tax is retroactive to the month in which a beneficiary starts living in another country or January of the current year, whichever is later . To comply with this requirement, the withhold rate for countries with a 25% taxation rate can be increased by up to twice the normal value. If doubling the withhold rate for countries with less than 25% taxation is not enough to recover monies owing within the same taxation year, the withhold rate can be increased to a maximum of 50% of the pension or benefit payment. Retroactive recovery is also required in situations where the rate of the non-resident tax withhold is increased by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Such an increase can occur because of CRA receiving additional income information after an original decision was made to reduce the non-resident tax withhold rate. In these situations, CRA will inform the Department by how much to increase the non-resident tax rate. In some instances, increasing the tax withhold rate to 50% is not enough to recover all non-resident taxes owing for a particular year. Since the rate of recovery must not exceed 50% of the payment amount, the CRA will be responsible for additional recovery. If, in December, the tax withhold rate is different from the rate of the country in which the individual resides, the system will automatically reset this rate in January of the following year to correspond with the rate of that particular country.

Canadian pensioners who vacation in other countries for the winter months are not subject to non-resident tax, as these are temporary changes of address of generally less than 6 months. They are not permanent moves.

Every January, NR4 supplementary forms are sent to individuals who receive OAS and CPP benefits outside of Canada. This form indicates the gross amount of benefits received and the amount of non-resident tax deducted during the previous year. The NR4 form is used for taxation purposes. The OAS and CPP systems automatically calculate the amount of tax to be withheld at 25% unless a tax treaty between Canada and another country lowers or exempts Canadian taxation. The withhold rates may be revised every January. The OAS and CPP systems either: make the necessary adjustments to the withhold rates of non-resident tax; or end the tax withhold entirely when individuals: change their address and leave Canada; move from one country to another; or return to Canada.

topic_title: Tax treaties and tax treaty changes
text: Tax treaties between Canada and other countries allow varying percentages of Canadian tax to be deducted, and in some cases, eliminates Canadian taxation. The individual's country of residence determines: whether or not non-resident tax is applicable, and, if so, the percentage of tax to be withheld from payments . When a new or revised tax treaty changes the non-resident tax rate, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) notifies the Innovation, Information and Technology Branch. The Department then changes the tax rate in the CPP and OAS systems and sends the Advisory Letter - Non Resident Tax to individuals affected by the change in the tax rate. These system-generated letters are issued each time a non-resident tax withhold is established, or if the percentage rate of a tax withhold changes. Corporate Finance forwards non-resident tax withheld on OAS and CPP accounts to CRA on a monthly basis using an interdepartmental settlement notice.

In most cases, the tax withhold rate for a non-resident receiving Canadian social security benefits is 25% of the benefit unless it is reduced or exempted by a tax treaty between Canada and the individual's country of residence. Tax treaties between Canada and other countries result in taxation rates varying between 0% and 25%. Individuals can apply for a reduced rate of non-resident tax withhold as per Section 217 of the Canadian Income Tax Act . The OAS and CPP systems apply the correct non-resident tax rate according to the residential address and country code. Events that can change the non-resident tax rate are: the submission and processing of an application by a non-resident of Canada for a reduction in the amount of non-resident tax required to be withheld for a given tax year (NR5); a new or revised tax treaty between Canada and other countries; a change of address to a different country; and when the Canada Revenue Agency advises the Department that the individual is a deemed resident of Canada. The amount of tax to be withheld is determined by applying the non-resident tax rate percentage to the gross amount of the pension or benefit payment. CPP pensions and benefits are indexed annually and the system automatically applies the tax rate to the new indexed benefit amount every January. OAS benefits are indexed quarterly ; therefore, the non-resident tax rate is adjusted every January, April, July, and October. System-generated letters [Advisory Letter - Non Resident Tax (ISP3525)] are issued to beneficiaries at month-end to advise of changes in the non-resident tax withhold rate.

topic_title: Transaction data received from the Canada Revenue Agency
text: The Canada Revenue Agency forwards requests for adjustment to the Department via magnetic tape weekly. The system receives these transactions and either: automatically updates the data system on which the account resides; creates an entry on a register produced in the appropriate regional operation ; or creates a discrepancy notice that is sent to CPP Business Operations. Discrepancies are investigated and a list of impacted accounts is sent to CPP Business Operations for distribution to the applicable region and program for correction.

topic_title: A request for reconsideration is submitted beyond the 90-day time limit as well as a New Facts request
text: If a request for an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit is received, as well as a request for a review of alleged New Facts , the Minister will assess the request for reconsideration using the 4 criteria identified above in the section entitled Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit . The review of the alleged New Facts is held in abeyance until the appeal rights have expired for the decision related to the extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit.

topic_title: A request for reconsideration is submitted beyond the 90-day time limit as well as a subsequent application
text: If a request for an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit is received, as well as a subsequent application, the Minister will assess the request for reconsideration using the 4 criteria identified above in the section entitled Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit , regardless of whether it was received within or beyond 365 days. The subsequent application is held in abeyance until the appeal rights have expired for the decision related to the extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit.

topic_title: Benefits and provisions subject to reconsideration
text: Under CPP legislation, decisions regarding the following benefits, pensions and provisions are subject to reconsideration: Retirement pension; Post Retirement Benefit; Death benefit; Survivor’s pension; Children’s benefit; Credit Splitting; Disability benefit; Post Retirement Disability Benefit; Assignment of Retirement pension (Pension Sharing); and Amount of the pension, benefit or provision. Under the OAS Act, decisions regarding the following pension and benefits are subject to reconsideration: OAS pension; Guaranteed Income Supplement; Allowance; and Allowance for the Survivor.

Canada Pension Plan Subsection 81(1)—Reconsiderations and Appeals—Appeal to Minister Subsection 82—Reconsiderations and Appeals—Appeal to Social Security Tribunal CPP regulations Section 74—Reconsideration and Appeal on Behalf of Certain Persons Subsections 74.1(2)(3)(4)—Request for Reconsideration Old Age Security Act Section 27.1—Reconsiderations and Appeals—Request for reconsideration by Minister OAS regulations Section 29.1(1)(2)(3)—Reconsiderations—Request for Reconsideration

A reconsideration is an administrative review by the Minister to confirm or vary the initial decision. The matter is considered completely anew, meaning the new decision does not take into consideration the previous initial decision. In accordance with the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act), an individual who is dissatisfied with an initial decision rendered under the legislation, known as the dissatisfied party, has the right to request a reconsideration of that decision. The reconsideration request must be made in writing or via the individual's My Service Canada Account (MSCA) within 90 days of the individual being notified of the decision. Requests for reconsiderations received by any means are acceptable, provided they are signed by the individual. If a written request or form does not have a signature, the Department will protect the date of the reconsideration request using the date the unsigned written request or form was received until the signed request is received. Requests that are original, certified true copies, or photocopies received by mail, fax, email, or submitted through an individual’s MSCA are all considered valid. When the requests are received by these means, the Department does not require the original reconsideration request with a wet signature. The legislation provides a time limit of 90 days to submit the request, as that is considered a reasonable time for the individual to: assess the impact of the decision; determine if reconsideration should be requested; and gather evidence to support the reconsideration request. The reconsideration process is a right granted to the applicant by statute. It is not a case of finding a mutually agreeable solution. The Department will review all factual elements on file to ensure that the criteria set out in the Acts apply to the applicant’s situation. This review determines whether the previous decision was correct. If it is determined that the previous decision was not correct, that decision is changed or varied.

The principles of “natural justice” guide the reconsideration process. These principles include providing the individual with a fair and impartial review of their case. The processes developed to conduct reconsideration must be transparent and fair. This includes being perceived as fair by the individual. In keeping with the administrative law principles of fairness and natural justice, the decision at reconsideration must be performed by a different decision-maker other than the decision-maker who made the initial decision.

topic_title: Reconsideration and appeals where penalty assessed
text: An individual (or any individual acting on their behalf) who was subject to an administrative monetary penalty and is dissatisfied with the decision or the penalty amount can request that the Minister reconsider that decision.

topic_title: Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit
text: The CPP and OAS regulations set out the criteria to be used for assessing a request for an extension of the 90-day time limit: within 365 days of the notification of the initial decision; and beyond 365 days following the notification of the initial decision. Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit but within 365 days If a request for reconsideration is received outside of the 90-day time limit but within 365 days of notification of the initial decision, the Minister’s delegate must assess the following 2 criteria: Is there a reasonable explanation for the delay? and Was there a continuing intention to request the reconsideration? Criterion 1—There is a reasonable explanation for the delay A reasonable explanation for the delay in requesting a reconsideration exists if there are exceptional or extenuating circumstances. Exceptional circumstances include information that relates to an applicant's or beneficiaries medical condition that prevents them from acting with reasonable diligence. Extenuating circumstances are related to situational factors that are unusual, unexpected or unavoidable and beyond the applicant's or beneficiary’s control and which have prevented them from submitting a timely request. Criterion 2—There is a continuing intention Continuing intention to request a reconsideration exists if the available information indicates the applicant or beneficiary had the intent to request a reconsideration during the 90-day time period. In some cases, there is an interaction between exceptional or extenuating circumstances and the demonstration of continuing intention, which should be taken into consideration when assessing the request. Reconsideration request is received beyond 365 days When a request for reconsideration is received beyond 365 days following the notification of the initial decision, the Minister’s delegate must assess the following 4 criteria: Is there a reasonable explanation for the delay in requesting a reconsideration? Was there a continuing intention to request a reconsideration ? If the request for reconsideration has a reasonable chance of success; and If the extension would cause prejudice to the Minister or another party. Criterion 3—A request for reconsideration has a reasonable chance of success A reasonable chance of success exists when the decision to deny a benefit or provision is disputable, debatable or open to question. Generally, for the purposes of considering whether the applicant or beneficiary has a reasonable chance of success in the context of an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit, the applicant or beneficiary must provide evidence to support their reconsideration request that was not presented to the initial decision-maker. If no new information is provided or no reasons are given to explain why the initial decision was incorrect, there is no reasonable chance of success for the reconsideration. Criterion 4—No prejudice would be caused to the Minister or another party by allowing a longer period to make the request In the majority of cases, it is not likely that unfairness to the Minister will be a significant factor in determining whether to allow the extension. Prejudice, or unfairness, can occur due to a time lapse of months or years. It can also be determined that there is a prejudice to the Minister or another party in situations where a file has been destroyed according to departmental file management guidelines. In these cases, the Minister may no longer have pertinent evidence available to reconsider the facts, which were present when the initial decision was made.

topic_title: Social Security Tribunal General Division and the extension denial decision
text: The Social Security Tribunal (SST) General Division has the jurisdiction to determine if the Minister fairly assessed the criteria for an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit. Original decision maintained If the SST General Division determines that the Minister fairly assessed the criteria for an extension, the original decision (i.e. initial or reassessment) will be maintained. The applicant or beneficiary can appeal the SST General Division decision to the SST Appeal Division. If no appeal is sought, the original decision regarding eligibility is final for that application. Extension of the 90-day time limit allowed If the SST General Division determines that the Minister did not fairly assess the criteria for an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit and makes a decision to allow the extension, the Minister can reconsider their decision or appeal the SST General Division’s decision to the SST Appeal Division. If the Minister reconsiders the eligibility and maintains the denial of a benefit or provision, the applicant or beneficiary will have the right to request an appeal to the SST General Division of the decision made on their application.

The Minister must make a determination as to whether to extend the 90-day time limit by assessing each of the criteria. Written reasons must also be given to support the decision to extend the time limit. The standard of proof for assessing a request to extend the 90-day limit for a reconsideration is “on the balance of probabilities”. That is, the Minister must be reasonably satisfied that the request meets the criteria to grant the extension of time. The decision-maker must: take into account all relevant information; use appropriate judgment; and consider each case on its own merits. The decision must be supported by the evidence. The analysis and written reasons must be clear.

If the applicant or beneficiary fails to provide sufficient information to allow the Minister to determine if there are circumstances that allow for a longer period in which to make the request, the Minister can take any steps necessary to obtain the required information, which includes contacting the applicant or beneficiary for further explanation. 90-day reconsideration time limit extension allowed When the Minister allows the extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit, a reconsideration determination must be made and the applicant or beneficiary notified of this decision in writing. As with any reconsideration decision, the applicant or beneficiary has the right to appeal this decision on the issue of benefit or provision entitlement to the SST General Division. 90-day reconsideration time limit extension not allowed and the right to appeal If, after considering the criteria, an extension of the reconsideration time limit is not allowed, the applicant or beneficiary must: be informed of the decision in writing; be provided with reasons for the decision; and be advised of their right to request an appeal to the SST General Division . Since a decision not to extend the reconsideration 90-day time limit can be appealed to the SST General Division, the decision must provide a rationale that clearly demonstrates that the criteria have been considered.

topic_title: Time frame for a request for reconsideration to be filed
text: The CPP and the OAS Act allow 90 days from the day an applicant or beneficiary is notified of: an initial decision on an application; or a reassessment decision to request a reconsideration of that initial decision. The files of individuals who do not submit a written request for a reconsideration within the 90-day period are closed. An extension to the 90-day time limit will be granted by the Minister only if a reasonable explanation based on exceptional or extenuating circumstances exists. Refer to the Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit section below for a description of exceptional or extenuating circumstances. A verbal request for reconsideration of the initial decision can be confirmed with the individual by telephone; however, the individual must still submit a written statement requesting reconsideration within the 90-day reconsideration period. CPP and OAS reconsideration forms are available to: provide clarity to individuals; streamline triage; and support faster processing. The reconsideration request forms allow the individual making the request to select all relevant pensions, benefits and provisions under the OAS and CPP programs, with the exception of the Child Rearing Provision. Requests for reconsideration of an initial CPP or OAS decision will continue to be accepted in writing or via MSCA, in any format (letter or reconsideration form), where the following required information is included: the name, address and Social Insurance Number or Account Number of the individual or contributor (CPP); for CPP, if the individual making the request for the reconsideration is not the contributor, that individual’s name and address and their relationship to the contributor; and the grounds for the request for the reconsideration and a statement of the facts that form the basis of that request.

The CPP and the OAS Act set out who can request a reconsideration and which of the Minister's decisions are subject to reconsideration. The following individuals can request a reconsideration: an applicant; a spouse or common-law partner —a spouse or a common-law partner cannot request a reconsideration of an OAS decision unless it affects them directly (e.g. Guaranteed Income Supplement or Allowance); a former spouse or common-law partner; the estate; a beneficiary; a beneficiary’s spouse or common-law partner; an added party; or any individual on behalf of one of the above.

topic_title: Withdrawal of a request for reconsideration New
text: A request for reconsideration can be withdrawn by the individual or their legal representative. The request must be: made in writing; dated and signed; and received before a decision is made. Once a reconsideration request is withdrawn, individuals must be advised in writing that a new reconsideration request will be required if they decide to request one in the future. The usual time frame for reconsideration requests apply. For further information, go to the Time frame for a request for reconsideration to be filed section.

The CPP Survivor's ( SVR ) pension is payable to the eligible survivor. Only one individual can be considered the eligible survivor. The following requirements must be met: Table 1. Requirement Details The contributor is deceased. Proof of death must be received. Information from a third party government data source, such as the Social Insurance Registry, or information from funeral directors, are acceptable proof of death. If these cannot be obtained, then other documentary evidence for proof of date of death is required. An application must be submitted. An application must be submitted in the prescribed manner. The deceased contributor had unadjusted pensionable earnings for the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP). The deceased must have contributed to the CPP for the MQP. The terms of an International Social Security Agreement and/or the Child Rearing Provision may also be applied to satisfy the MQP requirements. The applicant is considered to be the survivor of the deceased contributor. The applicant must be considered to be the legal spouse, separated legal spouse or common-law partner at the time of death in order to be considered the survivor of the deceased. In situations where there is a separated legal spouse and a common-law partner at the time of death, the common-law partner is considered the eligible survivor. Where a common-law partner withdraws their application or chooses not to apply, the separated spouse would not become the survivor. See the definitions for: legal spouse; separated legal spouse; common-law partner; and couples living apart for reasons beyond their control. The following disqualification conditions apply at the time of death: Table 2. Disqualification condition Details Separated Common-Law A voluntarily former common-law partner cannot be considered a survivor for CPP purposes. Divorced The deceased contributor and applicant must not have been divorced. Annulment The deceased contributor and the applicant must not have had a final annulment. Murder or Manslaughter An applicant must not be convicted of first or second degree murder or manslaughter of their spouse or common-law partner whose death would otherwise have made them eligible to receive the SVR pension. Married less than 1 year before date of death There is no entitlement to an SVR pension when: a contributor dies within one year from their date of marriage; and the Department is satisfied that the contributor expected to die within one year of the marriage. Disentitlement to CPP Survivor's Pension in cases of Credit Splitting effective January 1, 2025 An individual who receives a credit split in January 2025 or thereafter would not be eligible for an SVR pension due to the death of their separated spouse. For more information, please Credit Splitting (Policy) Credit Splitting (Policy)
