Sometimes, the applicant may sign more than one consent form, particularly if they received money from several sources. When an applicant signs more than one consent form, the following criteria must be used to determine priority of reimbursement: the date on which the individual signed the form; the date on which the form is received; and the type of institution making payments to the individual. If more than one consent form is signed on the same day, the form with the earliest received date stamp is processed first. If the date of signature and the date of receipt are the same on each form, then the consents must be prioritized by the type of organization. A form that authorizes reimbursement to a province is processed before one to a private insurer. If any arrears entitlement amounts remain after the reimbursement to the first organization, the remainder must be paid to the second organization seeking reimbursement.

The Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act allow reimbursement to disability insurers and provincial administrators. Reimbursement occurs when an individual is eligible for benefits or pensions and payments were made to the individual by a disability insurer or provincial administrator for the same period. Funds can be reimbursed to the following provincial governments and disability insurers: Provincial governments (Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia); Provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation programs (Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick); and Disability insurance companies. For approved disability insurers who have a signed agreement, refer to the National List of Status of Disability Insurers with an Existing Approval, Deduction and Payment Agreement with ESDC . National List of Status of Disability Insurers with an Existing Approval, Deduction and Payment Agreement with ESDC The above types of organizations must submit a valid consent to deduction and payment form for reimbursement of CPP or OAS arrears. Arrears may include the first monthly payment, if applicable. Consent allows the organizations to recover all or part of the monies advanced to the individual when CPP or OAS pension and/or benefit payments are approved. Reimburse only the pension(s) and/or benefit(s) that were applied for in cases where the consent form indicates only CPP or only OAS. Where the consent form indicates a specific benefit, for example CPP RTR pension, and the application submitted is for a CPP SVR pension, it must be clarified which benefit or pension the individual consented to reimburse. The reimbursement can only be deducted from the arrears amounts owed and the first monthly payment of the CPP or OAS pension or benefit.

topic_title: Reimbursement of CPP disability benefits to the administrator of a provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program
text: CPPD benefits applicant The applicant must be a beneficiary of the provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program with which the Department has a valid reimbursement agreement. Provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program The administrator of the provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program must have a signed agreement with reimbursement provisions with the Department. The provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program must : provide a valid Consent to Deduction and Payment – Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Disability Benefits to the Administrator of a Provincial Workers' Injury and Occupational Diseases Compensation Program (ISP-1619) form within one year after the date on which the ISP-1619 form is signed; request a total payment of greater than $50.00 in order to receive reimbursement. In addition, the provincial workers' injury and occupational diseases compensation program must not: reduce the contributor's payment while awaiting the adjudication of CPPD benefits; offset the children's benefit either directly or indirectly.

topic_title: Reimbursement of CPPD benefits to an insurer Updated
text: CPP allows for the reimbursement of CPPD retroactive benefit payments to disability insurers for the period in which individuals were eligible for both CPPD benefits and disability insurance payments. Disability insurers must have signed an agreement with the Department stipulating the terms and conditions under which such reimbursements are to be made. For approved disability insurers who have a signed agreement, refer to the National List of Status of Disability Insurers with an Existing Approval, Deduction and Payment Agreement with ESDC Conditions under which a one-time retroactive payment may be made to an insurer CPPD applicant For the reimbursement to take place, the CPPD applicant must: be a client of a disability insurer; have been granted a CPPD benefit with a retroactive payment owing; and have completed and signed a written irrevocable consent. Disability insurers To be reimbursed, the disability insurer must prepare and send the Department the following: Disability Benefits Retroactive Payment and Information Sharing Consent (ISP-1618A-B) form within one year of the date on which it was signed by the CPPD applicant; a Request to Deduct and Pay a One-Time Retroactive Payment to an Insurer (ISP-1618C) form with a request for a total payment greater than $50.00; and a copy of the disability insurer's record of payment. Additional CPPD reimbursement conditions for disability insurers Insurers agree to comply with the following additional conditions: The insurer will make no reduction in insurance payments while awaiting a decision. While an applicant is in receipt of payments from an insurer and awaiting the adjudication of their CPPD application, the insurer attests that they have maintained full monthly disability insurance benefit payments. Children's benefits: Insurers who request a reimbursement attest that they have not and will not offset children's benefits either directly or indirectly for that applicant.

topic_title: Reimbursement to provincial social services organizations
text: Depending on which CPP or OAS benefit or pension the individual has applied to receive, one of the following completed and signed forms is acceptable documentation for reimbursement: Consent to Deduction and Payment - Canada Pension Plan (ISP-1613) form; or Consent to Deduction and Payment - Old Age Security (ISP-3010) form. The following must also be met: a completed and signed ISP-1613 form or ISP-3010 form is received within 12 months from the date on which it was signed by both the applicant and the organization's representative; and the total amount to be reimbursed is greater than $50.00. Ontario only—CPP children's benefits Children's retroactive benefit payments are issued to eligible applicants and are exempt from reimbursement to the Ontario Disability Support Program or Ontario Works as of the following dates: CPP Surviving Child's benefits: January 1, 2017, for the Ontario Disability Support Program; and February 1, 2017, for Ontario Works. CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ): October 1, 2017, for both the Ontario Disability Support Program and Ontario Works. British Columbia only—CPP children's benefits Children's retroactive benefit payments for children under age 18 are issued to eligible individuals and exempt from reimbursement to the British Columbia provincial government as of the following dates: CPP Surviving Child's benefit as of September 1, 2015; and DCCB as of April 1, 2017. British Columbia—OAS The OAS reimbursement Information Sharing Agreement with the provincial government was terminated in 2009. Therefore, there is no mechanism in place to reimburse the province in the event that a British Columbia assistance recipient starts receiving OAS while also receiving provincial assistance during the same period of time.

text: During the review of the file, if you suspect misrepresentation or SIN misuse, do not contact the beneficiary by phone and do not suspend or cease the benefit. topic_title: Are the earnings from possible SIN misuse or error?
text: There are situations in which earnings are reported but, following a review of the file information, it is determined that they were not from the beneficiary's work activity. These situations can occur when work is done: by someone who is using the beneficiary's SIN; by someone deliberately impersonating the beneficiary; or as a result of an error (i.e. income is credited to the beneficiary instead of another employee with the same name who works at the same company). For more information, refer to CPPD Reassessment Referral to Integrity Services Branch A-03422 (article not available).

topic_title: Are there earnings with CPP contributions listed as $0? Updated
text: Earnings with CPP contributions listed as $0 in the ITRDS Earnings screen can be from: an honorarium which is a payment made in the beneficiary's name for services rendered without charge (i.e. a guest speaker or lecturer). These earnings can be from municipal governments, school boards, townships or management fees paid by corporations; or long-term disability benefits which can come from various sources including insurance companies, government agencies and employers. A reassessment is required to determine the nature of the earnings (i.e. if the earnings are indicative of work capacity).

text: For Record of Earnings (ROE) Triggers screened out of the automation process, a manual screening process is performed to determine if unreported earnings require a ROE reassessment. Once complete, a ROE reassessment may be opened in the Rules Based Reassessment System (RBRS). In PWS: Review for Active or On Hold items. In ITRDS: Review the beneficiary's Notes for any important information (i.e. did the beneficiary inform Service Canada of a Return to Work (RTW), receipt of vacation pay or severance, or of educational or volunteer activities?) and any actions taken. Review the Client Profile screen. If the beneficiary has died prior to the reassessment being initiated, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Go to the Enquiries section below. ROE reassessments focus on beneficiaries who have not reported earnings resulting from work activity. From this data, a ROE query (trigger) list is created. The ROE triggers are loaded into PWS in Auto status and an automation process begins. topic_title: When is a ROE reassessment not initiated? Updated
text: A ROE reassessment is not initiated in the following circumstances: The beneficiary is not in pay. However, a reassessment is still conducted in certain circumstances, such as if the beneficiary now receives an RTR pension or if they die before the reassessment is initiated. an assessment or reassessment is already in progress; the beneficiary is participating in CPP Vocational Rehabilitation Services; or the beneficiary's case is at any level of appeal, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or the Federal Court of Appeal. For beneficiaries reassessed previously with a continues to be decision based on sheltered or benevolent work, refer to the Sheltered/inclusive employment section. These beneficiaries still require a review to determine if there is a change in employment status, earnings, employer (or business under new management) or medical condition. A few examples of significant change may include one or more of the following situations: The employer changes. The number of hours worked per week increases by 5 or more hours. There is a promotion within the same organization (higher level of responsibility and salary). There is an increase in salary or wages above the standard cost of living increases. Minor increments in salary are not significant and do not indicate an increase in work capacity. The medical condition has improved, meaning the individual is no longer experiencing functional limitations that regularly prevents them from demonstrating overall work capacity. For these cases, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Share Point link (access is required). The CRA provides Service Canada with CPP Exempt registers that identify beneficiaries who have unreported earnings. The CRA flags an account as a CPP Exempt match when a beneficiary: is in receipt of a CPPD benefit and does not contribute to CPP; and reported, after their effective date of disability, one of the following types of substantially gainful earnings on their tax return: T1 earnings, suggesting self-employment work activity; T4 earnings, suggesting work activity for an employer; or a combination of both T1 and T4 earnings. For each beneficiary identified on the CPP Exempt trigger list, their relevant information is added into the Employment tab and into the Employment Details screen in RBRS . topic_title: When a CPP Exempt reassessment must not be initiated Updated
text: A CPP Exempt reassessment must not be initiated in the following circumstances: The beneficiary is not in pay. However, a reassessment is still conducted in certain circumstances, such as if the beneficiary now receives an RTR pension or if they die before the reassessment is initiated; An assessment or reassessment is already in progress; The beneficiary is participating in a CPP Vocational Rehabilitation Program; or The beneficiary's case is at any level of appeal, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or the Federal Court of Appeal. For beneficiaries who were previously reassessed with a "Continues to be" decision based on sheltered or benevolent work, go to the Sheltered or inclusive employment section. These beneficiaries still require a review to determine if there are changes in the medical condition, employment status, earnings or employer (or business under new management). A few examples of significant change may include one or more of the following: The employer changes. The number of hours worked per week increases by 5 or more hours. There is a promotion within the same organization (higher level of responsibility and salary). There is an increase in salary or wages above the standard cost of living increases. Minor increments in salary are not significant and do not indicate an increase in work capacity. The medical condition has improved, meaning the individual is no longer experiencing functional limitations that regularly prevents them from demonstrating overall work capacity. For these cases, send an enquiry to receive further instructions. Send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Share Point link (access is required). An informant lead (previously known as a third party complaint) is a notification to the Department—communicated by letter or telephone, electronically, in person or by any other means—by an individual (who may remain anonymous) that, in that individual's opinion, an investigation must be made into: CPP contributions made or pensions or benefits applied for or paid to a particular applicant, beneficiary or to a particular group of individuals; or OAS pensions or benefits applied fo r or paid to a particular applicant, beneficiary or to a particular group of individuals. It is essential that all informant leads received from all sources are documented to: investigate instances of alleged abuse; identify overpayments, suspected fraud or misrepresentation; and maintain the integrity of the programs.

In 1997, the Supreme Court of Canada decided that any information that might reveal the identity of an informant must not be divulged and must be kept in a way that would prevent disclosure. Unless the informant consents otherwise, the Department is legally bound to ensure that any information that might reveal the identity of an informant is not disclosed. The informant privilege rule provides informants with certain guarantees. Informant privilege must be strictly observed. The informant privilege belongs to the informant and, therefore, can only be waived by the informant. The identity of the informant lead must be protected if the informant either: wishes to remain anonymous; or has not indicated their wish to remain anonymous. The identity of the informant lead must not be used as a legal exhibit nor disclosed at any level of appeal. Cases are adjudicated based on the facts on file or obtained during the course of the investigation. Furthermore, the existence of the protected information must not be referred to in any documents, including those associated with appeals.

topic_title: Different categories of legal status Updated
text: There are different ways in which an individual is considered to be in Canada legally for OAS pension, ALW or ALWS benefit eligibility purposes. They are as follows: Table 1. Legal status Description Canadian Citizen An individual who was born in Canada or who has been granted Canadian citizenship and has not subsequently lost that citizenship. Permanent Resident An individual who has been granted permission to come to Canada to establish permanent resident status, but is not a Canadian Citizen. A permanent resident can be sponsored or non-sponsored. An individual's permanent resident status allows them to live in Canada, but there is also a time limit on how long they can live outside Canada. To keep the status of permanent resident, an individual must live in Canada for at least 2 years within a 5-year period. Sponsored Immigrant An individual who has been legally admitted to Canada under a sponsorship agreement. A sponsor is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who is 18 years of age or older and has agreed to financially support the sponsored immigrant while living in Canada for the duration of the sponsorship period. Income-tested benefits payable under the Old Age Security Act to sponsored immigrants have some limitations. Non-Sponsored Immigrant An individual who has been legally admitted to Canada without a sponsorship agreement. Temporary Resident Permit (formerly known as a Minister's Permit) An individual who is a member of an inadmissible class or who is in Canada in normally unacceptable circumstances can be issued a Temporary Resident Permit (formerly known as a Minister's Permit) at the Minister's discretion. Permits are normally issued for the length of the visit to Canada. The individual must leave the country by the expiry date of the permit or get a new permit before the current one expires. Convention refugee An individual who is lawfully in Canada because of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular group or political opinion, and has been granted refugee status. Order in Council An individual who is already in Canada but has no legal status may be issued an Order in Council by the Governor in Council Returning Permanent Resident Before the introduction of the permanent resident card, an individual who was outside of Canada for more than 183 days and had no intention of making a permanent home elsewhere but had permission to resume living in Canada as a permanent resident, could be granted this status. Temporary Resident An individual can be granted lawful permission to come to Canada for a temporary purpose as a visitor, as a student or to work for a specified period which can be renewed. The following types of permits can be issued: A visitor visa is an official document that can be issued for an individual to enter Canada for up to 6 months. A visitor record can be issued for an individual to extend or limit their stay in Canada. A study permit can be issued for an individual to study temporarily at designated learning institutions. A work permit can be issued for an individual to work temporarily in Canada. Individuals who have a visitor visa, visitor record, study permit or work permit are temporary residents of Canada who have legal status.

topic_title: Dual citizenship (dual nationality) and legal status
text: Applicants who were Canadian citizens and became citizens or nationals of another country prior to February 15, 1977, automatically lost their Canadian citizenship if: they resided outside Canada; were 21 years of age or over; and acquired another nationality or citizenship by a voluntary and formal act other than marriage. If they return to Canada, they are required to apply through the normal immigration channels to be legally re-admitted. Certain categories of individuals can qualify under the amendments to the Citizenship Act that came into force April 17, 2009 to automatically reinstate their Canadian citizenship. Applicants who are Canadian citizens and became citizens or nationals of another country on or after February 15, 1977 have not lost their Canadian citizenship, they hold dual citizenship. Citizenship is complex because of the great variety of citizenship laws throughout the world. Some countries allow dual citizenship, while others take away the citizenship of an individual who acquires another citizenship.

The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act provides that individuals who are registered as Indians pursuant to the Indian Act have the same rights and obligations under that Act as Canadian citizens, whether or not they are Canadian citizens. This applies only to registered Indians who are members of Canadian Indian reserves. Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada (INDC) issues a card called the "Certificate of Indian Status", more commonly referred to as a Status card. Any individual registered as an Indian under the Indian Act is eligible for a Status card, regardless of their age, and can apply for one. This card is acceptable in place of a Canadian Citizenship Certificate and is sufficient proof that applicants meet the legal status requirement.

topic_title: Interpretations of the Citizenship Act and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (justice.gc.ca)
text: The question of citizenship is a complex one, and under no circumstances can Service Canada personnel interpret the Citizenship Act or the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act for OAS applicants.

topic_title: Legal status of applicants resuming residence in Canada
text: Where an individual ceased to reside in Canada, then resumed residence in Canada and subsequently applies for an OAS pension, ALW or ALWS , the legal status requirement must be met on the day before the approval of the OAS application. Amendments to the Citizenship Act came into force April 17, 2009 (Bill C-37). Individuals who may be affected by these amendments to the Citizenship Act are those who were Canadian citizens (including Canadian-born individuals) who lost their citizenship when they departed from Canada, then became citizens of a foreign country before February 15, 1977. These individuals lost their Canadian citizenship automatically as Canada did not allow dual citizenship at that time. Until April 17, 2009, such individuals had to apply to IRCC to re-establish their legal status if and when they returned to Canada. These amendments to the Citizenship Act allow IRCC to automatically reinstate the Canadian citizenship of certain categories of individuals without requiring them to officially apply to have their citizenship reinstated. The categories for these amendments are as follows: The law restores citizenship to individuals who: became citizens when the first Citizenship Act took effect on January 1, 1947, including individuals born in Canada before 1947 and war brides. It also applies to other British subjects who had lived in Canada for at least 5 years before 1947, became citizens on January 1, 1947, then lost citizenship; and were born in Canada or became Canadian citizens on or after January 1, 1947, then lost their citizenship. The law also gives citizenship to some individuals who have never been citizens. This includes individuals who: were born outside Canada on or after January 1, 1947; are in the first generation born abroad; and were born to a Canadian citizen. OAS, ALW or ALWS applicants in any of the above situations are required to provide proof that citizenship has been restored by means of a citizenship certificate issued by IRCC. The citizenship goes back to the day the individual was born or lost citizenship depending on the situation.

It is important to differentiate legal status and residence as 2 separate requirements of eligibility under the OAS program. Residence refers to the period of time for which it can be established that applicants make their home and ordinarily live in any part of Canada. Legal status means that applicants are lawfully in Canada on the day before the day on which their application for benefits is approved. Similarly, in the case of those applicants who no longer reside in Canada, they must have been lawfully in Canada, pursuant to the immigration laws of Canada in force, on the day before they departed Canada for the last time. Applicants are not required to have been legally in Canada for each period of residence in Canada.

topic_title: Review of legal status at the time of conversion from an ALW / ALWS to an OAS pension
text: Legal status is an eligibility requirement for the ALW and ALWS . Therefore, if any concerns exist about an individual's legal status at the time of conversion from one of these benefits to an OAS pension (e.g. a possible interruption in residence which may have occurred within the last 5 years), that beneficiary's legal status must be reviewed.

topic_title: Has the beneficiary returned to unpaid educational or volunteer activities?
text: If the beneficiary self-reports their return to unpaid work-like activities (i.e. education and volunteer), they are entitled to a 4-month observation period. The observation period starts only after the completion of 4 months of participation in educational or volunteer activities of 15 hours or more per week. text: To cease a CPPD benefit in the Rules Based Reassessment System (RBRS) based on Regained Capacity , measurable changes in functional capacity must be supported. topic_title: Is fraud or misrepresentation suspected during the file review?
text: During the review of the file, if you suspect fraud or misrepresentation, do not contact the beneficiary by phone, and do not suspend or cease the CPPD benefit. In these cases, you must refer the file to the Integrity Services Branch. In the documentation, use words such as “discrepancy” or “anomaly”, but do not use words such as “fraud” or “abuse”. For more information, refer to CPPD Reassessment Referral to Integrity Services Branch (Action) KA-03422 (article not available).

topic_title: Is the beneficiary between the ages of 59 and 64?
text: If the DSB of a beneficiary between the ages of 59 and 64 ceases and they apply for an Early Retirement (ERTR) pension within 90 days from the date they were advised of the cease decision, their ERTR application is deemed to have been received in the month the DSB ceased. For more information, Applications Date of Receipt (Policy)

A beneficiary is considered non-compliant when the following occurs: Two letters were sent to the address on record and there is no indication that the beneficiary did not receive them. Contact with the beneficiary is successful but they do not provide the requested information or keep delaying without good cause. topic_title: Is there a claim or allegation of erroneous advice or administrative error?
text: A claim or allegation of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) made by a beneficiary or an authorized third party during the reassessment, at any level, must be fully investigated. The Minister may also initiate remedial action in the process of reviewing an application or file if it is noticed that an EA/AE occurred in the processing of a pension, benefit or provision. If the EA/AE is likely to result in an overpayment , the investigation must be completed after the decision on the reassessment has been made and appeal rights expired. If the EA/AE is likely to result in an underpayment , the investigation must be initiated immediately, prior to the completion of the reassessment decision. topic_title: What should be considered when setting a benefit cease date for a beneficiary who is non-compliant?
text: The date of non-compliance is the 30-day deadline indicated in the reminder letter. The benefit will cease at the end of the month of the deadline to respond. In most cases, the benefit cease date will be the same as the benefit suspension date, if there are no earnings prior that could justify an earlier cease date. The benefit cease effective date is the first month after the benefit cease date and is the first month the beneficiary will not receive a benefit payment. The benefit cease effective date must not be earlier than the date of non-compliance. For example, if the beneficiary does not respond by January 15, the 30-day deadline generated by the Rules Based Reassessment System (RBRS) in the reminder letter is the date of non-compliance. The benefit cease date will be January 31 (i.e. the end of the month of the deadline to respond) and the benefit cease effective date is February 1. When the beneficiary is non-compliant and there is no evidence of work activity, the cease reason in RBRS will be Non-Compliance . This type of decision could occur with an informant lead reassessment. When the beneficiary is non-compliant and there is evidence of work activity, the cease reason in RBRS will be Unreported Work Activity-N/C .

After a beneficiary has been reassessed and there is sufficient evidence to support a final decision, you will either cease the benefit, continue the benefit or refer to Vocational Rehabilitation (VR). Earnings are no longer required to be above the Substantially Gainful Occupation (SGO) amount in the observation month or in each month of the work trial prior to ceasing a benefit if work capacity is demonstrated. CPP For the following, the common-law relationship must have existed for a continuous period of at least one year, and evidence of the common-law relationship must be obtained when processing: an application for an SVR pension where an applicant states they were in a common-law relationship with the deceased contributor; an application or request for Pension Sharing , also referred to as an assignment of a RTR pension; or an application for Credit splitting, also referred to as a division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings. Acceptable evidence for the validation of a marital status New The determination of a marital status can be validated and accepted as evidence using: another program (i.e. OAS, CPP); third-party government data sources ( SVR pension only), pension sharing and credit split, implementation date to be determined information provided directly from funeral directors; and information provided from a foreign institution with whom the Department has an International Social Security Agreement. OAS For the following, the common-law relationship must have existed for a continuous period of at least one year, and evidence of the common-law relationship must be obtained when processing: a Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form where there is a change in marital status to "common-law” or a notification in writing or by telephone from a GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary that their marital status has changed to "common-law". Exceptions (OAS income-tested benefits only) Evidence of a common-law relationship is required if an initial application is received for the GIS or the ALW where an applicant indicates their marital status is "common-law", but they do not fall under one of the exceptions below. The requirement for marital status evidence for a common-law relationship is not required and will be waived for initial GIS and ALW benefit applications in the following situations: Both partners are eligible to receive the GIS (paid on Rate Table 2); Where the Minister has waived the requirement for a GIS application for individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment; Where an individual has been selected and subsequently automatically enrolled for the GIS and their non-pensioner common-law partner has applied for the ALW or their pensioner common-law partner has applied for the GIS, proof of a common-law relationship is not required if: the information and identity of the automatically enrolled individual are confirmed; and there have not been any changes to the marital status from the time the individual was selected for automatic enrolment to their 65th birthday; Where an individual's spouse's GIS effective date predates their GIS automatic enrolment effective date, proof of a common-law relationship is not required as long as there are no changes to or discrepancies with the marital status during the retroactive period; or When one member of the couple is an OAS pensioner and the other is not in receipt of any OAS benefits (Table 3); or when one member of the couple is an OAS pensioner and the other is applying for the ALW (Table 4); and the couple has the same Canadian address; and the start date of the common-law union is provided on the application(s); and the marital status declared on the application(s) by both individuals matches the marital status from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); and there is no change to the marital status reported during the retroactive period. If there is a change or discrepancy during the retroactive period, a review will need to be done and evidence of a common-law relationship is required. Proof of a common-law relationship is required if an ALWS benefit application is received where an applicant indicates they were in a "common-law" relationship with the deceased but do not fall under the exception below. The requirement for proof of marital status for the ALWS benefit will be waived for initial applications when the applicant: has a Canadian address; and has completed the appropriate sections of the application pertaining to “marital status”. This policy does not apply to changes of marital status that occur after the initial application. Acceptable documentary evidence In cases where validation is not acceptable or documentary evidence is required, acceptable evidence may consist of the following: Existing CPP or OAS records that confirm common-law relationship; A Statutory Declaration of Common-law Union (Single signature) (ISP-3104) form or a Statutory Declaration of Common Law Union (Dual Signatures) (ISP-3004) form which attest to the relationship of the common-law partners; Other evidence which supports a common-law relationship; or Documentary evidence that has been certified by an International Social Security Agreement partner. When assessing the validity of the relationship, there must be evidence that there was an agreement to set up a marital-like home. Casual liaisons, employee-employer or tenant-landlord associations are not considered a common-law relationship unless the association changed to a couple living in a matrimonial home situation for at least one year up to and including the date of death. The weight of the statements contained in the declaration and documents provided must be considered in order to make a sound decision. Statutory Declaration A Statutory Declaration must be obtained from the applicant when proof is required: for initial eligibility or entitlement; or when a beneficiary reports a change in marital status to "common-law". Although it is preferable to use existing forms, other formats of statutory declarations are acceptable as the types of forms are not a legislative requirement. However, if other compelling documents or evidence have been obtained during a file review or an integrity investigation, they may be used to change a beneficiary's marital status to "common-law" even if a Statutory Declaration is not received. All of the documents and/or evidence obtained must be reviewed and evaluated. A decision should be made based on the weight of the evidence provided. The statements included in the Statutory Declaration serve as evidence of the most common factors existing in a union and can usually be proven with documentation, if needed. Other evidence The applicant must provide other evidence of the common-law relationship in addition to the Statutory Declaration. However, when an existing pensioner is approved for the GIS benefit based on a "single" status and has the GIS for Life status (even if they are not entitled due to excess income) and they report a change to their marital status to common-law, a Statutory Declaration will be considered sufficient evidence in most cases. If the GIS pensioner's marital status changes to a married or a common-law relationship with another individual in receipt of an OAS pension, the requirement for marital status evidence is waived. Examples of other documentary evidence include: a Certificate of Civil Union in Quebec; a Domestic Partners Certificate in Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan; a Certificate of Common-law Relationship in Manitoba; a Marital status claimed on a current CPP or OAS benefit; an Income Tax and Benefit Return; provincial registration forms; an Adult interdependent partner agreement (in Alberta); a Cohabitation or Prenuptial Agreement; joint wills, bank accounts, charge accounts, loans, insurance policies, real estate papers, rental records, bills, receipts or contracts; Registered Retirement Savings Plan naming each other as beneficiaries in case of death; prescriptions or medical or hospital records indicating the nature of the relationship; child custody or school records; records showing the same address such as driver's license, tax, electoral, or census records; and any other type of record which reflects the nature of the relationship may be considered as evidence. Generally, the more objective the evidence, the more weight it carries. "Objective" means documentation that provides evidence attesting to the relationship of the common-law partners and, at the same time, is removed from the applicant's influence. For example, a legal document such as a will drafted before an event for which an application is being made could be considered as moderate to strong evidence. The strength of the document would depend on the level of detail provided (e.g. a life partner versus a friend).

Acceptable evidence for the validation of a marital status New The determination of a marital status can be validated and accepted as evidence using: another program (i.e. OAS, CPP); third-party government data sources ( SVR pension only), pension sharing and credit split, implementation date to be determined information provided directly from funeral directors; and information provided from a foreign institution with whom the Department has an International Social Security Agreement. OAS Evidence of marriage is required when processing: a Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form where there is a change in marital status to "married"; or a notification in writing or by telephone from a GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary that their marital status has changed to "married". Exceptions (OAS income-tested benefits only) Evidence of marital status is required if an initial application is received for the GIS or the ALW benefit where an applicant indicates that their marital status is "married" but they do not fall under one of the exceptions below. The requirement for marital status evidence for married couples is not required and will be waived for initial GIS and ALW applications in the following situations: If both spouses are eligible to receive the GIS benefit (paid on Rate Table 2); Where the Minister has waived the requirement for a GIS application for individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment; Where an individual has been selected and subsequently automatically enrolled for the GIS and their non-pensioner spouse has applied for the ALW or their pensioner spouse has applied for the GIS, proof of marriage is not required if: the information and identity of the automatically enrolled individual are confirmed; and there have been no changes to the marital status from the time the individual was selected for automatic enrolment to their 65th birthday; Where an individual's spouse's GIS effective date predates their GIS automatic enrolment effective date, proof of marriage is not required as long as there are no changes to or discrepancies with the marital status during the retroactive period; or When one member of the couple is an OAS pensioner and the other is not in receipt of any OAS benefits (Table 3); or when one member of the couple is an OAS pensioner and the other is applying for the ALW (Table 4); and the couple has the same Canadian address; and the date of marriage is provided on the application(s); and the marital status declared on the application(s) by both individuals matches the marital status from the CRA; and there is no change to the marital status reported during the retroactive period. If there is a change or discrepancy during the retroactive period, a review will need to be done, and evidence of marital status is required. Proof of marital status is required if an ALWS benefit application is received where an applicant indicates they were "married" to the deceased but do not fall under the exception below. The requirement for proof of marital status for the ALWS benefit will be waived for initial applications when the applicant: has a Canadian address; and has completed the appropriate sections of the application pertaining to “marital status”. This policy does not apply to changes of marital status that occur after the initial application. Acceptable documentary evidence In cases where validation is not acceptable or documentary evidence is required, acceptable evidence may consist of the following: Existing CPP or OAS records that confirm marriage. A marriage certificate, which can be: an official copy or extract of the church, synagogue, mosque, temple, etc.; or a civil record of marriage as issued by a competent authority. Marriage Registration Forms, if they are an official copy or extract of the record from Vital Statistics and indicate evidence of registration (e.g. registration number). A completed Statutory Declaration of Legal Marriage (ISP-1809) form. The Statutory Declaration must contain: the names of the couple; and the date and location of their marriage. A Decree Absolute or Judgment of Divorce under the Divorce Act of 1985 . The document may be used as proof of marriage, especially in the case of a Credit Splitting application. The document must specifically state the following details regarding the marriage that is being dissolved: the date of the marriage; and the parties to the marriage. Documentary evidence that has been certified by an International Social Security Agreement partner.

Legal marriage dissolution (i.e. divorce) or annulment must be verified. You must obtain evidence of divorce for: applications or requests for credit splitting; Pension Sharing (verification is required when conflicting information is received regarding the divorce); notifications provided in writing or by telephone for beneficiaries receiving the GIS or ALW benefits indicating that there is a change in marital status: from married to divorced; or from an existing legal marriage to an annulment. Acceptable documentary evidence for a legal marriage dissolution (divorce) In the case of a divorce, an original or certified true copy of the following documentation is required: Judgement of Divorce, if issued under the Divorce Act 1985 ; Certificate of Divorce; or Decree Absolute if issued before 1985. Acceptable documentary evidence for an annulment In the case of an annulment, an original or certified true copy of the Court Order of Nullity is required. Acceptable documentary evidence for foreign marriage dissolutions Where foreign residence of the individuals is being disputed (i.e. at least one person does not appear to be a foreign resident), evidence is required. The documents that can be used as proof of foreign residence include the following documents if the beneficiary was divorced or had a marriage annulled outside of Canada. These documents must show the petitioner's place of residence at the time of the marriage dissolution. They include the petitioner's: income tax returns; social insurance or social security records; immigration or citizenship records; business licenses; work permits or other identification cards; social welfare benefit records; passports or visas; or deeds, mortgages, rental agreements or leases, etc.

Documentary evidence is usually required to support an applicant, beneficiary or contributor's marital status when: eligibility or entitlement to a CPP or an OAS pension or benefit is impacted for an initial benefit; or there is a marital status change on an existing benefit. The following describes situations where documentary proof is required and identifies the type of documents that are appropriate.

In most cases, original or certified true copies of documents establishing the exact date of the separation of spouses or common-law partners is required as it can affect benefit eligibility and entitlement. However, unless there is conflicting information or a dispute regarding the date of separation, no documentary evidence is required to prove separation in the following situations: separation of spouses for credit splitting; or separation of spouses or common-law partners who are pension sharing. Acceptable documentary evidence for a separation When common-law partners separate and apply for credit splitting, a Statutory Declaration - Separation of Legal Spouses and Common-law Partners (ISP-1811) form is required. The following documents are acceptable to prove separation: legal separation papers; a written agreement or court order confirming the date of separation; an ISP-1811 form; or other statutory declaration forms stating the date and reasons for the separation, the names of the individuals separating and the signature of one or both of the individuals separating. Acceptable documentary evidence for living separate and apart while under the same roof When a couple claims to be living separate and apart while under the same roof, in addition to obtaining acceptable documentary evidence for a separation (from the above list), one or a combination of the following documents are acceptable as proof: a separation agreement stating specifically that the couple will continue to live separate and apart from each other, although they continue to live under the same roof; a Statutory Declaration where one spouse or common-law partner alleges that the former couple will continue to live separate and apart from each other, although they continue to live under the same roof; a completed questionnaire stating the arrangements made for the couple's living accommodations (e.g. who pays the bills, maintains the home); copies of the couple's Income Tax and Benefit Returns to confirm the marital status being claimed by the couple is single; or a written report from an investigation officer after an unannounced field visit.
No documentation is required when an applicant is claiming single status.

The full under age 65 SVR pension amount was paid when, at the time of the contributor's death, the survivor: was aged 45 or over but had not reached age 65; was under age 45 and had a dependent child; was under age 45 and was considered disabled as per the CPP; or some time after the contributor's death, was considered disabled as per the CPP prior to reaching age 65.

The over age 65 SVR pension amount was paid in the following situations: at the time of the contributor's death, the survivor had reached age 65; or some time after the contributor's death, the survivor reaches age 65.

Effective January 1, 2019, a full Survivor’s (SVR) pension is paid out to every survivor regardless of their age, the contributor’s date of death or the existence of dependent children or disability. That is, as of January 1, 2019, the SVR pension is always paid at the full rate with no reduction.

The reduced under age 65 SVR pension amount was paid when, at the time of the contributor's death, the survivor: was aged 35 to 45; and had no dependent children; and was not considered disabled as per the CPP; or some time after the contributor's death, and while in receipt of a full under age 65 pension: had ceased to be disabled while aged 35 to 45 and had no dependent children; or had ceased to have dependent children while aged 35 to 45 and was not considered disabled as per the CPP.

Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor aged 35 to 45 either must have a dependent child or be considered disabled as per CPP to receive an unreduced SVR pension were removed. Before January 2019, the amount of an SVR pension was established by some or all of the following factors: the earnings and contributions of the deceased contributor; the age of the survivor at the time of the contributor's death; whether or not the survivor had any dependent children at the time of the contributor's death; whether or not the survivor was considered disabled as per the CPP.

Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor under age 35 either must have a dependent child or be considered disabled as per CPP to be eligible for the SVR pension were removed. In order to determine if they meet eligibility requirements, survivors need to apply, or re-apply if they were previously denied.
Canada Pension Plan Section 63(6)—Only one survivor's pension payable

Under the CPP, an applicant is only entitled to receive one Survivor’s (SVR) pension at a time. Where an applicant is the survivor of 2 or more deceased contributors, only the greatest of the calculated SVR pensions will be paid. Note the following examples: If the SVR pension that is already in pay is the greater amount, the subsequent SVR pension application is denied. The applicant must be informed in writing of the decision. If the subsequent SVR pension application has the greater entitlement, the first SVR pension must be cancelled effective the month following the date of death of the subsequent deceased contributor. The cancellation results in an overpayment of the first SVR pension. The overpayment is then withheld from the arrears payment of the subsequent SVR pension and the balance is paid. The applicant must be informed in writing of the decision. If the greater SVR pension is subsequently reduced by a Credit Split, then the survivor becomes entitled to receive the previous SVR pension if it is the greater of the 2 SVR pensions. If the common-law partner of a deceased contributor either does not apply for the SVR pension, or applies and their application is denied based on the greater of 2 SVR pensions, the legal spouse is not eligible for the SVR pension.

Upon approval of a CPP Survivor’s (SVR) pension application, the effective date begins the latest of: the month following the month of death; or 11 months before the month in which the application was made.

Under CPP, only one person can be considered to be the survivor of the deceased contributor. As a result, only one individual can be entitled to receive the Survivor’s (SVR) pension. If there is more than one applicant for the CPP SVR pension, the applicant who meets the definition of "survivor" is the eligible beneficiary. There are times when the first beneficiary's SVR pension must be terminated in favour of the contesting applicant. To make such a change, the evidence submitted to support the second individual’s application must disprove the information and evidence submitted by the first person. In cases where it appears either applicant may have provided false or misleading information, the case is to be considered for referral to the Integrity Services Branch as per existing policies and procedures. If the second applicant is found to be eligible and the second application is approved: the SVR pension currently in pay must be cancelled; an overpayment must be set up; the original applicant must be advised: of the decision; and of their reconsideration rights; and the effective date of the SVR pension on the second application is the month after death or eleven months before the date of receipt of the application, whichever is later.

topic_title: Situations in which a paper statement of income is required from a pensioner/beneficiary who has a lifetime renewal designation .
text: If the pensioner or beneficiary has a lifetime renewal designation, but a paper statement of income is required to determine entitlement, the income information in the statement may be received from the pensioner or beneficiary on a statement of income form or as a separate written statement. Some situations include, but are not limited to the following: CRA receives income information that is not complete (e.g. in a bankruptcy, both the pre- and post-bankruptcy income information are not provided by CRA. The Department receives the pensioner’s or beneficiary’s income information, but not their spouse or common-law partner’s income information (i.e. a statement of income is required from the spouse or common-law partner to determine entitlement). The pensioner or beneficiary does not file an income tax and benefit return with CRA. The Department does not receive CRA one-way transmission.

topic_title: Situations in which a pensioner or beneficiary is no longer allowed to renew their income-tested benefit and must submit an application.
text: The following are situations in which the requirement for an application cannot be waived by the Department: The pensioner or beneficiary is absent from Canada for more than 6 months (not including the month of departure), and it is established that the absence is due to a permanent change in residence. The Department chooses not to waive the annual requirement for an application for a reason related to eligibility and entitlement. The pensioner or beneficiary no longer ha s a lifetime renewal designation . The pensioner is no longer in receipt of the OAS pension. The pensioner or beneficiary requests in writing that their benefit be ceased. An ALW beneficiary is no longer eligible for the ALW if a pensioner has their OAS pension cancelled upon request or is no longer eligible for the OAS pension (e.g. if the pensioner requested to cancel their OAS pension and the cancellation is granted, the beneficiary is no longer eligible for the ALW and they lose their lifetime renewal designation . If the Department chooses not to waive the requirement for an application, legislation requires that the pensioner or beneficiary be notified at least 15 days in advance to submit a subsequent application. Communicating to the pensioner/beneficiary that the Department is not waiving their renewal application means that the pensioner/beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewal designation until a new application is received and approved (e.g. a new application (GIS, ALW or ALWS)). It is required to confirm eligibility and entitlement if a pensioner or beneficiary loses their lifetime renewal designation .

On approval of an initial application, the effective date of the ALW is the latest of the following events: the month after the application or deemed application is approved; the month in which the pensioner's GIS is effective; or 11 months before the date in which the ALW application is received.

topic_title: Contributions and the age of the contributor
text: CPP and QPP retirement pension beneficiaries aged 60 to 65 Beneficiaries who have pensionable earnings from outside the province of Quebec that are greater than the year’s basic exemption must contribute to the CPP. CPP and QPP retirement pension beneficiaries aged 65 to 70 Beneficiaries who have pensionable earnings from outside the province of Quebec can make an election to not contribute to CPP.

topic_title: Election made to Canada Revenue Agency to stop contributing to the CPP
text: CPP and QPP retirement pension recipients aged 65 to 70 may make an election to stop contributing to the CPP. Once a contributor has made such an election, it remains in force until they revoke it next. The contributor may make the election only once in any given year. For employed individuals, the election becomes effective on the first day of the month following the month during which the election was made. For self-employed individuals, the election becomes effective on the first day of the month referred to in the election. The election affects all salary, wages or self-employment earnings from all sources of income. In other words, when an individual has more than one employment, it is not possible to opt out of making contributions to the plan for one job while remaining employed in another job.

CPP and QPP Retirement pension beneficiaries aged 60 to 70 are eligible for the Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) if they have pensionable earnings above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) and are alive January 1 of the year the PRB is payable. To be eligible for a PRB, the beneficiaries must meet all the following eligibility requirements: Eligibility requirements Description Effective date PRB contributions started on January 1, 2012 with the first PRB payments made on January 1, 2013. Application There is no application; a contributor must be in receipt of a retirement pension. The Minister will deem an application to be made on January 1 of the year following the year in which the contributions are made. Age An applicant must be 60 to 70 years of age. Contribution The beneficiary must have made Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings to the CPP greater than the YBE.

topic_title: End date of CPP contributions for a PRB
text: CPP contributions towards a PRB will end the earliest of the following dates: The month during which the contributor is deemed to have become disabled; The month during which the contributor dies; The month during which the contributor turns 70; or The last day of the month during which the contributor made an election to exclude salary, wages or the last day of the month before the election is made for self-employment earnings from contributions to the CPP.
Bill C-51—An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on January 27, 2009 and to implement other measures

When an individual previously made an election to stop contributing to CPP for the purposes of a PRB, they may later revoke that election by completing the appropriate Canada Revenue Agency form (employees), or by making an indication on their income tax return (self-employed). They may make a revocation once in any given year but not in the same year during which the election to stop the contribution is made. When an individual revokes an election, it is up to them to notify their employer. If they fail to do so, their salary or wages will continue to be excluded from contributions to the Plan and the employer will not be liable for the missing contributions. In such situations, they will have to pay both the employee and employer portions of the CPP contributions if they want their contributory salary or wages to count towards a PRB.

Both or either one of the spouses or common-law partners can apply for Pension Sharing (PNSH) on the same application form. If two applications are received, the information is verified and treated as one application. When only one spouse signs, the other spouse must be informed in writing of the application. In all cases, whether or not a PNSH application is approved, both spouses or common-law partners must be notified in writing of the decision and advised of their right to request a reconsideration.

topic_title: Calculating the amount of the PNSH
text: The portion of the CPP RTR pension of one spouse or common-law partner that is shared with the other spouse or common-law partner is calculated as follows: The total amount of the contributors' RTR pension payments after Pension Sharing (PNSH) is applied is equal to the total pension amounts before the PNSH. The amounts will have been redistributed between spouses or common-law partners.

To determine the RTR pension(s) amounts to be shared by the spouses or common-law partners, you must determine: the joint contributory period; and the period of cohabitation. Joint contributory period The joint contributory period for both single and double Pension Sharing (PNSH) starts with the later of: January 1, 1966; or the month in which the elder spouse or common-law partner reached 18 years of age. For single PNSH, the joint contributory period ends with the later of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which: the non-contributor reaches 70 years of age; and PNSH is approved. For double PNSH, the joint contributory period ends: the month before the later of the 2 CPP RTR pensions began. The spouses' and common-law partners' joint contributory period excludes any contributory months during which either person: was in receipt of a CPP DSB ; or could apply for the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) to their contributory period. Period of cohabitation The period of cohabitation represents the years that CPP contributions will be shared between the spouses or common-law partners. The period of cohabitation starts with the latest of: January 1, 1966; the month of marriage; or the month in which a common-law relationship starts. Periods when spouses lived together in a common-law relationship before getting married can also be included in the period of cohabitation. The period of cohabitation ends the month the joint contributory period ends.

Spouses or common-law partners may choose to share their CPP RTR pensions if the following eligibility requirements are met: A written application must be made in the prescribed manner using the Application for Canada Pension Plan Pension Sharing of Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1002) form. Both spouses or common-law partners must be at least 60 years of age at the effective date. At the time the couple applies for Pension Sharing (PNSH): spouses must be legally married and living together; or persons cohabiting in a common-law relationship who must have so cohabited for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the date the PNSH is approved. Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control are considered to be living together at the time of application for PNSH purposes. Neither spouses nor common-law partners can be voluntarily separated at the time of application. At least one of the applicants must have valid CPP or QPP contributions and either be receiving or have applied for a CPP or a QPP RTR pension.

As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in a new component of the CPP called CPP enhancement. The original CPP remains unchanged and is called Base CPP. The CPP enhancement is not a separate benefit, but a top-up to the Base CPP called Additional CPP. The CPP Pension Sharing Provision (single or double) is comprised of the Base CPP RTR pension amount and the first and second Additional CPP RTR pension amounts.

Since January 1, 1987, legal spouses or common-law partners can apply to share or assign, by means of a set formula, a portion of their CPP RTR pension with their legal spouse or common-law partner. This arrangement is usually referred to as Pension Sharing (PNSH), though the old term "assignment” is also sometimes used. CPP PNSH for RTR pension payments between spouses or common-law partners equalizes payments when one person may have had CPP pensionable earnings and contributions that were higher than the other person's or when the other person had no earnings at all. CPP PNSH for an RTR pension may help reduce a couple's taxes by equalizing the spouses' or partners' income levels; moving the higher income spouse or common-law partner into a lower income tax bracket. PNSH also affords some financial protection to the lowe income spouse or common-law partner in an intact relationship. When a PNSH application is approved, each spouse or common-law partner is assigned a portion of the other's CPP RTR pension. The assigned portion is then added to their pension entitlement.

Reinstating a single PNSH Reinstating a single Pension Sharing (PNSH) could result in a different sharing ratio if, at the time of approval of the first PNSH application, the non-contributor spouse had not yet reached age 70. In such cases, the joint contributory period and the period of cohabitation are extended to the month in which the contributor reached age 70 or the month the request for reinstatement of PNSH is approved, whichever is earliest . Reinstating a double PNSH When a double PNSH is reinstated, the ratio of the number of months in the period of cohabitation to the number of months in the joint contributory period remains the same ratio that had been calculated at the time of approval of the first PNSH.

There are 2 types of CPP Pension Sharing (PNSH): Single PNSH When only one spouse or common-law partner receives a CPP RTR pension and the other spouse or common-law partner is at least 60 years old and a non-contributor to CPP, the pension share is: single . The term "non-contributor" means that an individual has: never made a valid contribution to either CPP or QPP; and not been credited with earnings from a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings (credit split). Double PNSH When both spouses or common-law partners are receiving CPP RTR pensions or when one is receiving an CPP RTR pension and the other is receiving an CPP RTR pension from the QPP RTR , the pension share is: double .

topic_title: The CPP and QPP Pension Sharing agreement
text: The Pension Sharing (PNSH) agreement between the CPP and the QPP sets out the conditions and procedures for PNSH of both spouses' or common-law partners' RTR pensions. Each spouse or common-law partner receives 2 monthly payments, one from CPP and one from QPP. Due to the differences between the CPP and QPP provisions, PNSH may prove to be inequitable for one of the two parties or both. This can occur when there is a difference between the CPP and QPP periods of cohabitation and/or the joint contributory periods. An inequitable result occurs when the spouse or common-law partner who was receiving: the higher amount pension before the PNSH, either continues to receive a higher amount after the PNSH or becomes the spouse or common-law partner who receives the lower pension amount after the PNSH; or the lower amount of the 2 pensions before the PNSH, either continues to receive a lower amount after the PNSH or becomes the spouse or common-law partner who receives the higher pension after the PNSH. The CPP and the QPP agreed that a PNSH will be affected even if the result is inequitable. In such cases, if both spouses or common-law partners send a written request to end the PNSH, it will cease with the month following the month the written request is approved. Conditions of the CPP/QPP PNSH agreement For the administration of PNSH under both the CPP and the QPP, the following conditions and procedures take the following into consideration: An application for PNSH made to either the CPP or QPP is considered to have been made to both administrations. CPP and QPP independently determine eligibility according to their respective legislation. The CPP/QPP PNSH agreement is applicable to double PNSH only. One of the individuals must be in receipt of or eligible for a CPP RTR pension and the other for a QPP retirement pension. Both the CPP and the QPP calculate the portion of the RTR pension to be shared based on their own provisions and issues payments to both spouses or common-law partners. The PNSH for each spouse or common-law partner must start within the same month. The effective date of the PNSH must be the month after the month in which the PNSH is approved. If one administration determines (for whatever reason) that the PNSH must end, the other administration must also end the pension sharing effective the same month.

Pension Sharing (PNSH) ends at the time of the earliest of the following events: When either spouse or common-law partner dies, the PNSH ceases the month of death. Example: the spouse or common-law partner dies in July the last shared pension payment is July. The PNSH ceases as of August. For a single PNSH, sharing ends the month in which the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor. When the PNSH involves only CPP RTR pensions, sharing ends the 12th month following the month in which the spouses or common-law partners start voluntarily living separate and apart. When the PNSH involves both CPP and QPP RTR pensions, sharing ends the earliest of the 12th month after the spouses or common-law partners separated or the month in which the spouses legally separated. Example: if the date of separation was July 15, 2003, the last month their RTR pensions would be shared would be July 2004 and the pension sharing would end effective August 2004. The month in which a divorce is granted or a judgment of nullity of a marriage is issued. The last month the pensions would be shared is the month in which the divorce is granted or a judgment of nullity of a marriage is issued. The month after the month in which the Minister approves a written request(s) from both spouses or common-law partners to cancel the PNSH. If only one spouse or common-law partner requests a cancellation, the PNSH continues. When spouses or common-law partners voluntarily choose to end the PNSH, a written request, signed by both spouses or common-law partners must be made. If one or both spouses are incapable of signing, the spouses' representative(s) must sign the request to end PNSH on their behalf. Contributors or their authorized representative(s) may choose to submit a completed and signed form specifically for this purpose: Cancellation of Pension Sharing for Canada Pension Plan Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1014). Alternatively, they may submit a written request. Ceasing the PNSH retroactively There are cases where the Department does not become aware of an event that results in the termination of a PNSH until after the event. As a result, a spouse or common-law partner will have received a portion of the pension to which they were not entitled. In cases of divorce, separation, or where one spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor, the result will be an overpayment on one account and underpayment on the other account. When this happens, the Department will release the resulting underpayment to the contributor and will collect the overpayment. The contributor must receive their full entitlement for the months after the PNSH cease date. When there is both an underpayment and an overpayment on the same account, the underpayment can be applied to the overpayment. Any balance remaining on the overpayment will be recovered. When either spouse or common-law partner dies, the PNSH ceases the month of death. Any shared pension payment after death is a debt to the Crown and must be recovered. In cases where both spouses or common-law partners request to have the PNSH cancelled, this would not result in any overpayment or underpayment. The PNSH in this situation is cancelled the month after the month the Minister approves the written request, therefore the cancellation does not have monetary implications.

topic_title: Applying proration for DSB or PRDB —employees Updated
text: If a contributor is deemed to be disabled for DSB or PRDB purposes, the proration of the YBE or the DBE is the number of months in a year before that individual is deemed to have become disabled. In other words, it is the period from January of the year up to and including the date of onset. Proration for DSB or PRDB purposes also applies to the remainder of the year in which an individual is no longer considered disabled according to DSB or PRDB criteria. As a result, the contributory period resumes the month after the month that DSB or PRDB is terminated. Proration may apply for the period after the cessation of DSB or PRDB , if needed, to meet the earnings requirement for a subsequent DSB or PRDB application.

Self-employed earners do not benefit from having their earnings and contributions prorated when they fall under the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) or the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) because the formula used by the CRA for prorating self-employed earnings is different from the formula used to prorate employees' earnings. The CRA prorates earnings for self-employed earners by 12 months and for employees by the number of months leading up to, or following, the triggering event or DOO. If during a specific year, there are self-employment earnings (T1) and employment earnings (T4), both types of earnings and contributions can be considered to obtain a prorated MQP or LPDOO.

Applicants must be found disabled within their Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP). To qualify, the applicant must meet the definition of severe and prolonged by the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO), which coincides with the end of their MQP. The Date of Onset (DOO) or for late applicant, the established DOO, must be supported by objective medical evidence, employment and earnings information. A specific event leading to disability may not exist. Not all disabilities have a clear starting point or can be defined by a specific disabling event. The determination of whether someone meets the definition of severe and prolonged as defined by the CPP must be made “in respect of whom”. When proration is applied, the prorated year becomes the final valid year of the MQP. The DOO or the established DOO in the case of a late applicant, must be in the final valid year in order for the applicant to qualify.

Disability benefits Proration of UPE may apply for a year in which DSB or PRDB ( PRDB with a DOO of May 2023 or later), either starts or ceases to be paid (in a month other than December), and the UPE are below the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE). Proration of earnings or UPE for DSB or PRDB purposes may apply to a year in which the disabling event occurs (in a month other than December), where the earnings/UPE are below the DBE and the date of onset is: before 1998 and the earnings are equal to or below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE); or January 1998 and later and the UPE are below the DBE. When establishing the earnings eligibility requirements needed for a subsequent DSB or PRDB , proration may also apply to the remainder of the year in which a previous disability ceased (in a month other than December). A contributor must have made contributions for at least the Minimum Qualifying Period to be eligible to receive a benefit. A contributor will be considered to have made such contributions in a year only if they have made contributions on earnings that are not less than the YBE or DBE. Repayment of refunded contributions for current applications using proration New For a prorate year to be valid for the applicant, the contributor must repay some or all contributions that were refunded to them by CRA . The amount of the prorated UPE for the year will be used for benefit calculation purposes. Repayment of refunded contributions for Late Applicant Provision using proration New Late applicants who meet the Minimum Qualifying Period with a prorate date are no longer required to repay refunded contributions for the year of the established Date of Onset. The prorated year is not used for benefit calculation purposes in the case of a late applicant. General CPP An individual's Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) must be at least their basic exemption for the year to be deemed to have made a valid contribution. Normally, an individual's basic exemption for the year is the same as the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE), however, the legislation provides an exception to that provision. An individual whose UPE are equal to or less than the YBE can be deemed to have made a valid contribution for a year, for a proportion of the YBE months in that year, if during that year any of the following occur: the person reaches age 18 or 70 or has died; a retirement pension under the CPP or QPP becomes payable; the contributory period ends by reason of disability under the CPP or QPP, or a DSB or PRDB under the CPP or QPP ceases to be payable (other than in the month of December). In all cases, if a contributor has earnings but did not pay CPP contributions on them, the earnings are equivalent to zero for CPP purposes. CPP contributions, not earnings, are what allow a contributor to be entitled to receive CPP benefits. For example, if an individual earns over $100,000 a year for a few years, but never makes CPP contributions, the earnings may not be considered valid for CPP purposes.
