Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) may apply to a year in which "triggering" events occur (in a month other than December), where the UPE are equal to or below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE), or Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) for CPPD benefits. Triggering events include: reaching age 18; commencing a CPP or QPP Retirement pension; reaching age 70; and death. Years in which such events occur are prorated by the Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ); however, if the Department needs to use a year in which a triggering event occurs to qualify an individual for a benefit, a manual calculation can be done if the CRA hasn't already prorated that particular year. The UPE can only be prorated if sufficient CPP contributions have been deducted from the individual's earnings. If the contributions are insufficient to cover the earnings, the UPE will be less than the actual earnings. The number of months that can be prorated will be reduced. An individual cannot make CPP contributions before the age of 18.

topic_title: Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings for DSB or PRDB —Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) purposes Updated
text: In disability cases where proration of UPE may be available to an applicant, the following 2 dates must be determined: The date that the applicant last met the MQP requirements using years of valid earnings and contributions without proration; and The MQP with proration. A determination must first be made whether the applicant had a "severe and prolonged" disability when their MQP ended and continued thereafter. If it is determined that the applicant was not disabled when their MQP without proration ended, medical staff will proceed to determine if the applicant became disabled on or before the possible prorate period. In cases where the applicant became disabled before the prorated period, the DOO can be adjusted to the first possible date in the prorated period where the applicant meets all legislative requirements, including having a severe and prolonged medical condition and sufficient contributions into CPP.

topic_title: Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings for Survivor's pension or Death benefit purposes
text: Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) for SVR pension or Death ( DTH ) benefit purposes may be applicable to a year in which the death occurs, and the earnings are equal to or below the YBE. In January 1998, the YBE was frozen at $3,500. The CRA will automatically prorate the year since the date of death is a triggering/prorating event in a year as per the CPP. The year will be prorated when the CRA is notified.

topic_title: Attribution of a credit split New
text: Under the CPP, the same effective date of attribution should apply equally to former spouses, and former common-law partners. The effective date of the taking place or approval of the credit split is the last day of the month in which the request or application is received. The effective date of the attribution of pensionable earnings is the first day of the month following the month that the division takes place. For example, if a request or application is received in March, the earnings resulting from the approval of the credit split will be accredited to the record of earnings effective April. Any benefits requiring a credit split cannot be paid in the month the division takes place or any month prior. Any benefits currently in pay will be adjusted to be effective the month the division takes place.

topic_title: Disentitlement to CPP Survivor's Pension in cases of Credit Splitting New
text: Background and Rationale of Legislative Changes to the Canada Pension Plan: The legislative amendment to the Canada Pension Plan legislation means that an individual who has a credit split on or after January 1, 2025 with their former spouse is not entitled to an SVR pension when the former spouse dies. A credit split recognizes that spouses and common-law partners are economic partners who contribute to their shared household, which includes the accumulation of CPP pension credits. The division ensures that each former spouse or partner receives their rightful share of the pension credits earned through their joint efforts during the relationship. A credit splits signals that the economic partnership has ended. In contrast, the intent of the SVR pension is to provide a measure of income replacement to a survivor following the death of their spouse or partner. It is premised on the survivor being dependent on, to some extent, the income that their late spouse or partner brought to the shared household. Thus, credit splitting and SVR pension are intended to address contrasting circumstances. For example, with credit splitting, there is no longer a shared household because the spouses or partners have divorced or separated. With the SVR pension, there was a shared household at the time of death. While a separation signals the end of a relationship and economic partnership, some separated spouses opt to remain legally married and not divorce; such individuals may be eligible for an SVR pension, provided their spouse did not have a common-law partner at the time of death. Before this amendment, the existence of the loophole meant that a former spouse could benefit from both a credit split and an SVR pension, resulting in individuals being treated inconsistently on the basis of their relationship status. There was also the unintended possibility of an individual becoming eligible to an SVR pension or being granted a higher SVR pension amount by virtue of their own pensionable earnings that had been transferred to their former spouse. The amendment closes this loophole in the legislation, thus ensuring the consistent treatment of all individuals whose conjugal relationship has ended, regardless of the marital status. By applying for a credit split, individuals are signalling the end of their economic partnership with the former spouse. Individuals opting out of applying for a credit split signal that there is still some financial interdependence in spite of separation. Individuals applying for a credit split are therefore not eligible for the SVR pension. An individual cannot have both a credit split and an SVR pension; it is the responsibility of the individual to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each option, depending on their circumstances. Individuals applying for a credit split are therefore not eligible for the SVR pension. This amendment will be applicable to credit splits that occur in or after January 2025. The approval of a credit split with the former spouse disentitles that individual to an SVR pension. An individual who receives a credit split in respect of their former spouse in January 2025 or thereafter is not eligible for an SVR pension due to the death of their former spouse. If the individual first applies for and receives an SVR pension, they may subsequently apply for a credit split within the three-year time limit. In such cases, entitlement to the SVR pension will cease as of the effective date of the approval of the credit split. The effective date is the last day of the month in which the application for the credit split is received. The end of entitlement to an SVR pension in cases where a credit split has been done is only in respect of that particular former spouse. It does not exclude an individual from dividing their UPE with another former spouse; Subsequently re-marrying upon the death of that spouse; and upon the death of their second spouse (or third, fourth, etc.), applying to receive an SVR pension in respect of their second (or third, etc.) spouse's contributions. Credit splitting does not stop an individual from dividing their UPE with their former spouse then resuming their relationship with that spouse at a later date. Upon the death of their spouse, the individual can apply for and receive an SVR pension. As a condition of eligibility, they must have been continuously cohabiting with that spouse in a conjugal relationship for at least one year immediately before that spouse's death. In cases where a credit split has occurred, and the individual then decides to apply for an SVR instead, they will still have 60 days to withdraw their credit split application, after the date of receipt by the applicant of notification of the decision respecting the application. For a dual contributor who has had a credit split of RRQ earnings only, and who applies for a CPP SVR pension without having had a credit split of CPP earnings, there is still entitlement to the SVR pension, assuming other conditions of eligibility have been met. SVR pension payments made before the approval of the credit split can be suspended while credit splitting eligibility is being determined. For more information please refer to Suspension (Policy) . Suspension (Policy)

Non-binding written agreements on the Minister Under the CPP for credit splitting purposes, the provisions of a written agreement or a court order made on or after June 4, 1986, are not binding on the Minister. Binding written agreements on the Minister New A written agreement where common-law partners agree that they will not apply for a CPP credit split are binding on the Minister only if: The agreement, signed on or after June 4, 1986, contains a provision that expressly mentions CPP and indicates the parties' intention that CPP credits will not be divided. The specific provision of the written agreement is expressly permitted under the provincial law that governs the agreement. The Agreement allows for the opting out of CPP for the purposes of the credit split provision. Written agreements signed on or after June 4, 1986, in Saskatchewan, British Columbia, and Alberta and after July 1, 1989, in Quebec will preclude a division. The information and documentation cannot have been submitted earlier than January 1, 1987, for Saskatchewan, July 1, 1989, for Quebec, July 1, 1995, for British Columbia and October 1, 2005, for Alberta. For all other provinces, an agreement, dated on or after June 4, 1986, cannot preclude a credit split. The specific provision of the agreement has not been invalidated by a court order which is signed and dated in any of the provinces that invalidate an existing agreement signed in that province. For divorced individuals, the agreement was entered into before the judgement granting a divorce or the judgment of the nullity of the marriage was granted. For separated legal spouses and common-law partners, the agreement was entered into before the day of the credit split application. Disability A credit split is not permitted for any month that was excluded from the contributory period of one of the former spouses or common-law partners because they were considered to be disabled for the purpose of the CPP. Retirement pension Any months during which one of the former spouses or common-law partners was a beneficiary of a Retirement pension under the CPP or the QPP. Contributions to a provincial plan One or both spouses or common-law partners made contributions to a provincial plan (i.e. QPP) during the period of cohabitation. The CPP was amended in 1992 to allow credit splitting for months where there were no contributions to a provincial plan (i.e. QPP) during the period of cohabitation. If during the period of cohabitation one or both of the spouses makes a contribution to a provincial pension plan (i.e. QPP), then if no division is made by the provincial plan, that particular month is not divided and if applicable credit splitting will be allowed for other months in the period of cohabitation. The legislation also allows for credit splitting where one or both spouses was a contributor to a provincial plan (i.e. QPP) during the period of cohabitation and credit splitting is carried out by the provincial pension plan for that month. YBE A credit split is not permitted for a year where the total UPE of the person does not exceed twice the YBE.

topic_title: Divorce or legal annulment of marriage Updated
text: Since January 1, 1987, credit splitting is mandatory for spouses upon divorce or for legal spouses and common-law partners upon separation. In the case of spouses following a divorce or a legal annulment of marriage, credit splitting may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements have been met: Table 1. Requirement Description Credit split application Credit splitting shall take place the last day of the month in which the information and documentation required from the person requesting the division is received. The spouses named in the information provided were at one time legally married to each other; At least one of the spouses must have CPP credits; The marriage has been legally terminated at the time the information is provided by: divorce; or legal annulment; and such termination is recognized by Canadian law. Cohabitation The spouses must have cohabited for a period of at least one continuous year; A period of separation of any length is included in the cohabitation period if it was not voluntary by reason of the occupation, employment or illness of either spouse; If the spouses separate for less than one year before resuming cohabitation with reconciliation as the spouses primary purpose that lasts for more than 90 days, the period of separation is included in the period of cohabitation. Where the spouses are apart for one year or more and then resume cohabitation for at least one year, their time apart is not eligible for credit splitting. The period of time apart is deemed to start at the beginning of the calendar year they parted and ends with the last month of the year prior to the resumption of cohabitation. Death Under the CPP there is no legislative authority to return CPP credits to an individual when the former spouse dies. The CPP credit splitting provisions are designed to be a permanent division of unadjusted pensionable earnings (UPE). Once the division has been made, those credits belong to the former spouse or common-law permanently and cannot be returned later, even after death. Cancellation Credit splitting can be cancelled when it is detrimental to both spouses. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both spouses. This is only applicable when both spouses are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both spouses become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. No projected calculations are to be done to determine if credit splitting may be detrimental to both spouses at some time in the future. Withdrawal Withdrawal of the credit split request is not permitted for divorced individuals. Credit splitting is mandatory upon the Minister being informed of a decree absolute of divorce, a judgment granting divorce under the Divorce Act or a judgment of nullity in a marriage.

The credit splitting provision applies to the first and second additional UPE in the same way as it is applied to the base CPP. As with the base CPP, the additional earnings for each individual will be added and then divided equally, and the divided earnings will be attributed to each person. Additional pensionable earnings under QPP will be used to calculate the division. The first and second additional CPP contributory periods do not end with the month in which a beneficiary is determined to have become disabled. The disability exclusion does not apply. Therefore, unlike the Base CPP, it is possible to divide first and second additional pensionable earnings in periods where a beneficiary is in receipt of a DSB .

topic_title: Former common-law partners on or after January 1, 1987 Updated
text: Credit splitting for former common-law partners may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements are met: Table 3. Requirement Description Credit split application following the approval by the Minister of an application made: by or on behalf of either common-law partner; by the estate or succession of either common-law partner; or by any person that may be prescribed; and when an application for the provision is submitted in writing, the effective date of the approval of the credit splitting is the month the application is received; as being common-law partners requires verification, it is necessary that a statutory declaration be completed and submitted for the separation of common-law partners; for former common-law partners of the same sex, the date the common-law partners ceased cohabiting must be after the date July 31, 2000; when the application is submitted within 4 years after the day on which the common-law partners began to live separate and apart or if both common-law partners agree in writing, any time after the end of that 4 year period; when at least one of the common-law partners has valid CPP credits that can be split and the common-law partners' total Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) exceed at least twice the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) in the each of the years that are to be divided. Cohabitation The former common-law partners named in the application were at one time residing in a conjugal relationship and they must have cohabited for a period of at least one continuous year; Common-law partners must have cohabited for at least one continuous year in order for a division of pension credits to take place. The division begins the month that the partners began to cohabit together and ends the month before they commenced to live separate and apart; A period of separation of any length is included in the cohabitation period if it was not voluntary by reason of the occupation, employment or illness of either common-law partner; Where the common-law partners separate for less than one year before resuming cohabitation that lasts for more than 90 days with reconciliation as the primary purpose, the period of separation is included in the period of cohabitation. Where the common-law partners are apart for one year or more and subsequently resume cohabitation for at least one year, their time apart is not subject to credit splitting. The period of time apart is deemed to start at the beginning of the calendar year they parted and ends with the last month of the year prior to the resumption of cohabitation. Former common-law partners who resume cohabitation would not be eligible to apply for a credit split, as they are not living separate and apart at the time of the credit split application. Separation The applicant and former common-law partner must have been living separate and apart for a period of at least one year, or where one of the partners died, before the twelve-month period of living separate and apart had elapsed. The end of the cohabitation must be no earlier than January 1, 1987. Death Where one or both of the former common-law partners are deceased, an application for a credit split may be made: by the authorized representative(s) or by or on behalf of a child of a deceased former common-law partner. Under the CPP there is no legislative authority to return CPP credits to an individual when the former common-law partner dies. The CPP credit splitting provisions are designed to be a permanent division of UPE. Once the division has been made, those credits belong to the former spouse or common-law partner permanently and cannot be returned later, even after death. Cancellation Where credit splitting is detrimental to both common-law partners. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both common-law partners. This is only applicable when both common-law partners are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both common-law partners become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both common-law partners. Withdrawal The legislation allows the withdrawal of an application in those cases where: Separation occurred after January 1, 1987; and A written notice of withdrawal is submitted to the Department no later than 60 days after receiving notification of the division. The 60 days refers to the initial decision and not decisions which may be communicated as the result of a reconsideration or appeal. After the 60 days have passed, there is no discretion to withdraw the application even if both parties make a request; If the request for withdrawal is approved, the former common-law partner must be notified in writing of the withdrawal; When an application is withdrawn, the application cannot be used at a later date. A new application must be submitted.

Credit splitting provision The credit splitting provision in the CPP allows for the equal division of pension credits earned by: former spouses upon divorce; or separated legal spouses; and common-law partners. Credit splitting was introduced in the CPP on January 1, 1978. Under the 1978 provisions, all CPP credits earned by both spouses during the period of a marriage when the spouses cohabited were divided equally between the 2 spouses in the event of: a divorce; an annulment of a legal marriage upon application by either spouse within 36 months of the final divorce decree; or a judgment of nullity. Former spouses had to have cohabited for at least 36 continuous months during the marriage. Credit splitting did not extend to separated legal spouses and common-law partners. From the date of implementation of the credit splitting legislation in 1978, requests for a credit split were processed regardless of any separation agreement or court order entered into by the parties. The Minister was identified as a third party and, therefore, was not bound by the provisions of the agreement. In 1983, in Minister of N.H.W. v. Lawrence C. Preece et al. (the 1983 Preece decision), the CPP Pension Appeals Board ruled that if spouses had waived their rights to property claims other than those contained in a separation agreement or court order they were precluded from receiving a division of CPP pension credits. Because many separation agreements and court orders included a general property waiver against all future claims, the Preece decision often prevented Credit splitting. In March 15, 1991, the CPP was amended to add the Kempling remedy. This amendment allowed applicants denied by the 1983 Preece decision to qualify for credit splitting. By applying this remedy, credit splitting applications are not denied due to separation agreements or court orders made before June 4, 1986 having general property release clauses. Eligibility requirements

The range of division begins with the latest of: January 1966; January of the year the marriage took place; January of the year cohabitation started; or the month the youngest member of the couple reached age 18. The range of division ends with the earliest of: the month the eldest of the couple reaches age 70 the month of December before the year in which the couple last cohabitated; or the month of December before the year in which the marriage union was terminated (for divorces or legal annulments between January 1, 1978 and December 31, 1986).

topic_title: Separated legal spouses on or after January 1, 1987 Updated
text: When legal spouses are separated, credit splitting may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements are met: Table 2. Requirement Description Credit split application Credit splitting for separated legal spouses may only be considered: following the approval by the Minister of an application made: by or on behalf of either spouse; by the estate or succession of either spouse; or by any person that may be prescribed; and when a credit split application is submitted in writing. The effective date of the approval of the credit splitting is the month the application is received; when the spouses named in the application are still legally married to each other; when at least one of the spouses has valid CPP credits that can be split, and the spouses' total Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) must exceed at least twice the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) in the each of the years that are to be divided. Cohabitation The spouses must have cohabited for a period of at least one continuous year; A period of separation of any length is included in the cohabitation period if it was not voluntary by reason of the occupation, employment or illness of either spouse; Where the spouses separate for less than one year before resuming cohabitation with reconciliation as the spouses primary purpose that lasts for more than 90 days, the period of separation is included in the period of cohabitation. If the spouses are separated for one or more years and then resume cohabitation for at least one year, their time apart is not eligible for credit splitting. The period of time apart is deemed to start at the beginning of the calendar year they parted and ends with the last month of the year prior to the resumption of cohabitation. Separated spouses who resumed cohabitation would not be eligible to apply for a credit split, as they are not living separate and apart at the time of the credit split application. Separation The applicant and the spouse named in the application must have been living separate and apart for a period of one year or more, and that separation commenced no earlier than January 1, 1987. in the event of death of one of the spouses after they have been living separate and apart for a period of one year or more an application may be made by the authorized representative of the deceased former spouse Death The credit split application must be made within 3 years after death. An application may also be made by or on behalf of a child of a deceased former spouse. Under the CPP, there is no legislative authority to return CPP credits to an individual when the former spouse dies. The CPP credit splitting provisions are designed to be a permanent division of the UPE. Once the division has been made, those credits belong to the former spouse or common-law partner permanently and cannot be returned later, even after death. Cancellation A credit split is not permitted where credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both spouses. This is only applicable when both spouses are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both spouses become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. Withdrawal The legislation allows the withdrawal of an application in cases where: separation occurred after January 1, 1987, but the couple have not obtained a divorce; and a written notice of withdrawal is submitted to the Department no later than 60 days after receiving notification of the division of credits. The 60 days refers to the initial decision and not decisions which may be communicated as the result of a reconsideration or appeal. After the 60 days have passed, there is no discretion to withdraw the application even if both parties make a request. if the request for withdrawal is approved, the former spouse must be notified in writing of the withdrawal; when an application is withdrawn, the application cannot be used at a later date. A new application must be submitted.

Recalculation of benefits affects the following CPP pensions and benefits: Retirement pension; Post-Retirement Benefit; Disability benefit; and Survivor's pension, which includes combined benefits. The following benefits are paid at a flat rate and the recalculation of benefits does not affect the payment entitlement amount; however it could affect their eligibility: Death benefit; Post-Retirement Disability Benefit; Surviving Child's benefit; and Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit . To prevent any delays in starting to pay a CPP pension or benefit, legislation allows an interim calculation of a benefit to be made. The interim calculation is based on information already contained in the contributor's Record of Earnings (ROE). If necessary, an acceptable proof of earnings and contributions can be submitted covering a contributory period not shown in the ROE. Once the ROE is brought up-to-date, legislation allows a final calculation of the benefit to be made. Any retroactive payment owed can be made to rectify a benefit amount that had been paid based on an interim calculation. Alternatively, an appropriate recovery action can be taken on any overpayment incurred from an over-calculated interim benefit amount.

The amount of a Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) is based on the Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings of the previous year. The amount is also based on the contributor's age on January 1 of the year the PRB starts to be payable.
The Post-Retirement Benefit is paid during the lifetime of the beneficiary. Payments end with the final payment made the month of the beneficiary’s death.

The Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) is adjusted once per year, in January, to reflect the rate of inflation, i.e. changes to the cost of living as measured by changes in the Consumer Price Index. In years when the cost of living goes down, there is no change to PRB payment amounts.

topic_title: Payment of a Post-Retirement Benefit in the event of death
text: If a Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB)-eligible contributor dies before a payment is made, the PRB payment should be made to their estate, or next of kin, as per the hierarchy of payments in the event of the contributor's death. If a contributor dies before January 1 of the year following the year in which contributions to the Plan were made, then a PRB is not payable to the estate and their contributions are not reimbursed.

A CPP Retirement pension is based on such factors as: an individual's age at the pension effective date and how much they contributed to CPP over their contributory period. Similarly, a Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) is based on: an individual’s age at the effective date of the PRB; and how much they contributed to CPP over the course of the previous calendar year. A PRB is payable whenever valid CPP contributions were made in the previous calendar year. The PRB is: effective on January 1 of the year following the year in which the valid contributions were made; and calculated as soon as the Minister has received the earnings and contributions information from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The PRB calculation formula [(A * F/B) * C * D * E] /12 Legend * = multiply / = divide "A" = The calculated amount for the year before the year in which the PRB becomes payable. "F" = G/H G = Earnings on which a valid contribution has been made for the year under the CPP. H = Earnings on which a contribution has been made for the year under the CPP plus the earnings on which a contribution has been made for the year under the QPP. "B" = The Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the year before the year the PRB becomes payable. "C" = 0.00625 (25 percent of 1/40ths) "D" = The Maximum Pensionable Earnings (MPE) average for the year the PRB becomes payable. "E" = The actuarial adjustment factor which is based on the contributor's age on January 1 of the year the PRB becomes payable. Refer to additional information below in this section. Determining the value for "A" for the year the Retirement pension becomes payable To determine the Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) for the year the CPP retirement pension becomes payable, determine: which portion of those earnings will be used to calculate the retirement pension; and which portion (the remainder) will be used to calculate the PRB. The value for "A" to be used in the PRB calculation formula above is the greater of: $0; or the calculated amount arrived at by using the following formula: "A" = UPEs – [(YMPE x #months before retirement becomes payable)/12]

As per legislation, all benefits, including the Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB), become payable at the beginning of the month. The PRB becomes payable on January 1 of the year following the year in which eligible CPP contributions were made. The PRB first became payable effective January 1, 2013, based on pensionable earnings from the previous year.

The following provides an accountability framework that authorized officials must apply when dealing with overpayments: Managers must ensure that a process is in place to minimize or eliminate the occurrence of overpayments ; Employees must adhere to processes, such as suspending benefits in a timely manner, that minimize or eliminate the occurrence of overpayments, and must provide feedback to managers on the effectiveness of these processes; Managers and employees must ensure that overpayments are promptly identified, and are recovered in an efficient and effective manner by following the Department’s Overpayment Policy and Procedures ; and Managers and employees must take corrective measures to address situations of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error to ensure there is no recurrence.

topic_title: Administration of CPP and OAS overpayments
text: Departmental staff must act promptly when overpayments occur by: taking corrective measures, including correcting the error and ensuring the overpayment situation does not happen again in the future; informing individuals of the overpa yment (sending a letter in all cases); and attempting to recover the overpayment as the first course of action, with the exception of situations where Erroneous Advice (EA)/Administrative Error (AE) has already been established. Although no recovery is attempted in EA/AE situations a letter must be sent.

Departmental staff will: co mmunicate in a clear, easily understood manner when dealing with individuals; treat all individuals with dignity and respect; and treat all individuals consistently and equitably when applying the Department’s overpayment operational policy and procedures.

It is the Department’s policy to communicate efficiently and effectively with individuals. When an overpayment situation arises, the process begins with an overpayment letter being sent to the individual. For both active and inactive accounts, an initial overpayment letter is sent in all cases, including Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error situations. After the overpayment letter is sent, individuals are given a minimum of 30 days to reply. This can vary depending on the situation (e.g. if the individual lives outside Canada, if the individual is ill, etc.). After this period of time has elapsed, actions will be taken to initiate recovery of the overpayment. In cases where recovery action is deferred, individuals must be advised of the intended recovery action and provided with the opportunity to respond within a reasonable time frame (individuals will be given a minimum of 30 days to reply) before restarting recovery. If the individual objects, negotiations must take place. In cases of a sensitive nature, it is recommended that the individual be contacted by phone before effecting recovery and advised of the forthcoming letter. Discretion must be applied when determining what constitutes cases of a sensitive nature. Sensitive nature must be determined on a case-by-case basis. Examples of sensitive nature may include situations such as the death of a family member or undue hardship. It may also be applied whenever an individual responds to an overpayment letter indicating they are having difficulties in repaying their overpayments whe n they come due.

topic_title: GIS, ALW or ALWS overpayments related to options
text: An overpayment may occur when a GIS, ALW or ALWS entitlement is recalculated based on a comparison between actual and estimated income. In such cases, departmental staff will determine the full amount of any overpayments and attempt recovery.

topic_title: OAS time bar provision and common-law adjustments
text: Before Bill C-54, overpayments for OAS benefits (OAS pension, GIS, Allowance (ALW), Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) were recorded in their entirety, but recovery could only be enforced for amounts accrued in both the current year and the preceding fiscal year. The intent was that all overpayments over 2 years would be statute barred from recovery. This was based on the time bar provision of the OAS Act. After July 13, 1995, when Bill C-54 was given Royal Assent, the time bar provision was removed. At passage of the legislation, recovery of overpayments was limited to 2 years, but each passing year would increase the number of years that could be recovered. The Department will not recover any OAS pension, GIS, ALW or ALWS overpayment amount accrued before April 1, 1994 unless the overpayment was set-up before that date. Time bar provisions do not apply in cases where fraud or misrepresentation is proven. The full amount of the overpayment, including the time bar portion, must be set up as an overpayment. The time bar portion is remitted before the individual is advised of the outstanding overpayment. Overpayments due to recalculation of accounts with common-law adjustments are not recoverable earlier than July 2000 (the effective date of Bill C-23 where the definition of common-law was harmonized for CPP and OAS) unless they were established before that date. This means that adjustments to accounts can only be made back to July 2000. The individual is advised of the outstanding overpayment calculated on or after July 2000. T he Department will continue to collect overpayments on those accounts where overpayments were established before July 2000 and the individual has alrea dy been informed.

Overpayments can occur for a variety of reasons, including, but not limited to: original and duplicate cheques negotiated; amendments to periods of residence; a calculation error; income declared incorrectly; incorrect information provided; duplicate benefits paid to the same person; revision of estimated income; change of rate table for OAS benefits; or events such as: death; marriage; or separation. The use of the term "permanent write-off" in certain situations was introduced in 2011 to harmonize and align the Department’s recovery activities and data systems. Assets and liabilities are not included when assessing financial hardship with respect to debt repayment. Wher e an individual is granted a full discharge, the individual is rele ased from all pre-bankruptcy debts and all CPP or OAS overpayments before the date of filing, and not before the date of discharge, as was previously written. The Chief Financial Officer Branch is the delegated authority to approve write-offs. Also, an overpayment balance that remains after a compromise settlement, consumer proposal or a discharged bankruptcy is no longer considered a permanent write-off, but will instead be considered a write-off under the authorities of the Debt Write-off Regulations of the Financial Administration Act .

An overpayment refers to all CPP benefit and OAS pension payments that a person has received or obtained where there was no entitlement. A benefit payment includes all benefits and pensions available under the CPP and OAS programs. It also includes combined OAS/Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Disability/Survivor (SVR), Retirement (RTR)/Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) or RTR/SVR payments. This includes any amount related to a payment or cheque, regardless of whether or not it has been negotiated. An overpayment is incurred as soo n as a person receives a CPP benefit or an OAS pension amount to which they are not entitled.

topic_title: Alternate collection methods—garnishment and federal court certificate
text: When normal recovery methods are unsuccessful in obtaining repayment, the legislation empowers the Minister to recover overpayments through garnishment proceedings and the registration of Federal Court certificates. Garnishment Although there is authority under the Canada Pension Plan and the OAS Act for garnishment, these provisions were never implemented. A garnishment is defined as “seizing an individual's property, credit or salary, on the basis of a law that allows it for the purposes of reimbursing an overpayment”. If the Minister knows or suspects that an individual is or is about to become: indebted; or liable to make a payment to another individual who is liable to make a payment to His Majesty under the Canada Pension Plan and the OAS Act, the Minister may, by a notice served personally or by confirmed delivery service, require the first individual to pay the money otherwise payable to the second individual. This payment can be paid in whole or in part to the Receiver General on account of the second individual's liability. Garnishments are restricted to inactive accounts where normal recovery methods are unsuccessful in obtaining repayment of the overpayment. If information obtained from the individual or other sources indicates that the individual is capable of repayment or garnishment then garnishment may be initiated.The sources that may be repaid or garnished include: wages; bank deposits; or amounts owed to the individual by a third party.. Federal Court certificate Although there is authority under the Canada Pension Plan and the OAS Act for the Minister to certify overpayments with the Federal Court, these provisions were never implemented. A certificate is a legal document registered with the Federal Court to enforce recovery of an outstanding overpayment on an inactive account. The registered certificate has the same legal force and effect as a judgment obtained from the court. Court registration of the certificate allows the: seizure and sale of goods and chattels; placement of a lien; and sale of real property. After the certificate is registered with the Federal Court, the certificate can also be registered with any provincial or territorial superior court, as required. A record of the overpayment is kept on file by the court to ensure recovery from affected assets (i.e. any possession that has value in an exchange). The use of a certificate will only be considered as an exception to the rule on a case-by-case basis. If a decision is made to proceed with a certificate, the delegated authority can request that a certificate be issued. When existing recovery methods are unsuccessful and information is obtained indicating that the individual is capable of repayment, a certificate may be used for the immediate recovery of the overpayment. When the individual is currently incapable of repayment, a certificate may be used to protect the overpayment for future recovery. This would only occur after sending the notification to the individual that a request will be made for a certificate to be issued. If, at any time during this process, the individual claims undue hardship, the certificate process will continue since the intent is to protect the overpayment and does not place the individual in undue hardship.

The Department requires a formal written notification that an individual is declaring bankruptcy. Bankruptcy is the legal inability of an individual to repay their overpayments. When an individual files for bankruptcy, their assets are frozen and all unsecured creditors are required by law to cease all recovery action on overpayments until the disposition of the bankruptcy court is finalized. An absolute order of discharge from bankruptcy releases an individual from all overpayments incurred before the date of filing (including those not identified on the Statement of Affairs). This excludes 6 categories of debts listed under subsection 178(1) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act . After an absolute order of discharge is finalized, any new overpayments incurred on or after the date of filing or that were not part of the original claim of bankruptcy are collectible. This includes requests for money to be recovered on behalf of another federal agency or department (e.g. the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) or the Department of Justice). When the Department receives formal written notification or Notice/Matter of Bankruptcy from a court-appointed trustee that an individual has filed for bankruptcy, recovery action on CPP and OAS overpayments must be deferred or suspended immediately . If payments have already been recovered for periods covered under the bankruptcy, monies that should not have been withheld must be reimbursed. In some cases, the Department may be notified that a claim of bankruptcy status is “sine die”. This means that it has been adjourned indefinitely. The bankruptcy remains undischarged because the individual has not completed duties necessary for the court-appointed trustee to apply to the bankruptcy court to issue a discharge. All recovery actions on those overpayments that were part of that claim of bankruptcy remain on hold while the status is “sine die”. Formal notification of bankruptcy The licensed insolvency trustee must provide the Department with a formal written notification that an individual has declared bankruptcy. The trustee must submit a Notice/Matter of Bankruptcy to the Department. Recovery action of the overpayment continues until the Notice/Matter of Bankruptcy is received. Upon receipt of a Notice/Matter of Bankruptcy, suspend or defer all recovery action, including those on behalf of other federal departments until the absolute order of discharge by the bankruptcy court is finalized. If money is being recovered on behalf of another federal agency or department (e.g. the CRA or the Department of Justice), notify the other agency or department about the individual's declaration of bankruptcy. Simultaneously, a Form 31-Proof of Claim form must be filed immediately by the Department (even if it is incomplete) to advise the licensed insolvency trustee that the Department is making a claim against the assets of the individual. The Form 31 - Proof of Claim form must be completed regardless of the amount of the overpayment. A letter stating that the Department reserves the right to provide further details after discussions with the Department of Justice will accompany the Form 31-Proof of Claim form. Therefore, if fraud is suspected, a review can be carried out after filing the Form 31-Proof of Claim form. It is recommended that a legal representative from the Department attend the first meeting of creditors. By attending, they could assist the representative to decide whether to pursue recovery of the overpayment. All actions taken should be recorded on the individual's file. Bankruptcy court and discharge Bankruptcy proceedings are governed under the provisions of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act . In accordance with Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act , the trustee is required to apply for a discharge to the bankruptcy court no earlier than 3 months and not later than 12 months after the bankruptcy. Subsequent to this application, the bankruptcy court may: refuse a discharge; grant a discharge; or suspend a discharge. Each of these 3 above outcomes will result in a different course of action. There are different types of discharges as outlined in the following table: Table 1 Type of discharge Description Automatic This type of discharge occurs when an individual whose discharge is not opposed by the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, the trustee or a creditor and who has not refused or neglected to receive counselling. It is automatically discharged after 9, 12, 24 or 36 months, depending on whether it is a first or second bankruptcy. The discharge also depends on whether the insolvent individual is required to pay a portion of their surplus income into the bankruptcy estate as per the standard established by the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy. Order of Absolute This type of discharge is an official document issued by the court which relieves the individual of the overpayment incurred before declaring bankruptcy, taking under consideration the exceptions provided in the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act . Order of Conditional This type of discharge occurs when the court imposes certain conditions that must be met before a person's discharge becomes absolute. For example, the court may require a person to pay an amount to the trustee for distribution to the creditors. Order of Suspended This type of discharge occurs when the court orders a delay so that the discharge will not be effective until a certain date. The individual is refused a discharge In cases where the individual is refused a discharge, the overpayment is fully collectible and must be recovered. The individual is granted a discharge When an individual receives a benefit amount that they are not entitled to receive, they have incurred an overpayment. Incurred refers to when the overpayment was acquired or when it happened, which may cover periods before or after the date of filing for bankruptcy. When the individual is granted a full discharge, the individual is released from all pre-bankruptcy overpayments. Further, all CPP and OAS overpayments before the date of filing (allowable bankruptcy period) are written-off, except in limited circumstances such as false pretences or misrepresentation. Any portion of CPP and OAS overpayment amounts that cover or include periods on or after the date of filing are collectible and must be recovered. Suspended discharge When the discharge is suspended, no recovery action may be taken and full CPP or OAS pensions or benefits must be paid to the individual until the disposition by the bankruptcy court is finalized. Overpayments arising from false pretences or misrepresentation In accordance with paragraph 178(1)(e) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, overpayments caused by false pretences or misrepresentation are not released with a discharge of bankruptcy and must be recovered.

A compromise settlement is an agreement to finalize an overpayment by accepting a partial payment as full repayment of the overpayment. The individual is released from any obligation to pay the balance owed. A compromise settlement will only be considered when it is in the best interest of the Department. The individual or their representative must initiate the compromise settlement in writing. They must clearly indicate the reason for the request and the details of the proposal. All requests for a compromise settlement are forwarded to the Collections Litigations and Advisory Services section of the Canada Revenue Agency. They are the delegated authorities of the Department to negotiate and accept these requests. After a compromise settlement is finalized, the remaining balance of an overpayment is written-off.

Insolvency occurs when an individual cannot repay their overpayments at the time they are due. Under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act , an offer to repay under modified repayment terms is made through a consumer proposal. The Department defers or suspends recovery action on an individual's CPP and OAS overpayments upon formal written notification that the individual has filed a consumer proposal. Consumer proposal A consumer proposal is an arrangement between an individual and their creditors. It can range from an extension of the repayment time to asking creditors to accept cents on the dollar in satisfaction of their claim. When the Department receives formal written notification that a consumer proposal has been filed, while the file is under review, recovery action on the individual's overpayment is: deferred ( if recovery had not been initiated); or suspended (if recovery had been initiated). If the consumer proposal is accepted, payments from the court-appointed trustee are applied to the individual's overpayment. If the consumer proposal is rejected or a default occurs, normal overpayment recovery will start or resume.

Overpayment recovery is guided by the following key principles: be fiscally responsible by attempting recovery of overpayments in a timely manner; be flexible in establishing recovery rates or repayment schedules that reflect an individual's ability to repay; and ensure that the individual is not placed in undue hardship. When the individual cannot repay the full amount of the overpayment, a recovery rate is established in accordance with the above key principles. When calculating the recovery rate on an active account, the total of all the individual's CPP and OAS benefit entitlements must be considered. The Department cannot recover an overpayment from a pension or benefit payable to or on behalf of another individual other than the individual responsible for the overpayment. The only exception is if an individual other than the individual responsible for the overpayment voluntarily offers to refund the overpayment. The Department will accept written requests for a deduction from any current benefit payable. These offers must not be solicited by the Department. Voluntary payments and requests to increase the recovery rate can be accepted.

The liability to repay an overpayment rests with the beneficiary or another individual (e.g. spouse, common-law partner or relative of a deceased beneficiary) who received an amount that they are not entitled to receive. If a third party receives a benefit payment that they are not entitled to receive, the Department will attempt recovery if there is proof that this individual is the debtor and is responsible for the overpayment. Recovery action cannot be taken against a third party if it is based on an assumption made from looking at the beneficiary's file. An administrative investigation must be completed by the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) to determine whether a third party is liable for the overpayment. If the ISB determines that a third party is liable for the overpayment, we can recover from that individual even if there is no formal conviction by a court. However, the ISB must provide sufficient evidence that the third party is the debtor and is responsible for the overpayment. In general, overpayments are recoverable. The first course of action is to attempt recovery of the overpayment. If the recovery places the debtor in undue hardship, the recovery of the overpayment can be reviewed and modified accordingly. There are exceptions to the above when the following have been established: Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error; or Inactive account with an overpayment amount of $100 and under. There is no authority under the Canada Pension Plan or the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) to request a reconsideration or appeal the recovery rate of an overpayment or the overpayment amount. An individual may request a reconsideration or appeal the circumstances that caused the overpayment. These circumstances must be within the reconsideration or appeals provisions of the Canada Pension Plan or the OAS Act. When there is a reconsideration or an appeal on an account with an overpayment, recovery action must be deferred if it has not been initiated. If recovery has already been initiated, then it must be suspended until the outcome of the reconsideration or the appeal is known.

topic_title: Program recovery—same program and cross program
text: When an individual has an overpayment, it may be recovered from any pension or benefit payable under any act or program administered by the Minister. Recovery of an overpayment can be deducted and retained from the whole or a portion of a pension or benefit payment. This will ensure recovery of the overpayment (i.e. single payment or instalments) will not cause undue hardship in accordance with recovery rates of undue hardship and with the agreement of the paying program. Once a standard recovery rate is established based on the amount of all CPP and OAS pensions and benefits in pay, recovery of the overpayment is normally through a set-off or deduction from the same program's pension or benefit payments. If the Department is not able to recover the overpayment from the same program, a set-off from other programs within the Department (i.e. CPP and OAS) is considered.

Recovery rates apply only to ongoing monthly payments. If there is an overpayment on an account and the individual subsequently becomes entitled to an arrears payment under any program, 100% of that arrears payment must be applied towards the existing overpayment. This includes an underpayment after a recalculation of pension and benefits. Individuals must be informed in writing of the recovery action.

topic_title: Recovery of overpayments when individuals are deceased
text: A deceased individual's estate takes on their liabilities at the time of their death. A notification of death may be received by: a telephone call; correspondence from the deceased individual's representative; a letter; returned payments; informant leads; returned mail marked “deceased”; or information from the Social Insurance Registry or a death notification received from a provincial Vital Statistics. When applicable, the deceased individual's estate must be informed about the overpayment to be recovered. Outstanding overpayments at the time of the individual's death can be recovered from any CPP or OAS pensions or benefits owed to the deceased or to their estate. However, outstanding overpayments cannot be recovered from pensions and benefits paid to survivors or next of kin (e.g. SVR pension, ALWS benefit or Surviving Child's benefit). An overpayment can only be recovered from SVR pension and benefits if the recipient of these benefits voluntarily offers payment or is determined to be responsible for the overpayment after an administrative investigation is completed by the ISB. If the estate cannot be located, writing-off the overpayment can be considered. If it is established that there is no estate, the estate is closed or there are insufficient funds to make a partial or total repayment, remitting the balance of the overpayment can be considered. This consideration is based on whether the overpayment cannot be recovered in the reasonably foreseeable future. Recovery from the DTH benefit The CPP pays a one-time lump sum DTH benefit payment to or on behalf of the estate of a deceased CPP contributor to cover funeral expenses. Both the Canada Pension Plan and the OAS Act state that when a benefit is or becomes payable to the deceased individual's estate under any program administered by the Minister, an overpayment can be deducted and retained from the amount payable. Therefore, if the deceased individual's estate applies for and is eligible for the DTH benefit, it should be applied to any outstanding overpayment of more than $100 owed by the deceased or their estate. The consent of the deceased individual's estate representative is not required before initiating the recovery action against the DTH benefit. However, after the recovery is actioned, the deceased individual's estate representative must be notified in writing. Recovery from the pension and benefit payment in the month of death The Department is legislatively obligated to pay CPP and OAS pensions and benefits to the individual up to and including the month of their death. Month of death payments are not to be intercepted to apply towards a deceased individual's overpayment. Although the Department cannot intercept month of death payments, if it is returned to the Department, the payment can be applied towards the overpayment. No estate exists An individual is described as "intestate" when they die without a will. Once informed of the overpayment and if there are insufficient funds to repay it, the individual responsible for the financial affairs of the deceased individual must submit a written statement to the Department. This must state that the individual has died without a will and indicate there are insufficient funds to repay their overpayment. An estate exists Every effort must be made to inform the estate of any overpayment and to request recovery. The deceased individual's executor or representative is required to provide the Department with details of the estate administration. The estate is probated The deceased individual's estate representative must submit a written statement to the Department indicating whether the estate is probated. Letters of administration (or probate) legally establish a will as authentic and binding. Probate is the legal process of distributing assets according to the last will. The main advantages of this process are that: the probate court supervises the entire proceedings; and the probate laws are followed. The estate is not probated In some cases, the letters of probate will not be applied, even though the deceased left a will. It is likely in such cases that the estate was very small or simple and all assets were dispersed shortly after the death. Even when there is a will, it is not usually presented before the judge for appeal. The deceased individual's representative provides a written statement to the Department confirming that no application will be made for letters of probate. If there are insufficient funds to repay the overpayment, the statement should indicate that although the deceased left a will, the estate was very small and all assets were dispersed shortly after the death herefore, indicating that there are insufficient funds to repay the overpayment. The statement must include a description of the assets as well as claims against the assets. The estate is closed If the deceased individual's representative claims the estate is closed, the individual's representative must provide the Department with written confirmation.

An active account means there is a pension or benefit in pay under any of the programs (i.e. OAS, CPP or CPPD). Effective February 8, 2016, the recovery rates withheld from a monthly pension or benefit payment are as follows: For an overpayment amount of $100 and under : the full amount is deducted from the next or subsequent pension or benefit payments until the overpayment amount is recovered. For an overpayment amount over $100 : The standard recovery rate is equal to a monthly withhold of 25% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits until the overpayment amount is recovered (excluding children's benefits unless the overpayment consists of children's benefits). For individuals who are receiving income-tested benefits, the recovery rate will be equal to a monthly withhold of 10% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits until the overpayment is recovered. For individuals who are not receiving income-tested benefits and depending on an individual's situation, an initial recovery rate of a monthly withhold of 10% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits can be used. The recovery rate must not be less than $10 per month, unless their monthly entitlement is less than $10. When possible, the full overpayment should be recovered within 5 years. However, when there are large overpayments (i.e. $10,000 and over), the full overpayment should be recovered within 10 years. These guidelines are designed to help the Department establish consistent national recovery rates using discretion and good judgment. However, there will be cases where the overpayment cannot be recovered within the stated guidelines. Furthermore, depending on the circumstances, the established recovery rate does not prevent the Department from: determining a lower recovery rate; determining a higher recovery rate; or accepting repayment in full for individuals who request it.

An inactive account means there are no pensions or benefits in pay under any of the programs (i.e. OAS, CPP or CPPD). Effective February 8, 2016, all new or initial overpayments of $100 and under per benefit payment on inactive accounts are automatically remitted with no attempt to recover. This is due to the overall cost of recovery exceeding the amount of the overpayment. However, if unentitled payments are due to misrepresentation, fraud or duplicate payments cashed, they will be recovered.

When an individual claims the recovery of their overpayment (as a whole or in parts) would cause suffering or privation due to their limited household income, undue hardship may be considered. Household income is the total combined income of the individual and their spouse or common-law partner. Children's income is not considered when determining household income. In addition, assets and liabilities are excluded when determining a claim of undue hardship. Undue hardship exists when the individual cannot repay any portion of the overpayment, however small, without being deprived of the necessities of life. These necessities include food, shelter, medical attention, clothing and utilities (i.e. water, electricity and heating). A claim of undue hardship must come from the individual or from someone acting on their behalf. Reduced recovery rates for active accounts When an individual claims undue hardship, they indicate that they cannot repay at the established or proposed recovery rate. In response, the Department has the authority to reduce, suspend or defer recovery action for a period of time, while keeping with the key principles. In most cases, an individual must provide information about their household income and expenses on a Statement of Income and Expenses (ISP-0100) form. They must also provide documentation to the Department to support their claim. The Department has the discretion to accept or negotiate a reduced recovery rate without the need to request an ISP-0100 form. This reduced recovery is allowed as long as the overpayment will still be recovered within the suggested 5-year or 10-year time frames. In cases where the overpayment will not be recovered in the suggested time frames above based on the proposed reduced recovery rate, information about the individual's income and expenses is required. Once the ISP-0100 form is received, it is reviewed and the individual's ability or inability to repay their overpayment is determined. Additional information or clarification of details can be requested, if required. If the amount of an expense does not seem reasonable, the individual can be asked to provide an explanation. If the individual indicates they are currently making payments on loans and/or credit cards, they can be asked when these payments are expected to end. If the individual's yearly reasonable expenses are more than, equal to or approximate the yearly income, it may be concluded that undue hardship does exist. Discretion and judgement must be applied in each case. If it is determined that the individual is experiencing undue hardship and is not capable of repaying their overpayment at the proposed or established recovery rate, the recovery rate can be reduced. As a guideline for undue hardship claims, the reduced rate should be sufficient to recover the bulk of the overpayment within 10 years, but this is not always possible. Therefore, recovery rates are discretionary and can be reduced depending on the individual's financial situation. If the assessment of the individual's financial situation does not allow a reduced recovery rate, the original recovery rate should be maintained. If a reduced recovery rate is established and there is a possibility that the individual's financial situation may change in the future (i.e. loan payment is expected to end in the near future), the account can be reviewed every 6 to 12 months. Increased recovery rates for active accounts When it is determined that the individual can pay more than the established recovery rate, the recovery rate can be increased. However, the individual needs to agree on an increased recovery rate before it is implemented. Deferred recovery rate When it is determined that the individual is in a temporary (6 to 12 months) or long-term (5 years or less) situation of undue hardship, the recovery rate can be suspended (if recovery has started) or deferred (if recovery has not started). The account must be reviewed in 6 to 12 months or in 5 years or less, as applicable. Recovery after a period of deferral or suspension Before recovery begins or is restarted, individuals must be advised in writing of the intended recovery action after a period of deferral or suspension. They must also be provided with the opportunity to respond within a reasonable time frame. Individuals will be given a minimum of 30 days to reply. If the individual objects, negotiations must take place before restarting recovery.

The purpose of the EA/AE criterion under the remissions provisions is to enable the Department to remit an overpayment (in full or in part) when that overpayment was from erroneous advice or the result of an error by a Departmental employee. Erroneous advice Erroneous advice occurs when incorrect or misleading information is communicated or provided to an individual by a Departmental employee (i.e. orally or in writing) during the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act. This erroneous advice affects an individual's actions or conduct to their detriment in relation to the CPP or OAS program. Erroneous advice includes the omission of crucial information related to eligibility and entitlement to benefits. Specifically, if a Departmental employee does not provide an individual with all the required information available at that time and it affects the making of an informed decision regarding their benefit, it is considered just as erroneous as providing information that is incorrect. Administrative error An administrative error is an incorrect action, an error made or the failure to act by a Departmental employee during the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act that causes or increases an overpayment on an individual's account. Failure to act due to workload is not an administrative error. However, the failure of an employee to act on or to overlook information pertinent to eligibility and entitlement while administering the legislative provisions of the CPP or the OAS Act is an administrative error. When an overpayment is a result of EA/AE by a Departmental employee, it may be considered for remission in whole or in part. However, an overpayment caused by an employee's failure to act (e.g. not acting upon information on file) or to take corrective action when an error is found could result in the overpayment being considered for remission. In these situations, accounts should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. When overpayments are increased because of an employee's actions or inactions, there is flexibility to consider remitting all or portions of the overpayment in part or in full, depending on the circumstances of the case. There are also situations where the Department made an error that resulted in an overpayment and the individual is not aware that an error was made on their account. Specifically, the Department has determined that the overpayment is a result of EA/AE and that it is solely responsible for the overpayment. In these situations, the error is a clear fact and the individual was not aware of the error or that they were being overpaid. Situations where the Department made an error and is solely responsible for an overpayment include: systems errors where many beneficiaries were overpaid; encoding errors where the wrong benefit amounts are paid; or administrative errors where an individual is not aware that an error was made on their account. It would be unreasonable in these situations to request full recovery of the overpayment from the individual if the Department made the error and the individual could not have known they were being overpaid. This would create inequities and is inconsistent with the principles upon which the overpayment policy is based. Full remission—EA/AE An overpayment can be remitted in full if the Department's or a departmental employee's error is the sole cause of the overpayment and the individual could not have been aware of the error and that they were being overpaid. Partial remission—EA/AE An overpayment can be partially remitted when: the overpayment is originally caused by the Department or a departmental employee and the individual could have been aware of the error; or the overpayment is originally caused by an error or the actions or inactions of the individual and: an employee of the Department could have been aware of information on the account or in the file (including the error made by the individual) and could have taken corrective action but did not; or an employee of the Department made subsequent errors or omissions that increased the overpayment. In partial remission situations, it is appropriate for the Department to accept a percentage of the responsibility for the overpayment and remit that portion of it. For national consistency, this is generally set at 50%, but can be set to any percentage deemed appropriate, depending on the facts of the case. Discretion can be used to remit different percentages of an overpayment, as long as a rationale is provided for the recommended percentages based on the facts of each case. Depending on the case, certain portions or periods of the overpayment can be considered for a full or partial remission, while certain portions or periods may be fully recovered. When part of the overpayment is remitted, the balance remains as a recoverable overpayment and recovery action will continue.
Canada Pension Plan Subsection 66(3)—Remission of amount owing Section 107.1—Donations Income Tax Act Section 224(1)—Garnishment Old Age Security Act Subsection 37(4)—Remission of amount owing

According to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) and the Financial Administration Act , a remission is the decision to forgive an otherwise legally enforceable debt. This means that the debt is forgiven and the Crown gives up the right to resume collection at a future date. The debtor is released from the obligation to repay their overpayment. After a remission is approved on the overpayment or a specified portion of the overpayment, the Department gives up the right to resume recovery or collection of the overpayment at a future date. The individual is released from the obligation to repay because the overpayment is forgiven and no longer exists. As a rule, decisions to remit or not to remit an overpayment are upheld by the delegated official and will not be re-visited except in cases where there is: a gross error or misapplication of the legislation; new information that is discovered; or a jurisdictional error. Any payment received from an individual after their overpayment has been remitted must be returned to them since the overpayment no longer exists. However, if the individual insists on repaying the overpayment after it has been remitted, the Minister may accept the payment as a donation. In situations where a portion of an overpayment has already been recovered or repaid and a subsequent decision is made to remit the overpayment, the balance of the overpayment is remitted. There is no authority to reissue the already recovered funds to the individual when the Department has determined there was originally no entitlement to those funds. This includes situations where the cause of the overpayment was due to Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE).

The reasonably foreseeable future is the period of time over which the substantial portion of an overpayment is recovered. For example, this can be applied in situations where an individual dies and: leaves no estate; or the estate has been finalized and there is no other means of recovery. In this situation, the overpayment will not be recovered within the reasonably foreseeable future and can be considered for remission. In order to remit an overpayment, the Minister must be satisfied that the overpayment cannot be collected in the reasonably foreseeable future. When considering the remission under this condition, proof of attempted recovery actions taken (i.e. proof of the estate being insolvent or closed) and proof of death should be obtained before remitting the overpayment. The remission can only be completed once a response is received confirming that there are no funds to repay the overpayment or that the estate is closed or insolvent. In situations where recovery attempts are made but there is no response, the overpayment is written off and is not remitted.

topic_title: The cost of recovery exceeds the overpayment
text: Cost of recovery is applied when the administrative costs of collecting an overpayment are equal to or more than the amount of an overpayment. In these situations, remitting the overpayment can be considered. Service Canada determined it expends over $100.00 to recover an overpayment. Therefore, initial overpayments of $100.00 and under on inactive accounts are remitted automatically as the cost of recovery exceeds the overpayment amount.

Permanent undue hardship exists when it is determined that an individual will never be able to repay their overpayment without being deprived of the necessities of life. When an individual is in a permanent situation of undue hardship, remitting an overpayment can be considered. However, permanent undue hardship must be established before remitting an overpayment. Remission should not be considered initially, but on a case-by-case basis, after recovery has been attempted. You must obtain proof of attempted recovery actions taken, a statement from the individual claiming undue hardship and standardized financial assessments before remitting the overpayment.

topic_title: When will a remission be considered?
text: The first course of action is to attempt recovery of the overpayment. It is the Department's policy that recovery must be pursued on all overpayments. This excludes situations where EA/AE has been established and inactive accounts with an initial overpayment amount of $100.00 and under. The last course of action in the recovery process is remission. According to the provisions set out in the CPP and the OAS Act, consideration for remission must be carried out on a case-by-case basis. The CPP and the OAS Act specify that a remission of an overpayment may be considered under the condition that the Minister is satisfied that: the overpayment cannot be recovered within the reasonably foreseeable future; the cost of recovery exceeds the overpayment amount; the repayment of the overpayment would cause undue hardship; or the overpayment is the result of EA/AE. If one of the above conditions exist, then the Minister may remit all or a portion of the overpayment. However, it may be reconsidered if an individual is convicted of an offence under any provision of the CPP, the OAS Act or under the Criminal Code in connection with obtaining the benefit payment. If an individual is convicted of an offence (i.e. fraud, first or second-degree murder or manslaughter that disentitles them to benefits) in connection with an overpayment, the Department cannot remit the overpayment. The overpayment remains a recoverable overpayment and recovery action will continue. In addition, the overpayment cannot be considered under the write-off provisions, until every possible effort has been exhausted to recover and collect the overpayment. Whenever it is not 100% certain that one of the four conditions listed above are met, it is recommended that the overpayment be considered for a write-off rather than remission. According to the Treasury Board Policy within the Department, all approved remissions must be retained to establish an audit trail in accordance with general requirements on file retention.
