The Department’s policy ensures that any overpayment is recoverable and that the first course of action is to attempt recovery of the overpayment in full with the following exceptions: where Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) has been established; and on inactive accounts with an initial overpayment amount of $100.00 and under. No overpayment will be written-off until every possible effort has been made to recover it and all possibilities for collecting it have been exhausted. Only overpayments that are truly uncollectible should be written-off. A write-off, as it pertains to the Financial Administration Act , is the removal of an overpayment, in whole or in part, from the accounts receivable records. The writing-off of an overpayment obligation or claim does not, however, affect the right of Her Majesty to collect or recover the overpayment, obligation or claim in the future. There are no provisions in the CPP or the OAS Act regarding overpayment write-offs. The authority for overpayment write-off comes from the Financial Administration Act and its Debt Write-off Regulations. The Programs can recommend that overpayments be written-off, however the Chief Financial Officer Branch is the delegated authority to approve write-offs. UPDATED! The National Write-Off and Remissions Review Committee carries out a formal review for approval of any recommended write-off for overpayments $25,000.00 and over. When to consider a write-off? The Department may recommend a write-off for a CPP or OAS overpayment in the following situations: All avenues for recovery have been exhausted; An overpayment balance remains after a compromise settlement; An overpayment balance remains after a consumer proposal is accepted; An individual is bankrupt under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act with an overpayment balance before the date of filing and has been granted a full discharge by the bankruptcy court; or An individual has an overpayment that has arisen from a conviction of any offence under any provision of the CPP or OAS Act or the Criminal Code , and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts.

topic_title: Benefits, pensions and provisions that are processed post-mortem Updated
text: The following benefits are processed post-mortem: OAS pension; CPP RTR pension. If the individual is 70 + 1 month or older at the time of death Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ), as long as the contributor was receiving CPP DSB for the relevant period; SVR pension; Surviving Child's benefit; Credit Splitting requests or applications; and Child Rearing Provision (CRP) requests. CPP and OAS pension and benefit applications share the same rules (except for credit splitting and CRPs) regarding the payment of post-mortem benefits. The requirements are as follows: an application is made in writing and is received by the Department; the individual would have qualified for the pension or benefit before their death; and the application is received within one year of the person's date of death.

topic_title: Benefits that are not processed post-mortem Updated
text: CPP pension and benefits The following CPP pension and benefits are not processed post mortem if the application is received on or after January 1, 1998 : CPPD benefit, including an automatic reinstatement application received after the Date of Death (DOD); PRDB , including an automatic reinstatement application received after the DOD; and CPP RTR pension, if the individual is between the ages of 60 and 70 at the time of their death. Applications for the pensions and benefits above must be signed by the individual or their legal representative and received by the Department on or before the individual's DOD. Applications for these pensions and benefits received after the individual's DOD must be denied. OAS benefits The following OAS benefits are not processed post-mortem if the application is received on or after May 3, 2007 : the GIS; the ALW benefit; and the ALWS benefit. Applications for the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefits must be signed by the individual or their legal representative and received by the Department on or before the individual's DOD. Applications for the above benefits received after the DOD must be denied.

topic_title: Evidence to support a post-mortem application
text: The documentary evidence required to support a post-mortem application is the same as the evidence required if the application had been received before the individual's death. In addition, the following supporting documentation is necessary: acceptable evidence of death; and a written statement from the executor or administrator (in cases where the executor or court-appointed administrator has not already identified themselves on the application) which includes the following: a declaration they are responsible for the administration of the estate; and payment address information; or an indemnity agreement is required in cases where there is no estate, the estate is closed, or a benefit or pension application is submitted by any other person who is approved as a payee.

topic_title: Individuals who may apply on behalf of a deceased individual
text: The following individuals may apply on behalf of a deceased individual: the executor of the deceased individual's estate; the deceased individual's representative or heirs, when there is no estate; or the individual or agency (designated by the Minister) having custody and control of a child immediately before the child's death.

A CPP or OAS application is considered post-mortem when it is received after the Date of Death (DOD) of the individual. Even if the individual signs the application and it is received after the DOD, the application is considered post-mortem. Post-mortem applications are deemed to have been received on the DOD.

topic_title: Post-mortem GIS, ALW and ALWS benefit applications
text: Post-mortem applications for the GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits can only be processed if they have been received before May 3, 2007. The limitation on post-mortem GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits applies to the application for the benefit and not to the renewal of the benefit. Beneficiaries who have made a lifetime GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit application have met the requirement of making an initial application for the benefit. When renewing the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit, if a statement of income is provided on behalf of a deceased beneficiary, or if it is received after the Date of Death (DOD), the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit can be paid when there is continued eligibility or entitlement up to the DOD. The statement of income and the statement of estimated income are not considered post-mortem applications. In addition, the Canada Revenue Agency income feed is a statement of income and not an application for the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit.

topic_title: Time limit to receive a post-mortem application
text: OAS pension For an OAS pension, the Department must receive the application within one year of the Date of death (DOD) of the deceased individual. CPP CPP has similar provisions to OAS in that, for some benefits, the Department may receive the application within one year of the DOD of the deceased individual. However, for other benefits, the application must have been received by the Department on or before the individual's DOD. Specific rules for each benefit follow. RTR pension Where a contributor's DOD occurs in the month the individual turned age 70, or earlier, their RTR pension application must have been received by the Department on or before their DOD. Applications received after their month of death must be denied. For example, there is no provision to process an application on behalf of a deceased person where: the contributor dies: before age 70; or in the month of their 70th birthday; and the application is received after the month of their death. However, the application can be processed if: the contributor's date of death occurs anytime after the month the individual turned age 70; valid earnings and contributions have been made to the CPP; and the Department receives the RTR pension application within one year of the contributor's date of death. Credit splitting provision An application or request for a post-mortem credit splitting may be made by: the estate or succession of either spouse or common-law partner; a personal representative; the deceased individual's child; or someone on behalf of that child, if the child is under the age of 18. Applications or requests for credit splitting received after the death of an individual are treated differently than those for benefits and pensions under the CPP and OAS programs. The timelines for the submission of a post-mortem credit splitting request or application are based on whether the members forming the couple are: former spouses upon divorce or legal annulment; separated spouses; or former common-law partners requesting a Credit Split. The date of death is taken into consideration when applying the timelines for accepting a request. For more information on credit splitting application timelines, Canada Pension Plan – Credit Splitting (Policy)

Section 224.1 of the Income Tax Act empowers the Minister of National Revenue to request the recovery of an income tax debt from a CPP or OAS pension or benefit without obtaining authorization from the beneficiary.

Part II of the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act provides for the garnishment of designated federal monies to satisfy support orders or provisions. The following creditor types who are owed money under the terms of a defaulted support order can initiate a request for garnishment: the spouse or former spouse (creditor); the common-law partner or former common-law partner (creditor); the creditor's lawyer; or provincial or territorial enforcement services or social service agencies. To apply for assistance, a creditor can petition a court for a garnishee summons against the judgment debtor. In some jurisdictions, it is possible to obtain a garnishee summons without proceeding to court. The garnishee summons and an application for garnishment and support documents are then submitted to the Federal Minister of Justice. Upon receipt of a valid application, the Department of Justice informs the debtor that garnishable monies can be intercepted. As applicants do not specify the funds they believe will be paid to the debtor, the Department of Justice automatically requests searches of all eligible funds. The following federal monies can be intercepted at the source department: income tax refunds; employment insurance benefits; interest on unmatured Canada Savings Bonds held by the Bank of Canada; training income supplement; OAS benefits; benefits payable under the CPP, excluding: benefits payable in respect of children; and benefits paid on behalf of a beneficiary to a province or municipality and death benefits; agricultural stabilization payments; Western Grain stabilization payments; and Canadian Dairy Commission payments. Following notification, source departments report to the Department of Justice as to whether garnishable monies are payable (or may be payable in the future) to the debtor. If funds are available, the source department indicates to the Department of Justice both the amounts and the dates when those funds are payable. The Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Unit evaluates the funds available based on the information received from source departments, against the financial terms of the garnishee summons and instructs the source department to transfer all or some of the money to the Department of Justice. The funds are deposited in a trust account and a cheque is issued to the court or enforcement service that issued the summons. The garnishment order is binding for a period of 5 years or until the summons is satisfied in full. Exception An exception occurs where funds are garnished periodically. If a garnishee summons is of continuing effect and remains unsatisfied in full at the end of the 5-year period, it continues to bind any sources of money until the summons is satisfied. If, however, after the 5-year period is expired, no funds are garnished for a period of 180 consecutive days, the summons ceases to bind the government. Public trustee Note that applications received from the public trustee must be actioned even when a garnishment action has started.

The only accepted voluntary deductions from a CPP or OAS pension or benefit are from Veterans Affairs Canada. The individual must make the request in writing for voluntary deduction from their CPP or OAS benefit to repay a debt to Veterans Affairs Canada.

Recipients of CPP or OAS pensions or benefits may request that an amount be deducted each month from their benefit payment for income tax purposes. Income tax is not automatically deducted from CPP and OAS payments. The beneficiary is responsible for providing the amount or percentage that they would like to be withheld: Voluntary tax withholds can only be requested by residents of Canada. The withheld amounts can only be applied to the current year's income tax. They cannot be used to reimburse the Canada Revenue Agency for income tax owing from a previous year or to pay any other form of tax. Withholding a percentage of the benefit will automatically adjust the amount withheld when the benefit is indexed. If a dollar amount is withheld, it will not increase when the benefit is indexed. A withhold will remain in place until the beneficiary requests that it be removed or modified.

topic_title: Key principles common to both CPP and OAS benefits
text: Payments of a benefit can be suspended to determine continuing eligibility or entitlement in the following circumstances: failure to respond (e.g. attempts to correspond with beneficiaries by mail to request information to confirm their ongoing eligibility or entitlement to benefits and no response is received); the beneficiary fails to comply with the legislation (e.g. the beneficiary responds but refuses to provide the requested information); reviewing the third-party administration of a beneficiary's account; notification that a beneficiary's address has changed by way of returned correspondence, benefit payments, T4s, applications or cheques. The beneficiary's direct deposit payments could not be deposited because the account is closed. After making reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to locate a beneficiary, the Department must suspend payment of the benefit. the death of the beneficiary. When a beneficiary dies, the account is first suspended. However, once any outstanding receivables are recovered and proof of death is received (if applicable), the benefit is cancelled manual adjustments to the type or amount of the benefit are required; the monthly payments of a benefit are combined into one larger periodic payment; the beneficiary's eligibility or entitlement is in question.

topic_title: Other reasons specific to CPP Children's benefits Updated
text: Payments of CPP Children's benefits can be suspended to determine continuing eligibility when waiting for or reviewing documentation to determine the payee for a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit or Surviving Child's benefit from a new custodian.

topic_title: Other reasons specific to OAS pension and benefits
text: Although different situations can necessitate the suspension of a benefit, OAS pensions or benefits are usually suspended for the following reasons: the Canada Revenue Agency notifies the Department that the OAS pension recipient is living in a foreign country and has not submitted the OAS Return of Income form; reviewing residence for OAS pension, GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits if entitlement is questioned; the pensioner or beneficiary is not entitled due to incarceration. Suspension of all OAS benefit payments are effective the month following the month of incarceration; if the pensioner leaves Canada for a period exceeding 6 months, not including the month of departure, and the pensioner has fewer than an aggregate of 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18. Payment of the OAS pension may resume the month in which the pensioner returns to Canada or the month residence in Canada is resumed.

The Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act authorize the suspension of pension and benefit payments when a beneficiary's continuing eligibility or entitlement is in question and requires an investigation. If an individual is the subject of an investigation either by the Department or by the RCMP on behalf of the Department, consultation with the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) is required before any action to suspend the benefits is taken. The suspension of a benefit is an administrative measure used to temporarily stop the payment of a benefit to: confirm ongoing eligibility or entitlement; or take administrative actions. Suspensions are usually followed by an action to either resume the payments or to cancel the benefit. Beneficiaries expect that the benefit will be paid continuously after they have applied and been found to be eligible. Interruption in payments can have serious ramifications for beneficiaries. Therefore, all living CPP and OAS beneficiaries with a known address must receive a written notice a minimum of 30 days before the suspension of the benefits. A benefit remains suspended until the Minister is satisfied that the beneficiary continues to meet the eligibility criteria, in which case the benefit is reinstated. If an ISB investigation reveals a beneficiary is not eligible to the benefit in question, the payment of the benefit may be cancelled. A suspension must not remain in place for any longer than it takes to confirm continuing eligibility or to process transactions to correct the type, amount or method of benefit payment.

topic_title: Suspension of the GIS, ALW or ALWS
text: The GIS, ALW and ALWS can be suspended if: the pensioner spouse or common-law partner dies, in which case the ALW benefit can be converted into an ALWS benefit; the ALW or ALWS beneficiary reaches age 65, and the benefits are not automatically converted to the OAS pension and the GIS; the pensioner is no longer entitled to receive the GIS; the pensioner requests in writing that their OAS pension be cancelled, in which case the ALW will be suspended and must be repaid to the Department, if applicable; the ALW beneficiary becomes divorced or separated from their pensioner spouse or common-law partner, or the ALWS beneficiary no longer meets the definition of a survivor; the GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary has been absent from Canada for a period of more than 6 months excluding the month of departure; the GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary is not entitled due to a sponsorship agreement; there is no entitlement to the OAS pension for any month; or after the June payment, the income is in excess or the income information and has not been received in time to be processed before reversion. In most situations, the pensioner can retain their Lifetime renewal designation and the ALW or ALWS beneficiary can retain their Lifetime renewal designation when the benefit is suspended. As long as the individual is eligible to receive the ALW or ALWS benefit, the lifetime status cannot change. However, the Minister retains the right to request an ALW or ALWS application and a statement of income at any time to confirm eligibility or entitlement.

topic_title: When a suspension is not appropriate
text: Suspension may not be appropriate in the following circumstances: the beneficiary has not been notified that the suspension will take place, unless the address is not known, within the required timeline; the DSB or PRDB cannot be suspended solely at the request of a beneficiary; the DSB or PRDB beneficiary's medical condition must first be considered before a suspension can be approved; immediately upon receipt of an informant lead, or suspected fraud or misrepresentation. No suspension action is taken until the details of the informant lead, suspected fraud or the misrepresentation is confirmed by Integrity Services Branch.

topic_title: Cancellation of a CPP pension or benefit within 12 months
text: An individual may request to cancel any CPP benefit, including CPPD benefits, provided the following conditions are met: the request is made in writing; and the cancellation request is received within 12 months of the date the first payment commenced. The pension or benefit may then be cancelled provided the following conditions are met: the beneficiary repays all amounts received no later than 12 months after the day in which their request for a cancellation is granted; and the request is not an "in-favour" request to cancel a CPP RTR pension "in-favour" of a CPP DSB benefit. When the written cancellation request is received, as long as the request is granted and all amounts are repaid within the prescribed timeframes, the pension or benefit is cancelled retroactive to the initial effective date. The application is considered never to have been made and the pension or benefit is considered never to have been paid. Therefore, if an individual wishes to receive a pension or benefit at a future date, they must submit a new application. If the beneficiary does not repay the amounts within the 12-month period, the pension and any related benefits are reinstated and any amounts already recovered are returned to the beneficiary.

topic_title: Cancellation of an OAS pension and the GIS within 6 months Updated
text: An individual may request to cancel the OAS pension and/or the GIS provided the following conditions are met: the request is made in writing; and the cancellation request is received within 6 months of the date the first payment commenced. The pension or benefit may then be cancelled provided the beneficiary repays all amounts received no later than 6 months after the day on which their request for a cancellation is granted. When the written cancellation request is received, as long as the request is granted and all amounts are repaid within the prescribed timeframes, the OAS pension or GIS is cancelled retroactively to the initial effective date. When an OAS pension or GIS are cancelled, the application(s) is considered never to have been made (or the individual never automatically enrolled), and the pension and/or benefit are considered never to have been paid. In addition, the GIS beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewable designation. If the individual wishes to receive a pension or GIS at a future date, they must submit a new application. After the pension is cancelled, individuals can continue to: accumulate Canadian residence; or increase their OAS pension amount through an actuarial adjustment (voluntary deferral). Cancellation of the OAS pension and/or GIS and its effects on the ALW benefit When the OAS pensioner has requested to cancel their OAS pension and/or the GIS, the ALW benefit must also be repaid no later than 6 months after the day on which the request for the cancellation is granted. As a result of the cancellation of the OAS pension or GIS, the ALW benefit application is considered never to have been made and the benefit never to have been paid. In addition, the ALW beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewable designation and an application for the ALW is required in the future. If the ALW beneficiary fails to repay the amounts owed within the 6-month period, the OAS pension or GIS, and any related benefits (i.e. ALW benefit) are reinstated, and any recovered amounts are returned to the beneficiary. Automatic enrolment for the OAS pension and GIS The Minister retains the right to: cancel the OAS automatic enrolment process; and request an application before the individual's 65th birthday. ALW and ALWS There is no authority in the OAS Act to cancel an ALW or an ALWS benefit. However, a beneficiary may make a request, in writing, that the ALW or ALWS benefit be ceased.

topic_title: Cancellation of CPP and OAS benefits due to a conviction of the first or second-degree murder or manslaughter of the contributor or individual's spouse or common-law partner
text: Both the CPP and the OAS Act have the legislative authority to cancel a CPP SVR pension, DTH benefit, Surviving Child's benefit, or an ALWS benefit to an individual who has been convicted of the first or second degree murder or manslaughter of the CPP contributor or, in cases of the ALWS , the individual's spouse or common-law partner. When these pensions or benefits are cancelled, an overpayment is calculated back to the effective date of the benefit.

Operationally, cancellations may either be classified as internally or externally initiated. Internal cancellations are those which the system automatically actions. For example, the system automatically cancels a CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit or Surviving Child's benefit the month after the child's 25th birthday, as the child is no longer eligible to receive the benefit due to age. External cancellations refer to those that departmental staff initiate on the basis of information or documentary evidence received. For example, the beneficiary requests that their benefit be cancelled and their request is approved, or information is received indicating the individual is no longer eligible.

Canada Pension Plan Section 66.1—Request to cancel benefit CPP regulations Section 46.2—Cancellation of benefit Old Age Security Act Section 9.3—Request to cancel pension and Effect of cancellation Section 18.2—Request to cancel supplement and Effect of cancellation Section 26.2—Inviting persons to apply OAS regulations Section 26.1—Cancellation of Pension or Supplement

Beneficiaries request the cancellation of their pensions and benefits for a variety of reasons. For instance, the individual's financial needs may have changed or the individual has simply decided to cancel the benefit for personal reasons. A pension or benefit may be cancelled when an individual's request is made within the prescribed period of time: The CPP Regulations provide for the cancellation of a CPP pension or benefit if a request is made within 12 months of receipt of the first payment; The OAS Act provides for cancellation of the OAS pension and/or the GIS if a request is made within 6 months of the first payment. If it is determined that a beneficiary is no longer eligible to receive a CPP or an OAS pension or benefit, it is cancelled. In such cases, the term "cancellation" means the termination of payment of a benefit as the individual is no longer eligible to receive the benefit.

topic_title: Circumstances that require a suspended CPP pension or benefit to be reinstated Updated
text: Reinstating suspended or terminated CPP pension or benefit payments is required when: A pension or benefit that was previously suspended pending determination of the date of death and it is determined that the beneficiary: has not died; or has died sometime after the benefit was suspended. In such cases, the pension or benefit is first reinstated then terminated the month after the month of death. A pension or benefit was previously suspended at the beneficiary's request and the beneficiary now requests the pension or benefit be reinstated. A pension or benefit was previously suspended as the beneficiary's address was unknown, then the address is confirmed and entered into the system. A pension or benefit was previously suspended pending the establishment of a trustee and a trustee is now approved. In this case, it is necessary to: update the appropriate system with the new payee information; and reinstate the pension or benefit. A DSB or PRDB previously suspended pending an assessment of the case and it is determined that the beneficiary continues to be disabled. A DSB or PRDB was previously suspended pending an assessment of the case and it is determined that the beneficiary ceased to be disabled sometime after the benefit was suspended. In these cases, the benefit is: reinstated; and terminated the month after the month that the beneficiary ceased to be disabled. A Child's benefit for a -18 child that was previously suspended pending determination of decision-making responsibility of the child: and it has since been determined that the previous payee continues to have decision-making responsibility of the minor child; or it has since been determined that a new payee is eligible to receive the benefit on behalf of the minor child. In this case, it is necessary to: update the appropriate system with the new payee information; and reinstate the benefit. A Child's benefit for a +18 child was previously terminated effective the date the child left school or university and: it has since been determined that the child did not leave school or university; or a new Declaration of CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form is received and approved. A Child's benefit that was terminated when the child reached 18 years of age and it is determined that the child is eligible for a +18 Child's benefit and the CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form is received and approved. A Child's benefit that was suspended or terminated due to a legal adoption. Only Surviving children's benefits are not to be suspended or terminated following a legal adoption. If they are, such benefits are reinstated the month after the month of legal adoption.

topic_title: Effective date when reinstating CPP pensions and benefits
text: When reinstating CPP pensions and benefits, the reinstatement effective date must be the same as the suspension date.

topic_title: Exception for terminated CPP pensions and benefits Updated
text: When a CPP pension or benefit is terminated due to a beneficiary's request to withdraw their application, the pension or benefit cannot be reinstated. The beneficiary must submit a new application for the terminated pension or benefit should they wish to receive the pension or benefit again.

Reinstatement refers to reactivating a recurring CPP or OAS pension or benefit payment (excluding automatic CPP Disability).

If a pensioner has less than 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18 and is absent from Canada for more than 6 months, their OAS pension payments are suspended. Payment of their OAS pension is reinstated the month in which the pensioner returns or resumes residence in Canada. Payment of the OAS pension can also be reinstated after a suspension when the pensioner has: provided all of the information necessary to establish eligibility and entitlement; and complied with the provisions of OAS legislation. A pensioner who requests the cessation of their OAS pension after July 13, 1995 can request, in writing, the reinstatement of their pension at a later date. In such cases, the pension is reinstated either: the month after the month in which the written request for reinstatement is received; or the month chosen by the pensioner, whichever is later . A pensioner cannot accumulate additional periods of residence for any period before the date of reinstatement. However, they can still accumulate periods of time towards pension portability.

When a suspended CPP pension or benefit is resumed or a terminated CPP pension or benefit is reinstated, the recurring payment schedule is reactivated. Any amounts formerly deducted (e.g. a voluntary tax withhold) from a suspended account are reactivated, if applicable.

A beneficiary is not obligated to accept a Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), an Allowance ( ALW ) or an Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ) benefit for any particular period of time. After completing an application for an income-tested benefit, a beneficiary may decide to defer receipt of the benefit or, if already receiving the benefit, may wish that the payments be discontinued for a period of time. When a beneficiary requests, in writing, that the GIS, ALW or ALWS be reinstated, the payments can be issued for the remainder of the payment period for which the reinstatement is requested. Payments are reinstated the month after the month in which the request is received. Payment for this period of time is dependent upon: the beneficiary's continued eligibility throughout the payment period for which the reinstatement is requested; and income information being present on the beneficiary's file. Any subsequent benefits for a new payment period must be based on either an application or income information from the Canada Revenue Agency. If a beneficiary returns to Canada after an absence of 6 months or more after the month of their departure and it is established that their absence was of a temporary nature not involving a change in residence, the benefit is reinstated effective the month of the beneficiary's return. For a beneficiary who no longer resides in Canada, GIS and ALWS payments cannot be reinstated until the month the beneficiary actually resumes residence in Canada. When a beneficiary, their spouse or common-law partner or the couple no longer reside in Canada, the ALW cannot be reinstated until the month both individuals actually resume residence in Canada. When ALWS benefits are terminated because a spouse or common-law partner is charged with the murder or manslaughter of their spouse or common-law partner, and the survivor is convicted of a lesser charge or acquitted at the completion of the appeal process or new trial, the ALWS benefit is reinstated from the date of cancellation upon receipt of court documentation.

topic_title: Allowance and Allowance for the Survivor
text: An application for the Allowance is approved the later of: the day an individual turns 60; the day after an individual meets the residence requirements; the day after an individual meets the legal status requirement; twelve months before the date of receipt of the application, but not before the date that the individual turns 60; or the month the applicant's spouse or common-law partner is approved for the GIS. An application for the Allowance for the Survivor is approved the later of: the day an individual turns 60; the day after an individual meets the residence requirements; the day after an individual meets the legal status requirement; twelve months before the date of receipt of the application, but not before the date that the individual turns 60; or the month of the death of the spouse or common-law partner.

An application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) is approved the later of: the month that the individual is approved for an OAS pension; twelve months before the date the Department receives an application

Old Age Security Act Updated Section 5 — Approval of an Application for a Pension Section 10 — Approval of an Application for a Supplement Section 11 — Approval of an Application for an Allowance Section 12 — Approval of an Application for an Allowance

An application for an OAS pension is approved the later of: the day an individual turns 65; the day after an individual meets the residence requirements; the day after an individual meets the legal status requirement; twelve months before the date of receipt of the application, but not before the date that the individual turns 65; or the month immediately before the date specified on the application (in cases where the applicant is already 65 when the Department receives the application).

When an applicant meets all of the eligibility requirements, the OAS pension and/or benefit will be approved. The Minister reserves the right to request additional information or documentation if continued eligibility comes into question.
Canada Pension Plan Subsection 2 (1)—Interpretation—Definitions

Survivor is under the age of 35 years If a CPP Survivor's (SVR) pension applicant has no dependent children and is not deemed disabled as per the CPP, but is expecting the birth of the deceased contributor's child, the survivor must apply for the Surviving Child's benefit when the child is born. When the Surviving Child's benefit is approved, the survivor qualifies for the full rate SVR pension retroactive to the month after the contributor's death or 11 months from the date of the SVR pension application. Survivor is age 35 or older If a survivor is age 35 or older and expecting the deceased contributor's child, the survivor will be paid a reduced SVR pension. When the child is born, the survivor must apply for the Surviving Child's benefit. If the Surviving Child's benefit is approved, the SVR pension is converted to the full rate amount retroactive to the effective date of the SVR pension, that is, the month after the month of the deceased contributor's death.

Birth certificates issued in the People’s Republic of China are not acceptable as valid evidence of age as it is not possible to determine on what records these documents are based. Evidence of age submitted by applicants from the People’s Republic of China and Hong Kong can be based on different calendars and calculating methods. Examples of calendars used in the People’s Republic of China and Hong Kong are listed below: The Western (Gregorian) calendar has been used in the People’s Republic of China since 1950. The Gregorian calendar is the most widely used calendar in the world today. An evidence of age in which the year of birth is in relation to the governing regime and the month of birth is in relation to the moon For example, a person born on 10th day of the 8th moon of the 13th year of People’s Republic of China would have a birth date of September 8, 1924. The animal sign under which a person is born. Each sign recurs every 12 years. The Hebrew calendar has existed for over 5,700 years. It is a lunar calendar and differs from the Gregorian calendar in the following ways: The New Year begins in late summer or autumn; The leap years have an extra month (Adar Sheni meaning the 2nd Adar). The addition of this month brings the calendar months into alignment with Western calendar months over a period of time; The nights are considered as part of the following days; The spelling of the months is phonetic as shown in parentheses in the table below. To determine the month of birth in the Gregorian calendar according to the Hebrew calendar, consider: Tishri as the month of October, even though the day of Tishri falls between September 5 and October 4; and Adar Sheni, the extra month inserted in a leap year, as part of the Adar month. The corresponding months may not be entirely accurate in light of the above considerations: Month in the Gregorian calendar Corresponding months in the Hebrew calendar January Tevet (Teves, Tebet) February Shevat March Adar April Nisan May Ivar June Sivan July Tammuz August Ab September Eilul October Tishri November Cheshvan (Hesvan, Heshvan, Cheshvan) December Kislev Birth dates to remember in connection with the following religious holiday: Rosh Hashanah, New Year, which begins on the 1st day of Tishri; Yom Kippur, Day of Atonement, which begins on the 10th day of Tishri; Hanukkah, Feast of Lights, which begins on 25th day of Kislev; Purim, Feast of Lots, which begins on the 14th day of Adar or Adar Sheni in leap years; Pesach, Passover, which begins on the 15th day of Nisan.

The Julian calendar was used in Soviet Russia until 1918 when the Western calendar was adopted. It took several years for all areas and churches to change to the Western calendar. When you receive an item of documentary age evidence based on the Julian calendar, add 13 days to the date of birth to match the Western calendar. These documents are acceptable as evidence of age.

Combined benefits are subject to maximum payment amounts as follows: The most that can be paid to a person eligible for both CPP DSB benefit and the SVR pension is the maximum CPP DSB benefit (which is more than the maximum SVR pension); The most that can be paid to a person eligible for the RTR pension and the SVR pension is the maximum RTR pension (which is more than the maximum SVR pension); or The total amount of a combined RTR/SVR pension is adjusted based on the survivor's age (under 65 and 65 and over). When an individual is eligible for a combined RTR pension/SVR pension/PRDB, the greater of the2 flat rates (SVR or PRDB) is used in the calculation formula. A beneficiary cannot receive a full SVR pension and also receive a full RTR pension or DSB benefit.
To receive combined benefits, no additional documentary evidence is needed apart from that which is required for each individual benefit.

topic_title: Effective date of a combined benefit
text: The effective date of a combined benefit is the date the individual became eligible to start receiving the second benefit.

If an applicant meets the eligibility requirements for more than one benefit, they are eligible for and are required by CPP legislation to receive a combined benefit. CPP legislation states that a beneficiary must receive a combined benefit when they are eligible to receive a SVR pension and either: a CPP DSB benefit or a RTR pension; The PRDB is available and paid to disabled CPP RTR pension recipients who meet the PRDB eligibility requirements. A combined benefit can include either: a RTR and a SVR pension; a CPP DSB benefit and a SVR pension; or a RTR pension, a PRDB and a SVR pension. QPP Combined benefits may include a benefit paid under the QPP.

The CPP allows beneficiaries to receive the following combined benefits: Retirement (RTR) and Survivor (SVR); RTR and SVR, or RTR and Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB), whichever provides the greater flat rate; or SVR and CPP Disability (DSB) benefit. A combined benefit consists of 2 CPP benefits. One of the benefits could be paid under a provincial program (i.e. QPP).

The RTR pension provides a monthly benefit payment to eligible applicants. Eligible applicants can choose to receive: a full RTR pension at age 65; a reduced RTR pension if they begin receiving it as early as age 60; or an increased RTR pension if they defer receiving it until age 70. The Canada Pension Plan legislation contains drop-out and exclusion provisions to minimize any adverse effects that life events (unemployment, illness, attending school, caring for a child or other family member, etc.) may have on CPP benefit calculations. The exclusion provisions remove months of low or zero earnings from the applicant's contributory period and may increase the Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC). The Over Age 65 drop-out provision allows months of higher pensionable earnings, after reaching age 65, to replace months of low or zero pensionable earnings before reaching age 65, as long as this substitution does not reduce their contributory period below 120 months, minus any number of months of disability. Flexible retirement was introduced in January 1987 through Bill C-116, to allow contributors to take: a reduced RTR pension as early as age 60; and an increased benefit as late as age 70. At the same time, the Over Age 65 drop-out provision was modified to become a full drop-out, allowing individuals who defer their retirement pension after 65 to drop additional months of low earnings from their contributory period on a one-for-one basis. Exclusion provisions are applied to the contributory period, as applicable, in the following order: Disability Exclusion Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Over Age 65 Drop-Out Provision General Drop-Out Provision (Policy) Therefore, when an individual's contributory period ends after age 65, deduct the number of months accumulated in their contributory period after age 65 from the total number of months remaining in their entire contributory period. General Drop-Out Provision (Policy)

The CPP Retirement (RTR) pension provides a monthly pension to eligible applicants. Applicants can receive a CPP RTR pension: at age 65, paid in full; as early as age 60, with a reduction; and as late as age 70, with an increase. The amount of an RTR pension is decreased by 0.6% for each month the contributor starts receiving the pension before reaching age 65. Alternatively, the pension amount is increased by 0.7% for each month the contributor starts receiving the pension after reaching age 65. Title RTR Start Date Monthly % Increase Maximum % Increase at age 70 January 2013 0.70 42.0 January 2012 0.64 38.4 January 2011 0.57 34.2 1987 to 2010 0.50 30.0 All RTR pension calculations are based upon the Retirement For Benefit Calculation (RTR-FBC). The RTR-FBC is 25% of the contributor's Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings (AMPE). The AMPE is determined by escalating each year of the contributor’s Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) (the average of the last 5 years of Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE)) to current year value. This escalation of earnings is called the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE). The APE is divided by the remaining number of contributory months and is multiplied by 25%, resulting in the applicant's RTR-FBC. The CPP provides drop-out and exclusion provisions to allow for periods of unemployment, illness, attending school, caring for a child or other family member, for instance, to be excluded from the applicant's contributory period. These provisions exclude months of low or zero earnings from the applicant's contributory period and may increase the RTR-FBC. Drop-out and exclusion provisions are applied in the following order: Disability Exclusion Child Rearing Provision Over Age 65 Provisions General Drop-Out Provision The General Drop-Out Provision was introduced to allow for a defined percentage of months to be dropped from an applicant's contributory period when calculating their RTR pension's RTR-FBC. Over time, the percentage of periods that can be excluded has been amended. Effective January 2014, 17% of years with low or zero earnings may be excluded from a contributory period. A maximum of 96 months (8 years) may be excluded. Once all applicable drop-out provisions and exclusions are applied, the RTR-FBC is used in the calculation of the original CPP benefit and any subsequent CPP benefit when that subsequent CPP benefit starts the month after the original CPP benefit's cease date. Some benefit calculations will require a new RTR-FBC to be calculated and possibly a new General Drop-Out Provision rate to be used when there is at least one month between the original CPP benefit's cease date and the subsequent CPP benefit's start date. It is important to note that the drop-out provisions or exclusions will not be applied if the result is a disadvantage to the applicant.

topic_title: The applicant is living in Canada but is not considered a resident of Canada for specific reasons as outlined in the OAS Regulations
text: There are specific circumstances defined in the OAS Regulations where an applicant is physically present in Canada but is not considered resident in Canada during this period (e.g. an applicant who is not a citizen or permanent resident of Canada, but is living in Canada performing the duties as an official of a country other than Canada). For the complete list of these circumstances, Defining Residence (Policy) Any period where the applicant was living in Canada, whether ordinarily or not, for one of the circumstances listed, are not included as Canadian residence in the residence calculation. The applicant is considered present and not resident in Canada during this period.

topic_title: The applicant is living in or outside of Canada and making contributions to a country with which Canada has an International Social Security Agreement in force
text: An applicant will normally be considered a resident of Canada when they: ordinarily reside within Canada; or are living outside of Canada but are deemed to be a resident of Canada under a specified circumstance. However, it is possible that in either situation the applicant may have contributed to the social security program of a country with which Canada has an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) in force. With some exceptions, these periods are not considered as residence in Canada since ISSA s aim to prevent double coverage and entitlement to benefits. These periods are considered presence in Canada or an absence from Canada, depending on the applicant’s living situation. For more information, Defining Residence (Policy) If an applicant made contributions to a country with which Canada did not have an ISSA in force during such periods when they were residing or deemed to be residing in Canada, these periods can be considered as residence or deemed residence in Canada, depending on where the applicant was physically residing at the time. These same rules apply to the spouse or common-law partner and dependants who resided with the applicant during that period. However, the spouse, common-law partner or dependants are considered resident of Canada if, during that period, they: made contributions to the CPP ) or to the comprehensive pension plan of a province of Canada (e.g. QPP ); and did not make co ntributions to the social security scheme of the other country during the same time period. Effective Date: January 2019 to April 2023 To be eligible for PRDB , the contributor must: apply with a valid application (in writing or online); be in receipt of a CPP Early Retirement (ERTR) pension; be under age 65; meet the contributory requirements by having valid earnings and contributions in at least 4 of the last 6 years, or 3 of the last 6 years in the case of a contributor with 25 years or more of contributions, immediately prior to the date (year) of the CPPD application; and, have a severe and prolonged disability as defined in the CPP. Effective Date: May 2023 Eligibility for PRDB closely resembles DSB . Any disability application submitted by an individual in receipt of an early retirement (ERTR) is considered an application for both DSB and PRDB . To be eligible for PRDB , the contributor must: apply with a valid application (in writing or online); be in receipt of an ERTR; be under age 65; have valid contributions in at least 4 of the last 6 years, or 3 of the last 6 years in the case of a contributor with 25 years or more of valid contributions; have a severe and prolonged disability as defined in the CPP; have a Latest Possible Date of Onset of May 2023 or later; and either, have a disability date of onset (DOO) that is determined to be on or after the effective date of their ERTR; or have a disability DOO that is determined to be before the effective date of their ERTR pension, but because they applied for DSB more than 15 months after the effective date of their ERTR pension, they are not eligible for DSB . Eligibility for PRDB ends: when the beneficiary ceases to be disabled; when the beneficiary reaches 65 years of age; or the month in which the beneficiary dies.

The CPP received Royal Assent on May 3, 1965, requiring contributions on earnings from working Canadians as of January 1, 1966, or the month following the contributor's 18th birthday, whichever occurred later. The first pensions were paid January 1, 1967. The CPP was introduced in order to give some degree of protection to Canadian workers and their families against the loss of income due to retirement, disability or death. The CPP operates throughout Canada, except in Quebec where Retraite Quebec provides similar benefits through the QPP. The CPP and QPP work together to ensure that all contributors are protected, no matter where they live. Table 1. Significant changes have occurred since the enactment of the CPP Year Change 1974 The Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) amount increased for the first time. The YMPE specifies the earnings amount that can be used in calculating pension contributions for each year. Full annual cost-of-living indexation was introduced, allowing for benefits to be adjusted in January of each year to reflect increases in the cost of living as measured by the Consumer Price Index. The common-law surviving spouse of a deceased contributor was described as "the person who resided with the deceased contributor for a minimum of 3 years immediately prior to death where there was a bar to marriage, and for one year where there was no bar, and, was publicly represented by the contributor as the contributor's spouse". 1975 CPP pensions and benefits became available to male and female contributors as well as to their surviving spouses and dependent children. The retirement and employment earnings test for CPP Retirement pensions at age 65 was eliminated (a contributor can, upon application, receive his retirement pension the month following his or her 65th birthday, but can no longer contribute to the CPP). 1977 The CPP was included in some international and social security agreements. 1978 Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) (now known as Credit Split) was introduced, allowing a couple, in the event of divorce, to equally divide their CPP pension credits earned during the time they lived together. The Child Rearing Dropout Provision, (now known as the Child Rearing Provision) was introduced to ensure that contributors who reduced their participation in the workforce to look after children under the age of 7 are not penalized with lower CPP benefits. 1987 Flexible Retirement pensions became payable at age 60 if the beneficiary had wholly or substantially ceased work. The Pension Sharing provision, sometimes referred to as Assignment, was introduced to enable spouses in a continuing marriage or partners in a common-law relationship to apply to share their retirement pension or pensions. The Division of Unadjusted Pension Credits Provision expanded to cover the separation of married or common-law spouses. The CPP Disability benefit maximum entitlement increased. CPP Children's Benefit beneficiaries became eligible to receive a maximum of two full benefits. Beneficiaries of a CPP SVR pension were allowed to continue to receive their pension upon remarriage. Before January 1987, the common-law surviving spouse of a deceased contributor was described as: "the person who resided with the deceased contributor for a minimum of 3 years immediately prior to death where there was a bar to marriage, and for one year where there was no bar, and, was publicly represented by the contributor as the contributor's spouse". Effective January 1987, the definition of "spouse" was changed to: a person of the opposite sex who is cohabiting with the contributor in a conjugal relationship at the relevant time, having so cohabited with the contributor for a continuous period of at least one year; and if there is no person described in a., a person who is married to the contributor at the relevant time. 1991 The Credit Split provision was expanded to assist individuals who were denied CPP credit splitting because of a spousal agreement entered into before June 4, 1986. 1992 Provisions were enacted for individuals who were denied disability benefits due to late application. A 25-year schedule for employer-employee contribution rates was established. Children's benefits increased. 1998 Contribution rates increased to ensure 25% of a worker's average lifetime earnings was maintained. Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) frozen at $3,500.00. Death benefit frozen at a maximum of $2,500.00. Proration of Earnings (before 1998 and effective 1998). 2000 All CPP benefits and rights were extended to same-sex common-law relationships. 2009 Actuarial Adjustment Factor Post-65 adjusted. Actuarial Adjustment Factor Pre-65 adjusted. Work Cessation Test eliminated. General Drop-Out provision increased. PRB established. 2010 CPP legislation allowed the Minister to impose administrative penalties in cases of knowingly made misrepresentation. 2011 CPP legislation allowed the Minister to charge interest on the overpayment and penalty amount in cases of knowingly made misrepresentation. 2012 CPP and QPP retirement pension beneficiaries aged 60 to 65 who work in Canada (outside of Quebec) must make mandatory CPP contributions on pensionable self-employment or employment income. 2013 The SST was established. 2014 Jobs, Growth and Long-term Prosperity Act , 2014. Legislative changes brought about by the Jobs, Growth and Long-term Prosperity Act received Royal Assent on June 29, 2012, to amalgamate the privacy codes found in separate departmental acts, including those in the Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation) and the Department of Employment and Social Development Canada Act . Some CPP legislation sections were removed and amalgamated into the Department of Employment and Social Development Act . Some Canada Pension Plan Regulations were repealed so the 1-year expiration date on written consent forms is no longer legislated but continues to be the limit set by the Department's policy. 2016-2018 Triennial Review CPP Enhancement raises the ceiling on earnings covered was raised by 14% and will be phased in slowly between 2019 and 2025, resulting in a maximum annual CPP pension increase by about 50%. Benefits were enhanced to eventually cover 33% of average lifetime earnings, up from the original 25%. Addition of Child Rearing Drop-in for 5 years before the birth or adoption of a child. Addition of Disability Drop-in for 6 years before the applicant's disability. Elimination of the reduction factor for the Survivor pension beneficiaries under age 45. Flat rate death benefit of $2500 for all beneficiaries meeting the minimum qualifying period. Introduction of the Post-Retirement Disability Benefit for beneficiaries who become disabled before reaching age 65. 2022-2024 Triennial Review $2,500 top-up to the Death benefit, payable in cases where the deceased contributor was not paid an RTR pension or CPPD benefits, and no SVR pension is payable in respect of their contributions. A new child's benefit for the dependent children of disabled or deceased contributors aged 18 to 24 who attend school or university on a part-time basis corresponding to 50% of the benefit provided to full-time students. Extended eligibility for the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) in cases where a beneficiary was already receiving the benefit, but would have eventually lost eligibility due to the disabled contributor reaching the age 65 and would no longer be receiving a DSB or PRDB . A condition of ineligibility was added for the SVR pension where individuals who undertake a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings with their separated spouse are not entitled to a SVR pension upon the death of that spouse. Incapacity provision extended to the DCCB makes the CPP's incapacity provisions applicable to DCCB applications on behalf of a child, in cases where a disabled contributor with a child is determined to have been incapacitated, for the purpose of applying for a DSB or PRDB . Determination of payee for CPP child's benefits clarifies the determination of the payee for the DCCB and Surviving Child's Benefits to prioritize the disabled contributor or survivor. New terminology was introduced for decision-making responsibility and parenting time. 2025-2026 Regulatory Changes Streamlining of evidentiary requirements for benefit applications (staggered implementation 2025 and regulatory changes 2026): Using third-party data sources as validation for proof of death. The My child-rearing provision information page in MSCA outlines the requirements for using the online request for the Child Rearing Provision (CRP). After the applicant selects Request child-rearing provision , the Request my child-rearing provision screen opens. They will be asked a series of questions that require a Yes or No response. Based on the information provided by the applicant, they will either continue with the request or receive a message that instructs them to complete and mail the Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP-1640) form to the Department. If the child's SIN has been used for another client's CRP, it will result in an error. After the applicant enters their children's information, they must select the Certification checkbox to attest to the validity of their declaration.

Once registered, clients can access MSCA using one of the following sign in options: GCKey; Sign-in Partner; or Sign in with their province (Alberta and British Columbia only at this time). Clients that sign into MSCA using GCKey are prompted to opt in and register for multi-factor authentication. Multi-factor authentication is a security enhancement to the sign in process that helps confirm the identity of clients and prevent unauthorized access to MSCA. After enrolling for the multi-factor authentication service, clients must enter a security code sent to them via text or voice message each time they sign in with GCKey.

MSCA shows the client information already available to the Department. Applicants confirm this information is accurate and apply for benefits online via MSCA. An online application does not require a “wet signature”, but an electronic signature instead. After submitting an electronic application, an individual is given information about possible increased benefits or tax savings and can access the relevant forms for provisions and benefits, including the following: CPPD benefits CRP Pension Sharing provision Credit Splitting provision Voluntary tax deductions International agreements When an online application is submitted, the database automatically inserts a time-stamp, which is used as the date of receipt. The time-stamp protects the date of receipt of the application. Online applications are date and time-stamped in Atlantic Standard Time and must not be altered. Online applications submitted on the last day of a month are sometimes stamped the 1st day of the following month. The time-stamp depends on the date and time zone from which the client submits their online application. For example, if a client applies online in British Columbia on April 30 at 8:03 p.m., the Server in Moncton, NB stamps May 1st at 12:03 a.m. because of the time zone difference. In this case, the client would be eligible to receive their benefits effective June 1 instead of May 1. The confirmation page shows the timeline for when the applicant can expect to receive the Notice of Entitlement letter. For auto-adjudicated online applications, one of the following user IDs displays on the ITRDS Benefits and Benefits History screens: GOLVUPI; or GOLRTRA. The Data Capture Session screen displays Internet at Mode of Service .

This article provides information on Program Exception Process (PEP) for accounts that require processing outside the parameters of the ITRDS adjudication system.

Some scenarios prevent a CPP pension or benefit from being automatically adjudicated in ITRDS . This is due to insufficient client data merged from legacy systems or system limitations. Accounts that cannot be automatically adjudicated in ITRDS require adjudication using the PEP functionality. PEP users perform manual calculations such as the Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC) which is used by the system to calculate benefit entitlement. When this benefit information is entered in the PEP data capture block, the system bypasses the adjudication process. Currently, the PEP user profile is only accessible to staff in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. Accounts that have a benefit processed using the PEP functionality are referred to as PEP accounts. The PEP accounts are easily identified on the Client Profile screen by a PEP icon or by the message displayed in the Messages block. A new application can require PEP processing: when a decision is made to pay a benefit even if the client does not meet the legislative requirements (i.e. Minister's discretion); due to a Review Tribunal decision; where the applicant is an SVR pension class action member; for accounts with Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefits ( DCCB ) and Surviving Child's benefits with an effective date prior to 1975; for accounts identified by the Federal Courts; and for other reasons, such as situations that require PEP but do not fall into the above categories. For example: new legislation that is not yet coded in ITRDS but requires that the benefit be paid by a specific date; or system errors that impact the accuracy of the ITRDS adjudication system but the benefit can be processed using PEP and a calculated RTR -FBC. If the region processes an application for a benefit that requires the use of the PEP functionality for one of the reasons above, the system will deny the application and the file must be sent to the Program Exception Processing Unit for processing. For information on scenarios requiring PEP, refer to Special Handling Scenarios (PDF, 687 KB) Download link . Special Handling Scenarios When at least one benefit for a client is adjudicated using PEP, the client's account will have a PEP status. If you do not have the PEP user profile, you will not be able to data capture any benefits, pensions or provisions on that account. PEP users must process PEP accounts in the same manner as non-PEP accounts. However, additional information is captured in the PEP block on the Data Capture screen for each CPP pension and benefit (i.e. RTR pension, DSB , DTH benefit, SVR pension, Surviving Child's benefit and DCCB ). PEP functionality does not apply to the Child Rearing Provision or the Credit Splitting provision. Although there is a PEP block on the Pension Sharing (PNSH) provision Data Capture screen, it cannot be used as there is no override functionality that applies to PNSH. Once a benefit is adjudicated in ITRDS using the PEP block, the resulting pay pattern displayed on the current Benefits screen will indicate YES in the PEP indicator field. All PEP enquiries, maintenance work items or other work items for PEP accounts (i.e. dual accounts with PEP status) must be moved to the PEP location in PWS . Box 9430 St. John's NL A1A 2Y5 The following maintenance activities for PEP accounts are exceptions to the above and can be performed by regional processing staff: changes of address; adding or modifying contact information; and adding, modifying or deleting Federal Voluntary Tax Withholds. PEP functionality cannot always be used as a workaround. In some situations, benefit calculations may be incorrect and cannot be resolved using PEP. In these cases, the Super PEP functionality may be required to correct payment amounts and reduce the amount of manual priority payments issued. text: When a beneficiary self-reports a return to seasonal work, reaches allowable earnings and completes an observation month, they are case managed dependent upon if the substantially gainful occupation (SGO) amount is reached for the season. Canada Pension Plan Section 57(1.2)—Additional amount Section 60—Payment of Benefits: General Provisions

Eligibility requirements To establish eligibility for a Death ( DTH ) benefit, all of the following requirements must be met: Table 1. Eligibility requirements Description Application The applicant must submit an application for the DTH benefit; and The contributor must be deceased. Contributions The deceased contributor meets the contributory requirements. Effective January 1, 2025, the following eligibility requirements must be met for the DTH benefit top-up of $2,500: The contributor's death occured after January 1, 2025; The deceased contributor must not have received a DSB , PRDB , or an RTR pension and; No SVR pension is payable as a result of the contributor's death, with the exception of a Surviving Child's benefit. Minimum contributory requirements The minimum contributory requirements are met if the deceased contributor had unadjusted pensionable earnings in the lesser of: at least one third of the total number of years in their contributory period, subject to a minimum of 3 calendar years; or 10 years. To help contributors meet the minimum contributory requirements for a DTH benefit to be paid, the following can also be considered, where applicable: Credit Split Provision; Child Rearing Provision; Disability Exclusion; Social Security Agreements. A proration of the last year in the contributory period can also be performed when it is needed to meet the minimum contributory requirements.

CPP legislation prohibits any attempt to attach or assign a benefit payment. In that regard, the CPP program is under no obligation to pay a funeral home for expenses incurred. It is not unusual to receive an application for the DTH benefit from a funeral home. However, funeral homes do not meet the definition of an "institution" as understood by the CPP. An institution is generally considered an organization whose purpose is to further public objectives (e.g. social assistance, education and culture). In this context, funeral homes do not meet this definition. Payment of the DTH benefit to a funeral home is considered an "assignment" of benefits; the Minister has no authority to pay a funeral home for expenses incurred if the funeral home operator has been unsuccessful in obtaining payment for services rendered on behalf of a third party with whom it had a contract or agreement. Even if the funeral home ultimately provided the service and absorbed the costs, the fact remains that someone made the funeral arrangements and is responsible for the payment of those expenses. Therefore, non-payment of the funeral expenses is a private matter between the parties involved.

topic_title: Assignment of the benefit is not permitted
text: Eligible Death ( DTH ) benefit recipients cannot waive their right to the benefit in favour of another individual. Doing so contravenes CPP legislation. The 60-day waiting period must be applied in either of the following circumstances: an eligible DTH benefit recipient communicates in writing that they do not intend to apply for the benefit; or a request from an applicant to withdraw their DTH benefit application is approved. The Minister determines who the next eligible payee is, if any, in accordance with the hierarchy of payee.

topic_title: Contesting applications and double payments Updated
text: If payment of the CPP Death ( DTH ) benefit is made in accordance with the hierarchy of payee, the Minister is not legally obligated to make payment to any subsequent applicant (i.e. no double payments). Only one DTH benefit can be paid per contributor. If 2 or more parties have applied for the DTH benefit (i.e. there are contesting applications), care must be used in determining the appropriate payee or payees. DTH benefit applications from 2 or more different applicants can be received in the same period before the benefit is paid. A subsequent application can also be received from another applicant after payment has already been made to an earlier applicant. Generally, when there is no estate, the individual who paid for the funeral expenses or of having accepted responsibility for payment should be paid the DTH benefit on behalf of the estate. The amount paid cannot exceed the actual amount of the funeral expenses unless the applicant is the deceased contributor's survivor (or the surviving spouse or common-law partner) or their next of kin. If more than one applicant for the DTH benefit provides the amount of payment of the expenses normally associated with funeral costs, payment in each case is made proportionately, and cannot exceed the actual amount paid by each applicant. However, where one applicant is the survivor or surviving spouse, common-law partner or next of kin of the deceased contributor, any remaining amount of the DTH benefit is paid to that individual for the estate. There is no requirement to obtain a second application from that individual.
When the Death benefit is paid, an indemnity agreement is not used.
Canada Pension Plan Subsection 71—Death Benefit

A split payment of the Death ( DTH ) benefit can be considered under certain circumstances. Where there is no estate, one of the following organizations may submit a DTH benefit application: the Last Post Fund (Veterans Affairs Canada); a municipal, territorial or provincial ministry of social services; or a non-profit organization. In addition, as provincial or territorial succession laws can identify more than one appropriate next of kin (e.g. 2 siblings), the DTH benefit can be split between 2 or more payees. A split payment requires proof of funeral expenses when both applicants are applying as the person responsible for the funeral expenses.

topic_title: Applying from outside of Canada Updated
text: Departure date from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date Updated When the applicant's departure date from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date of the GIS, and all eligibility requirements are met, the application can be approved . The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period, after which the benefit is suspended. Departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date When the applicant's departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date of the GIS, the application must be denied.

topic_title: GIS application form and the statement of income
text: Initial application An application for the GIS must be made on a form prescribed by the Department, unless it has been waived or deemed, and the Department must receive the applicant's statement of income, which is a component of the GIS application. This statement of income can be waived if the income information is obtained via the CRA income feed. In addition, the statement of income can be considered as an application for the GIS for the individual's spouse or common-law partner if: their income information is complete on the statement of income for the GIS/ ALW or ALWS form; it includes their signature; and they are eligible for the OAS pension. If the income information provided by the applicant or the CRA does not coincide with the relevant payment period (e.g. 2019 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period), the application can still be approved as the receipt of income information fulfills the legislative requirement to provide a statement of income. However, the entitlement to the GIS cannot be determined until the income information for the applicable payment period is received (e.g. when the 2020 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period). A GIS application can also be considered for the applicant's spouse or common-law partner and a separate GIS application is not required if: the applicant submits a combined OAS pension and GIS application or a GIS application and the following sections are completed: Information about your spouse or common-law partner; and Declaration and signature for the spouse or common-law partner. their spouse or common-law partner is eligible to receive the OAS pension at the time their application is received. The application can be considered for the applicant's spouse or common-law partner even if the applicant does not want to receive the GIS, is not eligible to receive the GIS, chooses to withdraw their OAS pension application, or chooses to cease or cancel their OAS pension or GIS.
