topic_title: Legislative requirements to approve a new business application for the GIS Updated
text: Eligibility Requirements To approve a GIS application, all of the following eligibility requirements must be met: An application must be made, waived or deemed and it must include: a statement of income for the applicant received as part of the application or through the CRA income feed by one-way or two-way transmission; confirmation of the applicant's marital status. If the applicant has a spouse or common-law partner, we require their name and address. It must also be indicated if the spouse or common-law partner is an OAS pensioner. This requirement can be met by using data that the Department holds under the CPP and OAS programs; and the applicant's signature. The applicant must be eligible for the OAS pension. Entitlement requirements To determine entitlement, the following are required: A statement of income for the applicant's spouse or common-law partner. The spouse or common-law partner's signature. The spouse or common-law partner must: sign the applicant's initial application for the GIS; sign the statement of income form; sign the Spousal Consent and Declaration (ISS-0954) letter; or sign a separate written statement that includes their personal information and their income. A signature confirms they are the spouse or common-law partner of the applicant and that the information provided is valid. It also provides their consent for the Department to request their statement of income from the CRA , if required. Under the Old Age Security Act , the spouse or common-law partner is responsible for providing their statement of income and signature. The spouse or common-law partner's statement of income may be received: as part of the pensioner's GIS application; as part of a statement of income form; on a separate written statement; or from the CRA income feed by one-way or two-way transmission. If the applicant or their spouse or common-law partner provides their signature on the application, but the income information field is blank, the Department can request their income information from the CRA . Each person's signature provides their consent for the Department to request their income from the CRA . If the CRA does not have their income as they did not file their taxes, the applicant or their spouse or common-law partner must provide their income information. The spousal consent and declaration may be waived under certain circumstances. If the information has been previously received and there are no discrepancies between the information provided on the GIS application, the previous application, information from the CRA or any documentation submitted, it does not need to be requested again. When the spouse or common-law partner is deceased If the applicant's spouse or common-law partner is deceased, a statement of income and signature on their behalf as part of the pensioner's GIS application, are required if: they were never a beneficiary of an income-tested benefit; or they have never signed an income-tested benefit application or co-signed a joint income-tested benefit application A legal representative can sign on behalf of the deceased. This confirms the information provided on behalf of the deceased and ensures that we have consent to obtain the income information from the CRA , if required. However, if the survivor or another individual can provide income information via the income tax returns and notice of assessments for the required years, these documents can be accepted without the need to obtain the signature from the legal representative on the GIS application or statement of income. The income tax return would have been signed by the deceased or by an authorized representative, and the notice of assessment would show that the CRA accepted them. The applicant is eligible but not entitled for the GIS and the application is approved If an individual applies for the GIS and meets the legislative eligibility requirements for the GIS, but their spouse or common-law partner does not provide their statement of income or signature, the application can be approved, but the entitlement cannot be determined until the spouse or common-law partner provides their statement of income and signature. The GIS application can be approved with no entitlement if the individual meets the eligibility requirements for the GIS, but they are not entitled if: they are under a sponsorship agreement; they are incarcerated; or their income is in excess. Exception: If the individual's spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated, the application can be approved and entitlement paid if the applicant meets the eligibility requirements. The applicant is not eligible for the GIS and the application is denied If the applicant does not meet the required eligibility requirements, the application must be denied and the individual must be informed of their reconsideration rights.

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated GIS benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After 9 years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full GIS benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

As of January 1, 2019, the CPP enhancement was implemented. Individuals who make contributions to the enhanced CPP will receive higher CPP benefits. Enhancement of the Canada Pension Plan (Policy) CPP contributions consist of a base component and enhanced components. The base component (since 1966) is calculated on earnings between the year's minimum and maximum amounts of pensionable earnings. The current base contribution rate on these earnings is 9.9% (4.95% from the employer and 4.95% from the employee). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts. The enhanced components, referred to as first additional (since January 2019) and second additional (since January 2024), provide a top-up to the base component. The first additional component is calculated on the same range of earnings as the base and has a total contribution rate of 2% (1% from the employer and 1% from the employee). This additional rate was introduced gradually between 2019 and 2023. The base contribution rate of 9.9% gradually increased to include the first additional component as follows: Table 2. This higher limit is called the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE). Contributions to the second additional component are made on earnings between the YMPE ($71,300 in 2025) and the YAMPE ($81,200 in 2025). This range of earnings has a new set of contributions with a rate of 8% (4% from the employer and 4% from the employee). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts. When calculating the contributor's base Number of Contributory Months, the months when an individual is deemed disabled for the purpose of the CPP DSB or the QPP disability benefit are excluded from the calculation. This period is removed at the beginning of the base Number of Contributory Months calculation. Effective January 1, 1987, the contributory period of a disabled contributor ends the month the contributor is deemed disabled, otherwise known as the month of the Date of Onset (DOO). The disability exclusion starts the month following the DOO. Before January 1, 1987, the contributory period of a disabled contributor ended either the 3rd month after the month the contributor was deemed disabled, or the month before the month the CPP DSB payments began. The DSB exclusion began the month the CPP DSB benefit became payable. For more information, refer to the information on contributory period provisions in the CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

Effective January 2019, the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) and Disability Drop-In (DDI) provisions were introduced to protect the value of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings (e.g. due to child rearing or disability). The drop-in provisions only apply to a contributor's first additional earnings (as of January 2019) and second additional earnings (as of January 2024). These drop-in provisions are used to calculate the enhanced components of a CPP pension or benefit. For more information on CPP enhancement, go to the CPP enhancement section below. If the contributor's earnings are higher than the drop-in value, the drop-in provision will not be applied. In the calculation for the first and second additional contributory periods under the CPP enhancement, the number of contributory months is fixed at 480 months (40 years). The Department will use the best 480 months in the calculation of the enhanced components. Given that 480 months is always the number of months used, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months. For CPP base calculations, the disability exclusion and the drop-out provisions remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the average monthly pensionable earnings. In May 2023, system functionalities were introduced to "drop in" credits into the calculation of the first additional component of CPP benefits for periods of the CRDI and the DDI. In August 2025, system functionalities were introduced to "drop in" credits into the calculation of the second additional component of CPP benefits for periods of the CRDI and the DDI. Child Rearing Provision—CRDI (applicable to first additional and second additional components of the contributory period only) For contributors with low or no earnings due to raising children under the age of 7 for a period that includes 2019 or later, drop-in earnings may be included in the calculation of the first additional and second additional components of CPP benefits. When applied, the CRDI drops earnings into periods of low or no earnings from the month after the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility of the child until the month of the child's 7th birthday. The amount dropped in is equal to the contributor's average earnings for the 5-year period immediately before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility of the child. The earnings are only dropped in when the amount is higher than the contributor's actual first additional or second additional earnings during that period. The dropped-in credits act as Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) in the first additional or second additional contributory period when calculating the first or second additional component of a benefit. The CRDI does not help individuals meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) eligibility requirement for benefits as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced components. As CRDI credits are essentially first additional or second additional UPE, they are subject to credit splitting if a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed. Where a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed and the credit split changes the earnings amounts in any of the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child, any CRDI credits that were originally attributed within the period of cohabitation are not recalculated. The original CRDI credits are divided along with any other affected UPE. If a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed and the credit split changes any of the earnings amounts in the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child, and the CRDI period extends past the period of cohabitation, the CRDI credits for the post-cohabitation period are recalculated taking into account the newly divided earnings. If a credit split occurs prior to the CRDI calculation and any earnings from the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child were split, the credit split earnings are used in the CRDI calculation. For an example of a CRDI subject to the division of UPE, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) If the contributor does not have valid earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings for the drop-in, they do not receive the drop-in. If there are less than 5 years in the first additional or second additional contributory periods, the average is determined by the actual number of available months in the contributory period, down to a lower limit of 36 months (3 years). If there are less than 3 years in the first additional contributory period, the client is awarded 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e 1/12 of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each month outside of the contributory period, up to a maximum of 36 months for the CRDI. This is only applicable to the first additional contributory period, as second additional contributions are made on earnings between the YMPE and the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) amount. For CPP base calculations, the drop-out provisions remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings. For the enhanced components, the total number of months is always 480 months. Therefore, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months. For more information and calculation details on the CRDI, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) For additional examples of how to determine CRDI values, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) DDI (applicable to the first additional and second additional components of the contributory period only) For contributors with low or no earnings due to severe and prolonged disability, drop-in earnings may be added to the calculation of the first additional and second additional components of their RTR pension for the period they were deemed disabled if it is to the contributor's advantage. If a deceased contributor was receiving a DSB , the DDI can be applied to the enhanced components when calculating the SVR pension payable to the surviving spouse or common-law partner. The DDI does not help individuals meet the MQP eligibility requirements for benefits. DDI values are determined at the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) stage of calculating the enhanced component of a contributor's RTR pension, or the enhanced component of the SVR pension payable to a deceased contributor's surviving spouse or common-law partner. Because they are determined at the APE stage of the enhanced calculation, DDI values are not UPE and are not subject to credit splitting. The amount dropped into the contributor's first additional CPP contributory period equals 70% of their average first additional earnings compared to the YMPE made in the 6 years before the contributor became disabled. The amount dropped into the contributor's second additional contributory period is 70% of the average second additional pensionable earnings, made between the YMPE and the YAMPE. If a contributor does not have valid earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings amount for the drop-in, they will not receive the drop-in. If there are less than 6 years in the first or second additional periods, the drop-in rate is calculated using the actual number of available months in the contributory period; if the number of months is 0, there will be no drop-in amount. If the DSB beneficiary returns to work for a period of less than 6 years before qualifying for and receiving a second DSB , the higher DDI rate between the previous period of disability and the second period of disability is calculated. This will be applied to the second disability period in the beneficiary's contributory period. For more information on the DDI provision and for examples of its calculation, refer to Disability Drop-In (Knowledge) . For information on the formula and calculation details of the DDI, refer to Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) and to Disability Drop-In (Knowledge) Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool)

The drop-out provisions only apply to an individual's base contributory period and are not applicable to the first additional and second additional contributory periods. The drop-out provisions allow for months of low or no earnings to be removed from the total number of contributory months in an individual's base contributory period. Drop-out provisions may: help applicants meet the Minimum Qualifying Period requirement; or result in a higher pension or benefit amount. The system may apply one or all of the drop-out provisions in the base calculation, depending on the total number of contributory months remaining in the individual's base contributory period. The drop-out provisions are applied in the following order, when applicable: Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) +65 Drop-out General Drop-out The CRDO and the +65 drop-out provision will only be applied in the calculation if the total number of contributory months in an individual's base contributory period exceeds the basic number of contributory months required for the pension or benefit. The basic number of contributory months for: an RTR pension is 120 months; a DSB is 48 months; and a Death ( DTH ) benefit and an SVR pension is 36 months. Once applied, the CRDO and the +65 drop-out provision cannot reduce an individual's total number of contributory months to less than the basic number of contributory months. The general drop-out provision will only be applied if the total number of contributory months in an individual's contributory period exceeds 120. Once applied, the general drop-out provision cannot reduce the total number of contributory months to less than 120. Updated CRDO (applicable to the base contributory period only) The CRDO is applicable to qualifying contributors who had children born after December 31, 1958. It is only applied if it is to the advantage of the client. The CRDO may drop-out months with no or low earnings from the base contributory period, for the period beginning the month following the month of the birth of the child and ending with the month of the child's 7th birthday. For eligibility requirements, refer to Child Rearing Provision (Policy) . For guidance on determining the start and end dates of the Child Rearing Provision period, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) If, after applying this drop-out, the total number of months in the base contributory period exceeds the basic number of contributory months, the system will continue to the next drop-out provision. +65 Drop-out (applicable to the base contributory period only) Sometimes a person continues to work and contribute to the CPP beyond the age of 65. If a person contributes less after the age of 65, this provision allows the department to drop-out those years with no or low earnings. The system can only drop out the number of months over the age of 65 (e.g. if the client contributed to age 70, the system can drop out a maximum of 5 years, or 60 months, from the base contributory period). If a person's contributions after the age of 65 are higher than those made in some years before the age of 65, this provision allows the substitution of months with low pensionable earnings for months with higher pensionable earnings. This way the contributor can still take advantage of the +65 Drop-out provision even when some earnings after age 65 are high. If, after applying this drop-out, the total number of months in the base contributory period exceeds 120, the system will continue to the General Drop-out provision. For more information, refer to Over Age 65 Provision (Policy) (English article not available). KA-03418 The General Drop-out (applicable to the base contributory period only) This drop-out can be used to drop 17% of the contributor's total number of months after the disability exclusion and all other drop-out provisions have been applied. However, the remaining months cannot drop below 120. For more information, General Drop-Out Provision (Policy) The +65 Age Qualification provision effective January 1, 1992 (applicable to the base contributory period only, in certain cases) In rare cases, loss of eligibility for benefits (e.g. DTH , Survivor, Surviving Child's) which require at least 1/3 of the total number of years in their base contributory period, allows for exclusion of years after the contributor turns 65 where earnings are below the Year's Basic Exemption.

The MQP factor for year of DOO is equal to: 5 when the contributor's DOO is before 1998; 4 when the contributor's DOO is 1998 or later; or 3 when the contributor meets eligibility for DSB using 25 years of valid contributions with 3 in the last 6 years. Once you divide the contributor's total years of valid CPP contributions by the MQP factor for the year of the DOO, round the ratio to 5 decimal places (..R5d). The ratio cannot exceed 1.00000. If it does,1.00000 is used. Multiply the ratio by the full DSB flat-rate amount to find the prorated amount. Round the result to 2 decimal places (..R2d).

Use this formula when the disabled contributor's eligibility to DSB was established using an ISSA from: Portugal, Jamaica and Belgium; the United States if the DOO is prior to October 1, 1997; Greece if the DOO is prior to December 1, 1997; Italy if the DOO is prior to October 1, 2017; and France if the DOO is prior to August 1, 2017. Add only the minimum number of foreign years needed to meet the MQP to the total number of years the applicant has made valid contributions to CPP. Refer to the contributor's DOO to determine the minimum number of foreign years needed to meet the MQP. If the DOO is on or after January 1, 1998, the contribution must meet one of the following conditions: The contributor must have 4 years of valid contributions in the last 6 years. In this case, use 4 as the minimum number of foreign years needed to meet the MQP. The contributor must have 25 years of valid contributions, with 3 years of valid contributions within the last 6 years. In this case, use 3 as the minimum number of foreign years needed to meet the MQP. If the DOO is before January 1, 1998, the contributor must have 2 years of valid contributions within the last 3 years, or 5 years of valid contributions within the last 10 years. If the contributor: meets both of these conditions, use 2 as the minimum number of years needed to meet the MQP; or only meets the condition of 5 valid contributions within the last 10 years, use 5 as the minimum number of years needed to meet the MQP. Once you divide the total number of valid CPP contributions by the sum of the total number of years of valid CPP contributions and number of foreign years needed to meet the MQP, round the resulting ratio to 5 decimal places (..R5d). Multiply the ratio by the full DSB flat-rate amount to find the prorated DSB flat-rate amount. Round the result to 2 decimal places (..R2d).

topic_title: Earnings related portion and flat rate of CPP benefits or pensions
text: The earnings related portion is the calculation of the individual's contributions to the CPP, or to the CPP and QPP combined, based on their annual earnings and contributory period. An individual's contributory period is the years that person is eligible to contribute to CPP or to CPP and QPP combined. For more information on contributions and the contributory period, refer to CPP Contributions (Knowledge) or the CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Contributions (Knowledge) CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Some benefits or pensions may include a flat rate, which is a fixed amount. Both the earnings related and flat rate amounts increase every January if there's an increase in the cost of living, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. If the cost of living stays unchanged or if it goes down, the entitlement amounts will not increase or decrease. Since 1975, CPP benefits are adjusted every year in January by a factor based on the Pension Index. The Pension Index for a year is the average of the monthly Consumer Price Index figures for the 12-month period ending October 31 of the previous year. The adjustment factor for each January is not available until mid November of the preceding year because the Department must first receive the Consumer Price Index for October from Statistics Canada. For CPP purposes, the Pension Index for a year cannot be less than the previous year. In other words, benefits will never be adjusted downwards, even if the cost of living decreases. text: ISSAs for Greece, Italy and the United States were revised to calculate the proration of the DSB flat-rate amount using the DSB flat-rate proration formula 1. In cases where entitlement to the DSB existed for periods before the revised agreements came into force, entitlement was recalculated and became effective the date the revised agreement came into force. topic_title: How to calculate a combined benefit Updated
text: If a contributor is already receiving an RTR pension or a DSB and they apply for the SVR pension (or vice versa), the 2 benefits will be combined into a single monthly payment (combined benefit). You cannot receive 2 maximum benefit amounts. If a contributor is receiving an RTR pension, an SVR pension and a PRDB , the 3 benefits will be combined into a single monthly payment. The greater of the SVR pension flat-rate or the PRDB flat-rate is used in the calculation, while only the earnings-related portion is included for the pension or benefit with the lesser flat-rate amount. When calculating combined benefits, the following criteria impact the calculation procedure: the effective date of the combined benefit; the age of the applicant at the effective date of each individual benefit; and the benefit for which the applicant is making an application. As of January 1, 2019, CPP enhancement was implemented. With the enhancement to CPP combined benefit calculations will eventually have 3 separate components: combined benefits with an effective date on or after January 1, 2019, may include the base and first additional component ; as of January 1, 2024, they may also include the second additional component . As a result of CPP enhancement, there are 4 possible scenarios regarding the calculation of a combined benefit: No first additional and/or second additional earnings and contributions on either the RTR / DSB or SVR . The combined benefit is made up of only the base component. First additional and/or second additional earnings and contributions on the SVR pension only. First additional and/or second additional earnings and contributions on the RTR / DSB only. First additional and/or second additional earnings and contributions on both the RTR / DSB and the SVR pension. For more information and for procedures to calculate a combined pension for each scenario, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

topic_title: How to calculate a Retirement For Benefit Calculation, a 1st Retirement For Benefit Calculation and a 2nd Retirement For Benefit Calculation Updated
text: The Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC) is used to calculate all CPP benefits except children's benefits and the DTH benefit for contributors with a date of death on or after January 1, 2019. A contributor's base Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings (AMPE) is found by escalating each year of the contributor's base Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to current year value. Refer to Escalation Factors (Table 7) (PDF, 275 KB) Download link for yearly escalation factors and rates. The escalated base UPEs become base Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE). APEs are added together to get the base Total Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (TAPE) amount. Escalation Factors (Table 7) The appropriate drop-out and exclusion provisions are applied to drop out or exclude months from the base contributory period, in the following order: Disability exclusion Child Rearing Drop-Out Over Age 65 provisions General Drop-Out Provisions The remaining number of contributory months are known as the base Total Number of Contributory Months. The base RTR -FBC will continue to be calculated by: Multiplying the base UPE by the adjustment factor to bring them to current year values to find the base APE. Adding the base APE together to find the base TAPE. Applying appropriate exclusions and drop-out provisions to the base contributory period to find the Total Number of Contributory Months. Dividing the base TAPE by the Total Number of Contributory months to find the AMPE. Multiplying the base AMPE by 25%. Effective January 2019, contributions to the first additional component began, calculated on the same range of earnings as the base. Contributors who make contributions to the first additional component have a first additional RTR -FBC in addition to their base RTR -FBC. If the client has applied for the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) for a period that includes 2019 or later, they may be eligible to have the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) applied to the first additional contributory period. Any dropped-in amounts attributed to the first additional contributory period act as UPE. For more information on how the CRDI values are calculated, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) The first additional RTR -FBC is calculated by: Multiplying the first additional UPE (which could include any CRDI amounts attributed to the first additional component) by the adjustment factor to bring them to current year values to find the first APE. Calculating the Disability Drop-In (DDI) amount, if applicable. To calculate the DDI amount, refer to Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) and to Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool) . If the client was in pay for a CPP disability benefit that began in 2019 or later, a DDI value will be added into the first additional component if it is beneficial to the client. The greater of either the monthly DDI amount or the actual APE is applied to each month excluded due to disability for the year the amount is attributed and used in the benefit calculation. Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool) Adjusting the first APE by using the transitional factors in the table below. If DDI amounts are attributed for the years 2019-2023, the transitional factor must be applied to the first additional DDI value. Table 4. Transitional factors used for 2019-2023 Year Transitional factor 2019 15% 2020 30% 2021 50% 2022 75% 2023 and after 100% Adding all first APE together to determine the first TAPE amount. Dividing the first TAPE by 480 months to get the first base AMPE amount. Multiplying the first AMPE by 8.33% to get the first additional RTR -FBC amount. Effective January 2024, contributions to the second additional component are calculated on a range of pensionable earnings between the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings and the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings. Contributors who contribute to the second additional component have a second additional RTR -FBC, in addition to their base RTR -FBC and first additional RTR -FBC. If the client has applied for the CRP for a period that includes 2024 or later, they may be eligible to have the CRDI applied to the second additional contributory period. Any dropped in amounts attributed to the second additional contributory period act as UPE. For more information on how the CRDI values are calculated, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) The second additional RTR -FBC is calculated by: Multiplying the second additional UPE (which could include any CRDI amounts attributed to the second additional component) by the adjustment factor to bring it to current year values to find second APE. Calculating the DDI amount, if applicable. To calculate the DDI amount, refer to Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) and to Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool) . If the client was in pay for a CPP disability benefit that began in 2024 or later, a DDI value will be added into the second additional component if it is beneficial to the client. The greater of either the monthly DDI amount or the actual APE is applied to each month excluded due to disability for the year the amount is attributed and is used in the benefit calculation. Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool) Adding all second APE together to determine the second TAPE amount. Dividing the second TAPE by 480 months to get the second AMPE amount. Multiplying the second AMPE by 33.33% to get the second additional RTR -FBC amount.

topic_title: How to calculate Children's benefits Updated
text: Children's benefits are paid a flat rate amount. Refer to Maximum Monthly Amounts (PDF, 470 Kb) Download link . Maximum Monthly Amounts International Operations processors must use the proration formula to determine the prorated child's benefit flat-rate amount when an ISSA for any country (except France) is used to establish eligibility. Use the relevant flat-rate proration formula found in the How to calculate the Disability benefit section or the How to calculate the Survivor's pension section to replace the full value of the DSB or SVR pension flat-rate amount with the DCCB or Surviving child's benefit flat-rate amount.

Separated or divorced couples may divide their pension credits equally for the time they lived together. For more information on the eligibility requirements for credit splitting, Credit Split Application (Scenario) Range of division Determine the CPP period to divide. Periods excluded from credit splitting must be notated to ensure a division is not done for those periods. For divorced or legally separated individuals, the range of division begins with the latest of: January 1966; the month the youngest member of the couple reached age 18; or January of the year the marriage took place; unless cohabitation began before marriage, in which case the range begins in January of the year in which cohabitation started. The range of division ends with the earliest of: the month the eldest of the couple reaches age 70; the December prior to the year in which the couple last cohabited; or the December prior to the year in which the marriage/common-law union was terminated (for divorces or legal annulments between January 1, 1978 and December 31, 1986 only). For former common-law partners, the range of division begins with the latest of: January 1966; January of the year which cohabitation started; or the month the youngest member of the couple reached age 18. The range of division ends with the earliest of: the month the eldest of the couple reached age 70; December prior to the year the couple last cohabited; or December prior to the year the common-law union was terminated. Periods to be excluded from credit splitting are: any year where the combined base Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) does not exceed twice the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE); periods where one of the spouses receives a CPP or QPP RTR pension; periods where one of the spouses receive a Disability ( DSB ) benefit with CPP or QPP; or any months that spouses separated for over one year or more. As of January 1, 2019, the rules for a credit split of the first additional and second additional earnings follow the same rules as the base CPP or QPP, with 2 exceptions: the months for a beneficiary in receipt of CPP DSB are not excluded from credit splitting for the first additional earnings; and the YBE is not applicable for the second additional earnings. After determining the range of division and excluding periods, the base UPEs of both spouses or common-law partners are added together for the years in the base contributory period to be divided. The total base UPE for each eligible year is divided in half, and attributed to each spouse or common-law partner's base contributory period. The first additional UPEs of both spouses or common-law partners are added together for the years in the first additional contributory period to be divided. The total first additional UPE for each eligible year is divided in half, and attributed to each spouse or common-law partner's first additional period. As of January 1, 2024, the second additional UPEs of both spouses or common-law partners are added together for the years in the second additional contributory period to be divided. The total second additional UPE for each eligible year is divided in half, and attributed to each spouse or common-law partner's second additional period. The breakdown of division can be viewed in the Divided UPE screen in ITRDS , which will display the applicant's UPEs before and after the division, as well as the former spouse or common-law partner's UPEs before and after the division. The DSB , RTR pension and Survivor's pension are affected by a credit split.

Spouses or common-law partners may share a portion of each other's RTR pension based on the joint contributory period and their period of cohabitation. As of January 1, 2019, contributors who have made contributions to the enhanced CPP will be able to share their first additional RTR ; as of January 1, 2024, they will be able to share their second additional RTR . To calculate a pension sharing (PNSH), you must find the PNSH ratio for the spouses or common-law partners. Determine the base Joint Contributory Period To calculate the base PNSH, you must first calculate the number of months in the base joint contributory period. The base joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 1966; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The base joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. If only one spouse or common-law partner is a contributor, the base joint contributory period does not include those contributory months excluded due to disability or any month where the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) is applied. If both spouses or common-law partners are contributors, the base joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began and any months excluded from the base joint contributory period due to disability or the CRDO can only be excluded if they apply to both base contributory periods. Determine the base period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the base cohabitation period. Deduct any periods when they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If the spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 1966; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the base joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. As of January 1, 2019, determine the first additional joint contributory period when there is a first additional RTR pension to share The first additional joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 2019; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The first additional joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. The first additional joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began. Determine the first additional period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the first additional cohabitation period. Deduct any periods where they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 2019; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the first additional joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. As of January 1, 2024, determine the second additional joint contributory period when there is a second additional RTR pension to share The second additional joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 2024; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The second additional joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. The second additional joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began. Determine the second additional period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the second additional cohabitation period. Deduct any periods where they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 2024; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the first additional joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. Calculate the PNSH To calculate a PNSH, the formula is: If there is a first additional RTR pension to share, the following formula is used: If there is a second additional RTR pension to share, the following formula is used: To find the value of the PNSH amount to be shared to the individual's spouse or common-law partner, add: the base PNSH amount; plus the first additional PNSH amount; plus the second additional PNSH amount. The contributor's RTR monthly pension amount will be reduced by the amount shared to their spouse or common-law partner. To calculate a double PNSH, you must use the calculation above on each spouse or common-law partner to determine the RTR pension amount that each will share. For more information on PNSH, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

topic_title: How to calculate the Death benefit Updated
text: If the contributor meets the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP), the amount of the Death ( DTH ) benefit depends on when the contributor dies. If the contributor died: on or after January 1, 2019 , the DTH benefit payment amount is: a flat-rate amount of $2,500; or the actual cost of the funeral expenses. This can be up, to a maximum of $2,500 if the applicant is applying as the individual or institution responsible for the funeral expenses. on or after January 1, 2025 and the deceased contributor did not receive a CPP or a QPP RTR pension or a DSB and there is no SVR pension payable as a result of their death, the DTH benefit also includes a top- up amount of $2,500 in addition to the flat- rate amount. The DTH benefit amount is: a flat-rate amount of $2,500 plus the top- up amount of $2,500, for a total DTH benefit payment of $5,000; or the actual cost of the funeral expenses. This can be up to a maximum of $5,000 if the applicant is applying as the individual or institution responsible for the funeral expenses. International Operations processors must use the proration formula to determine the prorated DTH benefit amount when an ISSA for any country (except France) is used to establish eligibility. Once you divide the contributor's total number of years with valid CPP contributions by the number of years in the MQP. The ratio cannot exceed 1. If it does,1 is used. Multiply the ratio by the full DTH benefit flat-rate amount to find the prorated amount. Round the result to 2 decimal places (..R2d). If there is eligibility to the DTH benefit top-up amount, find the prorated top-up amount using the same formula. Substitute the full DTH benefit top-up amount in place of the full DTH benefit flat-rate amount. For more information on the ISSA between Canada and a country with which we hold an agreement, locate the country on the Foreign Benefits landing page under the International Social Security Agreements Countries tab. Foreign Benefits Historical DTH benefit calculations For deaths on or after January 1, 2019 until December 31, 2024 when the deceased contributor meets the MQP, the entitlement to the DTH benefit payment is: a flat-rate amount of $2,500; or the actual cost of the funeral expenses. This can be up to a maximum of $2,500 if the applicant is applying as the individual or institution responsible for the funeral expenses. For deaths on or after January 1, 1998 until December 31, 2018, when the deceased contributor meets the MQP, entitlement to the DTH benefit is the lesser of: 6 times the deceased contributor's monthly retirement pension at time of death—6 × Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC); the maximum DTH benefit amount of $2,500.00; or the actual cost of funeral expenses, to a maximum of $2,500 if applying as “ Responsible for Funeral Expenses”. For deaths before January 1, 2019, when eligibility to the DTH benefit is established using an ISSA, the amount is not prorated. In this example, the DTH benefit payable is $2,188.08. For deaths that occur before January 1, 1998, when the deceased contributor meets the MQP, the entitlement is the lesser of: 6 times the deceased contributor's monthly retirement pension at time of death (6 × RTR -FBC); 10% of the YMPE for the year the contributor died; or the actual cost of funeral expenses, to a maximum of $2,500 if applying as “Responsible for Funeral Expenses”. In this example, lesser amount of the DTH benefit payable is $2,188.08. For more information and for procedures to calculate a DTH benefit, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

topic_title: How to calculate the Disability benefit Updated
text: If a contributor is deemed disabled, the monthly DSB amount consists of the disability flat rate at their date of onset plus 75% of their Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC). Disability benefit when the contributor is deemed disabled after December 31, 2018, and before January 1, 2024 As of January 1, 2019, the CPP enhancement was implemented and the first additional component introduced. The value of the DSB is equal to: disability flat rate; plus 75% of base RTR -FBC; plus 75% of first additional RTR -FBC. Disability benefit when the contributor is deemed disabled after December 31, 2023 As of January 1, 2024, the second additional component of the CPP enhancement is implemented and the value of a DSB is equal to: disability flat rate; plus 75% of base RTR -FBC; plus 75% of first additional RTR -FBC; plus 75% of second additional RTR -FBC. The system calculates the disability flat rate component only once. The first additional RTR -FBC and second additional RTR -FBC used in the calculation of the DSB are based on calculation of the best 40 years (480-month denominator) and are not modified based on the date of onset of the contributor's disability. For additional guidance on manually calculating a DSB , refer to the CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide International Operations processors must refer to the following formulas to determine the prorated DSB flat-rate amount. Refer to the applicable formula based on the ISSA used to establish the disabled contributor's eligibility.

topic_title: How to calculate the Post-Retirement Benefit
text: The Post-Retirement Benefit ( PRB ) is calculated from Post-Retirement CPP contributions made in the previous year. To calculate the base PRB : Determine the client's base PRB Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) for the year prior to the PRB starting. UPE will be prorated if the client begins receiving an RTR pension or reaches the age of 70 in the year in which the PRB contributions are made. Divide those earnings by the same year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (MPE). Multiply this figure by a constant of 0.00625 (a constant derived from 1/40 × 25% - a base PRB is 1/40 of the base RTR payable pension, and the base RTR payable pension is 25% of the base Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings (AMPE)). Multiply the resulting figure from step 3 by the AMPE for the year the contributions were made. Multiply the number from step 4 by an adjustment factor. The amount of the adjustment depends upon how many months the client is below or above the age of 65 at the date the PRB begins. This is the same actuarial adjustment factor that would have determined the amount of the client's RTR pension if you had chosen to start it in that same month. Divide the resulting figure by 12 in order to determine the monthly benefit amount. CPP Enhancement and the PRB As of 2020, the value of the PRB will be equal to: the base PRB ; plus the first additional PRB . The first additional PRB will be calculated by means of a similar formula, namely, [(A × F / B) × C × D × E] divided by 12, where: A represents the first additional UPE for the year before the PRB comes into pay, with the following exception: For PRBs starting in 2020, the A amount is multiplied by 15%; For PRBs starting in 2021, the A amount is multiplied by 30%; For PRBs starting in 2022, the A amount is multiplied by 50%; For PRBs starting in 2023, the A amount is multiplied by 75%. B represents the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the year before the PRB comes into pay. C = 0.00208 (or 1/40th of 8.33%). D represents the average YMPE for the year in which the benefit becomes payable. The average YMPE is referred to as the Maximum Pensionable Earnings (MPE) average in the CPP Legislation and the CPP Calculation Guide. E represents the actuarial adjustment factor based on the age of the beneficiary as of January 1 of the year the first additional PRB becomes payable. F is G divided by H , rounded to 5 decimal places. ( F = G / H ) G represents the CPP first additional UPE as calculated using the B method of the ABC UPE calculation (excluding the basic exemption) rounded to 5 decimal places. H represents the CPP first additional UPE as calculated using the B method of the ABC UPE calculation (excluding the basic exemption), rounded to 5 decimal places plus the QPP first additional UPE as calculated using the B method of the ABC UPE calculation (excluding the basic exemption) rounded to 5 decimal places. (Earnings on which a contribution has been made to the first additional CPP plus earnings on which a contribution has been made to the QPP.) As of January 1, 2024, the value of the PRB will be equal to: the base PRB ; plus the first additional PRB ; plus the second additional PRB . The second additional component of the PRB will be calculated by means of the same formula as the first additional PRB , with " second additional " replacing " first additional " in all terms, and the A and C terms further modified as follows: A represents the second additional UPE for the year before the PRB comes into pay. C = 0.00833 (or 1/40th of 33.33%). For more information, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

topic_title: How to calculate the Post-Retirement Disability benefit
text: The Post-Retirement Disability Benefit ( PRDB ) is a flat-rate benefit that is equal to the Disability ( DSB ) benefit yearly flat rate. The contributor may receive a combined PRDB and RTR pension amount that is above the maximum RTR pension or DSB benefit amount. When a pensioner is eligible for both a combined Retirement and Survivor's pension and a PRDB , the greater of the survivor's flat rate or the PRDB flat rate is used in the formula. For more information, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

topic_title: How to calculate the RTR pension
text: To calculate an RTR pension: Determine the effective date using the RTR pension effective date calculation procedures. Refer to Effective Date—Retirement Pension (Policy) . Effective Date—Retirement Pension (Policy) Once the effective date is determined, proceed with calculating the contributor's base Retirement for Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC). The base RTR -FBC is 25% of the contributor's base Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings (AMPE). Once the base RTR -FBC is established, the procedure to calculate an RTR pension depends on the effective date of the RTR pension. Calculating an RTR pension with an effective date on or after January 1, 2011, and before January 1, 2019 Basic monthly amount at age 65 The basic monthly amount of an RTR pension payable the month after the contributor's 65th birthday is 25% of the contributor's AMPE. This is the contributor's base RTR -FBC. Flexible retirement provision—Actuarial factor adjustments for under 65 A contributor applying for RTR pension from age 60 to 65 receives a reduction depending on the age at which they choose to start their RTR pension. Effective January 2012, the actuarial factor used for calculating the RTR pension of applicants from age 60 to 65 changed. The monthly actuarial adjustment factor gradually increased from -0.5% to -0.6% over a five-year period, which will result in individuals receiving a slightly lower pension. The adjustment is permanent and the pension will remain reduced. CPP benefits are adjusted or escalated each year in January. As of January 2016, the monthly reduction is 0.6% per month. Therefore, the calculation is: 25% of the contributor's AMPE ($) × (0.6% × number of months until age 65) = $ (dollar amount) Benefit rate = $ (dollar amount) − RTR -FBC The table below shows the actuarial factor adjustments by year: Table 5. The value of the RTR pension is equal to the sum of the 3 RTR -FBCs, as follows: base RTR -FBC; plus first additional RTR -FBC; plus second additional RTR -FBC, all multiplied by the Actuarial Adjustment Factor. topic_title: How to calculate the Survivor's pension Updated
text: Earnings and contributions of the deceased contributor determine the Survivor's ( SVR ) pension rate. When the deceased contributor meets the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP), the entitlement is calculated based on the age of the surviving spouse at the time of the contributor's death. Where the survivor is under age 65, the SVR pension equals: 37.5% of the deceased's base Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC); plus survivor flat rate (based on the year of deceased contributor's death) pension portion. If the survivor has reached age 65, the SVR pension equals 60% of the RTR -FBC of the deceased contributor, escalated to the year the pension becomes effective. This calculation does not include a flat rate SVR pension portion. For more information, refer to Survivor's Pension—Entitlement and to Survivor's Pension—Entitlement SVR Pension Application (Scenario) Calculating an SVR pension with an effective date on or after January 1, 2019: When the contributor's date of death is on or after January 1, 2019 and before January 1, 2024, the value of the SVR 's pension for a recipient under the age of 65 will be equal to: SVR pension flat-rate; plus 37.5% of deceased's base RTR -FBC; plus 37.5% of the deceased's first additional RTR -FBC. The value of the SVR 's pension for a recipient aged 65 or older will be equal to: 60% of deceased's base RTR -FBC; plus 60% of the deceased's first additional RTR -FBC. When the contributor's date of death is on or after January 1, 2024, the value of the SVR 's pension for a recipient under the age of 65 will be equal to: SVR pension flat-rate; plus 37.5% of deceased's base RTR -FBC; plus 37.5% of first additional RTR -FBC; plus 37.5% of second additional RTR -FBC. The value of the SVR pension for a recipient aged 65 or older will be equal to: 60% of deceased's base RTR -FBC; plus 60% of first additional RTR -FBC; plus 60% of second additional RTR -FBC. For more information and for procedures to calculate an SVR pension, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide International Operations processors must use the proration formula to determine the prorated SVR pension flat-rate amount when an ISSA for any country (except France) is used to establish eligibility. Once you divide the contributor's total number of years the deceased contributor made valid CPP contributions by the number of years the deceased contributor's MQP. The ratio cannot exceed 1. If it does,1 is used. Multiply the ratio by the full SVR pension flat-rate amount to find the prorated amount. Round the result to 2 decimal places (..R2d). A survivor who, at the time of the contributor's death, was between the ages of 35 and 45, had no dependent children, and was not disabled, received the survivor flat rate + 37.5% of the RTR -FBC of the deceased contributor, reduced by a factor of 1/120th for each month the survivor was under age 45. A survivor who, at the time of the contributor's death, had not yet reached age 35, had no dependent children, and was not disabled, was not entitled to any amount of a survivor's pension until they reached age 65, unless they became disabled.

To meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for a CPP pension or benefit, the contributor must have valid base contributions for a certain number of years in their base contributory period. A valid base contribution appears as a base Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings amount in the contributor's Record of Earnings. The number of years required to meet the minimum contributory requirement is dependent on the CPP pension or benefit. To be eligible for a CPP RTR pension, a contributor must have at least one valid base contribution. Eligibility Requirements–Retirement Pension To meet the MQP for a CPPD benefit, the disabled contributor must have made valid base contributions: in 4 of the last 6 years; for at least 25 years with at least 3 valid contributions made within the last 6 years; or for each year after the month of cessation of the individual's previous DSB or PRDB . The deceased contributor must have made valid base contributions in the lesser of: at least one third of the total number of years in their base contributory period with a minimum of three calendar years; or ten years. The purpose of this article is to provide an explanation of how to calculate CPP benefits and provisions.

When an individual dies, any of the following can apply for a one time, lump-sum payment: the estate's executor; the individual or agency responsible for paying funeral costs; the individual's survivor; or the deceased's next-of-kin. For a Death ( DTH ) benefit to be payable, the deceased individual must have made sufficient contributions to the CPP. Contributor died on January 1, 2025 or later New Effective January 1, 2025, for a death occurring on January 1, 2025 or later, the DTH benefit is made up of a flat-rate amount of $2,500 and a top-up amount of $2,500 for a maximum of $5,000 in cases where the contributor receives: a flat-rate amount of $2,500 when they meet the minimum qualifying period; and a top-up amount of $2,500 if they never received a DSB , PRDB or RTR pension and no SVR pension is payable as a result of the contributor's death (with the exception of a Surviving Child's Benefit). If eligibility for the DTH benefit is established by using an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA), the base flat-rate amount and the top-up amount will be prorated based on the actual number of CPP contributory years. Contributor died on January 1, 2019 or later For a death occurring on January 1, 2019 or later, the entitlement of the DTH benefit is a flat rate of $2,500 when the contributor meets the minimum qualifying period. If eligibility for the DTH benefit is established by using an ISSA, the flat-rate amount will be prorated based on the actual number of CPP contributory years. Contributor died after December 31, 1997 and before January 1, 2019 For a death occurring on January 1, 1998 or later, the CPP DTH benefit payable is equal to the lesser of: 6 times the calculated monthly RTR benefit amount of the deceased contributor at the time of death [6x(Retirement For Benefit Calculation)]; or $2,500, the maximum benefit payable. For contributors who died on December 31, 1997 or earlier, the DTH benefit amount is not subject to the $2,500 limitation, even though the benefit can be paid in 1998 or later. Contributor died on December 31, 1997 or earlier For a death occurring on December 31, 1997 or earlier, the DTH benefit payable is equal to the lesser of: 6 times the calculated monthly RTR benefit amount of the deceased contributor at the time of death [6x(Retirement For Benefit Calculation)]; or 10% of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings for the year in which the contributor died.

topic_title: ALW benefit application form and the statement of income
text: An application for the ALW benefit must be made on a form prescribed by the Department, and the Department must receive the applicant's statement of income information. The statement of income may be received: as part of the pensioner's GIS application; as part of the ALW applicant's statement of income form; on a separate written statement; or through the CRA income feed (e.g. one-way or two-way transmission). If the income information provided by the applicant or the CRA does not coincide with the relevant payment period (e.g. 2019 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period), the application can still be approved as the receipt of income information fulfills the legislative requirement to provide a statement of income. However, the entitlement to the ALW benefit cannot be determined until the income information for the applicable payment period is received (e.g. when the 2020 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period).

topic_title: Applying from outside of Canada Updated
text: Departure date from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date Updated When the applicant's departure from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date of the ALW benefit, the application can be approved if the applicant: has an aggregate period of 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18; or has an aggregate period of 10 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18, but has less than 20 years and was a resident of Canada on the day before the day the application is approved. The applicant can receive the payments for the remainder of the 6-month period, after which the benefit is suspended. The residence period can be met either through: Canadian residence alone; or aggregate residence obtained through an International Social Security Agreement that Canada has with another country. Departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date When the applicant's departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date of the ALW benefit, the application must be denied .

topic_title: Entitlement to the ALW benefit after the GIS pensioner departs Canada
text: In cases where the GIS pensioner is absent from Canada and their GIS is suspended in the 7th month after their departure from Canada, the ALW benefit is also suspended. Since the GIS pensioner is not entitled to receive the GIS, there is no entitlement to the ALW benefit.

topic_title: Legislative requirements to approve an ALW application Updated
text: Eligibility requirements To approve an ALW application, all of the following requirements must be met: an application must be received, and it must include: the applicant's signature; and confirmation of the applicant's eligibility based on their age, residence, legal status and marital status (e.g. married or in a common-law relationship with a GIS pensioner who is eligible for the GIS); and a statement of income from the applicant. Entitlement requirements To determine entitlement, the following are required: a statement of income from the applicant's spouse or common-law partner; and the spouse or common-law partner's signature. A signature confirms they are the spouse or common-law partner of the applicant and that the information provided is valid. It also provides their consent for the Department to request their statement of income from the CRA, if required. Under the Old Age Security Act , the spouse or common-law partner is responsible for providing their statement of income and signature. If the applicant or the spouse or common-law partner provides their signature on the application or statement of income form, but the income information field is blank, the Department can request their income information from the CRA. If the CRA does not have their income as they did not file their taxes, the applicant or the spouse or common-law partner must provide their income information. The applicant is eligible but not entitled for the ALW and the application is approved If an individual applies for the ALW benefit and meets the legislative eligibility requirements for the ALW , but their spouse or common-law partner does not provide their statement of income or signature, the application can be approved, but the entitlement cannot be determined until the spouse or common-law partner provides their statement of income and signature. The ALW benefit application can be approved with no entitlement if the individual meets the eligibility requirements for the ALW , but they are not entitled if: they are under a sponsorship agreement; they are incarcerated; the GIS pensioner is eligible for the GIS but not entitled as they are under a sponsorship agreement; or the GIS pensioner is eligible for the GIS but not entitled as the couple's combined income is in excess. Exceptions: There are exceptions where the ALW applicant can still meet the entitlement requirements for the ALW even though the pensioner is not entitled to the GIS. The exceptions include: when the pensioner is incarcerated; and when the pensioner is entitled to the GIS but chooses not to receive it. The applicant is not eligible for the ALW benefit and the application is denied If the applicant does not meet the required eligibility requirements, the application must be denied and the individual informed of their reconsideration rights.

topic_title: OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment and the ALW benefit application
text: For OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment and the ALW benefit application, consider the following: An individual selected for OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment may apply separately for the ALW benefit. Since there is no automatic enrolment for the ALW benefit, the individual must prove that they meet the eligibility criteria for the ALW benefit in the usual manner and with the relevant documentation. The selection criteria for the OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment process cannot be used to approve the ALW benefit before age 65. The eligibility criteria are not proven until the OAS pension and GIS application are waived and the applicant is approved for the OAS pension and GIS. The ALW benefit application cannot be held until the applicant's 65th birthday because there is no legislative authority to hold it. ALW benefit applications must be processed in a timely manner.

Eligibility requirements To be eligible for the ALW benefit, an individual must be a resident of Canada and meet all of the following eligibility requirements: Table 1. Eligibility requirements Eligibility requirements Description Application An initial application must be made on a prescribed form and a statement of income received. Age An applicant must be 60 to 64 years of age inclusive. Residence For payment in Canada, the minimum period of residence to qualify for the ALW benefit is 10 years of residence in Canada after reaching age 18, either through: Canadian residence alone; or aggregate residence obtained through an International Social Security Agreement that Canada has with another country. The minimum 10-year residence period must have occurred before the day on which the application is approved. Legal status An applicant must be lawfully in Canada on the day before their application is approved. Marital status An applicant must be the spouse or common-law partner of a pensioner who is eligible for the GIS.

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated ALW benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After nine years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full ALW benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

Everyone has an estate at the time of death, except when an individual has absolutely no real property (i.e. land and buildings, also referred to as real estate) or personal property (i.e. property other than land and buildings, also referred to as possessions and capital investments). In the administration of the estate of a deceased individual, an individual dies: with a will (i.e. testate); or without a will (i.e. intestate). When an individual dies without a will or there is no executor, an administrator can be appointed by a provincial court.

topic_title: Individual or institution paying for the funeral expenses
text: The DTH benefit payment can be made to the individual or institution who paid for or is responsible for paying the deceased contributor's funeral expenses if: there is no estate; or the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor. If the DTH benefit payment is being made to the individual or institution (e.g. Veterans Affairs Canada (Last Post Fund), a municipal or provincial ministry or agency of social services, a non-profit organization) who has paid for or is responsible for payment of the funeral expenses, the amount of the payment cannot exceed the actual amount of the funeral expenses. The individual or institution may be required to submit the receipt (i.e evidence of payment) and the invoice or contract (i.e. evidence of responsibility to pay). Proof of funeral expenses (e.g. funeral receipt or contract) are not required from the individual or institution who has paid or was responsible for the payment of the funeral expenses. The Minister reserves the right to request proof of funeral expenses at any time. The information regarding the amount of the funeral expenses or service provider may be obtained by a phone call if it is not submitted on the application. However, proof of funeral expenses must be submitted if there are multiple applications received or any discrepancies with the information provided.

Per the payment hierarchy, the DTH benefit can be made to the next of kin if: there is no estate; the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor; there is no other individual or institution who has paid or is responsible for the payment of the funeral expenses; there is a letter from the individual or institution who has paid or was responsible for the payment of the funeral expenses stating they will not apply; and there is no survivor. The following is the order of priority for next of kin common to the succession rules of each province and territory: child or children of the deceased parent of the deceased sibling of the deceased When clarification is required or the next of kin cannot be determined, submit an enquiry through the Business Expertise Request Tool for guidance.

topic_title: No funeral or more than one funeral
text: There is no requirement that funeral services be performed for the deceased contributor before a DTH benefit can be paid. For example, this may be the case if the deceased contributor had donated their body to an educational or research institution or if there has been a presumption of death following a disappearance.

topic_title: Paying an individual or institution other than an estate (date of death before January 1, 2019)
text: The DTH benefit payment can be made to another eligible applicant if: there is no estate; the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor; or the DTH benefit is less than $2,387 (the amount prescribed in the CPP regulations). Before paying the DTH benefit to someone other than an estate representative (e.g. executor, court-appointed administrator, public trustee), the Minister must make reasonable enquiries to ensure that the estate representative has sufficient time to apply (i.e. 60 days). If there is no estate or the benefit amount is below the amount prescribed in the legislation, the payment of the benefit can be made immediately to the appropriate applicant as per the hierarchy prescribed in the legislation.

Once the CPP Death (DTH) benefit eligibility criteria are met, the payee must be determined. When the payment of a DTH benefit has been approved, the benefit is payable to the estate of a deceased contributor except when indicated in the legislation. For the CPP DTH benefit, estate means that an estate representative has been appointed and has accepted the responsibility to administer the deceased contributor's assets and debts, including the distribution of any benefits, and is considered the first payee. The estate representative can be: an individual or agency (e.g. law firm) appointed by the deceased contributor in their last will and testament as their executor; an individual appointed by the court of the relevant provincial jurisdiction; or a provincial public trustee. The legislation allows for the payment of the DTH benefit (in whole or in part) to be made to an individual or agency other than the estate when: there is no estate; or the estate has not applied for the DTH benefit within the prescribed time of 60 days following the contributor's death. In the absence of a DTH benefit application by the deceased contributor's estate, the hierarchy for paying the DTH benefit is as follows: to an individual, agency or institution who has paid or is responsible for the payment of a deceased contributor's funeral expenses; in the absence of an individual or institution described in paragraph (a), to the survivor of the deceased contributor; or in the absence of an individual or institution referred to in paragraph (a) and a survivor referred to in paragraph (b), to the next of kin of the deceased contributor. For the DTH benefit, an institution is an organization who has taken responsibility for the funeral expenses of the deceased contributor (e.g. Last Post Fund, Community and Social Services).

topic_title: Survivor of the deceased contributor Updated
text: Upon application, the payment can be made to the survivor of the deceased contributor in the hierarchy if: there is no estate; the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor; and there is no other individual or institution who has paid or is responsible for the payment of the funeral expenses.

topic_title: ALWS benefit application form and the statement of income
text: An application for the ALWS benefit must be made on a form prescribed by the Department, unless this requirement has been waived, and the Department must receive the applicant's statement of income. The statement of income may be received: as part of the ALWS benefit applicant's statement of income form; on a separate written statement; or through the CRA income feed (i.e. one-way or two-way transmission when an ALWS benefit application has been submitted). If the income information provided by the applicant or the CRA does not coincide with the relevant payment period, e.g. 2019 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period, the application can still be approved as the receipt of income information fulfills the legislative requirement to provide a statement of income. However, the entitlement to the ALWS benefit cannot be determined until the income information for the applicable payment period is received, e.g. when the 2020 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period.

topic_title: Applying from outside of Canada Updated
text: Departure date from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date Updated When the applicant's departure from Canada is within 6 months of the effective date of the ALWS benefit, the application can be approved if the applicant: has an aggregate period of 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18; or has an aggregate period of 10 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18, but has less than 20 years and was a resident of Canada on the day before the day the application is approved. The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period, after which the benefit is suspended. The residence period can be met either through: Canadian residence alone; or aggregate residence obtained through an International Social Security Agreement that Canada has with another country. Departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date When the applicant's departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date of the ALWS benefit, the application must be denied .
