topic_title: Legislative requirements to approve an ALWS benefit application Updated
text: Eligibility requirements To approve an ALWS benefit application, all of the following requirements must be met: An application must be received or waived; and it must include: the applicant's signature; confirmation of the applicant's eligibility based on their age, residence, legal status and marital status (meet definition of common-law partner at the time of death of their partner or have been married without termination by divorce or annulment at the time of their spouse's death); and verification that the ALWS benefit applicant meets the definition of a survivor and has not remarried or entered into a common-law relationship since the death of their spouse or common-law partner; A statement of income from the applicant. If the applicant provides their signature on their application or statement of income form, but the income information field is blank, the Department can request their income information from the CRA. Their signature provides their consent for the Department to request their income from the CRA. If the CRA does not have their income as they did not file their taxes, the applicant must provide their income information. Entitlement requirements Once the applicable income information is provided by the applicant or the CRA for the applicable payment period, entitlement can be determined. The applicant is eligible but not entitled for the ALWS benefit and the application is approved The ALWS benefit application can be approved with no entitlement if the individual meets the eligibility requirements for the ALWS , but they are not entitled if: they are under a sponsorship agreement; they are incarcerated; or their income is in excess. The applicant is not eligible for the ALWS benefit and the application is denied If the applicant does not meet the required eligibility requirements, the application must be denied and the individual must be informed of their reconsideration rights.

topic_title: OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment and the ALWS benefit application
text: For OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment and the ALWS benefit application, consider the following: An individual selected for OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment may apply separately for the ALWS benefit. Since there is no automatic enrolment for the ALWS benefit, the individual must prove that they meet the eligibility criteria for the ALWS benefit in the usual manner and with the relevant documentation. The selection criteria for the OAS pension and GIS automatic enrolment process cannot be used to approve the ALWS benefit before age 65. The eligibility criteria cannot be applied until the OAS pension and GIS application are waived and the individual is approved for the OAS pension and GIS. An ALWS benefit application cannot be held until the applicant's 65th birthday because there is no legislative authority to hold it. ALWS benefit applications must be processed in a timely manner.

Eligibility requirements To be eligible for the ALWS benefit an individual must be a resident of Canada and meet all of the following eligibility requirements: Table 1. Eligibility requirements Eligibility requirements Description Application An application must be made or waived: the application must be submitted on a prescribed form and a statement of income received; or the application may be waived where the ALW benefit is converted to the ALWS benefit. The Old Age Security Act allows the requirement for an initial ALWS benefit application to be waived if the individual was eligible for the ALW benefit, even if there was no entitlement for the month in which the pensioner died. Age An applicant must be 60 to 64 years of age inclusive. Residence For payment in Canada, the minimum period of residence to qualify for an ALWS benefit is 10 years of residence in Canada after reaching age 18, either through: Canadian residence alone; or aggregate residence obtained through an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) that Canada has with another country. The 10-year residence period must have occurred before the day on which the application is approved. Legal Status An applicant must be lawfully in Canada on the day before their application is approved. Marital Status The applicant must: be a survivor (they must not have remarried or entered into a common-law relationship since the death of their spouse or common-law partner); and either meet the definition of common-law partner at the time of death of their partner or have been married without termination by divorce or annulment at the time of the spouse's death; and not be convicted of first or second degree murder or manslaughter of their spouse or common-law partner, whose death would otherwise have made them eligible to receive the ALWS benefit.

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated ALWS benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After nine years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full ALWS benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

topic_title: Contact when administering the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit
text: Do not initiate contact with the child or the individual or agency with custody and control of the child if: the disabled contributor has not provided their written consent; or the disabled contributor instructs the Department not to initiate contact. "Contact" includes sending the following forms: the Application for benefits for under age 18 children of a Disabled Contributor (ISP1152) form; the Application for a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit (ISP1400) form; and the Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) form. However, if an application is received from the child or the individual or agency with custody and control of the child, process the application and communicate the decision to the applicant in writing. In this case, do not communicate the decision to the disabled contributor, even if the disabled contributor did not provide consent or if they instructed the Department not to initiate contact.

Send a DCC - ORP +18, Info missing to establish eligibility (651) letter to the disabled contributor if: the contributor have not yet provided their consent to contact the individual or agency that has custody and control of the child; and the contributor have indicated that they: do not have custody and control of the under age 18 child; or have a child aged 18 to 25 or a child under age 18 who is managing their own affairs. Set a bring forward (BF) on the file to obtain the disabled contributor's consent to initiate contact. If you do not receive the required documents, Bring Forward (BF)
Canada Pension Plan Subsection 42(2)—When person deemed disabled

When an applicant applies for a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit, they can b e found to meet the severe criterion on the basis of a single medical condition. However, if a single medical condition is insufficient to make a determination of severe, the combined impact of all of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical conditions on their functional capacity is assessed to see if the severe criterion is met. Whenever the applicant or beneficiary has 2 or more medical conditions that, when considered individually, are not sufficient to meet the severe criterion, an assessment must be made regarding the combined effect of all of the relevant medical conditions on their work capacity. Each medical condition is not to be considered individually or in isolation when determining if the applicant or beneficiary meets the definition of severe and prolonged under the CPP. All medical conditions that are likely to affect an applicant or beneficiary’s employability (i.e. not just the main or dominant medical condition) must be considered. This includes taking into consideration all relevant physical and mental conditions identified on their file. When there is insufficient information on file to substantiate a condition, including a self-reported condition, the decision-maker should determine whether additional information is available. Other considerations When considering the combined effect of all reported medical conditions, consideration must also be given to the progressive nature of chronic conditions and the impact they have on an applicant or beneficiary’s overall functional capacity. The following factors need to be considered as all may contribute to higher stress levels: the impact on activities of daily living; the responses to medication (e.g. trials, dosage, and side effects); the impacts of various interventions and treatments; the increased complexity of self-care (e.g. eating, bathing); and the increased likelihood of having multiple medical appointments.

The National Search Unit within the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security Directorate of the Benefits Delivery Services Branch (BDSB) no longer conducts database searches of individuals whose location is unknown.

The National Search Unit was introduced in 1980 to conduct database searches for individuals whose location was unknown to third parties, such as: private pension providers; insurers; government agencies; friends or family members. Third parties submitted requests asking the National Search Unit to locate and contact an individual on their behalf, for a small fee. The increased accessibility of online information and the availability of private sector service providers have since made personal information more easily obtainable. As a result, Service Canada, acting on its mandate to find efficiencies and improve services, decommissioned the National Search Unit effective September 26, 2014. A letter to inform of the service changes was sent to all organizations that submitted a request after this date. If you receive enquiries related to the National Search Unit, submit them to the Operational Service Desk

topic_title: Child Rearing Drop-In calculation when there are less than 36 months in the first additional contributory period Updated
text: When there are fewer than 5 years (60 months) in the first additional contributory period, because the individual either had a child before the age of 23 or had a child before 2023, only the actual number of contributory months will be used to calculate the Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ). The minimum number of contributory months required is in the first additional contributory period 36 months. When fewer than 36 months exist in the first additional contributory period, the formula applicable to the first additional contributory period attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YMPE ) for each missing month up to 36 months. Example: A contributor had a child in June 2020 and was eligible to receive the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ) in July 2020. Table 2. Earnings from 2019-2020 Year Months Earnings YMPE 1st Additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings 2019 12 $36,296 $57,400 $36,296 2020 6 $19,289 $58,700 $19,289 Ratios are calculated by dividing the first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) by the YMPE for each of the 5 years (60 months) prior to the recipient's start date for a CCB . Each ratio is then multiplied by the number of months in the first additional contributory period for that year. As there are not 60 months in the contributor's first additional contributory period, the value of the contributor's CRDI for 2020 is calculated based on the actual number of contributory months. However, the minimum number of contributory months required is 36 months, and in this case, the contributor has a first additional contributory period of only 18 months (from January 2019 up to and including June 2020). Since there are fewer than 36 months in the contributor's first additional contributory period, 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE will be attributed for each missing month up to 36 months. This is represented by the value Q below. [[(M1 × A) + (M2 × B) + (M3 × C) + (M4 × D) + (M5 × E) + (M6 × F) + Q] / R = [[(0) + (0) + (0) + (0) + (12 × ($36,296 / $57,400)) + (6 × ($19,289 / $29,350) + Q))] / 36] × YMPE = [[(12 × 0.63233) + (6 × 0.65721) + Q] / 36] × YMPE Q is [36 - (M1 + M2 + M3 +M4 + M5 + M6)] × 0.4 In the case of this contributor, Q = [36 - (0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 12 + 6)] × 0.4 [36 - 18] × 0.4 = 7.2. Q is input into the equation to find the CRDI , t hen the average is calculated and multiplied by the YMPE for the year the drop-in is attributed. The YMPE for 2020 is $58,700. [[(7.58796) + (3.94326) + 7.2] / 36] × 58,700 = [[18.73122 / 36] × 58,700 = 0.52031 ( CRDI Factor) × 58,700 = a CRDI of $30,542 for 2020. Since this amount is greater than the contributor's actual 2020 earnings of $19,289, the drop-in amount will be attributed for 2020. It will cover the whole year despite the fact that the contributor had their child in June 2020.

topic_title: Child Rearing Drop-In calculation when there are less than 60 months in the first additional or second additional contributory period Updated
text: When there are fewer than 5 years (60 months) in the first additional contributory period, because the individual either had a child before the age of 23 or had a child before 2023, only the actual number of contributory months will be used to calculate the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) attributed to the first additional contributory period. The minimum number of contributory months required in the first additional contributory period is 36 months. Similarly, when there are fewer than 5 years (60 months) in the second additional contributory period because the individual either had a child before the age of 23 or had a child before 2028, only the actual number of contributory months will be used to calculate the CRDI for the second additional contributory period. The minimum number of contributory months required in the second additional contributory period is 36 months. Example: A contributor had a child in February 2022 and was eligible to receive the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ) in March 2022. Table 1. Earnings from 2019-2022 Year Months Earnings Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings 1st Additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings 2019 12 $52,124 $57,400 $52,124 2020 12 $54,225 $58,700 $54,225 2021 12 $56,235 $61,600 $56,235 2022 2 $4,753 $64,900 $4,753 Ratios are calculated by dividing the first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each of the 5 years (60 months) prior to the recipient's start date for a CCB . Each ratio is then multiplied by the number of months in the first additional contributory period for that year. As there are not 60 months in the contributor's first additional contributory period, the value of the contributor's CRDI for 2022 is calculated based on the actual number of contributory months. In this case, the contributor has a first additional contributory period of 38 months (from January 2019 up to and including February 2022). [[(M1 × A) + (M2 × B) + (M3 × C) + (M4 × D) + (M5 × E) + (M6 × F) + Q] / R = [[(0) + (0) + (12 × ($52,124 / $57,400)) + (12 × ($54,225 / $58,700)) + (12 × ($56,235 / $61,600)) + (2 × ($4,753 / $10,817) + Q))] / 38] × YMPE = [[(12 × 0.90808) + (12 × 0.92376) + (12 x 0.91291) + (2 × 0.43940) + 0] / 38] × YMPE Next, the average is calculated and multiplied by the YMPE for the year the drop-in is attributed. The YMPE for 2022 is $64,900. = [(10.89696 + 11.08512 + 10.95492 + 0.8788) + 0 / 38] × 64,900 = (33.8158 / 38) × 64,900 = 0.88989 ( CRDI Factor) × 64,900 = a CRDI of $57,754 for 2022. Since this amount is greater than the contributor's actual 2022 earnings of $4,753, the drop-in amount will be attributed for 2022. It will cover the whole year despite the fact that the contributor had their child in February 2022. There are no second additional UPE in this example because this period is prior to the second additional contributory period.

topic_title: Child Rearing Drop-In formulas for the first and second additional contributory periods Updated
text: Formula for the first additional contributory period Where: M1 to M6 represent the number of months in the first additional contributory period for each of the 5 years (60 months) before the contributor becomes a Family Allowance recipient. There is a special calculation for M1 and M6 . If, for example, a child is born or adopted in May, the value of M6 will be 5 months (January to May) and the value of M1 will be 7 months for a total of 12 months. A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YMPE ) for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. ( A to E = UPE ∕ YMPE ) F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods—if there was a previous child— F provides that a previous drop-in amount be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the first additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by a prorated YMPE amount. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. Q attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE for each missing contributory month, up to 36 months. R is the denominator used to calculate the average ratio of earnings to YMPE . The value of R will be between 36 and 60 and represents the number of contributory months in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. T represents the YMPE for the year to which the drop-in is attributed. The product of multiplying the average ratio by T is the value of the child-rearing drop-in (CRDI) for the year to which it is attributed. Formula for the second additional contributory period This formula is similar to that applied to the first additional contributory period. The only differences are: A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the additional UPE by the difference between the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YAMPE ) and YMPE , for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. YAMPE is the new pensionable earning ceiling introduced by the CPP enhancement. Its value is 114% of YMPE . ( A to E = UPE ∕ YAMPE − YMPE ). F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods (i.e. if there was a previous child) F allows a previous drop-in amount to be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the second additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by the difference between the prorated YAMPE and YMPE amounts. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. There is no Q in the second additional contributory period formula. 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE cannot be attributed to the second additional contributions, since contributions to that period are made on earnings between the YMPE and YAMPE . For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) When a contributor’s first additional and second additional contributory period ends within 7 years after the birth, adoption, or date on which the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child (e.g. the contributor starts to receive their CPP RTR pension, reaches age 70 or dies) the calculated amount of the CRDI must be prorated over 12 months, using the following formulas: First additional CRDI: First additional CRDI value = first additional CRDI factor × Prorated YMPE Second additional: Second additional CRDI value = Second additional CRDI factor × (Prorated YAMPE – Prorated YMPE)

topic_title: DSB additional component recalculation following the attribution of the Child Rearing Drop-In
text: A contributor had a child in 2026 who will turn 7 in 2033. This means that as long as the contributor keeps custody of the child, they are eligible for the Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ) from 2026 to 2033. The contributor becomes disabled in June of 2028 and qualifies for the DSB . A CRDI is attributed in 2028 and because it is an annual drop-in, the calculation of the DSB includes the drop-in. Even though the contributor became disabled in June 2028, the value of the drop-in is not prorated. The contributor gets the full-year benefit of the drop-in, unless it is a year that the contributory period starts or ends. In January 2029, the contributor's DSB is increased due to the standard indexation. It is not increased due to the CRDI at that time because the contributor has already received the drop-in's full value for 2028, and a DSB calculated in January of 2029 would not include any UPE for 2029. However, when the contributor's benefit is increased due to indexation in January 2030, there is also a UPE for 2029 which is not yet included in determining the amount of the DSB . This triggers a recalculation based on the date that the DSB was first put into pay (i.e. 2028). The recalculation proceeds as follows: The 2029 earnings are converted into Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) for 2028. A new benefit amount is determined. The new benefit amount is then indexed to 2030 amounts by applying the 2 Pension Indexes (2029 and 2030). However, this recalculation is not retroactive and reflects an increased amount payable in and after 2030. In January 2031, as was the case in 2030, the CRDI provides a UPE from the previous year (2030) that was not included in the DSB calculation. The benefit recalculation proceeds as follows: The benefit is recalculated again with the UPE converted to a 2028 APE (i.e. the year the disability started). The 2028 APE is used to determine the DSB amount. The DSB amount is indexed for each subsequent year to determine the amount payable in and after 2031. Steps 1 to 3 are repeated each January until 2034 (i.e. the last year of recalculation) due to the drop-in of 2033. For more information, Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge)

The onus of proving a claim is on the individual who claims a violation of their Charter rights. Once they prove their claim, the government must demonstrate that the violation is reasonable and demonstrably justifiable in a free and democratic society. This is the justification test as set out in Section 1 – Reasonable limits External link of the Charter. Section 1 – Reasonable limits Section 1 of the Charter states: “The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” If the government fails to meet the justification test, the type of remedy available differs between a court and an administrative tribunal. While courts have the power to strike out or declare certain statutory provisions as invalid, an administrative tribunal such as the SST can only decide that a provision is invalid for determining the matter before it. In addition, the decision of the SST does not establish a precedent and applies only to the case before it. For more information, refer to the workflow How to Handle Charter challenges at Reconsideration and SST Appeal Levels External link . How to Handle Charter challenges at Reconsideration and SST Appeal Levels

An individual may claim in a request for reconsideration of a CPP or OAS decision, that the Minister's decision or the legislation is unfair given their personal circumstances. You must process such requests using current reconsideration procedures. Occasionally, an individual claims that the decision or legislation is against or violates the Charter. That is, the individual identifies Section 15. (1) of the Charter or states “discrimination” in their reconsideration letter. In either case, no additional actions are required at the reconsideration stage.

As identification of a Charter challenge is the responsibility of the SST , it reviews all files for charter references. When the SST determines that the appeal is a Charter challenge, it will advise the regional Appeals Documentation Unit (ADU). Once confirmation of a Charter challenge is received from the SST , the regional ADU must notify the National Headquarters (NHQ) CPP or OAS Policy group from the Income Security and Social Development Branch by email, as per the following table. Table 1: List of Contacts Program Contacts to cc in email to the SST CPP or CPPD appeals Chantal Mrak Chantal Mrak OAS or GIS appeals Kevin Wagdin Kevin Wagdin The SST then sends a letter to advise the appellant of procedures. The SST includes Charter information and information on the Canada Pension Plan or Old Age Security Act with their letter to the appellant. Administration procedures at the SST The appellant must inform the SST about what they are going to challenge. The SST then forwards this information to Legal Services and the Income Security and Social Development branch in NHQ. The Income Security and Social Development branch then handles the Charter challenge in collaboration with Legal Services. If the Income Security and Social Development branch requires a file or specific documents, it contacts the regional Appeals Documentation Unit directly. Charter hearing If the appellant fails to confirm their intent to proceed with a Charter challenge, the SST informs all parties and convenes a normal hearing. Once the appeal is no longer a Charter challenge, the responsibility for the appeal returns to the region. Depending on the nature of the Charter challenge, the CPP or OAS Policy and Legislation Directorate drafts an expert report and written legal submissions are made. At the hearing, counsel from the Department of Justice represents the Minister and an officer from the Policy and Legislation Directorate appears as an expert witness. Staff from the regional office are not normally involved in Charter challenges before the SST . If the Charter challenge is decided in the appellant's favour, the benefit entitlement issue may be dealt with at the same hearing. A party who is dissatisfied with the SST -GD (General Division) decision may request leave to appeal to the SST -AD (Appeals Division). The party could be the Minister or the Appellant. If a Charter challenge is raised for the first time at the SST hearing, the departmental representative must request an adjournment for the Minister to make submissions and arguments on the constitutional issue(s). Once the adjournment is granted, the departmental representative must notify the appropriate regional Appeals Documentation Unit, who, in turn informs the CPP or OAS Policy and Legislation Directorate of Employment and Social Development Canada at NHQ. If the request for adjournment is refused, the departmental representative must immediately forward a summary of the hearing to the CPP or OAS Policy and Legislation Directorate.
This article provides information about Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (the Charter) challenges.

All laws and legislation (including CPP and OAS legislation and decision making) are subject to the Charter. Therefore, CPP and OAS decision-makers must ensure they do not breach guaranteed Charter rights when exercising their duties and powers. Subsection 15. (1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms states: “Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.” The Charter sets out established protections of basic rights, which guarantee Canadians certain rights and freedoms and protects them from laws and government action that offend these basic rights. For the purposes of CPP and OAS, the most common challenge is that a legislative provision discriminates, contrary to the equality provision under Section 15. (1) of the Charter. If an individual claims a violation of one or more Charter rights, the issue may become a Charter challenge case.

Reassessment Enquiry Chart Referring to vocational rehabilitation at reassessment There will be beneficiaries who continue to meet the severe and prolonged medical criteria. However, reasonable rehabilitation measures may result in improvement in their capacity for employment. Identification of rehabilitation potential and a subsequent referral to a Vocational Rehabilitation Case Manager (VRCM) are required. It is important that each case will be decided on its own merit by the VRCM. If there is an immediate need for referral, refer to a VRCM. Certain conditions are required to improve a beneficiary's chance of success in the program. At least one of the following criteria must be met to refer a file to a VRCM for a more in-depth review of the file: beneficiary motivation; early intervention; potential for a return to work; evidence of co-insurance; and requirement for retraining to facilitate an RTW. Factors for a referral to Vocational Rehabilitation include: the beneficiary requires assistance to identify skills they would need to acquire in order to RTW; cost-effectiveness when considering time left in the workforce versus the cost of the rehabilitation program; and a lack of a clear relationship between the impairment and the beneficiary's previous occupation (e.g. a paraplegic with computer skills may be able to perform their previous occupation with some adjustment to their workplace). Exclusion Conditions Any one of the following criteria may be sufficient to exclude referral to a VRCM: terminal illness; chronic or progressive debilitating disease; major cognitive impairment; mental capability needing a sheltered or inclusive work environment; incapacity; or high level disabling behaviour leaving the beneficiary unemployable. topic_title: Introduction to the Reassessment Program Updated
text: The Department may conduct a reassessment of beneficiaries receiving a CPPD benefit to determine if they continue to be disabled in accordance with CPP legislation and policy. For the purposes of this process, CPPD benefits refer to both the DSB and the PRDB . There are several reasons to initiate a review of a beneficiary's file. To confirm if a beneficiary remains eligible for the benefit, the Department may assess continuing eligibility based on: new or recent earnings information; or a pre-scheduled return to work notification; or notification from the beneficiary or other parties of a change in circumstances, including: self-reported Return to Work (RTW); unreported RTW; improvement in the beneficiary's medical condition; and participation in volunteer or educational activities. If a beneficiary self-reports work, volunteer or educational activities, it is considered an assessment. Triggers associated with unreported work activity are considered a reassessment. When conducting a review, you must examine all evidence on the file since the last time the beneficiary received a decision. There may be times when it is necessary to request additional information from sources other than the beneficiary. You have the discretion to make a decision based on information on file and any information obtained during the reassessment. A decision only needs to ensure that the contributor is more likely disabled than not. For more information, refer to Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) . In most cases, the beneficiary should be able to: Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) provide all necessary information concerning their overall work capacity; and serve as the primary source of information to determine continuing eligibility during an assessment or reassessment. For more information, refer to Final Decision section below.

topic_title: Is there a claim or allegation of erroneous advice or administrative error?
text: A claim or allegation of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) made at any level by a beneficiary or an authorized third party during the reassessment must be fully investigated. The Minister may also initiate remedial action in the process of reviewing an application or file if it is noticed that an EA/AE has occurred in the processing of a pension, benefit or provision. If the EA/AE investigation is likely to result in an overpayment , an investigation must be completed after the decision on the reassessment has been made and appeal rights expired. If the EA/AE investigation is likely to result in an underpayment , an investigation must be initiated immediately, prior to the completion of the reassessment decision. The Child Rearing Drop-In supports primary caregivers who stop working or reduce their work hours to care for children under the age of 7. The drop-in is only applied if it benefits the client. Each year after 2019, the CPP enhancement will "drop in" an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average earnings during the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child if the following are met: the drop-in amount is higher than their actual earnings during that period; and the child is under the age of 7. The Child Rearing Drop-In is also applied for any contributor who, at the birth or adoption of a child, receives the Canada Child Benefit and acts as the primary caregiver. An eligible contributor will receive earnings dropped into the calculation of the enhanced portion of their CPP benefit for the time when the child was under 7 years old. The earnings dropped in as a result of the Child Rearing Drop-In are eligible for a Credit Split provision (division of pensionable earnings).

topic_title: How is the Child Rearing Drop-In determined?
text: The Child Rearing Drop-In will drop in unadjusted pensionable earnings (UPE) in the first and second additional contributory periods. For the first additional contributory period, the UPE will be equal to the average percentage of earnings the contributor has made in relation to the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) for the 5 years before birth or adoption of the child. For the second additional contributory period, the UPE are based on earnings between the YMPE and the year’s additional maximum pensionable earnings, which equals to 114% of the YMPE. Only higher earners who make more than the YMPE will contribute to the second additional contributory period.

topic_title: How is the Child Rearing Drop-In different from the current Child Rearing Drop-Out?
text: The Child Rearing Drop-Out only applies to the base calculation of the CPP. The drop-out removes contributory months with low or zero earnings from the base calculation. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average of monthly pensionable earnings. The Child Rearing Drop-In only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. The drop-in adds earnings into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement portion of a benefit. The eligibility requirements for the Child Rearing Provision remain the same.

topic_title: What happens if the applicant applies for a benefit after 2019, and the child rearing period begins before 2019 and ends after January 2019?
text: Since the CPP enhancement begins in 2019, the period before January 1, 2019 is outside of the CPP first additional contributory period and cannot be protected. However, if the child is under the age of 7 in 2019, the Child Rearing Drop-In will be applied. In this case, the individual would have no months in their first additional contributory period with which to calculate the drop-in value. The client would then be treated as if they had earnings of 40% of the YMPE when determining the value of the drop-in.

topic_title: What happens if there are no average earnings to drop in?
text: The Child Rearing Drop-In is based on the first and second additional pensionable earnings. It is possible for a client to receive a drop-in with a $0 value. This can occur when a client is a valid contributor but has no earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings for the drop-in. If there are less than 5 years in the first or second contributory periods, the average is determined by the actual number of available months in the contributory period, down to a lower limit of 36 months (3 years). If there are less than 3 years in the first contributory period, the client is awarded 40% of the YMPE for each month outside of the contributory period, up to a maximum of 36 months for the Child Rearing Drop-In.

topic_title: Why drop-in earnings and not drop-out periods or months of no earnings?
text: In the calculation for the first and second additional contributory periods under the CPP enhancement, the number of contributory months is fixed at 480 months (40 years). The Department will use the best 480 months in the calculation of the enhancement. With the CPP base calculations, the drop-outs remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the average monthly pensionable earnings. With the enhancements, given that 480 months is always the number of months, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months.

topic_title: Will a beneficiary be affected by the Child Rearing Drop-In if they are currently receiving a benefit with a child rearing period that ends before 2019?
text: The Child Rearing Drop-In will not be applied to any benefit calculation unless the child rearing period includes January 2019 or later, when the CPP enhancement takes effect.

topic_title: Will the Child Rearing Drop-In impact other CPP provisions?
text: The Child Rearing Drop-In can impact the Credit Split provision. This is because the Child Rearing Drop-In will drop in a client's UPE, which can be divided by the Credit Split provision.

The CPP enhancement adds 2 additional contributory periods. The first additional contributory period begins January 1, 2019. The second additional contributory period begins January 1, 2024. With the CPP enhancement, the number of contributory months is set at 480. The contributor's best 480 months are used in the calculation of the enhanced components. When the first additional and second additional calculations are done, earnings are dropped in to increase the average maximum pensionable earnings which results in a higher average of earnings over the period of 480 months. For more information, Enhancement of the Canada Pension Plan (Policy)

The Disability Drop-In (DDI) rate (credits) for the first additional contributory period is determined by taking 70% of the contributor's average first additional pensionable earnings made in relation to the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) in the 6 years (72 months) before the Date of Onset (DOO), including the month of the DOO. For the second additional contributory period, the drop-in is similarly determined by taking 70% of the contributor's average second additional pensionable earnings, made between the YMPE and the year's additional maximum pensionable earnings in the 6 years (72 months) before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. A client can receive a first additional or second additional drop-in rate with a $0 value. This can occur when a client is a valid contributor but has no earnings in the period with which to calculate the average earnings amount for the first additional or second additional drop-in. If there are less than 6 years in the first or second additional contributory period, the drop-in rate is calculated using the actual number of available months in the contributory period. If the number of months is zero (0), there is no DDI amount provided. If a contributor's disability ceases due to a return to work, and the contributor becomes disabled again and has additional pensionable earnings for less than 6 years, the amount of drop-in for the second disability is the greater of: the drop-in rate for the previous period of disability; or the drop-in rate for the second period of disability (calculated using the previous 6-year period, including unadjusted additional pensionable earnings plus the drop-in from the previous period of disability). If the Child Rearing Drop-In or credit split Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) amounts within the 6 years before the contributor became disabled are higher than the first additional or second additional DDI value, the greater value will be used. These credits are dropped in during the APE calculation for an RTR or SVR pension. This means the additional APE resulting from the DDI are added to the total first additional APE and total second additional APE during the calculation of the pension. For more information, Examples—Disability Drop-In

The Disability Exclusion only applies to the base calculation. The exclusion removes contributory months when the client was disabled, starting with the month following the month of DOO, from the calculation of the CPP base rate. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average monthly pensionable earnings. The eligibility requirements for the Disability Exclusion remain the same. The Disability Drop-In (DDI) only applies to the enhanced calculations and only if it is to the advantage of the contributor. The drop-in adds earnings into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the first additional and second additional components of an RTR or SVR pension. The DDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility and minimum qualifying period requirements for CPP benefits. If a contributor becomes disabled and receives a DSB in 2019, but never makes CPP enhanced contributions, the drop-in earnings for those months or years of disability will be $0 and will not affect the CPP benefit or pension calculations.

This knowledge article provides you with information on how the Disability Drop-In (DDI) provision impacts the calculation of the enhanced components of an RTR or SVR pension.

On January 1, 2019, changes to the CPP legislation came into effect as a result of the 2016-2018 Triennial Review. The DDI provision was introduced as a support for contributors with disabilities. The DDI provision is not used in the calculation of a DSB amount; rather, the DDI helps to protect the value of the enhanced components of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings for individuals who were in receipt of DSB . Earnings are credited to the contributor's first additional and second additional CPP contributory periods for the months when they were disabled as defined by the CPP. The drop-in amounts are used only for the purpose of calculating future RTR or SVR pension amounts, and are only calculated if the RTR or SVR pension is calculated. To apply the DDI provision to the enhanced components of the RTR or SVR pension calculations, the following criteria must be met: the contributor's disability Date of Onset (DOO) must be on or after January 1, 2019; to apply the DDI provision to the first additional component of the applicable benefit, the contributor must have first additional pensionable earnings in 2019 or thereafter; and to apply the DDI provision to the second additional component of the applicable benefit, the contributor must have second additional pensionable earnings in 2024 or thereafter. The DDI provision can only be attributed if it is to the advantage of the disabled contributor. The provision might not necessarily be to their advantage, as while the contributor cannot work and contribute during the disability period, they may have already received the following other credits: as a result of a Credit splitting provision; or from the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI). The DDI is only applied if it is greater than the credit split or CRDI earnings amount. An eligible contributor will receive earnings dropped into the calculation of the enhanced components of their CPP RTR pension and any SVR pension paid to their eligible surviving spouse or common-law partner. Earnings are dropped in for the month-based period of time the contributor is disabled, beginning the month after the contributor's DOO and ending the month their DSB ceases. The DDI values are not subject to a credit split (division of pensionable earnings between former spouses or common-law partners). The values may change if there is a division that affects the 6 years before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. If a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings occurs after the drop-in values have been calculated and there is a change to the pensionable values used to calculate the drop-in values, then both the drop-in earnings and benefit amount must be recalculated. For more information, Disability Drop-In Provision (Policy) The dollar amount of earnings dropped into the client's first additional and second additional CPP contributory period equals 70% of the client's average first additional pensionable earnings and 70% of the client's average second additional pensionable earnings for the 6 years (72 months) before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. A disability beneficiary may cease to be disabled and return to work. If they have contributions and additional pensionable earnings for less than 6 years and then becomes disabled again, the value of the drop-in for the second period of disability will be the greater of: the drop-in value for the previous period of disability; or the drop-in value for the second period of disability, calculated using the previous 6-year period, which will include unadjusted additional pensionable earnings from pensionable employment plus the drop-in amounts from the previous period of disability. This is applicable even in cases when a contributor returns to work and then suffers a relapse within 2 years ( DSB Auto Reinstate).

The base and enhanced components of the CPP will work together seamlessly as there is no separate application process to receive the CPP enhanced component of CPP benefits. The CPP enhanced component will be included in the CPP payments that clients receive and combined into one amount. Starting in June 2022, clients who made valid contributions in January 2019 or later will start to receive the first additional component of their benefit, including any retroactive amounts. Those who begin receiving a benefit in June 2022 or later will be paid the first additional component as part of their regular monthly amount. The enhanced component of CPP benefits is considered taxable income. Although income tax is not automatically withheld from CPP benefit payments, it can be withheld upon request.

CPP contributors can receive estimates of their future benefits via: the Canadian Retirement Income Calculator; a Statement of Contributions ( SOC ); or benefits simulations performed by Service Canada staff. In many cases, these estimates use projected CPP contributions, which are based on the contributor maintaining their current average earnings pattern. The Canadian Retirement Income Calculator, the SOC and the benefit simulations in ITRDS have been updated to reflect the CPP enhancement. topic_title: Child Rearing Drop-in and Disability Drop-in Provisions
text: Effective January 2019, the drop-in provisions will help to further protect the value of the enhanced component of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings for primary caregivers and individuals with disabilities. Pension credits are "dropped in" for these periods based on an average of their earnings prior to the child's birth, adoption, date they came under the custody and control of the client or the date the client became disabled. Similar to the child rearing drop-out provision and the disability exclusion, the drop-in provisions can help increase the amount of CPP benefits. However they will not be considered when determining eligibility or the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. The child rearing drop-out provision and the disability exclusion apply to the base component of CPP benefits and the drop-in provisions apply to the enhanced component. Eligibility criteria for the child rearing drop-in and drop-out provisions are the same. For more information, refer to Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) and Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) Disability Drop-In (Knowledge)

CPP consists of: a base or original component (since January 1, 1966) that is calculated on earnings between the year's minimum and maximum amounts of pensionable earnings. The current base contribution rate is 9.9% (4.95% from the employer and 4.95% from the employee). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts; and additional or enhanced components which provide a top-up to the base and are broken down into first (effective January 1, 2019) and second (effective January 1, 2024). The first additional component is calculated on the same range of earnings as the base and has a total contribution rate of 2% (1% from the employer and 1% from the employee). Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee amounts. This additional rate is being introduced gradually between 2019 and 2023 and will continue throughout a client's contributory period. With the implementation of CPP enhancement, First Nations employees on reserves will still be able to choose whether to contribute to the CPP . However, if First Nations employees and employers contribute to the CPP , they and their employers will do so at the new contribution rates resulting from the enhancement. These higher contributions will increase the amount of their CPP benefits. If the employer chooses not to participate, First Nations employees may still elect to be covered by the CPP . They are required, however, to pay both the employee and employer contributions at the new enhanced rate. First Nations people who are employed off reserves have always participated in the CPP and will participate in the CPP enhancement. For more information, CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy)

The CPP enhancement will impact the following: Retirement Pension ; Retirement Pension Post-Retirement Benefit ; Post-Retirement Benefit Disability Benefit (refer to CPPD Benefits Application (Scenario) for more information); CPPD Benefits Application (Scenario) Survivor's Pension ; Survivor's Pension Combined Benefits ; Combined Benefits Credit Split Provision ; and Credit Split Provision Pension Sharing Provision . Pension Sharing Provision The eligibility criteria for CPP benefits are not affected by the enhancement as only the base component is used to determine eligibility and the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. The flat rate benefit amount of the Death benefit, Post-Retirement Disability Benefit and benefits for children of deceased or disabled contributors will not be affected by the CPP enhancement. In addition, the current formula used to calculate the combined benefits under the base CPP continues to apply. However, there is no maximum placed on the enhanced component of a combined SVR and RTR pension or of a combined SVR pension and DSB benefit.

As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in the CPP enhancement; a new component of the CPP . The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but a "top-up" to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP . This means working Canadians will receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. Gradual increases to CPP contribution rates will take place over a 7-year period (2019 to 2025). The enhanced component of benefits will grow over time, affected by total earnings and a person's enhanced contributions. 40 years of enhanced contributions are required to achieve the maximum effect of CPP enhancement on a person's benefit. Before January 2019, the RTR pension replaced one quarter (25%) of the average monthly pensionable earnings. This average is based on an individual's work earnings up to the year's maximum pensionable earnings set by CPP . The CPP enhancement increases this to one third (33.33%) of the average pensionable earnings. The eligibility criteria for CPP benefits are not affected by the enhancement as only the base component is used to determine eligibility and the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. QPP is also being enhanced in a similar way , allowing for an alignment of enhanced benefits.

In order to support the CPP enhancements, the Department is implementing changes to CPP earnings and contribution rates and to how a number of CPP benefits are calculated. ITRDS is gradually being modified to accommodate these changes. Updates to the earnings and contributions screens and additional system changes related to calculations of the first additional component have been implemented. Additional system changes to calculate the second additional component of the enhancement will be implemented at a later date. For more information, Enhancement of the Canada Pension Plan (Policy)

If an individual works in Quebec, they contribute to the QPP rather than CPP . If they also reside in Quebec, they will apply for the benefits under the QPP where similar enhanced benefits are available.

To be eligible for a CPP Retirement (RTR) pension, an individual must meet the following requirements. Application An application for an RTR pension must be made to the Minister in writing or electronically using the My CPP Retirement application. The electronic process does not require a wet signature, but instead allows applicants to meet the "in-writing" requirement with an electronic signature. In the majority of cases, all the necessary information to process an RTR pension application is not always included in the written request. As a practice, a completed application form should be obtained, if possible . For more information on proactive enrolments, such as in cases where the legislative requirement for an RTR pension application has been waived for clients who have reached age 70 and meet the eligibility requirements, RTR70—Proactive Enrolment Age The contributor must have reached age 60. Contributions The contributor must have unadjusted pensionable earnings in at least one year of their contributory period.

The effective date of a DSB and a PRDB is the date the benefit becomes payable. First application The effective date for a DSB and a PRDB on a first application is either: 4 months after the date the applicant is deemed disabled, if maximum benefit retroactivity has not been provided; or 15 months, with a 4-month waiting period, if maximum benefit retroactivity is provided. When an applicant was previously in pay for a DSB or a PRDB If a DSB or a PRDB ceases and either benefit becomes payable within 5 years of the cessation date of the previous benefit, the 4-month waiting period is waived. The benefit effective date is then determined to be the later of: the month after the date the applicant is deemed disabled, if maximum retroactivity has not been provided; or 12 months, with a one-month waiting period, if maximum retroactivity has been provided. If a new DSB or PRDB application is received more than 5 years after the previous benefit's cessation date, but there is a medically determined disability date within the 5-year period of the previous benefit's cease date, the effective date will be 12 months before the date of the application. Effective date when credit splitting—date of attribution is used Updated When credit splitting is required to establish a minimum qualifying period, the DSB or PRDB cannot be paid for any month prior to the date of attribution of pension credits. Following the approval of the credit split, the divided pension credits are attributed to the contributor's account the month of the month the credit splitting request was received. If the Date of Onset or the Earliest Possible Date of Onset (if maximum retroactivity was provided) is before the date of attribution, the payment effective date is the month of the date of attribution.

topic_title: A DSB converted to an RTR pension Updated
text: The RTR pension replaces the DSB effective the month after the beneficiary reaches age 65. The individual's DSB will automatically be converted to an RTR pension. A child's eligibility to the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit may continue even after the beneficiary reaches age 65, Eligibility Requirements—CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit (Policy) An application is not required, however the beneficiary must be notified of the conversion in writing.

When a contributor reaches age 60 but has not yet reached age 65, their RTR pension starts with the latest of: the month the applicant reaches age 60; the month after the month of application; or the month the applicant chose, which must not be more than 12 months after the month the application was received. When a contributor reaches age 65, their RTR pension starts with the latest of: the month the applicant reaches age 65; the 11th month before the month of application; or the month the applicant chose, which must not be more than 12 months after the month the application was received.

Effective date CPP contributors may apply for their RTR pension up to 12 months before their effective date. Applicants who reach age 65 may be entitled to up to 12 months of retroactive payments. However, no retroactive payment may be made for any months before: January 1995; or the individual reaches age 65. The date the Department receives an application for an RTR pension, whether on paper or online, is the date from which an individual's pension start date can be determined. Change in the effective date The effective date of an RTR pension may be advanced or deferred in the following circumstances: When an RTR pension is not in pay and a different effective date is desired, the applicant must submit a written request to change the effective date. However, the newly proposed effective date must fall within the requirements listed above. When an RTR pension is in pay and a later effective date is desired, the recipient must submit a written request to cancel the pension within 12 months of the first retirement payment being issued. When an RTR pension is in pay and an earlier effective date is requested, the recipient must submit a written request and the earlier date must fall within the parameters listed above under Effective Date . A school or university is defined as a school, college, university or educational institution that provides training or instruction of an educational, professional, vocational or technical nature. Acceptable institutions include but are not limited to: Universities Composite High Schools Comprehensive Schools High Schools Colleges (regular) Community Colleges Military Colleges Business Colleges Bible Colleges Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Collegiate Institutes Convents Novitiates Institutes of Technology Music Academy (School) Polytechnic School School of Applied Arts and Technology Schools of Nursing Technical Schools Vocational Schools Use the following factors to determine if an educational institution is acceptable for CPP purposes: It is recognized as an educational institution by a province or territory, or its course of study is affiliated with an institution that is recognized; It offers the student a diploma or certificate upon completion of the course of study; It provides training that will directly prepare the student for further study at a recognized educational institution; and It can demonstrate that the student must attend or otherwise participate in courses (e.g. submit papers, make presentations, write tests, pass examinations and other activities) that would indicate full-time study.

To receive a child's benefit, a child aged 18 to 25 who was not previously paid as a child under the age of 18 must submit: an Application for a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit (ISP-1400) form; a Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP-1401) form; or a CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP1402) form; and proof of birth (if required). If a child is applying for 2 benefits (e.g. Surviving Child's benefit and Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit), an ISP-1400 form is required for each benefit. However, one ISP-1402 form may be accepted for both benefits.

Benefit payments are made to dependent children only for periods they are deemed to be in approved attendance at school or university. The vacation period is part of the school year. Full-time and part-time status continues during the school vacation if the child was attending school or deemed to be attending school full-time or part-time at the end of the school term, semester or school year. Benefits for dependent children, who are 18 to 25 years old and attending school on an approved basis, start the later of either: the month in which a DSB or a PRDB is payable to the contributor; the month following the month in which the contributor dies; the 11th month before the month the child's benefit application is received; or the month in which classes begin (a school vacation may be considered part of the full-time or part-time attendance class period). The benefit ends either: the last month the dependent child is considered to be in approved attendance at school or university (a school vacation may be considered part of the approved attendance period); the month the dependent child turns 25; the month the dependent child dies; or the month the contributor ceases to be disabled with the exception of when the DSB converts to an RTR pension or the PRDB stops due to the contributor turning age 65. Once a child reaches the age of 18, they must provide proof of approved attendance at school or university to continue their benefit. If the Department does not receive proof of attendance by the end of the bring forward period, the child no longer meets the definition of a "dependent child" and will no longer be eligible for the benefit. As a result, their Surviving Child's benefit and Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) will cease. If the Department does not receive proof of approved attendance at school or university by the end of the second month of the relevant period of study, the child no longer meets the definition of a "dependent child" and will no longer be eligible for the benefit. As a result, the Surviving Child's benefit and DCCB will cease.

CPP legislation recognizes that although a child may not be attending school, they may be deemed to be in approved attendance in the following situations: School vacations; or An absence due to illness. Children who are absent due to illness can in certain circumstances be considered in approved attendance at school. For benefit payments to continue to be paid to the dependent child, they must submit the required Canada Pension Plan Illness Certificate (ISP-1403) form and it must be consistent with the type of attendance (full-time or part-time) at the time the illness begins. If a disabled contributor's child was absent from school due to illness but continued to receive benefit payments as they provided the ISP-1403 form, their benefit payments will cease the month the contributor's benefit payments cease. If a disabled contributor's child was absent from school or university due to illness and the DSB ceases, that child will be eligible for benefits up to the date the DSB ceases. This is only applicable if the child resumes full-time or part-time attendance during that year or the following school year. They must also submit an ISP-1403 form confirming that the absence was due to illness. Upon notification from a student that their school is not able to provide classes (teacher strike, temporary closure, etc.) and they have returned to school with an extended end date, proof is required to extend the end date. Proof can come in the form of: a letter from the school with all relevant information; a completed CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form that confirms approved attendance; or official proof of enrolment signed by an authorized school official that contains all required information.

A determination of what constitutes full-time school attendance is essential in deciding eligibility for benefits. A dependent child is normally considered to be in full-time attendance at school for CPP purposes if they are recognized to be a full-time student by an acceptable educational institution.

Effective January 1, 2025, a determination of what constitutes part-time school attendance is essential in deciding eligibility for benefits. Dependent children of deceased or disabled contributors can be eligible for a benefit when they are attending part-time school and meet all eligibility requirements. The educational institution determines the part-time status. The amount they could receive is 50% of the rate for full-time students. A dependent child is normally considered to be in part-time attendance at school for CPP purposes if they: are recognized to be a part-time student by an acceptable educational institution; and enrolled in courses that make up at least 20% of a full course load as recognized by their educational institution.

CPP children's benefits provide financial assistance to eligible dependent children that would otherwise be provided by the disabled or deceased contributor. To be eligible for children's benefits, a dependent child who is 18 to 25 years old must be in full-time or part-time attendance at a school or university as defined in the Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation).

topic_title: A child adopted "in fact" by the contributor
text: An adoption "in fact" can involve an agreement in which the legal parents or a guardian agree to place a child under the decision-making responsibility and parenting time of an adopting parent (the contributor) who cares for the child as they would for their own child. On the other hand, situations can occur where no actual agreement exists. Examples of no actual agreement being in place are situations: where a child has been abandoned and a contributor assumes long-term parental responsibility for the abandoned child; or where the contributor is living with the child's legal parent and cares for the child as though the child was their own. Adoption "in fact" is based on a factual situation normally involving a long-term or permanent child-contributor relationship. The contributor cares for, and behaves towards the child, as if the child was their legal child. The child-contributor relationship must be supported by obtaining evidence described later in this document. Adoption "in fact" ends when the child-contributor relationship ends. A child adopted "in fact" by the deceased contributor When the contributor is deceased, the child may be considered to have been adopted "in fact" by the deceased contributor provided: the "in fact" adoption occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and the relationship between the child and the contributor existed at the time of the contributor's death. A child adopted "in fact" by the disabled contributor When the contributor is disabled, the child may be considered adopted "in fact" provided the "in fact" adoption: occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and was in effect before the date the disability is deemed to have commenced for any date before January 1, 1992; or may be effective before or after the date the disability is deemed to have commenced on January 1,1992,or any date after January 1,1992.

topic_title: A child under the contributor's "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time
text: An "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time arrangement can often involve short-term relationships or situations where a child is "in fact" under the decision-making responsibility and parenting time of a relative or family friend (e.g. older sibling, grandparent, godparent). An "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time arrangement can also arise in situations where the contributor marries or becomes the common-law partner of one of the child's legal parents. In such situations, the child is residing with the contributor, but the nature of the relationship (e.g. the degree of influence and discipline the contributor exercises over the child) may not be such that adoption "in fact" can be established. A child under the "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the deceased contributor When the contributor is deceased, the child may be considered to have been "in fact" under the deceased contributor's decision-making responsibility and parenting time provided the agreement: occurred before the child's 21st birthday;and the relationship between the child and the contributor existed at the time of the contributor's death. A child under the "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the disabled contributor When the contributor is disabled, the child may be considered to be "in fact" under the decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the disabled contributor provided the agreement: occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and was in effect before the date the disability is deemed to have commenced for any date before January 1, 1992; or may be effective before or after the date the disability is deemed to have commenced on January 1, 1992, or any date after January 1, 1992.

topic_title: A child under the contributor's legal decision-making responsibility Updated
text: A child who is legally under the decision-making responsibility of a contributor is placed there by a court action. An example would be when a court gives a contributor legal guardianship of a dependent child. A child under the legal decision-making responsibility or parenting time of the deceased contributor Updated When the contributor is deceased, the child may be considered legally to have been under the deceased contributor's decision-making responsibility and parenting time provided: the legal order detailing decision-making responsibility and parenting time occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and the relationship between the child and the contributor existed at the time of the contributor's death. A child under the legal decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the disabled contributor Updated When the contributor is disabled, the child may be considered legally to have been under the disabled contributor's decision-making responsibility and parenting time provided the agreement: occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and was in effect before the date the disability is deemed to have commenced for any date before January 1, 1992; or may be effective before or after the date the disability is deemed to have commenced on January 1, 1992, or any date after January 1, 1992.

Under the CPP, adoption "in fact" describes a long-term relationship between a contributor and a child provided the adoption "in fact" occurred before the child's 21st birthday. Adoption "in fact" must be based on a factual situation where, usually , a natural or legal parent or legal guardian of the child agrees to submit the child into the care and responsibility of the "in fact" parent. The natural or legal parent or legal guardian may be the partner of the "in fact" parent.

Under the CPP, the term "child" means and includes a child: of the contributor, whether born before or after the contributor's death; adopted legally or adopted “in fact” by the contributor while the child was under 21 years of age; or of the contributor who has either legal or “in fact” decision-making responsibility or parenting time while the child was under 21 years of age. The CPP definition does not include a child of the contributor who is adopted legally or adopted “in fact” by someone other than the contributor or the contributor's spouse or common-law partner before the death or disability of the contributor, unless the contributor was maintaining the child as defined by CPP.

Under the CPP, the term "dependent child" of a contributor means and includes a child of the contributor who: is younger than 18 years of age; or is 18 to 25 years of age and in full-time or part-time attendance at a school or university. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: Health; Education; Culture, language, religion and spirituality; and Significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time means the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is at school) Maintaining a dependent child of the disabled or deceased contributor (adoption or “in fact” by someone other than the contributor) Updated CPP Regulation 65.1 states that maintaining the child with reference to the child of a disabled contributor means making financial provisions for the child amounting to not less than the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit payable under the CPP. CPP Regulation 65.1 further states that maintaining the child with reference to the child of a deceased contributor means making financial provisions for the child, until the contributor's death, amounting to not less than the Surviving Child's benefit payable under the CPP.

topic_title: Evidence for children born after the death of a contributor
text: The following documents may be used to support a parent's claim that the deceased contributor was a legal parent of the child in cases where a child is born after the death of the contributor: a written statement verifying that the birth occurred within 301 days of the date of the contributor's death; and a long form birth certificate. The applicant who is unable to obtain a long form birth certificate must provide a written statement stating that the deceased contributor is the child's parent completed either by: the family physician; or a member of the deceased contributor's family.

topic_title: Evidence for children who are legally under the "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the contributor
text: An applicant who applies for a CPP children's benefit for a child who is adopted "in fact", may have an agreement with the child's legal parents. This agreement gives the applicant decision-making responsibility and parenting time. To establish if a child is legally under the decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the contributor, the following appropriate official documents must be obtained: a court order; or another legal agreement.
The documents identified by CPP for this purpose are: a copy of the adoption order; and a birth certificate; or a baptismal certificate.
The documents identified by CPP Regulation 47(2) for this purpose are: a birth certificate; or a baptismal certificate.

topic_title: "In fact" decision-making or parenting time Updated
text: Under the CPP, "in fact" decision-making responsibility or parenting time describes a child who: is under the decision-making responsibility of the contributor before the child's 21st birthday and whom the contributor maintains; and for whom the contributor has some parenting time but lacks a parent-child relationship.
Under the CPP, the term "legal parent" means: a biological or natural parent; or an adoptive parent.

topic_title: Legally adopted child of the contributor
text: A court order is required for a child to be legally adopted. When the adoption is finalized, the child is no longer considered the child of the previous natural or adoptive parents. A new birth certificate is issued which identifies the new adoptive parents as the child's legal parents. Legally adopted child of the deceased or disabled contributor When the contributor is deceased or disabled, the child may be considered the legally adopted child of the contributor provided the legal adoption: occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and was finalized before the contributor's death for a deceased contributor; or became effective either before, on or after the deemed date of disability for a disabled contributor.

Deceased contributor's natural child A natural child may be considered the child of a deceased contributor whether born before or after the contributor's death. If the child is born after the death of the contributor, the birth must occur within 301 days of the date of death of the deceased contributor. The child's birth certificate identifies the contributor as a parent. Disabled contributor's natural child A natural child may be considered the child of a disabled contributor whether born before or after the date the contributor's CPP DSB application is approved.

topic_title: Other evidence for children under the "in fact" decision-making responsibility and parenting time or who are adopted "in fact" by the contributor
text: If there is no legal agreement, the CPP requires the applicant to submit the following documents: A written statement from the applicant which must contain the following information: the period of time the child was in the contributor's care; a description of how the child was represented to the public by the contributor (e.g. as the contributor's child or adopted child); the name(s) and address(es) of the child's parent(s) or guardian(s), and the reason why the child was not living with them; a description of the influence, direction, nature and degree of discipline; exercised over the child by the contributor, or others (and if so, by whom); a detailed description of the decision-making responsibility and parenting time exercised by the contributor over the child using supporting evidence signed by a third party such as school records, health insurance claims, medical records, etc.; a description of the nature and extent of maintenance provided for the child by the contributor, or others (and if so, by whom). A written statement, if obtainable, from the child's parent(s) or guardian(s). A written statement is designed to verify the applicant or contributor's claim. CPP requests that this statement provides the following information: the date that they gave decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child to the contributor; the terms that were outlined in the agreement (if any) regarding the child (e.g. was the child left with the contributor on a permanent or temporary basis); and a description of the nature and extent of maintenance provided for the child by the parent(s) or guardian(s).

It is one of the factors used to determine the child's eligibility for CPP Children's benefits.
