Contributory periods cannot be excluded from the CPP enhancement portions. Therefore, Child Rearing Drop-in ( CRDI ) amounts are used to drop earnings into the contributor's first and second additional contributory periods for the purpose of CPP benefit calculation. Pension credits equal to the amount of the primary caregiver’s average earnings during the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child are dropped into their first additional contributory period. There will be a maximum of 7 years of drop-ins per child. When there are overlapping drop-in periods due to the birth of more than one child in a given time frame, the highest of the 2 or more drop-in average earnings amounts is used. Beginning January 1, 2024, the provision will attribute to the primary caregiver’s second additional contributory period an amount equal to the average of their second additional UPE in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. Child-Rearing Drop-ins result in additional UPE The drop-in amounts function like additional UPE . They are used to calculate the additional CPP portion of the RTR pension and the additional CPP earnings-related portions of the DSB (including the PRDB and SVR pension). Their value must be adjusted upward at the time a pension or benefit is calculated. Use the same adjustment methodology as that used for the upward adjustment of the value of UPE . Child-Rearing Drop-ins and CPP Credit Splitting The drop-in amounts will be subject to division upon divorce or separation. The drop-in amount, once attributed to the contributory period, is not recalculated during the period of cohabitation due to the division. Changes to the earnings in the years before the birth or adoption of the child due to the division do not trigger a recalculation of the amount of the drop-in within the period of cohabitation. (The original amount attributed is divided along with the other UPE.) If the CRDI period extends past the period of cohabitation (i.e. the period subject to division), then the CRDI amount for that post-cohabitation period is recalculated, taking into account the newly-divided earnings. Therefore, if a division of additional UPE occurs after the CRDI has been attributed and affects the pension credits that were used to calculate the drop-ins, the amount of the CRDI must be recalculated. If there is a benefit in pay, the benefit amount must also be recalculated as the CRDI impacts other provisions. Bookend years The amount of the CRDI must be prorated for both the first and second additional contributory periods for the year in which the contributor: reaches 18 years of age; reaches 70 years of age; dies; or begins their RTR pension. The calculated amount of the CRDI for such years is prorated over 12 months. Less than 5 years in the contributory period If the individual either had a child before they turned 23 years of age or had a child before the year 2023, there are less than 5 years (60 months) in the first additional contributory period. In such cases, only the actual number of contributory months is used to calculate the average since CPP contributions can only begin at age 18. The minimum number of contributory months required is 36. In cases where there are less than 36 months in the first additional contributory period, the formula used for the first additional contributory period attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e 1/12 of the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each missing month, up to 36 months. Child rearing period ends and then restarts There are cases in which one period of child rearing may end when custody and control of a child is lost. When this occurs, the individual no longer receives the CCB . If, however, custody and control of the child is regained, the individual again receives the CCB . In such cases, the drop-in value for the second period of child rearing is calculated using the previous 5 year period, which, will include (if the individual worked during this time), additional UPE from pensionable employment in addition to the drop-in amounts from the previous child rearing period. Calculation The CRDI formulas for the first additional and second additional contributory periods are found in the Canada Pension Plan. The 2 calculations differ slightly from one another: Formula for the first additional contributory period Where: M1 to M6 represent the number of months in the first additional contributory period for each of the 5 years (60 months) before the contributor becomes a Family Allowance recipient . There is a special calculation for M1 and M6 . If, for example, a child is born or adopted in May, the value of M6 will be 5 months (January to May) and the value of M1 will be 7 months for a total of 12 months. A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the first additional UPE by the YMPE for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. ( A to E = UPE ∕ YMPE ) F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods—if there was a previous child— F provides that a previous drop-in amount be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the first additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by a prorated YMPE amount. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. Q attributes 40% of the monthly maximum, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE for each missing contributory month, up to 36 months. R is the denominator used to calculate the average ratio of earnings to YMPE . The value of R will be between 36 and 60 and represents the number of contributory months in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. T represents the YMPE for the year to which the drop-in is attributed. The product of multiplying the average ratio by T is the value of the child-rearing drop-in for the year to which it is attributed. Formula for the second additional contributory period This formula is similar to that applied to the first additional contributory period.The only differences are: A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the additional UPE by the difference between the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YAMPE ) and YMPE , for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. YAMPE is the new pensionable earning ceiling introduced by the CPP enhancement. Its value is 114% of YMPE . ( A to E = UPE ∕ YAMPE − YMPE ). F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods, (i.e. if there was a previous child) F allows a previous drop-in amount to be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the first additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by the difference between the prorated YAMPE and YMPE amounts. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. There is no Q in the second additional contributory period formula. 40% of the monthly maximum, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE cannot be attributed to the second additional contributions since contributions to that period are made on earnings between the YMPE and YAMPE .

The CPP Child Rearing Drop-out ( CRDO ) provision helps contributors maintain their level of pensionable earnings by excluding eligible child rearing years from their contributory period when calculating their CPP benefits. The purpose of the CRDO is to ensure that a CPP contributor will not be penalized for periods of low or zero earnings while they cared for a child under 7 years of age. The provision may help a contributor to qualify for benefits or to increase the amount payable.

topic_title: Child Rearing Provision eligibility conditions Updated
text: The following eligibility conditions must exist before a contributor can be considered under the Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ): The contributor or the contributor's survivor must have made an application for a pension or benefit under the CPP . The request for the CRP must be submitted in writing. The Request for a Child Rearing Provi sion (ISP1640) form facilitates the process when properly completed. The CRP declaration is also built into the application form for the CPP Retirement ( RTR ) pension as well as the application for CPP Disability ( DSB ) benefits. The contributor must be deemed to have been either a Family Allowance recipient or the individual eligible for the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ) for the children for which the CRP is requested. This condition is met when the contributor: received Family Allowance payments; or remained at home and was the primary caregiver for the child(ren) under 7 years of age and is the spouse or common-law partner of the person who received Family Allowance payments and the Family Allowance recipient waives their rights to the CRP ; and/or is the individual eligible for the CCB ; or is the person who would have been eligible for the CCB had they applied for the benefit and no other person was considered to be an eligible individual in respect of the same child for the same period of time. The contributor must have been the Family Allowance recipient and/or a CCB -eligible individual for at least one child under 7 years of age, however, the month of the child's: birth cannot be included since the Family Allowance and the CCB are not payable for that month; and 7th birthday is included.

The CPP Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ) has 2 ways to help contributors maintain their level of pensionable earnings during the time when the child was under 7 years old: excluding eligible child rearing years from their CPP calculation. This is called the Child Rearing Drop-out ( CRDO ); and dropping earnings into the CPP calculation of the enhanced portion of the contributory period. This is called the Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ).

The CPP does not provide the right to request a reconsideration for the Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ). Reconsideration rights are only provided with respect to decisions regarding pension or benefit eligibility and/or entitlement. The CPP Regulations state that notifications of appealable decisions must be sent to the individual or beneficiary in writing by the Minister. Since the CRP is not appealable, there is no legislative authority that states the individual or beneficiary must be notified of the outcome of CRP processing to accounts. The Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP1640) form is a declaration and not an application. It does not carry the rights and obligations of an application and, therefore, must not be referred to as an application in any forms or communications.

topic_title: Waiving rights to the Child Rearing Provision
text: The Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ) is typically intended for Family Allowance recipients and individuals eligible for the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ). However, the spouse or common-law partner of a Family Allowance recipient may use the CRP if they remained at home and were the primary caregiver for children under 7 years of age. In this situation, the Family Allowance recipient must waive their rights to use the CRP in favour of their spouse or common-law partner. For CCB purposes, as described by Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ) in gendered terms, when a male and a female parent live together in the same household as the child, the female parent is usually considered primarily responsible for the child. The female would therefore be the individual eligible for the CRP . If it was the male parent who stayed home to care for the children, but the female parent received the CCB by default from CRA , the male parent would not be considered eligible for the CRP even though his record of earnings would reflect that he was, in fact, the stay-at-home parent. In these cases, the contributor must contact CRA to request they send a letter so the CRP can be applied to the parent who actually stayed home to care for the child(ren). Family Allowance recipient Under the Family Allowance program, if the contributor is the spouse or common-law partner of a Family Allowance recipient, the contributor must provide CPP administration with a completed and signed Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP1640) or a CRP request embedded in the CPP DSB or RTR pension application forms. The contributor spouse or common-law partner must state the periods during which they remained at home as the primary caregiver for the child(ren). However, according to CPP Regulations, the contributor's spouse or common-law partner will benefit from the CRP for the stated periods only if the Family Allowance recipient: confirms the periods claimed; and waives their right to use the CRP in favour of the contributor spouse for those same periods. Canada Child Benefit-eligible individual Under the CCB program, only the CCB -eligible individual can benefit from the CRP as specified in the CPP Regulations. There have been cases, however, where a parent stayed home to raise the child(ren) and was denied CPP benefits because the other parent received the CCB . CRA has agreed to provide a letter confirming that the parent who stayed home would have been determined to have been the CCB -eligible individual for the dates indicated. Before CRA can issue this letter, they must receive a signed declaration from the CCB -eligible recipient, attesting to the fact that the other parent was, in fact , the primary caregiver of the child(ren). The CCB -eligible recipient must specify the period of time in which the other parent was the primary caregiver of the child(ren). All other periods would remain with the parent who had originally been identified as the CCB -eligible recipient. Individuals are advised of their options for qualifying as the CCB -eligible individual. Contributors are advised to contact officials at the appropriate CRA regional tax centre to obtain the letter noted above. After the CRP has been applied to the CPP account of the primary caregiver based on the letter from CRA , the CRP cannot be revoked and applied to the CPP account of the parent who actually received the Family Allowance or the CCB . Individuals must be well advised of the possible consequences of applying for the transfer of the CRP . The primary caregiver must advise the CCB -eligible parent that they will not be able to use the CRP if they agree to waive their rights to the CRP in favour of the primary caregiver. It is the primary caregiver's responsibility to advise the CCB -eligible parent unless the CPP has written authorization to communicate with the CCB -eligible parent that future eligibility for CPP pensions and benefits may be affected if they waive their rights to CRP . The Department cannot advise a person to waive their CRP eligibility. The eligibility for the CRP is proven by the CRA letter.

The evidence required to establish the conditions of eligibility to a DCCB are as follows: If the contributor is eligible for a DSB or a PRDB , the evidence required is the approval of the DSB or the PRDB . Effective January 1, 2025, at 65 years of age, when the DSB converts to the RTR pension or when the PRDB ends, the child will remain eligible for the DCCB , provided that they continue to meet all eligibility criteria (i.e. child-contributor relationship, school attendance for children 18 to 25 years of age). An application for the DCCB is made in the prescribed manner and at the prescribed location by: the disabled contributor for children under 18 years of age, if the children are under their decision-making responsibility and parenting time; the person or agency having decision-making responsibility and parenting time of children under 18 years of age; the child who has reached 18 years of age; or a disabled contributor's child under 18 years of age. In exceptional circumstances, the DCCB may be paid directly to the child. The child is the child of the disabled contributor; In addition to being the disabled contributor's child, the child must be a dependent child of the disabled contributor. If the child is 18 to 25 years of age, to be eligible for a CPP Child's benefit, they must also submit a CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form to confirm their full-time or part-time attendance at school or university. The CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) is a monthly, flat rate benefit that is adjusted annually. The CPP pays benefits to dependent children of disabled contributors provided they meet specific eligibility requirements for the DCCB .

topic_title: Protection and disclosure of the disabled contributor's information
text: To protect the privacy and personal information of a disabled contributor, the Department will not initiate contact with, or solicit a DCCB application or information from the child or the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child (i.e. an individual other than the disabled contributor) unless the Department receives the disabled contributor's written consent to do so. To ensure that their privacy and personal information is protected, disabled contributors may decide to: inform the child, individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child of possible entitlement to the DCCB ; provide their written consent for the Department to contact the child, the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child regarding possible entitlement to the DCCB ; or make no contact with the child, the individual or agency having custody and control of the child, and not provide their written consent for the Department to initiate contact with these individuals. If the disabled contributor decides not to make contact and not to provide their written consent for the Department to contact the child and, as a result, no one submits an application for the DCCB , the DCCB cannot be paid. Under the CPP, the Department is obligated to make decisions on all applications received. This includes all DCCB applications, even if the disabled contributor: has not provided written consent to initiate contact with the custodial parent; or instructs the Department not to initiate contact with the child or individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child. The disabled contributor may revoke their consent to contact the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child or the child directly, in writing, if contact has not been initiated.

text: If the client has requested their DSB benefit to be maximized rather than the SVR pension (for personal financial reasons), an alternate combined calculation can be used. Though this alternate calculation does not change the client's total entitlement amount, it could result in a change to the benefit split on their tax slip.

You are responsible for understanding and explaining to clients how we use the formulas to calculate the amount of combined CPP benefits. When calculating these benefits, a portion of the payment is assigned to each benefit. The CPP legislation states that the amount of a combined pension is subject to a ceiling for the year the contributor "first becomes entitled" to the second benefit. For the purposes of combined pension calculation, the year in which the survivor first became entitled to an SVR pension should be the year in which the survivor would have been eligible had the applicant applied. A combined benefit may create a receivable and a suspended payable. The system does not automatically recover the receivable. You must do a manual offset by recovering the receivable amount(s) from the payable. topic_title: Effective date of a combined benefit
text: The effective date of a combined benefit is the date the second CPP or QPP benefit became payable. For example, the effective date of a combined pension, where the second benefit is a DSB or an RTR pension, is considered the effective date of that benefit. In situations where the SVR pension is the second benefit, the effective date will be defined as the date of the combined first payment.

topic_title: Eligibility for receiving a combined benefit
text: You must determine if an applicant is eligible for a combined benefit. If an applicant meets the eligibility requirements for more than one benefit, they are eligible for and are required by CPP legislation to receive a combined benefit. A combined benefit can include either: a DSB and an SVR pension in which a contributor is in receipt of a DSB benefit based on their own contributions and is in receipt of an SVR pension based on the contributions of a deceased contributor; an RTR and an SVR pension in which a contributor is in receipt of an RTR pension based on their own contributions and is in receipt of an SVR pension based on the contributions of a deceased contributor; or an RTR , an SVR pension and a PRDB in which a contributor is in receipt of an RTR and PRDB based on their own contributions and is in receipt of an SVR pension based on the contributions of a deceased contributor. When calculating an RTR pension, an SVR pension and a PRDB , use the PRDB flat rate portion in the calculation. Subtract the SVR pension flat rate from the PRDB flat rate and add the difference to the RTR and the SVR combined pensions amount issued to the client. For more information on the policy, Combined Benefits (Policy)

As of January 1, 2019, the Department will begin the enhancement phase of the CPP components. The first additional and second additional components are not separate benefits, but top-ups to the original base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. The current formula used to calculate the base CPP combined benefits continues to apply and the maximum payable for the base component of a combined benefit cannot exceed the maximum base retirement or base disability rate. If there is a first additional or second additional SVR pension, RTR pension and/or DSB component, it will be added to the amount of the base component of the combined benefit. The eligibility criteria for CPP benefits are not affected by the enhancement as only the base component is used to determine eligibility and the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. CPP applicants The Department uses the client's SIN to identify and control a CPP contributor's account in ITRDS. To properly identify the contributor's Record of Earnings, applicants who apply for CPP pensions, benefits or provisions, or who request their Statement of Contributions, must provide their SIN. You have the authority to request a SIN from or on behalf of the following individuals: the former spouse or common-law partner of the applicant who is applying for CPP Credit Splitting; a surviving child or disabled contributor's child for whom an application for CPP Children's benefits is made; a disabled CPP contributor; a deceased CPP contributor; or the spouse or common-law partner of a disabled CPP contributor or the survivor of a deceased CPP contributor. OAS applicants To apply for the OAS pension, Allowance (ALW) and Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefits, the applicant must provide their SIN. If the applicant does not have a SIN and does not apply for one, the Department assigns a 9-digit number to process their application. Refer to Applicant does not have a SIN . You have the authority to request a SIN from or on behalf of the following individuals: Applicant does not have a SIN the applicant, where the applicant and the contributor are not the same person (e.g. ALWS benefits). SIN validation System validation When you enter a SIN in ITRDS, the system automatically validates it. If you enter even a single incorrect digit in the 9-digit SIN, ITRDS indicates it is invalid. The SIN, surname, given name and the date of birth provided on the application are matched against the SIN Validation file (M3001). The Social Insurance Registry (SIR) updates the M3001 file on a bi-weekly basis with new and amended SIN information. Manual validation To validate a SIN: Check the first 3 digits of the SIN to ensure that the range of the SIN has been issued by the SIR. The ninth digit is a check digit and must equal the result of the check digit calculation performed on the first 8 digits as follows: Add together the digits in the first, third, fifth and seventh positions in the SIN; Multiply each of the digits in the second, fourth, sixth and eighth positions in the SIN by 2, then add together each product of these calculations; Add the results of a) + b); and Subtract the last digit of the result of c) from 10 to get the check digit. Example To illustrate the process, the SIN 408-162-576 is used. Step Calculation 2 a) 4 + 8 + 6 + 5 = 23 2 b) (0 x 2 = 0 ; 1 x 2 = 2 ; 2 x 2 = 4 ; 7 x 2 = 14 [1 + 4]) ; 0 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 4 = 11 2 c) 23 + 11 = 4 4 (the last digit is 4) 2 d) 10 - 4 = 6 (6 is the ninth (check) digit in the SIN)

You must bring forward the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) request and contact the client to find out if they intend to apply for a CPP pension or benefit when: a CRP request form is received; there is no primary pension or benefit in pay; and no application for a CPP pension or benefit has been received. You must force deny the CRP request with a reason of Insufficient Documentation/Proof and update the client's notes in ITRDS if the following situations occur: The CRP data capture session is in Pending status and you have confirmed that either: the client does not intend to apply; or you were unable to contact them. There is no proof of birth and no eligibility for the CRP. In such cases, do not request proof of birth and send the appropriate denial letter to the applicant. For example, you must Force Deny the CRP request with the reason Insufficient documentation/Proof : if proof of birth is not provided after being requested; or if a child was born outside of Canada and did not enter Canada until after they had turned 7 years of age. You must then send a letter to the applicant explaining the reason for the denial (e.g. proof of birth not provided or ineligible because the child did not enter Canada until after they were 7 years old). When you review the pension or benefit information and notice the benefit is at the maximum rate before adjudicating the CRP: force deny the provision with the reason Insufficient documentation/Proof ; update the client's notes in ITRDS ; and send a letter to the client with the reason the CRP is denied. If you adjudicate the CRP request and there is no change in the benefit rate or the MQP has still not been met on a new benefit: withdraw the CRP; update the client's notes in ITRDS ; and send a letter to the client with the reason the CRP is denied. If you withdraw a CPP pension or benefit, you must also withdraw the CRP.

Once you force deny the credit split application, the benefit Status on the Credit Splitting screen will show as Denied and the reason will be Insufficient Documentation/Proof . ITRDS does not recognize the fact that there is no proof of divorce. If proof of divorce is not provided when processing a Credit Split application, do not submit the Data Capture Session. You must Force Deny the application.

You can select Ineligible Applicant or Insufficient Documentation/Proof as reasons to force deny a Death ( DTH ) benefit. If an application for a DTH benefit is received and the applicant is not the individual eligible to apply for it, you must first create a Contact to allow the Data Capture - DTH screen to become available. On the Data Capture - DTH screen, select Ineligible Applicant from the Force Deny Reason block and click Force Deny to submit. The Benefits screen opens and displays a DTH benefit Status of: Denied . If there is no proof of birth on the deceased's account and the applicant did not supply the documentation in the allowable time frame, force deny the DTH benefit with the reason Insufficient Documentation/Proof . If the deceased client does not have a social insurance number and there are no valid contributions, force deny the application with the reason Insufficient documentation and update the client's notes with the denial reason: Does not meet MQP . Then send the applicable denial letter to the applicant.

Former guidance products available through sites such as the EReference Library form the basis for new content found in the KMT. The KMT homepage was designed to comply with Treasury Board Secretariat standards on web accessibility and usability. It provides a number of ways to access various pensions processing resources. topic_title: How to access a landing page
text: Each drop-down menu in the Main Menu contains a "duplicate" entry that is identical to the corresponding menu heading. This duplicate entry appears as the top item of the drop-down menu. Clicking on these duplicate entries opens the Landing Page for the related drop-down menu. Example of a "duplicate" menu entry An example of the "duplicate" entry for the Monetary menu.

A Landing Page provides an expanded view that displays the contents of one of the drop-down menus described above. Specifically, a Landing Page displays all of the business scenarios found under one of the drop-down menus, grouped together by subject. A detailed description of a business scenario (or Scenario , as appearing in the KMT) is available in the Content Structure section below. A Landing Page serves as a visual aid for quickly locating content found under one of the drop-down menus of the Main Menu . Locating content on a Landing Page is often more effective than using other search methods, such as performing a key term search in the Search Bar . There are 2 main types of procedural content in the KMT, identified as either Scenarios or Actions . It is easy to distinguish between these 2 types of content in the KMT, as either the word Scenario or Action appears in brackets () following each document title. Scenarios A Scenario provides a complete outline of the knowledge needed to perform a work process (i.e. a business scenario). Scenarios often deal with complex situations involving multiple considerations. A Scenario serves as a map of how to complete a business process by providing a list of topics to consider and where to go for more information. It may help to think of a Scenario as an "umbrella", as it covers all of the reference material and action-based steps needed to complete a particular business process. To illustrate, the Retirement Pension Application (Scenario) covers all of the customary topics that may be present when processing a Retirement (RTR) pension application. It also covers procedural guidance for all of the tasks required to process an RTR pension application. Links to these action-based tasks, such as Data Capturing the Application in ITRDS, Requesting Documentation by Telephone or Mail, and Signing off the Application, are all types of Actions . The Retirement Pension Application (Scenario) also contains links to other Scenarios when more information is required in complex situations (e.g. dealing with a Third Party Request). Example of a Scenario in the KMT An example of a Scenario in the KMT. Actions Actions provide detailed instructions in a step-by-step format on how to perform specific tasks. It is common for multiple Actions to appear as links within a Scenario . For example, Actions appearing as links in the Retirement Pension Application (Scenario) as a non-exhaustive list include: Home Address, Correspondence Address or Payment Destination—Modify (Action) ; Retirement Pension Application—Data Capture in ITRDS (Action) ; and ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete (Action) . An agent must complete all of the Actions listed above to process an RTR pension application.

CPP and QPP agreements mandate that benefit amounts and qualification criteria are determined by the paying jurisdiction. The paying jurisdictions bill the other jurisdiction for the amount paid to the contributor on its behalf. After a data capture session, you may receive an On Hold - Awaiting RRQ Input message after you click Submit . This indicator means that the client may have QPP earnings. This information gets requested manually by the RRQ Request function in ITRDS. The transaction is held while the system requests and receives information from QPP. The RRQ Request screen in ITRDS is used to request earnings, credit splitting and benefits data from QPP. This can be done for single or multiple accounts. It can also be used to view the status of a request. Multiple selections can be made for each client. However, greyed out selections cannot be selected as they have already been requested. The status of the requests can be as follows: None will change to Pending when the request is submitted. Pending - AS and Pending - SDA will change to Received when QPP responds to the request. The status will also indicate Received if the answer from QPP is a blank record.

topic_title: Date of onset when prolonged criterion is subsequent to severe
text: In some situations, while the decision-maker may be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the applicant or beneficiary has a severe and prolonged disability at the time of adjudication, the disability may only have become prolonged at a time after the decision-maker is satisfied that the disability was severe. In such cases, the date of onset is determined to be when the disability became severe.

When considering whether a severe disability will be of indefinite duration, it is important to consider factors such as: the likelihood that existing or expected treatment(s) or intervention(s) will be successful; treatment failures; and the side effects associated with treatment(s). The prolonged criterion is met when, based on the factors listed above and any other factors, the duration of the severe disability is uncertain and cannot be predicted.

Canada Pension Plan Section 42(2)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Interpretation—Definitions—When person deemed disabled Section 44(1)(b)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Benefits Payable CPP regulations Section 68(1)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Determination of Disability Section 68.1(1)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Determination of Disability—Substantially gainful, in respect of an occupation

topic_title: Likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration
text: If a disability is found to be severe and is long continued and of an indefinite duration, that is, there is no reasonable end in sight for the disability based on existing or expected treatment(s) or intervention(s) or any other relevant factors, the disability is considered prolonged. It is possible that evidence demonstrates a disability is long continued but does not demonstrate that it is of indefinite duration. Such applications should be denied. The following examples illustrate this concept. Examples An applicant or beneficiary with a severe medical condition who is expected to recover following treatment or therapy, or who has a favourable prognosis for recovery despite the length of time does not meet prolonged criterion; When a disability is of indefinite duration, it is also long continued and therefore prolonged. However, a disability that is long continued is not necessarily of indefinite duration.
The prolonged criterion is met if a disability is found to be severe and the evidence on file is conclusive that the disability is likely to result in death.

For the purposes of CPP, an applicant or beneficiary must meet both the severe and prolonged criteria to be considered disabled. To establish that a disability is prolonged, one of the following 2 components must be met: the disability is likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration; or the disability is likely to result in death.

topic_title: Prolonged considerations when there is a favourable prognosis
text: Evidence of a favourable prognosis is not always sufficient to lead to a determination that the prolonged criterion is not met. In such circumstances, medical knowledge and experience is used to establish and explain how the applicant or beneficiary meets the prolonged criteria despite a favourable prognosis.
CPP regulations Subsection 68(1)—Determination of Disability

The Minister can determine initial and continuing eligibility for CPP Disability benefits based on medical reports and information completed by: Nurse pra ctitioners (no restrictions); and Registered nurses only for applicants or beneficiaries residing in geographically isolated areas. Registered nurses must use records maintained by treating physicians or n urse practitioners . When there is insufficient information on a file to make an eligibility determination, additional information is requested only from physicians and N urse practitioners . Geographic isolation Consider the following factors when determining geographical isolation: regional area; availability of medical services; and accessible roads. This same practice applies to arranging functional capacity evaluation or combined functional capacity evaluation/independent medical examination for applicants and beneficiaries. functional capacity evaluation or combined functional capacity evaluation/independent medical examination Invoices I f the conditions above are met and payments for medical reports are requested, CPP compensates physicians, nurse practitioners and registered nurses based on the current fee schedule.

Impact of age on medical condition With increasing age, the findings related to the medical condition(s) change. There can be an associated increase in the incidence and severity of cognitive and physical impairments, leading to disability. The same medical condition(s) may cause significantly different functional limitations in applicants/beneficiaries of different ages. For example, a younger applicant or beneficiary will more likely than not, have better recovery after surgery or treatment. Impact of age on employability It must be determined how the applicant or beneficiary’s functional capacity for work is affected or influenced by their age. As individuals are impacted by the aging process differently, determining how age affects their ability to retrain or adjust to other work should be performed for each applicant or beneficiary according to their specific circumstances. The following age ranges are guidelines to assist in determining the potential impact of an applicant’s or beneficiary’s age on their employability. These ranges reflect an understanding that younger persons are usually better able to adapt to other work. In certain situations, it is the combination of age, medical condition(s), or expected recovery and treatment time that suggests it is unlikely that the applicant or beneficiary would be capable of returning to work. Age** Impact on employability Under 45 Age is not usually a significant factor in limiting their ability to adjust to other work. 45 to 49 While not usually significantly affected in their ability to adjust to other work, age could be more a factor for making an adjustment to other work. 50 to 54 May be affected in their ability to adjust to other work when combined with other factors, such as limited work experience and a medical condition(s). 55 and over May be significantly affected in their ability to adjust to other work. **These categories are not intended to replace any information on the applicant’s or beneficiary’s file that provides particular information about them.

Education includes formal and informal education as well as training. Higher levels of education or training demonstrate the likelihood an individual will be capable of additional training in the future. Formal education completed many years ago may no longer be relevant in terms of the applicant’s or beneficiary’s capacity to pursue any substantially gainful occupation (SGO). Therefore: less emphasis should be given to formal education which occurred in the remote past; and consider education, training, or knowledge acquired or used in their most recent work in the context of their capacity to perform other types of SGO. Impact of medical condition on ability to retrain It should be confirmed as to whether there are any physical or cognitive limitations related to the applicant’s or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) that would affect their ability to retrain. Despite previous education, some medical condition(s) could make learning new tasks and responsibilities difficult. Personal characteristics must be considered when determining whether the combination of medical condition(s) and personal characteristics make it more likely than not that the contributor is disabled according to the CPP. Consideration must be given in a real world context, regarding what effect the combination of the applicant’s or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) and personal characteristics have on their functional capacity and ability to pursue any substantially gainful occupation (SGO). Consideration must be given to the combined effect of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) and their: age; education; work experience; and language proficiency. Examples of socio-economic factors not to consider: Regional unemployment rates; Local access to specific jobs; Types of major industry in the region; Types of occupations offered by regional industries; and Occupational skills needed for those industries. The included parameters serve only as a baseline to help in decision making, not to quantify how to consider personal characteristics. Personal characteristics should be considered in the same manner that a medical condition is evaluated. A simple diagnosis may not always be sufficient to evaluate an applicant’s or beneficiary’s level of disability.
The intent of this policy is to help decision makers evaluate the implications of personal characteristics in relation to the medical condition and functional capacity as a whole.

A determination must be made as to whether the applicant ’s or beneficiary’s past work and life experience may have provided them with any transferable skills that could enhance their capacity for substantially gainful work, including: on-the-job training; occupation-specific courses ; or volunteer work, etc. Impact of medical condition on ability to work It should be confirmed as to whether there are physical or cognitive limitations related to the applicant’s or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) that would affect their ability to use skills they had previously obtained. Impact of work experience on employability While in the past, many individuals worked for the same employer during their entire career, it is common today for an individual to work in a variety of jobs during their working years. This variation in work experience indicates they are likely capable of adjusting to other work. Similarly, individuals with transferable skills commonly have an advantage over low-skilled workers in the labour market. Skill level corresponds to the type or amount of training and education required to work in an occupation. It also reflects the experience required and the complexity of the responsibilities involved in the work. In most cases, progression to a highly skilled occupation is not possible without the completion of additional formal education, whereas progression from a low skilled occupation to one with higher skills is often achievable through on-the-job training and experience. Essential skills are the skills that provide the foundation for learning all other skills and enable individuals to better prepare for, get and keep a job, and adapt and succeed at work. Essential skills are used in the workplace in different ways and at different levels of complexity. The level of complexity can range from basic to advanced, and varies based on the work being performed. Where the applicant or beneficiary has a work history characterized by physically active work, consideration must be given as to whether it is likely they can perform sedentary work. Usually, these jobs require the ability to do light work with your hands, to do repetitive tasks which require fine motor skills, and literacy. During the assessment of eligibility and continued eligibility, it is to be determined if the associated functional limitations related to the medical condition(s) impact the applicant’s or beneficiary’s ability to regularly pursue any substantially gainful occupation. A functional limitation hinders an individual’s ability to perform tasks or participate in activities. For CPP DSB and PRDB purposes, the focus is on those functional limitations affecting an individual’s work capacity. How these limitations affect the ability to function in both daily and work life requires a holistic assessment to determine eligibility and continued eligibility. Limitations may occur in one or more domains: physical abilities; behaviours and emotional abilities; communication and thinking abilities; and other daily abilities. Consideration should be given to possible linkages across domains in order to understand how difficulty in one domain may be affecting another. Both the individual’s self-reported functional limitations and the perspectives of their healthcare provider(s) should be considered.

topic_title: Impact of treatment and interventions Updated
text: The purpose of treatment and interventions is to stabilize, restore or improve health and function. Treatment and interventions may vary depending on the nature and severity of the medical condition(s). They may also depend on the individual’s response to treatment interventions. The goal of treatment may be: curative; therapeutic; to help control the progression or deterioration of a medical condition; to provide relief of symptoms (e.g. alleviate pain); to maintain quality of life; or to assist in providing insight and development of necessary coping mechanisms. The treating practitioner, in collaboration with the applicant or beneficiary, determines the most appropriate course of treatment. Certain treatments may not be attempted, or may be discontinued, due to reasons such as: suitability; availability; or affordability. Consideration should be given to how medical treatments and interventions are impacting the work capacity of an individual.

The Late Applicant Provision (LAP) is for individuals applying for a DSB or a PRDB who do not have sufficient earnings and contributions in the 6 years prior to the date of their application. The LAP protects contributors who would have met the earnings, contributions and medical criteria had they applied at an earlier time. There is no restriction to the number of times an individual can apply for benefits or the number of times the LAP can be used. Conditions of the provision For the DSB , the LAP can be considered if: other applicable provisions, such as: the Child Rearing Provision (CRP); the proration of earnings; credit splitting; additional earnings; International Agreements (IA); and previous DSB periods have been considered and the applicant still does not meet the current DSB contributory requirements. the applicant meets the contributory requirements at an earlier date. For the PRDB , when the Date of Onset (DOO) or established DOO falls between January 2019 and April 2023, the LAP can be considered if: the applicant does not meet the contributory requirements at the date of application; the applicable provisions (e.g. credit splitting and IA) have been considered; the applicant still does not meet the contributory requirements; and the considered date of application cannot be earlier than the individual’s Early Retirement (ERTR) pension effective date. Considered Date of Application The application for the LAP with respect to a PRDB Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) calculation requires that the application must be received earlier than it was. The considered date of application creates a new 6-year window during which the earnings and contributions must be present. The considered date of application cannot be before 2019, the year PRDB came into force, or the year the individual started receiving their ERTR pension. Determination of the DSB Latest Possible Date of Onset The Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) will be established based on an applicant’s earnings, contributions and all applicable legislative provisions. The legislative contributory requirements in effect at the DOO or established DOO must be met to determine the LPDOO. LPDOO and PRDB For the purpose of a PRDB , it is not necessary for the individual’s DOO to have started within the MQP. It is only necessary that the individual meets the contributory requirements, has a DOO or established DOO on or after January 2019 and before their 65th birthday.

These include: the Child Rearing Provision; the proration of earnings; Credit splitting; additional earnings; International Agreements; and previous DSB or PRDB periods. topic_title: Applicable circumstances for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control
text: Table 1. Circumstance Description Long-term care and nursing homes One spouse or common-law partner remains in the matrimonial home and the other is placed in a nursing home or long-term care facility. Both members of the couple are in a nursing home or long-term care facility. This may be the same or different facilities, including the same room. Medical condition One member of the couple needs ongoing medical care and assistance with activities of daily living and moves into an alternate dwelling with someone who takes care of their needs (e.g. a family member), while the other spouse or common-law partner remains in the matrimonial home. This move may be of a temporary or permanent nature. Transitional situations One member of the couple is hospitalized, awaiting a bed in a long-term care facility, while the other spouse or common-law partner remains in the matrimonial home. Employment The couple must live apart for economic or employment reasons such as availability of work or proximity to medical assistance.

A Statutory Declaration is not needed to prove a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control. The following documents are acceptable: a written statement with the date and reasons for living apart, the names and addresses of the persons living apart, and the signature of one or both of the persons living apart; or the "Statement - Spouses or Common-law Partners Living Apart for Reasons beyond their Control" form indicating the date and reasons for living apart, the names and addresses of the persons living apart, and the signature of one, or both of the persons living apart.

On January 1, 2017, the change in benefit calculation for couples living apart beyond their control became effective the month after the month in which the event causing them to live apart occurs. Retroactive adjustments can be made back to that month as long as eligibility and entitlement existed throughout the period. However, the retroactive adjustment for couples receiving the GIS or ALW benefits can only go back as far as January 1, 2017, as that is the date the provision came into force for the ALW benefit

topic_title: End date for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control
text: A couple will continue to be paid at the single rate because of living apart for reasons beyond their control until such time that the circumstances change and the provision no longer applies. For instance, the provision no longer applies when: the couple begins to share a dwelling that is maintained by them (e.g. when they both start living in the matrimonial home again); the couple separates; one of them dies.
Old Age Security Act Section 15(3)—Continuing direction

In recognition of the difficulties that couples face when they are forced to live apart as a result of circumstances beyond their control, the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) has a provision that allows the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) and the Allowance ( ALW ) benefits to be calculated at a more favourable rate. To use their income for the purposes of calculating a more favourable benefit rate, the couple must: be living apart as a result of circumstances not attributable to either party; and not be living together in a dwelling maintained by either of them. For the GIS and the ALW benefits, where it has been determined that a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control and there is no change in their marital status, their benefit(s) may be calculated at a more favourable rate. This provision is applicable to couples where: One person is eligible for the GIS benefit Both persons are eligible for the GIS benefit or One person is eligible for the GIS benefit and the other person is eligible for the ALW benefit. It allows each member of the couple to have their entitlement calculated at the single rate based on their individual income and it is not intended to place the couple in a worse financial situation. If the single rate is calculated on individual income and it is not advantageous to the couple, the benefit(s) will continue to be calculated based on the couple's combined income. If, as a result of applying this provision, the benefit of one person in the couple is reduced or no longer entitled, but it is to the overall advantage of the couple, written authorization by that person or their Power of Attorney, trustee or legal representative must be obtained before benefits can be recalculated.

A person who is not satisfied with a decision or determination made under the OAS Act for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control is subject to the same reconsideration rights as an individual who is not satisfied with the benefit amount or denial of the benefit. Therefore, reconsideration rights should be given for a decision to deem or not deem a beneficiary living apart for reasons beyond their control for the purposes of the GIS and ALW .
Canada Pension Plan Section 42(2)—Interpretation—Definitions

Definition of terminal illness For CPP purposes, a Terminal Illness (TI) is defined as a medical condition that cannot be cured or adequately treated and is reasonably expected to result in death within 6 months. When a doctor, nurse practitioner or a registered nurse in a geographically isolated area completes a medical attestation or medical report, they use this definition to attest that an applicant has a TI. TI attestation The Terminal Illness Medical Attestation for a Disability Benefits Application under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530B) form or section 4 a) of the Medical Report for Canada Pension Plan Disability Benefits (ISP-2519) form is sufficient evidence to determine that an applicant has a severe and prolonged disability. The attestation should be taken at face value and development should only be undertaken in unique circumstances, such as late applications or if the applicant is working at the date of application. In cases where the medical condition is suggestive of a TI, but an attestation is not completed, screening for a grave medical condition should take place.

Determining whether an applicant is disabled or a beneficiary continues to be disabled, according to the CPP, is an administrative decision. Administrative decisions are to be made based on the civil standard of proof: a balance of probabilities. To grant or continue paying a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit, the civil standard of proof must be met. That is, on a balance of probabilities, the applicant or beneficiary in respect of whom the determination is made, is determined to: be disabled; or continue to be disabled. The civil standard of proof is not a standard of certainty but rather a nuanced approach intended to give the decision-maker, when reviewing all of the evidence, the ability to come to a conclusion as to which is more likely to be true, the applicant or beneficiary is: disabled or not disabled.

topic_title: The Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities standard
text: The satisfied on a balance of probabilities standard is to be applied in determining an applicant or beneficiary's eligibility or continuing eligibility for a Disability (DSB) benefit under the CPP. All of the objective and subjective evidence provided to the decision-maker to determine whether an applicant or beneficiary meets the CPP definition of disability, must be weighed. That is, a decision-maker must be satisfied that the applicant or beneficiary has, or continues to have, a severe and prolonged disability. Absolute proof of disability is not required. For the purposes of determining eligibility or continuing eligibility for a DSB benefit, the standard of proof used is the civil standard on a balance of probabilities rather than the criminal standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. To say that something is proven on a balance of probabilities means that it is more likely than not to have occurred—it is probable. Therefore, an applicant or beneficiary must be found more likely than not to be, or still be, disabled according to the definition of disability under the CPP. Additionally, a balance of probabilities standard of proof requires the disability be considered in the context of the whole person. That is, not only the medical condition(s) are considered, but also how the capacity to work and personal characteristics affect the particular applicant or beneficiary.

topic_title: To be satisfied on a balance of probabilities
text: It must be determined that it is more likely than not the CPP severe and prolonged criteria is met/continues to be met after considering, weighing, and analyzing the objective and subjective evidence about the nature and extent of the applicant's/beneficiary’s: medical condition(s); treatment and impact; limitations; prognosis; work capacity; and personal characteristics.

1. The Knowledge Management Tool (KMT) for Pensions was designed for you! Over 150 processing staff from all regions and levels helped play a role in shaping a tool that was built “with processing, for processing”. This includes Program Services Officers, Program Support Clerks, Service Canada Benefit Officers, Team Leaders, Business Expertise and Medical Adjudicators from all pensions programs. Representatives from regional processing also participated in our National Working Group and helped design and test the KMT layout and content. 2. Some key KMT features were borrowed, not invented The KMT design team worked with representatives from processing to learn what regional tools and features worked best for them and which ones they would like to see included in the new national tool. The Benefits Toolbox, which appears on the KMT homepage, and the automatically generated Bring Forward date calculator were popular features that were integrated into your tool as a result of feedback. 3. The KMT was initially referred to as the “Pensions eTool” Before being given its new name, you may have heard of the “Pensions eTool”. This was the name initially used to refer to the KMT project. Perhaps you or someone you know was involved in early focus group discussions which lead to the project being initiated in 2015. Perhaps you know someone who participated in the Pensions eTool National Working Group or was involved in testing the tool’s functionality and content over the past two years. Either way, the KMT has been the result of the combined efforts of many of your colleagues. Give them a big thanks! 4. The KMT is being released to CPP first, but plans are underway to onboard OAS, CPPD and International Operations (IO) While CPP processing has been on boarded to the tool first, we are not stopping there. Work is ongoing on developing specific OAS, CPPD and IO content, as well as integrating content for these programs into the KMT’s common procedures. 5. The KMT needs you to make it better! The KMT will continue to grow and evolve with your help and feedback. Are you having trouble finding something or expecting to see an item in a different place? Use the KMT feedback button for these kinds of navigational suggestions, as well as for any broken links or typos you may find. You can also use the KMT feedback button to share suggestions or ask questions about missing information, the clarity of procedures, or site improvements. Remember that client-specific enquiries as well as suggestions for general improvements to pensions programs should be sent through to your Business Expertise contact.

topic_title: Contributor criteria for an ITRDS SOC request
text: If a CPP contributor requests a SOC , you can generate a CPP SOC automatically from the ITRDS Contributions screen. Providing you have the authority, a button to request the SOC will be present. You must ensure that the contributor criteria listed below are met before processing the SOC request. The CPP contributor must: be 18 years of age or older; have a prime social insurance number ( SIN ); have a valid name; have made at least one valid contribution; be a CPP only contributor with a home address or a dual ( CPP and QPP ) contributor with a home address outside Quebec; have a foreign address of 4 lines or less; have credit split UPE for QPP and none from CPP , if applicable; not have a fraud warning on their account; and not have a pending or processed CPP Death or Survivor's benefit, if deceased. topic_title: SOC and Canada Revenue Agency Updated
text: The SOC provides contributors with a year by year summary statement of their: CPP earnings and contributions (and QPP , if applicable); and estimates of their CPP pension and benefit dollar amounts. Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ) and Revenu Québec are responsible for collecting CPP and QPP earnings and contributions data from the following documents: copies of T4 and Relevé 1 forms submitted by employers; or T1 and TP1 general forms submitted by the self-employed. CRA and Revenu Québec regularly transfer this data to Employment and Social Development Canada ( ESDC ) where it is posted to each contributor's Record of Earnings (ROE). A contributor's CPP ROE account is used to: determine eligibility for CPP benefits; calculate the CPP benefits entitlement amount; calculate the estimated monthly CPP benefits on the CPP SOC ; display earnings and contributions data on the CPP SOC , including any divided pensionable earnings and any Child Rearing Drop-in credits; calculate the Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) by year; and prepare and send a manual CPP or CPP / QPP SOC . When a CPP pension or benefit application is processed, the CPP benefit entitlement amount is often based on interim earnings due to the delay between the moment CRA reports the contributor's income and the income appearing on the contributor's ROE. When ESDC receives earnings updates from CRA or QPP , the new data will trigger a recalculation. When the account is readjudicated in ITRDS , the CPP benefit amount is adjusted accordingly.

Some individuals may be entitled to Disability (DSB) benefits as well as benefits from other jurisdictions, notably provincial Workers’ Compensation Boards. The “stacking” of such benefits can result in combined benefits equal to or even more than the pre-disability income. This is a disincentive to rehabilitation and Return to Work. The CPP provides authority for the Minister to enter into agreements that would set rules for determining the amount of such DSB benefits to be paid by CPP and the amount to be paid by the other jurisdiction. In no case can the agreement result in the individual receiving a total benefit that is less than the amount that would otherwise be payable under the CPP.

topic_title: Conversion from a Disability benefit to a Retirement pension
text: When a Disability (DSB) beneficiary reaches age 65, the benefit is automatically converted to an Retirement (RTR) pension. An RTR pension is calculated for the year the disability started. Full price indexing to the effective date of the RTR pension is provided. There is also a further adjustment if the beneficiary’s disability commenced in 1987 or earlier to account for the manner in which the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) was calculated before that time. Former DSB beneficiary becomes eligible for an RTR pension If a DSB benefit was paid for an y period age 60 or beyond the special conversion calculation i s applicable. If DSB benefits are ceased before age 60, conversion from DSB benefit to RTR pension is not applicable. The calculation of the RTR pension is based on the YMPE average for the year the RTR pension starts.

topic_title: Special adjustment—Disability benefit effect on a Retirement pension
text: Beneficiaries who receive or received CPP Disability (DSB) benefits have their Retirement (RTR) pension calculated using the average of the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings for the year the RTR pension starts and the 2 previous years. This provides wage indexation protection from the time the DSB benefit started. The legislation introduces a special RTR pension calculation for persons who received DSB benefits for any period beyond age 60. While contributors who received a DSB benefit continue to receive a higher than average RTR pension compared to other contributors, the difference will be less.

In situations where individuals are widowed twice (or more), the greater of the calculated Survivor's (SVR) pension entitlements will be paid. If a pensioner’s SVR pension is subsequently reduced following a credit split, as the SVR entitlement amount is based on: the deceased contributor’s earnings and contributions; age at the time of death; and the deceased ex-spouse submitted a credit split application within the legal time frame from the date of death, then the pensioner becomes eligible for the other pension, which is now the greater of the 2.

topic_title: 2+ years of earnings at or above the SGO benchmark
text: Earnings above the SGO benchmark for 2 or more years likely indicate the individual has work capacity. However, an assessment of these earnings should occur to ensure they are due to work activity and not from other sources. Development may be required. If it is determined the earnings are not due to work activity, assess the applicant/beneficiary considering the Severe Criterion: Medical Condition and Functional Limitations guidance.

The number of hours an applicant or beneficiary participates in paid employment each week is part of a holistic assessment in determining if this activity is reflective of work capacity. General Guidelines for Work Activity

The predictability of attendance may be reflected in an individual’s ability to work scheduled shifts, in a predictable manner, over a sustained period. Consideration must be given to individuals with unpredictable or irregularly occurring medical conditions and resulting functional limitations (for example, those with mental health diagnoses or cyclical conditions which have periods of exacerbations and remissions). The limitations associated with these condition may prevent them from being able to sustain predictable employment. These applicants or beneficiaries may therefore not be regularly capable of work. For applicants and beneficiaries with varied weekly hours of work or work attendance, a longitudinal assessment of work activity may be necessary to determine their work capacity. Development may be required.

topic_title: Assessing Work Capacity When Earnings are Below SGO
text: When an applicant or beneficiary has earnings below the SGO benchmark, a holistic assessment is to occur to help determine each individual's circumstances and overall work capacity, including: predictability of attendance; the number of hours worked; earnings (in the case of self-employed individuals, gross business earnings); the effect of their medical condition(s) and functional limitations; non-medical reasons affecting work activity; and any evidence to the contrary/information that suggests otherwise. All evidence is to be weighed and the balance of probabilities approach is to be used in determining the eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPP DSB benefits.

topic_title: Assessment of Earnings from Work Activity
text: In May 2014, a subsection of the CPP Regulations came into force which defined “any substantially gainful occupation” (SGO) as one that provides a salary or wage equal to or greater than the maximum amount a beneficiary would receive as a CPP DSB benefit. With this definition, a benchmark of earnings has now been set which clearly defines SGO and serves as a measurement for work capacity. Considering this, earnings can be categorized as follows:

Earnings below the SGO benchmark require a holistic assessment to determine if the individual has work capacity. Refer to the section Assessing Work Capacity when earnings are below SGO for further guidance.

topic_title: Earnings at or above the SGO benchmark
text: Earnings above the SGO benchmark likely indicate an individual has work capacity. However, an assessment of these earnings should occur to ensure they are due to work activity and not from other sources. Development may be required. If it is determined the earnings are not due to work activity, assess the applicant/beneficiary considering the Severe Criterion: Medical Condition and Functional Limitations guidance.

In legislation, the phrase “incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation” defines the severe criterion. The severe criterion is a measure of work capacity. For applicants and beneficiaries engaged in work activity, work capacity is defined with two indicators: work activity (incapable regularly pursuing) income earned from work activity (any substantially gainful occupation).

This policy provides guidance on the assessment of work capacity where there is evidence of work activity. It applies to both applicants and beneficiaries of the CPP disability (DSB) benefit and the Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB). The guidance should be used in the assessment of work capacity for: individuals who are currently working (either for an employer or are self-employed); beneficiaries who have worked since they were determined to be eligible for the CPP DSB benefit or PRDB; applicants who qualify under the late applicant provision and who may not be currently working, but have worked on or after their latest possible date of onset (LPDOO).
Individuals participating in paid employment between 15 and 30 hours per week may be demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity should occur.

topic_title: Working less than 15 hours per week
text: Individuals participating in paid employment for less than 15 hours per week are usually not demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity is required.
Individuals participating in paid employment over 30 hours per week are likely demonstrating work capacity, unless the evidence on file supports otherwise.

Lifetime renewal designation Before May 3, 2007, pensioners or beneficiaries were only eligible to automatically renew their GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit without an application if they were in receipt of a benefit in the month before the start of the next payment period (i.e. June). Effective May 3, 2007, pensioners or beneficiaries are eligible to be automatically renewed for benefits without an application beginning with the 2008-2009 payment period, provided they meet the following requirements: A GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary was in receipt of benefits on May 3, 2007. An applicant's initial GIS, ALW or ALWS application was received before May 3, 2007, but processed and approved on or after this date. In this situation, even if the applicant is not entitled due to excess income, they are still considered a lifetime renewal applicant. An applicant's initial GIS, ALW or ALWS application is received and approved on or after May 3, 2007. In this situation, even if the applicant is not entitled due to excess income, they are still considered a lifetime renewal applicant. Requirement for an application is waived The requirement for a GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit application can be waived for any subsequent year for which the pensioner or beneficiary's income information is provided to the Department via the CRA one-way transmission, or by a statement of income received directly from the pensioner or beneficiary where they must have a lifetime renewal designation. Lifetime renewal designation lost Communicating to the pensioner or beneficiary that the Department is not waiving their renewal application means the pensioner or beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewal designation until a new application is received and approved (e.g. a new application (GIS, ALW or ALWS )). It is required to confirm eligibility and entitlement if a pensioner or beneficiary loses their lifetime renewal designation. Situations in which the lifetime renewal designation is no longer applicable: The ALW or ALWS beneficiary: ALW beneficiary becomes divorced or separated for more than 3 months from their pensioner spouse or common-law partner; or ALWS beneficiary no longer meets the definition of survivor. If the pensioner is no longer eligible for the OAS pension, the pensioner or beneficiary is no longer eligible to receive the GIS or ALW benefits and their lifetime renewal designation ends. When the pensioner or beneficiary leaves Canada for more than 6 months, their entitlement stops 6 months after the month of departure. If their absence is considered: permanent (i.e. involving a change in residence) and they no longer reside in Canada, they are no longer eligible to receive GIS, ALW or ALWS benefits, and their lifetime renewal designation ends. temporary (i.e. not involving a change in residence), they will continue to be eligible to receive GIS, ALW or ALWS benefits and will retain their lifetime renewal designation. Sponsored immigrants Sponsored individuals who have applied for a GIS, an ALW or an ALWS benefit and who meet all other eligibility and entitlement criteria can be approved for the benefit but may not be entitled for payment because they are under a sponsorship agreement. The approval of their benefits allows the Department to consider them a lifetime renewal applicant. This allows them to have subsequent applications for their respective benefits waived as part of the lifetime renewal designation process. The decision to waive a future application is at the discretion of the Department.

Since the inception of the CPP disability program in 1966, there has been a significant shift in how disability and persons with disabilities are seen in relation to their ability to participate in the workforce. Disability is now seen as the result of environmental, social, and attitudinal barriers preventing an individual from fully participating in society. Persons with disabilities have the right to full and equal participation and inclusion in society. Considering this, a consistent and equitable approach to assessment of work activity and SGO criteria are applied to all individuals engaged in any type of work. Accommodation Employers have an obligation to accommodate employees as long as the accommodation(s) do not result in undue hardship to the employer. Sheltered Work Exception In rare circumstances, it may be determined an applicant or beneficiary is employed in a truly sheltered employment setting. The primary purpose of this type of therapeutic work is for social connection and cognitive stimulation, rather than to provide an income. Examples of these types of settings include: employment of institutionalized individuals in mental health facilities; and community run programs for individuals with specific disabilities, often for those with developmental delays. A defining characteristic of this work is the highly supportive nature of this type of work. Thus a modified approach to assessment of work activity and income earned should occur.

The profitability must be considered together with: the medical condition; performance and productivity factors; and personal characteristics. Medical evidence may be the most important evidence in assessing a self-employed applicant or beneficiary's performance and productivity.

topic_title: Adverse side effects of health care treatment
text: There may be well documented adverse side effects of treatment. An evaluation of the magnitude of these adverse side effects should be made to determine whether it constitutes a reasonable reason for non-compliance.

An applicant or beneficiary may not have access to the appropriate medical facility, institution or clinic because financial pressures on the health care system have resulted in significant rationing or the elimination of certain treatments. For example, there may be long waiting lists to access the required health care treatments that make it impractical to expect the applicant/beneficiary to comply.

An applicant or beneficiary with a chronic medical condition for an extensive period of time may: have tried health care treatments in the past that were unsuccessful; and be reluctant to follow the recommended treatment again.

topic_title: Cognitive difficulties or mental health illness
text: An illness, injury or the effect of medications can hamper an applicant or beneficiary’s cognitive ability to evaluate the: benefits; risks; and nature of h ealth care treatments.

The assessment of compliance with treatment should not rely solely on expectations of what appropriate treatment might be for a given illness or impairment. It is the actual treatment recommendations documented on file which must form the basis of an evaluation of compliance.

Not all forms of health care treatment are financially subsidized by public or private health care systems in Canada. Not all CPP disability applicants or beneficiaries have access to extended health care coverage. Although an applicant or beneficiary might choose to be compliant with the health care treatment, their financial situation may be such that they cannot afford to pay directly for the health care treatment, if that is the only way it can be accessed.

topic_title: Knowledge and understanding of health care treatment protocol
text: An applicant or beneficiary may not completely understand the benefits, risks and nature of treatment recommendations due to problems with literacy and cultural or language barriers.
