Disabled applicants or beneficiaries may have difficulty coping with stressful life situations. This may be a combination of: la ck of child care; transportation problems; or la ck of financial and/or social supports.

Non-compliance with health treatment is the failure or refusal to accept and follow investigation or treatment recommendations. Non-compliance with health care treatment can include: not attending investigation or treatment appointments; not taking prescribed medications; not accepting to undergo surgical interventions; not accepting other specialized forms of treatment (e.g. radiation, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychotherapy and counselling, substance abuse programs); not adhering to dietary recommendations; and inconsistent adherence to an exercise program.

The determination of eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPP Disability benefits includes the assessment of the impact of non-compliance with recommended treatment on the beneficiary’s ability to work. Non-compliance with health care treatment is an element to be considered and is generally not the sole reason for denying benefits. Various factors may lead to non-compliance by an applicant/beneficiary with health care treatment recommendations and a need to be assessed. Any combination of the following factors need to be considered in assessing the applicant or beneficiary’s decision about complying with health care treatment.

topic_title: Reasons for non-compliance with health care treatment
text: An applicant or beneficiary’s failure to comply with recommended health care treatments can be affected by a number of factors which need to be documented and assessed to determine the impact on their capacity to work. Reasonable cause or efforts are present where the known facts and circumstances are such that a reasonable person in the same situation would make a similar decision or exhibit similar behaviour. If an applicant or beneficiary refuses or fails to follow recommended treatment, it must be determined: whether or not the reason for non-compliance constitutes reasonable cause; and if they made reasonable efforts to follow the recommended treatment.

topic_title: Risks associated with health care treatment
text: There are varying degrees of risk associated with any health care treatment. The degree of risk can be: dependent on the type of health care treatment. associated with well kno wn and conventional treatments that may be lower than the degree of risk associated with experimental treatments. associated with medications, physiotherapy, exercise programs, etc. that may be lower than the degree of risk associated with major surgery or other invasive health care treatments. associated with a health care treatment that may be higher if the applicant/beneficiary has multiple medical conditions where the health care treatments for each particular medical condition may increase the risk of complications.

topic_title: Transportation limitations, geographical location and lack of social supports
text: Access to appropriate transportation to attend health care assessment or treatment needs to be considered in assessing non-compliance. An applicant or beneficiary may not have access to health care treatment because of where they live. Urban areas have greater accessibility in terms of: av ailability of a wide range of services; proximity to services; and continuity of care for health care treatment. An applicant or beneficiary in a rural or remote area may not have access to regular health care treatment services and facilities. The range of services may be limited or require long-distance travel. They may not have family and/or community supports that enable them to participate in health care treatment.

Compliance with health care treatment is a personal health issue between the applicant or beneficiary and their health care provider. The decision to comply with treatment is an ethical and legal question involving informed valid consent. It implies that an individual, after having been informed of the benefits/risks, has the right and freedom to: make their own treatment decisions; and deal with the consequences of these decisions.

The Minister has the authority to ask an applicant to undergo a Functional Capacity Evaluation (FCE) and an Independent Medical Examination to assess their eligibility, or continuing eligibility, for CPP Disability (DSB) benefits. Written consent must be obtained if there is: medical clearance from a physician; and consent from the applicant or beneficiary before sending for an FCE. In situations where the physician suggests in the medical report that the applicant or beneficiary be sent for an FCE, written medical clearance from the physician is required. If the applicant or beneficiary’s physician does not provide written consent, the Department cannot take any further action on the FCE. This procedure provides you with the steps to follow when processing an application, file or account for co-workers, relatives or friends.

Report to your manager or team leader if you: receive applications, files, or accounts for yourself, co-workers, former co-workers, relatives or friends. Your manager will distribute these to another team member or region, if necessary; discover an employee is processing an application, file or account for themselves, co-workers, former co-workers, relatives or friends; or are a Power of Attorney or trustee for a client. Managers or team leaders will ensure that you do not receive these files.

You must not knowingly witness, process, amend, or otherwise handle any application, file or account for benefits for: yourself; co-workers; relatives by blood or marriage (including common-law relationships); or friends. The term "friend" is defined in the broadest possible sense. Avoid being or appearing to be under obligation to any person or organization that might profit from special consideration by you. Do not offer assistance in dealing with the government to any individual or entity where such assistance is outside the official role of an employee without first obtaining written permission from your supervisor. No employee should exert any form of influence over the processing of any application, file or account and particularly those involving benefits for: themselves; co-workers; relatives by blood or by marriage (including common-law); or friends. Influence can include, but is not limited to, an employee: asking another employee to process an application, file or account for benefits for themselves, a co-worker, relative or friend before other applications, files or accounts, where it would not normally be processed at that time; requesting that any subsequent action on an application, file or account for benefits for themselves, a co-worker, relative or friend be discussed with them before proceeding; or using knowledge of the benefit adjudication process to provide an unfair advantage to the processing of a co-worker's, relative's or friend's application, file or account. The Department recognizes that employees may have Power of Attorney or trustee status for a client. However, an employee who has Power of Attorney or trustee status for a client may not handle that client's application, file or account in their capacity as an employee. Employees can request information concerning an application, file or account for a client for whom they have Power of Attorney or trustee status. However, all such requests for information must conform to the normal rules and procedures that guide Powers of Attorney and trustees who are not employees. Adherence to these guiding principles should not significantly compromise service delivery or client service. Managers and team leaders must apply these principles and procedures to minimize impacts on the client as much as possible. Every employee has signed a document certifying that they have read and understood the Conflict of Interest and Post-Employment Code for the Public Service. Failure to comply will result in disciplinary action, including dismissal. For more information, refer to the ESDC Code of Conduct

topic_title: Did the applicant list children in the Child Rearing Provision section of the application?
text: The Child Rearing Provision (CRP) may help an applicant qualify for CPPD benefits or receive a higher DSB amount. The CRP can also be used to improve a Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). The CRP applies only to the time period when the individual had little or no earnings and was the primary caregiver for children under the age of 7. The CRP includes the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO), which allows for the removal of months or years of low or no earnings to be removed from an individual's contributory period when calculating a CPP pension or benefit. As of January 1, 2019, the CRP includes the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) which adds Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement component of a benefit for the time when the child was under the age of 7. The CRDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility requirements or Minimum Qualifying Period, as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. When a client is in pay for a DSB and has UPE attributed from the CRDI for any year(s) during which they are in pay, it triggers a recalculation of the additional components of their DSB every year following the attribution of the CRDI UPE. Recalculations occur in January to coincide with the indexation of the DSB entitlement. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) If using the CRP can help an applicant to qualify for CPPD benefits or improve their LPDOO, CPPD Earnings and Contributions Criteria (Scenario)

text: To be eligible for a CPPD benefit under the Late Applicant Provision, the applicant must meet the following criteria: Be considered disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements. topic_title: Is the applicant receiving or have they applied for the SVR pension? Updated
text: Before January 2019, a surviving spouse under the age of 35 could only qualify for the CPP SVR pension if: they had a dependent child or children at the time of the contributor's death; they were disabled; or both. Surviving spouses between the ages of 35 and 45 without any dependents and who were not disabled received a reduced SVR pension entitlement. Effective January 2019, applicants under the age of 45 are no longer required to have dependent children or be considered disabled under the Canada Pension Plan legislation to qualify for the full under-65 SVR pension. The SCBO must advise the Medical Adjudicator (MA) if the applicant: was under the age of 45 at the time of the deceased contributor's date of death; and has received a reduced SVR pension, if applicable. The MA will determine if and when the applicant met the severe and prolonged criteria to assess entitlement to a full SVR pension prior to 2019. Applicants who were under the age of 35 at the time of the contributor's death and who have an account status of Eligible but No Entitlement in ITRDS , must re-apply for the CPP SVR pension to be considered under the post-January 2019 rules. For more information, SVR Pension Application (Scenario)

For more information, refer to Process a Fast-Track Reapplication (Scenario) or Process a Fast-Track Reapplication (Scenario) Fast Track Reapplication (Policy)

text: Automatic reinstatement allows CPPD benefits to be reinstated for an applicant whose previous benefit was ceased due to a Return to Work or participation in volunteer or educational activities, regardless of whether the applicant self-reported or not. text: When a Death ( DTH ) benefit application is received and a there is a DSB with an On Hold status on the Benefits screen in ITRDS , the DTH benefit data capture cannot be submitted. When you receive notification that CPP has a DTH benefit application to process and an immediate determination cannot be made on the CPPD benefits application, you must modify the DSB on the Benefits screen in ITRDS and select Release . topic_title: Establishing a cease date when a beneficiary is non-compliant and their earnings are below the SGO amount
text: If there are no SGO earnings to support the beneficiary was capable of a SGO before the date of non-compliance, benefits cannot be ceased earlier than the date of non-compliance. Benefits must be ceased at the end of the month in which the non-compliance occurred.

topic_title: Establishing a cease date when a beneficiary is non-compliant and is self-employed with a gross income above the SGO amount
text: When a self-employed beneficiary fails to provide the information requested by the Minister regarding their self-employed earnings and/or business activities, an assessment of their work activity in the business is more difficult and may not be possible. In cases where a non-compliant, self-employed beneficiary has a gross income above the SGO amount, it is reasonable to conclude that the business is profitable. Since the beneficiary has not provided the information requested by the Minister, work capacity cannot be confirmed. However, it is reasonable to conclude since their self-employed work activity is profitable, that the beneficiary has the capacity to regularly pursue some type of work. Failure on the beneficiary's part to provide information or details to explain their self-employed earnings, results in their CPPD benefit being ceased. In these cases, the cease date is based on the available earnings information. When the period of self-employment of a non-compliant beneficiary cannot be determined, January of the first year of SGO earnings is deemed to be the month in which the beneficiary returned to work and their CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of that month (January).

topic_title: Establishing a cease date when a beneficiary is non-compliant and their earnings are at or above the SGO amount Updated
text: In some cases, information available to the Minister (e.g. work activity with SGO earnings since the beneficiary began receiving CPPD benefits) suggests the beneficiary may have become ineligible for CPPD benefits at some point before the date their non-compliance occurred. Beneficiaries who are non-compliant and have earnings equal to or greater than the SGO amount must have these earnings investigated to determine: the period of employment; the source of those earnings; and if those earnings are reflective of the beneficiary being able to work at any SGO. If the earnings are confirmed and a period of employment is verified, CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of the month the beneficiary returned to work. Files may be transferred to ISB to confirm the source of earnings, if required. If the earnings cannot be confirmed or verified, January of the first year of SGO earnings is deemed to be the month in which the beneficiary returned to work. In such a case, the beneficiary's CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of January.

To continue receiving CPPD benefits, beneficiaries must continue to meet the eligibility requirements. To ensure that beneficiaries remain eligible, the Department may reassess them to determine continuing eligibility. The regulations give the Minister the authority to request information regarding: the beneficiary's occupation and earnings for any period; and changes in the beneficiary's medical condition. This policy guidance addresses a beneficiary's non-compliance to requests for this information. It does not address non-compliance with health care treatment. Non-Compliance with Health Care Treatment (Policy) A beneficiary is considered non-compliant when: the Minister receives no response from the beneficiary after 2 written requests have been sent (the original request and the reminder to the original request) asking for specific information by a prescribed date; or the beneficiary responds to the Minister's written request but fails to provide the specific information sought, as solicited by the Department, which is necessary to make a decision regarding their continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits. A beneficiary is not considered non-compliant when: the beneficiary has good cause; the nature of the beneficiary's medical condition is such that it could be reasonably anticipated they will be unable to respond to the request for information (i.e. incapacity); or the beneficiary is missing. Suspending CPPD benefits based on non-compliance When a beneficiary does not respond to the Minister's requests for information, the payment of CPPD benefits is generally suspended. Suspending payment of the benefit when a beneficiary becomes non-compliant: may prompt the beneficiary to respond to the Minister's request for information; and limits the potential of any overpayment of benefits that the beneficiary could incur. While benefits are suspended, the beneficiary does not have the right to request a reconsideration or to appeal. Reaching a decision concerning the beneficiary's continuing eligibility and informing them of the decision enables the beneficiary to exercise these rights. Ceasing CPPD benefits when non-compliance occurs If a beneficiary fails to provide the information requested by the Minister within the suspension period, their DSB benefits can be ceased. These files may be transferred to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for further investigation before determining a cease date. If confirmed that earnings are from work activity, the cease date is based on the evidence rather than non-compliance. Files with evidence of fraud, misrepresentation or missing beneficiaries must be sent to ISB for investigation. Establishing a CPPD benefits cease date In situations where a beneficiary has not provided the required information requested by the Department to determine their continuing eligibility, CPPD benefits are ceased based on the available earnings information. The following are not to be used when determining a CPPD benefits cease date: Earnings confirmed through an employer to be from sources other than work activity such as: earnings related to sickness benefits; or payment to the beneficiary for unused vacation leave. Earnings that have been fully investigated either: at the time of the initial eligibility determination; or during a previous reassessment.

topic_title: Beneficiary—60 years of age or over
text: If a beneficiary is 60 years of age or older, they may choose to apply for an RTR pension. If it is approved, thei r CPP DSB benefits will cease the month before their RTR pension starts.

It is important to ensure that beneficiaries understand the effect of terminating their benefits. The matter must be discussed factually and no effort is to be made to influence a beneficiary's decision. The beneficiary must be contacted to ensure they have a full understanding of the implications of terminating their CPP DSB benefits including: loss of income; prolonging the contributory period which can result in a lower RTR and Survivor pension amount(s); loss of any children's benefits; and should they become disabled again at a future date, they may not have enough earnings and contributions to re-qualify for CPP DSB benefits.

Caution must be exercised when dealing with a termination (or cancellation) request from a beneficiary whose disability is based on a psychiatric disorder. A special effort must be made to ensure they fully understand the implications of terminating the ir CPP DS B benefits.

topic_title: Beneficiary—Under 60 years of age and not eligible for an RTR pension
text: If a beneficiary would like their benefit terminated and they are under 60 years of age and, therefore, are not eligible fo r an RTR pension, a reassessment of continuing eligibility must occur. If the provided medical report(s) support that the beneficiary has regained capacity, the benefits are normally ceased effective the month the termination is processed. In some instances, another date may be more appropriate (e.g. the doctor indicates that the beneficiary will be able to return to work at a specified future date). If a medical report is not provided, a written statement from the beneficiary will be sufficient as long as the statement includes some indication of regained capacity for work (e.g. an improvement in their functional status or a return to work activi ty). Written statement Phrases such as the following should be considered: I am feeling much better... I am now looking for a job... I do not consider myself disabled anymore... I will be going on Employment Insurance next week... I should be able to get back to work soon... I do not believe that I am entitled any longer... If no evidence is provided to support the fact that the beneficiary is no longer disabled, th e CPP DSB benefits cannot be terminated. Date CPP DSB benefits are ceased A CPP DSB benefit is ceased the month the termination request is processed.

If a request for cancellation of CPP DSB benefits (including the PRDB ) is received more than 12 months after the date of the first payment of the benefit, t he request is treated as a request to terminate CPP DSB benefits. CPP DSB benefits can only be terminated if: the person is 60 years of age and applied for a CPP Retirement (RTR) pension ; or evidence is provided to show that the beneficiary has ceased to be disabled.

Past beneficiary dies after completing an automatic reinstatement request If the Department receives the required documentation from the past beneficiary or their legal representative prior to their death and within one year of the date the same or related disability reoccurred, their DSB or PRDB can be reinstated. Post-Mortem Applications (Policy) In pay for the CPP RTR pension A past beneficiary cannot cancel their Early Retirement (ERTR) pension in favour of a DSB if the recurrence of their medical condition occurred after the start of their ERTR pension. They must have become unable to work due to a recurrence of their medical condition prior to the effective date of their ERTR pension. If the recurrence of the past beneficiary's medical condition occurs after the effective date of their ERTR pension, they may be eligible for the PRDB if specific conditions are met. Documentation An AR request must be made in writing. The past beneficiary is required to supply information about the recurrence of the same or related disability and the date they: stopped working; were unable to participate in educational activity; or were unable to participate in volunteer activity. When the benefit ceased, the beneficiary was provided with: a personalized Reinstatement of CPPD Benefits form; and a Physician or Nurse Practitioner Confirmation form. These completed forms will be accepted as a confirmation of AR eligibility. Generally, no additional information is requested unless further clarification is required. Earnings and Contributions If the past beneficiary does not meet the eligibility criteria for AR, they will be required to meet the Earnings and Contributions (E & C) requirements if they choose to apply using the fast-track reapplication or the initial application for a CPPD benefit. Although past beneficiaries do not require E & C to be eligible for AR, any valid contributions made while they were working will be included in the entitlement calculation for the: DSB ; RTR pension; DTH benefit; and SVR pension. Past beneficiary returning to work or residing in Québec Past beneficiaries whose CPPD benefit ceased due to a return to work are eligible for the AR even if they contribute to the Québec Pension Plan (QPP) or reside in Québec. Their QPP contributions will be used to recalculate their reinstated DSB . The eligibility is established when the DSB is ceased. Effective date If it is determined that the past beneficiary meets the criteria for AR, their CPPD benefit will start the month following the month they stopped work activity or work-like activity or 12 months prior to the date of the request (maximum retroactivity). If the past beneficiary was laid off, dismissed, terminated, or quit and subsequently has a recurrence of the same or related disability, their CPPD benefit will be reinstated effective the month following the date when their disability recurred and not the date stopped work or work-like activity. Payment amount The amount of the reinstated CPPD benefit will generally not be less than what the past beneficiary would have received However, if their personal or family situation (e.g. credit splitting, change in custody of children) changed since the cessation of benefits, the CPPD benefit monthly entitlement amount could be affected. In the case of PRDB , the amount of the RTR pension could be affected. Other CPP benefits The Disabled Contributor's Child Benefit will be paid if the eligibility requirements are met at the time the CPPD benefit is reinstated.

To be eligible for AR, the past beneficiary must: be under age 65; not be receiving a CPP RTR pension at the date of the recurrence of the same or related medical condition when the DSB was previously in pay; have had their CPPD benefit ceased due to: a return to work; participation in educational activity; or participation in volunteer activity. have a recurrence of the same or related disability within 2 years of the date the CPPD benefit was ceased; submit a request for reinstatement within one year of the recurrence of their disability causing them to: stop working; stop participating in educational activity; or stop participating in volunteer activity; When a past beneficiary requests an appeal of a cease decision and asks for AR before the appeal decision, the AR request should be held in abeyance pending the outcome of the appeal.

Automatic reinstatement (AR) is an incentive which provides financial security to beneficiaries of CPPD benefits who are unsuccessful at their: return to work; participation in educational activities; or participation in volunteer activity. AR allows past beneficiaries of CPPD benefits who meet the AR eligibility criteria to have their CPPD benefit reinstated if they are unable to continue working or participating in educational or volunteer activities due to the same or related disability. This incentive is available for 2 years following the month benefits were ceased. AR is particularly helpful to past beneficiaries with episodic or recurring conditions. Each additional recurrence of the medical condition has an impact on treatment, recovery and likelihood of deterioration. Recurrences may result in: shorter intervals between relapses; additional functional limitations or a further reduction in functional abilities; more aggressive treatment and medical interventions; and longer absences from the workplace. A beneficiary may experience multiple episodes of exacerbation and remission over their lifetime while receiving a CPPD benefit. Eligibility requirements Appeal rights AR decisions are subject to reconsideration and appeal to the SST . Protection of initial and fast-track reapplication If it is determined the past beneficiary does not meet the criteria for AR, the date the signed reinstatement form was received may be used as the application date for a subsequent CPPD benefit application or fast-track reapplication. For more information, Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy)

topic_title: Who is eligible for AR Updated
text: AR is not a re-adjudication of eligibility for CPPD benefits. When the DSB or PRDB is approved, the beneficiary is determined to have met the severe and prolonged criteria for that medical condition. If a past beneficiary stops work activity or work-like activity (i.e. volunteer or educational activities) due to a recurrence of the same or related medical condition, the criteria do not need to be met again and a review of eligibility is not undertaken. Past beneficiaries who request the reinstatement of benefits do not have to meet earnings and contributions requirements and are not required to undergo a medical review of eligibility. If the past beneficiary does not meet the AR requirements as outlined below, they are still able to reapply for a CPPD benefit as a fast-track reapplication or a new application.

topic_title: Who is not eligible for AR Updated
text: A past beneficiary is not eligible for AR if the benefit was ceased due to: regained capacity; or non-compliance without evidence the past beneficiary returned to work. An enquiry must be submitted to National Headquarters via the Business Expertise Request Tool in the following situations if: considering ceasing benefits on regained capacity alone; a past beneficiary was ceased due to regained capacity alone and submits a new application for CPPD benefits or an AR request within AR timeframes.

Review the response and documents received from the applicant: If the documents received confirm all of the applicant's stated employment periods, these periods can be deemed as residence in Canada. If the documents received do not support the applicant's stated employment periods, these periods cannot be deemed as residence in Canada, continue processing the application considering these periods as presence in Canada.

Certain ISSAs contain a provision that allows a period of presence in Canada to be deemed as residence for OAS purposes if the applicant: contributed to the CPP; ordinarily resided in one of the applicable countries; and was present in Canada after the date the applicable ISSA came into force. The applicant does not need to meet the definition of resident in these periods, but they must meet the legal status requirement. Refer to Legal Status (Scenario) for more information. Legal Status (Scenario) There are 6 countries whose ISSA with Canada includes this provision. They are listed in the table below. Periods of presence in Canada can be deemed as residence if they occurred after the date the ISSA came into force. The date of entry into force of Canada's ISSA with these 6 countries are as follows: Table 1. Countries and date of entry into force of the Agreement Country Date of entry into force of the Agreement Antigua and Barbuda January 1, 1994 Dominica January 1, 1989 Grenada February 1, 1999 Saint Vincent and the Grenadines November 1, 1998 Trinidad and Tobago July 1, 1999 St. Kitts and Nevis July 1, 1999 Contributions to CPP during periods of presence Only the days that the applicant was present in Canada and contributed to the CPP are considered as residence for calculation purposes. The applicant is not credited for an entire year of residence for each year of contributions to the CPP. Proof of employment must be obtained for all periods in which the applicant was deemed present in Canada. Documentary proof required The applicant must provide an official document to demonstrate the start and end dates of all periods that they were in Canada to confirm whether this provision applies to them. For periods when they contributed to the CPP, the applicant must present one of the following documents to support all of the stated periods of employment in Canada: a Record of Employment; an official letter from their employer that provides details of the employment period with the start and end dates; or any other official document that supports the applicant's claimed periods of employment in Canada.

topic_title: Determine eligibility for a DSB benefit
text: Determine eligibility for a DSB benefit by reviewing the Earnings screen in ITRDS. The client must have Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings equal to or more than the Disability Basic Exemption for: 4 of the last 6 years; or 3 of the last 6 years, with 25 or more years of contributions. The Disability Basic Exemption for each year can be found on the CPP Rates and Benefits sheet

topic_title: Determine eligibility for a DTH benefit and a SVR pension
text: Determine eligibility for a DTH benefit and a SVR pension by reviewing the Earnings screen in ITRDS. The client must have Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings for the lesser of: 1/3 of their contributory period; or 10 years. If the client’s contributory period is 9 years or less, a minimum of 3 years of valid contributions are needed to be eligible for the DTH benefit or the SVR pension. Example A client’s contributory period lasts from 1966 to 1991. The calculation is made as follows: Base contributory period starts: January 1966 Base contributory period ends: March 1991 Total years in base contributory period: 26 (1966 to 1991 = 26 years) Minus years in pay for base DSB benefit: 0 Total base years minus base disability: 26 Divided by 3: 9 (8.66 round up to 9) The contributory period must be at least 9 years and indicated on the Record of Earnings to qualify for the DTH benefit or SVR pension.

The contributory period is the period of time in which the individual makes contributions based on their earnings to the CPP or the QPP. A dual contributor is one who has contributed to both the CPP and the QPP. Under the CPP, individuals pay contributions during their contributory period on annual earnings between a set minimum and a set maximum level: The minimum level, known as the Year’s Basic Exemption, is set at $3,500. The maximum level is set every year by the CPP and known as the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings.

If an applicant has contributed to both CPP and QPP (at least one valid unadjusted pensionable earning in each Plan), the jurisdiction responsible for administering their account is determined by the following: If there was no previous benefit activity: the contributor’s usual place of residence at the time of application (Quebec residents apply to the QPP while all others apply to the CPP); the contributor’s last province of residence if the contributor is living outside of Canada at the time of application; the contributor’s residence at the time of death for Survivor’s pension s. If there was previous benefit activity: the jurisdiction that is or was responsible for benefit activity on the cancelled account. CPP and QPP agreements for dual accounts mandate that benefit amounts and qualification criteria are determined by the paying jurisdiction, in accordance with legislation governing that jurisdiction. The respective paying jurisdiction bills the other jurisdiction for the amount paid to the contributor on its behalf.

A dual contributor is an individual who has made a valid contribution to both the CPP and the QPP during their lifetime. The CPP and the QPP have a number of agreements that govern contributions and benefits from their respective plans. Some workers and some self-employed individuals will contribute to both plans during their working life. The agreements stipulate that workers and self-employed individuals contribute to either the CPP or the QPP, depending on the province of their employment or business. In addition, these agreements determine that applications from individuals are processed by either CPP or QPP based on the province of residence of the contributor. Individuals who have pensionable earnings in Quebec while also having pensionable earnings in Canada outside of Quebec could potentially earn both: a Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) based on CPP contributions; and a Retirement Pension Supplement based on QPP contributions. These individuals are subject to: the year’s basic exemption in each respective jurisdiction; and in addition, they are subject to the year’s maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) across both jurisdictions. As a result, the individual is not able to earn both a maximum CPP PRB and a maximum QPP Retirement pension supplement. For individuals with total earnings above the YMPE, the individual's contributions and, by extension, benefits, are calculated based on the proportion of the total earnings in each jurisdiction. For example, consider an individual who earned 75% of YMPE in Quebec and 50% of YMPE in New Brunswick (a 3:2 ratio). The individual would therefore contribute 60% of YMPE to the QPP and 40% of YMPE to the CPP, earning an appropriate Retirement pension supplement from the QPP and PRB from the CPP.

To provide information on the CPP Record of Earnings (ROE). The CPP is financed by contributions from employees, employers and self-employed persons, along with interest from the Canada Pension Plan Fund. The CPP covers nearly all working persons in Canada between the ages of 18 and 70 who earn more than a minimum level of earnings in a calendar year. Canada Revenue Agency is responsible for the collection of earnings and/or contributions from: T4 forms submitted directly to them by employers; and T1 General forms for self-employed individuals. The ROE is a computer file which contains a record for each Social Insurance Number that has recorded earnings and/or contributions. An individual’s ROE is used to calculate CPP, QPP and Dual contributor benefits, and to calculate any financial adjustments between programs. To receive CPP benefits, a person must have a valid contribution to the CPP for a minimum number of years or have received credits from a credit split. CPP benefit amounts are based on how much a person contributes and on the length of time they have contributed and, in some cases, the age of the person when the benefit becomes payable. It is very important to ensure that each person’s earnings and contributions are recorded accurately so that when they apply for a benefit, they will get the full amount they are entitled to.

Incorrect earnings posted Under the CPP, an entry in the Record of Earnings (ROE) shall be conclusively presumed to be accurate and may not be called into question after 4 years have elapsed from the end of the year to which the entry was made. Whenever any reduction is made to a contributor's ROE and it appears that the contributor has received a statement of earnings, the Minister shall notify the contributor of the adjustment. If the contributor is not satisfied with the adjustment, they may make a request to the Minister to reconsider the reduction. Adjustments are made to the ROE in all cases and any benefit in pay or previously paid is calculated retroactive to the effective date. When an adjustment results in an overpayment, the decision to collect or remit the overpayment is made in accordance with the Overpayment Policy. In cases where a person has worked and contributed to the CPP up to the point in time that a benefit becomes payable, the contributor's ROE may not contain information with respect to this person's most current unadjusted pensionable earnings. This is due to the fact that confirmed information concerning Earnings and Contributions (E & C) for a year is not received from Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) until approximately November of the following year. To prevent lengthy delays in the payment of benefits, the legislation provides for the interim calculation of a benefit to be made. The interim calculation is based on information contained in the ROE at the time the benefit is processed. In rare instances, the interim calculation might be based on earnings information which is manually entered by processing staff. Interim earnings requirements Evidence of the contributor’s earnings and contributions for the effective year of the benefit and the previous year is mandatory if such evidence is required to establish the minimum qualifying period (MQP) provided under the legislation for the Death benefit, the Survivor’s pension or the Disability (DSB) benefit. In cases where a self-employed contributor is applying for a DSB benefit and contributions for the year of application and/or the previous year are required to meet the MQP, evidence of earnings is required. Documentary evidence of earnings The following subsections list examples of documentary evidence of earnings. Employees Information T4 Slip. An acceptable T4 slip is one that meets the following standards: it identifies the contributor through name and Social Insurance Number (SIN); it identifies salary, wages and contributions (CPP or QPP); and in the judgement of processing staff, there is no reason to believe that the relevant information contained on the T4 slip is incorrect, fraudulent or invalid. Income Tax Slip (Relevé 1) for QPP contributors. Statement of Contributory Salary and Wages (ISP2011) form completed in full by the employer or another authorized official. Signed letter from the contributor's employer on the company's stationery outlining the contributor's name, SIN and earnings and contributions for each applicable year. Self-employed persons Notice of Assessment or Re-assessment from CRA which indicates the amount of contributions assessed on self-employed earnings. A completed working copy of pages 1 through 4 inclusive of the Individual income Tax Return CRA form along with: a Notice of Assessment issued by CRA marked "as declared"; and a Statement of Income and Expenses; or Installment receipts or photocopies of the front and back of cancelled cheques and details showing how installment payments were calculated from income tax and CPP contributions. A financial statement signed by the contributor's auditor and showing net self-employed earnings for the year, along with: installment receipts or photocopies of the front and back of cancelled cheques; and details concerning how payments were calculated for Income Tax and CPP. QPP contributions Any documentary evidence of QPP contributions should be referred to the Contributor Client Services for further investigation. Requesting an earnings investigation and the reasons for the request The following are examples of where an earnings investigation may occur: The ROE indicates pensionable earnings which vary from the amount indicated by evidence submitted by the applicant; The ROE appears to be incomplete for one or more years in the contributory period; A contributor has indicated that there are discrepancies in the Statement of Contributions; Double postings (i.e. 2 identical postings for the same calendar year with the same employer code); Evidence submitted for one year is recorded under a different year; Incorrect or no SIN on earnings evidence; E & C evidence on file but no entry in the ROE; or Other unusual circumstances.

Contributory period The CPP provides that the contributory period no longer ends automatically at age 65 or the month contributions were last made if made after age 65. For a CPP Retirement (RTR) pension and CPP Disability (DSB) benefit calculation, the contributory period ends the earliest of the month: of the contributor’s 70th birthday; of death; or before the CPP or QPP RTR pension begins. The contributory period excludes: Any month the contributor received a CPP or QPP DSB benefit; Any month the contributor received Family Allowance or was eligible for the Canada Child Benefit. Refund of contributions For individuals who continue to work and contribute to the CPP beyond age 65, approval of a retroactive RTR pension will result in the individual becoming eligible for a refund of contributions. Individuals who satisfy the following conditions may be eligible for a refund of contributions: they are between ages 65 and 69; they have worked and contributed to CPP after reaching age 65; they satisfy all eligibility requirements for an RTR pension; they opt for retroactive payment rather than an actuarially increased pension. Retroactive period completely within one calendar year The manner in which contributions are refunded varies depending on the period of retroactivity. Contributions will be automatically refunded to individuals where the period of retroactivity falls completely within the same calendar year. Retroactive period covers 2 calendar years If the retroactive payment spans 2 calendar years, the client will have to apply for a portion of the refund.

The standard age to begin receiving the CPP RTR pension is 65. However, the CPP allows contributors to start as early as age 60 with a permanent reduction in the pension amount, or to defer until up to age 70 with a permanent increase. Because there are no actuarial increases to the pension past the age of 70, there is no financial advantage in waiting to start the pension. Due to a retroactive payment limitation of 12 months, an individual who waits too long to apply would be unable to collect all of the benefits they would have received if they had applied at age 70. Under the CPP, an application must be made before an RTR pension is paid to a beneficiary. As a result, a small but significant number of eligible seniors miss out on receiving their RTR pension because they apply late or not at all. In an effort to ensure that payments are made to eligible clients aged 70 years or older, effective January 1, 2020, the Department is waiving the requirement for an RTR pension application.

Situation Scenario Action Account suspended and released within the same year A disability recipient is residing in Canada. In June 2019, the account is suspended due to a reassessment. In August 2019, the client informs the Department of a move to Japan for health reasons. In November 2019, the disability account is released and payment is made for the period of June 2019 to November 2019. At the time of payment, the client is a non-resident and, therefore, the tax withhold will apply on the total amount of the released benefit. Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) reporting must be updated to reflect periods of non-residence resulting in the issuance of: a T4A(P) for January to May 2019; and an NR4 for June to December 2019 Account suspended and released within the same year A disability recipient is residing in Japan. In June 2019, the account is suspended due to a reassessment. In August 2019, the Department is informed of the client's move back to Canada. In November 2019, the disability account is released and payment is made for the period of June 2019 to November 2019. NRT is not withheld because the client is a Canadian resident at the time of payment. Account suspended but released in the following year An OAS recipient is residing in Canada. In September 2018, the account is suspended due to an investigation. In November 2018, the Department is advised of the client's move to Bermuda for health reasons. In February 2019, the OAS account is released and payment is made for the period of September 2018 to February 2019. The NRT withhold will apply to the total amount of the released benefit because the client is a non-resident of Canada at the time of payment. Account suspended but released in the following year An OAS recipient is residing in Greece. In September 2018, the account is suspended as the client is considered missing (i.e. unable to locate client). In December 2018, the Department is advised of the client's move back to Canada. In January 2019, the client's OAS account is released and payment is made for the period of September 2018 to January 2019. NRT will not be withheld from the amount of the released benefit because the client is a Canadian resident at the time of payment. Notification received of client's departure from Canada in previous year A client informs the Department in March 2019, of a move to France in October 2018. The NRT withhold takes effect in April 2019 and includes recovery of taxes owing for January 2019 to March 2019 only. Taxes owed for October to December 2018 will not be recovered because the client has already received a T4A for 2018. Taxes must be recovered within the same taxation year. Refer to the Retroactive recovery of tax example below to determine how to recover retroactive tax. Retroactive recovery of tax Retroactive recovery of tax In March 2019, a client informs the Department of a move to Jamaica as of January 2019. An NRT withhold of 25% effective April 2019 would allow the department t o recover the NRT from April to December 2019 but the client would still owe NRT from January to March 2019. Effective April 2019, an NRT rate of 50% should be set up from April to June 2019 to recover the tax owing from January to March 2019. If the tax withhold rate remains at 50% in December, the system will automatically reset the withhold rate to 25% effective January of the following year. The NRT must then be reduced to 25% effective July 2019.

An NRT withhold starts when the beneficiary’s country of residence in ITRDS changes from domestic to foreign or from one foreign country to another. If the country of residence is not in the Non-Resident Tax Table , the Country of Residence is set to Other and the rate is set to 25%. The tax withhold comes into effect the month in which the beneficiary starts residing in another country, which is considered as their place of residence for income tax purposes. The NRT applies to the beneficiary’s taxable payables. Non-Resident Tax Table An NRT cannot be manually added as the Canada Revenue Agency automatically sends it to the Department and it is add ed by ITRDS. However, in certain situations, you can modify an NRT rate, reason and end date. When either you or the system modify an NRT rate, the Start Date defaults to the current accounting month and cannot be changed. You cannot enter an NRT End Date that is earlier than: the Start Date or more than 5 years after (if the NRT rate reason is "Retroactive"); or the Start Date or later than December of the current tax year (whichever date is earliest). You must modify an NRT when: CRA approves a reduced tax withhold rate; the withhold rate increases because of a retroactive recovery of NRT; or Financial and Benefit Management Systems identify an account with system irregularities.

The Income Tax Act allows the taxation of Canadian social security benefits paid to non-residents. The NRT is 25% unless there is a tax treaty between Canada and the country of residence, or the client has applied for and received a reduction in their NRT rate. The country in which a client resides determines whether or not the NRT is applicable and, if so, the percentage of tax to be withheld. NRT rates can vary for OAS and CPP payments. A country can have up to 3 rates: CPP (other than the Death (DTH) benefit) DTH OAS NRT rates are only percentages, not dollar amounts. Withhold rates are reviewed every January and revised accordingly. ITRDS displays the adjusted NRT rates or ends the tax withhold entirely if a client does the following: changes their address and leaves Canada; moves from one country to another; or returns to Canada.

In situations where multiple withholds are required on the same account, you must follow the overpayment hierarchy. Refer to policy article Priority of Withholds—Set-offs, Withholds, Deductions, Reimbursements and Overpayments . You must verify if a foreign address exists before entering a Federal Voluntary Tax Withhold (FVTW). If an FVTW exists on a foreign account, you must manually remove the FVTW by setting the withhold rate to zero. topic_title: T4A and NR4 slips issued in the same year
text: If a client has resided both in Canada and in another country in the same year, a T4A and NR4 slip should be issued to reflect the appropriate portions paid. CPMS tracks the individual monthly payments and issues these slips automatically. If inappropriate slips were issued for that year’s withholds, the account will be reported on a discrepancy listing (e.g. voluntary tax for an NR4 slip or NRT for a domestic T4 slip). In such cases, you must issue the appropriate slips manually. For example: Situation Actions A client advises that they will become a non-resident by permanently relocating to another country in April. They will be subject to an NRT withhold effective April of that year. The client's benefit entitlement is cancelled in July of that year. A T4A should be issued to reflect the payments made from January to March (i.e. the period the client was a Canadian resident). An NR4 slip should be issued to reflect the payments made and the NRT withheld from April to July (i.e. the period they resided outside of Canada). The client had voluntary tax withheld for the period they resided in Canada Th e FVTW rate m ust be set to zero before the foreign address change. CPMS would stop withholding voluntary tax once the domestic address was changed to a foreign address. The T4A would reflect not only the benefit amount from January to March, but also the amount of voluntary tax withheld.

A cessation of an OAS pension is an action initiated by a pensioner to voluntarily stop receiving their pension for a period of time or indefinitely. It is different from a suspension of benefits. Cessation of the OAS pension A pensioner can make a request in writing that their OAS pension be ceased. Cessation of the OAS pension also results in the cessation of other supplementary benefits such as the GIS and the ALW benefit. If the benefits for the spouse or common-law partner are impacted, the spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing. The pension ceases to be payable effective: the month in which the pensioner's request is actioned; or the month indicated by the pensioner (if it is in the future). Should a pensioner choose to receive their pension at a later date, it can be reinstated. Cessation of the GIS, ALW or ALWS A beneficiary is not obligated to accept a GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit for any particular period that they do not wish. After completing an application, the individual can decide not to receive the benefit right away or, if they are already receiving the benefit, may discontinue that payment for a period of time. The GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits cease to be payable effective: the month in which the request is actioned by the Department; or the month indicated by the pensioner (if it is in the future). When a beneficiary chooses to cease the payment of the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit, the lifetime renewal designation ends. Should a beneficiary choose to receive their benefit at a later date, it can be reinstated: however, a new application is required. When the request to cease is approved for the GIS or the ALW and if the benefits for the spouse or common-law partner are impacted, the spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing.

topic_title: Payment cessation for Surviving Child's and Disabled Contributor's Child benefits Updated
text: The Surviving Child's benefit and the Disabled Contributor's Child Benefit ( DCCB ) cease the month after the month in which any of the following occur: the child reaches age 18 and does not attend school on a full-time or part-time basis; the child who is 18 years of age or older stops attending school on a full-time or part-time basis; the child who is 18 years of age or older who attends school on a full-time or part-time basis reaches the age of 25; or the child dies. In addition, DCCB payments cease the month after the month in which any of the following events occur: the DSB or PRDB ceases because the contributor ceases to be disabled; the contributor dies; the child is legally or "in fact" adopted by someone other than the disabled contributor or their spouse or common-law partner; the "in fact" adoption relationship changes to the extent that the parent DSB or PRDB beneficiary-child-contributor relationship has permanently ended, not merely that some of the circumstances have changed. The DCCB can be reinstated if it can be demonstrated that the child-contributor DSB or PRDB beneficiary relationship is re-established; the disabled contributor ceases to have decision-making responsibility or parenting time with respect to the child; the child ceases to be under the legal or "in fact" decision-making responsibility or parenting time of the DSB or PRDB beneficiary, where the child was originally a child of the beneficiary by reason of legal or "in fact" . The DCCB can be reinstated if it can be demonstrated that the child- DSB or PRDB beneficiary relationship is re-established; or the conversion of a DCCB for a child over the age 18 to a Surviving Child's benefit. A DCCB in pay or payable to a child between the ages of 18 and 25 at the time of the DSB or PRDB beneficiary's death is converted automatically to a Surviving Child's benefit without the need to complete an application providing that all conditions of eligibility for a Surviving Child's benefit are met.

In such cases, the first SVR pension is cancelled effective the month after the death of the second spouse or common-law partner. Before January 1, 2019 An SVR pension was payable up to and including the month the survivor: dies; or who was under the age of 35, ceased to have dependent children and was not disabled. Before January 1, 1987 If a survivor remarried before January 1, 1987, their SVR pension ceased with the final payment occurring the month of remarriage. This only applied in cases of legal marriage. A common-law union did not terminate an SVR pension. Had the new marriage been terminated by divorce (recognized by Canadian law) before January 1987 or had been annulled at any time, the SVR pension was payable again upon notification by the former beneficiary. In such cases, the SVR pension was reinstated effective the month after the divorce. In the case of annulment, however, the pension was reinstated retroactively back to the month it was cancelled due to the remarriage.

topic_title: How to determine an OCON Updated
text: A client's account is generally serviced based on their place of residence. Their place of residence also determines to which OCON their account will be assigned. For Ontario accounts, the postal code determines the OCON. If an application is submitted from outside of Canada, and there has been no previous activity on the account, the contributor's last province of residence determines the OCON. If no province is indicated on the application, the last province of contribution is used. If the last province is Ontario and there is no previous activity, the OCON is 0501. A client's account can be assigned an OCON for a specialized processing unit (i.e. Dual Processing Unit, International Operations Unit or Program Exception Processing Unit), regardless of the client's address. Determine the OCON as follows: Table 4. How to Determine the OCON Benefit or pension Situation RTR pension The permanent residence of the contributor determines the OCON. If the client's residence is outside of Canada, the last province or territory of residence determines the OCON. If you cannot determine the last province of residence, the last province of contribution is used. DSB The permanent residence of the contributor determines the OCON. If the client's residence is outside of Canada, the last province or territory of residence determines the OCON. If you cannot determine the last province of residence, the last province of contribution is used. Death ( DTH ) benefit If there is no previous benefit activity, you must determine the OCON based on the province or territory in which the applicant for the DTH benefit resides. If there is no previous benefit activity, the applicant does not reside in Canada and the last province of residence of the deceased is unknown, you must determine the OCON based on the last province of contribution. If the deceased has no contributions, the OCON is 0501. If there is previous or current benefit activity, the OCON stays the same. SVR pension You must use the province or territory in which the spouse or common-law partner is located to determine the OCON. If the spouse or common-law partner has never resided in Canada, the OCON is determined by the last province of contribution of the deceased contributor. If the deceased has no contributions, the OCON is 0501. If there are 2 or more SVR pensions, the OCON is the province or territory in which the spouse or common-law partner currently resides. When a reinstatement of spousal benefits occurs, the OCON is the province or territory in which the spouse or common-law partner currently resides. Surviving child's benefit If there is no spouse or common-law partner or if the spouse or common-law partner is deceased, you must determine the OCON based on the province or territory in which the payee for the youngest child is located. The OCON is determined by the province or territory in which the survivor resides if they are the payee for the child. If the payee for the youngest child is cancelled, the province or territory where the payee for the next youngest child is located determines the OCON. Disabled contributor's child benefit The OCON is determined by the province or territory in which the disabled contributor resides. Combined pension The OCON is determined by the province or territory of the living client (i.e. RTR pension/ SVR pension or DSB / SVR pension). Contesting applications The OCON is determined by the province or territory where the first application was received. Any office that receives a second application must send it, along with all necessary documents, to the appropriate office. The receiving office will be responsible for both applications. For recipients of the CPP Retirement (RTR) pension who apply for CPP Disability (DSB) benefits and are deemed to have become disabled before the month the RTR pension became payable, the application for DSB benefits is deemed to be a request for the cancellation of the RTR pension. This is referred to as an in-favour cancellation. Effective January 1, 2019, CPP RTR pensioners no longer have to submit a written request to cancel their RTR pension in favour of receiving the CPP DSB benefit. Instead, their application for DSB benefits is deemed to be the request for the cancellation of their RTR pension. Once cancelled, the RTR pension is considered never to have been paid. A Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB) recipient can cancel their RTR pension in-favour of a CPP DSB benefit if specific conditions are met. When their RTR pension is cancelled, the amounts of RTR pension, Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB), if applicable, and PRDB they received must be repaid. The amount of all RTR pension entitlements paid is recovered from the DSB benefit arrears payment. The balance, if any, is recovered from subsequent monthly DSB benefit payments. text: When the DSB benefit is approved, it is processed immediately upon approval. Written notification of the DSB benefit decision must be sent to the beneficiary. topic_title: Complete the Notification of Cash Receipts (ISP1671) form
text: Field Direction Period of overpayment (if known) Enter the period of the receivable, if it is known. OCON Enter the 4-digit number that identifies the account's Office of Control (OCON) for CPP only. Office of Control Office of Control Payment history code Enter the payment history code: Enter 0 when the payment history should be updated. Enter 1 when the payment history should be bypassed. The following are examples of when the payment history should be bypassed: original and duplicate cheques are cashed; funds must be redirected to another OCON or to OAS; funds must be redirected to another government department (CPP only). Apply to overpayment Check this box if the money must be applied against a receivable. Original and duplicate cheques cashed Check th is box if the refund is applied to an overpayment because of the cashing of original or duplicate cheques. Address Locator This field is no longer required. Historically, the Address Locator was a 2-digit number related to the address set to the beneficiary. On the NCR, an address locator was provided for the beneficiary against whom a receivable was lodged where a single remittance covered multiple beneficiaries (e.g. for a spouse and a -18 surviving child, an address locator existed for each beneficiary). A separate NCR was prepared for +18 surviving children or disabled contributor's children. Benefit Enter the 3-letter code for the benefit type that is overpaid from the following: Retirement pension: RTR Disability benefit: DSB Disabled Contributor's Child Benefit: DCC Survivor's pension: SVR Surviving Child's benefit: ORP Death benefit: DTH Amount Enter the total amount or portion of the remittance to be applied to each receivable. The individual portions allocated to each benefit type must be added together and totalled to equal the amount received. When a portion applies to more than one ORP or DCC, you must indicate the total amount refunded for the portion of ORP or DCC. Tax Code Enter T or NT to indicate if the amount should be reported as taxable or non-taxable for all monies received which represent a refund of CPP benefits. Examples by benefit type and tax status are shown below (CPP only): RTR: Taxable (code T) DSB: Taxable (code T) Surviving spouse: Taxable (code T) DTH: Taxable (code T) +18 ORP or DCC: Taxable (code T) -18 ORP or DCC: Taxable but Non-reportable (code NT) Combined SVR/RTR: Taxable (code T) Combined SVR/DSB: Taxable (code T) Other Enter any instructions related to the disposition of the remittance. If the remitter is deceased: Delete any post-dated cheque information by entering "DELETE INFORMATION - REMITTER DECEASED" in the Other field of the NCR. Do not complete the other fields of the NCR. Forward copy 1 of the NCR to Input/Output and retain copy 2 on the benefit file. Retrieve any post-dated cheques which cannot be negotiated due to the remitter's death from Finance. Correspond with the estate regarding the return of the post-dated cheques. Request a new refund. If a cash receipt does not belong to CPP: Notify Finance by completing the NCR and entering "REFUND REDIRECT - NO CPP OVERPAYMENT" in the Other field of the form. Enter the name and address of the correct payee on the NCR, if it is known. Enter 1 in the Payment history code field to ensure the payment history is not updated with the amount of the cash receipt. After you complete the lower portion of the NCR, sign and date the form. Forward the benefit file, copies 1 and 2 of the NCR and the change order to the batching clerk in the usual manner.

Retroactivity provisions apply based on when an application is received, deemed to have been made or the requirement for an application has been waived. The benefit cannot be paid to a beneficiary for any month that is more than 11 months before the month in which the initial application is deemed to have been made or waived. However, retroactive payments may go beyond the period normally allowed in cases of : erroneous advice and administrative error; incapacity.

When a benefit is granted after the start of the month in which payment becomes effective, a lump sum payment is made back to the effective date. However, for a Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB), the Department will likely not have the required information to pay the PRB in January of a given year. Once the Department receives the earnings and contributions information from the Canada Revenue Agency, payment will start and include a back payment to January.

Applicants who have reached age 65 may be entitled to up to 12 months of retroactive payments. However, no retroactive payment will be made for any months before January 1995 or before the individual reaches age 65. Proactive enrolment at age 70 In cases where a person is at age 70 or older at the time the requirement for a Retirement (RTR) pension application is waived, retroactive monthly payments of the RTR pension are provided for up to 12 months. Retroactivity for proactive enrolment does not apply to individuals under the age of 70.

Survivors under age 35 Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor under age 35 must either have a dependent child or be considered disabled according to the CPP to be eligible for the Survivor’s (SVR) pension, were removed. In such cases, survivors must apply or re-apply. For new eligibility determinations, the maximum retroactive period will continue to be 11 months before the date of application. However, in no case is an SVR pension payable without the prescribed qualifying conditions for any month before January 2019. Survivors aged 35 to 45 Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor aged 35 to 45 must either have a dependent child or be considered disabled according to the CPP to receive an unreduced SVR pension, were removed. For new eligibility determinations, the maximum retroactive period will continue to be 11 months before the date of application.

Benefits can be paid retroactively for up to one year from the date of death or from the point at which the deceased was eligible for the benefit, whichever is less. For a deferral, an actuarial adjustment factor of 0.6% may be applied towards a retroactive post-mortem OAS pension.

Retroactivity provisions apply based on when an application is received, deemed to have been made or the requirement for an application has been waived. The benefit cannot be paid to a beneficiary for any month that is more than 11 months before the month in which the initial application is deemed to have been made or waived. However, retroactive payments may go beyond the period normally allowed in cases of : erroneous advice and administrative error; incapacity. Other eligibility requirements must be met in order for the retroactivity period to be extended.

Individuals who apply for an OAS pension after their initial date of eligibility can receive: a retroactive payment for up to 11 months; an actuarially adjusted pension (if a full pension) for the whole period of deferral; an actuarially adjusted pension or additional 40ths for accumulated periods of residence for the whole period of deferral (if a partial pension); or a combination of both measures. It is important to note that for individuals who have a combination of both measures because they deferred their OAS pension and applied after their initial date of eligibility, the actuarial adjustment (or additional 40th for accumulated periods for partial pensions) cannot be applied to the retroactive period. The actuarial adjustment or additional 40th for accumulated periods for partial pensions can only be applied to the months between the initial date of eligibility and the effective date.

The requirement for a renewal application is waived when: one-way transmission is received from Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); or a statement of income is received directly from the beneficiary. For beneficiaries who do not file their income tax and benefit returns or are late filers, Service Canada may not receive income information from the CRA in a timely manner. Renewal of benefits and any retroactivity for previous months of entitlement are protected based on the date the income is received via the CRA one-way income transmission or the date of receipt of a paper income statement. When income information is received, the beneficiary has satisfied the requirement to waive the renewal application and thus retroactivity rules apply based on the date the income information is received up to a maximum of 11 months.

Bill C-26, An Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board Act and the Income Tax Act, came into force in March 2017. As of January 2019, working Canadians began paying more into their CPP in exchange for higher retirement, survivor, and disability benefits. The legislative changes required to enable the implementation of the CPP enhancement are being applied gradually over 7 years (from 2019 to 2025). This provides time for individuals and employers to adjust to the higher contributions. The base and enhanced components of the CPP are intended to work seamlessly so that citizens only need to apply once. Work has since begun within Employment and Social Development Canada and Canada Revenue Agency to ensure that the CPP is being gradually enhanced. November 2019 is a milestone in this implementation as changes to calculation estimate tools are released. Review the client's notes for any information that may be important. Statistics Canada provides the Consumer Price Index figures to the Department. The Department is then responsible for calculating the escalation factor for CPP and OAS pensions and benefits payment rates. Escalation of CPP pension s and benefits payment rates CPP pensions and benefits payment rates may be adjusted or escalated each year in January to reflect increases in the cost of living as measured by the Consumer Price Index. The average of the monthly Consumer Price Index figures for the 12-month period ending October 31 of the previous year is the Pension Index. The pension and benefits payment rates are adjusted by a factor based on the Pension Index. The adjustment factor for each January is not available until mid-November of the preceding year because the Consumer Price Index for October must first be received from Statistics Canada. For CPP purposes, the Pension Index for a year cannot be less than that of the previous year. This means that the dollar amount of a CPP pension or benefit cannot drop to correspond with a similar drop in the Consumer Price Index. Escalation of OAS pension and benefits payment rates OAS pension and benefits payment rate increases are legislated under the Old Age Security Act . The rates are calculated 4 times a year (January, April, July and October) using data from the Consumer Price Index's All-Items Index so that pensions and benefits payments keep up with the cost of living. OAS pension and benefits rates are increased every 3 months by a factor based on the Consumer Price Index. For example, the factor used for increasing OAS benefits in April is equal to the ratio between the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous January to the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous October.

A tax convention between Canada and Azerbaijan was ratified and came into effect January 2007. Effective January 1, 2007, all periodic payments of social security benefits (i.e. CPP and/or OAS) are subject to the tax treaty rate of 15%. All lump sum CPP Death benefit payments remain subject to the withholding rate of 25%.

Effective November 25, 2011, Canada entered into a revised tax treaty with Italy. Many of the changes affecting pension payments took effect January 2013. Effective January 2013, OAS and/or CPP recipients residing in Italy had the following changes to the NRT rates applied to their Canadian pensions and benefits: Recipient type NRT rates OAS An increase to 25% CPP (excluding the Death benefit) 15% CPP Death benefit 25% To reduce the applicable tax rate, residents of Italy must each year submit a completed NR5 form to CRA. Where the non-resident does not complete the NR5 form, the Canadian payer withholds the following: Payment type Withhold rate OAS 25% CPP 15% Lump sum 25% of the gross amount In addition to this change, OAS payments are now subject to the OAS Recovery Tax. Since 2011, to determine the amount of recovery tax payable and to continue receiving OAS benefits, residents of Italy who receive OAS payments must file an Old Age Security Return of Income (OASRI) (T1136) form every year. The CRA guide T4155, Old Age Security Return of Income Guide for Non-Residents helps OAS clients to complete the Old Age Security Return of Income form.

Effective January 2012, Canada entered into a revised tax treaty with Switzerland. Since then, OAS beneficiaries who reside in Switzerland do not need to file an Old Age Security Return of Income. Residents of Switzerland who are OAS and/or CPP recipients are entitled to a Non-Resident Tax (NRT) exemption on the first $15,000 of pensions that originate in Canada. However, in the case of periodic pension payments, the NRT charged in this manner shall not exceed the lesser of: 15% of the gross periodic pension payments exceeding $15,000 of the total pensions that originate in Canada or its equivalent in Euros; or the tax that would otherwise be payable in Canada, were the recipient a Canadian resident. To reduce the applicable NRT rate, residents of Switzerland must, on an annual basis, submit a completed NR5 - Application by a Non-Resident of Canada for a Reduction in the Amount of Non-Resident Tax Required to be Withheld for Tax Year ___ form to Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). If the non-resident does not complete and return the NR5 form, the Canadian payer withholds 15% of the gross periodic pension payments of OAS and CPP, and 25% of the gross from any lump sum payments. Residents of Switzerland who wish to benefit from a further reduced NRT rate must complete and return the NR5 form.

text: When a beneficiary's ALW or ALWS benefit was approved with 40 years of residence in Canada and is suspended at age 65, their ALW or ALWS benefit can be converted to the OAS pension and the GIS benefit without having to confirm their information (i.e. address and direct deposit) by phone or mail when: the beneficiary is still eligible for the ALW or ALWS benefit (even if they were not entitled); the beneficiary's lifetime renewal designation continues to be set to Yes ; the beneficiary has a Canadian address; the beneficiary is being paid a CPP benefit and the CPP and OAS home address match, as well as either the mailing address or direct deposit information; and the Department has received the beneficiary's CRA income information for the previous or current income year. The OAS Act allows the Minister to waive the requirement for an OAS pension and an initial GIS application if the ALW or ALWS benefit ceases to be payable when the beneficiary reaches the age of 65. For the purpose of the OAS Act, "payable" means the beneficiary is "eligible to receive a benefit" as opposed to being "entitled to (in receipt of) a benefit". When an ALW or ALWS beneficiary who has a lifetime renewal designation reaches age 65, using the information on file, it is possible to determine whether an OAS/GIS application is necessary to convert their account to an OAS/GIS based on whether they continue to meet all the eligibility requirements and entitlement.

Beneficiaries who are sponsored when they reach the age of 65 during their sponsorship period are not automatically converted to the OAS pension and the GIS benefit. These individuals are required to submit an application which can be met through the submission of a conversion application or the OAS pension and GIS benefit combined application.
Old Age Security Act Section 21(5.1)—Payment of allowance to survivors, Waiver of requirement for application

The Old Age Security Act allows the requirement for an initial Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) application to be waived if the Allowance (ALW) would have been or was payable for the month in which the OAS pensioner spouse or common-law partner died. A separate application for the ALWS is not required. The ALW application is used and the ALW benefit is automatically converted to ALWS. For the purposes of the OAS Act, "Payable" means the beneficiary is "eligible to receive a benefit" as opposed to "being entitled to (in receipt of) a benefit". The Minister retains the right to solicit in certain circumstances where: residence or marital status requires verification; or an income tax return has not been filed for a number of years.
