Children's benefits are paid on behalf of the child to the individual or agency for periods during which the individual or agency had decision-making responsibility for the -18 child. If an individual or agency receives Children's benefit payments for periods during which they had no decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan, an overpayment is established and is subject to recovery in accordance with policy. Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) The recipient or payee of a -18 Child's benefit can be: a disabled contributor or survivor who has decision-making responsibility (at least 20% of the parenting time) for the child; a person or agency who has decision-making responsibility for a deceased or disabled contributor's child; or under exceptional circumstances, a -18 child who is not living with a parent, individual or agency that exercises decision-making responsibility (i.e. a child living alone). Payees must notify the Department when a change of parenting time occurs that rebuts the presumption of decision-making responsibility (the disabled contributor or the survivor are presumed to have decision-making responsibility if they have at least 20% of the parenting time). When these periods are confirmed, payments are made to each payee for the months that they had decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan. When the child reaches 18 years of age and is in full-time or part-time (effective January 1, 2025) attendance at school or university, any retroactive amount for the periods when the child was under age 18 years of age is paid to the individual or agency that had decision-making responsibility for that child. The portion of the Children's benefit owed for any months after the child's 18th birthday is payable directly to the child if the child is in full-time or part-time attendance at school or university.

The Department only makes Children's benefit payments to a -18 child in exceptional circumstances. When a request for direct payment of a -18 Child's benefit is received from a -18 child, the Department must confirm that the child-contributor relationship still exists (Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) only) and that the request is from a child living alone. Documents supporting the circumstances described in the child's request for direct payment are also required. The following 2 documents are mandatory: written statements from neutral third parties (e.g. school teachers, family physician) who have knowledge of the situation regarding the decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the -18 child; and a written observation document obtained by Service Canada staff through direct contact with the child and community workers which states that the community worker recommends that the -18 Child's benefit be paid directly to the child based on case-specific information collected. This document must provide details about: the reasons and circumstances which require payment of the -18 Child's benefit directly to the child; and where known, the ability of the -18 child to manage their own affairs. If possible, obtain a written statement from: the disabled contributor or the survivor of a deceased contributor; or the parent, individual or agency who had decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the -18 child.

topic_title: Disputed dates of decision-making responsibility Updated
text: If there is a dispute between the parties about the periods when each individual or agency had decision-making responsibility for the -18 child, the party requesting such a change must provide the following documents to the Department in support of their request: a court order detailing the allocation of decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the -18 child to an individual or agency; or a written statement from the individual or agency requesting the change which includes details about the dates the change in decision-making responsibility occurred; and a description of the circumstances that led to the change in parenting time, causing the change in decision-making responsibility. In such situations, to verify the date of the change in decision-making responsibility between the parties in the dispute, one or more of the following documents should be obtained: the record of the person who received the Canada Child Benefit for the periods under review; a written statement from third parties (e.g. family physician, school teacher) who are familiar with the situation; or separation agreements or court orders. The following documents can be used as additional supporting evidence: school registration forms; provincial health care registration; and private insurance records. Review the information or the evidence to determine who the child lives with (i.e. schedule). The disabled contributor or survivor must have 20% of parenting time or more to be the eligible payee. Once the actual periods of decision-making responsibility are verified through examination of the required evidence, separate -18 Children's benefit payments can be made to each party for the appropriate periods.

topic_title: Effective date of the change in decision-making responsibility
text: The effective date of the change in decision-making responsibility for payment purposes is the month after the month that a notification of the change in decision-making responsibility is received. However, notification of a change in decision-making responsibility may be received months or even years after a change has occurred. In these situations, the party requesting the change in decision-making responsibility must provide documents that support their claim. In some cases the evidence provided by the requesting party demonstrates that they did not understand the meaning of decision-making responsibility. For example, the requester may state that they provided financial support for the -18 child but confirm that they had no parenting time for the -18 child during the disputed period.

topic_title: Evidence of parenting time or decision-making responsibility to substantiate a change in payee

This policy provides guidelines to identify who the payee should be for CPP Children's benefits for a dependant child under the age of 18 (-18 child) when there is a change in decision-making responsibility. Custody and control has been replaced with decision-making responsibility. When the child is under the age of 18, the payment of Children's benefits is made to the person or agency who has decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: health; education; culture, language, religion and spirituality; and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is a new term introduced in the legislation. Its purpose is to help determine if the disabled contributor or survivor can be presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, to have decision-making responsibility for a child or orphan and receive the benefit on their behalf. Under the new legislation, a disabled contributor or a survivor is presumed to have decision-making responsibility for a child or surviving child, unless they have less than 20% of the parenting time. Parenting time means the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is at school).

In most situations, a request for a change in payee for a -18 child is not disputed by any other parties. The party requesting such a change must provide the following documents to the Department in support of an undisputed request: a court order detailing the allocation of decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the -18 child to an individual or agency; or a written statement from the individual or agency requesting the change which includes details about: the dates the change in decision-making responsibility occurred; and the circumstances that led to the change of parenting time, which led to a change in decision-making responsibility; and a written or verbal confirmation from the payee at the time of notification acknowledging the change which includes details about: the dates the change in decision making responsibility occurred; and the circumstances that led to the change in parenting time which led to a change in decision-making responsibility.

topic_title: Effective date of Children's benefits for a child under the age of 18
text: If, at the time the CPP contributor is deemed disabled, there is eligibility for a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ), the DCCB begins the later of: the month the DSB begins; or the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made. If a natural child is born to the contributor, the DCCB for that child becomes payable the later of: the month after the child is born; the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made; or the month the DSB or PRDB begins. If the contributor legally adopts a child, the DCCB for that child becomes payable the later of: the month after the child is legally adopted; the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made; or the month the DSB or PRDB begins. Legal or “in fact” decision-making responsibility or parenting time may be effective before or after the date the contributor's disability is deemed to have commenced. In such cases, the DCCB becomes payable the later of: the month after the disabled contributor has legal decision-making responsibility for the child, “in fact” decision-making responsibility for the child or adopted ‟in fact”; the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made; or the month the DSB or PRDB begins.

topic_title: Effective date of Children's benefits for children between the ages of 18 and 25 Updated
text: For children who are between 18 and 25 years of age and attending school or university on a full-time or part-time basis (effective January 1, 2025), the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) can begin the later of: the month the contributor's DSB or PRDB begins; the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made; or the month in which classes begin (a school vacation may be considered part of a full-time or part-time attendance period). A written request to apply for a DCCB which contains all of the required information is acceptable. The 11-month maximum retroactivity period applies to all applications for children's benefits. There is no exception to this rule. If no information about the children is provided on the CPPD benefits application and the Department later learns that the disabled contributor had children, the effective date of payment of a DCCB for any of the children would be subject to the 11 months of retroactivity from the date of receipt of the DCCB application.

The purpose of this report is to identify entitlement to an income-tested benefit for the year in which a client declared bankruptcy. topic_title: Enter the income and pay retroactive benefits
text: Pre-reversion/renewal (April to June accounting months) Process future income from the work item on the Renewal (REN) screen. If the income required to calculate entitlement for the current payment period is available from a Statement of Income form, the CRA screen or the ITRDS Income History screen, but was not previously encoded, enter this income on the Income (INC) screen. Calculate retroactive entitlement on the CAL screen for the applicable months. For each applicable month, enter the Payment Income , AS , Account Type (AT) , Indicator (Ind) , MS , and Eligible Years (ElgYr) fields to calculate the benefit entitlement. A comment may also be added. Review each previous payment period to determine if there are missing periods of potential GIS eligibility. The GIS eligibility is date protected by the receipt date of an Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP3025) form, Statement of income for the Renewal of the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP3026) form or the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) one-way income feed. GIS benefits may be paid the latest of the following events: the effective date of the OAS pension; or 11 months before the receipt date of ISP3025 form, ISP3026 form or the CRA one-way income feed. For any missing months of entitlement, determine if the required income is available: If yes, use the income to perform the GIS entitlement calculation for the applicable period on the CAL screen. If no, request the income for the applicable payment period. If the income year is within the past 3 years, request the income from the CRA on the GEN screen. If the income year required is beyond 3 years, send an ISP3026 to the client to obtain their income. Once the income has been received, perform the GIS entitlement calculation for the applicable period. Go to the Underpayment (OVP) screen and issue any resulting GIS underpayment to the client. Send the GIS, Initial application/Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control (024) or the GIS-ALW-ALWS, Renewal/Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control (019) award letter for any retroactive benefits or for benefits starting in the current accounting month. Future GIS award letters will be system-generated. In ITRDS, go to the Notes screen. Add a note to include the following: year(s) and the source of the income amounts encoded; period and amount of retroactive payments; and other pertinent information. Add a note In PWS, complete the work item. Post-reversion (July to March accounting months) Enter the current income on the INC screen. Calculate retroactive entitlement on the CAL screen for the applicable months. For each applicable month, enter the Payment Income , AS , AT , Ind , MS , and ElgYr fields to calculate the benefit entitlement. A comment may also be added. Review each previous payment period to determine if there are missing periods of potential GIS eligibility. The GIS eligibility is date protected by the receipt date of the ISP3025, ISP3026 or the CRA one-way income feed. GIS benefits may be paid the latest of the following events: the effective date of the OAS pension; or 11 months before the receipt date of the ISP3025, ISP3026 or the CRA one-way income feed. For any missing months of entitlement, determine if the required income is available. If yes, use the income to perform the GIS entitlement calculation for the applicable period on the CAL screen. If no, request the income for the applicable payment period. If the income year is within the past 3 years, request the income from CRA on the GEN screen. If the income year required is beyond 3 years, send an ISP3026 to the client to obtain their income. Add a note and include the following: year and the report advising source of income amounts encoded; period and amount of retroactive payments; and other pertinent information. The following pensions and benefits will have an additional portion and are included in the CPP enhancement: Survivor pension; Retirement pension; Disability benefit; Post-Retirement benefit and Combined benefits. Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) form the basis of benefit calculations. The 2 new contributory periods add 2 new sets of UPE. Under the enhancement, there are a total of 3 sets of UPE: one for each of the Base CPP, the first additional period and the second additional CPP. The UPE details are as follows: Base UPE = UPE up to the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), based on contributions made at 9.9%. First additional UPE = UPE up to the YMPE, based on contributions made at an extra 2% contribution rate. Second additional UPE = UPE from the YMPE to the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings, based on contributions made at an extra 8% contribution rate. The base CPP determines eligibility for a pension or benefit. When an individual meets the minimum qualifying period (MQP) in the Base CPP period, they are eligible for the pension or benefit, including any additional portions.

Under the enhancement, combined benefits are calculated using the same formula as the one used for the Base CPP. The only difference is that there is no flat-rate component for combined benefits under the additional CPP enhancement.. The rules for combined benefits under the base CPP portion are as follows: If there are 2 flat-rate components, the beneficiary receives the larger one. For the earnings-related components, the beneficiary receives the larger one plus 60% of the smaller one. The ceiling on the earnings-related component is the maximum earnings-related amount. When the retirement pension is taken early (between ages 60 and 65) for a combined survivor-retirement pension, the actuarial reduction factor is applied to the final retirement pension amount.

The contribution rates corresponding to the base, first and second contributory periods are structured as follows: Table 1. Contributory period Contribution rate structure Base CPP Contributions made on earnings from the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) up to the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) continue at a combined (employee and employer) contribution rate of 9.9% (4.95% each for the employee and the employer or 9.9% for self-employed contributors). First additional period Contributions made on earnings from the YBE up to the YMPE at a combined contribution rate of 2% (1% each for the employee and the employer or 2% for self-employed contributors). Second additional period Contributions made on earnings between the YMPE and Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings at a combined contribution rate of 8% (4% each for the employee and the employer or 8% for self-employed contributors). Phase-in period A 7-year phase-in period for the enhanced rates beginning January 1, 2019 will occur as follows: A 5-year phase-in of the 2% first additional contribution rates from 2019 to 2023 inclusively, broken down according to the table below: Table 2. Year Contribution % for employee Contribution % for employer Contribution % for self-employed contributors 2019 0.15 0.15 0.3 2020 0.3 0.3 0.6 2021 0.5 0.5 1.0 2022 0.75 0.75 1.5 2023 and each subsequent year 1.0 1.0 2.0 A 2-year phase-in of the upper earnings limit — the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings — in 2024 and 2025, along with a new contribution rate of 8% (4% each for the employee and the employer or 8% for self-employed contributors) on earnings between the YMPE and the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings.

The enhancement adds 2 additional contributory periods to the base CPP contributory period. The first additional contributory period begins January 1, 2019, or the month an individual reaches age 18 (whichever is later ) and ends the earliest of: the month before a contributor reaches age 70; the month in which the contributor dies; or the month before the month in which the retirement pension commences. The second additional contributory period begins January 1, 2024, or the month an individual reaches age 18 (whichever is later ) and ends the earliest of: the month before a contributor reaches age 70; the month in which the contributor dies; or the month before the month in which the retirement pension commences.

The credit splitting provision applies to the first and second additional unadjusted pensionable earnings in the same way as it is applied to the base CPP. As with the base CPP, the additional earnings for each individual will be added and then divided equally, and the divided earnings will be attributed to each person. Additional pensionable earnings under the QPP will be used to calculate the division. The first and second additional CPP contributory periods do not end with the month in which a beneficiary is determined to have become disabled. The disability exclusion does not apply. Therefore, unlike the Base CPP, it is possible to divide first and second additional pensionable earnings in periods where a beneficiary is in receipt of a CPP disability (DSB) pension.

The amount of the disability benefit is: the disability flat-rate amount; and 75% of the amount of the contributor’s Retirement pension (calculated as the sum of its base, first and second additional portions).

The enhancement of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) serves as a top-up to the benefits provided by the base CPP. The result is that working Canadians will receive higher amount benefits in exchange for making higher CPP contributions. For people who contributed to the CPP through paid work or self-employment in 2019, and continued to do so thereafter, the enhancement increases the amounts of the following CPP pensions and benefits: Retirement pension; Disability benefit; Survivor’s pension; Post-Retirement Benefit; and Combined benefits. Enhanced benefits will increase over time as people make enhanced contributions, eventually increasing benefit by up to 50%. The features of the enhancement are as follows: The CPP enhancement began in 2019, with the contribution rate of 2% being phased-in gradually from 2019-2023; The upper earnings limit will be 114% of the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) upon full implementation of the enhancement in 2025. This new amount is called the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings ; and The enhancement, when combined with the base CPP , offers a replacement rate of 33.33% on earnings up to 114% of the YMPE. The original CPP remains unchanged since its introduction in 1966 and is called the "Base CPP". The CPP enhancement creates a top-up to the "Base CPP" called "Additional CPP". The additional CPP contains its own: contributory periods; contribution rates; replacement rates; and benefit calculations. As a part of the CPP enhancement, the additional CPP will introduce child rearing and disability drop-Ins. For both the child rearing drop-in and the disability drop-in, qualifying earnings are dropped into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement portion of a pension or benefit.
The total amount of the Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) is the sum of its base, first and second additional portions.

Rates under the enhancement for the retirement pension calculation are as follows: 25% of the contributor's average monthly pensionable earnings (Base CPP). 8.33% of the contributor's best 40 years of first additional monthly pensionable earnings . This means that the Base CPP income replacement rate of 25% will be supplemented by an additional 8.33% to give a total income replacement rate of 33.33%. 33.33% of the contributor's best 40 years of second additional monthly pensionable earnings.

The total amount of an retirement pension paid to a beneficiary is the sum of the base, the first and the second additional portions. Since both the base CPP contributions and the first additional CPP contributions apply to earnings between the Year’s Basic Exemption amount and the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings, the base and first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) will usually be the same amount. The calculation of first and second additional UPE also takes into account any UPE acquired under the QPP.

The amount of the survivor pension for survivors under age 65 is : the survivor pension flat-rate amount; and 37.5% of the amount of the deceased contributor’s retirement pension (calculated as the sum of its base, first and second additional portions). The amount of the survivor pension for survivors aged 65 or over is: 60% of the amount of the deceased contributor’s retirement pension (calculated as the sum of its base, first and second additional portions).

topic_title: Assignment of benefits to nursing homes
text: Some private and public nursing homes ask their residents to sign a form, giving the home authorization to direct deposit pension benefits directly into the home's bank account. This type of authorization must not be accepted as it is considered an assignment of benefits and is not permitted by legislation.

Authority to communicate is different than authority to legally act on behalf of an individual and the two must not be confused. Lawyers Lawyers are "authorized contacts" and cannot make decisions on behalf of applicants or beneficiaries unless they have also been given POA. As a contact, their scope is limited to communication and the parameters described in the authorizing document. The exception is signing a request for a reconsideration or appeal as this is prescribed in legislation. Legislation allows anyone to request a reconsideration on behalf of an applicant. The authorizing letter should be read carefully to see what lawyer is the individual's authorized contact. A written notice from the individual is not required. A letter written on a lawyer's letterhead that advises the Department that they are representing an individual is sufficient proof that the lawyer or the paralegal working for the lawyer is the individual's authorized contact. A written notice from the individual is not required. Other authorized contacts An individual or organization who has been given authority to communicate on behalf of a beneficiary through a consent to communicate form or letter is also known as an "authorized contact". Although the consent is a legal document, it only provides the individual with the authority to receive and provide information. The individual or organization is not authorized to make decisions on behalf of the beneficiary, such as initiate voluntary tax withholds, or change payment details.

The Department often receives applications and court orders, certificates, or letters from provincial or territorial public trustees, (or public guardian and trustees) stating that they or another third party (individual or agency) have been appointed to administer an individual's financial affairs. A legal representative, public trustee, guardian or committee is appointed under provincial or territorial legislation to act on behalf of an incapable individual only after many factors have been considered by the province or territory, including whether the individual had granted an enduring POA before they became incapable of managing their affairs. However, a court ruling may remove a POA and replace it with a public trustee if the attorney is not acting in the best interests of the grantor. As each province or territory has its own process for appointing the public trustee, not every public trustee will submit the same document to prove that they have been appointed to act on behalf of an incapable individual. When a public trustee does not send in a court order or a certificate of guardianship, but sends a letter that identifies the following criteria, the letter can be accepted as proof of appointment in order to pay CPP or OAS benefits to the public trustee: the name of the individual they are assisting; their role on behalf of the individual (the letter must state that the representative must be appointed to administer the property of the incapable individual and not their personal care); that the individual is incapable; and the legislation under which they are acting. OAS and CPP benefits are paid directly to federally, provincially or territorially appointed administrators on behalf of an incapable individual when the Department is notified of the arrangement by the Province or Territory and the administrator sends in proof of their appointment as described above. Legal representatives appointed by a court or by the public trustee are accountable to the Court for monies received on behalf of incapable individuals. Court orders Where a province or territory requires the Court to decide whether a guardian, committee, or trustee needs to be appointed to manage the finances of an incapable adult, the process is as follows: The Court makes a decision on capacity taking into consideration evaluations made by a qualified capacity assessor, and then issues a court order which may have a seal and a docket number. The court order designates the public trustee, a private citizen or an agency as the committee or guardian to handle either the personal care or property, or both for an individual who is deemed not competent. The public trustee, agency or individual(s) identified above may be given permanent or temporary custody of the individual. The Department has no authority to cancel or revoke a court order unless the Department receives: another court order revoking the first one; or a certificate from the public trustee naming a private citizen responsible for administering the individual's benefits. Committees Certain provincial or territorial legislative statutes specify the appointment of a committee. A committee may consist of one or more individuals. If an individual is found to be incapable of managing their own affairs, the public trustee may be appointed automatically (without a court hearing) as committee when there is no existing valid legal representative (i.e. an existing committee, or an enduring POA). Upon application to the applicable provincial or territorial court, a third party may be appointed as committee in place of the public trustee to manage the financial affairs of the incapable individual. Since committees may be given authority over the individual's financial affairs, their personal affairs, or both it is very important that staff read the authorizing document carefully. Guardianships Some provinces and territories allow the appointment of guardians for incapable individuals. Guardianship law falls under provincial or territorial legislation and guardianship orders, or certificates are unique to each province or territory. A guardian may be appointed by the provincial or territorial court or by the public trustee. A private guardianship order or certificate is issued by a court after it approves an application made by a private citizen to look after the affairs of an incapable individual. A statutory guardianship means that a statute or law allows a guardian to be appointed without court involvement. When someone is appointed by the public trustee without a court order, this type of appointment is called statutory guardianship. The guardian is usually a relative, spouse or partner of the incapable individual. In some provinces or territories, where an incapable adult is in need of assistance and there is no legal representative, and no family or friends willing or able to act as a committee or private guardian, the public trustee may be appointed as statutory guardian without a court hearing. After a medical and a functional assessment is submitted to a designated health authority (a government-appointed medical officer), this official has the authority to issue a certificate of incapability which allows the public trustee to automatically become the incapable adult's statutory guardian and take over their financial and legal affairs. Some guardianships are for personal matters (guardianships of the individual), while others are for financial matters (guardianships of property). If a party is appointed a guardian of the individual, they have the legal authority to make or assist the beneficiary in making decisions about their personal care but not their financial matters. A guardian of property cares for and manages all property belonging to the incapable individual or minor that is not otherwise held in trust.

topic_title: Indigenous Services Canada and Veterans Affairs Canada
text: The Department may receive a letter from an official of Indigenous Services Canada or Veterans Affairs Canada informing that they now administer the affairs of a particular individual. In order to process this request, the following conditions must be met: the letter must contain the federal logo, be dated, and be signed by an official who provides an official title and a physical address; the letter must quote from the relevant legislation (Section 51, 52, or 52.1 of the Indian Act or subsection 5(d) of the Department of Veterans Affairs Act ); and all documents needed to support a change in payee must be provided. Each time the payee is changed to one of these federal departments, the official must be asked to inform the Department if any of the following situations occur: the individual dies or regains capability; or the individual moves or leaves Canada.

If the individual dies, any legal representation that was in place while the individual was alive ends and legal representation for the estate takes over. A legal representative for the estate after the individual's death is an executor named in the individual's will or, if there was no will and no named executor, it is an estate administrator appointed by a court. The role of the executor or court-appointed administrator is to act and communicate on behalf of the estate. They have signing authority for the estate and can: continue the process for a valid application that was submitted before the individual's death (signed by the individual and received before their death); make requests for a reconsideration, or an appeal; and apply for post-mortem benefits that the individual could have received but did not receive before they died, excluding : a CPPD benefit; an initial GIS, ALW benefit , ALWS benefit ; and an application for a CPP RTR pension for an under age 70 contributor.

Legal representation is governed provincially and territorially. The term "legal representative" covers all types of representatives that have been given authority through an authorizing document to act in some capacity on behalf of an individual. What a legal representative is authorized to do is prescribed in legal documents. Legal representatives include: individuals with Power of Attorney (POA); trustees; executors and estate administrators; committees; guardians; mandates (in Quebec); tutors; and liquidators of a succession (in Quebec). The individual chooses POAs, mandates, executors and liquidators of a succession. Trustees, committees and guardians are appointed through legislation, by the court or by the Minister when the individual is deemed incapable of managing their own affairs. Estate administrators are appointed by the court when the individual dies without a will. If it is determined the authorizing document is valid for the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act purposes, a legal representative has all the rights and responsibilities of the individual they represent, as outlined in the authorizing document. That is, the legal representative may make decisions on behalf of the individual, including taking actions such as: changing their address; providing direct deposit information; and signing application forms. Benefits cannot be made payable to a third party unless the beneficiary has been proven to be incapable of handling their own affairs and the third party has been legally appointed by a court, by provincial or territorial legislation, or by the Department as the legal representative to act on their behalf. Paying a third party when the beneficiary is capable of managing their affairs is considered an assignment of benefits, which is not permitted by legislation.

A POA is executed (written and signed) according to the laws of the province, territory, or country where they are drafted; and, therefore, may be executed differently. A POA is said to exist when an individual authorizes another individual or agency to act on their behalf. The individual giving the power is called the “grantor”; the individual receiving it is called the “attorney”. The grantor must be mentally capable of making their own decisions at the time the POA is executed. The relationship between the grantor and the attorney is governed, except in the province of Quebec, by the common law of agency and by provincial statutes and legislation. In Quebec, it is governed by the Civil Code. The POAs and Protection Mandates in Quebec section below provides more information on this topic. A general POA gives the attorney the authority to do anything the grantor could do themselves, within the terms listed in the POA document. A limited POA gives the attorney authority to act for a specific purpose (e.g. to buy or sell a particular piece of property). As a general rule, the POA will be recognized for CPP and OAS purposes if it complies with the laws of the place where it was executed. However, ultimately, it is up to the discretion of the Department whether it will accept a POA. A POA document may authorize the appointment of one or more attorneys to act jointly (together), severally (independently) or successively (independently but successive by order of attorney named). If a POA specifies that co-attorneys must act jointly and there is not an option for them to act severally, the signatures of both attorneys are required to make a decision on behalf of the grantor. If the POA names more than one attorney and does not state whether they can act alone, then it is to be assumed that they must act jointly. If a POA allows the attorneys to act jointly and severally, and a signature is required on a document, the signature of one attorney is sufficient. If a POA requires attorneys to act jointly, signatures of all attorneys are required on a document. The Department can however for communication purposes communicate with each attorney separately. The authority given in a POA may come into effect on a date specified in the document, or it may only “spring” into effect once an event that is specified in the document occurs (i.e. disability, incapability or an overseas posting). This is known as a "springing" POA. If there is no specified date or event, a POA starts immediately upon execution. POAs usually cover 2 areas of decision-making: decisions about property; and decisions about personal care. The Department will only recognize a POA that is intended for property, as CPP and OAS benefits are considered property. A POA that has been given for banking purposes only will not be recognized. A POA for personal care is not acceptable for the administration of CPP and OAS pensions and benefits. A POA may be described as "ordinary" or as "enduring" (also known as "general" or as "continuing"). If the POA document does not contain wording that it will continue or endure despite the incapability of the grantor, then it is an ordinary POA. An ordinary POA ends automatically when the grantor becomes incapable. While both types of POA are acceptable for CPP and OAS purposes, it is important to note on file if it is an ordinary or enduring POA to indicate when the authority of the attorney will end. If the Department accepts a POA, it will be applied to both programs, OAS and CPP. If the Department already has a POA on file for an individual, and then receives a POA that was executed more recently, the Department must confirm with the grantor they have revoked the previously issued POA. Springing POA A springing POA takes effect when the event that is specified in the POA document takes place. The event may be: the physical or mental incapability of the grantor; or a non-medical event. For example, the grantor requires someone to manage their affairs while they are residing outside of Canada temporarily. The POA springs into effect when the grantor leaves Canada. When the grantor returns to Canada, the POA ends. If the springing event is incapability of the beneficiary (grantor), confirmation of the grantor's incapability is required before recognizing the authority of the attorney. Confirmation can be an assessment from a medical professional or a court document. A Certificate of Incapability (ISP-3505) form is also acceptable; however, it is not required as the form's intended purpose is for appointing a trustee and not for recognizing a springing POA. A springing POA that comes into effect when the grantor becomes incapable is an enduring POA. If the springing POA is not conditional on a physical or mental incapability (as in the example of a temporary absence from Canada), confirmation that the springing event has occurred could be a phone call or letter from the grantor informing the Department of the springing event, or the Department confirming the event with the grantor. The type of notification required would depend on the wording in the POA. On the other hand, the POA itself could provide specific terms that make it clear that the event has occurred, and confirmation is not required. For example, the POA document may state that the lawyer can only provide a copy of the POA document to the attorney to inform them they have been given POA when the springing event has taken place. When the attorney presents a copy of the POA to the Department, this proves that the springing condition has been met. POAs and Protection Mandates in Quebec In Quebec, an individual can choose to grant a POA and a protection mandate. A POA in Quebec is similar to a general POA, but it is not enduring. The POA allows the grantor to name one or more individuals to manage their property, but not their personal care, and to perform administrative duties such as paying bills, withdrawing money from a bank account or other financial transactions as described in the POA document. The POA only provides authority for the attorneys to act on behalf of the grantor while the grantor has the mental capability to act on their own and to oversee the actions of the attorney. In Quebec, a grantor can also name one or more individuals to look after their personal care and to manage their property in the event that they become incapacitated. This is called a protection mandate; the grantor is the mandator and the attorney is the mandatary. The protection mandate only comes into effect once 2 conditions are met: an attorney or notary, at the request of the mandatary, applies for homologation of the mandate; and a medical assessment confirms that the mandator is incapacitated. Once a protection mandate is in force, it replaces the POA for CPP and OAS purposes. Since the beneficiary/mandator has been deemed incapable of managing their affairs, benefits will be made payable to the mandatary. Since the mandatary has the authority to act on the mandator's behalf they will have access to the mandator's account and finances in order to manage their benefits. As of November 1, 2022, there are also 3 types of representatives that may be relevant for CPP and OAS purposes: tutor; assistant; and temporary representative. Tutor A tutor is a court-appointed individual who represents an individual who is incapable of caring for themselves or of administering their property. The role of tutor may also be assigned to the public curator by the court. The court must issue a judgment specifying: the acts that the incapable individuals can perform themselves, either alone or with the assistance of their tutor; and the acts that they cannot perform alone and that must be done by their tutor. As of November 1, 2022, a previous form of protective supervision—the curator— will no longer exist. Any outstanding curators will become tutors. Assistant An assistant is an individual chosen by someone living with a difficulty to help with the administration of their property or the exercise of their rights. Although assistants are not court-appointed, they are recognized by the public curator and are publicly registered to act as an intermediary between the individual living with a difficulty and third parties, including government departments. Temporary Representative A temporary representative of an incapable individual is a court-authorized individual who performs a specific act on their behalf. The court sets the terms and conditions of the exercise of the temporary representative's powers. Given that this is a temporary measure, there is an end to the period of the temporary representation, after which the incapable individual regains their rights. When is a POA valid? In Canada, since legal representation is legislated provincially or territorially and is unique to each province and territory, a POA is valid when it meets the legislated standards of the province or territory in which it is issued. An authorizing instrument issued in one province or territory is acceptable in another province or territory, provided it meets the requirements of the province or territory receiving the POA. Therefore, should the grantor move to another province or territory after executing the POA, the POA executed in the one province or territory will be honoured in whatever province or territory the grantor resides as long as the initial authorizing instrument meets the requirements of the province or territory. Provincial or territorial legislation allow for a POA to be executed without the involvement of a lawyer, but it must be executed according to the laws of the province or territory where it is being executed. The provinces or territories provide direction on how POAs should be written and signed if they are executed without legal assistance (a lawyer or notary public). They often provide a template that the grantor can use. An individual can grant a POA to whomever, with whatever duties, and under whatever conditions they choose, which could include allowing the appointed attorney to delegate their duties to others. Although it is the individual's right to grant their authority to someone that they trust to act on their behalf, accepting a POA for CPP and OAS purposes is up to the discretion of the Department. A POA document executed with or without legal assistance may be a valid POA for CPP or OAS purposes if it meets the legal requirements under the provincial or territorial Act in which it is executed. The following list provides some general information needed to determine if a POA is valid (including a foreign-issued POA) for CPP or OAS purposes: a title that describes the contents; the name or names of individuals who have the power to act on behalf of the grantor (jointly and severally) (independently); a description of what the appointed third party or parties can do on behalf of the grantor; the date the POA takes effect (on the date it is executed or upon a specific event for a springing POA); the duration of the appointment; information about whether the power continues to act after the grantor becomes incapable (enduring or continuing); the conditions under which the POA continues; the name and signature of the grantor; the date on which the document was drafted; the name and signature of the individual (s) named to act on behalf of the grantor (the signature of an individual who has been granted POA is only required on the POA document where the requirement is prescribed by legislation. Not all Acts require the attorney named in the POA to sign the POA document); the names and signatures of the witness(es). The POA will only be acceptable for program purposes if it is witnessed in accordance with the appropriate Act. If there is only one witness, they cannot be the same individual that is being given the POA, an individual related to the grantor by blood, adoption, adoption-in-fact or through marriage, or someone of minor age; and in the case of a foreign POA, it must be witnessed either by a lawyer and accompanied by legal advice and witness certificate in the prescribed form; or by two adults who are not named as the POA or who are not family members of either the POA or grantor. The POA must contain the grantor's signature. It must indicate where it was executed and that its purpose is for property and not for personal care. Although a POA does not have to be enduring or continuing, it is important to take note whether the POA is enduring or continuing should the grantor become incapable. When a POA is signed with a mark instead of a signature A POA signed by a mark is acceptable. The mark might be anything from an “x” to a thumbprint. A statement from the witness(es) or a lawyer must accompany the POA document that has been signed with a mark confirming they saw the grantor sign the document with their mark and that they appeared to understand what they were signing. POAs and payment of benefits Unlike trusteeship, when the Department has been advised that a third party has been granted a POA, whether springing or enduring, it does not result in changing the payee to that third party. Even if the grantor becomes incapable, payments continue to be made payable to the grantor in care of the POA. When is a POA not valid? A POA document that does not meet the legal requirements under provincial or territorial law cannot be accepted, nor will a written statement be accepted as a substitute. A third party indicating that they are the holder of a POA who cannot produce a copy of the document cannot be recognized by the Department as the individual's legal representative. When does a POA end? A POA remains in effect until: it is voluntarily revoked. The grantor can only revoke a POA while they are mentally capable. This revocation must be done in writing and witnessed by a lawyer, notary public or 1 to 2 witnesses (depending on the province or territory where it is being signed); the grantor completes a new POA. The Department will need to confirm with the grantor that they have revoked the previous POA; or it is involuntarily revoked through: bankruptcy of the grantor; mental incapability of the grantor (if the POA is not an enduring or continuing POA); or death of the grantor. it is revoked by a Court order, either through a direct order or by the appointment of another representative, which automatically rescinds the POA (the appointment of the public trustee, or a guardian, etc.). The authority of an attorney under an enduring POA ends if a court is satisfied, on the application of any interested individual, that an attorney has abused their authority and a guardian is subsequently appointed under provincial or territorial law; the individual having the POA: advises the Department in writing that they no longer have POA (e.g. the POA has been revoked); has renounced their role as POA and there is no joint or substitute attorney named in the POA document; is no longer physically or mentally capable of performing duties; or dies. A POA document may name an alternate attorney in case the primary attorney is unwilling or unable to act or dies. If the primary attorney is unwilling or unable to act on behalf of the grantor, the Department will require written notification of the primary's resignation or proof of their death before the Department will recognize the alternate's authority to act on behalf of the grantor for OAS and CPP purposes. Protection of employees of the Department Generally, some protection is given under the various provincial Acts when the actual notice of revocation of the POA is not received by the attorney or by the Department. If the attorney and the Department act in good faith and without knowledge that the grantor has terminated or revoked the POA, the Department's actions resulting from the attorney's requests are valid and binding.

The province of British Columbia (BC) has both a Power of Attorney Act and a Representation Agreement Act . The BC Representation Agreement Act provides an opportunity for adults to appoint a representative if they do not meet the capability requirements to appoint a POA under the BC Power of Attorney Act . An adult who requires a representative but who does not meet the capability requirements to legally grant a POA can still make a representation agreement. For example, these adults who have: a developmental disability and communicate through gestures; had a stroke and cannot sign a contract; or mild dementia. Since the representation agreement allows individuals to plan for the possibility of future incapability, by its very nature, it is enduring and continues despite any future incapability of the individual. These agreements are treated similar to enduring POAs, are recognized for CPP and OAS purposes and do not require proof of incapability. Under section, 7 of the Representation Agreement Act an adult may name a representative to help them make decisions, or to make decisions on their behalf, with respect to personal care, and the routine management of their financial affairs, which includes pensions. The representation agreement, like a POA, allows the representative to sign documents on behalf of the individual; and, benefits continue to be paid to the individual, despite any future incapability of the individual. It is possible that an individual has both a representation agreement and a POA in place. Should a conflict arise or there is an inconsistency between a POA and a representation agreement, under the BC Power of Attorney Act, the issue will be resolved in favour of the provision in the enduring POA. For CPP and OAS purposes, only representatives appointed under Section 7 of Representation Agreement Act after September 1, 2011, (or under Section 9 before September 1, 2011) are recognized.

When does the Department appoint a trustee? The Department can appoint a trustee when an individual who is eligible to receive benefits is incapable of managing their own affairs and an individual or agency has come forward requesting to administer benefits on that individual's behalf. The Department can only appoint a trustee when there is no existing legally binding arrangement in place for another individual or agency to act on the individual's behalf, i.e. an attorney named in an enduring POA, or a federally, provincially or territorially-appointed administrator (e.g. public trustee, court-appointed committee or guardian). OAS and CPP benefits are paid directly to a government-appointed administrator on behalf of an incapable individual when the Department is notified of the arrangement and receives proof of appointment. If the Department is aware that the beneficiary had granted an enduring, continuing or springing POA before they became incapable, the Department cannot appoint a trustee, even if it is the attorneys themselves requesting to be paid as trustee. This would go against provincial POA legislation. When there is no legal representative appointed under a law of Canada (province or territory) to act on behalf of an incapable individual, the Department may appoint an individual, institution, or agency to administer benefits if they come forward to request to be appointed. This individual, institution or agency is referred to as a Departmental trustee and may apply for, receive and administer benefits on behalf of the incapable individual. The appointment may only be made when it has been concluded that the beneficiary is incapable of managing their own affairs and the third party (individual or agency) has entered into an agreement with the Minister to receive and administer benefits on behalf of that individual. If the Department suspects that an individual is incapable of managing their affairs, but no one comes forward to identify themselves as the individual's legal representative (POA or Court appointed), the Department cannot solicit a third party or approach the public trustee to assist or to take over as trustee. Instead, a Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP-1603) form can be mailed to the individual's address. Either the individual will then authorize someone to communicate on their behalf, or someone who is helping the individual may come forward to inform the Department that they are their legal representative or to apply for trusteeship. Documentation required to appoint a trustee Certificate of i ncapability A Certificate of Incapability (ISP-3505) form is required to confirm that an individual is incapable of managing their affairs before the Minister can appoint a third party to act on their behalf. Whenever possible, the individual's treating physician must complete the ISP-3505 form. If there is no treating physician, or if another physician is better-suited to attest to the individual's incapability, then it can be filled out by that physician. If there is no physician available who can fill out the ISP-3505 form, the following designated licensed medical professionals may complete it: a registered nurse; a nurse practitioner; a professional social worker; or a clinical psychologist. The physician or licensed medical professional needs to provide a medical diagnosis of: impairment; infirmity; insanity; or illness. When there is no licensed medical professional, the following designated licensed professionals may complete the ISP-3505 form: a member of the clergy who is in a position to know the facts; a professional social worker; or a lawyer who has been handling the affairs of the individual. The designated licensed professional has to provide a description of the incapability (i.e. whether the underlying cause of the incapability is infirmity, illness, insanity or another cause) to support their assessment of incapability. The reasons provided by the non-medical licensed professional will constitute evidence that the Department will have to evaluate. If necessary, further evidence or information can be sought from the certifier if there is any doubt about the individual's incapability. The Department must be satisfied that the applicant or beneficiary is incapable of managing their affairs. Agreement to administer benefits Before the Department appoints a trustee, the individual or agency must agree , in writing, to administer the funds. By signing the Agreement to administer benefits under the Old Age Security Act and/or the Canada Pension Plan by a Private Trustee (ISP-3506) form or the Agreement to administer benefits under the Old Age Security Act and/or the Canada Pension Plan by an Agency or Institution (ISP-3507) form they agree to: act on behalf of the beneficiary by accounting for all benefits received from OAS and CPP and indicate how this money was spent; notify the Department of any changes regarding the beneficiary's condition (the trustee must inform the Department if the individual has regained capability. The Department will then ask the trustee to produce a new certificate of incapability or a doctor's narrative to assess the beneficiary's capability. If the beneficiary has regained capability, the trusteeship would end, and benefits would be made payable directly to the beneficiary); return the payment for any month in which the beneficiary is no longer in their care; inform the Department if the beneficiary moves outside of Canada or they lose contact with the beneficiary; inform the Department if they feel that they are no longer in a position to administer the benefits effectively; and return any benefits paid for month(s) following the month of a beneficiary's death. Private trustee Before the Department can appoint an individual, it must receive the ISP-3505 and ISP-3506 forms duly completed, dated and signed. Agency or institution Before the Department can appoint an agency, it must receive the ISP-3505 and ISP-3507 forms duly completed, dated and signed. Foreign Trustees Legislation allows payment of OAS and CPP benefits directly to a legal representative who has been appointed by a provincial, territorial or federal court of Canada for the purposes of managing the property of a beneficiary who has been deemed incapable of handling their own affairs. If an incapable beneficiary lives abroad and there is no Canadian provincially, territorially or federally appointed administrator to manage their affairs, the Department can appoint a foreign-based administrator after receiving either the ISP-3505 and ISP-3506 (for an individual) forms or the ISP-3507 (for an organization) form. These trustees will be responsible for completing a Trustee's Accounting Report (ISP-3509) form when requested to do so by the Department. Non-profit organizations, registered charities or municipalities administering benefits on behalf of vulnerable seniors aged 65 or over To ensure that vulnerable seniors, aged 65 and over, receive the benefits to which they are entitled, non-profit or charitable organizations and municipalities may apply to administer and expend benefits on behalf of homeless, or at imminent risk of being homeless. The Department will only appoint the organization as a trustee if the Department is satisfied that the eligible individual is incapable of managing their own affairs and the organization has entered into an agreement with the Department to administer benefits. The Department must also be satisfied that no other individual (i.e. a family member, close friend, or an individual) who has POA or agency is already authorized by, or pursuant to, a law of Canada, a province or a territory to represent an incapable beneficiary or potential beneficiary through an existing arrangement as in the following situations: valid enduring POA; trusteeship; committee; or guardianship. Before the Department appoints the organization as trustee, certain criteria must be met. The organization must provide an attestation of the individual's homelessness and that the homeless senior lives in Canada. The organization or municipality determines that a senior is homeless, or at imminent risk of being homeless, by assessing the individual's living situation, which could include the following factors: the absence of a fixed home address; a regular pattern of shelter usage; a precarious, unsafe, or inadequate housing arrangement; or a self-identification of being homeless. The organization must be either: a municipality incorporated under the relevant provincial or territorial act; a non-profit organization; or a registered charity possessing an exemption under the Income Tax Act . The organization must also be recognized as valid or reputable. This may be determined through various ways. A charitable organization will be listed as a charity on the CRA website. A non-profit organization may be recognized by CRA , yet it may not be listed on the CRA website, in which case it would have to provide proof of its status by submitting one of the following: a copy of its constitution and/or by-laws; letters of incorporation; or documentation indicating a history of recognition of its excellence in delivering services to homeless, or at imminent risk of being homeless seniors. The organization must submit an ISP-3505 form and an ISP-3507 form. A professional in the organization who falls under the list of designated professionals who can sign the ISP-3505 form cannot be the same individual who signs the ISP-3507 form; however, the different individual can work for the same organization. The organization must also have liability insurance of at least $1,000,000.00 (or, in the case of a municipality, the capacity to fund a liability of at least $1,000,000.00), or their request to administer the benefits will be denied. Although an individual may be homeless and incapable, the individual must still meet all eligibility requirements to receive a benefit. As this group of individuals and the organizations applying to act as trustees on behalf of the individual may have difficulty obtaining standard documents to prove eligibility requirements, there may be a higher incidence of other acceptable evidence being presented to meet the requirements (e.g. statutory declarations for OAS residence). When does a Department-appointed trusteeship end? The Department may terminate the appointment of a trustee for the following reasons: the beneficiary regains the capability to manage their own affairs; the beneficiary attains the age of majority; the beneficiary dies; the trustee dies; the trustee fails to notify the Department of any changes to the beneficiary's condition; the trustee has lost contact with the beneficiary; the trustee fails to respond to an accounting request; the trustee fails to demonstrate consistent accountings; the trustee fails to act on behalf of or in the best interests of the beneficiary; there is a change of trustee; the Department is informed that another legal representation exists that takes precedence. For example, provincial or federal legislation may terminate a Departmentally-appointed trusteeship based on something else being put into place (i.e. another third party may be appointed through a court order in such a way that the previous authorization is no longer valid); or the organization's reliable status changes. Department-appointed trustee accounting Legislation requires a Department-appointed trustee to account for all monies they received to ensure that the monies were used for the benefit of the individual. The Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act prescribe the Minister's authority to request a ISP-3509 form at such time or times as the Minister deems it necessary. Trustees must maintain yearly records of the monies received and spent for the beneficiary. Should the Minister deem it necessary to obtain an accounting report, the trustee must be able to readily provide the requested documentation for the applicable year(s). The Department requires an accounting report from the trustee a minimum of every 2 years from the date of the last accounting request, but has the authority to request one more often depending on the circumstances (e.g. trustees receiving benefits on behalf of homeless or at risk of being homeless seniors). If a Department-appointed trustee dies and the beneficiary lives on, the trusteeship ends unless there are multiple trustees or a substitute is named, and the benefits must be suspended. A new trustee must be appointed as soon as possible, and a final accounting ISP-3509 form must be obtained from the executor handling the estate of the deceased trustee. No effort is to be made to recover unexpended funds, as this becomes a civil matter between the new trustee and the former trustee's estate. If a Department-appointed trusteeship ends for any reason other than the death of the trustee, the trustee must return to the Department any funds they received on behalf of the incapable individual that they did not disburse to the incapable individual or expend on their behalf; and complete a final accounting report. Charitable, non-profit organizations and municipalities approved as legal representatives are required to provide independently audited statements to ensure the validity and reliability of the information that they provide. As reporting mechanisms are already in place for federal and provincial government departments and agencies that are acting on behalf of an incapable beneficiary, the Department will not normally request an accounting report from these representatives unless there is doubt regarding the disbursement of the beneficiary's monies. Responsibility of the Department In the case of a Department-appointed trusteeship, the Department must investigate when a complaint is received where benefits are not being administrated properly on behalf of the CPP and or OAS beneficiary. The Department can remove a trustee in circumstances where the trustee fails to act appropriately and meet the requirements of the appointment. If the trustee must be removed and no one else comes forward to request trusteeship, the Department cannot solicit another third party or approach the provincial public trustee to assist or to take over as trustee. Benefits would then be paid directly to the beneficiary. In these situations, Integrity Services can be consulted to investigate whether there is a contact for the beneficiary. Whenever there is a dispute between a POA, trustee, committee, etc., the Department is responsible for determining which legal representation should take precedence.

topic_title: Accumulating residence under an International Social Security Agreement Updated
text: When an OAS pensioner residing outside Canada has not accumulated enough Canadian residence (i.e. 20 years) to allow portability of the pension, the totalization provisions of Canada's International Social Security Agreements (ISSAs) can be used to satisfy these requirements. While the way Canadian residence is measured under the various agreements may vary, the basic premise is that years of residence or contributions in an ISSA country can be added to an applicant's Canadian residence (totalization). If the combination of Canadian residence and qualifying international residence or contributions is greater than 20 years, the OAS pension becomes fully portable. If a pensioner leaves Canada permanently and their pension is not portable, entitlement may be reinstated if they accrue creditable periods in a country with whom Canada has an ISSA without having to return to Canada.
Old Age Security Act Section 9—Suspension of pension where pensioner leaves Canada Subsection 9(1)—Suspension of pension where pensioner leaves Canada

Portability is the term used to refer to a pensioner's ability to receive their pension abroad. After an OAS pensioner leaves Canada, the portability rules determine the length of time that the Department can continue to pay the pension. The basic intent of the OAS pension is to provide seniors with modest economic support. The amount of support and an individual's eligibility for the support is based on their contribution to Canadian society. The primary targets of the OAS pension are seniors living in Canada. For OAS purposes, the contribution that an individual makes to Canadian society is measured by the amount of time an applicant has been a resident of Canada. After having made a significant contribution to our society, many seniors may choose to leave Canada to live elsewhere.

As a rule, OAS income-tested benefits (i.e. GIS, ALW and ALWS ) are not portable. These benefits are intended to provide immediate economic support to lower income Canadians while they are residents of Canada. The payment of OAS income tested benefits is extended for 6 months beyond the month of departure from Canada but are not continued beyond that point.

topic_title: Portability and the amount of an OAS pension Updated
text: In most cases, the amount of an OAS pension that is portable will be the same as the pensioner's original entitlement. This includes any escalation to the pension amount based on changes in the Consumer Price Index since the pension originally became payable. Once a partial pension has been approved, the amount may not be increased based on subsequent residence in Canada or deemed residence while outside of Canada. While the net amount could change, as it could now be subject to additional non-resident and recovery tax deductions, the gross entitlement will remain the same. Some scenarios include: A pensioner receiving a full OAS pension based on 40 years of Canadian residence is entitled to continued payment of the pension despite leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 24 years of Canadian residence is entitled to continued payment of the pension when they leave Canada. A pensioner has been receiving a partial OAS pension for 3 years. As the partial pension was based on 18 years of Canadian residence, the pensioner is entitled to continued payment of the pension despite leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 4 years of Canadian residence in combination with 18 years of residence or contributions in a country with which Canada has an ISSA has satisfied the portability requirements and is entitled to continued payment of the pension when they leave Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 16 years of Canadian residence and who does not have sufficient foreign creditable periods under an ISSA is not entitled to continued payment of the pension upon leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 18 years of Canadian residence is living outside of Canada working as a Missionary (i.e. is considered a deemed resident) is entitled to 6 months after the month of departure from Canada. Once the pensioner returns to Canada, the pension is reinstated. The absence can be counted as an uninterrupted residence towards the 20 years required for portability purposes. An applicant applies for an OAS pension. Upon reaching age 65, the applicant is absent from Canada but considered a deemed resident. All residence before age 65 is used to determine eligibility. If the applicant has a minimum of 10 years of residence after age 18 but less than 20, the benefit can be paid for 6 months after the month of departure. The pension is reinstated the month of return or the month residence is resumed in Canada.

topic_title: Portability of entitlement established under the 3 for 1 or 10-year rules Updated
text: While the scenarios listed in the Portability and the amount of an OAS pension section above are some common or typical portability situations, other circumstances require a closer examination. Under the 10-year and 3 for 1 rule, it is possible for an individual to qualify for a full pension (i.e. the equivalent of 40/40ths) with less than 20 years of Canadian residence. In these situations, the individual may qualify for a full pension while in Canada but may not have sufficient Canadian residence for portability purposes. Upon notification that an OAS pensioner is leaving the country, their residence must be reviewed to determine if the pension should be paid on a continuing basis for more than 6 months after the month of departure. This is particularly true for the pensioner who qualified for a full pension by virtue of the 3 for 1 or 10-year rules as their eligibility was determined without necessarily establishing that they had 20 years of Canadian residence. There are 2 possible outcomes: The pensioner has more than 20 years of Canadian residence With 20 years of Canadian residence, the OAS pension is fully portable, and the pensioner is entitled to continuing payment of the equivalent of a full (i.e. 40/40ths) pension for the duration of their eligibility. The pensioner has less than 20 years of Canadian residence Payment of the OAS pension will be suspended effective the 7th month after leaving Canada unless the pensioner can take advantage of the totalization provisions of an ISSA to meet the 20-year portability requirement. If the pensioner must rely on the totalization provisions of an ISSA, the file must be transferred to International Operations. If the pensioner is entitled to a full OAS pension based on the 3 for 1 or the 10-year rules, this will be reduced to a partial pension reflecting only the individual's Canadian residence, with certain rare exceptions.

topic_title: Portability requirements for an OAS pension
text: To satisfy the portability requirements, an applicant must have accumulated a minimum of 20 years of Canadian residence, at which time an OAS pensioner is considered to have made a significant enough contribution to warrant the continued payment (portability) of the OAS pension after leaving Canada. However, this requirement is not applied at the time of application unless the applicant applies from outside of Canada. Instead, the portability requirement is applied 6 months after the month that a pensioner left Canada. This means that pensioners who were originally entitled to an OAS pension based on less than 20 years of Canadian residence could have accumulated sufficient residence to allow portability of the pension. A pensioner may be paid a full pension under the 10 Year Rule or the 3 for 1 Rule but may not have accumulated the required 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18 for the pension to be portable. The same applies to a pensioner in receipt of a partial pension in which they have not accumulated the required 20 years of Canadian residence. A partial pension based on 18/40ths will, after 2 additional years of Canadian residence (from the effective date of the OAS pension), become fully portable. It was not portable at the time of application but later becomes so; however, there will be no adjustment to the rate. If an applicant chooses to voluntarily defer a partial pension for a higher pension amount, the adjustment to the pension may be based on the actuarial adjustment, not on the further accumulation of residence. However, residence will continue to be accumulated for portability purposes.

topic_title: Portability rules between March 11, 2020 and June 1, 2021 New
text: Beneficiaries in receipt of non-portable OAS benefits who were unable to return to Canada within 6 months of their departure from Canada due to restrictions caused by the pandemic (between March 11, 2020 and June 1, 2021) did not have their benefits suspended. When beneficiaries notified the Department that they could not return for reasons related to COVID-19, payments continued beyond the 6-month limitation. This interim measure was rescinded, and regular portability rules resumed effective June 2021.

Proactive enrolment allows the Minister to waive the requirement for an application for an RTR pension if the Minister is satisfied that: the person has contributed to the CPP; the person is 70 years old or older; and the person either: receive: another CPP benefit; an OAS benefit; a QPP benefit; or has filed an income tax return for the tax year that precedes the year in which the Minister intends to waive the requirement. The amended legislation provides that an application for an RTR pension is deemed to have been made and received on the day the requirement for an application is waived. When the requirement for an application is waived, an approved RTR pension is payable for each month after the month the requirement is waived.

A CPP Retirement (RTR) pension is payable to CPP contributors who have reached the eligible age. Legislation allows an individual to begin receiving their RTR pension as early as age 60 with a permanent reduction in the pension amount or to defer up to age 70 with a permanent escalation. Current legislation requires that an application or a request in writing be made in order for a beneficiary to receive their RTR pension. A significant number of eligible seniors have not applied for their RTR pension by age 70 and, therefore, may not be receiving benefits to which they may be entitled. Effective January 1, 2020, Bill C-97 will allow the Minister to waive the requirement for an application for an RTR pension under specific criteria and proactively enroll eligible individuals for their RTR pension at age 70. In situations where there is insufficient information for the Minister to assess these criteria, the requirement to submit an application for the RTR pension still applies. The CPP regulations allowing a CPP beneficiary to cancel their benefit has been amended to extend the current 6-month window for requesting the cancellation and repayment of a CPP benefit to 12 months.
