topic_title: +18 child left school before ITRDS Release 7 implementation
text: Mario submitted an ISP1401 form in January 2009 for the Winter 2009 semester. September 2009 was entered as the school end date. Mario left school in March 2009. His Child's benefit was terminated March 31, 2009. Mario returned to school in September 2009. Although the benefit was properly terminated in March 2009, the school end date of September 2009 remained in the CPP/Continuous Supplementary Cheque Legacy System and was converted to ITRDS . When the new school period is entered, the ITRDS determines that Mario was underpaid for the period from April to September 2009 and a payable is created. In such a situation, you must modify the converted school attendance period (i.e. the end date) to reflect when the +18 child left school.

topic_title: A school period prior to migration New
text: Mary turned 18 in October 2024. Mary was in full-time attendance at school beginning in September 2024. However, Mary did not submit a Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP-1401) form for September to December 2024. Mary submitted an ISP-1401 form for the winter semester only (beginning January 2025). Mary was not paid from November to December 2024 in the IA Legacy system. Mary then submitted an ISP-1401 form for the period from September to December 2024. As the second ISP-1401 form covers a school period before CPP IA migration, do not enter this school period into ITRDS . Only enter periods after January 2025. You must: Enter the school period after January 2025 in ITRDS . You must use the Super Program Exception Process functionality to data capture the child's benefit starting in January. Issue a manual priority payment for the 2 months that were previously withheld (November and December 2024). Update the client's notes.

topic_title: CPP International Agreements migration to ITRDS —release December 2024 New
text: In the International Agreement (IA) Legacy system, children's benefits were displayed with a single pay pattern where the start date was the effective date of the benefit. You would have entered the future end date for a child's benefit for a child over the age of 18 (+18 child) by entering the school end date. In the Legacy system, the school end date was automatically updated when a benefit had been terminated. If a break in benefit entitlement occurred (e.g. a gap in school attendance), you had to manually withhold payment for the period of non-entitlement. Information concerning breaks in benefit entitlement was not visible on the Benefits information screen (1I5) and +18 child periods appeared as a single continuous period. As it was not possible to separate the individual benefit periods, the data was converted to ITRDS as a single period. For more information, Interpreting Converted Data on ITRDS Screens It is possible to experience adjudication issues while processing declaration of attendance at school or university requests in the situations below.

topic_title: Entry of a previously-withheld school period
text: Mary turned 18 in October 2008. She was in full-time attendance at school beginning in September 2008. However, she submitted an ISP1401 form for the winter semester only (beginning January 2009). In the CPP/Continuous Supplementary Cheque Legacy System, a school end date of September 2009 was entered. The payments for November 2008 and December 2008 were withheld. Mary submitted an ISP1401 form for the period from September to December 2008. As the ISP1401 form covers a school period before ITRDS implementation and the payment for this period was previously withheld, this school period is not entered into ITRDS . You must: Issue a priority payment for the 2 months that were previously withheld (November and December 2008). Update the client's notes.

In the CPP/Continuing Supplementary Cheque Legacy system, Children's benefits were displayed with a single pay pattern where the start date was the effective date of the benefit. You would have entered the "future end date" of a +18 Child's benefit by entering the school end date. In the Legacy system, the school end date was automatically updated when a benefit had been terminated. If a break in benefit entitlement occurred (e.g. a gap in school attendance), you had to manually withhold payment for the period of non-entitlement. Information concerning breaks in benefit entitlement was not visible on the Benefits information screen (1B1) and +18 Child's benefit periods appeared as a single continuous period. As it was not possible to separate the individual benefit periods, the data was converted to ITRDS as a single period. For more information, Interpreting Converted Data on ITRDS Screens This situation did not cause adjudication issues during regular Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) form processing except in the following situations.

Jason attended school after his 18th birthday in August 2007. After completing the fall semester in December 2007, he did not return to school until September 2008. Jason's mother Susan receives a Survivor's ( SVR ) pension. When Jason leaves school after December 2007, Susan is 40 years of age. Because Susan is under age 45, her SVR pension amount is reduced when Jason leaves school. When Jason returns to school in September 2008, Susan is again eligible for a full SVR pension. The agent correctly entered the dependency end and start dates (date dependency starts (DPNS) and date dependency ends (DPNE) transactions) in the CPP/Continuous Supplementary Cheque Legacy System. Jason submits a new ISP1401 form for the September 2009 semester. Jason's school attendance period is converted to ITRDS from the CPP/Continuous Supplementary Cheque Legacy System as September 2007 to September 2009. His benefit information goes from incorrect to correct when you add the new school period. A review of Susan's benefit information shows a change in her SVR pension rate and a corresponding payable because the attendance appears to be continuous (i.e. no loss in dependency). This is incorrect . When this error occurs, the agent must rebuild the child's school attendance period completely as follows: Retrieve the hard copy account file. Determine whether the child's account is in balance, considering: the ISP1401 form submitted; eligibility; amounts previously withheld; and whether the child: is owed additional payments; or has been overpaid. Determine the exact balance. In the child's account, delete the existing converted school period entirely on the School Declaration screen. Refer to the ISP1401 forms from the file and add each school attendance period individually to ITRDS . In extreme circumstances where the file is not available, the following information may be available: in the client's notes in ITRDS ; or by reviewing the information available on the CPP/Continuous Supplementary Cheque Legacy System 1B4 and 1T7 screens. When the data from all ISP1401 forms have been entered in ITRDS , access the Benefits screen. This causes a re-adjudication of the account and any related accounts. Access the Overview screen in CPMS . In such a situation, monetary results (payables) occur. These should equal the amounts previously withheld. Adjust the payable in CPMS : Adjust the Supplementary Payable using the Adjustment Reason Not Entitled and Adjustment Type Decrease Payable Amount . Enter the amount previously withheld in Adjustment Amount . Change the Payable Status to Pending . Update the Client's Notes in ITRDS . The +18 Child's benefit should now be correctly “in pay”, with no additional monetary results. Access the SVR account by clicking on Interrelationships in the navigation menu. The Interrelationships screen opens. Access the survivor's Benefits screen. Confirm all pay patterns have been correctly re-established and that the benefit rate is correct. Access the Overview screen in CPMS . Confirm all monetary results have been correctly adjusted. No payable should be present.

The CPP recognizes that in respect of Pension Sharing, Credit Splitting and the Survivor’s pension, a separation does not constitute an interruption of cohabitation when a couple did not have the intention to live separate and apart, but were separated by reason of : occupation; employment; or illness of either individual. In most cases, these conditions are met when one spouse or common-law partner can no longer live in the family home due to age or illness. Circumstances for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control Medical condition A couple can be considered to be living apart for reasons beyond their control when one member of the couple: needs ongoing medical care and assistance with activities of daily living and lives in an alternate dwelling with someone who takes care of their needs (such as a family member, hospital, nursing home or care facility), while the other spouse or common-law partner remains in the matrimonial home; and/or needs to move closer to receive medical assistance, while the other spouse or common-law partner remains in the matrimonial home. Such a move can be of a temporary or permanent nature. Employment or occupation In cases where the couple must live separately for employment or occupation reasons (i.e. availability of work), they can be considered as living apart for reasons beyond their control. Incarceration If one spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated, to be considered separated for reasons beyond their control, the applicant must prove that this is a temporary separation and that the spouses or common-law partners intend to resume living together (cohabitating) after the period of incarceration. Pension sharing for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control For Retirement Pension Sharing, the pension sharing will continue if a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control, such time that the Minister is sa tisfied that the circumstances have changed in the following situations: the couple becomes separated or divorced; or one spouse or common-law partner dies.

topic_title: Continued consent to communicate personal information
text: The Department must obtain written consent in cases where the individual is seeking to allow the Department to disclose their information to another individual, agency or organization (who is not a legal representative) over a continuous period of time. A departmental form that is available for this purpose: Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP-1603) form. The intended use of the ISP-1603 form is not to communicate with an agency or organization. An agency or organization's form is acceptable consent as long as it provides all the required information. The individual can also provide all the required information to the Department with their own written statement authorizing us to communicate with that agency or organization. As it is an individual's right to share their personal information with whomever and however they choose, the Department cannot insist on the individual using a departmental consent form for communication purposes with an authorized person or agency. However, to protect the privacy of the individual and the integrity of the programs, the consent needs to be in writing, signed and dated. If the individual uses a letter of authorization or another agency or organization's form for consent to communicate their personal information, it should provide: the name, address and telephone number of the authorized person, agency or organization; what information can be shared; and any restrictions. For example, a consent may be received restricting the purpose for communication with the authorized person to the reconsideration process. Once a decision is made on the reconsideration, the consent expires. By signing the consent form or letter, the individual is declaring they understand that they are allowing the Department to communicate their personal information to a third party. The Department will only release information that is permitted by the form or letter and under the specified circumstances and conditions stated on the consent form or letter. If an individual has provided written consent, they may withdraw their consent at any time. For records and audit purposes, it would be preferable the withdrawal bein writing. However, if the individual cannot send a written request and the employee had validated their identity over the phone, the Department can accept their verbal request to withdraw their consent. The staff must document the withdrawal request.

The Privacy Act defines personal information as information about an identifiable individual that is recorded in any form. Personal information includes: race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age or marital status of the individual; education and medical, criminal or employment history; financial transactions in which they were involved; any identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, such as a SIN; an address, fingerprints or blood type; their personal opinions or views, except where they are about another individual; correspondence sent to a government institution by the individual that is implicitly or explicitly of a private or confidential nature, and replies to such correspondence that would reveal the contents of the original correspondence; the views or opinions of another individual about the individual; and their name where it appears with other personal information relating to them or where the disclosure of the name itself would reveal information about them.

Requests for information made on the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat Policies (Directive on Privacy Practices) forms, e.g. Access to Information Request Form (TBC 350-57) and Personal Information Request Form (TBC 350-58) are formal requests. Written requests that refer to an Act such as the Privacy Act , Access to Information Act , and Freedom of Information Act are also considered formal requests. Formal requests are sent to the regional privacy coordinators to manage. The director of Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) and Employment and Social Development Canada, along with the National Headquarters ATIP coordinator are the only authorities who can deny formal requests for access to personal information received from an individual or their legal representative. The privacy coordinator provides an explanation for the denial to access the information to the individual, if requested.

Generally, when receiving a written request that does not mention the Privacy Act specifically, it is considered an informal request for information. Once the Department identifies the identity and authority of the individual who will receive the information, they release the information under the legislative provisions of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the CPP legislation and the OAS Act. However, if information on an individual's file is exempt from disclosure, the Department cannot respond to an individual's informal request to provide them access to the personal information on their file. The privacy coordinator will provide the reasons for denying access to the individual. Denying access can occur for information that contains the following: references to other individuals; sensitive medical information; information that cannot be disclosed for legal or security reasons; and information that is subject to solicitor-client or litigation privilege. Requests for copies of the following are to be referred toAccess to Information and Privacy: medical reports; statements made by a third party; applications for benefits; letters sent to a third party; documents related to an integrity investigation; entire files, as they usually contain personal information of another individual (e.g. SIN and date of birth); information on another individual's file; and documents that contain the personal information of other individuals.

topic_title: One-time consent to communicate personal information
text: The Department accepts verbal consent in cases where an individual calls and requests that CPP or OAS staff speak with a third party who is in the room with them at the time of the call. Personal information can be shared with the third party once the caller is authenticated as the applicant, beneficiary or contributor. The verbal consent is deemed valid only for the duration of that telephone call. Details of the conversation must be recorded for accountability purposes.

The government defines privacy as an individual's right to the protection of their personal information. Protection of personal information is a requirement of the government to control the extent to which an individual's personal information is collected, used, disclosed, retained and disposed. All employees are responsible for being aware of the importance of: protecting personal information in their care; ensuring that security requirements are being met; and reporting real and suspected incidents to management. Consent to communicate personal information In the course of administering and delivering benefits for CPP and OAS programs, the Department frequently receives requests for personal information. Personal information that is on a departmental file (e.g. an application, correspondence) belongs to the individual. Before sharing information from an individual's file with a third party, there must be authority to do so. Authorization to release information may be granted by relevant legislation or by the individual to whom the information pertains. The individual can authorize this release of information through a legal instrument such as a power of attorney, will, letter of authorization or consent form. They can authorize the release of information verbally depending on the circumstances of the request. If the individual cannot provide authority because they become mentally incapable or die, legislation allows for the appointment of a legal representative to act on their or their estate's behalf. The legal instrument will specify what personal information can be shared and the conditions for the release. Requests received for disclosure of personal information There are differences in how the Department responds to requests for information when they are of a formal or informal nature and based on who requests the information. Transmission of personal information (Protected A, B and C) The policy regarding the transmission of personal information by hand, mail, fax or email depends on the classification of the information. Information is classified as Protected A, B, or C. To learn what is considered Protected A, B, and C information and the rules on how it can be transmitted, refer to the Information Categorization Tool Internal link . Information Categorization Tool

topic_title: Principles on the protection of personal information
text: An individual's personal information, whether the individual is alive or deceased, is governed by the following 2 overriding principles: the individual (or their legal representative) has the right to access it; and it is privileged and thereby protected. Personal information may only be released as specified in the applicable provisions of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP legislation), the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act), Department of Employment and Social Development Act and Regulations or under the Privacy Act . Legislation governing the protection and disclosure of personal information applies to all personal information obtained by the Department in the course of administering an individual's file. This includes the information of the individual or of a third party mentioned on their file. All personal information is protected whether it is provided to or generated by the Department. The collection, use, disclosure, retention and disposition of personal information must be carried out in a way that respects the privacy principles. These privacy principles are outlined in the Privacy Act and other applicable laws, regulations and policies. This includes the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat Policies (Directive on Privacy Practices) and ESDC's Departmental Policy on Privacy Management. The stewardship of personal information and the protection of privacy are key components of the Department's code of conduct, which are described as follows: employees are responsible for the safekeeping of personal information collected, handled, stored and transmitted, and are responsible to ensure that, no matter the format of the information, (e.g. electronic, paper or other format), it must only be seen or handled by those who have the right to see it; employees are permitted to access only the personal information that is necessary for their work; The individual's personal information can only be disclosed as legally authorized; and the Privacy Act gives Canadians the right to see their own personal information in records that are under the Department's control. The Department of Employment and Social Development Act states that any individual or group who makes available information that is privileged is committing a breach of privacy. A privacy breach occurs when there is improper or unauthorized collection, use, disclosure, retention and disposal of personal information. A privacy breach can be the result of inadvertent errors or malicious actions by employees, third parties, partners in information-sharing agreements or intruders. A breach of the Department's code of conduct or any of the related laws, policies or procedures can lead to administrative or disciplinary measures, up to and including termination of employment. In addition, it is considered an offence and can be subject to additional punishment that includes a fine and imprisonment if any individual or group does the following: obstructs access to personal information; uses an individual's personal information; or knowingly makes available privileged information that is not authorized under Part 4 of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act.
Protected A information is of low sensitivity and of limited injury to individuals. It includes routine correspondence with name, address, gender, date of birth or SIN.

Protected B information is information that is particularly sensitive and may cause serious injury to the individual. Examples include: personnel screening; test results; character references; eligibility for social benefits; and medical and financial information

Protected C information is information that is extremely sensitive and can cause extreme injury to individuals (e.g. investigations into threats of individuals). Protected C information can only be transmitted via a secure method.

topic_title: Requests for corrections to personal information and complaints
text: Under the Privacy Act , an individual has the right to request corrections be made to their personal information on a government file in the case of an error or omission. They also have the right to register a complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada if they are dissatisfied with the information provided or any information exempt from disclosure.

topic_title: Requests for medical information from the individual
text: Individuals may request medical information from their file under the Privacy Act . Requests for copies of medical information must be in writing and not released on the basis of a verbal request. However, medical adjudicators have the flexibility of discussing medical evidence with the applicant, contributor or their legal representative over the phone. Medical adjudicators may also confirm the receipt of a medical report based on a verbal request. Requests for copies of medical information are forwarded to the regional or National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) coordinator. Medical information cannot be released unless the program authorizes the release. The coordinator will consult with a medical adjudicator before releasing the information. In situations where the disclosure of a medical report may not be in the best interests of the individual, the ATIP coordinator will obtain written confirmation from the physician who wrote the report on whether or not to release the medical information. The physician will advise the coordinator whether or not the release of the information would have an adverse effect on the physical, mental or emotional health of the individual or cause harm to a third party. In cases where the ATIP coordinator consults with a medical adjudicator before releasing information, the medical adjudicator may provide the ATIP coordinator with a recommendation, along with a rationale, as to why the medical information should not be released.

topic_title: Requests for medical reports from other program areas within the Department
text: Medical information may be disclosed from one program to another within the Department. However, only medical information that relates directly to the administration of the other program can be disclosed. The program that holds the information must authorize the disclosure. The program area must make a written request for the medical information of another program. As with requests for medical information from individuals, the requests are forwarded to the regional or National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy coordinator. Before releasing any medical information, ensure: the need for the requested information is clearly identified; the doctor's report does not specify that the information is not to be released because it could cause harm to the individual or to someone else; only information that is relevant for the administration of the program is released; and caution is applied when disclosing medical information. For example, Employment Insurance (EI) requests a copy of a letter contained in the Department's files. In the letter, the individual references their work activity. However, it also contains information on the individual's medical condition. Since work activity is relevant to the administration of the Employment Insurance Act (EI Act), information in the letter regarding their work activity can be released. However, since their medical information is not relevant to the administration of the EI Act, it cannot be released.

topic_title: Requests for personal information when there is an informant lead on file or a file is under investigation by the Integrity Services Branch occur
text: In some situations when receiving a request for information, there is an informant lead on file or the file is under investigation with the Integrity Services Branch (ISB). If this occurs, a decision on if and what information can be released can only be made after consulting with the proper departmental authorities (including Access to Information and Privacy and ISB).

topic_title: Requests from a friend, relative or other
text: There can often be situations when a third party (friend, relative, translator, etc.) requests information on behalf of an applicant or beneficiary and there is no authorizing instrument on file. In this situation, the Department cannot consider the third party to be an authorized contact and cannot release detailed information from the applicant or beneficiary's file. However, the Department can provide the third party with generic, non file-specific information. The only time personal information from the applicant or beneficiary's file can be shared with a friend or relative who is not recorded on file as an authorized contact is if they are in the room with the individual and the individual provides their verbal consent.

A lawyer can request information either in writing or verbally (i.e. in-person or by telephone). Supporting documentation must be on file (either a letter of authorization from the individual to whom the supporting documentation relates to or a letter from the lawyer written on a letterhead clearly indicating they are representing the individual) before releasing information from the file to them. If there is any doubt as to who the lawyer is representing, the individual's written authorization will be required. Letterhead is acceptable documentation for representation even if an assistant or a paralegal who is working for the lawyer signs it. If there is proof on file of the lawyer's authorization to communicate with the Department, information can be released to the lawyer and to the paralegal who is working for the lawyer.
Paralegals who are not working with the individual's lawyer are considered a third party and require the individual's authorization before any information can be released to them.

topic_title: Requests from a trustee in bankruptcy
text: A trustee that has been appointed under the rules of the Bankruptcy Insolvency Act must provide a legal authorizing document signed by the individual showing that the individual allows their personal information to be disclosed to the trustee.

topic_title: Requests from authorized contacts (other than legal representatives)
text: An authorized contact can be anyone who is authorized by the individual to communicate on their behalf. They can be an individual, an agency or an organization. In order to release any personal information to an authorized contact, the Department must first have on file the written consent of the individual to whom the personal information relates to. Consent can be a letter of authorization, or a departmental or other organization's consent form. Upon receiving written consent from the individual, the Department can communicate information about the individual's file with the authorized contact based on the specified information in the letter or form. Only information not restricted by the individual, by the legislation and by the Department can be discussed with the contact. Copies of documents from the individual's file cannot be released to a contact unless the letter of authorization instructs the Department to do so. If it does, the release of information must follow the rules set out by Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP). When in doubt regarding what information to release from a file to an authorized contact, the ATIP coordinator can provide assistance.

topic_title: Requests from disabled contributors for information about a disabled contributor's child's file
text: The Department cannot confirm to a contributor that an application for a CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) has been submitted on behalf of their child. The Department can also not confirm the approval of DCCB for that child. This applies even when it was the contributor who provided the child's personal information and information about the other parent or guardian with whom the child is living with on their CPPD benefits application. This information is confidential and only the third party caring for the child or the adult child themself can disclose this information to the contributor or provide consent for the disclosure.

The CPP legislation defines representative while the OAS Act does not. For consistency and ease, the definition of representative for both CPP and OAS purposes is as follows: guardian; curator; committee; executor; lawyer*; trustee; individuals with a Power of Attorney (POA); or any other legal representative of that individual. A legal representative has all the same rights of access to the individual's information as the individual does themselves. Only a legal representative with the authority to make decisions and sign documents on behalf of an individual can request and be given all information from an individual's file. All legal representatives must provide proof of their legal authority by means of an authorizing instrument. *In the case of lawyers, if the individual has retained them for representation in specific matters and has not granted them POA, the lawyer cannot be given access to information outside of those matters. When an individual dies, any existing POA or authorization to communicate that the individual gave to the Department while they were alive ends with their death. The Department can then only communicate with an estate legal representative such as an executor or a court-appointed administrator, if one exists. If it is not known whether or not an executor or a court-appointed administrator exists and the Department requires information from the estate, correspondence can be sent to the deceased individual's last known address. Whoever is looking after the deceased's affairs can provide the Department with the information or documentation needed or inform the Department if there is an executor or an estate administrator.

topic_title: Requests from Members of Parliament and Senators
text: Members of Parliament and Senators do not need to obtain written consent from individuals to obtain information from the Department on their behalf if they have completed a Departmental Registration Agreement Letter and have been placed on the Regional Enquiries Unit list of parliamentarians. This list grants them the authority to access services provided by the Department via a direct telephone line. The Department can provide Members of Parliament and Senators with information about an individual or information relating to a third party (e.g. requesting credit splitting or pension sharing of an RTR pension) on the condition that the information is relevant to: the individual's application for a benefit; the receipt of a benefit; credit splitting; or pension sharing of an RTR pension. When the information requested involves a third party, the Department only releases information that is essential for the individual to receive or apply for a benefit to a Member of Parliament, as in an application for credit splitting. Following the dissolution of Parliament when an election has been called, information that is essential for the individual to receive or apply for a benefit cannot be released to a Member of Parliament without the individual's written consent.

topic_title: Requests from provincial or territorial members of legislature
text: The Department can only disclose personal information to a provincial or territorial member of legislature (i.e. Member of Provincial Parliaments, Member of the Legislative Assembly) who is trying to help their constituent resolve a problem. In this situation, the Department can disclose personal information when: they receive a written authorization from the individual naming the member; and the written authorization is on the individual's file.

topic_title: Requests from third parties for personal information from a CPP disabled contributor file in order to solicit a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit application
text: Disabled contributors are under no obligation to disclose that they have children on their application for CPPD benefits. To protect the disabled contributor's privacy, the Department must not initiate contact with the child, the other parent or guardian or the agency that has custody and control of the child to solicit a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit application or information unless the Department receives the disabled contributor's written consent to do so. Disclosing a CPP contributor's eligibility for CPPD benefits may put the contributor in a vulnerable position given their medical condition. Some contributors prefer to keep their sensitive information private. This choice is their fundamental right and the Department must respect their decision. Failure of the Department to respect the privacy of a disabled contributor could result in tangible and negative consequences for them. For example, disclosing the disability status of the contributor could provide their former spouse with evidence when seeking to end or limit the contributor's custody of their child(ren). Authorization to communicate with a third party ends when the applicant who has given authorization dies. However, the applicant's consent to contact the guardian or the adult child for the purpose of applying for a child benefit is still valid after the CPPD benefit applicant's death. The reason why the consent is still valid is because it simply provides authorization to mail out an application to the child's guardian or the adult child. It does not provide authorization to communicate personal information from the contributor's file. This was the wish of the CPPD benefit applicant before they died.

topic_title: Requests from trustees or Public Guardians and Trustees
text: A provincial trustee or Public Guardian and Trustee must present proof of appointment to the Department to receive personal information from an individual's CPP or OAS file. Proof can be a letter stating they have been appointed under provincial law to act on behalf of the individual.

An individual can request information about their own file in writing (i.e. a dated letter with a wet signature) or verbally (i.e. in-person or by telephone). If an individual requests information about their application or about their CPP or OAS benefits in this manner, the Department can send them a letter with this information without consulting with their Service Canada Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) privacy coordinator. The agent must authenticate the individual's identity prior to releasing the information. However, if an individual requests a copy of their application or documents from their file, Service Canada staff must consult with an ATIP coordinator. Alternatively, the individual can be advised to submit a formal Personal Information Request Form (TBC 350-58) under the Privacy Act to obtain a copy of the application or documents.

The legislative authority related to the collection and use of personal information for the purpose of administering the CPP and OAS programs is found within the following federal statutes: Privacy Act Department of Employment and Social Development Act Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation) and regulations Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) and regulations This policy direction is derived from these authorities and the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat Policies (Directive on Privacy Practices).

The Privacy Notice Statement on CPP and OAS applications for benefits and provisions informs applicants of: the nature of the information being sought and of the purpose of the collection; the source of the information collection; the consequences of refusing to consent to the collection (i.e. that refusing to consent to the collection cannot result in any adverse decision about the applicant) where: the information is essential to making a decision directly affecting the individual; or the information is not essential to making a decision directly affecting the individual; the registration number of the personal information bank in which the information is to be contained; the individual's right of access and protection under the CPP legislation, the OAS Act, the Department of Employment and Social Development Act and the Privacy Act , where the information is collected directly from the individual concerned; and that the information requested can be accessible to the individual concerned, where the information is collected from another individual.

topic_title: The Department of Employment and Social Development Act
text: When obtaining personal information for the administration or enforcement of the CPP and OAS programs, the Department of Employment and Social Development Act allows the Minister to enter into agreements with federal institutions, provincial and territorial governments or public bodies created under: provincial or territorial law; governments of foreign states; and international organizations of foreign states. When obtaining personal information and in any subsequent disclosure of this information, the Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) is governed by the legislation under which the information was originally collected. Under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , ESDC can obtain personal information that other federal departments collect regarding an application for a SIN, as well as the SIN.

The Privacy Act sets out the basic authorities for the Government of Canada regarding the collection and use of personal information. The Privacy Act provides for the protection of individuals' personal information that is collected or held by a government institution, regardless of whether the information is publicly available. The Privacy Act requires that information, whenever possible, be collected directly from the individual, unless: the individual provides a written consent for collecting their information from another source; there is a legal representative responsible for the applicant or beneficiary's affairs; or another government institution has the information and can disclose it through an Information Sharing Agreement (ISA), a Memorandum of Understanding or an International Social Security Agreement. The Privacy Act requires that government institutions only collect personal information if the collection is necessary and relevant to the administration of the institution's programs. Once collected, the information can only be used for the purpose that it was collected or for a use that is consistent with that purpose. The Privacy Act does not permit the collection of personal information, just in case it may have value in the foreseeable future. The Department is expected to take all reasonable steps to ensure that personal information used for an administrative purpose is as accurate, up to date and complete as possible. Departmental employees responsible for determining the initial or continuing eligibility and entitlement of individuals for CPP or OAS benefits and provisions must only use properly collected personal information for the purposes of determining initial or continuing eligibility and entitlement. This is personal information that has been: collected directly from the individual; validated for accuracy and reliability by the individual; or collected under a legislative authority. Under the terms and conditions of ISAs, the Department is authorized to collect specific personal information indirectly from: another federal department; a provincial or territorial government; a foreign government; or a third party. An ISA is a written record of understanding between government parties that outlines the terms and conditions under which personal information is shared between the parties. In this context, information sharing means that either one party is disclosing information while the other party is collecting information (i.e. one-way sharing) or that both parties are disclosing and collecting information (i.e. two-way or reciprocal sharing). An ISA may also document an information sharing arrangement involving more than two parties. Once an ISA or a Memorandum of Understanding is in place, the Minister can collect information from: any designated federal institution; the Retraite Québec; and provincial or territorial governments; or public bodies created under their provincial or territorial laws for the purpose of obtaining information relevant to the administration of the CPP or OAS program. The transfer of earnings or income information from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) is an example of the indirect collection of personal information from a government institution that is authorized by legislation to collect information in order to administer the CPP legislation and OAS Act. ESDC can obtain personal information that other federal departments collect regarding an application for a SIN and also the address information provided by the CRA, which is also found on the Record of Earnings screen. Other examples of indirect collection of personal information which does not affect the individual's eligibility and entitlement to CPP or OAS benefits and provisions are: research purposes; statistical purposes; or audit and evaluation purposes. When determining eligibility and entitlement for CPP and OAS benefits and provisions, individuals are notified via privacy notices of the external sources that can collect personal information and the purpose of the collections. The individuals are notified at the time of application or automatic enrolment. Departmental employees responsible for determining initial and continuing eligibility and entitlement of individuals for CPP and OAS benefits and provisions can also collect personal information from a third party (e.g. doctor, employer, family member). They can only collect information from a third party if valid authorization or consent is obtained from the individual or their legal representative. Collection of publicly available personal information The Privacy Act provides for the protection of individuals' personal information that is collected or held by a government institution, regardless of whether the information is publicly available. The Department must be transparent to the individual concerned when making a decision on initial or continuing eligibility and entitlement for a CPP or OAS benefit or provision. Publicly available personal information is any personal information that is currently available to the public that is circulated through media (e.g. newspapers, television, radio or the Internet). It can also be information available on publicly accessible records, such as a court file (e.g. provincial court judgment or decision) or a publicly accessible data bank. Departmental employees responsible for determining the initial or continuing eligibility and entitlement of individuals for CPP or OAS benefits and provisions (including employees preparing submissions to the Social Security Tribunal ( SST ) must not collect or use publicly available personal information unless expressly authorized by law or by written consent from the individual to do so. Even if personal information is published in a public telephone directory, an individual's telephone number and address are still personal information that cannot be used to determine CPP or OAS benefit and provision eligibility and entitlement. However, it can be used for the purpose of contacting an individual, as this use is consistent with the original purpose for which the information was collected and compiled by the telecommunication company (i.e. to find contact information for individuals or organizations). Departmental employees responsible for reviewing and making decisions on an individual's CPP or OAS file regarding initial and continuing eligibility and entitlement (including employees preparing submissions to the Social Security Tribunal ( SST ) are: authorized to collect information directly from: the individual; another individual or organization who has been given written consent from the individual; the individual's legal representative; or a government department under an ISA or Memorandum of Understanding; and not authorized to: seek, collect or use publicly available personal information unless expressly authorized by law; undertake investigation or surveillance; or access or use publicly available personal information (e.g. from the Internet, newspapers, online funeral home sites or any other public sources) in the: administration; determination of initial eligibility and entitlement; or review of continued eligibility and entitlement to a benefit or provision for the CPP and OAS programs. The collection and use of personal information beyond the scope of what the legislative authorities permit (i.e. pertaining to the determination of eligibility and entitlement under the CPP legislation and the OAS Act, including preparing submissions to the Social Security Tribunal ( SST ) is an invasion of privacy and can contravene the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Privacy Act . Publicly available personal information already collected and on file Employees may come across personal information which has been sent to the Department by a third party (e.g. an informant lead). They may also find personal information that is on an individual's file because it was obtained by administrative staff. If the information indicates possible abuse or fraud by an individual, the employee is not authorized to use this information for administrative purposes or to discuss the information with the individual concerned. The file must be sent to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for investigation. Only ISB employees may access publicly available personal information as they have investigative authorities under the CPP legislation and the OAS Act. Any matter that compromises the integrity of the programs must be dealt with exclusively by ISB. This includes the management of informant leads also known as third party complaints. Publicly available personal information that has already been accessed, placed on an individual's CPP or OAS file and used in making an administrative decision on a benefit or provision must remain on the file for legal purposes, in accordance with the Privacy Act , and cannot be removed from the file or destroyed. The information must be identified and a note must be included to explain what the information is. Although this information must remain on the individual's file, there is no authority to use it when making a new decision if the file is subsequently reviewed. Although the information cannot be used in making a new decision, it cannot be ignored if it places doubt on continuing eligibility and entitlement. The personal information must be referred to ISB for investigation. Any unauthorized collection or misuse of publicly available personal information must be reported as a security incident pursuant to the Privacy Breach Directive and be investigated to determine whether it constitutes a breach of privacy. Refer to Privacy Breach Directive Internal link . The collection and use of publicly available personal information can be considered a violation of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act and the departmental Code of Conduct (specifically the Respect for Democracy, Integrity or Stewardship sections). Privacy Breach Directive

topic_title: Use of information for research and evaluation purposes
text: The Department of Employment and Social Development Act allows information (including information that can identify the individual to whom it relates) to be made available to any individual or body for research or statistical purposes, provided the research is consistent with the principles set out in the Act. The Department of Employment and Social Development Act allows information to be released only under the conditions set out in an agreement and if the Minister is of the opinion that there is no other way the purpose of the research or statistics could be accomplished without releasing the personal information and possibly identifying the individual. The individual is advised of possible disclosure in a disclosure statement on Department forms.

The SIN is the Government of Canada's national identifier used to administer various government programs for individuals. The CPP legislation, OAS Act, Department of Social Development Act or Privacy Act does not prohibit the SIN from being included on letters to CPP and OAS applicants, beneficiaries, contributors or to their legal representatives. The only exception is in cases where the Department is sending information about the individual to a third party who is not an authorized representative.

Under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act, primary and secondary release of information can be made available to a prescribed federal institution subject to the conditions agreed upon between the parties in an ISA or a Memorandum of Understanding. The exception is that an ISA between Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) and the Department of Justice Canada is not required when the Department receives a Family Orders Enforcement request for garnishment of monies from CPP and OAS benefits. Under Part I of the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act , the Department must comply with the order to release personal information from an individual's file to the Department of Justice Canada for garnishment purposes. Under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act and its regulations, the Department is authorized to release personal information held by CPP or OAS programs to the following federal institutions for the administration or enforcement of their Acts: the CRA for the Income Tax Act and Part I of the Energy Costs and Assistance Measures Act; the Correctional Service Canada for the Corrections and Conditional Release Act; the Department of Justice Canada or the RCMP for the purpose of investigations or prosecutions in relation to war crimes or crimes against humanity or any activities in relation to the extradition from Canada for such crimes; Veterans Affairs Canada for the administration of any of their 6 Acts (i.e. Canadian Forces Members and Veterans Re-establishment and Compensation Act, Children of Deceased Veterans Education Assistance Act, Civilian War-related Benefits Act, Civilian War-related Benefits Act, Pension Act and War Veterans Allowance Act ); the Library and Archives of Canada for the Library and Archives Act of Canada Act; Statistics Canada for the Statistics Act; and the Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) for the Public Service Superannuation Act, Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act (for CPP only). Under the OAS Act, other federal institutions such as the CRA, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) and Correctional Service Canada can make information they obtained for the administration of their Acts available to the Minister of ESDC if the information is necessary for the administration of the OAS program. For example, this authority allows Service Canada to obtain income information from the CRA for the spouse or common-law partner of the GIS beneficiary to administer the benefit. Under the CPP legislation, any information obtained by the bodies below may be made available to the same bodies, as well as to the department of ESDC or the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions for the purpose of the administration of the CPP: the CRA; the Department of Finance; PSPC; or IRCC.

Under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , if the Minister considers it advisable and there is an agreement or contract between the Minister and other persons or bodies (e.g. a person or a non-government group or organization), personal information can be disclosed for the administration of any federal law or activity or any provincial law as per the terms of the contract.

To share personal information about an individual, there must be legal authority. The Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation) and the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) authorize the Department of Employment and Social Development to share or exchange an individual's personal information in the administration and the enforcement of the program for which the information was obtained or for another program. The Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the CPP legislation and the OAS Act enable the Minister to enter into agreements with the following for the purpose of information gathering for the administration or enforcement of a program: federal institutions; governments of provinces or territories and public bodies created under their laws; governments of foreign states; international organizations of foreign states; and other persons or bodies. The conditions for the exchange of information are set out in an Information Sharing Agreement (ISA) or a Memorandum of Understanding. Information can only be released as set out in the legislation or as per the terms of the agreement or contract. For specific information that can be released, Information Sharing Agreements Regional and Federal Tools

The Department of Employment and Social Development Act authorizes the Minister to provide information to the government of a province or territory or to a public body created under the law of a province or territory subject to the conditions agreed upon by the Minister and the government or body in a signed ISA. The agreements outline what information to release, under what conditions, and to whom.

It is an offence for Service Canada partners to disclose any information they receive from the Department, unless the disclosure is allowed by a specific agreement between the Minister and the partner as described in the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the CPP legislation and the OAS Act.

topic_title: Sharing information when the beneficiary is deceased and there is no estate
text: An individual's personal information is protected even after their death. If an individual is deceased and there is no legal representative (i.e. executor or court-appointed estate trustee), no information can be released to a third party in the interest of protecting the deceased beneficiary's personal information. The only exceptions to this rule are: the release of information regarding benefits received by the deceased if the third party makes a request on a Deemed Person to Represent the Deceased Client for the Purpose of Issuing a T4A (OAS), T4A (P) and NR4 (ISP-1202) form; and the release of information may be required when a request is sent to the deceased's bank for the return of payments made after the date of death.

Legislation permits personal information about an individual to be provided by one program to another within the Department to administer their programs or activities. Only information relating directly to the administration of the programs can be disclosed.

Amendments to the OAS Act increased the enhancement of Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) benefit for single OAS pensioners effective July 1, 2016. The increase also applies to the GIS enhancement for pensioners whose spouse or common-law partner is not eligible for OAS benefits, and to the Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefit. As the enhancement is applied to the beneficiary's GIS, Allowance (ALW) or ALWS benefit entitlement, no additional application is required from the individual. Eligibility for the enhancement is based on the beneficiary’s information, originally used to determine their eligibility for an OAS income-tested benefit. Enhancement parameters As the enhancements are part of the GIS, the ALW, or the ALWS benefits, all of the current payment parameters (i.e. limits on retroactive payment, limits on payments abroad, indexation, etc.) that apply to these benefits also apply to the enhancements. Enhancement details follow: Individuals for whom a special qualifying factor applies, the GIS/ALW/ALWS benefit enhancement is : equally prorated at the rate of 1/10th of the enhancement for each year of residence the individual has in Canada after age 18, increasing gradually over a 10 year period. If an individual applies late and is eligible to receive an OAS income-tested benefit, the individual could also be eligible for a retroactive payment of the OAS income-tested benefit, including the enhancement of up to 11 months plus the month in which the Department received their application. The enhancement is subject to the same quarterly indexation, in accordance with changes in the Consumer Price Index, as applied to the pertinent benefit. topic_title: Civil proceedings not related to the Canada Pension Plan legislation or the Old Age Security Act
text: Personal information is not released in civil proceedings that do not relate to the administration of the Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation) or the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act). If a legal instrument is received requiring the release of information, the decision to release information is made by the Access to Information and Privacy coordinator based on whether: there are other avenues for the parties to obtain the information; there is a public interest or public funds at issue under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the CPP legislation or the OAS Act; or it is purely a private dispute in which there are no compelling or exceptional circumstances favouring release (e.g. on moral, ethical or humanitarian grounds).

topic_title: Civil proceedings related to the Canada Pension Plan legislation or the Old Age Security Act
text: Civil proceedings may involve the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (the Charter) challenges or appeals with the SST . They may be proceedings initiated by the Department or that are related to the CPP and OAS programs but not initiated by the Department. If an individual claims that a piece of legislation violates their Charter rights, they can challenge the validity of the legislation. Legal Services is contacted for advice in Charter challenge cases. Only information that was used in the Department's decision is released. In civil proceedings that are related to, but not initiated by the Department, a valid legal instrument is required before any information can be released to the requester. All requests for personal information are referred to National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy. All requests for personal information initiated by the Department in civil proceedings are referred to Integrity Services Branch. A legal instrument is not required because the Minister is normally named as party to the proceedings. When the Social Security Tribunal—General Division hears a case, the Department releases only the information that is required by the SST for making a decision.

topic_title: Criminal proceedings not related to the Canada Pension Plan legislation or the Old Age Security Act
text: The Department is not required to give evidence or produce documents in legal proceedings not related to Canada Pension Plan legislation (CPP legislation) or Old Age Security Act (OAS Act), unless the Minister considers it appropriate to do so under the authority of: the Department of Employment and Social Development Act ; the CPP legislation; or the OAS Act. Information can only be released when a charge is laid, or a legal instrument is issued and when the information is necessary for that particular prosecution or investigation. If the RCMP requests information from an individual's file and the Department did not initiate the investigation, the RCMP must provide a legal instrument. If a criminal investigation is conducted by the RCMP, the Department, for its part, can initiate an administrative investigation on the same file. Sometimes, documents such as search warrants or subpoenas are received from other federal, provincial, territorial or municipal agencies (e.g. social services). These documents may include requests to provide evidence of negotiated payments where charges have been laid under the Criminal Code . Although Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) is responsible for issuing and retaining those payments that have been negotiated, the information contained in those payments is the property of the Department. The Cheque Redemption Control Directorate (CRCD) within PSPC retains direct deposit payment records and negotiated cheques for 6 years. If a search warrant or subpoena has been issued requesting evidence of negotiated payments, the Department's regional offices are responsible for obtaining the originals or certified copies of negotiated payments from the CRCD within an established time frame.

topic_title: Criminal proceedings related to the Canada Pension Plan legislation or the Old Age Security Act
text: The RCMP is the investigative body authorized to conduct criminal investigations on behalf of the Department. The Memorandum of Understanding between the Department and the RCMP defines the roles and responsibilities of the Department and the RCMP in the investigation and prosecution of an offence against the CPP and OAS programs. Charges do not have to be laid. and a legal instrument is not required for the Department to release information to the RCMP if the investigation is initiated by the Department.

Canada Evidence Act Cabinet documents, records of Cabinet decisions and draft legislation cannot be released under the Access to Information Act and the Canada Evidence Act. The National Headquarters (NHQ) Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) coordinator is responsible for responding to requests for this type of information. Client-solicitor privilege Information between the Department and Legal Services is privileged. Documents containing such information cannot be disclosed without consulting with Legal Services. The NHQ ATIP coordinator is responsible for responding to requests for this information. Situations requiring the denial of information in response to a subpoena, court order or search warrant Any subpoena, court order or search warrant is automatically denied in the following situations: the information requested is general in nature and the lawyer or person responsible refuses to be more specific; releasing the information would be damaging to an ongoing departmental investigation by the RCMP; the documents contain information belonging to a third party not related to the investigation or court procedure; or releasing the information would jeopardize the safety of an individual (beneficiary or third party).
