The Department of Employment and Social Development Act provides that in legal proceedings, whether criminal or civil, the Minister, or the Minister's delegate, as per the Delegation of Authorities, is not required to give evidence with respect to personal information. The Minister will provide evidence when it is appropriate to do so, or when the legal proceeding directly concerns the administration or enforcement of the CPP or OAS program. Before the Department of Employment and Social Development can provide any personal information from an individual's file for a legal proceeding, it requires either a written request from the individual, their authorized third party or legal representative, or a legal instrument from any other third party. A legal instrument can be: a search warrant; a subpoena; a summons; or a court order. Whether personal information can be released or not, and under what conditions, will depend on: who has initiated the proceedings; who has requested the information; and the case itself. When a subpoena or summons is received by the Department, the decision to release the information is made by either: the Integrity Services Branch (if the investigation was initiated by the Department); or the Access to Information and Privacy coordinator (if the proceedings were initiated from outside the Department).

Under the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , an individual's personal information may be disclosed if the Minister is of the opinion that: the public interest in disclosing the information outweighs any invasion of an individual's privacy; or the individual to whom the information relates would clearly benefit from the disclosure. This provision is used only in the most serious of situations, such as: a health or medical emergency; a terrorism incident; or a national disaster. In these situations, requests for personal information must be sent to National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy.

topic_title: Releasing personal information in exceptional circumstances
text: The decision to release information in exceptional circumstances rests with the Director of National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy.

topic_title: War crimes and crimes against humanity
text: Only National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy can release personal information to the Commissioner of the RCMP, the Minister of Justice or the Attorney General of Canada where the information is required for the investigation, prosecution, and extradition activities in Canada that relate to war crimes and crimes against humanity.

topic_title: Absences and payment of benefits outside of Canada Updated
text: For the purpose of OAS benefits (i.e. partial OAS pension, GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits), absences of sufficient duration (temporary or otherwise) will stop the continuing payment of benefits. Payment of these benefits will continue for only 6 months after the month of departure. An individual's absence may be considered temporary for the purpose of initial eligibility, but this determination will not supersede the restrictions on the payment of benefits outside of Canada. The rules regarding the portability of benefits must be applied, regardless of whether the Department considers the absence to be temporary in nature.

topic_title: Absences for the purpose of attending school or university
text: An individual's residence and presence in Canada will not be interrupted by absences for the purpose of attending school or university. An individual attending school abroad will be considered a resident of Canada for OAS purposes, regardless of the periods of time spent outside of Canada. Given the number and diversity of educational institutions abroad, the variety of acceptable forms of documentary evidence that may substantiate these absences cannot be comprehensively listed here. If an individual was outside of Canada to attend school or university, they will be deemed to have been a resident and present in Canada throughout the period of attendance. Unlike with a specified circumstance, they do not have to return to Canada to have that period of attendance deemed as residence in Canada.

topic_title: Calculation of residence periods for individuals who were absent from Canada under Specified Circumstances during the COVID-19 pandemic New
text: Under the Specified Circumstances provision there is a requirement for individuals, and their spouses or common-law partners, to return to Canada within 6-months of their employment or assignment ending in order to have their time abroad deemed as Canadian residence. During the pandemic, individuals may have been prevented from returning to Canada due to travel bans or restrictions, involuntary quarantine or self-isolation. Therefore, interim measures were implemented effective March 11, 2020 . For individuals who were absent from Canada under a specified circumstance and who were unable to return to Canada within 6 months of their employment or assignment ending due to restrictions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, consideration can be given to deem the period abroad as residence in Canada. These individuals must attest to and provide Service Canada with the reasons why they were unable to return to Canada within the 6-month period. This consideration may be given for those absent from Canada under specified circumstances and who should have returned to Canada during the period of March 11, 2020 to June 1, 2021 , when the interim measures were rescinded.

topic_title: Delayed receipt of the OAS pension
text: Some individuals may not have accumulated sufficient residence to be entitled to a full OAS pension at age 65. These individuals may choose to delay receipt of their OAS pension until they have accumulated sufficient residence to be entitled to a greater amount.

Each absence is evaluated based on its duration. If there are numerous absences throughout the individual's residence history, these absences must be reviewed collectively. Updated Absences of less than one year In most cases, an absence of less than one year does not interrupt residence. However, if there is a pattern of frequent short-term absences from Canada, an individual's residence history must be reviewed to determine if the pensioner was and still can be considered a resident of Canada. In cases where it is clearly indicated that the individual has severed all residential ties with Canada, a review of an applicant's residence during a short-term absence is required. Updated Absences greater than one year An absence from Canada greater than one year may be determined to have interrupted residence. As a rule of thumb, the longer the absence from Canada, the greater the chance that residence may have been interrupted. Any absence may be considered temporary if the individual can prove residential ties to Canada and that they: were a resident of Canada at the time of departure; did not establish residence in the other country; maintained strong ties with Canada during their absence; and showed intent of returning to Canada within a reasonable time period. This determination can only be made upon return to Canada. The individual may be required to submit supporting evidence of the reason for the prolonged absence. Frequent absences of 6 months or more within a period of several years may constitute a break in Canadian residence or they may be determined to be temporary absences.

topic_title: Family members and specified circumstances Updated
text: Generally, an individual's residence is determined by the location and activity they themselves undertook while outside of Canada. However, the OAS regulations also recognize that there can be situations where individuals find themselves absent from Canada while accompanying their spouse or common-law partner. Spouses and common-law partners residing with an individual absent from Canada under a specified circumstance or attending school or university In situations where individuals are absent from Canada while accompanying their spouse or common-law partner, their absence from Canada can be considered residence in Canada provided the individual on whom they are dependent is absent from Canada under one of the specified circumstances or for the purpose of attending school or university. In simpler terms, if an individual is considered a resident of Canada by virtue of a specified circumstance, their spouse or common-law partner will also be considered a resident of Canada during this period. The spouse or common-law partner's absence while accompanying the individual on whom they are dependent will only be considered as Canadian residence if: the spouse or common-law partner returns to Canada either before or within 6 months after the return of the individual on whom they are dependent; the spouse or common-law partner returns within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or the spouse or common-law partner reaches an age at which they would be eligible for the OAS pension while absent from Canada. If the spouse or common-law partner worked and contributed to the social security scheme of the other country for the same period, these periods may not be considered deemed periods of residence in Canada. Entering into a marriage or common-law relationship while absent from Canada under a specified circumstance If a resident of Canada who was absent under a specified circumstance marries or enters into a common-law relationship during the absence,the spouse or common-law partner must count the period after the date of the marriage or date the common-law partnership as residence in Canada. The spouse or common-law partner's absence while accompanying the individual on whom they are dependent will only be considered as Canadian residence if: the spouse or common-law partner returns to Canada either before or within 6 months after the return of the individual on whom they are dependent; the spouse or common-law partner returns within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or the spouse or common-law partner reaches an age at which they would be eligible for the OAS pension while absent from Canada. If the spouse or common-law partner worked and contributed to the social security scheme of the other country for the same period, these periods may not be considered deemed periods of residence in Canada. Dependants residing with an individual absent from Canada under a specified circumstance Similar requirements apply to dependants, including an individual's mother, father, mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother, sister and the natural, adoptive or foster child(ren) living abroad with the individual who is absent from Canada under a specified circumstance. These individuals may be considered residents in Canada during this period provided they: return within 6 months of the return of the individual on whom they were dependent; return within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or reach an age where they would be eligible for an OAS pension under the OAS Act while absent from Canada.

An individual may qualify for a full OAS pension under the 40-Year Rule, the 10-Year Rule or the 3 for 1 Rule. 40-Year Rule An individual can qualify for a full OAS pension by accumulating 40 years of residence in Canada after age 18. When all periods of residence in Canada after age 18 have been counted and they do not total 40 years, applicants may still be able to qualify for the full OAS pension under the 10-Year Rule or the 3 for 1 Rule, or they may reside in Canada for the additional period required for a full pension. 10-Year Rule An individual can qualify for a full OAS pension based on as little as 10 years of residence in Canada accumulated after age 18. The following situations describe the eligibility requirements that allow an applicant who has reached age 65 to qualify for a full OAS pension under the 10-Year Rule: On July 1, 1977 , the applicant was 25 years of age or older, was a resident of Canada and resided in Canada for the 10 years immediately preceding the day that their application is approved. On July 1, 1977 , the applicant was 25 years of age or older but was not a resident of Canada. They did however, reside in Canada for any period of time after age 18 and prior to July 1, 1977 , and resided in Canada for the 10 years immediately preceding the day that their application is approved. On July 1, 1977 , the applicant was 25 years of age or older but had no residence in Canada on or before that date. They did however, possess a valid immigration visa on or before July 1, 1977 and resided in Canada for the 10 years immediately preceding the day that their application is approved. Determining the 10-year period immediately before the date of approval of the application The day on which the application is approved is normally the applicant's 65th birthday. This means that applicants must have resided in Canada for the 10 years immediately preceding their 65th birthday to be eligible for payment of the pension to begin effective the following month. In the case of applicants who cannot fulfill the residence requirements when they reach age 65, their application is approved the day after they meet the 10-year period of residence in Canada. Where there have been absences from Canada in the 10-year period, the nature and duration of each one must be evaluated to determine whether the applicant remained a resident of Canada during the absence. If residence has been interrupted during the 10-year period, the application must be considered under the 3 for 1 Rule. 3 for 1 Rule When residence during the 10-year period has been interrupted by absences, it is still possible for an individual to qualify for a full OAS pension using the 3 for 1 Rule. This allows the applicant to make up for absences during the 10-year period by substituting, on a 3 for 1 basis, prior periods of time in Canada. The eligibility requirements to qualify for a full OAS pension are the same under the 3 for 1 and 10-Year Rules, with the exception of the following: The applicant does not have to have been a resident of Canada for a continuous period of 10 years immediately before the approval of the application. They can have absences during the 10-year period, provided that they are supplemented by prior time in Canada equal to at least 3 times the periods of the absences in the 10-year period. Any time spent in Canada after the applicant has reached age 18 and before the 10-year period (whether the applicant was a resident or present in Canada) can be used to make up for absences in the 10-year period. The applicant must be a resident of Canada for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the day the application is approved. If there has not been a lengthy presence in Canada after age 18 and before the 10-year period, applicants may not be able to satisfy the residence requirements at the time of their 65th birthday or when submitting their application, whichever is later. It must then be determined on what date they will have sufficient make-up time to qualify, assuming that up to the date of approval, they will have no absences that interrupt residence in Canada. Once the effective date for a full OAS pension under the 3 for 1 Rule is calculated, applicants are informed of the earliest date on which they may qualify. They must also be informed that the calculation was made on the assumption that they would have no absences that would interrupt their residence in Canada up to that date and that any absences must be reported to the Department. When applicants applying from outside of Canada must return to Canada for one year to qualify under the 3 for 1 Rule, they are considered to have completed their year of residence on the day before the anniversary of the date on which the period of residence began.

topic_title: Impact of residence determinations under the OAS program
text: Determining an individual to have been a resident of Canada can result in the individual becoming eligible for payment of an OAS pension and other OAS benefits. In some cases, the actual benefit amount (entitlement) that is calculated will vary depending on the length of an individual's residence in Canada. After residence has been used to qualify and calculate a benefit amount, it can also have an impact on the continuing payment of the benefit. In some cases, when a pensioner has been outside of Canada for some time, they may be required to re-establish residence in Canada or confirm that residence was not interrupted in order for payments to resume.

topic_title: Individuals not considered resident in Canada
text: Individuals in Canada will not be considered residents of Canada under the following circumstances: individuals living on a ship outside of the territorial waters of Canada; or individuals who are not citizens or permanent residents of Canada who are in Canada: performing the duties as a properly accredited diplomat consular officer, representative or official of: a country other than Canada; the United Nations or any of its agencies; or any intergovernmental organization in which Canada participates. as a member of a military force present in Canada for training or for any other purpose in connection with the defence or security interests of Canada, or under any treaty or agreement between Canada and another country; or as the spouse, common-law partner or dependant of an individual described above; as the staff or as an individual otherwise accompanying any of the individuals described above.

Individuals engaged locally outside of Canada by a Canadian embassy or consulate are sometimes natives of the country in which they are employed by the Canadian embassy. Others are Canadian citizens residing abroad who accept employment during their residence. In some cases, a Canadian may go abroad to accept employment as a locally-engaged individual. Periods of absence during which the individual was employed as a member of locally-engaged staff abroad may be accepted as residence in Canada provided the following conditions are met: the individual was considered to be a resident of Canada immediately before the date on which they became locally-engaged staff members of Global Affairs Canada; the individual's income throughout the absence was subject to Canadian income tax; and the individual returned to Canada within 6 months after the end of the employment or attained, while employed outside of Canada, an age at which they are eligible to an OAS pension. It should be emphasized that the purpose of the legislation is to provide coverage for residents of Canada employed abroad. This policy does not cover foreign nationals engaged in Canadian posts abroad, regardless of their tax status under Canadian law.

To be considered eligible for an OAS pension and, if applicable, the related supplementary benefits such as the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Allowance ( ALW ) and the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ), the applicant must have sufficient residence in Canada to meet the legislated eligibility requirements. There are several ways in which an individual's residence can satisfy the residence eligibility requirements for OAS benefits. The residence requirements vary depending on whether an individual qualifies for a partial or a full OAS pension or related income tested benefit.

Applicants who do not qualify for a full OAS pension and do not wish to complete the additional residence required to do so may qualify for a partial OAS pension once they reach age 65 or later. A partial OAS pension is calculated at the rate of 1/40th of the full pension for each complete year of residence in Canada after age 18. The minimum period of residence required to qualify for a partial OAS pension is 10 years of residence in Canada after age 18 for payment in Canada. If the applicant is not considered a resident of Canada at the time of the application (i.e. the day before the approval of the application), the minimum period of residence required is 20 years of residence after age 18 to export the Canadian pension. Once a partial OAS pension has been approved, the monthly OAS pension entitlement cannot be increased based on subsequent residence in Canada. However, residence can continue to accrue towards the 20 years minimum for portability of the pension abroad. When aggregating residence, only actual residence and not periods of presence in Canada can be counted. Once all periods of residence have been established, they must be added together to arrive at the aggregate. If the aggregate contains a fraction of a year, it must be rounded to the next lower multiple of a year. For example, if all periods of actual residence total 25 years and 3 months, the number of years on which the eligibility must be based is 25 years or 25/40ths.

topic_title: Periods not considered deemed residence in Canada and the interaction with ISSAs Updated
text: Canada's ISSAs with other countries seek to eliminate gaps in coverage for individuals who are sent to work abroad. This means that if the applicant had creditable periods to another country's social security scheme and these periods of contributions coincide with periods of deemed residence, these periods may not be considered residence in Canada for OAS purposes. Canada's ISSAs seek to prevent double coverage or double entitlement to benefits. Agreements define certain periods that are not to be considered periods of residence in Canada for OAS entitlement purposes in cases where individuals are making contributions under the social security scheme of the other country. They eliminate situations where an individual who contributes to the social security program of the other country can also count these same periods as residence in Canada for OAS purposes. When investigating the specified circumstances of an applicant under the OAS program, it is important to note that the duplicate (double) coverage provisions of an agreement may have to be reviewed. These exclusions also extend to the spouse or common-law partner and dependants of that individual who reside with them unless the spouse, common-law partner or dependant makes or has made contributions to the CPP or the QPP and is not making or has not made work-related contributions under the social security scheme of the other country during the same time period. Canada-United States border workers Border workers are individuals that are permanently living in the United States but who are employed in Canada, or vice-versa. Under the Canada-United States agreement, clients residing in the United States but making contributions to the CPP or the QPP are considered residents of Canada for those periods, unless contributions were made to the United States pension plan for the same period. At the same time, clients residing in Canada but making contributions to the United States pension plan are considered Canadian residents for that period. There is no requirement to remove periods of United States contributions from Canadian residence. Non-detached workers Non-detached workers are individuals who reside in another country, contribute to CPP and/or QPP but have not been sent there by their Canadian employer. Periods of residence in the other country may be counted as residence in Canada for OAS purposes when contributions have been made to the CPP and/or QPP, even if the individual has never resided in Canada. It is to be noted, however, that periods of time where overlapping contributions have been made to both the CPP and/or QPP and another social security plan are not considered periods of residence in Canada for OAS purposes. These periods of foreign contributions must be verified by International Operations (IO). Specific issues relating to the interaction of the residence provisions and ISSAs require direction from IO since some sections in the ISSA have precedence over the OAS Act. If IO confirms that a situation is not covered by a provision of an agreement, a determination must be made based on the OAS Act and Regulations alone, which means it must be determined whether the applicant meets the definition of residence for the purposes of OAS benefits.

Residence in Canada is one of the three primary eligibility factors for OAS benefits. In order to pay benefits under the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act), the Department must ensure that the residence, age and legal status requirements have been met. Residence Specified circumstances and exceptions to residence rules There are several provisions where individuals may be deemed a resident of Canada despite being physically absent. These exceptions to the general residence rules are frequently referred to as specified circumstances . The deeming of residence is also considered for individuals who are subject to the legislation of another country's pension scheme with which Canada has an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) in force. At the same time, provisions exist that prevent the Department from considering certain periods of physical presence to be considered as residence in Canada. The following subsections describe the various circumstances under which an individual may be considered to reside in Canada despite being physically absent. Residence requirements To be found eligible for an OAS pension and where applicable, the related supplementary benefits: GIS, ALW , and ALWS ; the Department must be satisfied that the applicant has sufficient residence in Canada to meet the legislated eligibility requirements. There are several ways an individual will satisfy the residence eligibility requirements for an OAS pension. Similarly, there are various residence requirements depending on whether an individual qualifies for a partial or full OAS pension, or a related income-tested benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW , ALWS ). Absences
Common to all residence requirements is one underlying rule: periods of Canadian residence before an individual reaches age 18 cannot be used to satisfy any of the residence requirements.

Residence outside of Canada may be considered Canadian residence for foreign nationals if they lived on Canadian embassy grounds. Applicants should be asked specifically if the claimed residence was on embassy soil or not: If yes , applicants must request information from Global Affairs Canada confirming the period of residence on embassy soil for OAS purposes. If no , the normal application of the OAS regulations apply. There is a requirement that an individual returns to Canada within 6 months of completing their employment or specified activity outside of the country. However, this requirement does not apply if the individual reaches an age where they are eligible for the OAS pension while outside of Canada and the pension meets the portability requirement under the OAS Act.

Residence must not be confused with presence. To be considered a resident of Canada for the purpose of OAS benefits, an individual must ordinarily live and make their home in Canada. An individual is considered present in Canada when they are physically present in any part of Canada. An individual who is present in Canada is physically within Canada,but is not necessarily a resident of Canada. Similarly, an individual can be considered a resident of Canada although they are not present in Canada. Some scenarios involving residence versus presence include: An individual resides in Canada but is not considered to be a resident of Canada (e.g. foreign diplomats); An individual is present in Canada but does not reside in Canada (e.g. United States residents who own a summer cottage in Canada); An individual resides in another country but is considered a resident of Canada (e.g. members of the Canadian Armed Forces, Canadian diplomats). The Department must determine whether an individual is a resident of Canada or simply present in Canada. When making this determination, the primary assumption is that an individual can only be resident of one country at any given time. While an individual may own property in many countries and spend some time in each of them, only one country will be considered their place of residence. This country will be the one with which the individual has the most significant attachment. An individual's attachment to a country is measured by evaluating the residential ties between the individual and the country.

For domestic accounts, a residential or home address assists the Minister in being satisfied that the residence requirement is met. A home address is required for the approval of a domestic partial OAS pension and income tested benefits. No civic number There are cases where the applicant may only have a Postal Office (PO) box or General Delivery (GD) box. The individual must provide a viable reason as to why they only have a PO box or GD Box, e.g. the person is living on a reserve or living rurally. If the Minister is satisfied based on information on file that the individual meets the residence requirement, a civic number may not be required. No fixed address Where an applicant identifies as having no fixed address, the need for a home address may be met when an address is provided where the applicant can receive mail, and where an individual or an organization can be contacted to verify that the applicant, to the best of their knowledge, has no fixed address and they or the organization have contact with the applicant. This may be an address (e.g. bank, hospital, shelter, church, a friend's house etc.) provided the organization or individual agrees that it can be used as the mailing address. This address and contact, combined with the resident statement, assists the Minister in being satisfied that residence has been met.

Absences from Canada during periods of employment with the organizations below may be considered residence in Canada, provided the individual: returned to Canada within 6 months of completing their employment or reached an age where they are eligible for the OAS pension outside of Canada; had a permanent home in Canada or maintained a self-contained domestic establishment in Canada; and was not covered under the pension scheme of the country in which they were present, depending on the terms of the ISSA with that country. These organizations are: the United Nations or one of its specialized agencies; the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; the Commonwealth Secretariat; the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development; the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie; or a Canadian firm or corporation as a representative or member thereof.

topic_title: Specified absences during or immediately after World War II
text: An individual will be considered a resident of Canada while they were awaiting transportation to Canada during or immediately after World War II if: they were unable to return to Canada due to the dislocation of transportation facilities; and returned to Canada when transportation became available. Proof of the date of application for transportation should be requested. If no supporting evidence can be obtained, a statutory declaration from the applicant may be considered.

Employment in certain occupations or engagement with certain organizations while outside of Canada can also be considered as Canadian residence. There is a requirement for the individual to return to Canada within 6 months after completing the employment or activity (this requirement does not apply if the individual reaches an age where they are eligible for the OAS pension while outside of Canada). However, individuals in the following occupations or organizations do not have to maintain a permanent place of abode throughout the period of absence. Examples of specified occupations and organizations include: the Government of Canada or the government of a municipal corporation of any province; a missionary with any religious group or organization; an employee, a member or an officer of an international charitable organization; performing of services in another country under a development or assistance program that is sponsored or operated in that country by the Government of Canada or of a province or by a non-profit Canadian agency; a member of the Canadian Forces, pursuant to and in connection with the requirements of their duties; working for Canada connected with the prosecution of any war; a member of the armed forces of any ally of Canada during any war; a worker in lumbering, harvesting, fishing or other seasonal employment; and a transport worker on trains, aircrafts, ships or buses running between Canada and points outside of Canada or other similar employment. Missionaries Missionaries are individuals sent on a mission to perform the specified functions of propagating a religious faith and/or doing humanitarian work. To be considered a missionary, individuals must: have been sent, while residing in Canada, to another country by any religious group or organization to carry out missionary duties. These could include religion, education, medicine, agriculture or engineering; and have retained their Canadian citizenship or their legal right under the immigration laws of Canada to resume residence in Canada and were not formally admitted for permanent residence to the country in which the missionary work was performed. Missionary duties performed outside of Canada with the following organizations have been recognized as residence for OAS purposes, although there may be others: Wycliffe Bible Translators of Canada Incorporated The Mennonite Brethren Missions/ Services In some cases, the members of religious organizations cannot be considered as missionaries but may be considered as members of a Canadian firm or corporation and would therefore have to have maintained a permanent abode or a self-contained domestic establishment in Canada while they are absent in the course of their duties. Example Members of the Salvation Army who provided auxiliary services to the Canadian Forces in Germany fall into this category. In view of the nature of the services provided, which were mainly recreational, these individuals were not considered to be performing missionary duties while abroad. However, they were considered to be members of a Canadian Corporation who had a permanent place of abode in Canada during the absence. International charitable organizations Members of an international charitable organization can be considered residents of Canada despite being absent from Canada. An international charitable organization has substantial presence in multiple countries and uses its resources for charitable activities such as relief of poverty, the advancement of education, the advancement of religion, or other purposes that benefit the community. The individual must have been considered a resident prior to engaging in employment outside of Canada. It should be noted that, to be eligible for consideration under this provision, an individual must be an employee, a member, or an officer of the organization. Examples The United Israel Appeal of Canada solicits donations of money from Canadians for indigent people living in Israel. They maintain a small office and staff in Jerusalem to administer and distribute the funds collected in Canada. Although the United Israel Appeal of Canada does assist the poor in Israel, it also resembles, in some ways, a business firm or corporation because of its emphasis on collecting money in Canada. Its activity in Canada is fund raising, not social work. While accepting this aspect of work of this organization, the United Israel Appeal of Canada Inc. clearly falls within the definition of an international charitable organization and the time that the employees spend in Israel may be considered as residence in Canada for OAS purposes. It has been established that CARE Canada is registered as a charitable organization with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). It can therefore be considered as such for OAS purposes. Non-profit Canadian agencies There are circumstances under which individuals who are performing services in another country under a development or assistance program that is sponsored or operated in that country by the Government of Canada, a province of Canada or a non-profit Canadian agency can be considered residents of Canada despite being absent from Canada. Example Upon review of the organization, its activities and the role it plays in developing countries and on the basis of the information available, it meets the criteria of a non-profit Canadian agency.

An individual meets the residence requirements for the ALW and ALWS benefits when they have a minimum of 10 years of residence in Canada after age 18 before the day the application is approved. If the applicant has less than 20 years of residence after age 18, they must be a resident of Canada on the day before the application is approved.

An absence is defined as a period of absence from Canada of a Canadian resident that is of a temporary nature and: does not exceed one year; is for the purpose of attending school or university; or is a specified circumstance. Exceptions to residence rules can be deemed not to have interrupted an individual's residence in Canada. Residence in Canada may include temporary absences (i.e. periods of time during which an individual was outside of Canada). Temporary absences are of a nature and duration which do not interrupt residence in Canada. To maintain residence in Canada during periods of temporary absences, an individual must be able to demonstrate 2 distinct ties with Canada: that a centralized mode of living in Canada was established before the period of absence; and that a principle and centralized mode of living was maintained during the period of absence. To prove continuing residence in Canada, evidence is required to show that the absences were temporary in nature (i.e. there was a clear intent to return to Canada and the individual maintained factual ties with Canada). A determination of residence must be made on a case by case basis. There is no single rule to determine whether an individual is a resident of Canada. Many factors must be considered and analyzed. If there is greater evidence showing a continuing residential relationship with Canada, the individual's residence in Canada may be assumed. If it is determined that an individual maintained residence in Canada during periods of temporary absences, the individual is considered to have been in Canada throughout the period of absence. For qualification and benefit calculation purposes, the period of absence will contribute to the residence requirements.

text: A combined T4A and NR4 Insert is included with the tax slips and contains the following information: Changes to the beneficiary's information can affect their payments. It is the beneficiary's responsibility to contact Service Canada if there are any changes to the following: address; banking information; death of a beneficiary; marital status; leaving Canada for more than 6 months; or children (e.g. a child enters or leaves their custody). The beneficiary is advised that their OAS pension will permanently increase by 10% the month after they turn the age of 75.

CPP Tax slips Amended and duplicate T4A(P) and NR4 tax slips can be provided any time after the original slip has been issued. The processing centre responsible for the account must issue the amended, duplicate or the manual T4A(P) and NR4 tax slip. CPP tax slips, with the exception of duplicates, are sent to the CRA electronically: every Monday, Wednesday and Friday during the month of February; and weekly starting in March. In most cases, amended tax slips are not issued before the originals are mailed to beneficiaries. Amended tax slips can be sent if a death occurred during or before December 2025 and processed in January 2026. In these cases, retrieve the T4A(P) from E-forms and send to the appropriate contact when requested. For both residents and non-residents of Canada, refer to Tax Slips (Scenario) in the following situations: Tax Slips (Scenario) issuing a duplicate or amended T4A(P) or NR4 slip; or adding a manual T4A(P) or NR4 slip. OAS tax slips New Amended, cancelled and duplicate T4A(OAS), NR4-OAS and NR4(ITB) tax slips can be provided any time after the original slip has been issued. Processing centres can issue amended, cancelled and duplicate tax slips while call centres can only issue duplicate tax slips. OAS tax slips, excluding cancelled and duplicate slips, are sent electronically to the CRA and Revenu Québec. Amended, cancelled and duplicate OAS tax slips are printed on a weekly basis. Amended tax slips Amended tax slips cannot be issued before the original tax slip has been issued. Amended tax slips can only be sent to indicate that changes were made to the financial data generated for a specific client, tax slip form type and tax year after the original has been issued. For example, a priority payment was issued in 2025 but not recorded in Cúram until 2026. Cancelled tax slips New Cancelled tax slips indicate that the tax slip was invalidated because it was sent in error. Cancelled tax slips can be sent in any of the following circumstances: a tax slip was sent to the wrong individual or confirmation is received that an individual previously identified as deceased is not deceased; an incorrect tax slip was issued (e.g. a T4A was issued instead of a NR4, or vice versa); or the benefits were cancelled. Duplicate tax slips Duplicate T4A(OAS), NR4-OAS and NR4(ITB) tax slips can be provided any time after the original tax slip has been issued. Duplicate tax slips can be sent in any of the following circumstances: after an address change; the client requests another tax slip be mailed to them; or a verified third party requests a copy.

This review code (05) is automatically set by OAS Online to identify a client who has a court-appointed or Department-appointed trustee who administers their benefits. The default review date is set one year from the date when the trustee is added to the system. To differentiate between Department-appointed trustees and court-appointed trustees, staff must change the review date to: YY01 (January) for Department-appointed trustees who are required to complete accounting reports; and YY07 (July) for court-appointed trustees who are not required to complete accounting reports unless there is doubt about the disbursement of the client's monies. The purpose of this review code is to ensure that the Trustee's Accounting Report (ISP-3509) form is sent to the Department-appointed trustee, as required. For court-appointed trustees, the Department will not request an accounting report unless there is doubt about the disbursement of the client's monies. For more information, Trusteeship (Scenario) The ISP-3509 form must be sent to the Department-appointed trustee for completion at least: every year for a trustee who administers benefits for an incapable homeless senior or an incapable at-risk of being homeless senior; or every 2 years , for all other Department-appointed trustees.

Eligibility to the ALW benefit during the incarceration of a spouse or common-law partner When an application for the ALW benefit is submitted by the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the application may be approved provided that the applicant meets all the ALW eligibility criteria. The incarcerated spouse or common-law partner must also apply and be eligible for an OAS pension and the GIS in order for the spouse or common-law partner to receive an ALW benefit. Payment of the ALW benefit to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated OAS pensioners Payment of the ALW benefit to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated OAS pensioners will continue even though the incarcerated individual's OAS pension and GIS are suspended. During the period of incarceration, the ALW beneficiary will maintain their entitlement to the ALW benefit and their benefit may be calculated on the basis of their individual income. The ALW benefit can be paid based on Rate Table 4, using either combined income or individual income, whichever is more advantageous. The new payment rate may be paid at the effective date (i.e. the normal rules regarding retroactivity apply) as long as the ALW benefit applicant's spouse or common-law partner meets the definition of incarcerated on the effective date. Otherwise, the new payment rate would be effective the month following the month of the individual's incarceration. The new payment rate may be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual's release. Should the individual be released to a transitional living facility (i.e. halfway house), the combined income test does not apply until the couple resumes living together. Although the incarcerated individual must notify the Department of the date of their release, the legislation prescribes that spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals who are in receipt of a more advantageous rate by this measure will have to notify the Department of their spouse or common-law partner's release date, if known, or of any change in their marital status in a timely manner in order to avoid overpayments. The date of release provided by either the incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner must correspond to the release date on the transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory.

GIS payments will be suspended simultaneously with the OAS pension since this benefit can only be paid to individuals who are receiving the OAS pension. At the time of the individual's release, the GIS may be resumed at the same time as the OAS pension, as long as the pensioner meets all of the OAS eligibility requirements to receive the GIS and provided that the Department has their income information. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. Entitlement to the GIS during the incarceration of a spouse or common-law partner When an application for the GIS is submitted by the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the application may be approved provided that the applicant meets all the GIS eligibility and entitlement criteria. In addition, payment of the GIS to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated ALW beneficiaries continues even though the incarcerated individual's ALW benefit is suspended. During the individual's period of incarceration, their spouse or common-law partner's GIS entitlement should be paid based on which ever rate is to their advantage. If a pensioner is married or in a common-law relationship with an incarcerated pensioner, the GIS can be paid based on Rate Table 2 using combined income or Rate Table 1 using individual income. If a pensioner is married or in a common-law relationship with an incarcerated ALW recipient, the GIS can be paid based on Rate Table 4 using combined income, Rate Table 3 using combined income or Rate Table 1 using individual income. Exception: If the incarcerated spouse or common-law partner is a non -pensioner, the pensioner spouse or common-law partner will continue to be paid GIS based on Rate Table 3 using combined income. The income information for both individuals is still needed. The single rate may be paid at the effective date (i.e. the normal rules regarding retroactivity apply) as long as the GIS applicant's spouse or common-law partner meets the definition of incarcerated on the effective date. Otherwise, the single rate would be effective starting the month following the month of the individual's incarceration. The single rate may be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual's release. If the individual is released to a transition living facility (i.e. halfway house), the combined income test does not apply until the couple resumes living together. Although the incarcerated individual must notify the Department of the date of their release, the legislation prescribes that spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals that are advantaged by this measure have to notify the Department of their spouse or common-law partner's release date, if known, or of any change in their marital status in a timely manner in order to avoid overpayments. The date of release provided by either the incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner must correspond to the release date on the transfer of information from the Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory.

topic_title: OAS benefits applications and suspensions Updated
text: No OAS benefit may be paid for any period of incarceration (exclusive of the first month of that period) to an individual who is incarcerated. The suspension of all OAS benefit payments is effective the month following the month of incarceration. Only incarcerated pensioners and beneficiaries will have their OAS benefits suspended. Low income spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated individuals will not lose their entitlement to the GIS or ALW benefit. Initial suspensions of OAS benefit payments following Royal Assent or Information Sharing Agreements concluded with provinces or territories The initial suspensions of OAS benefit payments were effective the month following the first transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or from the province or territory that identifies the OAS pensioner or beneficiary as incarcerated. Subsequent suspensions of OAS benefit payments for existing pensioners and beneficiaries Based on the transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or from the province or territory, OAS benefit payments will be suspended effective the month following the month of incarceration. OAS benefit applications submitted during incarceration When an application for an OAS benefit is submitted by an individual while they are incarcerated, the application may be approved at that time provided that the applicant meets all the OAS benefit eligibility criteria. However, payment of the benefit will only begin the month the individual is released, provided that they continue to meet all the eligibility requirements. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. An individual whose OAS benefit application is approved while incarcerated is entitled to receive retroactive payment for any months (within 11 months) in which they were not incarcerated, including the first month of incarceration. OAS benefit applications submitted after release from incarceration If an application for an OAS benefit is received within 11 months of the individual's release from prison, no retroactive payment may be made for any month in which the individual was incarcerated (except for the first month of incarceration and the month of release). The application will be assessed to determine if the period of incarceration falls within the provision to limit payment of the OAS benefit based on sentence period and jurisdiction.

OAS applicants, pensioners and beneficiaries sentenced to imprisonment do not receive OAS benefit payments during of a period of incarceration. The provisions limit payment of OAS benefits to pensioners and beneficiaries by suspending their OAS benefits while they are incarcerated. They also limit payment to those who apply for OAS benefits while incarcerated. Should an individual apply after release from incarceration, the legislation also provides that there is no entitlement to retroactivity for any periods of incarceration except for the first month of incarceration and the month of release. Incarceration under the provisions of the OAS Act means that due to a sentence of imprisonment, an individual is confined in a penitentiary or a correctional facility for a period: of 2 years or more to be served in a federal penitentiary; or exceeding 90 days to be served in a provincial correctional facility in a province where an Information Sharing Agreement has been negotiated. There are 2 implementation stages for these provisions: In the first stage , OAS benefit payments are suspended during the period of incarceration to an individual who is sentenced to imprisonment in a federal penitentiary for a term of 2 years or more. In the second stage , Information Sharing Agreements will be pursued with the provinces and territories and implemented as they are concluded. Once an Information Sharing Agreement is in place with a province or a territory, the suspension of payments will be extended to individuals during the period of incarceration serving a term exceeding 90 days in a prison in that jurisdiction. This provision does not apply to individuals incarcerated outside of Canada. The Department has a one-way agreement with Correctional Services Canada that permits the disclosure of Correctional Services Canada information to the Department for the purpose of administering the OAS program exclusively. Currently there are no Information Sharing Agreements (ISAs) with provinces or territories allowing for the exchange of personal information between the Department and the province or territory for the purpose of limiting OAS benefit payments. Until ISAs are reached with provinces or territories, OAS payments cannot be withheld from these individuals. OAS benefits Murder or manslaughter of a spouse or common-law partner A spouse or common-law partner who has been convicted of 1st or 2nd degree murder or manslaughter will not be eligible to the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ) benefit as a result of the death of the murdered individual. Benefits are either denied or cancelled back to the effective date. In these cases, there is no eligibility to the ALWS benefit due to the murdered spouse or common-law partner policy as opposed to limiting payments of OAS benefits due to incarceration. Pension income splitting To ensure that the lower income spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual is not disadvantaged by a pension income split when calculating the GIS or the ALW benefit based on their own income, the non-incarcerated spouse or common-law partner may ask to exclude the amount of pension income split they received from their spouse or common-law partner. Notifications on the limitations of OAS pension and benefits payments OAS pensioners or beneficiaries must be informed in writing immediately of the suspension of their pension and benefits once it has happened. However, the limitations on payment of OAS benefits generated by the provision do not require that the pensioner or beneficiary be notified 30 days before the suspension of their OAS benefits. The non-entitlement to OAS benefits has been already determined by the information received from Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory. Letters will need to be sent to the spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals who have had their GIS or ALW benefit adjusted due to the provision. Overpayments As of January 2011, any OAS payment received or obtained by the pensioner or beneficiary to which they are not entitled due to incarceration will be set up as an overpayment and will be recovered according to the overpayment policy and procedures. Reconsiderations and appeals Individuals whose OAS benefits are suspended or reinstated under this provision have recourse via the regular appeal process. If an individual is dissatisfied with a decision made, they may request a reconsideration of the decision by writing to the Minister within 90 days of being notified of the original decision. Individuals that remain unsatisfied with the reconsideration decision may request an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal-General Division. Family Orders and garnishment If an account suspended under this provision is also subject to a garnishment order under the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act or a set-off agreement with the CRA , the withhold or garnishment activity on the account will also be suspended. The Department will notify the appropriate department (i.e. Department of Justice, the CRA ) of the suspension of OAS payments and the suspension of the garnishment or withhold. Reinstating OAS benefits when incarceration period ends New The OAS benefit payment will resume the month the individual is released, provided that they continue to meet all the eligibility requirements. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. The individual can send the notification before or after the date of release. The date provided must correspond with the release date on the transfer of information from Correctional Service Canada or the province or territory before payments are resumed. There is no requirement for a new application as the beneficiary was eligible for the benefit throughout the period of incarceration but was not entitled to receive it. For income-tested benefits, a statement of income is required in order to calculate entitlement. The statement of income can be submitted by the beneficiary on a prescribed form or as a separate written statement. The requirement of a paper statement of income can be waived if the income information is received from the CRA .

Information used to make the decision After graduating from the University of Alberta, the applicant was accepted to study medicine at a university in England. They spent 2 years abroad. During their stay in England, the applicant's primary purpose was to attend university. When applying for OAS benefits, they provided documentation from the university to confirm enrolment and the dates they had attended university. The applicant also provided passport records that confirmed their entries and departures from England and re-entry to Canada. They advised that they had returned home to Canada on several occasions to visit family. Decision The applicant’s absence is not considered to interrupt residence in Canada since the purpose of the absence was to attend school rather than to reside in that country.

Information used to make the decision The applicant arrived in Canada from Taiwan in April 2008 and became a permanent resident. In May 2018, they may be entitled to a partial OAS pension. While in Canada, they alternate living arrangements between their daughter, a cousin and a third relative. They are registered with a provincial health plan, have a current bank account and are active in social and religious organizations. From 2012 to 2015, they were outside Canada twice a year to visit family members in Taiwan, the United States and England. The pattern of absences was: June 11 to September 12, 2012 (94 days); December 6, 2012 to January 2, 2013 (27 days); June 29 to September 2, 2013 (65 days); February 23 to March 27, 2014 (32 days); June 28 to August 26, 2014 (59 days); and December 4, 2014 to April 1, 2015 (116 days). Decision These multiple short-term absences are considered temporary. The length and nature of the applicant's absences from Canada indicate that they were temporary and not associated with a change in residence. The applicant was physically present in Canada a great majority of the time during this period. Furthermore, they maintained significant residential ties with Canada as they were registered with a provincial health plan, had a current Canadian bank account and remained active in social and religious organizations.

Information used to make the decision On November 5, 2016, the applicant took a trip to England and returned to Canada in April 2017. While they were outside of Canada, their neighbour took care of their home. Decision The applicant was absent from Canada for less than one year. They maintained a permanent place of residence in Canada and they kept close ties with neighbours. As a result, the applicant's absence did not interrupt their residence in Canada.

Information used to make the decision The applicant took a trip to the United States. During their stay, the applicant was offered employment and decided to relocate there permanently. They purchased a home in the United States and resided there for 8 months. The applicant returned to Canada to arrange the sale of their home in Canada and make arrangements for their ultimate move to the United States. The applicant contacted and informed the Department of their plans upon their return. Decision Although the applicant's absence was less than one year, they interrupted their residential ties in Canada by accepting employment in the United States, selling their home in Canada and purchasing another home in the United States. Therefore, the applicant's absence is deemed to have interrupted their Canadian residence.

Information used to make the decision The applicant was born in Chile on July 8, 1954, and they entered Canada as a landed immigrant on June 28, 1999. They resided with their daughter, sharing utilities and other costs. In December 1999, the applicant started to work and became a member of various clubs and social organizations. They obtained a bank card, social insurance number and a health card. In February 2014, the applicant left Canada for Chile and returned in June 2015 as a returning resident. The extended absence of 15 months was due to their mother's critical health and their desire to obtain retirement benefits from the Chilean government. The applicant applied for an OAS pension on January 6, 2019. Decision The applicant's residence history indicates that they entered Canada as a landed immigrant, showing their intention to make Canada their home. They established a centralized mode of living by obtaining employment and involving themselves in various social organizations. The applicant's Canadian bank accounts remained open and they kept club memberships current while they were in Chile. There is no indication that the applicant intended to reestablish residence in Chile and they returned to Canada as a resident, not a visitor. The absence is deemed to be temporary even though it exceeded one year. The applicant is considered to have established a centralized mode of living in Canada before their departure to Chile in 2014 and is considered to have Canadian residence during the period of February 2014 to June 2015.

Information used to make the decision The applicant was born in Malaysia in March 1954 and applied for their OAS pension in February 2019. The applicant entered Canada with their spouse in October 2003 as a Permanent Resident. While in Canada, they live with their daughter and do not pay rent or share utility expenses. The applicant brought some personal effects with them to Canada, has a current Canadian bank account, and is registered with a provincial health plan. Their engagement in Canadian social life is limited. The applicant's spouse returned to Malaysia in 2005 to reside there permanently. Every year, the applicant returns to Malaysia to live with their spouse for 6 or 7 months. Decision The applicant does not qualify for OAS benefits. Their residence history indicates that they have not established a centralized mode of living in Canada or maintained strong residential ties in Canada. Their continued migration between their daughter and spouse's residence is characteristic of a long-term visitor in Canada, not a resident. The spouse's permanent residence in Malaysia constitutes a principal residential tie for the applicant.

The following list of factors must be considered to make a decision regarding residential ties. Any determination of residence must be made on a case by case basis. The majority of the factors must demonstrate an individual’s residence in Canada.

Did/Does the individual have extensive ties outside of Canada, such as: family, property, business assets/interests? filing taxes in another country? medical insurance coverage, driver’s licence, etc. in another country? What is/Was: the extent of the absences from Canada? the individual present i n Canada the majority of the time, despite repeated absences from Canada? What were: the reasons given for the extended or frequent absences from Canada? the medical or humanitarian reasons, i.e. caring for sick relatives? Does the individual show a pattern of physical presence in Canada after each absence from Canada, such as: returning home as a resident (with a "returning resident" permit)? living as a visitor?

Did/Does the individual: own or rent a dwelling ? live in the family home of friends/relatives ? maintain the property, e.g. utilities, insurance, snow removal, etc.? retain furniture and personal effects in Canada? pay income tax as a resident of Canada? have "returning resident" permits? have immediate family members in Canada (i.e. spouse, dependent children )? have statements from neighbours verifying residence ? have registration with a provincial health plan? have current bank accounts in Canada? have a Canadian driver’s license/car registration? have a mailing addres s and a telephone listing?

topic_title: Can the Department use the Credit Splitting provision to improve the Latest Possible Date of Onset or help meet the eligibility requirements?
text: You must send the appropriate letter to the applicant if: they indicate that they are separated or divorced; and the Department can improve their Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) or establish their eligibility for CPPD benefits using the Credit Splitting provision. Effective January 1, 2025, upon receipt and approval of a Credit Split application for separated legal spouses, there is no eligibility to a CPP SVR pension when one of the separated legal spouses dies. If a separated legal spouse is receiving an SVR pension and the Department receives a Credit Split application on or after January 1, 2025 for the same deceased separated legal spouse, the SVR pension ceases as of the effective date of the credit split approval. The effective date of the credit split approval is the last day of the month in which the Department receives the Credit Split application or request. If the Department can improve the MQP or establish eligibility for CPPD benefits using Credit Splitting, call the applicant before sending a letter inviting them to apply for a Credit Split when they receive an SVR pension. Confirm whether the periods of cohabitation provided on the CPPD benefits application are for the same deceased spouse for whom the applicant is receiving an SVR pension. If yes, inform the applicant if a separated legal spouse is receiving an SVR pension and the Department receives a Credit Split application for the same deceased separated legal spouse, the SVR pension ceases as of the effective date of the Credit Split approval. If the CPPD benefit applicant still chooses to submit a Credit Split application, it will be reviewed by the CPP processing unit when received. If there is a CPPD benefits application in PWS or on hold in ITRDS , the CPP processing unit will notify the CPPD processing unit that a Credit Split application was received and will provide: the receipt date of the Credit Split application; the separated spouses' account information; the periods of cohabitation provided on the Credit Split application; and the Bring Forward (BF) date you set on the Credit Split application, if applicable. The CPP processing unit will proceed with the adjudication of the Credit Split application and confirm the decision (i.e approval or denial) with the CPPD processing unit. You must send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) Internal link to request expedited processing of the CPPD benefits application if the following conditions are met: Business Expertise Request Tool the CPPD processing unit sent the Credit Split application during the Earnings and Contributions review; the CPP processing unit approved the Credit Split for the same separated spouse for whom the applicant was receiving an SVR pension; the SVR pension is terminated; and your Earnings and Contributions review is complete and ready for medical adjudication. If the Credit Split did not improve the applicant's MQP or establish eligibility, add an important ITRDS note to indicate the Credit Split is not required for the MQP. For more information, Credit Split Application (Scenario)

The Child Rearing Provision (CRP) helps an applicant maintain their level of pensionable earnings by excluding periods of low or no earnings during the years spent raising children under the age of 7. The CRP can help an individual meet or improve the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) or increase the monthly rate of their CPPD benefit. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Scenario)

A contributory period is the period of time when an individual is eligible to contribute to the CPP and/or QPP. For more information, refer to CPP Contributions (Knowledge) and to CPP Contributions (Knowledge) CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy)

The Credit Split provision allows CPP unadjusted pensionable earnings earned by both common-law partners or spouses during the common-law union or marriage to be divided equally between both individuals. The attributed pensionable earnings following the approval of a request for a Credit Split provision may help an individual meet or improve the Minimum Qualifying Period for a CPPD benefit. For more information, Credit Split Application (Scenario)

text: If the applicant was employed and worked during the previous or current year: request a certified copy of their T4 income slip; or send the applicant a Statement of Contributory Salary and Wages - Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2011) form, to be completed by the applicant and their employer. If the applicant was self-employed request a certified copy of: their T1 Tax Statement; and the Notice of Assessment or the Notice of Reassessment they received from the Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ). For self-employed applicants, CRA assesses the amount of their employment earnings which determines the amount of contributions the applicant pays into CPP. The Earliest Possible Date of Onset (EPDOO) is based on the applicant's Date of Application (DOA) and is the earliest date an applicant can be deemed disabled for the purpose of paying a CPPD benefit. The EPDOO is either: 15 months before the DOA; or 12 months before the DOA for a subsequent CPPD benefit application where the previous CPPD benefit ended within the past 5 years.

The established Date of Onset (DOO) is a term used for late applicants only. The established DOO is the date on which the applicant's disability started. It is a medically determined date that is separate from the DOO and the LPDOO. The CPPD benefit can be approved using the LAP only if the established DOO is on or before the LPDOO. topic_title: Is the applicant already receiving an RTR pension?
text: An applicant cannot receive both an RTR pension and a DSB for the same period. If an RTR pension has been in pay 15 months or more from the date of the CPPD benefits application, the applicant is not eligible for a DSB . As of January 1, 2019, all applications, requests for reconsideration and appeals for DSB are accepted and reviewed for the DSB and the PRDB . PRDB is available to a retired pensioner who meets the eligibility requirements and whose: disability Date of Onset (DOO) is determined to be on or after the effective date of their RTR pension; or disability DOO is determined to be before the effective date of their RTR pension and applied 15 months or more after the effective date of their RTR pension. If a CPPD benefits application is received with an RTR pension application, the CPPD benefits application will be considered for a DSB and a PRDB when the RTR pension is effective the month following its receipt date. For more information, refer to the Process a PRDB (Scenario)

topic_title: Is the Child Rearing Provision needed to improve the Minimum Qualifying Period?
text: Any months that can be dropped out because of the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) period will no longer be used to establish the applicant's Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP). Only the years below the Year's Basic Exemption (before 1998) or below the Disability Basic Exemption (effective January 1998) will be dropped. For MQP purposes, only CRP full years can be dropped from the applicant's contributory period. If the CRP overlaps with the LPDOO, the LPDOO may be able to slide to the month in which the CRP period ends. In these situations, the LPDOO moves to the last month of the CRP. If there is no time gap between the end of the MQP and the first month of the CRP period, the LPDOO can be established as the last month in the CRP period. If the CRP period begins before January 1998 and ends after January 1998, you must watch for the change in the MQP rule. The MQP rule must be met at the new LPDOO. If you require a CRP application to meet or improve the MQP, you must obtain the information required to process the CRP by sending the appropriate letter to the applicant before forwarding the file to the Medical Adjudicator for medical determination. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Scenario)
The Latest Possible Date of Onset is the last month in which the applicant can be found disabled and still meets the Minimum Qualifying Period requirements.

topic_title: Manual calculation of Minimum Qualifying Period
text: You must complete a manual Earnings Investigation Worksheet External link in the following situations: Earnings Investigation Worksheet a Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) that is based on prorated earnings; there are valid earnings after the Latest Possible Date of Onset; a Late Applicant Provision pre-1987 MQP; a credit split exists on the account; an applicant is in pay for an RTR pension; a subsequent CPPD benefits application is received after a decision to cease the benefits is made; or any scenario where ITRDS does not calculate the correct MQP. topic_title: Minimum contributory requirements for CPPD benefits
text: To determine the minimum contributory requirements, refer to Non-Medical Eligibility—CPPD Benefits (Policy) and to Non-Medical Eligibility—CPPD Benefits (Policy) Eligibility Requirements— PRDB (Policy)

Earnings with CPP contributions that are below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) (before 1988) or below the Disability Basic Exemption (effective January 1998) can be prorated if the applicant is deemed disabled in the prorate year by the end of the prorated month. If earnings are available on the Record of Earnings, ITRDS calculates and displays a prorated latest possible date of onset. If earnings are available on the Record of Earnings, ITRDS calculates and displays a prorated Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). The Canada Revenue Agency assesses the CPP contributions of self-employed individuals at the end of the year when they file their income tax return. If 100% of their earnings are below the YBE and are self-employed, no contributions are made to the CPP, and there are no valid CPP contribution to prorate. Following the cessation of a CPPD benefit, the contributory period restarts the month following cessation of the benefit. If the year during which the benefit ceased is required to meet the earnings requirements, that year may be prorated. Proration can be used to establish or extend an LPDOO for PRDB for applicants with a Date of Onset (DOO) or an established DOO in May 2023 or later. For more information, refer to Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (Policy) and to Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (Policy) Process a PRDB (Scenario)

topic_title: Valid Earnings after the Latest Possible Date of Onset
text: Valid Earnings after the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) are earnings that exceed the Disability Basic Exemption that appear after the LPDOO and must be investigated. Earnings gained through a CPP credit split are not considered valid earnings for the purposes of determining work capacity. topic_title: Was a subsequent application received after a decision to deny CPPD benefits?
text: If the subsequent application is received outside the appeal period, and the Department did not receive a request for reconsideration, proceed as follows: Complete the earnings investigation; and if the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) is met, forward the file to the Medical Adjudicator for a medical determination; or if the MQP is not met, deny on the basis of insufficient earnings and contributions. topic_title: Was the Credit Split provision used to calculate the applicant's Minimum Qualifying Period?
text: The attribution date is the month following the month in which the credit split is approved. When a new benefit is put in pay as a result of earnings from a credit split, the effective date will be the month following the month the credit split is approved. A benefit that was not payable in the absence of the credit split cannot be paid for any months before the month in which the earnings are attributed. Prior to January 1, 1998, valid earnings must be above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) and effective January 1, 1998, valid earnings must be above the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE). The exception to this rule applies when a credit split causes the earnings to drop below the DBE. Effective 1998, if a contributor's earnings for any year are greater than the DBE before the credit split, and after the credit split are less than the DBE but more than the YBE for that year, the earnings are used as a valid year when determining if the Minimum Qualifying Period has been met. For more information, refer to Credit Split Application (Scenario) and to Credit Split Application (Scenario) CPP Credit Splitting (Policy) When considering the Late Applicant Provision and the Credit Split provision, as long as the applicant was separated from their spouse or common-law partner for at least one year or divorced before the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO), the divided earnings could be used to meet the earnings and contributions requirements. If the Department uses the CPP Credit Splitting provision to improve the LPDOO, ensure the earnings investigation worksheet includes the LPDOO with and without the applied credit split. Refer to IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP External link . IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP For more information, Credit Split and the Late Applicant Provision for CPPD benefits (Policy)

topic_title: Was there a previous CPPD benefit in pay?
text: As of January 1987, the contributory period of a disabled applicant ends the month the applicant is deemed disabled. If the applicant was previously in pay for a CPPD benefit, you can exclude those months from the contributory period when determining the Latest Possible Date of Onset of a subsequent application. For Minimum Qualifying Period purposes, only full years (from the Date of Onset to the last month in pay) will be excluded from the contributory period.

If you need to manually determine non-medical eligibility, complete an Earnings Investigation Worksheet External link . Earnings Investigation Worksheet To determine non-medical eligibility under an International Social Security Agreement, complete an earnings investigation worksheet. Refer to IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP External link . IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP

To be considered a current Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP), the applicant's MQP must be: no later than 15 months before the date of application; or within 12 months from the date of application if the applicant received a CPPD benefit within the last 5 years. If the MQP is not current, consider the Late Applicant Provision which provides eligibility protection to applicants who would have met the MQP requirements if they had applied earlier.
