Before March 2019, NHQ loaded all option recalculations in the PWS on an annual basis; current year option recalculations were loaded in the spring and previous year option recalculations were loaded in the fall.

Option recalculations where the required income information has been received, and a work item has been created in PWS, will be reviewed as usual, according to existing procedures for Income - Options: Effective July 1, 2008 All option recalculations for which the required income information has not been received will be loaded in the PWS with the specific barcodes: NHQOPTRECALC-CYY-NOINCOME for current year options; and NHQOPTRECALC-PYY-NOINCOME for previous year options. To action these work items by priority, Option Recalculation—Follow-Up Income Not Received

A consistent practice throughout the network for finalizing option recalculations for which no follow-up income has been received, has been developed. Starting in March 2019, a process was implemented by National Headquarters (NHQ) to identify and create work items in PWS once it has been confirmed that the required income information has been received by the Department to perform the option recalculation. Each year, beginning with the April accounting month up until reversion, NHQ will conduct scans of ITRDS for required income information. These scans will be conducted on a weekly basis for current year option recalculations and on a monthly basis for previous year option recalculations. Work items for option recalculations will be created in PWS where the required income information has been received. A client who was granted an option must submit their income for the following payment period so that an option reconciliation can be performed. Reporting of actual income must include all income that is considered income for GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit purposes regardless of how that income was used in the option calculation. You must compare the statement of actual income for the base calendar year against the statement of estimated income previously made. You must question any discrepancies that you are unable to resolve when reviewing the information on file to ensure the accuracy of the benefit rate paid. Options are generally processed in 2 parts: current year and previous year. Each part of the option must be reviewed and reconciled individually, based on the respective year of the estimated income. For more information regarding option reconciliations, Reconcile Options For options in the OAS Online system with a C or P option code, National Headquarters will perform regular scans from April to July of each year to determine if a CRA income feed has been received. A final scan will be performed in October. If the Department has not received the required income, a PWS work item will be created in the appropriate mail processing centre for follow-up. To identify these items, a unique barcode will be added to PWS: NHQOPTRECALC-CYY-NOINCOME for current year options; and NHQOPTRECALC-PYY-NOINCOME for previous year options. Once it has been confirmed that the Department has not received the income required to perform the option reconciliation, the period previously paid on the estimated income may have to be reverted to the original base calendar year income, and the entitlement recalculated accordingly.

Due to an OAS Online system enhancement, an issue has been identified that causes a delay in the weekly updates of the Calc Flag 4 to be implemented on a client’s OAS account. The issue is triggered when an agent sets the GIS for Life Flag to N and links or delinks the account during the same week. When this series of transactions are completed during the same weekly update, the Calc Flag 4 will take 2 weekly updates to be implemented on the account in lieu of 1 weekly update. This issue is especially concerning during the last week of an OAS Accounting month, where the Calc Flag on the account will not be set to 4 in time for the Month-End Payment process and the client could have a GIS benefit issued when they is not entitled. OAS Production Support is running a monthly scan to identify accounts that may have been impacted by this issue, which will be loaded into PWS and sent to regions for review.

topic_title: Are there multiple online applications listed in ITRDS? Updated
text: When multiple online applications are listed in ITRDS, you must confirm if they are duplicates of the same application or separate applications. In ITRDS, compare the following: the information in the sections of the online applications on the Application Status screen, particularly the free form text sections such as the Medical Information; and the Adjudication Timestamp when the benefit row is expanded on the Benefits screen. Generally, identical applications will be within seconds or minutes of each other. However, there can also be large gaps in between identical applications. An additional tool to use is the View Access History screen in the Government Online system. If it is available, you can verify if the client pressed the Submit button multiple times on the same application. However, it may not be clear if they are duplicate applications. As of April 6, 2021, CPP processing staff will no longer record and apply cash receipts in CPMS. The National Accounts Receivable (NAR) team in the Chief Financial Officer Branch (CFOB) will record incoming payments into the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements (PSCD) system. Due to the automatic interface between PSCD and CPMS, this action will automatically update the client’s account in CPMS. Incoming payments refers to the process of receiving payments to pay off program debts. These payments can be received via automated or manual transactions by: walk-in; mail; online banking; in-person banking; recoupment; and withhold. These payments create an incoming payment file, which are uploaded to PSCD. Incoming payments recorded by the NAR team during the December calendar month will automatically update the debtor’s account in CPMS during the same calendar year. When PSCD interfaces with CPMS, it will update the debtor’s: payment history, year-to-date totals; benefit amounts; and receivables. This worklist identifies work items that need further investigation by the CFOB before any payments can be applied to an account. Incoming payments that cannot be applied against a debt in PSCD for the following reasons will create a credit that will be refunded to the client by the NAR team: the client is not aware that the debt is paid in full and continues to make payments; a payment is received after a debt has been remitted; a bankruptcy or judgment was applied on the account for a previous date and payments were applied after that date; or a set-off was applied after the client paid the account. You will no longer create a manual priority payment to issue refunds; this action will now be completed by the NAR team. Payments that require a refund will have a status of Awaiting Section 20 approval on the Payment Clarification worklist in PSCD. Once the refund is investigated and approved by the NAR team, the credit (i.e. refund) displays a document type of RF (i.e. refund) in PSCD).

In the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system, the term write-off is used generically to include write-offs, remissions, rescissions and forgiveness. Generally, the write-off process consists of manually or automatically writing off, in whole or in part, any debt or obligation due to the Crown. In most cases, the write-off process goes through the following lifecycle: Create the recommendation for a write-off. Review the recommendation and generate a report. Approve or reject the recommendation for a write-off. Process and post the approved recommendations. Definitions of each type of write-off appear in the following table: Term Definition Forgiveness A forgiveness extinguishes a debt and applies only to the Canada Student Loans Program. Forgiveness releases the debtor from all liability, waives the Crown’s right to reinstate the debt, and permits both the Crown and the debtor to remove the debt from their accounts. Remission A remission deems the debt to be paid and applies only to CPP and OAS Programs. Remission releases the debtor from all liability, waives the Crown’s right to reinstate the debt, and permits both the Crown and the debtor to remove the debt from their accounts. Rescission A rescission relates to penalties. Penalties can be reduced in whole or in part and are only applicable to penalties imposed by Employment Insurance, OAS and CPP. Write-Off A write-off is an accounting action which removes primarily debts owed to the Crown from the accounts receivable records that are not collectible, but does not release the debtor from the obligation to pay and does not affect the right of the Crown to collect the debt in the future, except where prohibited by legislation. Waiver A waiver is the action of relinquishing the Crown’s right to charge an amount. Waivers usually apply to penalties, interest or other additional charges. When an amount is waived, it is considered never to have existed so there is no debt to write-off.

Effective January 1987, the term "common-law partners" applies to persons who are not married to each other and who have been cohabiting in a conjugal relationship for a continuous period of at least one year. They have the same rights and obligations as married individuals when they apply for benefits. "Cohabitation" means to live together, while "conjugal" implies a commitment of both common-law partners to live in a marriage-like state, thereby assuming those marital rights, duties and obligations typically applied to married couples. Since July 31, 2000, the definition of common-law partner includes same-sex partners as long as they meet the definition of common-law partners. Individuals do not have to publicly represent themselves as husband and wife to be considered common-law partners under the OAS Act. Cohabitation between common-law partners can be interrupted by temporary separations during the year before the contributor's death and still be considered as continuous. If there is an interruption in cohabitation that is involuntary and beyond the control of the couple (i.e. neither party had any intention of separating), their cohabitation is considered as uninterrupted and not grounds for modifying or denying a benefit. The intent of the parties must be considered when assessing if there was a break in their cohabitation during the one-year period before the contributor's death. If it is not clear that the partners were cohabiting, the courts attempt to determine if there is an intention on the part of both common-law partners to set up a matrimonial home together. Criteria used to determine if this intention exists include the following: Do both common-law partners live in the same house, with responsibility for the day-to-day household jobs (e.g. cooking, cleaning, laundry, gardening) assumed by one common-law partner on behalf of both parties or shared by both common-law partners? How do the common-law partners represent themselves socially? Does one common-law partner provide money to their partner and to their partner's children? In the case of a physical separation: Are there trips for the purpose of visiting with the other common-law partner? If another party alleges that cohabitation has ceased, is there clear evidence of an intention to terminate cohabitation? This list is not exhaustive, but gives an idea of what type of information the applicant can provide to establish the common-law relationship. After the request is made, it becomes the applicant's responsibility to prove to the Minister's satisfaction that the conditions of eligibility are met.

Conflicting information on a couple's marital status must be resolved before a benefit can be paid. If it is determined after review that false or misleading information has been given concerning a beneficiary's marital status, appropriate action must be taken according to current policies and procedures.

Canadian law must recognize a marriage for it to be considered legal. As of July 2005, the Civil Marriage Act defines marriage as the lawful union of 2 persons to the exclusion of all others. This Act legalized same-sex marriage in Canada.

Legal marriage dissolution means that 2 people who were legally married have terminated the marriage either by divorce or by annulment. Divorce A couple is not divorced until a court order finalizes the divorce and ends the marriage. In Canada, such a court order is referred to as a "Judgment of Divorce" if it is issued under the Divorce Act of 1985. If the court order was issued before 1985, it was called a “Decree Absolute”. The Divorce Act of 1985 states that the dissolution of a marriage takes effect, subject to special circumstances or rights of appeal, 30 days after the Judgment of Divorce is rendered. Annulment Under both the CPP and the OAS Act, only legal (not church) annulments are recognized. A legal annulment is one that has been ordered by a court of law. An annulment is a legal declaration that either: a marriage never existed because it was invalid; or a legal marriage existed until it was ended by a court order or decree of nullity. Foreign marriage dissolution Some OAS or CPP beneficiaries petition and receive a divorce or a marriage annulment outside of Canada. Under the Divorce Act , such marriage dissolutions are acceptable if, at the time the dissolution procedures were carried out, one of the former spouses was habitually resident of the foreign country for at least one year immediately preceding the commencement of proceedings for the divorce. The term "habitually resident" is interpreted to mean the person's domicile of choice, the place where the person's life is centred and where the individual intends to reside. Foreign countries may grant a divorce for couples that were not residing in the country for a year or more, contrary to the Divorce Act . However, such divorces may still be valid in Canada. The courts have developed a two part test that should be applied in order to recognize a foreign divorce under the Divorce Act where the couple has not resided in the foreign country for a year or more: Determine whether the divorce is legally valid in the jurisdiction where it was granted. Determine whether either former spouse had a real and substantial connection to that jurisdiction, as allowing Canadian residents to divorce in a jurisdiction with which they had no connection "of any substantive nature" would offend Canadians' notion of fairness and not be in harmony with Canadian public policy. Therefore, when one of the former spouses in the divorce had a connection to the jurisdiction in which the divorce was granted, unless it can be proven that the divorce was not legally valid in that jurisdiction, the divorce should be recognized in Canada.

Marital status can be validated using a third-party. However, if there is a discrepancy between the information provided by the applicant and the third-party, or there are contesting applications, documentary evidence to prove marital status must be requested.

A couple is considered to be "reconciled" when they have resumed cohabitation. Separated married couples OAS benefits When a separated married couple reconciles, they are considered to be “married”, effective the month after the month of reconciliation. Separated common-law partners OAS benefits When a separated common-law couple reconciles after a breakdown period of less than 3 months, the marital status does not change from the "married rate". A separation of more than 3 months is seen as evidence that the relationship has ended. If more than 3 months have passed after the month in which the separation occurred and the couple resumes cohabitation, they are required to live together for one year before they may be considered as common-law partners under the OAS Act.

Separation occurs when a couple, married or common-law, lives separate and apart by either: mutual agreement; legal separation; or desertion, where one person has deserted the other according to the law of the Canadian province or territory where they last resided together. Since the separation of spouses or common-law partners can affect benefit eligibility and/or entitlement, it is important to establish: if the couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control; or if the separated couple is separated by mutual agreement or did one desert the other; and the exact date the separation occurred.

Old Age Security Act A survivor is a person whose spouse or common-law partner has died and who has not become the spouse or common-law partner of another person since the spouse or common-law partner's death. Canada Pension Plan If the death of the contributor occurred on or after January 1,1987, the survivor in relation to the deceased contributor is the person who was the common-law partner at the time of the contributor's death. If the contributor was not in a common-law relationship at the time of death, the survivor is the person who was legally married to the deceased contributor at the time of the contributor's death. Legally married at the time of death includes if the couple was separated or if divorce proceedings had been initiated but had not been finalized. If the deceased contributor was in a common-law relationship at the time of their death, the common-law partner is the survivor and even if the common-law partner withdraws their application or chooses not to apply, the legal spouse cannot be the eligible survivor.

topic_title: Arrange for a Functional Capacity Evaluation or an Independent Medical Examination at an assessment facility Updated
text: The following criteria will help identify applicants or beneficiaries who may be asked to attend a Functional Capacity Evaluation (FCE) or an Independent Medical Examination (IME): The applicant or beneficiary is under the age of 60. There is insufficient objective medical evidence to support eligibility or continuing eligibility. There is conflicting medical information. The applicant or beneficiary has not been examined by a specialist in the recent past. The medical diagnosis at the time of granting was expected to improve or stabilize but the applicant or beneficiary's condition is unchanged at the time of the reassessment. There may be times where the applicant or beneficiary is asked to attend both an FCE and IME at the same time. As well, in rare instances, an applicant or beneficiary over the age of 60 may be asked to attend an FCE. Arrange for a Functional Capacity Evaluation (FCE), an Independent Medical Examination (IME) or a combined FCE and IME.

The FCE and the IME can be arranged at any level of adjudication, reassessment or appeals to aid in the assessment of eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits. This type of assessment is most often arranged at the reassessment level and requests are rare. While they can provide an impartial second opinion, they are: costly; lengthy; arranged in rare circumstances only; and require manager approval. You can arrange for a FCE or an IME after you: develop the file to obtain additional information. Refer to CPPD-File Development (Scenario) (KA-01878) (article not available); evaluate all the evidence; determine you are unable to make a decision based on a balance of probabilities. Refer to Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) ; Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) consult with the regional Medical Adjudicator Consultant via the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) Internal link for their agreement to organize an impartial second opinion; and Business Expertise Request Tool have approval from your manager to proceed. When arranging for a FCE or an IME at the reassessment level, you must send an enquiry via BERT. Business Expertise will review the enquiry and escalate to CPPD Business Operations, as necessary. Prior to making any arrangements, you must obtain written medical clearance from the applicant's or beneficiary's regular physician: It is not sufficient for the physician to suggest arranging an FCE in the medical report. If the physician does not provide written consent, you cannot take any further action on the FCE. If the applicant or beneficiary does not have a physician, you may send them for an IME and inform the IME specialist to arrange for an FCE if they deem it necessary. You must also obtain: written consent from the applicant or beneficiary; and the Consent to attend FCE (FCE-CONSENT) form and the Consent to attend IME (IME-CONSENT) form which are are used in conjunction with a Consent for Service Canada to Collect Personal Information (ISP-2502) form. The information sheet that is sent to the client with the consent form informs them that Service Canada will be charged for missed appointments. For more information, Functional Capacity Evaluation or Combined Functional Capacity Evaluation/Independent Medical Examination (Policy)

Amendments to the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada’s regulations came into force in January 2014 and individuals began entering Canada under a 20-year Parents and Grandparents (PGP) sponsorship agreement around January 2016. Since it is expected that most 10-year sponsorship agreements will have lapsed by the time the amendments to the Old Age Security Act come into force, grandfathering rules will apply under limited situations. Effective date is before October 1, 2025 Individuals under a sponsorship agreement who submit an application with an effective date before October 1, 2025, will continue to be assessed under the old rules, even if the application is received after this date. Old Rules Individuals under a 10-year PGP sponsorship agreement with an effective date prior to October 1, 2025, who have not yet applied for benefits, will be subjected to the old rules even if their sponsorship agreement has not yet ended. Under the old rules, sponsored immigrants are not entitled to receive the GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit for the duration of their sponsorship agreement. The limitation on entitlement remains in effect until: the beneficiary accumulates 10 full years of residence in Canada after age 18; the sponsorship agreement ends; or the sponsorship agreement breaks down. Effective date is on or after October 1, 2025 Individuals under a sponsorship agreement who submit an application with an effective date on or after October 1, 2025 will be assessed under the new rule, regardless of the length of their sponsorship agreement. The rule being that an individual under a sponsorship agreement is not entitled to receive the GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit for the duration of their sponsorship period.

A sponsored immigrant is an individual who is legally admitted to Canada under a sponsorship agreement. A sponsor is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who is 18 years of age or older and has agreed to financially support the sponsored immigrant while living in Canada for the duration of the sponsorship period. Effective October 1, 2025, individuals under a sponsorship agreement are not entitled to receive the GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit for the duration of their sponsorship period. Additionally, the duration of the Parents and Grandparents (PGP) sponsorship period has been extended from 10-years to 20-years in all provinces and territories except Quebec. This limitation on entitlement remains in effect until: the sponsorship agreement ends; or the sponsorship agreement breaks down. Once the sponsorship agreement ends or breaks down, the sponsored individual is entitled to receive the GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit in the same manner as a non-sponsored immigrant.

Income-tested benefits may be paid to sponsored individuals before the end of their sponsorship agreement only in the event of a sponsorship breakdown. The following conditions may qualify as a sponsorship breakdown: the sponsor dies; the sponsor is convicted of an offence under the Criminal Code in respect of the sponsored individual; the sponsor is determined to be bankrupt as defined in section 2 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act. ; or the sponsor is sentenced to a term of imprisonment of more than 6 months. text: If you need to review earlier guidance related to this interim measure, click the Previous Versions at the bottom of this page and select version 2.26 .

Effective Date: March 11, 2020 Issue or purpose This interim product was developed in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The interim measures have undergone changes, including certain measures: were rescinded; were incorporated into regular policy; and will remain active pending legislative amendments. Background In December 2019, a novel coronavirus and subsequent disease outbreak were reported (COVID-19). As the virus spread, rules with regard to travel, quarantine and self-isolation were imposed by affected countries. The rules established by foreign governments and commercial entities (e.g. travel industry) prevented some Canadian citizens and permanent residents from returning to Canada, impacting entitlement to OAS benefits. OAS pensioners and GIS recipients who ordinarily reside in Canada were sometimes prevented or delayed from returning to Canada due to travel bans or restrictions, involuntary quarantine or self-isolation. Given the portability and specified circumstances provisions for residence under the Old Age Security Act , some individuals with non-portable OAS pensions or benefits, or who were employed or engaged abroad, may also have been impacted. The pandemic resulted in delayed receipt of applications and documents affecting benefit entitlement, notifications from Service Canada to individuals, recovery of overpayments, claims of undue hardship and unsigned CPP declarations of attendance due to school closures. It made it difficult for an applicant or beneficiary to have a commissioner for oaths complete and sign their portion of a statutory declaration. Effective Date: March 11, 2020 Purpose This interim product was developed to address difficulties individuals were experiencing with adhering to program requirements due to the global COVID-19 pandemic. The interim measures have evolved with some rescinded, others incorporated into regular business and some still active as they require regulatory amendments. The interim measures provide revised operational policy and procedural direction regarding the requirement for documentation: to establish marital status for Old Age Security (OAS) benefits, the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Survivor's pension and CPP pension sharing; for proof of funeral expenses for CPP death benefits; and to establish legal status for certain OAS applicants when processing initial applications for the (OAS) pension, Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), the Allowance ( ALW ) and Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ). It also amends the requirement to provide proof of the date of death for the ALWS and applications for CPP death benefits, Survivor's pensions and Surviving Child's benefits. In addition, it amends some of the requirements to provide proof of the date of death when terminating or cancelling CPP, Canada Pension Plan Disability (CPPD) and OAS benefits after a beneficiary dies. Documentary evidence requirements related to the reconsideration of the Minister's decision, appeals to the Social Security Tribunal ( SST ), and referrals to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) are not impacted by the direction in this document. Background In December 2019, a novel coronavirus and subsequent disease outbreak was reported (COVID-19). As the virus spread, rules regarding travel, quarantine and self- isolation were imposed by affected countries and in Canada. To ease the burden on applicants, beneficiaries and the service delivery network, these interim measures were created to simplify the processing of applications and are now being implemented into regular business. Previously, the processing network had to obtain lists of accounts from EDS or Cognos/IRIS that were identified in various operational reports and that required action. The Tracking All Work initiative has been developed to resolve the following issues: reports were difficult to use; reports were unavailable in PWS; many of the accounts listed did not require action, although there was no way to identify them ahead of time; and there was no integrated client perspective (i.e. no way to link clients appearing on different reports). The SharePoint site has been designed to filter out any reports where action is not required.

You must no longer access these operational reports from either the Electronic Document System (EDS) or Cognos/IRIS. Instead, National Headquarters will automatically upload any accounts that require action to PWS as work items. The regions will manage and assign the work items, and you are responsible for those that have been assigned to you. You can access a list that includes all reports, their current report name and number and the new PWS work items. Each PWS work type can have multiple associated barcodes to help identify the action required. list Once a PWS work item is assigned to you, look up the account in the SharePoint Digital Repository by entering the client’s social insurance number or account number. The SharePoint Digital Repository has been designed to eventually capture all reports for that client. For now, the functionality includes a subset of accounts. For example, a client could appear on 4 CPP credit reports and 2 CPP debit reports. Likewise, a client could appear on the OAS Reject report and the Marital Status Incompatible report. This functionality will allow you to action all reports at the same time. The SharePoint Digital Repository also removes any duplication between a daily, weekly or monthly version of a particular report. Therefore, only one PWS work item will be created regardless if it previously appeared on both a weekly and monthly operational report. Once you complete the required action, close the work item in PWS. Refer to the instructions on how to use the Reports SharePoint site . Effective July 2022, the following emergency benefits received in 2021 or later are exempted from the calculation of income-tested benefits, i.e. the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), the Allowance (ALW) and the Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefits. Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Emergency benefits received in 2020 For the July 2021 to June 2022 payment period, based on an individual’s 2020 income, the EI-ERB, CERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB are considered income when determining entitlement to income-tested benefits. In some cases, the receipt of these emergency benefits in 2020 resulted in a reduction or cessation of income-tested benefits in July 2021. To alleviate the financial hardship of GIS, ALW and ALWS recipients who received emergency benefits in 2020, individuals may qualify for the One-time grant for GIS Recipients who received Pandemic Benefits Options Under the OAS Regulations, pension income for the purpose of an "option" includes amounts received as “employment insurance benefits”. Therefore, prior to July 2022, EI ERB is considered “pension income” in the same manner as EI benefits. However, CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB are not considered pension income. The cessation of EI ERB can trigger an "option". However, the cessation of the CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB cannot trigger an "option” as these benefits are not considered pension income under the OAS Regulations. An "option" for the cessation of EI-ERB may be granted even if an individual qualifies for the "One-time grant for GIS Recipients who received Pandemic Benefits", if it is to their advantage. When estimating income for a separate event (i.e. retirement or reduction in retirement pension), EI ERB is included in the estimated income. Any EI ERB received would continue to be part of the estimated income for the July 2021 to June 2022 payment period. Effective July 2022, any EI ERB would be removed from the estimated income. The CERB, CRB, CRBC, CRSB and CWLB continue to be part of the base calendar year income of an estimate until June 2022. Effective July 2022, the base calendar year will no longer include income from these sources. Claims of dire need For accounts where individuals claimed they were in a dire need situation and were granted options when their emergency benefits ended, the option is still valid as this was the direction in place at the time. In addition, these options will continue until the income from the emergency benefit no longer forms part of the base calendar year income. In other words, if a beneficiary was granted a current year option due to their emergency benefit ending, they may continue to be granted a previous year option for this event. Claims of suspected CERB/EI ERB fraud or identity theft For accounts where income-tested benefits stopped or were reduced in July 2021 due to CERB/EI ERB income, but individuals claim they did not receive this income and are victims of fraud or identity theft, the income cannot be removed without confirmation that the Canada Revenue Agency will be amending the taxpayer’s 2020 income.

In order to provide similar support for workers who would generally be eligible for the Employment Insurance (EI) program, the Minister made an interim order on March 31, 2020, providing for the Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) to be administered through Service Canada. Publicly, this benefit was also referred to as the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB). For most Canadians, the CERB/ EI ERB ended on October 3, 2020. Where continued support is needed, the Government of Canada introduced additional temporary recovery benefits to support those who are still unable to work for reasons related to COVID-19. These new benefits are: the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); the Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); and the Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Not all individuals who were in receipt of the CERB/EI ERB will be eligible for continuing support under the new Government of Canada initiatives. The CERB/EI ERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB are taxable benefits that are considered income under the Income Tax Act and are considered income when determining entitlement to income-tested benefits up to June 2022. Effective July 2022, legislative amendments were made to the Old Age Security Act, allowing for the exclusion of these benefits received in 2021 or later when calculating income. CPP and CPPD If a CPP Retirement (RTR) pension or CPPD beneficiary is working, they could be eligible for the CERB/EI ERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB or CWLB. RTR pension and CPPD beneficiaries should contact the CRA to determine whether they may be eligible for this income support. These emergency benefits will not be considered employment income and receipt of these benefits will not affect eligibility for CPPD benefits. CPPD applicants and beneficiaries will continue to be assessed on the legislated eligibility criteria and will be paid in full if they are found to be disabled as defined under the CPP. There is no need to report the receipt of the CERB/EI ERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB or CWLB to Service Canada. However, for CPPD benefit purposes, employment or self-employment work activity must be reported as per the beneficiary's responsibilities. OAS

topic_title: Absence greater than 5 years after February 15, 1977
text: The applicant was born in Canada on May 16, 1958. On their OAS application, the applicant indicated that they are a Canadian Citizen. The residence statement indicates they left Canada on September 9, 1980, and lived in Italy until October 21, 1990. During this absence, the applicant became an Italian citizen. The applicant did not lose their Canadian citizenship as they left Canada after February 15, 1977, and now hold dual citizenship with Canada and Italy. Since the applicant was Canadian at birth and never left Canada before February 15, 1977, they must provide documentation that shows Canada as their place of birth for proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or the SIR .

topic_title: Absence greater than 5 years before February 15, 1977
text: Example 1—The applicant did not become a citizen of another country during the absence The applicant was born in Canada on July 27, 1945. On their OAS application, they indicated that they are a Canadian citizen. The residence statement indicates they went to France from 1965 to 1972 (i.e. an absence greater than 5 years before February 15, 1977) to take care of a sick relative. The applicant did not become a French citizen during that period and as a result, would not have lost their Canadian citizenship. When processing the applicant’s OAS application, review the application and any provided documentation to ensure there are no discrepancies. If no discrepancies are found, the applicant must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth for proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or the Social Insurance Registry (SIR). If discrepancies are found, the applicant must do one of the following: Complete and sign the Statutory Declaration - Confirmation of Canadian Citizenship (ISP-1899) form to confirm they did not become a citizen of France during their absence. If the applicant completes and signs the ISP-1899 form, they must provide documentation showing Canada as their place of birth for proof of legal status, unless proof of age was established through the CPP program or the SIR ; or Provide proof of Canadian citizenship reinstatement, if the applicant became a citizen of France during their absence. If the citizenship was reinstated, they can provide their Canadian Citizenship Certificate. Example 2—The applicant became a citizen of another country during the absence The applicant was born in Canada in May 1948. In April 1970, they moved to the United States of America and, in April 1975, they were granted United States citizenship. The applicant lost their Canadian citizenship as they became a citizen of another country before February 15, 1977. In June 1990, the applicant returned to Canada to reside permanently. In January 2023, they applied for their OAS pension, and provided proof that their Canadian citizenship had been restored by submitting a citizenship certificate. Since proof of reinstatement of Canadian citizenship has been provided, the legal status requirement is met.

topic_title: The applicant indicated Canadian Citizen on their application, but only provided proof of landed immigrant status
text: The applicant was born in Germany on July 23, 1958, and came to Canada as a landed immigrant on July 7, 1986. In January 2023, the applicant applied for the OAS pension and indicated on the application that they are a Canadian citizen. The residence history indicates that they have remained in Canada since their first entry date in 1986. The applicant provided a certified copy of their landed immigrant document (IMM1000) which proves their landed immigrant status as well as the date of entry. Although the document provided (IMM1000) does not support the legal status stated on the application (Canadian Citizen), the legal status requirement is met as the applicant met all the following criteria: The applicant has indicated on their OAS pension application that they are currently a Canadian citizen; The applicant originally entered Canada as a permanent resident and has provided acceptable proof of this status; The applicant has no absences from Canada where legal status may have been lost; The applicant is currently residing in Canada; and There is nothing about the applicant’s account that would make you question their legal status.

Table 1. Example 1 Residence Statement and Documents on file Residence Statement Documents on file Initial date of entry in November 1981. No absences since their date of entry into Canada. Permanent Resident Card showing the permanent residence date as March 1983. In this situation, it is common for an individual to be living in Canada before obtaining permanent residence status. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Clarification regarding the applicant’s intent to reside in Canada between these dates is not required. The applicant’s period of Canadian residence begins with the original date of entry (November 1981).

Table 2. Example 2 Residence statement and Documents on file Residence statement Documents on file Initial date of entry into Canada in July 2002. Absence from Canada from November 2002 to June 2003. Re-entry into Canada from July 2003 to the present. Record of Landing (IMM1000) showing: the original date of entry into Canada in July 2002; and the landed date in December 2004. In this situation, due to the absence before the landed date in December 2004, clarification is required. This clarification will assist you in determining whether to consider the period between the original date of entry and the landed date as residence or presence in Canada. You must call the applicant to clarify their intent to reside in Canada from the original date of entry. If, during the call, the applicant indicates that: their intent was to reside in Canada from their original date of entry, the Canadian residence period begins with the original date of entry, July 2002; or they did not intend to live in Canada until their return in June 2003, the Canadian residence period begins with the date the applicant decided to make Canada their home in July 2003. The period before July 2003 is considered as presence in Canada. Since there are no changes required to the residence statement on the application, the applicant’s clarification is not required to be in writing. Record the details of the phone call on a Telephone Call (ISP-0112) form and in ITRDS notes.

Table 3. Example 3 Residence statement and Documents on file Residence statement Documents on file Initial date of entry into Canada in October 1991. Absence from Canada from January 1992 to May 1992. Re-entry into Canada from June 1992 to the present. Permanent Resident Card showing permanent residence date in February 1993 In this situation, due to the absence before the permanent residence date, clarification is required. This clarification will assist you in determining whether to consider the period between the original date of entry and the permanent residence date as residence or presence in Canada. You must call the applicant to obtain information in regards to the applicant’s intent to reside in Canada from their original date of entry. During the call, the applicant indicates that: their intent was to reside in Canada from their original date of entry; the short absence was to finalize the sale of their home in the other country; they actually entered Canada in December 1990 (not October 1991) under a temporary work visa and did not include this period as they thought it would not be considered as Canadian residence. Since the period in December 1990 can be considered as residence in Canada and was not originally included on the residence statement, you must obtain the new residence information in writing. Once the new residence statement is received, the Canadian residence period begins with the new original entry date (December 1990) and the absence from January 1992 to May 1992 can be considered as residence as the absence was temporary in nature.

While an applicant for a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit can have a Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) based on their own earnings and contrib utions, they can also be eligible for a credit split and have divided Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) attributed to their Reco rd of Earnings. The applicant may gain UPE from a credit split after the LPDOO. In some cases, the UPE may be attributed for a period of less than 4 years. Such a case could result in the applicant gaining from 1 to 3 years of UPE after they last met the contributory requirements to qualify for a DSB benefit. A medical review will determine if the applicant meets the severe and prolonged criteria for a CPP DSB benefit at their LPDOO. The LPDOO will be determined by using both the applicant's own UPE as well as the UPE acquired through credit splitting.

The balance of probabilities is used to determine if the applicant was more likely than not disabled at the Latest Possible Date of Onset. All medical and non-medical evidence on file, as well as the progressive nature of the applicant’s medical condition (s) and whole medical history must be considered. Consideration of the progressive nature of the medical condition (s) is particularly pertinent when adjudicating under the LAP.

topic_title: Determination of the established date of onset
text: The established Date of Onset (DOO) is a medically determined date that and is separate from the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). At times, the medical evidence will not be sufficient to determine the established DOO. In such cases, the balance of probabilities approach must be considered.

The retrospective medical determination associated with late applicant cases is often difficult to make because medical evidence relevant for that period of time is not always available. The fact that an applicant cannot provide this evidence does not always mean they were not disabled when they last qualified for benefits.

The Late Applicant Provision (LAP) can extend eligibility to CPP disability (DSB) benefits to protect those contributors who would have met the earnings and medical eligibility had they applied for a CPP DSB benefit at an earlier time. The LAP can be applied if the applicant meets the following contributory requirements: they were conside red disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements, th e Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO); they continue to meet the severe and prolonged criteria since their LPDOO; they were disab led at the date of adjudication; and they are likel y to be disabled into the future and considered incapable of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation (equal to 12 times the maximum monthly disability amount). The LAP allows for the determination as to whether or not an applicant qualifies for CPP DSB benefits at a time when they had coverage under the CPP . Once it is established that the applicant has met the contributory requirements at some point in time, it must be determined if the applicant meets the definition of “disabled” within the meaning of the CPP. T o make a medical determination, it must be established if the applicant met the definition of a “severe and prolonged” disability when they last qualified for a benefit and continuously thereafter. In order to make a defendable and sustainable denial decision, the evidence must demonstrate: the applicant was not disabled at their LPDOO; and the information supports the applicant’s work capacity after their LPDOO.

As of January 1, 1998, valid earnings are earnings that exceed the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year. Earnings below the DBE are not considered to be valid earnings for the purposes of the CPP Disability benefit and do not require investigation. An applicant may have valid earnings after their Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) because they wanted to maintain a connection to the workforce or were attempting to continue working despite their disability and were unsuccessful. To recognize and support the applicant's attempt to remain in the workforce, these years must be investigated to determine if the applicant had capacity for work after their LPDOO. If an applicant has one to 3 years of valid earnings after they last met the contributory requirements, investigation of the valid earnings after the LPDOO will determine their work capacity. The assessment of work capacity for those years is based on: performance; productivity; and profitability. If an applicant has valid earnings after the LPDOO and it is determined that the earnings do not represent the work capacity, it must be established if the applicant had a severe and prolonged disability: on or before their LPDOO; and continuously since their LPDOO to the date of application and into the future. Both employer and medical evidence is required to determine capacity from the LPDOO, including the valid years of earnings. The evidence is to be used to support the continuous nature of the disability determination. There are times when information regarding an applicant’s work activity may not be available (e.g. the business has closed, the files destroyed). When this occurs, consider all evidence (medical and non-medical): what is known about the applicant’s work activity; information about the applicant’s medical condition; and the Medical Adjudicator's knowledge of CPP legislation and policy. The balance of probabilities standard is used to determine if the applicant was more likely than not disabled at their LPDOO.

topic_title: Insufficient CPP contributions to meet contributory requirements for CPP DSB benefits and foreign work activity is identified
text: The applicant does not have sufficient earnings and contributions to qualify for CPP DSB benefits, however, there is evidence on file that they worked in another country or countries. An International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) may help the applicant meet the minimum contributory requirements for CPP DSB benefits. There are 2 possible scenarios: If Canada does not have an ISSA in force with the relevant country or countries, the application is denied based on insufficient earnings and contributions; or If Canada has an ISSA in force with the relevant country or countries, the file is transferred to International Operations to determine if there is contributory eligibility for the CPP DSB benefit under the ISSA.

Canada Pension Plan Subsection 42 (2)(a)(b)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Interpretation—When person deemed disabled Subsection 44 (1)(b)(ii)—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Benefits Payable Section 56—Calculation of Benefits—Disability Pension—Amount of disability pension Section 69—Payment of Benefits: Special Rules Applicable—Disability Pension and Post-retirement Disability Benefit—Commencement of pension CPP regulations Section 68—Pensions and Supplementary Benefits—Determination of Disability

International Social Security Agreements Canada has reciprocal agreements related to social benefits in force with many countries. These International Social Security Agreements (ISSA) allow social program credits from other countries to be considered when determining eligibility for benefits in Canada. Some applicants may have lived and worked in Canada and in other countries. Their work activity in another country may occur before or after their work in Canada. The social security systems of certain countries allow voluntary contributions to be made without work activity. Such voluntary contributions can also be used in determining an individual's eligibility for benefits in Canada. Interaction between the Late Applicant Provision and an ISSA It is important to determine an applicant's eligibility for CPP Disability (DSB) benefits by first using their domestic (i.e. Canadian) contributions before considering the use of an ISSA. This includes consideration under the Late Applicant Provision (LAP). If the applicant has lived or worked in a country with which Canada has an ISSA in force, it is the responsibility of International Operations to review the CPP DSB benefits application if it is determined that the LAP cannot be applied in the applicant's case. topic_title: The applicant has sufficient CPP contributions to meet contributory requirements and foreign work activity is identified. However, the foreign work activity occurs after their latest possible date of onset
text: Any foreign work activity identified after their Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) could indicate work capacity. In such cases the application must be assessed to determine the applicants work capacity after their LPDOO. If it is found that the foreign work activity represents work capacity and the applicant is not eligible for CPP DSB benefits using their domestic LPDOO, it must then be determined if Canada has an ISSA in force with the country or countries where the applicant worked. If Canada: has an ISSA with the country or countries, a final decision on the application is not made and the file is transferred to International Operations for determination if there is eligibility for CPP DSB benefits under the ISSA; does not have an ISSA with country or countries, the CPP DSB benefits application is denied medically based on their LPDOO.

topic_title: The applicant has sufficient CPP contributions to meet contributory requirements for CPP DSB benefits and foreign work activity is identified before the latest possible date of onset
text: If the applicant has sufficient domestic earnings and contributions to establish a Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) and there is evidence on file that they worked in another country or countries before their LPDOO, the file is referred for medical adjudication for a determination of disability based on their LPDOO. If the applicant is eligible for CPP DSB benefits, the file is processed for payment. If the applicant is not eligible for CPP DSB benefits, it must first be determined if Canada has an ISSA with the country or countries where the applicant worked. If Canada: has an ISSA with the country or countries, a final decision is not made and the file is transferred to International Operations to determine if there is eligibility for CPP DSB benefits under the relevant ISSA(s); does not have an ISSA with the country or countries, the CPP DSB benefits application is denied medically using their LPDOO.

Currently, operational policy states that when there is a reversal of decision(s) on the SVR pension based on who is determined to be the survivor of a deceased contributor, the initial decision is considered valid and there is no overpayment. The policy presumed that the initial decision was correct at the time it was made based on the information at hand and, therefore, any overpayment created was not valid and could not be recovered. While policy did not consider these situations to be recoverable overpayments by the Department, procedurally, an overpayment would be created on the system and remitted as "uncollectible".

The updated policy stipulates that payments made to an initial beneficiary who is subsequently determined not to be entitled to a SVR pension constitutes a debt to the Crown and must be repaid. While there is authority to remit all or part of a debt to the Crown due to erroneous advice or administrative error, the evidence-based decision to pay a SVR pension to an initial applicant followed by a determination that the new applicant meets the definition of survivor does not, in itself, constitute an administrative error. This direction is effective as of the date of publication and will not to be applied retroactively. Closed cases will not be overturned or reviewed. For more information on the p olicy, refer to the iFGP Reversal of Decisions—Survivor’s Pension For instructions on how to process a contesting application, Survivor's Pension Application

Effective immediately, policy and procedures have been updated on what to do in the case of contesting CPP Survivor’s (SVR) pension applicants or beneficiaries, when one is already in pay. Therefore, there are new guidelines for recovering receivables when a reversal of a decision is made.

The fast track reapplication is an incentive offered to past CPPD beneficiaries who attempted to return to work or participated in work-like activities. The fast track reapplication is an accelerated process for previous CPPD beneficiaries who stop working within 5 years of their benefit cease date. It is offered if the beneficiary stopped work due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were originally granted benefits. Fast-track reapplication only applies to the same benefit that was previously in pay. A past beneficiary may request a fast track reapplication kit: in writing or via the My Service Canada Account (MSCA); by phone; or in person. Eligibility criteria To qualify for a CPPD benefit under the fast track reapplication, the past beneficiary must meet the following eligibility criteria: be under the age of 65; for DSB , not be receiving a CPP retirement pension at the date of the recurrence of the same or related medical condition; have received a CPPD benefit in the past; have had their CPPD benefit ceased (i.e. benefit is not currently suspended) and they must not be appealing the cease decision; have stopped work or work-like activity due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were previously granted a CPPD benefit; reapply within 1 year of the recurrence of the same or a related disability within 5 years of the date their DSB or PRDB was ceased; meet the earnings and contributions requirements. Earnings and contributions considerations Refer to the Eligibility Requirements— PRDB (Policy) . Commencement of payments Past beneficiaries who are deemed eligible under the fast track reapplication process and are found to be disabled are to receive payment within 2 months of the date of reapplication. The date of Onset will be the later of: The month after the month in which the past beneficiary stopped work or is found to be disabled, if maximum retroactivity has not been provided; or 12 months before the date of application (maximum retroactivity). If the fast-track reapplication is refused, a subsequent application may be date protected to the receipt of the fast-track reapplication.

Each year, an individual's ongoing entitlement to the GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits must be reviewed based on their latest income. Individuals will be notified by letter about their ongoing entitlement in a staggered approach, based on letter type and printer capabilities. This year, letters will be mailed in July and August. In most cases, individuals remain entitled to their income-tested benefit. However, their payments could increase or decrease depending on their income compared to the previous year. For example, an individual could see a decrease in benefits if their 2023 income is higher than their 2022 income. In other cases, an individual's benefit will not continue for one of the following three reasons: Their income or combined income exceeded the maximum amount (excess income); They indicated that they do not wish to receive the benefit; or Service Canada did not receive all of the necessary income information. Suspension letters requesting income information will include a Statement of income for the Renewal of the GIS, the ALW or ALWS for payment period of July (2024) to June (2025) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026 form) to give clients the means to provide their income information and renew their benefits. The letters informing clients of their entitlement to benefits for the 2024 to 2025 payment period will be mailed in 3 phases: The first phase will be the suspension letters. These letters will be sent starting the week of July 15, 2024; The second phase will be the entitlement letters. These letters will be mailed to individuals once the mailing of the suspension letters is complete. The anticipated start date is July 23, 2024; and The third phase will be the non-entitlement letters . The anticipated start date is August 13, 2024. These letters will be sent to individuals who are GIS for Life but who were not receiving a benefit in the 2023 to 2024 payment period and are not entitled to a benefit in the 2024 to 2025 payment period. The following entitlement letters will be mailed to the beneficiary: GIS/ ALW / ALWS Entitlement Letter (ISP-3057) GIS Suspension Letter (ISP-3067) GIS Suspension Letter - IO (ISP-3067-IO) ALW / ALWS Suspension Letter (ISP-3068) ALW / ALWS Suspension Letter - IO (ISP-3068-IO) GIS/ ALW / ALWS Non-Entitlement Letter (ISP-3056)

The OAS Recovery Tax applies to higher-income OAS pensioners who file an income tax return and whose individual net income (for a given base taxation year) is above the threshold set by the Department of Finance. Criteria for applying the OAS Recovery Tax OAS pensioners who file an income tax return and whose individual net income including the OAS pension exceeds the established indexed threshold, have a calculated portion of their monthly OAS pension payment deducted as Recovery Tax at source. Those pensioners with a net individual income higher than the ceiling threshold have their OAS pension payment 100% recovered at source. The total Recovery Tax amount may not exceed the total monthly OAS pension entitlement. Recovery tax calculation Each July, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) calculates the total amount of the OAS Recovery Tax payable for the entire payment period from July of the current year to June of the year following. The amount of Recovery Tax calculated is based on the pensioner's assessed income for the calendar year (often referred to as the "base calendar year") preceding the start of the deduction period. The Recovery Tax amount is equal to 15% of the amount by which the pensioner's net income (reported on line 234 of the income tax return), including the OAS pension, exceeds the established threshold amount. The 15% amount is then divided by 12 to determine the amount of OAS Recovery Tax to deduct monthly. To determine the "base calendar year" in relation to the months January to December, proceed as follows: for OAS pensions paid from January to June, the "base calendar year" is the calendar year before the preceding year. For example, for pensions paid from January to June 2019, the Recovery Tax calculation is based on the pensioner's income reported for 2017. for OAS pensions paid from July to December, the "base calendar year" is the immediately preceding calendar year. For example, for pensions paid from July to December 2019, the OAS Recovery Tax calculation is based on the beneficiaries income reported for 2018. The notice of assessment issued by the CRA notifies OAS pensioners of the OAS Recovery Tax amount to be deducted at source from their monthly pension payments. Affected pensioners receive a letter indicating the: effective date; amount; and, where applicable; and voluntary tax amount deducted at source.
Income Tax Act

For non-residents of Canada, the OAS Recovery Tax is an additional monthly tax on higher-income OAS pensioners whose individual net world income for a given base taxation year exceeds the threshold amount set by the Department of Finance. The OAS Recovery Tax generally applies to residents of any non-exempt country that have a 25% non-resident tax withhold rate. OAS beneficiaries who reside in a non-exempt country are subject to the OAS Recovery Tax as well as the non-resident tax withhold. Criteria for applying the OAS Recovery Tax Non-resident OAS pensioners may be subject to the OAS Recovery Tax if they meet both residence and income criteria. Residence OAS pensioners are considered non-resident OAS pensioners for the purposes of the OAS Recovery Tax when: they do not reside in Canada; their residential address is identified by the Department as being in a country with a non-resident tax withhold rate of 25%; and they file with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) as a non-resident. Residents of countries which have concluded tax treaties with Canada that reduce the rate of the non-resident tax withhold below 25% are exempt from the OAS Recovery Tax. In some cases, pensioners identified as non-residents are considered by the CRA as factual or deemed Canadian residents and file taxes as such. These pensioners may still be subject to the OAS Recovery Tax if their income is above the established threshold amount. Income Non-resident OAS pensioners: must file an annual OAS Return of Income form. The CRA, however, will not insist that pensioners residing in a tax-recovery-exempt country file an OAS Return of Income form; who reside in a non-exempt country must submit an annual OAS Return of Income form to the CRA declaring their net world income. Pensioners whose income exceeds the established threshold amount are subject to the OAS Recovery Tax. If the CRA grants a beneficiary a reduction or waiver in the non-resident tax withhold rate (NR5) for a given calendar year, the system automatically stops the Recovery Tax deduction for that specific calendar year also. Recovery tax calculation The CRA calculates the OAS Recovery Tax amount using the individual's declared net world income, including the OAS pension. The OAS Recovery Tax amount is calculated yearly for the payment period beginning in July and ending in June of the following year, by referring to a preceding year defined by the CRA as the "base taxation year". The "base taxation year" is the calendar year that precedes the start of the OAS Recovery Tax withholding period. In relation to a calendar year (i.e. January to December), for OAS pensions paid during the first 6 months of a year, the "base taxation year" is the year before the preceding year; for benefits paid during the last 6 months of a year, the "base taxation year" is the immediately preceding year. The OAS Recovery Tax amount equals 15% of the amount by which the beneficiary's net world income reported on the OAS Return of Income form exceeds the established threshold amount for the "base taxation year". The 15% amount is then divided by 12 to determine the amount of OAS Recovery Tax to deduct monthly. However, because the pension is also subject to a 25% non-resident tax withhold, the rate of the OAS Recovery Tax is reduced from 15% to 11.25% of the amount by which the beneficiary's reported net world income exceeds the established threshold amount. The actual OAS Recovery Tax amount as calculated by the OAS system is 75% of the posted amount posted by the CRA. For pensioners whose net world income, including the OAS pension exceeds the ceiling threshold amount, their OAS pension is 100% recovered. However, the combined total of the non-resident tax withhold and the OAS Recovery Tax amounts cannot exceed the total OAS pension amount. The CRA advises beneficiaries who file an OAS Return of Income form about their calculated OAS Recovery Tax amount by means of a notice of assessment. The CRA issues an advisory letter to all affected beneficiaries, including those whose OAS pension is recovered at 100%. The letter indicates the following: the effective month of the OAS Recovery Tax withhold; the non-resident tax withhold amount; and the OAS Recovery Tax amount: OAS Recovery tax—100% withhold.

Since 1989, higher-income seniors must repay some, or all, of their OAS pension. Originally, the repayment was made in a lump sum at tax-time and the amount repaid was calculated based on the pensioner's income from the previous year. For this reason, the repayment became known as a "claw back". Since July 1996, the OAS pension repayment is made through monthly deductions at source. The monthly deductions are referred to as the OAS Recovery Tax. OAS Recovery Tax effective date and the time period covered The effective date for the OAS Recovery Tax is the later of: the accounting month when the amount is posted to the account; or the date the OAS pension payments begin. The monthly recovery amount is based on the "base taxation year" and covers the period from July of a given year to June of the following year. This is defined as the payment period. Revision to and reduction (waiver) of the calculated OAS Recovery Tax amount The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) may revise a pensioner's monthly OAS Recovery Tax amount as a result of a reassessment, and issue a notice of assessment to the pensioner. The CRA may also reduce an OAS Recovery Tax deduction amount upon receiving a request claiming "undue hardship" from a pensioner, referred to as a "waiver". If the pensioner's request to reduce the recovery tax deduction is approved based on "undue hardship", they notify the pensioner by letter. In both circumstances, the data transfer from the CRA to the Department is automated and the pensioner receives a system-generated letter detailing the revised amount to be deducted. Refunding excess OAS Recovery Tax withheld The CRA retains sole responsibility for the authorization of refunds of the OAS Recovery Tax. The Department's role in the reimbursement of excess taxes withheld is limited to an internal corrective measure. There may be cases where the amount of the OAS Recovery Tax withheld is revised as a result of a reassessment or is reduced due to a "waiver". A pensioner may request a refund of the amount that was deducted in excess of the reduced (waived) amount transmitted by the CRA. Departmental processing staff calculate the total amount of excess Recovery Tax to be refunded using the appropriate OAS screens, transactions, commands and system procedures. The OAS underpayment—calculated due to a refund of excess tax deducted—is included with the next regular monthly payment. A priority payment may be issued if it is considered necessary. The year-to-date totals must be adjusted to reflect: the total OAS pension amount paid; and where applicable, the total OAS Recovery Tax deducted. Increasing the OAS Recovery Tax deduction When there is an increase to the OAS Recovery Tax amount to be withheld, the revised amount is transmitted by the CRA to the Department. This is done electronically for residents and manually on the Request to Change OAS Recovery Tax/Repayment (T1151) form for non-residents. Reconsiderations and appeals Beneficiaries cannot request a reconsideration or appeal the amount calculated or the recovery of the OAS Recovery Tax since the Department is recovering the tax on behalf of the CRA.

A security incident aimed at gaining access to the GCKey client accounts and Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) My Account online services by using compromised user IDs and passwords has occurred. Although the GCKey service itself was not compromised, the Government of Canada authorized the immediate cancellation of all affected accounts. The GCKey is a service provider used by the Government of Canada to support clients in gaining secure access to their accounts. It is composed of a user ID and password which allows users to access Government of Canada online services and to conduct secure online transactions.

An updated OAS database allows each region to correctly identify clients residing in their respective province. Clients must appear on the correct provincial file exchanges, therefore the region codes in the OAS Online system must match the client’s home address. Each Regional Processing Centre is responsible for the accounts of payees living in their respective province. When a client moves from one province to another, the Regional Processing Centre in their former province of residence must transfer out the client’s file to the new region of residency. If additional guidance is required, send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool by following normal channels. Business Expertise Request Tool

Preventing additional mismatches When a client moves out of province, processing staff must ensure that the change of address and the transfer out transactions are performed to ensure the client’s account appears on the correct provincial exchange. Where the change of address is performed through My Service Canada Account (MSCA) or by a call centre agent, processing staff must ensure that the change of address is reviewed and that the transfer out transaction is performed. Correcting existing mismatches National Headquarters (NHQ) will review all mismatches where the client is in pay for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) benefit and will perform the transfer out transaction directly in the OAS Online system where necessary. All OAS only or inactive GIS accounts will be loaded into PWS as non-client generated work items under the following barcodes: NHQREGCODEMISMATCH-OAS-ACT NHQREGCODEMISMATCH-OAS-INACT NHQREGCODEMISMATCH-GIS-INACT When processing staff are working on an account where one of these work types exist, staff must verify and validate the client’s home address and region code. If the discrepancy is valid, no further action is required and the work item can be closed. If the region code is incorrect, processing staff must follow the Transfer Out procedures where applicable. Refer to the National Training Package: OAS Account Maintenance - Participants Guide, Section 13.10 Transfers for how to perform a transfer out transaction. There are 89,000 accounts in the OAS Online system where the province code and the region code do not match. Although this discrepancy has no direct impact on clients’ OAS benefits, it does have a direct impact on the clients appearing on the proper provincial file exchange. Therefore, the clients may be at risk of not receiving the provincial benefits to which they are eligible and entitled to. Ongoing monthly scans will be conducted and validated to ensure additional mismatches do not continue to exist.
