The following timeline is specific to CPPD Legislative History. Year Direction 1964 British North America Act (now the Constitution Act) amended, authorizing the federal government to make laws relating to supplementary benefits (including Survivor’s (SVR) and Disability (DSB) benefits) irrespective of age. 1965 In 1965, the CPP took over administration of the CPPD. Provincial governments were no longer required to share the costs. 1966 CPP was enacted effective January 1, 1966, in all provinces and territories except for Quebec, which enacted a separate QPP. 1970 First DSB benefit pensions payable in February 1970. 1974 CPP amended, effective January 1, 1974: Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) increased from $5,600.00 in 1973 to $6,600.00 in 1974 and $7,400.00 in 1975; CPP benefits to be increased each year effective January 1974, to fully reflect annual increases in the Consumer Price Index (i.e. 2% cap eliminated). 1975 CPP amended, effective January 1, 1975: Limit to 12 months for the period in which dissatisfied applicants or beneficiaries may appeal to the Minister; Provided that appeals may be made on behalf of incapacitated persons; Provided for payment of reasonable legal fees incurred by a respondent in an appeal to the Pension Appeals Board (PAB). 1978 CPP amended, effective January 1, 1978: Eliminated the previously applicable reduction in CPP children’s benefit when an eligible deceased or disabled contributor had more than 4 children; Introduced the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) to accommodate parents who leave or reduce their participation in the workforce to raise children . 1987 Major and wide ranging CPP amendments, effective January 1, 1987, including: Flat-rate portion of a CPP DSB benefit increased from $91.06 to $242.95 per month; Minimum contributory requirements eased (5 of the last 10 years or 2 of the last 3 years) 1 ; 2 children’s benefits payable when both parents are deceased or disabled; Retroactivity extended from 12 to 15 months 2 . Revisions to the CPP appeals system: Review the tribunal established as second CPP level of appeals, replacing ad hoc Review Committees; Decisions by the PAB, the third and previously final level of appeals, may be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal. 1 1969 to 1986 minimum contributory requirements: 5 years if only 5 years in a contributory period, or 1/3 of a contributory period; 5 of the last 10 years if more than 10 years in the contributory period. 2 Allowed disabled beneficiaries to receive retroactive payments for up to 12 months (because of the 3-month wait period before benefits become payable) instead of the prior maximum of 9 months. 1989 Dissolution of the Disability Determination Board. 1992 CPP amended, effective January 27, 1992: $35.00 increase in children’s benefits; Revised 25 year schedule of CPP contributions; Provisions to ensure that benefit eligibility is protected for individuals who are incapacitated; Provisions to pay children’s benefits to a child adopted in fact or coming under the custody and control of a contributor after a benefit is in pay; Automatic conversion from an over age 18 Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit (DCCB) to a Surviving Child’s benefit; Assignment of CPP DSB benefits to insurance companies (reimbursement through one time lump sum payment); Reduction from one year to 90 days to request a reconsideration of initial decision. CPP amended, effective June 1992: Introduction of the Late Applicant Provision, which provides a measure of protection for contributors by allowing an assessment of disability at the time the applicant last met the contributory requirements. 1995 CPP amended, effective July 13, 1995: Reconsideration becomes an administrative process outside of the appeal system; OAS amended to have appeals made to the Review Tribunal (along with CPP appeals). In 1995, a number of work incentive policies were introduced, including: allowing beneficiaries to volunteer or attend school without automatically having their disability status reviewed; a work trial where beneficiaries are able to work and still collect CPP DSB benefits; a fast track reapplication process for those who return to work, but cannot continue because of a recurrence of the same or related disability; allowing beneficiaries to work and earn up to the allowable earnings estimated amount in a calendar year without informing the CPP Department and without losing their benefits; Vocational Rehabilitation . 1998 CPP amendments to the way benefits were administered and calculated in order to moderate the escalating costs, effective January 1, 1998, including: Creation of the CPP Investment Board; Move from “pay-as-you-go” funding to fuller funding; Contribution rates amended to reach 9.9%; Year’s Basic Exemption is frozen at $3,500.00; Introduction of the Disability Basic Exemption; Changes to combined benefit rules (Disability-Survivor); Minimum contributory requirements tighten (4 of the last 6 years and contributions of at least 10% of each YMPE during that period); Introduction of penalty provisions. 2000 CPP amended, effective July 31, 2000 to extend benefits and obligations to common-law same-sex partners on the same basis as opposite-sex partners. 2005 CPP amended, effective January 1, 2005: Allowed for reinstatement of a DSB pension that had ceased to be payable because a person had returned to work, and, if the person becomes incapable of working within a 2 years period after the date when payment of the pension ceased (automatic reinstatement); Allowed the consequential reinstatement of the DCCB. 2008 CPP amended, effective March 3, 2008: Eased contributory requirements for long term contributors (3 of the last 6 years with at least 25 years of contributions); Fully integrated the full funding provision into actuarial reporting and contribution rate setting. 2010 CPP amended, effective April 1, 2010: Updated penalty provisions; Provisions providing the authority to set terms and conditions for charging interest in case of misrepresentation. CPP amended, effective September 2010: 2 technical amendments concerning late applicants in relation to the proration provision and the end of the contributory period; The work cessation test, the provision on which the policy for the “substantially gainful occupation” amount was based, was removed with the creation of the Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB) (the regulation was actually repealed in 2013); General “drop-out” increased from 15% to 16% in 2012 and 17% in 2014 and has had implications for individual pension amounts. 2011 CPP amended, effective retroactively to 2006: Restored longstanding policy and legislative intent to require CPP contributions on employer-funded long-term DSB benefits paid to an employee retroactively to January 1, 2006. 2012 The Social Security Tribunal (SST) was established under the Department of Human Resources and Skills Development Act on June 29, 2012. CPP amended, effective December 12, 2012: Provided regulation-making authority to prescribe the meaning of the term “substantially gainful” for disability purposes, in relation to any occupation; Allows CPP disability late applicants to use the CRP when determining the minimum qualifying period in the same manner as those applicants who apply for the DSB pension on time. 2013 April 1, 2013, the SST replaces the Review Tribunal and the PAB for Income Security appeals and the Board of Referees and Employment Insurance Umpires for Employment Insurance appeals: SST Regulations come into force; CPP Regulations amended, effective April 1, 2013: Prescribes the circumstances (based on the Gattellaro criteria) in which the Minister may allow a longer period to make a request for reconsideration. 2014 In May 2014, the administrative policy that was established substantially gainful was replaced with Regulation 68.1 (1). CPP Regulations amended, effective May 29, 2014: Introduces “substantially gainful in respect of an occupation”. 2016 CPP amended: Adoption of the CPP enhancement which expands the CPP to include 2 additional components: First, the CPP earnings replacement will increase from 25% to 33%; Second, there will be an increase in the maximum level of pensionable earnings by 14%, as of 2025. Maximum amount of Retirement (RTR) pension, SVR pension, DSB pension and PRBs to increase following adoption of CPP enhancement; Individual benefit amount remains subject to the amount of additional contributions made and the number of years over which those contributions are made. 2018 CPP amended, February 27, 2018: Eliminate age-based restrictions on the SVR pension; The Death benefit is amended to consist of a lump sum flat rate of $2,500.00 rather than a variable earnings related amount; Introduction of a Post-Retirement Disability Benefit which will provide benefits to disabled individuals under the age of 65 who are in receipt of a RTR pension; Provide drop-ins for the enhancement portion of the benefits in order to protect the benefit amounts for parents with lower earnings during child-rearing years and individuals who are disabled; Maintain portability between the CPP and the QPP.

You must triage DSB benefits applications involving a COVID-19 diagnosis based on relevant clinical features and tag as Terminally Ill, Gravely Ill or Regular. Evidence suggests physical or mental health deterioration post-recovery is possible. The potential trauma that may have been sustained as a result of the COVID-19 illness (e.g. a protracted intensive care unit admission, intubation, and other aggressive interventions) must be considered. These factors must be given added weight where an underlying mental health condition is present.

Infected individuals will typically begin showing symptoms 5 to 6 days after infection. Approximately 20% of infected individuals will experience dyspnea at this time and will seek medical attention. In Canada, approximately 14% of cases are hospitalized. This typically occurs around the 7th day following the onset of symptoms. Approximately 20% of hospitalizations (3% of all cases) will require intensive care. Intensive care unit admission often occurs around the 11th day, triggered by the onset of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome secondary to a cytokine storm, an exaggerated immune response triggered by the infection. Overall, individuals over the age of 60 account for over 96% of COVID-19 deaths in hospital in Canada.

Over 65% of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 in Canada are of working age, with the highest proportion being in the 40-59 age bracket. The risk of negative outcomes increases with age. Overall, a higher proportion of cases are women. While hospitalizations are higher among men, deaths are higher amongst women.

COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus and primarily affects the respiratory system. The illness may be contracted by up to 80% of the population, but with the containment measures being undertaken, it is projected to be restricted to 25-50% of the population. The majority (up to 80-85%) of infected individuals will be asymptomatic or will experience mild to moderate symptoms such as fever, dry cough and fatigue with no residual sequelae. The remaining 15% will have a more serious clinical presentation. Evolving reports suggest that some individuals may develop severe and permanent impairments involving pulmonary, cardiac, renal, neurological and other body systems. As of August 20, 2020, the case fatality rate in Canada was 7.3%.

The medical community’s understanding of complications related to COVID-19 continues to evolve and its impacts are not necessarily limited to the respiratory system. The most critically ill may suffer long-term complications secondary to the illness and/or treatments. The extent of COVID-19 specific sequelae remains unclear, as little research has been published given the recency of the outbreak. However, the impact of related treatments is better understood. As many as 50% of individuals treated in an intensive care unit will experience residual effects known as post-intensive care syndrome, particularly where ventilator support was required. This is especially true for individuals with underlying physical and mental health conditions. They will often experience a significant decline in long-term functional capacity. Ventilator support risks complications such as barotrauma, perforation and muscular atrophy, which may result in a subsequent disabling condition (e.g. pulmonary fibrosis). Complications of this nature represent potential prolonged sequelae that may emerge from both the illness and related treatments that could lead to disability during or after infection.

Intensive care unit admission criteria vary widely across jurisdictions and individual hospitals. Intensive care unit admittance on its own should not be relied upon as an indication of severity or a predictor of outcomes. However, the need for invasive ventilator support is a strong predictor of death. Descriptive reports indicate as many as 88% of individuals with underlying health conditions who received invasive ventilation did not recover.

CPP disability applications involving a COVID-19 diagnosis must be triaged based on relevant clinical features and queued as Terminally Ill, Gravely Ill or regular. For applications with a COVID-19 diagnosis submitted using a regular application, rather than a terminal illness medical attestation, a closer examination must occur if the following key indicators are present as they are suggestive of a possible terminal application: Invasive Ventilation Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation; Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome; Septic Shock; and/or Multiple Organ Failure. Additionally, the following may help in conceptualizing the severity of the disease process when triaging applications: Severity Description Mild Absence of pre-existing conditions and less advanced age are predictive of a successful recovery. The majority (~80%) of individuals who contract COVID-19 will recover in the community with mild symptoms, if any. Moderate These individuals will generally recover at home. Often, older individuals who have pre-existing conditions may experience complications requiring medical intervention or hospitalization. Most will recover; however, some may experience complications that will present new sequelae and/or exacerbate existing conditions. Severe Advanced age and presence of pre-existing conditions requiring hospitalization and aggressive medical intervention is expected among this group and is associated with a higher case-fatality rate. The chance of recovery is low where the patient is in septic shock, experiencing Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome or multiple organ failure. This segment has so far been relatively small in Canada and the majority of these cases are not of working age.

Several pre-existing conditions have been found to be associated with the requirement for aggressive medical intervention and are predictors of unfavorable outcomes. Old Age Security Act Section 15—Spouses and Common-law Partners

A beneficiary may be: married; single; in a common-law partnership; divorced; separated; a surviving spouse or surviving common-law partner; or living apart for reasons beyond their control. Marriage, common-law partnership, separation, divorce, reconciliation and death are all events that will change a beneficiary's marital status. Marriage Since July 1, 1999, when beneficiaries marry, the change of marital status to "married" is effective the month following the month of the marriage. When a beneficiary in receipt of an ALWS benefit marries, the ALWS benefit payment ceases the month following the month of marriage. Common-law partnership Beneficiaries who begin living in a common-law partnership during a payment period are considered to be "single" until they meet the requirement of living together in a conjugal relationship for a continuous period of at least one year. Public representation as husband and wife was a requirement for common-law partners when applying for benefits under the Old Age Security Act before July 2000 . Since July 1, 1999, when beneficiaries meet the requirement of living in a common-law partnership (and publicly represented themselves as husband and wife if before July 2000), the marital status changes to "married" effective the following month. When a beneficiary in receipt of an ALWS benefit enters into a new common-law partnership, the ALWS benefit payment ceases as of the effective month of the marital status change. Once the couple meets the definition of common-law, should either person in that common-law partnership marry someone else, the Department must determine when the common-law partnership ended. The recalculation of the entitlement is based on that information. Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control Where a couple lives apart for reasons beyond their control, they continue to qualify for their respective benefit. They are paid at the single rate when it is to their advantage. The change of marital status to "single" is effective the month following the month in which the couples began living apart for reasons beyond their control. Separation of married or common-law partners Since July 1, 1999, separated spouses or common-law partners are considered to be "married" for the first 3 consecutive months of separation following the month in which the separation occurred. Then, the marital status changes to "single". For the ALW benefit, where a couple is separated for a period of more than 3 months, there is no longer eligibility to the ALW benefit and the lifetime renewal designation ends. ALW benefit payments continue for the first 3 consecutive months of separation following the month in which the separation occurred. Then, the ALW benefit payments cease. Divorce or annulment of legal marriage Since July 1, 1999, when a couple divorces, the marital status is changed to "single" the month following the divorce or annulment. For ALW benefits, there is no longer eligibility to the ALW benefit and the lifetime renewal designation ends. ALW benefit payments cease the month following the month of the divorce or annulment. Married couples resume cohabitation after separation Since July 1, 1999, when a married couple reconciles and the breakdown was for a period of less than 3 months, the marital status does not change, meaning that the couple will continue to be considered as "married". Since July 1, 1999, when a reconciliation occurs after a period of more than 3 months, the couple is considered to be "married" effective the month following the month of reconciliation. For the ALW benefit, the lifetime renewal designation is lost after a separation of more than 3 months; therefore, if reconciliation occurs after a separation of more than 3 months, a new ALW benefit application is needed. Common-law partners resume cohabitation after separation Since July 1, 1999, when a common law couple reconciles and the breakdown was for a period of less than 3 months , the marital status does not change, meaning that the couple will continue to be considered as "married". A separation of more than 3 months is seen as evidence that the relationship has ended. If more than 3 months have passed following the month in which the separation occurred and the couple resumes cohabitation, they are required to live together for one year before they may be considered as common-law partners under the Old Age Security Act. For the ALW benefit, the lifetime renewal designation is lost after a separation of more than 3 months; therefore, if reconciliation occurs after a separation of more than 3 months, a new ALW benefit application is needed. Death Since July 1, 1999, when a spouse or common-law partner dies, the survivor is considered to be "single", effective the month following the month of death. ALWS benefit—Survivor remarries or becomes the common-law partner of another individual When an ALWS beneficiary remarries or meets the definition of common-law with another person, their marital status changes from "survivor" to "married" or "common-law" ("single" to "married" rate). There is no longer eligibility to the ALWS benefit and their lifetime renewal designation ends. If this second relationship ends, the former ALWS beneficiary cannot reclaim their previous marital status of a survivor of their first spouse or common-law partner.

Entitlement to income-tested benefits under the Old Age Security Act such as the GIS, the ALW and the ALWS is based on: the beneficiary's current marital status; and net income received in the base calendar year.

topic_title: The spouse or common-law partner does not apply for a benefit or complete a statement of income Updated
text: If a pensioner indicates that they are married or living in a common-law partnership, the Department must inform the pensioner that the application cannot be processed until the spouse or common-law partner either applies for a benefit or provides their income information and signature. A statement of income may be completed and signed on the pensioner's initial application for the GIS, a prescribed statement of income form or as a separate written statement. If the spouse or common-law partner refuses or is unable to complete and sign a statement of income or the CRA cannot provide income information, the Department can consider calculating the pensioner's GIS entitlement at the single rate depending on the circumstances. Calculating the pensioner's GIS benefit entitlement at the single rate should only be considered in rare circumstances when the Department cannot obtain the spouse or common-law partner's income. This could include a situation where an individual's spouse lives in a different country.

topic_title: The spouse or common-law partner is deceased and income is required for retroactive GIS entitlement
text: The applicant's retroactive entitlement can be calculated at the single rate if: the applicant's spouse or common-law partner is deceased; there is no legal representative for the estate; and the applicant or next of kin cannot obtain the required income information (e.g. income tax returns and notice of assessments).

topic_title: The spouse or common-law partner is eligible for a benefit but has not applied
text: If a GIS pensioner's spouse or common-law partner, who is age 60 to 64 and who would otherwise be eligible for an ALW benefit, chooses not to apply, the pensioner's GIS is calculated according to the rate table associated with the marital status, "pensioner married to a non-pensioner". If a GIS pensioner's spouse or common-law partner, who is age 65 or over, and who would otherwise be eligible for an OAS pension and the GIS, does not apply, the pensioner's GIS is calculated according to the rate table associated with the marital status, "pensioner married to a non-pensioner". If a GIS pensioner's spouse or common-law partner, who is aged 65 or over, is in receipt of the OAS pension but does not apply or chooses not to apply for the GIS, the pensioner's GIS is calculated according to the rate table associated with the marital status, "married to a pensioner".

topic_title: When the spouse or common-law partner of a GIS pensioner becomes eligible for a benefit during a payment period
text: The spouse or common-law partner's in come information, in most cases, will not be required since the couple's income has already been provided or reported. The earlier available income may be used to determine the entitlement. This same statement of income or income feed from the CRA also serves to authorize payment of an income-tested benefit from the date of eligibility to the end of that payment period.

Service Canada currently receives all CPP, CPPD and OAS requests for reconsideration for pensions, benefits and/or provisions in paper form or written communication only. Effective October 24, 2020, clients are able to submit a request for reconsideration of an initial decision made on their CPP, CPPD and OAS applications for pensions, benefits and/or provisions online through their My Service Canada Account. The Online Request for Reconsideration reflects the current paper forms available to each program and follows the same layout. The main difference is that the Online Request for Reconsideration contains a dynamic component, which directs clients to the next appropriate section of the application based on the information they have provided. As part of this release, clients requesting a reconsideration of a decision made on their CPPD benefits also have the ability to upload supporting documentation using the Document Upload Solution. The Online Request for Reconsideration is available for clients within My Service Canada Account (MSCA) in order to request for reconsideration of a decision received for their OAS, CPP and CPPD benefits, pensions or provisions online. Existing clients can log into their MSCA account, while new clients will be required to register for an account in order to proceed to the online form. The eligibility criteria for requesting a reconsideration online are as follows: The client must be over the age of 18; The client must not have a payee on file; The client’s account must not be under control of a Trustee or Power of Attorney (i.e. third party); The client must have a Canadian address (clients that currently live outside of Canada will not be able to request a reconsideration online); and A dual contributor residing in Quebec will not be able to request for reconsideration for CPP or CPPD benefits. A dual contributor living in Quebec will be able to request a reconsideration for OAS, the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Allowance and Allowance for the Survivor. Clients will be required to complete one request for reconsideration for each benefit, pension and/or provisions they are asking Service Canada to reconsider (e.g. if clients wish to request for reconsideration on both their OAS and GIS applications, they will need to submit 2 separate online requests). Leveraging existing MSCA functionalities, clients will also have the opportunity to update their address and telephone number with the current View and Update Personal Information functionality. When clients submit their request, MSCA will populate their information within a PDF version of the form and will submit it to the Digital Repository for storage. The clients will then be directed to the applicable confirmation page based on the program to which the request is related. Request for Reconsideration of OAS and CPP Clients requesting a reconsideration of their OAS and CPP benefits, pensions or provisions will be directed to a confirmation page containing the statement of acknowledgement of receipt, the time and date stamps and the service standards. Request for Reconsideration of CPPD Clients requesting a reconsideration of their CPPD benefits will be directed to a similar confirmation page with added instructions. It will also contain the link to the Document Upload Solution (DUS) functionality, which will enable these clients to upload the required supporting documentation for their request. For information specific to the DUS functionality, refer to the Document Upload Solution Implementation Bulletin. Document Upload Solution

Service Canada receives an estimated 50,000 Declarations at School or University (ISP1401) forms from eligible child beneficiaries annually. Currently, students wishing to renew or re-establish their benefits must complete the paper form, visit their learning institution Registrar’s Office to obtain a hand signature for Section C on the ISP1401 form, and then mail it into a Service Canada for processing. This new e-Service will lessen the burden for both students and the institution’s administrative staff, as well as help streamline service delivery operations.

Along with the current ISP1401, students will now be able to submit official documentation retrieved from their online student portal as an alternative to seeking signature of Section C of the ISP1401 from Registrar’s Office for valid proof of enrolment to support their declaration, whether they are renewing their benefits online or on paper. In order to be accepted, the proof of enrolment must contain clear and concise information about the student’s current academic status and will confirm their full-time enrolment status in a recognized educational institution. It must include the following information: Student name; School oﬃcial's original or electronic signature; Degree; Program; Semester(s), term(s) or school year; Student ID number; Start and end dates for each semester(s), term(s) or school year; Name and address of school or university (may also include a logo or watermark); and, Enrolment status for each semester(s), term(s) or school year (full-time, half time, less than half time). A revised ISP1401 E-Form will be made available in late 2020 (date TBD) on the Service Canada website to inform students who download the form about the new proof of enrolment option and the new online service. The e-Form includes radio buttons, which serve as a list of available options to validate their attendance; however, these are not mandatory in order to process the revised ISP1401. The ISP1401A, will be updated with the first mail-out in early 2021 (date TBD) to inform students of the new proof of enrolment option and the new online service. MSCA clients must accept the MSCA Terms and Conditions of Use and confirm that they understand and agree to the Privacy Notice as well as the Terms of Use specific to Document Upload . In these situations, agents will be required to: contact the client by phone or by mail to inform them that we cannot accept the upload; include a note in the PWS work item and ITRDS; and complete the work item in PWS. topic_title: Examples of determining the effective date
text: Determining the effective date for couples when the notification is received January 1, 2017 or later. The Department receives notification in February 2017 that spouse A and spouse B, both 85 years old, have been living apart for reasons beyond their control since July 2007. This is when spouse A moved to a long-term care facility. As notification was received after January 1, 2017, the account was reviewed and it was found that the couple had eligibility to their GIS continuously throughout the period being reviewed. The couple may have their GIS benefits recalculated retroactively to August 2007, the month after spouse A moved to the long-term care facility. Determining the effective date for couples when the notification is received before January 1, 2017. The Department receives notification in November 2016 that spouse A and spouse B, both 90 years old, have been living apart for reasons beyond their control since July 2014. This is when spouse A moved to a long-term care facility. As the notification of separation for reasons beyond their control was received in November 2016, the rules in place before January 2017 must be followed. The effective date for calculating the GIS benefits based on their individual income can only be retroactive back to July 2015. This date would be the start of the previous payment period.

topic_title: Examples of situations where couples are living apart for a reason that is considered beyond their control.
text: For more information regarding applicable circumstances for couples living apart for reasons beyond their control, Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy) The following chart provides questions and examples for various situations. If you can answer yes to any of these questions, the couple may be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control. Are one or both individuals in a long-term care facility or nursing home? This includes when the couple is sharing a room. Example: Spouse A is placed in a nursing home because they are in the advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease. Spouse B remains in the family home. The couple may be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control the month after spouse A moves into the nursing home. Spouse B fractures their hip 6 months later. Due to complications they are unable to return to the family home to care for themselves. Spouse B is then placed in a semi-private room with their spouse at the nursing home. In this situation, the couple may continue to be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control. Is the couple living apart because one member needs ongoing medical care and assistance with daily living and has moved into an alternate dwelling? Example: Spouse A and spouse B live in a rural area. Spouse B is an ALW benefit recipient and requires hospital treatment for several hours three times a week. The treatment is expected to continue indefinitely. The closest available hospital that provides the treatment is a 4-hour drive from the couple's home. The couple's son lives less than a kilometre from the hospital and offers a home and ongoing assistance for the duration of spouse B's treatment. Spouse A remains in the family home. The couple may be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control the month after spouse B moves into their son's home. Is one member of the couple medically discharged but waiting in a hospital until they can be transferred to a long-term care facility or nursing home? Example: Spouse A and spouse B were involved in a car accident. Spouse A was badly injured and required months of treatment and recuperation. After a hospitalization of 2 months for medical treatment, spouse A was medically discharged. Although discharged, they waited in the hospital for 2 additional months until they were transferred to a nursing home that provides rehabilitation services. The couple may be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control the month following the month spouse A was admitted to the hospital. During their recovery, spouse A was allowed to return home for short periods of time to allow them to slowly re-integrate back to their regular mode of living. In between these short stays, spouse A had to stay in the nursing home. The couple would continue to be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control as the return home is not of a permanent nature and the visits home were of short duration. Is the client's spouse currently incarcerated? Refer to: Incarceration—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) ; and Incarceration—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) Incarceration—Limiting Payment of OAS Pension and Benefits (Scenario) . Incarceration—Limiting Payment of OAS Pension and Benefits (Scenario) Is the couple living apart for economic or employment reasons such as availability of work or proximity to medical assistance? Example: Spouse A and spouse B live in a rural area. Spouse B was employed with a company close to their home. The company decided to close the office where Spouse B was employed. The company offered Spouse B a position at their head office which is 6 hours from the couple's home. As there are no suitable employment opportunities close to home and Spouse A only has 3 years left before they can retire with a pension from this company, they had no choice but to accept the position and move to the larger city where the head office is located. Spouse B requires a wheelchair for mobility purposes and the couple had their home designed to be wheelchair accessible. Spouse A was unable to find an affordable home close to the new employment that is suitable for Spouse B. Renovating to prepare a new home to be wheelchair accessible is just not feasible. The couple made the difficult decision that Spouse A would rent a small one-bedroom apartment in the city and they would live separately until Spouse A's retirement. The couple may be considered living apart for reasons beyond their control the month after spouse A moves into their new apartment in the city.

To use the document upload feature, clients must first register to My Service Canada Account (MSCA). During the registration process, they will confirm their date of birth, SIN and other personal information. MSCA also provides clients the opportunity to update their personal information. Any change made in MSCA instantly updates the client's profile in ITRDS . MSCA connects to ITRDS , PWS and the digital repository, which are secured environments that store the uploaded supporting documents. If one of these systems is down, the client receives a "Systems unavailable" message. For more information, My Service Canada Account (Knowledge)

Do not print uploaded documents when processing the file to uphold the privacy statement and terms of use provided to the client. The document will remain accessible in the digital repository as per Retention and Disposition Procedures for CPP, CPPD and OAS Client Files However, there are 2 situations where staff may need to print the uploaded document: for an Access to Information and Privacy request; or for an SST appeal. The following PWS profiles have print functionality: PWS —Program Support Clerk, Program Services Officer, SCBO , Business Expertise Advisor PWS —Team Leader—Workload Manager PWS —National PWS —Pensions Program Performance Administration To print documents, click the File tab in the PDF viewer and click Print . This gives the user the ability to print or save the document. To ensure adherence to the Privacy statement, saving is strongly discouraged and should only be done if absolutely necessary.

Each document will have a separate PWS work item that links to the document in the digital repository. The work item for online documents will remain in Active status until it is reviewed or actioned by the person with the delegated authority. This ensures the work item shows in the Work Items list. These Active work items are categorized as an “Online Document” and will not be counted in regional processing inventories for workload management. Program Performance monitors this workload and changes the source to "online" for any application and reconsideration for work items included in the inventory. Once logged into the CCT, you can create a new client document based on a template selected from a content repository and provide additional information using the interactive editor. The interactive editor provides an accurate view of the final printed document and, based on the rules and controls specified within the template, you can modify certain aspects of the document as needed. This policy describes the interaction between the CPPD Late Applicant Provision (LAP) and the CPP credit splitting provision. When a CPPD benefits applicant does not meet the current contributory requirements to be eligible for disability benefits, the LAP is considered. Criteria To be considered for both the credit splitting provision and the LAP, the applicant must: apply for CPPD benefits; require the LAP to qualify; be eligible for a credit split; and either qualify for a DSB or a PRDB with the credit split; or have their latest possible date of onset (LPDOO) enhanced with the credit split. Application of the credit splitting provision and the LAP To determine if the credit split will improve the applicant’s CPPD benefit LPDOO, it is necessary to determine: the LPDOO using the credit split; and if the applicant was eligible for a credit split at the time of the calculated LPDOO. The effect of a credit split on the DSB or the PRDB effective date If the credit split is required to meet the minimum qualifying period rules, the effective date of the DSB or the PRDB will be the later of: the date of attribution of the credit split; or 4 months after the date of onset (DOO), or for subsequent DSB or PRDB applications, the month after the DOO. Woodcock and Ash Federal Court of Appeal decisions in 2002, Woodcock and Ash, resulted in the following rule governing the relationship between CPPD benefits, the LAP, and the credit splitting provision: The Woodcock appeal challenged how the LAP and the credit split provision were used to establish an LPDOO. The Ash appeal challenged how the LAP and the credit split provision were used to improve an LPDOO. As long as the CPPD benefits applicant was separated from their former spouse or common-law partner for at least one year, or divorced prior to the LPDOO, the credit split can be used to meet the earnings and contributions requirement for a DSB or a PRDB . To apply the Woodcock or Ash decision, the following circumstances must all be present: The applicant has applied for CPPD benefits and is eligible for credit splitting; The applicant meets the earnings and contributions requirements, or their LPDOO for a DSB or a PRDB is improved by using the credit split; and The applicant requires the LAP to qualify for a DSB or a PRDB . For more information, Non-Medical Processing and the Late Applicant Provision (Policy)

In January 2020, the Department implemented a solution to allow clients to apply for CPP DSB benefits online within their MSCA. This release marked an important milestone in digitizing the CPPD application process; however, up until this release of the Document Upload Solution clients still had to provide supporting documentation for DSB benefit applications either by mail or in person. Their application was not considered complete until Service Canada received the required documents. Until now, Service Canada received all CPP, CPPD and OAS requests for reconsideration for pensions, benefits and/or provisions via paper or written communication only . Moreover, until this release, students wishing to renew or reinstate their Children's benefits had to: complete a paper ISP1401 form; visit the registrar’s office at their institution of learning to obtain a wet signature for Section C on the ISP1401 form; and finally mail the completed and signed ISP1401 form to Service Canada for processing. The new online ISP1401 form for Children's benefits renewal reduces the burden for both students and the learning institution’s administrative staff. Together, the 3 additional e-service options now available through MSCA support Service Canada’s commitment to deliver easy to use, seamless, digitally enabled services that put the needs and expectations of Canadians first.

MSCA links to the PWS. When the client uses one of these e-services available through their MSCA, a new work item opens in PWS, which is similar to the process for online applications. There is no change to the paper process, so, you may receive both online and paper forms and/or documents for the same client file. A Current Year Option is effective the later of: the month the income-tested benefit became effective; the month following the month of retirement; the first month the pension is not paid; or the first month the pension income reduction occurs. Retirement Reduction or termination of pension income The following table lists the payment periods and the effective dates of option: Table 1 Frequency of payment Effective date of option Monthly Semi-monthly Bi-weekly Weekly The effective date of an option for these payment frequencies is the month that the pension is either not paid or is paid at a reduced rate. Example 1—Reduction of pension income A client receives a semi-monthly payment of $275.00 on the 10th and 25th of each month. In May, the client’s payments were reduced to $175.00 beginning with the payment they received on the 25th. Since the reduction occurred in May, the option is effective May . Example 2—Termination of pension income A client was receiving a monthly pension payment of $750.00. The pension ended and the client received a final payment in October. The client did not receive a payment in November. Since the client received the final payment in October, November is the first month when the pension is not paid. Therefore, the option is effective November and is calculated excluding the pension income. Quarterly The effective date of option for this payment frequency is the first month of the three-month period (i.e. January, April, July and October) that the payment is reduced or stopped, regardless of which month the payment is received within each quarter . Example 1—Reduction of pension income A client receives a quarterly pension payment of $500.00. The client receives these payments in March, June, September and December each year. In June, the client’s payment was reduced to $300.00 per payment. The option is effective the first month of the quarter that the payment was reduced. Since the client’s pension was reduced in the second quarter of the year, the option is effective April . Example 2—Termination of pension income A client receives a quarterly Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) payment of $955.00. The client receives these payments in February, May, August and November each year. In August, the client received a final payment of $426.00, depleting the fund. There are two events to consider for this client: the reduction of the RRIF payments in one quarter and the termination of the payments in the next. For the first event (the reduction), the option is effective the first month of the quarter that the reduction occurred. Since the client’s RRIF reduced in the third quarter of the year, the option for this event is effective July . For the second event (the termination), the option is effective the first month of the quarter that the loss occurred (i.e. the first quarter where no payment was received). Since the client did not receive a payment in the fourth quarter of the year, the option for this event is effective October and is calculated excluding the pension income. Semi-annual The effective date of an option for this payment frequency is the first month of the six-month period (i.e. January and July) that the payment is reduced or stopped, regardless of which months within each half of the year the payment is received. Example 1—Reduction of pension income A client receives a semi-annual pension payment of $2,400.00. The client receives these payments in March and September each year. In September, the client’s payment was reduced to $1,800.00 per payment. The option is effective the first month of the semi-annual period that the payment was reduced. Since the client’s pension was reduced in the second semi-annual period of the year, the option is effective July . Example 2—Termination of pension income A client receives a semi-annual pension payment of $4,150.00. The client receives these payments in June and December each year. In December 2021, the client received their final payment. The option is effective the first month of the semi-annual period that the loss occurred (i.e. the first period where no payment was received). Since the client did not receive a payment in the first semi-annual period of the following year, the option is effective January 2022 and is calculated excluding the pension income. Annual The effective date of an option for this payment frequency is the first month of the year (i.e. January) that the payment is reduced or stopped, regardless of which month during the year the payment is received . Example 1—Reduction of pension income A client receives annual pension payments of $4,800.00. The client receives these payments in May each year. In May 2021, the client’s annual payment was reduced to $2,400.00 per payment. The option is effective the first month of the year that the payment was reduced. Since the client’s pension reduced in 2021, the option is effective January 2021 . Example 2—Termination of pension income A client receives annual pension payments of $6,000.00. The client receives these payments in October each year. In October 2021, the client received their final payment of $5,244.00. There are two events to consider for this client: the reduction of the payments in one year and the termination of the payments in the next. For the first event (the reduction), the option is effective the first month of the year that the reduction occurred. Since the client’s pension reduced in 2021, the option for this event is effective January 2021 . For the second event (the termination), the option is effective the first month of the year that the loss occurred (i.e. the first year where no payment was received). Since the client did not receive a payment in 2022, the option for this event is effective January 2022 and is calculated excluding the pension income. Irregular payments The payment frequency for clients who do not have a regular payment schedule is considered annual. The total estimated amount that the client will receive in the current calendar year will be compared to the total amount received in the previous calendar year. If there is a decrease, the optionable event is considered to have occurred in the January of the year of the decrease. The effective date of the option will be January of the same year. Example 1—Reduction of pension income The client receives irregular RRIF payments each year. Over the last 4 years, the client's payments have been the following: 2018: $700.00 in February $600.00 in August $1,500.00 in September $1,000.00 in December Total of payments received in 2018: $3,800.00 2019: $900.00 in April $1,000.00 in July $1,100.00 in September $1,500.00 in December Total of payments received in 2019: $4,500.00 2020: $1,700.00 in July $2,500.00 in December Total of payments received in 2020: $4,200.00 2021: $1,500.00 in April $1,500.00 in July $1,200.00 in November Total of payments received in 2021: $4,200.00 The client did not follow a pattern of regular and predetermined payment rates. Therefore, the client's periodic payments are considered annual. Since the total of the client's payments decreased in 2020, the option effective date is January 2020 . Example 2—Termination of pension income The client receives irregular RRIF payments each year. Over the last 3 years, the client's payments have been the following: 2019: $1,500.00 in April, $900.00 in July, and $1,200.00 in September. Total of payments received in 2019: $3,600.00 2020: $1,100.00 in February, $1,000.00 in July, $400.00 in October (final payment, RRIF depleted). Total of payments received in 2020: $2,500.00 2021: client did not receive any payments in 2021 as the RRIF is depleted. The client did not follow a pattern of regular and predetermined rate of payments. Therefore, the periodic payments are considered annual. The total of the client's payments decreased in 2020, therefore the first option effective date is January 2020 for the reduction in the pension income. In 2021, the client did not receive any RRIF payments, therefore the second option effective date is January 2021 for the termination of pension income. One-time lump-sum payments If the lump sum is the only event in the calendar year, only a previous year option will be granted effective July of the payment period following the calendar year that the event occurred. If the lump sum payment is not the only event that occurred in the calendar year, the effective date of the option for the lump sum payment event will be the month following the month the payment was received. Whether the lump-sum payment income will be included in the estimated income for the other events depends on whether the lump-sum payment was received before or after the other events. topic_title: Review codes and user k eys
text: Final month-end reports will be produced at the end of the December accounting month. Regions should review these reports as usual in order to take any needed follow up actions on accounts in January within ITRDS and CPMS, etc. OAS and IA review codes are not being converted into the new system. Many review codes will be replaced with new functionality. Scans will be run post migration to provide regions with reports of review codes that may require follow up after migration. OAS System User key data will not be converted at migration. If you need to extract data on an urgent basis that is in the user key fields, you should consider collecting this in January. National Headquarters will run scans to identify user key information and provide these to the regions sometime after implementation in case follow up work is needed.

As part of the OAS Service Improvement Strategy, adjudication and payment of OAS and International Agreements (IA) client benefits will be migrated to the CPP platforms (ITRDS and CPMS) at the end of 2020. In order to ensure all accounts merge accurately at migration, several activities are underway to: establish a single version of all clients in ITRDS ; address outstanding balances; and identify discrepancies that would prevent a successful merge of client accounts. In preparation for the migration of accounts in OAS Online and the IA systems to the ITRDS platform, there will be several OAS Online and IA system transactional limitations for the December 2020 accounting month.
In order to ensure a smooth transition and minimize possible data issues, the following guidance is provided when processing benefits in the OAS or IA system in December 2020.

NHQ is aware of some accounts that fall into this situation and will reach out to the regions directly for those. We ask that the processing centres review their OAS and IO fraud or misrepresentation cases, where known, and update the accounts according to the below instructions. Where a fraud or misrepresentation case exists where the debtor applied for benefits under multiple SINs that are the debtors alternate SINs, take the following action : Situation Direction The debtor has an account in OAS or IO under the Prime SIN Move all overpayment information contained under the alternate SINs to the prime SIN account. Remove all outstanding debt information from the alternate SINs. If the total debt is over $99,999.99, add the following note in ITRDS : " Overpayment(s) merged under Prime SIN, account left out of balance as overpayment over 100K, account to be adjusted in CPMS in December 2020. " T he debtor does not have an account in OAS or IO under the Prime SIN S end an email to OAS-IA INITIATIVES / INITATIVES SV-AI (EDSC/ESDC) for guidance. OAS-IA INITIATIVES / INITATIVES SV-AI (EDSC/ESDC) These accounts must be corrected by November 30, 2020 in order to have the correct debt established in CPMS. Further direction will be provided in the near future on how to handle overpayments where the fraud or misrepresentation was committed on another person's SIN.
There is no reference material.

As part of the OAS Service Improvement Strategy (SIS), adjudication and payment of OAS and IA client benefits will migrate to the CPP platforms (ITRDS and CPMS) at the end of December 2020. Common client data elements from multiple system sources need to be merged to provide a single version of an individual client and ensure appropriate adjudication of all CPP, OAS and IA benefits. A clean copy of all OAS and IA client data is required post migration. Accounts where the client data elements cannot be automatically merged at system implementation will be excluded from systematic processing and adjudication or calculation of benefits will need payment exception processes.

There are currently a number of accounts that are or were being paid under an account number or SIN that is not considered the Prime SIN. As ITRDS uses only Prime SIN for each client, the account number in either the OAS or IA systems needs to be updated to the Prime SIN. A client data migration scan was sent to the regions in October 2020 to correct or update the OAS accounts to be paid under the Prime SIN. Included in the SIN scan were a number of fraud or misrepresentation accounts with outstanding overpayments on multiple SINs, most of them alternate SINs. These accounts require further clean up prior to m igration. In these situations, when the data migrates to ITRDS, anything stored under the alternate SIN will be loaded as history on the client profile . D epending on the situation, an incorrect overpayment value or no overpayment will be created in CPMS. Prior to the end of the December 2020 accounting month , the uncollected overpayment must be deleted from the alternate SIN and added to the primary SIN for the OAS or IA account prior to migration. This will allow the correct amount of the overpayment to be created in ITRDS and CPMS at migration.

Determining the payee for the child under the age of 18 The person or agency who has decision-making responsibility for the child under the age of 18 (-18 child) is the eligible payee for the Surviving Child’s benefit. The survivor is presumed to have decision-making responsibility if they have at least 20% of parenting time. The benefit can be paid directly to a surviving -18 child in exceptional circumstances.
Canada Pension Plan Section 75—Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit and Orphan's Benefit, payment of benefit

Determining the payee for a child under the age of 18 Updated The CPP provides payment of a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) for a child under the age of 18 to the person or agency that has decision-making responsibility on behalf of that child. Custody and control has been replaced with decision-making responsibility. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: health; education; culture, language, religion and spirituality; and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is defined as the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is in school). Unless there is evidence of the contrary, the disabled contributor is presumed to have decision-making responsibility for the child unless they have less than 20% of the parenting time. The DCCB is payable to the disabled contributor when the above is satisfied and they: apply for the DCCB ; and inform the Department that they have decision-making responsibility for the child. Refer to the Disputed dates of custody section of Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) . Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) Decision-making responsibility or parenting time includes, but is not limited to: formal and informal parenting arrangements; or sole, shared, joint and similar parenting arrangements. All DCCB eligibility requirements must be met. Child-Contributor Relationship—Children’s Benefit (Policy) By applying for the DCCB and indicating they have a minimum of 20% parenting time for the child, the disabled contributor is making an attestation that they have decision-making responsibility, which is sufficient to determine that they are the payee on the initial application only. The change in payee is effective the month following the change in decision-making responsibility or the current accounting month when the request is actioned (this is for change the payee based on policy updates only). Refer to Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) for more information. Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) When the disabled contributor shares decision-making responsibility, the Department will pay the full amount of the DCCB to the disabled contributor as there is no legislative authority to allow the DCCB payment to be split. When the disabled contributor does not live with the child at least 20% of the parenting time, you must determine if the other parent, guardian or child can be contacted (i.e. when they are available to be contacted and how they want to be contacted). Refer to the Protection and disclosure of the disabled contributor's information section of Eligibility Requirements—CPP Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit (Policy)

Service Canada may make bulk payments of CPP and OAS benefits to: provincial or territorial Public Trustees; or guardians and private agencies who hold trusteeships for multiple CPP or OAS beneficiaries. Service Canada can make a bulk payment to a Public trustee or a Private trustee, such as a: Public trustee or the Public curator (Quebec); and Private trustee (agency). If the applicable provincial or territorial Public trustee or Public curator (Quebec) has been appointed as the legal representative for a beneficiary, then the provincial, territorial Public trustee or Public curator must remit to Service Canada a dated letter or notice. If a Private trustee (agency) has been appointed as trustee by Service Canada for a beneficiary (or several beneficiaries), Service Canada must have a Certificate of Incapability-OAS/CPP (ISP3505) form and an Agreement to administer benefits under the Old Age Security Act and/or the Canada Pension Plan by an Agency or Institution (ISP3507) form on file for each beneficiary. The use of a single “Agreement to administer benefits under the Old Age Security Act and/or the Canada Pension Plan by an Agency or Institution” form by an agency to cover multiple beneficiaries (referred to as a Blanket Agreement) is not sufficient. All Service Canada appointed Trusteeships that are established must be completed by using: both a Certificate of Incapability and an Agreement to Administer Benefits under CPP; and/or OAS by an Agency or Institution for each Trusteeship.

topic_title: Direct deposit to an account other than the beneficiary’s account
text: CPP or OAS benefits directed to a bank account where the beneficiary is not named as an account holder is considered an assignment of benefits and prohibited by the CPP and the OAS Act. The Department can however direct payments into an account that is held by a third party in trust for an incapable beneficiary. The Department would first need a direct deposit request from the third party along with satisfactory evidence showing that the beneficiary is incapable of managing their own affairs by reason of: infirmity; illness; insanity; or other cause. The third party administrator can be: a Public trustee; a trustee or a guardian appointed by legislation or by the Court ; or an agency or individual appointed by the Department. If the Department has appointed the third party as trustee, the evidence and payee’s contact information must be on file, including the Certificate of Incapability and Agreement to Administer Benefits form.

Types of financial institutions and accounts included A direct deposit may be made to financial institutions physically located in Canada. The term “financial institution” includes: trust companies; credit unions; and some foreign banks located in Canada.

Types of financial institutions and accounts A direct deposit may be made to financial institutions physically located in the United States or in any other country in which the direct deposit service is available.

topic_title: Who can apply for direct deposit
text: All CPP and OAS beneficiaries are encouraged to enrol in direct deposit. Legal representatives, who have been given the legal authority to act on behalf of a beneficiary or contributor, may also enrol the beneficiary in direct deposit. Legal representatives include attorneys who have been given power of attorney (POA) for property, or third party administrators for property who have been appointed by: Legislation; a provincia l or territorial court (trustees, guardians, committees); or a Department (trustee) acting on behalf of an incapable individual. An individual who has been authorized by the applicant, beneficiary or contributor, either by letter or by the “Consent to Communicate Information to a Representative” form, to give and receive information with the Department on behalf of the beneficiary is not authorized to enrol for direct deposit on the beneficiary’s behalf. If an attorney named in a POA document requests direct deposit, the request will only be accepted if the beneficiary is named on the bank account, since the beneficiary and not the attorney is the payee. Documentary evidence of the third party’s authority to act on behalf of the beneficiary must be on file before accepting a direct deposit request on behalf of the beneficiary.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada introduced the following emergency benefits to support Canadians by providing temporary income support for workers (employed and self-employed) who were directly impacted by the pandemic: Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); the Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); and the Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). The CERB/EI ERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB are taxable benefits that are considered income under the Income Tax Act and are considered income for determining entitlement for income-tested benefits up to June 2022. Effective July 2022, legislative amendments were made to the Old Age Security Act , allowing for the exclusion of these benefits received in 2021 or later when calculating income.

Procedures are now available for processing renewal accounts for the July 2022 to June 2023 payment year, that includes EI ERB in the 2021 Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income. The PWS work item will include a note that provides the amount of EI ERB and Employment Insurance benefits received in 2021. The amount of income identified as EI ERB must be manually removed from the client's income. If this income was not removed before the end of the July accounting month a recalculation of benefits may be required. When a couple is separated for 12 months or more, the PNSH ceases with the current processing month. If either spouse makes a request for reconsideration of the Department's decision to cease the PNSH with the current month, the Department must apply the legislation as it reads and effect the cessation with the month the event took place. If neither individual requests a reconsideration, remove all payables and receivables from both accounts in CPMS. If there is a reconsideration request asking the Department to cease the PNSH retroactively to 12 months after the separation or end of a common-law relationship, you must action the monetary in accordance with the Overpayment Policy, if: an individual’s payable is applied to their receivable; any remaining payable is issued to the individual; and any remaining receivable is recovered. The CPP legislation does not support this process.
If additional guidance is required, send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool by following normal channels. Business Expertise Request Tool

For cases where a couple is separated for 12 months or more, the cessation date will no longer be the month in which the PNSH is terminated by the Department. It is no longer a requirement for either spouse to submit a request for reconsideration before actioning the monetary results. This direction is effective from the date of publication and must not be applied retroactively. Closed cases must not be reviewed or overturned. Connect is a digital delivery platform that facilitates sending and receiving Protected B correspondence with one or multiple recipients. It enables secure collaboration through one common platform. IO staff can communicate through Connect to exchange: liaison forms; Canadian or foreign application forms; and supporting documents. Similar to an email inbox, Connect allows IO staff to create "conversations" with specific recipients and manage messages with replies and notifications. Forms and documents can be uploaded to the Connect platform for secure electronic delivery to a recipient. The Connect procedures for exchanging information with Canadian and foreign institutions are largely the same as the current procedures. The only difference is the elimination of the outgoing physical copy of correspondence by mail unless the recipient requests it. For each participating institution, 2 conversations will be created to facilitate document transfer and reduce the quantity of documents in each conversation. They conversations are as follows: one for processing staff to upload outgoing correspondence; and one for support staff to retrieve incoming correspondence.
IO processing sites have implemented the use of Canada Post's Connect service to exchange Protected B personal information with participating Canadian and foreign institutions.

CPP credit and debit reports identify accounts where credits remain unpaid and debts that remain outstanding at the end of a month. CPP regional processing staff are required to release credits, apply credits to an outstanding debt, or set recovery on debts.

The work items listed in the credit and debit report are created with an Auto status in PWS . Where possible, all monetary actions in the CPMS as well as the resulting letters will be automated. Where applicable, the automated process will release payables, apply payables to receivables, or will set recovery of the receivables, and send letters. topic_title: Creating an Enquiry work item type
text: The Call Centre or In-Person agent selects one of the plus ( + ) buttons corresponding to the program related to the work item being created. Once the page has loaded, the Source must be Call Centre or In Person by default. All of the following fields in the form (marked with red asterisks) must be completed: Field Direction Location The agent must select the appropriate Processing Centre in the Location field that is responsible for processing the client's benefits, as per the Common Reference Tool's – Escalating a Call procedure or the client's Office of Control specified in ITRDS. Assignment Status By default, Unassigned is the status that appears in this field. Do not alter this field; it remains set at Unassigned . The Assignment Status field is completed by the Processing clerk who assigns the work item to the appropriate Service Canada Benefits Officer. When an agent is further escalating a previously-created Enquiry work type, this field must not be modified. Date Received When creating a new Enquiry work type, Call Center and In Person agents must check the Received Today box. Checking this box automatically populates the Date Received to the day the escalation is made by the client. The agent must not make changes to this field when escalating an existing Enquiry work item in PWS. Client To facilitate the entry of the client's name, Call Centre and In-Person agents must enter the client’s Social Insurance Number (SIN), which populates the client’s information. Program This field should automatically populate if the agents used one of the plus ( + ) buttons. If not, the Call Centre or In-Person agent selects the program related to the work item being created. Category The Category is always Maintenance . Type One of the new Enquiry work types must be selected in this field. Call Centre and In-Person agents must type in the word Enquiry , select the Search button and the list of available Enquiry work types will be shown. The agent must select the work type which best describes the nature of the client’s enquiry. The Enquiry – Other work type should only be used if the alternate work types are not applicable for the escalation. For that reason, the use of this work type must be limited. Once the Enquiry work types have been selected, the following fields appear: Field Direction Callback If the client has requested a callback, the agent selects Yes in this field. If not, this field must remain at the default setting: No . Escalate If this is the first enquiry made by the client, this field should be 1st Level . If the agent is escalating an existing enquiry made by the client, then the agent must select the next escalation. Last Escalated On This field will be automatically populated based on the date when the Escalate field is updated and will be locked for any manual intervention. Escalation Due Date Once the previous fields have been set, the agent must select Save on the Work Item Detail screen. After saving the work item, the Escalation Due Date automatically calculates depending on the Last Escalated On field and on the escalation timeframes. PWS Notes Once the agent has completed the required fields, they must enter the notes into PWS that were entered into ITRDS, with the exception of SINs, to ensure coherence amongst the systems. This also ensures proper tracking of all the modifications as all the escalations are done within the one work item. Once these fields have been completed, the agent clicks the Save and Close button.

topic_title: Enquiry work types in PWS and new Enquiry Follow-up work type Updated
text: Call Centre and In-Person agents should only be creating Enquiry work types and Processing agents should not be changing Enquiry work types created by Call Centre and/or In-Person agents in PWS to a different work type. This ensures the ability to: potentially escalate this work; communicate back to the client; and effectively track this work. Enquiry work types are meant to capture the client’s initial call and subsequent escalations. The Enquiry work item should be completed when a response has been provided to the enquiry (e.g. call back made, updated ITRDS notes, or other processing action taken). This will ensure that if a client calls back, the Call Centre and In-Person agents can clearly recognize that the Enquiry work item has been addressed. Completed Enquiry work items should not be reactivated, rather a new Enquiry established if needed.

Effective July 24, 2021, a new Enquiry Follow-up work type was created in PWS to capture any additional work that is required on the client account based on a client enquiry. This work type is included for all current Programs (OAS/CPP/DSB/IO) under the Category: Maintenance . If additional work is required based on the client enquiry (e.g. letter with Bring Forward), the new Enquiry Follow-up work type must be created to capture that work, and the underlying Enquiry work type must be completed. An alternate work type, such as Death Notification or Reassessment , can also be used. In either case, the underlying Enquiry work type must be completed and ITRDS Notes must reflect the response to the underlying Enquiry. The work type Report Follow-up must not be used. Work Type in the Application and Appeals categories must also not be used. Use of the Enquiry Follow-up work type assists Call Centre and In-Person agents to quickly identify that processing action related to the underlying Enquiry is underway with ITRDS Notes providing additional information.

topic_title: Applications for CPP or OAS pensions and benefits made under International Social Security Agreements
text: Special forms to apply for CPP and OAS pensions and benefits have been developed for individuals who have worked or lived in countries with which Canada has an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA). Provided the form clearly identifies the applicant and the CPP or OAS benefits they are applying for, and it is signed by the applicant, it must be considered a valid benefits application. These special forms are accepted as valid applications whether an ISSA was used to determine benefit eligibility or not. For more information on which countries have an ISSA with Canada, consult Foreign Benefits
The applicant's identity is confirmed by: SIN; name, address and date of birth; and applicant's signature.

A My Service Canada Account online application, a signed written statement, or a completed departmental form for a specific CPP benefit is considered an application, e.g. DSB , PRDB , DTH benefit, SVR pension. If a request for a benefit is made on the wrong CPP form, it does not date-protect the intended benefit.

The following will be considered applications for CPPD benefits: a signed written statement; a signed application for CPP DSBs; or a signed terminal illness application for DSB . The above documents will be accepted and adjudicated for both the DSB and PRDB when: the applicant is in receipt of an Early Retirement (ERTR) pension on the date the disability application is received; the applicant is in receipt of an ERTR pension prior to the initial decision being communicated to the individual; or an individual applies for both DSB and an ERTR pension at the same time. In certain cases, the ERTR pension only starts the month following the month the application was received. Despite this, there can be cases where an application is received in May, while the benefit payment will only start in June. If the individual applies for an ERTR pension after an initial decision on the DSB is made and communicated to the individual, a separate written statement or an Application for a Canada Pension Plan Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (ISP-1170) form will be required to determine their eligibility for the PRDB . This will not be considered a simultaneous application for both benefits.
