When an individual is married or in a common-law relationship and is applying online for the GIS, their spouse or common-law partner must provide consent to obtain their information from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and declare that the information provided about them is true. The spouse or common-law partner's consent and declaration are considered obtained through their GIS or ALW application process if: the details of their marital status match the information provided on the online GIS application you are processing; the CRA Marital Status flag and the CRA Spousal SIN found on the CRA Income (CRA) screen in OAS Online match the information provided, if available; and one of the following conditions are met: both spouses or common-law partners have signed a previously submitted paper OAS/GIS or paper GIS application; the spouse or common-law partner previously submitted an online OAS/GIS or online GIS application and a signed Spousal Consent and Declaration (ISS0954) letter or a Spousal Consent and Declaration GIS (ISS0954A) letter was received; the spouse or common-law partner has been approved for automatic enrolment of the GIS (i.e. the process is not in Pending status); or the spouse or common-law partner has also submitted an online OAS/GIS, online GIS or online ALW benefit application that is being processed at the same time as the applicant’s online GIS application. If there are any discrepancies between the information provided in the spouse or common-law partner's GIS or ALW benefit application process, the CRA Income (CRA) screen and the information provided in the online GIS application you are processing affecting eligibility and entitlement, they must be resolved as per regular procedures, before processing the online GIS application. If the spouse or common-law partner's consent and declaration have not been obtained through the GIS application process, this consent can be obtained by sending the ISS0954A letter to the spouse or common-law partner to complete. The ISS0954A letter allows the spouse or common-law partner to provide: confirmation that the information provided on their behalf is correct; consent for the Department to request and use their CRA income information to determine their spouse or common-law partner's entitlement for the GIS; and advise the spouse or common-law partner that, if they have already been deemed eligible for the OAS pension, their partner's online application for the GIS will also be considered their application for the GIS, if applicable. If all other eligibility criteria are met, the online application can be approved without the consent and declaration from the spouse or common-law partner; however, the applicant's GIS entitlement cannot be calculated until the consent and declaration is received from the spouse or common-law partner.
This procedure provides the guidance necessary to retrieve and process an online GIS application.

Table 1.Timeline of the Development of the Old Age Security Act Year Update 1951 British North America Act, 1951, 14-15 George VI, c. 32 (U.K.) (R.S.C. 1970, Appendix II, page 439). The Canadian Constitution was amended to give Parliament the power to enact laws on old age pensions. 1952 Old Age Security Act, S.C. 1951 (2nd Sess), c. 18—Effective January 1, 1952. The Old Age Security Act came into force on January 1. The OAS pension was set at a flat rate of $40 a month ($480 a year and was payable at age 70). The applicants had to have lived in Canada for 20 years immediately preceding approval of the application. Payment was suspended when the pensioner left the country and reinstated upon his or her return. The pension was financed by taxes from taxable personal income, corporate income, sales tax and loans from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. 1957 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1957-1958, c. 3—Effective November 1, 1957. In order to encourage immigration to Canada, the residency requirements for the OAS were lowered to 10 years of residence in Canada immediately preceding approval of the application. Persons who could not meet this condition had to have been present in Canada before these ten years, for periods totalling twice the length of the gaps in the ten year period and had to have resided in Canada during at least a year immediately preceding the approval of the application. The duration of the payment of the pension to pensioners absent from Canada was increased from 3 to 6 months in a calendar year. The amount of the OAS pension was raised to $55 a month ($660 a year). 1960 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1960, c. 34—Assented to July 7, 1960. The Old Age Security Act was amended to provide for indefinite portability with regard to pensioners who had at least 25 years of residence in Canada after the age of 21. As well, the unconditional payment of OAS pensions abroad was possible for a period of 6 months, not counting the month of departure. 1962 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1962, c. 5—Effective February 1, 1962. The amount of the OAS pension was raised to $65 a month ($780 a year). 1963 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1963, c. 16—Effective October 1, 1963. The amount of the OAS pension was raised, this time to $75 a month ($900 a year). 1964 British North America Act, 1964, 12-13 Elizabeth II, c. 73 (U.K.) The Canadian Constitution was amended again to give Parliament the power to enact laws on supplemental old age benefits, including survivor and disability benefits, whatever the age of the recipient. 1965 Canada Pension Plan , S.C. 1964-1965, c. 51, s. 119, 120 and 122—Effective May 5, 1965. The Old Age Security Act was amended to set the age of eligibility for an OAS pension at 65, lowering the age by one year, each year, starting from age 69 in 1966. The requirements for the residency period were amended to extend the old residency requirements to 40 years after the age of 18, without requiring residence in Canada during the year immediately preceding the approval of the application. Starting in 1968, OAS pensions increased each year based on the changes in the Pension Index, as is the case for the Canada Pension Plan. 1966 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1966-1967, c. 65—Effective January 1, 1967. The monthly Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) was established for OAS pensioners born on December 31, 1910 or before whose income was below a fixed amount. The maximum GIS payment was set at $30 for 1967 and subsequently at 40% of the OAS pension amount. The GIS was income-tested and reduced by $1 for each full $2 portion of monthly base income calculated at 1/12 of the income, excluding the OAS pension for the preceding year. In the case of married pensioners, the GIS was reduced by $1 for each full $4 of the couple's combined income excluding the OAS pension. Where one spouse has not reached the pensionable age, the reduction to be made on their combined income excluding the OAS pension and an amount equal to the OAS pension for the younger spouse. The authorized payment of the GIS for periods of absence from Canada up to 6 months in addition to the month of the pensioner's departure from Canada. 1970 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1970-1971-1972, c. 9 (also see R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp. ) c. 21)—Effective January 1, 1971. The amount of the OAS pension was raised to $80 a month ($960 a year). The residency requirements of the OAS were amended. Applicants absent from Canada during the 10-year period preceding the approval of the application must have been present in Canada during the preceding years but after the age of 18, for periods equal to 3 times the aggregate period of absence prior to the 10-year period. As well, they must have resided in Canada at least one year immediately preceding the approval of the application (3 for 1 formula—came into force on December 18, 1971). The increase introduced on the basis of changes in the Pension Index only applied to the GIS and OAS combined and added to the supplement; the increase in the pension alone ended. It was no longer required for a person to have been born on or before December 31, 1910 to be eligible for the supplement. 1972 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1972, c. 10—Effective January 1, 1972. The portability formula of 25 years was changed to 20 years, in order to meet the needs of immigrants, who had worked in Canada and wanted to return to the country of their birth. As well, the payment of OAS pensions abroad was authorized indefinitely, if the pensioner had resided in Canada for 20 years after the age of 18. The annual increase in the OAS and the GIS was from this point on based on the Consumer Price Index rather than the Pension Index. 1973 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1973-1974, c. 8—Effective April 1, 1973. The amount of the OAS pension was raised to $100 a month. 1973 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act ,S.C. 1973-1974, c. 35—Effective October 1, 1973. The OAS and GIS pensions were from this point on adjusted quarterly rather than annually, based on the Consumer Price Index. 1975 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1974-1975, c. 58—Effective October 1, 1975. The Old Age Security Act was amended to introduce the Spouse's Allowance, now known as the Allowance ( ALW ), payable to persons aged 60 to 64 who are married to and living with OAS pensioners. The residency requirements for the ALW were the same as those required for the OAS pension. The Old Age Security Regulations were also amended to introduce the definition of residence and presence, as well as the periods of absence, which could be deemed to have not interrupted residence or presence in Canada. The OAS Fund was abolished; pensions were paid directly from the Consolidated Revenue Fund as a statutory appropriation. 1977 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1976-1977, c. 35—Effective July 1, 1977. The residency requirements were amended to allow for the payment of partial pensions calculated at a rate of 1/40th of the full OAS pension, for each year of residence in Canada after the age of 18. As this change completely overhauled the previous rules for granting a pension, the government "grandfathered" a large segment of the Canadian and immigrant population by providing a transition period of 40 years. The new Act applied to residents of Canada under the age of 25 on July 1, 1977, and to persons of any age who were abroad on this date, had not resided in Canada after the age of 18 and did not hold a valid immigration visa. The new or old rules, whichever was the most advantageous, applied to residents of Canada aged 25 or older and resident in Canada on July 1, 1977, or if they were abroad being aged 25 or older and had already resided in Canada after the age of 18 or held a valid immigration visa on July 1, 1977. Amendments to the secondary benefits legislation provided for the payment of GIS benefits to recipients of partial OAS benefits. As well, partial Spouse's Allowance (now known as the ALW ) benefits became payable based on the same residency requirements as for OAS pensions. The Old Age Security Act was amended to permit international social security agreements to be concluded to protect the acquired old age security rights of persons who had emigrated across international borders. 1978 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , R.S.C. 1978-1979, c. 3 —Assented to November 20, 1978. The ALW continued to be paid for the 6 months following the death of a pensioner, when this death occurred on or after November 20, 1978. 1979 An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act , S.C. 1979, c. 4—Effective October 31, 1979. Repayments to provincial governments of social assistance advances through deductions from OAS, GIS or ALW benefits where the advances were made while the applicant awaited to receive benefits. The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board Act included, among others, penalties for unreturned overpayments. Bill C-36 changed these provisions to clarify that the purpose of penalties is not to punish, but to promote compliance. Therefore, knowledge that one was lying was set as a necessary condition of applying penalties. In addition, penalties were now considered a "debt due to Her Majesty" thereby giving the Government authority to force payment through litigation. In addition to penalties, the Act extended the consideration of a "debt due to Her Majesty" to the interest of any overpayments instead of just the overpayment itself. When interest would be applied and how it would be applied will be decided through Governor in Council regulation. Economic Action Plan Act , S.C. 2014, c. 20 In January 2014, changes were made to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations , which increased the length of the parent and grandparent sponsorship period from 10 to 20 years in all provinces except Quebec. Effective May 21, 2021, individuals can apply online through their My Service Canada Account (MSCA) for the Death (DTH) benefit, a one-time lump sum payment payable to the estate or to an eligible individual, on behalf of a deceased CPP contributor. The online DTH benefit application does not replace the Application for CPP Death Benefit (ISP1200) form. However, it is another channel by which eligible applicants can apply for the benefit. If an estate exists , the executor named in the will or the administrator named by the Court to administer the estate applies for the DTH benefit. The executor should apply within 60 days of the contributor's date of death. If no estate exists or, if the executor has not applied for the DTH benefit, payment may be made to other individuals who apply for the benefit in the following order of priority: The person or institution that has paid for, or that is responsible for paying the funeral expenses of the deceased; The surviving spouse or common-law partner of the deceased; or The next-of-kin of the deceased. The online DTH benefit application contains a dynamic component by which it displays appropriate application questions based on the information input by the applicant and mirrors the ISP1200 form. Furthermore, the online application for a CPP DTH benefit asks the following 2 questions, if applicable: Are you the person responsible for the funeral expenses? The response to this question may affect the hierarchy of payment of the DTH benefit. Refer to Paying the Death Benefit . Paying the Death Benefit Who is the person to represent the deceased client for the purpose of filing income tax? This question does not change the current process to determine the person who is being issued a T4 for the purpose of filing income tax. If the applicant provides their contact information online, the Deemed Person to Represent the Deceased Client for the Purpose of Issuing a T4A(OAS), T4A(P) and NR4 (ISP1202) form is not required. topic_title: Calculation of the earnings exemption before July 1, 2020
text: Effective July 1, 2008 to June 30, 2020, the employment earnings exemption was a flat rate of $3,500 applied to the client's net employment income only. The net employment income after the exemption is applied cannot be a negative amount; therefore, when the exemption is greater than the employment income, the net employment income will be nil.

topic_title: Combined employment and self-employment income is less than or equal to $5,000 but greater than $0.00 Updated
text: When the combined employment and self-employment income is greater than $0.00 and less than or equal to $5,000, the entire amount of the combined earnings income is deducted. Example 1 Income source Net income reported by the applicant Earnings exemption amount calculated by Cúram Income amounts in the system after the exemption is applied Employment (block 7) $3,000 $3,000 $0.00 Self-employment (block 8) $1,000 $1,000 $0.00 Manually enter the net employment and self-employment amounts reported by the applicant into Cúram. Do not manually apply the earnings exemption to the income. Cúram will calculate and apply the total earnings exemption of $4,000 to the manually entered income. Since the combined employment and self-employment income is less than $5,000, the total amount is exempted. Once the exemption is applied to the income blocks by the system, the GIS entitlement will be calculated based on no employment or self-employment income.

topic_title: Combined employment and self-employment income is greater than $15,000 Updated
text: When the combined employment and self-employment income is greater than $15,000, the $5,000 exemption is added to an additional exempted amount equal to 50% of $10,000. Therefore, the client is entitled to a $10,000 exemption ($5,000 + $5,000). Example 4 Income source Net income reported by the applicant Earnings exemption amount calculated by Cúram Income amounts in the system after the exemption is applied Employment (block 7) $3,000 $3,000 $0.00 Self-employment (block 8) $18,000 $7,000 $11,000 Manually enter the net employment and net self-employment amounts reported by the applicant into Cúram. Do not manually apply the earnings exemption to the income. Cúram will calculate and apply the total earnings exemption of $10,000. This deduction is calculated as follows: Determine the total combined income: Deduct $5,000 from the total combined income: Since the balance is over $10,000, calculate 50% of $10,000: $5,000 Add the $5,000 exemption to the 50% exempted amount: Since the total earnings exemption amount is more than the total employment income amount, Cúram will apply the first $3,000 of the exempted amount to block 7 with the remaining $7,000 applied to block 8. Once the exemption is applied to the income blocks by the system, the GIS entitlement will be calculated based on $11,000 of self-employment income.

text: When the combined employment and self-employment income is equal to or greater than $5,000, but less than or equal to $15,000, the client is entitled to a $5,000 exemption plus 50% of the amount of combined employment and self-employment income that exceeds $5,000 but does not exceed $15,000 (up to a maximum of $5,000; $10,000 in total). This exemption is calculated as follows: Determine the total combined income: Deduct $5,000 from the total combined income: Calculate 50% of the amount that exceeds $5,000: Add the $5,000 exemption to the 50% exempted amount: Since the total earnings exemption amount is equal to the total employment income amount, Cúram will apply the full exemption to the employment income block in the system. Once the exemption is applied, the GIS entitlement will be calculated based on $2,000 of self-employment income. This exemption is calculated as follows: Determine the total combined income: Deduct $5,000 from the total combined income: Calculate 50% of the amount that exceeds $5,000: Add the $5,000 exemption to the 50% exempted amount: Since the total earnings exemption amount is more than the total employment income amount, Cúram will apply the first $2,000 of the exempted amount to block 7 with the remaining $7,000 applied to block 8. topic_title: Employment income is less than $3,500 Updated
text: Example 7 Income source Net income reported by the applicant Earnings exemption amount calculated by Cúram Income amounts in the system after the exemption is applied Employment (block 7) $2,750 $2,750 $0.00 Self-employment (block 8) $8,000 $0.00 $8,000 Manually enter the net employment and net self-employment amounts reported by the applicant into Cúram. This deduction is calculated as follows: Determine the amount of employment income: $2,750. Deduct the flat rate employment earnings exemption of $3,500: Since the employment income cannot be reduced to a negative amount, the total earnings exemption is $2,750 and is applied to block 7 by the system. text: When the self-employment income is a negative amount and the employment income is a positive amount. Currently, individuals who want to apply for the Allowance (ALW) or the Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefits can only do so using the paper application form: Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor - Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP3008). Individuals who want to apply for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) benefit can only do so using: the relevant paper application form: Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP3025); or Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement with Statement of Income (ISP3025B); or the combined OAS pension and GIS benefit online application. Effective May 28, 2021 individuals may apply for the ALW or ALWS benefits and, effective June 4, 2021, individuals may apply for the GIS benefit through their My Service Canada Account (MSCA) secure online portal.

My Service Canada Account unavailability MSCA will not be accessible for one hour very early EST on May 28, 2021 for ALW or ALWS benefit applications and again on June 4, 2021 for the GIS benefit application. Process for Clients The same policies and processes for accessing MSCA apply for clients, including the Department’s Registration and Authentication process. To register for an MSCA account a client needs a Personal Access Code (PAC). Normal practices to obtain a PAC continue to apply.

Effective May 28, 2021 and June 4, 2021, new functionality in My Service Canada Account (MSCA) will enable individuals, both those residing within Canada and those residing abroad, to apply for the Allowance (ALW), Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) or Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) benefits online. Under the heading OAS/GIS Applications , clients can apply online for an ALW, ALWS or GIS benefit if they meet the conditions that follow. Individuals are eligible to apply online for ALW or ALWS benefits starting May 28, 2021 if they: are between 59+1 month and 65+11 months years of age; though the age for benefit eligibility is between 60 and 64 years of age (including the month of the individual's 65th birthday), individuals can apply 11 months early or, for a retroactive payment, up to 11 months in the past (i.e. back to 65+0 ) ; have no third party representation on file (e.g. Power of attorney, Trustee etc.). Individuals are eligible to apply online for GIS benefit starting June 4, 2021 if they: are age 64+1 month or older; are in pay for an OAS pension or have an OAS pension in Future/Pending status; are not already in pay for the GIS benefit and do not have a GIS benefit in Future/Pending status; and have no third party representation on file (e.g. Power of attorney, Trustee etc.). The online applications for the ALW, ALWS and GIS benefits offer a simplified client experience, asking only relevant questions. This means that clients are only asked questions that are specific to their situation (e.g. applicants born and having always lived in Canada will not be asked to complete the residence question). For ALW and ALWS benefits, clients face a single interface when they start the application. If their spouse or common-law partner is deceased, they receive the ALWS application stream of questions. Otherwise, they receive the ALW stream of questions. When an individual submits an application for the ALW, ALWS or GIS benefits online, based on the individual's home address and marital status, their confirmation page presents: the most applicable proof documentation the individual is required to submit; along with the relevant Service Canada processing centre address to which the individual will send their supporting documentation. Once submitted online, applications for ALW, ALWS or GIS benefits are linked as PDF documents directly to the PWS rather than as a paper form. The application will be processed as per existing processes. A new work item linked to the application is created in PWS and it is assigned it to the applicable processing centre location. Processing agents currently obtain the OAS pension and GIS benefit combined online application work item through Government On Line (GOL) Support Services. This step will no longer be necessary for these new applications because of the direct link from PWS to the ALW/ALWS or GIS benefit online applications. Instead, the PDF applications will be retrieved directly from PWS to be processed as per the existing process for paper applications. There are no actions needed on the part of processing agents to change the status of the application in MSCA. For situations where an applicant does not meet the access rules to apply using MSCA, the system presents an “Unable to continue” page which describes to the applicant the reason(s) why they cannot use this service. The page will offer to the applicant: a link to the Service Canada website for more information; and alternate service channels (e.g. a paper application form).

There are no changes that will affect the paper-based application process for the ALW/ALWS or GIS benefits. The paper application forms for the ALW and the ALWS benefits (ISP3008) as well as for the GIS benefit (ISP3025/3025B) will continue to be available and accepted. When an applicant is applying for the GIS benefit and has indicated that they have a spouse or common-law partner, send a letter to that spouse or common-law partner to: verify or correct the information provided by the applicant; declare that they have read and agreed to the terms and conditions outlined in the letter; and obtain their agreement that if the spouse/common-law partner is currently eligible to receive the OAS pension, the information provided will also be considered as their application for the GIS benefit.

topic_title: Calculating estimated income when CPP PRB is not the event but is included in the estimate
text: When you process an option, you must review ITRDS and CPMS to confirm that the correct CPP monthly rate is used in the estimate calculation. If the client receives a PRB , the CPP monthly rate payable will be displayed along with the PRB rate payable for each applicable year. All rates added together equal the monthly entitlement issued to the client. The PRB entitlement for the current year may not be available in ITRDS at the time of processing the option due to the PRB payment pattern described above. To ensure that you are using the most accurate CPP monthly rate in the estimate calculation, you must review the applicant’s CPP entitlement to determine if a PRB is normally received as part of their CPP income or if there is an indication that a PRB will be adjudicated for the year of the estimate. You may have to perform a PRB simulation in ITRDS to determine the PRB entitlement for the current year. In June, when the option is being reviewed for the upcoming payment period, you must confirm the CPP rate that was used in the estimate calculation. If the PRB amount is now available and is different than what was used to perform the original calculation, recalculate the estimate and adjust the benefit accordingly.

The PRB is a taxable monthly benefit that is payable to a CPP or QPP RTR pension recipient who works and makes valid contributions on earnings above the Year’s Basic Exemption (YBE). It is payable for the client's lifetime, even when they are already receiving the maximum RTR pension. For more information, Post-Retirement Benefit (Knowledge) The normal pay pattern for a PRB is an automated retroactive payment for January to March, issued with the April CPP or QPP payment. Regular CPP or QPP payments, including the PRB amounts for each year, begin in April and continue to December. This process is repeated each year. Since CPP and QPP are considered pensionable income for option purposes, clients may submit a Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form to: report the retroactive PRB payment as an event; or include the PRB entitlement as part of the estimated income for a separate optionable event.

topic_title: Valid application with insufficient or missing information or documentation
text: If you determine that a CPP or OAS departmental pension or benefit application, online application or written request for a CPP benefit is valid, but there is missing information or documentation to make an eligibility determination, you must contact the applicant to request them (e.g. questionnaires, statutory declarations, medical reports, consent forms). If the applicant provides the requested information, refer to the applicable application procedures to process the application and make a decision on eligibility. If the applicant fails to provide the missing information or documentation within the bring forward periods, you must make an eligibility determination using the information provided and communicate the appropriate appeal rights to the applicant. A decision must be made on all valid applications and appeal rights offered. CPPD—Determine if an Application or Request for Reconsideration is Complete (Scenario)

An application under CPP and OAS must meet certain criteria to be valid before making an eligibility decision. When an invalid application or intent to apply is received, the Department communicates with the applicant to gather the missing components to make an application valid. If the application remains invalid, the Department administratively closes the file. For clarity, "application" used in this article includes all pensions and benefits applications for all program benefits as well as a written request for a CPP program benefit. An applicant is defined as the individual applying for or requesting the benefit, or their legal representative applying on their behalf. Each program specifies how applicants may apply. To make an application valid it requires a signature with a clear indication of the benefit and the person to receive the benefits. For more information, Valid Applications (Policy)

"Discretion" means the Minister must consider all relevant factors when deciding whether to release a payable. There is also an onus on the Minister to make a reasonable effort to find the appropriate payee.

If eligibility requirements have been met and a benefit has been approved, the Minister is legally obligated to pay the benefit. If the beneficiary is alive, the payment is made to them directly or to their authorized legal representative i.e. custodial parent, trustee, etc. In the event that the beneficiary dies, the payee must be determined. If there is a will, the Minister must make reasonable efforts to advise and pay the estate. If the estate is closed or declines the unpaid benefit, the Minister has the discretionary authority to pay another person or agency.

The hierarchy used for identifying the payee for unpaid benefits at death is not the same as the hierarchy used to pay the DTH benefit. The payee hierarchy used to identify the appropriate payee for Benefits Unpaid at Death is as follows: The deceased’s estate. A person sufficiently connected to the deceased beneficiary to be financially affected by their death. The next of kin. While the estate must be the first payee, the Minister has discretion in identifying the payee and paying someone other than the estate representative when it cannot be determined if the deceased had a will. To ensure the unpaid benefits are released appropriately, careful consideration must be given when applying this discretion.

In all cases where unpaid benefits are to be paid to a recipient other than to an estate, an indemnity agreement is required. The main purpose of the indemnity agreement is to protect Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) in the event that the distribution to the chosen recipient is challenged in court. Since there is no estate, the designated recipient is receiving and distributing the benefit. This agreement protects ESDC from having to defend its distribution in court and from having to pay out the benefit more than once, should it be determined by a court that the incorrect person or agency was paid. The wording in the indemnity agreement imposes an obligation on the recipient to deal with the payment and to account for its disposition in the same manner as would be required by a personal representative. However, it does not impose an obligation upon ESDC to monitor the distribution of the monies by the recipient. The indemnity agreement must not be provided to a recipient until it has been determined that as signee, they are the designated recipient of the unpaid funds because they agree to indemnify ESDC in exchange for the receipt of the monies. As a result, the indemnity agreement will not come into effect until the monies are actually paid. The indemnity agreement does not bind ESDC into distributing the benefits to the signee. Although this is a Service Canada form, an official of ESDC does not sign the indemnity agreement. As a result, the indemnity agreement will not contain a promise (expressly or implied) by the Minister that the recipient in question will receive the funds. The covering letter accompanying the indemnity agreement must not contain a promise (expressly or implied) to pay the signee who completes and submits it. This is because another person who is more entitled may be identified between the time the indemnity agreement is signed and the entitlement is actually paid.
Canada Pension Plan Section 2—Definitions CPP regulations Section 57—Benefits Unpaid at Death Old Age Security Act Section 2—Definitions OAS regulations Section 24(5)—Benefits Unpaid at Death

If there is no estate or the estate representative is either deceased or cannot be located, the Minister has the discretion to pay it to another person or agency. Although not formalized in CPP or OAS legislation, the following hierarchy should be used as a guide: a person who is sufficiently connected to the deceased contributor individual and who is financially affected by their death; or the next of kin. Person c onnected to the d eceased In determining the appropriate payee, the intent of the CPP and OAS programs should be kept in mind. The intent of the CPP program is to provide contributors and their families with a basic level of financial support. The intent of the OAS program is to provide partial income security for senior Canadians in recognition of the contribution they have made to Canadian society and the economy. The recipient of the unpaid benefit should therefore be significantly connected to the deceased and be financially affected by their death. Generally, the deceased’s survivor or children would be the most appropriate choice. The following questions can help identify a payee (list provided for descriptive purposes only which is not intended to be exhaustive): Is there evidence of a SVR application in pay, i.e. a surviving spouse or common-law partner? Is there evidence that child benefits are or were in pay, i.e. confirmation the deceased had children? Was the deceased living with a person who was dependent in some way on the deceased’s income? For example, perhaps they paid “rent” to their parents. Before the beneficiary's death, was someone caring for them? Was the caregiver financially responsible for covering all or part of the deceased's care costs? Provincial s uccession l aws Processing staff may also look to the laws of succession from the relevant province as a guide to help them identify an appropriate payee. Most provinces generally follow the same order. First in line is generally the eligible surviving spouse or common-law partner. If there is no survivor, the payment goes to the children (natural or adopted), or grandchildren; otherwise, it could be distributed to the surviving parents. If there are no surviving parents, then to the deceased’s siblings. If there are no siblings, then to the nieces and nephews, etc.

In the event that a beneficiary of a CPP and/or OAS pension or benefits dies, any benefits to which they are entitled that were unpaid at the time of their death are still owed, even though they are deceased. Benefits intended to be payable to the beneficiary before their death are valid payables that can be paid to: the deceased beneficiary’s estate; or another appropriate payee. Benefits can remain unpaid in the following circumstances: Employment and Social Development Canada is notified of the beneficiary’s death before the payment is released; the payment or cheque for the month of death is returned by the bank or by another party; adjustments were made to a deceased beneficiary’s account which resulted in an underpayment i.e. new earnings posted to their CPP Record of Earnings; or there is a frozen underpayment.

The Department should make a reasonable effort to determine and contact the eligible payee, such as the estate representative, the next of kin, etc. Processing staff must follow a logical approach to release all payables. For the purposes of this operational policy, “reasonable efforts” means a degree of effort that is reasonable given the existing circumstances. It does not mean, "all efforts" or “leave no stone unturned”; or that all possible steps must be taken. It also does not mean expending an amount of effort causing an excessive administrative burden or result in unreasonable administrative costs to administer the department. How the processing centres define, “reasonable efforts” depends on the facts of a particular case, and must be weighed against the Minister’s duty to pay. “Reasonable”, in itself, is a subjective concept that is difficult to define, and its close synonyms are “sensible”, “suitable”, and “usual”. Processing staff should consider the following circumstances: the amount of the underpayment; how easily someone is identifiable; and the relationship of the potential payee to the deceased beneficiary. If, after making reasonable attempts to identify a payee, it is evident that pursuing the matter would become futile or would involve unreasonable costs to administer, the Minister has the discretion to release or not the benefits that were unpaid at the time of the contributor's death.

Any unpaid benefit entitlement on the beneficiary's file at the time of their death must be paid to the estate, with the exception of CPP children’s benefits. If a deceased payee was receiving payment of a Disabled Contributor’s Child 's B enefit or a Surviving Child’s benefit on behalf of a child, and there remained unpaid child benefits when the payee died, the deceased’s estate is not entitled to receive those payments. Should any child's benefit remain unpaid at the time of the payee’s death, the relevant benefits are paid to the person or institution who assumes custody and control of the child or they are paid to the child directly if they are now +18. There may be cases where an estate is closed and the representative does not wish to re-open the estate or does not wish to accept the unpaid benefit. In cases where the former executor, administrator or trustee advises they do not wish to administer the underpayment for distribution, they should send a letter of “No Intent” advising the Department the estate does not wish to pursue the matter. Upon receipt of the letter, the Minister has discretionary authority to release the payment to someone else (usually to the survivor or the next of kin).

If benefit payments remain unpaid at the time of death, the Minister has: a duty to make reasonable efforts to identify an appropriate payee; and to issue the payments. There is no time limit from the Date of Death by which the payments must be claimed and paid. However, once a payee is identified, the unpaid benefit should be released as quickly as possible.

topic_title: Example 2—Using the first additional contributory period Disability Drop-in ratio when calculating a benefit Updated
text: Disability Drop-in values and Adjusted Pensionable Earnings when calculating a benefit Disability Drop-in (DDI) values are dropped in during the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) calculation for an RTR or an SVR pension. The first additional or second additional DDI value will only be dropped into the benefit calculation if it is greater than the actual first additional or second additional APE amount and is to the client's benefit. If the DSB recipient has received additional pension credits as a result of a credit split or has had Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) amounts attributed for the period of disability, the actual APE may be higher than the DDI amount. The DDI amount cannot be attributed to any month that is outside the period the client is deemed disabled. The DDI and the actual APE values must be broken down into monthly amounts and compared because there could be some months where the DDI amount is greater and others where the actual APE is greater. The greater of the monthly DDI amount or the actual APE is applied to each month excluded due to disability for the year the amount is attributed and used in the benefit calculation. Using Taylor from Example 1, let us assume Taylor's DSB converted into an RTR pension when they reached age 65 in January of 2024. The Average Yearly Maximum Pensionable Earnings (AYMPE) used to calculate the RTR-FBC for an RTR is: The AYMPE of the year the DSB started, if a DSB was paid after age 60; or The AYMPE of the year the RTR starts, if there was not a DSB paid after age 60. The phase-in factor must be applied to the first additional DDI values for 2021-2023. To determine the Yearly DDI Value with a Phase-in, the formula is: 1st DDI factor (rounded to 5 decimal places) × phase in factor (rounded to 4 decimal places) × AYMPE used in the calculation of the Retirement or Survivor = Yearly DDI factor (rounded to 0 decimal places) In Taylor's case, they were paid a DSB after age 60 and it began in 2021, so the 2021 AYMPE of $57,780 will be used. 2021 - 0.64966 × 0.5000 × $57,780 = $18,769 2022 - 0.64966 × 0.7500 × $57,780 = $28,153 2023 - 0.64966 × 1.0000 × $57,780 = $37,537 To determine the monthly DDI, divide the DDI value by 12. 2021 - $18,769 ∕ 12 = $1,564.08 2022 - $28,153 ∕ 12 = $2,346.08 2023 - $37,537 ∕ 12 = $3,128.08 The phase-in factor must also be applied to first additional APE values for 2021-2023. To determine the yearly APE Value with a phase-in factor, the formula is: (CPP UPE + QPP UPE, rounded to 0 decimal places) × Adjustment Factor (rounded to 5 decimal places) × Phase-in factor (rounded to 4 decimal places) As we saw in Example 1, Taylor's UPE in 2021 was $40,410. In Taylor's case, they were paid a DSB after age 60 and it began in 2021, so the 2021 AYMPE of $57,780 will be divided by the 2021 YMPE amount of $61,600 to find the adjustment factor of 0.93799. The phase-in factor for 2021 is 0.5000. 40,410 × 0.93799 × 0.5000 = $18,952 To determine the monthly amount of the first additional APE, divide the APE amount by the number of contributory months with earnings and contributions. 2021 - $18,952 ∕ 12 = $1,579.33 2022 - $0 ∕ 12 = $0 2023 - $0 ∕ 12 = $0 Compare the monthly DDI amounts and the monthly APE amount and apply the greater amount. 2021 - The APE amount of $1,579.33 is higher than the DDI amount of $1,564.08 therefore the client gets 12 months of APE. 2022 - The DDI amount of $2,346.08 is higher than the APE amount of $0 therefore the client gets 12 months of DDI. 2023 - The DDI amount of $3,128.08 is higher than the APE amount of $0 therefore the client gets 12 months of DDI.

M7 is the number of months in the contributor's additional contributory period in the year in which they were deemed disabled that are before the month following the month in which they were deemed to have become disabled. The value of the Disability Drop-in ( DDI ) will be equal to 70% of the average of the first additional pensionable earnings and 70% of the second additional pensionable earnings for the 6 years (72 months) before the onset of disability, which includes the month they are deemed disabled. The 6-year average is used because those are the earnings considered when determining eligibility for a CPP DSB benefit. Providing a 70% credit is consistent with most private disability insurance plans in Canada. Drop-ins are calculated when the department converts unadjusted additional pensionable earnings into adjusted additional pensionable earnings. Therefore, they are dropped into the benefit calculation and not the individual’s earnings history. The month they are deemed disabled is included in the range for calculating the DDI values for the first and second additional contributory periods; however, the DDI starts the month after they are deemed disabled. topic_title: CPP DSB benefit ceases and an individual becomes disabled again
text: There are cases where one period of disability ceases; then a beneficiary: returns to work; has contributions and additional pensionable earnings for less than 6 years; and becomes disabled again. In such cases, the amount of the drop-in for the second period of disability is the greater of: the drop-in amount for the previous period of disability; or the drop-in amount for the second period of disability calculated using the previous 6-year period, which includes unadjusted additional pensionable earnings from pensionable employment and the drop-in amounts from the previous period of disability. This applies to multiple periods of the DSB including the reinstatement of the DSB .

topic_title: Credit Splitting (Division of first and second additional unadjusted pensionable earnings)
text: The Disability Drop-ins ( DDI ) are not subject to division upon divorce or separation (as additional unadjusted pensionable earnings are subject to division), given that they apply only at the time of a benefit calculation when unadjusted additional pensionable earnings are converted into adjusted pensionable earnings. A CPP disability beneficiary may still receive additional pension credits from their former spouse or common-law partner as a result of a division, given that the additional contributory periods do not end when disability starts. If, as a result of division of additional unadjusted pensionable earnings, the disability beneficiary has received pension credits while disabled, the greater of the 2 will be used: the drop-in value; or the pension credits. The amount of the DDI can change after a division if it affects the 6 years before the onset of disability. Given that these added credits need to be factored in, if a division of unadjusted additional pensionable earnings occurs after the drop-in amount has been calculated, and there is a change to the pensionable earnings that were used to calculate the drop-in, then both the drop-in and benefit amounts must be recalculated.

As of January 1, 2019, (first additional), and January 1, 2024, (second additional), the contributory period of CPPD beneficiaries will also be credited with drop-in amounts. The Disability Drop-in ( DDI ) provision is applicable only where the disability date of onset is after December 31, 2018. The DDI amounts are attributed only if they are advantageous for the disabled contributor. They might not necessarily be to their advantage, as while the contributor cannot work and contribute during the disability period, they may have received credits: as a result of a credit-split following divorce or separation; or from the child rearing drop-in . The drop-in amounts are used only for the purpose of calculating future benefit amounts, apart from the DSB benefit (i.e. the retirement pension and SVR pension). DDIs are applied only at the time of a benefit calculation. In 2018, Québec enhanced the QPP in the same way as the CPP enhancement. Therefore, for dual contributors, the first additional and second additional pensionable earnings under the QPP will be taken into account in calculating the DDIs. If, in the 6 years before the disability, there are child rearing drop-in amounts, these amounts will be used in the calculation of the amount of the DDI . The period covered by the DDI is the month-based period of time that an individual is disabled (rather than the period of time in receipt of a DSB benefit, which starts the fourth month after an individual is deemed disabled). Therefore, in those years where a disability starts or ends, the amount of the drop-in is prorated to take into account the fraction of the year that an individual is disabled.

During the phase-in of the CPP enhancement as of 2019 there may be fewer than 6 years (72 months) in the additional contributory period for the purpose of calculating the drop-in amount. In such cases, the actual number of months in the additional contributory period is used to determine the value. If there are no additional pensionable earnings, the value is zero. There is a maximum of 34 years of Disability Drop-ins (i.e. the CPP enhancement accumulation period of 40 years minus the 6 years that forms the basis of eligibility for the DSB benefit).

The base CPP protects Disability ( DSB ) benefit beneficiaries by excluding from the base contributory period the months that an individual is determined to be disabled. This ensures the calculation of benefit amounts is not adversely affected by periods of no earnings, and protects eligibility for the survivor’s ( SVR ) pension and subsequent DSB benefit. The CPP enhancement is designed differently. Rather than a variable contributory period, as exists in the base CPP , the CPP enhancement has 2 fixed 40-year contributory periods. Therefore, the concept of excluding periods from the CPP enhancement contributory periods is incompatible with the design of the additional CPP . Since periods cannot be excluded, periods of disability under the CPP are protected by means of a drop-in amount. As of January 1, 2019 (first additional) and as of January 1, 2024 (second additional), for each month that an individual is deemed disabled, the provision attributes to their first or second additional contributory period an amount equal to 70% of the average of their first or second additional pensionable earnings in the 6 years (72 months—including the month they are deemed disabled) before becoming disabled.

topic_title: Assessment type at reassessment—Prescheduled Return to Work assessment Updated
text: When a beneficiary self-reports educational or volunteer activities, the Reassessment work type will be created in PWS with the Description Volunteer or Education . Record it in the Rules Based Reassessment System as a Prescheduled Return to Work assessment. The goal of this assessment is to confirm continuing eligibility of the individual for disability benefits. Considerations for the assessment include: determining the level of skill or physical effort required to participate in a volunteer activity; determining if the educational activity is structured or unstructured; assessing the number of hours spent on the activity and the beneficiary's predictability of attendance; reviewing all information added to the file since the last decision; updating medical, employment, education, and other information, as required; and providing information concerning other Service Canada benefits and programs where appropriate. Factors to analyze during the assessment: results of prior reassessments and vocational rehabilitation experience; earnings, employment activity, educational activity, and volunteer activity. topic_title: Self-report of activity to Service Canada Centre or Call Centre Updated
text: Beneficiaries engaging in educational or volunteer activities for 15 hours or more per week for 4 months are required to report their activity to Service Canada. When a representative receives a report of educational or volunteer activity of 15 hours per week or more for 4 months, they must create an Enquiry – Volunteer/Education work item and update systems. The PWS maintenance work item identifies the self-reported educational or volunteer activity to the processing network. The Medical Adjudicator contacts the beneficiary within 15 business days of receipt of the PWS work item. No Enquiry-Volunteer/Education work item is created in PWS for beneficiaries reporting educational or volunteer activity less than 15 hours per week and less than 4 months to a Service Canada Centre or Call Centre representative. The beneficiary is informed to update Service Canada if the activity increases to more than 15 hours per week for 4 months.

Assess educational or volunteer activity at initial application, reconsideration or reassessment. These procedures also describe how to follow up with a beneficiary after a self-reported educational or volunteer activity assessment.

Since the inception of the CPPD program in 1966, there has been a significant shift in how disability and persons with disabilities are seen in relation to their ability to participate in the workforce. Disability is now seen as the result of environmental, social, and attitudinal barriers preventing an individual from fully participating in society. Persons with disabilities have the right to full and equal participation and inclusion in society. In light of this, a consistent and equitable approach to the assessment of work activity and SGO criteria are applied to all individuals engaged in any type of work. Accommodation Employers have an obligation to accommodate employees as long as the accommodations do not result in undue hardship to the employer. Sheltered work exception In rare cases, it may be determined an applicant or beneficiary is employed in a truly sheltered employment setting. The main purpose of this type of work is therapeutic for social connection and cognitive stimulation, rather than to provide an income. Examples of these types of sheltered settings include: the employment of institutionalized individuals in mental health facilities; and community-run programs for individuals with specific disabilities, often for those with developmental delays. A defining characteristic of sheltered work is its highly supportive nature. In light of this, a modified approach to the assessment of work and income earned should occur.

The number of hours an applicant or beneficiary participates in paid employment each week is part of the assessment in determining if this activity is reflective of work capacity. Table 1. General guideline for work activity Work hours per week Description Less than 15 hours Individuals participating in paid employment for less than 15 hours per week are usually not demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity is required. 15-30 hours Individuals participating in paid employment between 15 and 30 hours per week may be demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity should occur. More than 30 hours Individuals participating in paid employment over 30 hours per week are likely demonstrating work capacity unless there is evidence to the contrary on file.

The predictability of attendance may be reflected in an individual's ability to work scheduled shifts, in a predictable manner, over a sustained period. Consideration must be given to individuals with unpredictable or irregularly occurring medical conditions and resulting functional limitations. For example, consideration must be given to those with mental health diagnoses or cyclical conditions which have alternating periods of exacerbation and remissions. The limitations associated with such conditions may prevent the individual from being able to sustain predictable employment. These applicants or beneficiaries may therefore not be capable regularly of pursuing work. For applicants and beneficiaries with varied weekly hours of work or work attendance, a longitudinal assessment of work activity may be necessary to determine their work capacity. Development may be required.

topic_title: Assessing work capacity when earnings are at or above the SGO benchmark Updated
text: When an applicant or beneficiary has earnings at or above the SGO benchmark amount, these earnings are likely an indicator of work capacity. To ensure these earnings are due to work activity and not other factors, an assessment must be done. This includes an assessment of the: number of hours worked per week; and predictability of attendance. If it is determined that the earnings are not due to work activity, assess the applicant or beneficiary. Severe Criterion—Medical Condition and Functional Limitations (Policy) When a beneficiary is being reassessed retroactively, gaps in the earnings history may be a sign of a failed attempt to return to work. Retroactive reassessment files with up to one calendar year of earnings at or above the SGO benchmark, followed by no earnings in subsequent years, may be treated as a failed attempt to return to work where appropriate and supported by the evidence.

topic_title: Assessing work capacity when earnings are below the SGO benchmark
text: When an applicant or beneficiary has earnings below the SGO benchmark, a holistic assessment is to occur to help determine each individual's circumstances and overall work capacity. The assessment may include: the number of hours worked per week; predictability of attendance; earnings (and in the case of self-employed individuals, gross business earnings); the effect of their medical conditions and functional limitations; non-medical reasons affecting work activity; and any evidence to the contrary or information that suggests otherwise. Refer to the Evidence to the contrary section below. All evidence is to be weighed and the balance of probabilities approach is to be used in determining the eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits. For more information, Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy)

An applicant or beneficiary may report other activities which factor into the determination of the “capable regularly” portion of severe, such as: educational activities; and volunteer activities. Using the balance of probabilities standard of review, the components of hours worked and predictability of attendance should be applied to non-income generating activities to develop a better understanding of an individual's work capacity. Any educational or volunteer activities are to be considered alongside any demonstrative paid work activity as part of the assessment of overall work capacity. Educational activities Educational activities can have an important impact on an individual's future employability, particularly those from an accredited educational institution, as it builds towards a post-secondary diploma or degree. Current enrolment in an accredited educational or training program, or enrolment after the disability claim date for late applicants, are to be assessed in relation to the individual's capacity to pursue any SGO. Structured educational activities Structured educational activities are meant to provide the individual with skills and competencies that improve their capacity for work. Structured educational activities at a credential granting institution require the individual to: complete assignments; regularly attend classes (in-person or online); and potentially earn a certificate, diploma or degree. If an educational activity meets the criteria for a structured educational activity, it should be included in the assessment of an individual's overall work capacity. This assessment will include: determining the number of hours spent on the structured educational activity (includes class time and time spent studying and completing assignments, research, etc.); and the individual's predictability in attending the scheduled educational activity or training. Unstructured educational activities Unstructured educational activities are usually self-directed and do not typically result in the individual obtaining employer-recognized credentials. These activities: do not result in an increased level of employability; and do not require the same level or effort and predictability of attendance that a structured educational activity requires. Volunteer activities Current volunteer activities, or participation after the disability claim date for late applicants, are to be assessed in relation to the individual's capacity to pursue any SGO. The factors to be assessed are the same as those for paid work and include: the level of skill or physical effort required to complete the tasks; and the hours and predictability of attendance required for the volunteer position. Volunteer positions which require specialized training or work experience can be seen as equivalent to paid occupations requiring the same level of expertise or effort as per the list below. HIGHLY SKILLED (Typically sedentary work) HIGHLY SKILLED (Typically sedentary work) SKILLED (Typically sedentary work, but may include physical work which is light to medium in nature) SKILLED (Typically sedentary work, but may include physical work which is light to medium in nature) SEMI-SKILLED (Typically physical work which is medium to heavy in nature) SEMI-SKILLED (Typically physical work which is medium to heavy in nature) LOW SKILLED (Typically physical work which is heavy in nature) LOW SKILLED (Typically physical work which is heavy in nature) Skill level and volunteer Essential and universally transferable skills (Reading, Writing, Document use, Numeracy, Oral communication, Working with others, Thinking, Computer use/Digital skills, Continuous learning) HIGHLY SKILLED (Typically sedentary work) Examples: Accountant Language Instructor HR Coordinator Issues Advocate Social Policy Researcher Typically advanced level of all essential skills. Performance of duties requires specialized training (gained in post-secondary education) or experience. Volunteers require advanced skills and would command above-average wages for this position in the paid labour force. Skill level and volunteer Essential and universally transferable skills (Reading, Writing, Document use, Numeracy, Oral communication, Working with others, Thinking, Computer use/Digital skills, Continuous learning) SKILLED (Typically sedentary work, but may include physical work which is light to medium in nature) Examples: Board Member Office Administrative Assistant Child Care Provider Event Organizer/Supervisor Amateur Hockey Coach Typically advanced to moderate level of all essential skills. Performance of duties requires some specialized training (likely post-secondary education) or work experience. Volunteers may require the ability to manage or organize other volunteers or clients. Occupations with supervisory responsibilities are included here. Skill level and volunteer Essential and universally transferable skills (Reading, Writing, Document use, Numeracy, Oral communication, Working with others, Thinking, Computer use/Digital skills, Continuous learning) SEMI-SKILLED (Typically physical work which is medium to heavy in nature) Examples: Home Support Worker Fundraiser Homelessness Outreach Worker Mental Health Peer Supporter Typically moderate to basic level of essential skills Performance of duties requires little to no specialized training (with some post-secondary education typically at a college diploma or certificate level). Volunteers may engage with a public in a customer service role or be required to perform repetitive physical tasks. Skill level and volunteer Essential and universally transferable skills (Reading, Writing, Document use, Numeracy, Oral communication, Working with others, Thinking, Computer use/Digital skills, Continuous learning) LOW SKILLED (Typically physical work which is heavy in nature) Examples: Food Delivery Driver Kitchen Helper Cleaner Charity Store Stock Worker Typically basic level of essential skills. Performance of duties requires no specialized skills or experience other than some on-the-job training. Volunteers will likely be required to lift heavy objects, perform repetitive physical tasks, and be on their feet for a significant amount of time.

A decision on initial or continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits is made in “respect of whom the determination is made”. Evidence to the contrary is evidence on file (e.g. medical, employment) that shows that the individual does not have the work capacity for any SGO despite their earnings or work activity. Cases with evidence to the contrary are rare. If information is identified that suggests an individual does not have work capacity despite engaging in paid work, the decision rationale must clearly articulate what information (e.g. medical evidence, predictability) led to the determination of initial or continuing eligibility.

Effective December 13, 2021, this policy provides guidance on the assessment of work capacity where there is evidence of work activity. It applies to both applicants and beneficiaries of the CPPD benefits. The guidance is to be used in the assessment of work capacity for: individuals who are currently working (either for an employer or who are self-employed); beneficiaries who have worked since they were determined to be eligible for the CPPD benefits; and applicants who qualify under the Late Applicant Provision (LAP) who may not be working currently, but who have worked on or after their latest possible date of onset. For more information on the LAP, refer to Medical Adjudication and the Late Applicant Provision (Policy) . Medical Adjudication and the Late Applicant Provision (Policy) Interpreting the severe criterion In the Canada Pension Plan legislation, the phrase "incapable regularly of pursuing any Substantially Gainful Occupation" (SGO) defines the severe criterion. The severe criterion is a measure of work capacity. For applicants and beneficiaries engaged in paid work, work capacity is defined by 2 indicators: work activity (incapable regularly of pursuing); and income earnings from a work activity (any SGO). Assessment of earnings from work activity In May 2014, CPP Regulations came into force which defined any SGO as one that provides a salary or wage equal to or greater than the maximum amount a person could receive for CPPD benefits. This definition sets an earnings benchmark that clearly defines an SGO and serves as a measurement of work capacity. Considering this, earnings can be categorized as: earnings below the SGO benchmark; and earnings at or above the SGO benchmark. Other considerations

Seasonal work is work activity that occurs at around the same time each year for the duration of a season, or longer if required for the completion of a specific job. Generally, seasonal work has predetermined beginning and end dates due to seasonal factors. Assessment of work capacity for individuals engaged in seasonal work is the same as for those engaged in other work activities. For more information, refer to the Assessment of earnings from work activity section above. Additional considerations for seasonal work include: work history; earnings history; identified patterns of work activity; and a determination as to the beneficiary having stopped working due to: a shortage of work; their medical condition; or a combination of both. If the applicant or beneficiary demonstrates the ability to work predictably in a seasonal capacity, they are demonstrating work capacity and benefits will likely be denied or ceased. The assessment of earnings and work activity for self-employed individuals considers gross business earnings but is otherwise the same as the assessment used for employed individuals. topic_title: Determining the deemed date of an OAS/CPP pensions application
text: The deemed date of receipt is earlier than the eligibility date The deemed date of receipt of a CPP pension application is more than 11 months after the earliest eligibility date Medically determining the deemed Date of Application for CPPD benefits Diagnosis : chronic vegetative state, meningitis, encephalitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis. March 22, 2016 The applicant was referred to the intensive care unit because the applicant: had a resurgence of fever; had an alteration in mental status and hypotension; failed to regain consciousness; and eventually had to be intubated and ventilated. At the Date of Application (DOA), the applicant remains in a vegetative comatose state without the ability to respond in any way to their environment. The applicant had an acute event resulting in a hospitalization in March 2016. Table 1. The facts Event Date DOA January 7, 2018 (55 years old) Date stopped work March 3, 2016 (due to medical reasons) Claim date of disability March 2016 Latest Possible Date of Onset December 2018 Earliest Possible Date of Onset October 2016 Determination of the deemed DOA The medical evidence shows the applicant became disabled within the meaning of CPP in March 2016. The applicant has been unable to form or express the intent to apply for benefits since March 2016 when they lost consciousness. The incapacity provision allows you to provide a new earlier deemed DOA. The applicant's new earlier deemed DOA is the later of: the month before the first month the relevant benefit could have started to be paid; or the month the applicant's last relevant period of incapacity started. The applicant became disabled in March 2016 and the effective date of payment could have been July 2016. The month before this is June 2016, therefore, the incapacity started in March 2016. The latest of these 2 dates is June 2016. The new deemed DOA is June 2016 and the applicant's disability Date of Onset will be March 2016 with benefits becoming payable in July 2016.

Diagnosis : Longstanding bipolar disorder with worsening of symptoms and severe traumatic brain injury. September 2021 The applicant was involved in a car accident which resulted in: traumatic brain injury; hospitalization for urgent care; subsequent admission to a rehabilitation facility for one year; and dependent for full-time care. At the Date of Application (DOA), the applicant has made minimal recovery from the traumatic brain injury and continues to require full-time care. The applicant had an acute event in September 2021 resulting in hospitalization followed by extensive rehabilitation. Prior to this event, the applicant stopped working in November 2020 due to significant worsening of their longstanding bipolar disorder. Table 2. The facts Event Date DOA September 2023 Date stopped work November 2020 Claim date of disability November 2020 Early Retirement (ERTR) pension in pay January 2021 Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) N/A (receiving ERTR >15 months) Earliest Possible Date of Onset (EPDOO) N/A Determination of the deemed date of application The medical evidence shows the applicant became disabled within the meaning of CPP in November 2020. The applicant has been unable to form or express the intent to apply for benefits since September 2021, when they suffered a traumatic brain injury, and despite rehabilitation, impairments remained, resulting in the need for full-time care. The incapacity provision allows you to provide a new earlier deemed DOA. The applicant’s new earlier deemed DOA is the later of: the month before the first month the relevant benefit could have started to be paid; or the month the applicant’s last relevant period of incapacity started. The applicant became disabled in November 2020 and the effective date of payment could have been March 2021. The month before this is February 2021 . The incapacity started September 2021 . The latest of these 2 dates is September 2021. In this situation, the new earlier deemed DOA is September 2021. The new earlier deemed DOA changes the length of time the applicant has been in pay for ERTR, it is now less than 15 months. A new earnings and contributions review is needed to determine the LPDOO for CPP benefits. Once this review is completed by the SCBO, the file is reviewed to clarify eligibility for DSB and PRDB. Table 3. The facts Event Date New earlier deemed DOA September 2021 Date stopped work November 2020 Claim date of disability November 2020 In pay for ERTR January 2021 LPDOO December 2020 PRDB LPDOO (2019) May 2023 PRDB LPDOO (2023) December 2023 EPDOO June 2020 Determination of the Date of Onset The medical evidence shows the applicant was disabled within the meaning of CPP in November 2020 when they were no longer able to work due to worsening of their medical condition.

topic_title: The claim of incapacity is received beyond the 90-day reconsideration or appeal period
text: The applicant turned 65 years of age in June 2015. An application for an OAS pension is submitted on their behalf in January 2017. In May 2017, the applicant was approved for an OAS pension with a retroactive effective date of February 2016. In February 2021, a Declaration of Incapacity - Physician's Report (ISP-1800) form was received by the Department indicating that the applicant became incapacitated in October 2014 due to a serious illness and remains incapacitated to this day. The applicant may have been incapacitated since October 2014; however, the claim of incapacity was received after the 90-day reconsideration period of the initial decision. For the claim of incapacity to be reviewed and considered, the applicant would need to submit a reconsideration request for an extension of the 90-day time limit. If the criteria is met to extend the 90-day time limit, the claim of incapacity can be reviewed and considered. If the criteria to extend the 90-day time limit are not met, the claim of incapacity cannot be considered.

topic_title: GIS/ALW/ALWS and Emergency COVID Benefits: Questions and Answers
text: Q1. Why has my Guaranteed Income Supplement/Allowance/Allowance for the Survivor payment gone down or stopped? If you received one of the emergency COVID benefits such as Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB)/Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB), Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) , Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB) and Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB), they are taxable benefits that are considered income under the Income Tax Act and will be included in the calculation of your Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS)/Allowance (ALW)/Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefits in July 2021. This may affect the amount you will receive for the period of July 2021 to June 2022. Q2. Who is affected by this? Individuals, or couples, who received emergency COVID benefits and saw an increase in their 2020 income could see a change in the amount of their benefits. Q3. Why is this happening now? Every July, the Department reassesses an individual’s entitlement for income-tested benefits based on the individual’s income, or the combined income of a couple. Therefore, payments can increase, decrease or even cease according to reported changes in annual net income. Q4. Does the Department have to include the emergency COVID benefits in the calculation for income-tested benefits? Yes, the emergency COVID benefits are considered income under the Income Tax Act and must be included in the calculation of GIS/ALW/ALWS benefits. Q5. Are there differences between CERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and EI ERB for GIS purposes? Yes, there are differences. As EI ERB is considered an employment insurance benefit, its cessation can be considered an optionable event. CERB, CRB, CRSB and CRCB are not considered as pension income or employment income and cannot trigger an option request. Q6. I am no longer receiving the emergency COVID benefits and my GIS/ALW/ALWS has gone down. Is there anything I can do? If you received EI ERB payments issued by Service Canada, you can complete a Statement of Estimated Income form. This will be processed and your entitlement for the GIS/ALW/ALWS will be reviewed. Q7. My GIS/ALW/ALWS stopped in July. Are there any other benefits I can receive? Seniors are encouraged to visit the Benefits Finder on the Canada.ca website to ensure they are receiving all the benefits to which they are entitled. This website also provides information on provincial benefits. Assess gross business earnings for the self-employed individual. Gross business earnings is the total sum of the money from work activities that lead to producing a product or service for the purpose of generating income. Similar to a highly paid employee where the Substantially Gainful Occupation (SGO) threshold can be reached in a short amount of time, earnings from work activities that are above the SGO threshold are an indicator of work capacity regardless of the hours spent working. The client's application for benefits will likely be denied or their benefits ceased based on earnings alone. Relationship between types of self-employment and gross business earnings In a sole proprietorship : a business is owned exclusively by one person; there is no separation between the business and the owner; and the owner is responsible for any debts or liabilities. In a sole proprietorship, the gross business earnings are gross personal earnings. In a partnership , 2 or more legal entities operate a shared business as: a general partnership—the partners share both profits and liabilities; or a limited partnership—a limited partner may only contribute financially and be involved in financial decisions but is not otherwise involved in the business. In a partnership, gross business earnings are split based on the percentage each partner has in the business. Example If the individual is in a partnership with a 40% share of the business, calculate 40% of the gross business earnings as follows: $40,000 gross business earnings multiplied by 40% = $16,000 gross business earnings for the individual. In a corporation : the business is a distinct legal entity separate from the owner(s); the owner(s) are not responsible for debts and liabilities; and the owner(s) can withdraw a salary or dividend from the business that becomes their personal income. Gross business earnings represent work effort. The self-employed person may choose to draw a salary or dividends from the business, but this amount is based on factors other than work activity. A corporation can have owners with different percentages of shares in the company. Gross business earnings should be split when considering the individual's gross business earnings percentage. Example If the individual is in a partnership with a 40% share of the business, calculate 40% of the gross business earnings as follows: $40,000 gross business earnings multiplied by 40% - $16,000 gross business earnings for the individual.
