An individual may decline, up until the day of their 65th birthday, the automatic enrolment of: an OAS pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) benefit at the same time; the GIS benefit alone; or an OAS pension after the GIS benefit has already been declined. Automatic enrolment may be declined by: opting out through MSCA; sending a letter declining OAS and GIS, GIS alone or OAS after the GIS has already been declined; or returning the OAS Automatic Enrolment Notification letter (ISP3009 or ISP3030) to the Department with a note (separately or made directly on the notification letter) declining the OAS and GIS, GIS alone or OAS after the GIS has already been declined. If an individual opts out of automatic enrolment through MSCA, an online confirmation and a transaction record are generated. There are two reports generated for individuals who opt out through MSCA: OAS Early Auto-Enrolment - MSCA Opt Out: this report flags accounts with a “pending” account status (A/S 4); OAS-GIS Opt Out Date in Month of Clients 65th Birthday: this report flags accounts with an “in-pay” account status (A/S 1). The reports are loaded as work items on individual accounts in PWS. The barcodes used are RPT-OPTOUT-MSCA-OASGIS and RPT-OPTOUT-INMONTH65.

topic_title: Adjustment of estimated income and cancellation of an option
text: Individuals who were granted an option are required to advise the Department if they have underestimated or overestimated their income should they become aware of these situations. Individuals who are receiving benefits based on estimated income may cancel their option at any time. If a revised estimate results in the beneficiary losing entitlement to a benefit or is entitled to less than they would be if the base calendar year income were used, the benefit must be adjusted. If this review results in an underpayment or an overpayment, the necessary actions must be taken to balance the account and the beneficiary must be advised accordingly in writing.

The effective date of an option is the month following the month of retirement, the first month in which the pension is not paid, or the month the reduction of the pension income takes place. Effective date of retirement The date of retirement is the last day the individual receives income from that office or employment. This could occur in the month the employee actually performs the duties of the position, or it could be the last day the employee receives regular salary or wages, i.e. where an employee is on leave and is being paid regular salary or wages (e.g. vacation or sick leave) until the date of actual retirement. For a self-employed person, the date of retirement is the last day in which they actively carry on that business or terminate their business activities. Where an individual gives the first day of a month as the date of retirement, it should be clarified as to when the actual last day of employment or self-employment occurred. Effective date of option The option is effective in the month following retirement. Effective date of termination or reduction of pension income For pension income, the loss is suffered: in the first month or periodic payment period the individual receives no pension; or the first month or periodic payment period they receive a reduced pension. Effective date of option The option is effective for the first month or periodic payment period in which the pension is either not paid or is paid at a reduced rate. If the periodic payment is annual , the effective date of the option is the first month of the year ( January ) in which the payment is reduced or the first month of the year ( January ) the pension is not paid. If the periodic payment is semi-annual , the effective date of the option is the first month of the 6-month period ( January and July ) in which the payment is reduced or the first 6-month period ( January and July ) the pension is not paid. If the periodic payment is quarterl y, the effective date of the option is the first month of the 3-month period ( January, April, July, and Octobe r) in which the payment is reduced or the first 3-month period ( January, April, July and October ) the pension is not paid. If the payment is monthly , the effective date of the option is the month the payment is reduced or the first month the pension is not paid.

An option may be granted to an individual who has retired from employment or self-employment, has ceased to carry on a business, or has a loss of income due to termination or reduction of pension income. These are called "optionable events". When an option is granted, entitlement to an income-tested benefit is determined based on estimated income for the current calendar year rather than on actual income for the base calendar year. The base calendar year is the last calendar year ending before the current payment period. Estimated income is what an individual foresees receiving after the event. One event may result in two options referred to as the "Current Year Option" and the "Previous Year Option". The event date determines the type of option. If the event occurs in the current payment period or the previous 6 months, it is a current year option. If the event is in the calendar year immediately preceding the payment period, it is a previous year option. An option is intended to act as a buffer from the financial impact of retirement, or from the termination or reduction of a pension income. It must only be granted if it is to the pensioner's or beneficiary's advantage. Each payment period is looked at separately to determine if an option is beneficial. If the current year option is not beneficial but the previous year option is, then the previous year option may be granted and vice versa. They are not dependent on one another.

topic_title: Events to be considered to grant an option Updated
text: Loss of employment or self-employment income Individuals may be granted an option when they cease to be employed, or cease to carry on a business. Individuals "retire for option purposes" when they no longer receive income from employment or at the end of the month in which they cease to actively carry on a business. Retirement from employment Individuals are considered "retired" from their employment when their regular relationship with the employer has been interrupted. "Regular" means at least 2 consecutive payments of a biweekly salary or four consecutive payments of a weekly wage. They could also be retired if there has been a significant reduction in their normal work period and earnings. Individuals may also be considered retired in the following situations: They retire from their regular employment and subsequently find another job. They would be considered retired from the first place of employment. They return to work for a former employer but occupy a different position at a lower wage, regardless of when the return to work took place. In these situations, any income earned after the event would be included in the estimate of income unless otherwise stated. Retirement from self-employment Self-employed individuals may be considered to have retired if they have taken steps to discontinue their business. In the case of a fisher, this might mean the sale of their license. Where a farmer is concerned, the land may have been sold or left fallow. Loss of pension income An option may be granted when an individual has a loss of income due to termination or reduction of pension income. For option purposes, "pension income" is defined as: Any annuity payments, including Registered Retirement Income Fund payments and Registered Retirement Savings Plan regular payments. CPP or QPP benefits, other than a death benefit. Superannuation or pension payments. Wage loss replacement income, i.e. a private disability pension, health insurance and salary insurance, if they are considered as pension income for income tax purposes (a T4 is issued). Spousal and child support payments received after a formal agreement or a court order. Pension income unduly received. Payments under a Provincial or Territorial Workers' Compensation known as Commission des normes de l'équité de la santé et de la securité du travail in Quebec. Employment Insurance benefits. Foreign pension income.

A retroactive option may be granted once the following conditions are met: There is eligibility for income-tested benefits for the period of the option. An application or statement of income must have already been submitted for the income-tested benefit or the data transfer of income must have already been received from the Canada Revenue Agency. Receipt of the option form is within the legislated timeframes.

Seasonal work If an individual temporarily ceases seasonal employment (school crossing guards, fishing guides, construction workers, etc.), an option is not granted when the seasonal employment ends. "Seasonal work" is generally used to describe a work situation that is irregular in nature, i.e. road work construction crews who may work April-October, or a server who only works during the peak Christmas period or summer months when the restaurant is busiest. The employee does not "retire" or terminate work each year. They have a habitual relationship with their employer and the intention is to return during the next cycle. A seasonal worker is not entitled to an option each time their work ends because there is no true loss of income. There may be variations in earnings, but it is "regular" in the sense that they return to the same employer and earn approximately the same wage each year. A seasonal worker would be entitled to an option when the habitual relationship with the employer terminates, and they do not intend to return to work for the next cycle. The option would be effective in the month following retirement, i.e. the last month duties are performed. CPP or QPP income CPP or QPP Pension Sharing An option cannot be granted in cases where CPP pensioners share a portion of their CPP or QPP RTR pension with their spouse or common-law partner as there is no actual loss of income for the couple. However, the termination of pension sharing due to separation, divorce or death constitutes a reduction of pension income for one of the two individuals involved and an option may be granted effective the month the pension sharing ceases. CPP or QPP Credit Splitting An option may be granted where there is a termination or reduction of a CPP or QPP pension or benefit because of a Credit Split. PRB PRB payments are included as income for the purposes of calculating entitlement to OAS income-tested benefits. In addition, the PRB is considered a benefit under the CPP or QPP, and as such, considered pension income as per the OAS Regulations. The PRB is normally paid on a monthly basis. However, the first payment is generally issued in April as a lump-sum payment for the months of January to March. A beneficiary who has received an arrears lump-sum PRB may experience a reduction in PRB income the following month when the regular monthly payments resume. The fluctuation in PRB income from one month to the next is part of the normal payment pattern. Therefore, there is no overall loss of PRB income from year to year and an option cannot be granted and should be denied. However, when the PRB lump-sum payment has a retroactive payment for previous years' entitlement that is not part of the regular payment pattern, consideration can be given to granting an option if there is a loss or reduction in pension income. CPP or QPP lump-sum payments In order to prevent lengthy delays in the payment of benefits, the CPP or QPP provides for the interim calculation of a CPP or QPP benefit based on the earnings that are posted to the Record of Earnings at the time the application is being processed. Once the total earnings have been posted, the CPP or QPP benefit can be revised and recalculated. This could result in a retroactive lump-sum payment to a beneficiary. A delay in processing a CPP or QPP pension, such as an RTR or SVR pension or DSB , could also result in a retroactive lump-sum payment. If the CPP or QPP lump-sum is a retroactive payment that includes entitlement for a previous year and the amount is not considered under the Notional Tax Provision (i.e. the retroactive amount from previous years is less than $300.00), entitlement to an option can be considered. Lump-sum CPP or QPP payments that remain after the notional tax has been applied, or that do not consist of arrears from previous years, are not optionable. As there is no loss of pension income within the calendar year in which the lump-sum was received, there is no need to use the option provision. CPP or QPP enhancement As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in the CPP or/ QPP enhancement; a new component of the CPP or/ QPP. The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but a "top-up" to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP or/ QPP. The enhancement is called "Additional CPP or/ QPP". Gradual increases to CPP or/ QPP contribution rates will take place over a 7-year period (2019 to 2025). Starting in June 2022, beneficiaries who made valid contributions in January 2019 or later will start to receive the first additional component of their benefit, including any retroactive amounts. Those who begin receiving a benefit in June 2022 or later will be paid the first additional component as part of their regular monthly amount. The lump-sum payments received are to be treated as described in the CPP or QPP lump-sum payments section above. Wage loss replacement income Salary insurance payments Payments from this source are generally issued in the same amount as the salary they replace so an option is not granted when the individual stops working, as there has been no actual loss of income. An option could be granted when the insurance payments cease and work does not resume. Wage loss replacement income Wage loss replacement income can be optionable depending on the source of the income and whether or not the individual is the sole contributor to the plan. Payments from a plan to which the individual was the sole contributor are not considered income for income tax purposes, or for GIS/ ALW / ALWS purposes, and therefore would not be granted an option. In these cases, an option may be granted when the individual stops working, but not when the wage loss replacement income reduces or ceases. Health or disability insurance (if considered income for income tax purposes - T4 issued) Payments from this source generally cover 80% of the salary replaced. An option is granted when the person stops working and again when the health insurance ceases if the individual does not return to work. Income from a Plan to which the applicant was the sole contributor An option may be granted when the individual stops working but not when this income ceases or reduces as it is not considered income for income tax purposes or for GIS/ ALW / ALWS . Child or spousal support payments Spousal support payments These payments are included in the definition of pension income and, if such payments are considered income for income tax purposes, an option may be granted when they cease or reduce. Generally, spousal support payments are received on a monthly basis; however, a different schedule can be negotiated. In cases where there is a different or irregular schedule, the option would be effective when the loss occurs. For irregular schedules (no fixed schedule), the pension would be assessed year over year. The individual could be granted an option effective January of the year the loss occurred (i.e. the year the income reduces, or the first year no income is received). Child support payments Child support payments made after April 30, 1997, as a result of a court order or written agreement are not included in the income of the recipient, nor are they considered as deductions from the income of the payer, and would therefore not be granted an option. However, for agreements made prior to May 1, 1997, the new tax rules may not apply. If the payments are considered income for the recipient, then an option could be granted when the child support payments end or are reduced. Pension income splitting Under the Income Tax Act , an individual may elect to share their eligible pension income (private pension, superannuation, Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP)/Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) including life income fund, annuity income, etc.) with their spouse or common-law partner in order to lower their joint tax liability. This is known as the "pension income splitting" provision. Since OAS income-tested benefits are calculated on the combined income of a couple, the pension income splitting provision does not affect the majority of beneficiaries. However, it may have a negative impact in cases where couples' income-tested benefits are calculated on estimated income, but elected to split their pension income in the base calendar year. When individuals are eligible to have their income calculated based on an estimate, do not include the split pension amount if it is now disadvantageous to the couple. Any member of the couple so disadvantaged may submit a new statement of income or an "Election to Remove Pension Income Splitting" form in order to disregard the pension income split. Foreign pension income Pension income also includes foreign pensions i.e. British pensions, U.S. Social Security pensions, German war widows' pensions, etc. However, not all foreign pensions are considered income for OAS income-tested benefit purposes. If a foreign pension income is considered income for OAS income-tested benefit purposes, then an option could be offered if it ceases or reduces. Pension income unduly received An individual is not entitled to a pension if the pension income is unduly received. In such a case, the pension is terminated and the individual must repay it. Pension income is optionable and therefore, if that pension income ceases, an option may be granted in certain situations. If the pension is repaid in the same calendar year that it was received, the total amount of the benefits paid in that year will either be adjusted prior to the tax slip being issued (for a net amount of $0.00), or the pension repayment will be reported as a deduction in the same calendar year. In both scenarios, no actual loss has occurred and no option can be offered unless the beneficiary is negatively impacted after calculating an option for another event. If the pension has been received in one calendar year and the repayment(s) occur in subsequent calendar years, the income reported is not offset. This is considered a loss and the individual would be entitled to an option for the termination of the pension. In cases where the individual continues to receive a pension from the same source and a recovery rate is applied to repay the overpayment, the amount will be netted on the tax slip for that year. This is often seen when CPP DSB are ceased and recovered from a CPP RTR pension. In these cases, it appears that the retirement pension was reduced however, it is not an actual reduction in the individual's entitlement (rate) and an option cannot be granted. However, an option can be granted for the termination of the DSB benefits. Estimating pension income unduly received If an option is granted for another event and the individual is repaying the pension income from an ongoing benefit (e.g. CPP DSB from their RTR pension), the benefits are estimated using the entitlement rate minus the repayment amount. If an option is granted for another event and the individual has repaid the pension income as a lump sum, the repayment is reported as a deduction and will appear on Block 9 . This is often seen with Employment Insurance (EI) benefits. The benefit income received must be included in the estimated income per regular procedure, however the repayment is not included when calculating the estimated income. The deduction for the overpayment recovery is captured and used as part of the base calendar year income. Proof of reimbursement must be obtained or confirmed through the CRA income feed. Provincial workers' compensation payments Payments under Provincial and Territorial Workers' Compensation (known as La Commission des normes de l'équité de la santé et de la securité du travail in Quebec) that cease or reduce are entitled to an option effective the first month no payment or a reduced amount is received. The option is calculated based on the reduced rate, even if a payment at the higher rate was made in that month. EI benefits EI benefits are calculated on a weekly basis and paid for calendar weeks commencing Sunday and ending Saturday and are normally paid in arrears. For option purposes, EI benefits terminate when the entitlement ceases (not at the last payment). The effective date of the option is the first month of no EI entitlement. Weekly EI payments can fluctuate over the course of a person's entitlement if they have earnings or are unavailable for work. An option may be granted when an individual has a loss of income due to a termination of or reduction in pension income. For EI purposes this means that their EI entitlement must actually cease or their actual entitlement must reduce due to a recalculation. If the EI payments are less 1 week or their payment is $0.00 for a few weeks, their entitlement may not have changed. The benefit must actually end as it would when they return to work or when they have claimed all the weeks that they were entitled to claim. Estimating EI income When estimating EI income, the estimate must include all pension income received beginning the effective month of the option. Therefore, it is the payments received that are used in the calculation of the estimated income, not the entitlement for the month. If an individual retires in January, and the individual's entitlement to EI begins in January, but the payment for all or part of that January entitlement is paid in February, that amount received in February is included in the estimate. Under this same concept, EI benefits are reported to the CRA in the same year they are received. Therefore, if an individual retires in December and the individual's EI entitlement begins in December but the payment for all or part of that December entitlement is paid in January, that amount received in January is included in the estimate. For ease of processing and alignment purposes, use the ‘date processed' from Full Text Screens as the 'date received'. Intermittent or seasonal work If an individual draws EI benefits intermittently between jobs, or as a seasonal worker, their regular income consists of employment income followed by EI income from year to year. This forms a consistent pattern of a relatively steady income from year to year and therefore there is no overall loss of income. When this EI entitlement ends, it is not an optionable event. However, when EI benefits are paid for the last time and the individual does not resume work, they may be considered to have had a loss in pension income and an option could be offered. In such cases, if the individual subsequently returns to work after a significant break, any income derived from employment during that calendar year must be included in the estimate of income, as EI benefits are considered to be pension income and not employment income. Provincial programs funded through EI The EI program transfers funds to provinces to implement and administer job creation work projects. The income an individual gains from these projects can be considered as pension income for the purposes of calculating GIS/ ALW / ALWS entitlement and an option can be granted when the program ends depending on how it is reported to the CRA. COVID-19 emergency benefits Effective July 2022, Bill C-12 amended the definition of "income" under Section 2 of the OAS Act to exempt certain federal emergency benefits from the calculation of income for GIS, ALW or the ALWS purposes. These emergency benefits include: the Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); the Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and the Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Benefits received in the 2021 taxation year or later, which have been reduced or ceased, are not entitled to an option. Prior to Bill C-12 coming into effect, emergency benefits were taxable benefits considered net income under the Income Tax Act, and were considered income when determining entitlement to income-tested benefits. EI ERB Under the OAS Regulations, pension income for the purpose of an option includes amounts received as “EI benefits”. Therefore, prior to Bill C-12 coming into effect, EI ERB was considered pension income in the same manner as EI benefits and the cessation or reduction of EI ERB could trigger an option. If an EI ERB ceases, an individual is entitled to an option regardless of whether the individual returned to work or started to receive another emergency benefit, i.e. CRB, CERB, etc. All additional employment income is to be estimated for the year and combined with any income received from the base calendar year. CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB The cessation of CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB cannot trigger an option as these benefits are not considered pension income under the OAS Regulations. For accounts where individuals claimed they were in a dire need situation and were granted an option after their emergency benefits ceased, the option is still valid as this was the direction in place at the time. These options will continue until the income from an emergency benefit is no longer part of the base calendar year income. RRSP income RRSP Income is considered as income in the year that it is withdrawn and is not considered pension income. Therefore, it is not eligible for an option. RRSP lump-sum withdrawals are included as other income and is included in the base calendar year's income. This source of income cannot be excluded from the individual's total income. Contributions made to a RRSP or RRIF are deducted from the base calendar year income. The net total from the base calendar year is added to/or deducted from the estimate of optionable income when calculating the income to be used for an option. Annuity payment from a RRSP An annuity payment from an RRSP, received by an individual who has attained the age of 65 before the end of the taxation year, is considered pension income. Since these annuity payments are considered pension income, an option is granted if they cease or reduce. RRIF income (including transfers from an RRSP) Income from a RRIF is considered pension income. All RRIF accounts have a minimum amount that must be withdrawn annually. An individual may be entitled to an option if there is a reduction in their regularly scheduled withdrawals, where the RRIF payments cease or a lump sum is withdrawn and the fund is depleted. If there is an option after the reduction of the RRIF payment, the reduced payment for the remainder of the calendar year starting in the month/period of reduction is prorated and included in the calculation of the estimated income. Regular and predetermined RRIF payments If RRIF payments are received at a regular and predetermined schedule and rate (periodic payments), any reduction or termination of the payments is considered to have occurred the month after the end of the RRIF periodic payment. The optionable event occurs in the first month of the period in which the payment is reduced or stopped. Irregular RRIF payments For individuals who do not have a regular and predetermined schedule for RRIF payments, their periodic payments are considered as annual payments. The total amount that is estimated to be received in the current calendar year will be compared to the total amount received in the previous calendar year. If there is a decrease, the optionable event occurs in January of the current calendar year. The effective date of the option will be January of the same year. Lump-sum RRIF payments An option will be granted only when the total amount of the RRIF is withdrawn, that is, if the RRIF is depleted. An option cannot be granted after a partial lump-sum RRIF withdrawal. If the total amount of the RRIF is withdrawn, the effective date of the option is the first month following the period in which the lump sum was withdrawn. Lump-sum RRIF payments with regular RRIF payments If an individual who receives regular and predetermined RRIF payments also withdraws a lump sum (where the fund is not depleted), the lump-sum payment will be considered to have been received in the calendar year in which it was withdrawn. Therefore, the lump-sum payment will be included (without prorating) with the estimated income whether the lump-sum payment is withdrawn before or after the optional event. Multiple RRIF payments If an individual receives payments from more than one RRIF, the same rules must be applied to each RRIF, as each RRIF is considered a separate fund. Residual payments on RRIF accounts When an RRIF is depleted, the financial institution can issue a final payment known as the residual payment if there is any money left in the fund, e.g. interest, financial charges, etc. Even though the residual RRIF payment is part of the RRIF that was depleted, the receipt of the residual payment is considered as a separate lump-sum payment and not as a regular RRIF payment. An option can be granted the month after it is received. RRIF income transferred from a deceased spouse or common-law partner RRIF income received as a result of a transfer of funds from a deceased spouse or common-law partner (usually in a lump sum) is optionable if the RRIF income is not re-invested in whole or in part. If the transferred RRIF income is reinvested in an RRSP, into another RRIF or into an annuity, the RRIF income will not be eligible for an option. The individual has not had a loss of pension income because they can deduct the eligible amount of the transferred RRIF income from their total income. If the individual is already being paid benefits based on an option when a transfer of RRIF income from the deceased spouse or common-law partner occurs, and they reinvest it in whole or in part (and this lump-sum amount was not granted an option), it could disadvantage them in one year (as this payment would be included as income), and over-advantage them the following year (when the eligible amount of the transferred RRIF income is deducted from their total income). Extension of RRSP contributions to age 71 Options are not granted to individuals who choose to stop receiving their RRIF payments because they want to contribute more to a RRSP. There is no loss of income is these situations. Lump-sum pension income Lump-sum payments that fall under the definition of “pension income” may qualify for an option. Lump-sum payments are declared as other income to the CRA. These payments may include a retroactive lump-sum payment (arrears), an amount replacing future payments or a simple one-time payment. To review payments of lump-sum pension income for options, the following 2 criteria must be considered: Is the lump-sum payment considered as “pension income”? Has the individual had a loss of income as a result of the cessation or reduction of pension income? If the answer is “no” to either of the questions above, the individual cannot be granted an option. Any pension income received in a calendar year after an optionable event is included in the estimate of income. Therefore "pension income" must include the lump sum for prior optionable events until the month following the receipt of the lump sum. The lump-sum amount is excluded the month after its receipt, as this is when the loss of income occurs. Effective date of lump-sum options The effective date of the option is the beginning of the payment period, where the receipt of the lump sum falls in the base calendar year unless the lump sum is impacted by another event. Single event lump-sum payments If a lump-sum payment is the only optionable event occurring in the current payment period, and it is not impacted by any other statement of estimated income, then it is considered to be a single event lump-sum payment. The individual does not have a loss of income until the payment period when the lump-sum payment becomes part of the base year income. As a result, for single event lump-sum payments, only a previous year option will be granted to the individual. Multiple event lump-sum payments If the lump-sum payment is not the only event in the current payment period or it affects or is affected by the statement of estimated income for another optionable event, the option is treated as a multiple event lump sum. This is to ensure that the individual is not disadvantaged by the interaction. If there are multiple events, including a lump-sum payment, it must be included in any option period that is prior to the receipt of the lump-sum payment and must be excluded the month following the receipt of the lump-sum payment. Option following the retirement of fishing licences Each fishing licence is considered to be a separate business and, therefore, subject to an option when that business ceases. A holder of 3 different fishing licences could be granted 3 options because of ceasing the businesses for which the licences were designated. Options are also available for employees of the business.

topic_title: Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income for the Year 20XX (ISP-3041)
text: For income-tested benefit purposes, the option provision offers the individual and/or their spouse or common-law partner a choice to have their income calculated based on an estimate or based on their income from the base calendar year. The individual must provide a written request to calculate their income using an estimate. To process an option, an individual must submit their income for the base calendar year, and must provide it via a statement of income, or via the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income feed. An individual must also submit the Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income for the Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form for the year of the event. This form meets the legislative requirements and provides the authorization to calculate the individual's income based on their estimated income. The statement of estimated income form must capture all the information required, including: a clear request for an option; a statement confirming the month of retirement or loss or reduction of pension income; a statement of estimated employment or self-employment; or pension income for the year of the event or for the year following the event. The form also informs the individual of his or her responsibilities to estimate their income as accurately as possible, and that the consequence of underestimating their income could be an overpayment that must be repaid. If multiple events occur in the same calendar year, a single form can be used if the dates of all of the events within that year are recorded on the form. If the individual has another event that has not been recorded, then another statement for the same calendar year would have to be obtained. It is important that the Department has a statement of estimated income form that accurately reflects the individual's estimated income for the calendar year. If an event occurs in the future and the individual does not know the details at the time of reporting, the necessary form(s) is sent at the time the event actually occurred. Any entitlement is then recalculated after the form is received from the individual.

topic_title: Submission of an option form by an estate
text: If an applicant dies after submitting a GIS, ALW or ALWS application and it is determined that the deceased had an optionable event before their death, the estate, or legal representative may be asked to complete and sign an option form. If the beneficiary dies intestate or the estate has been closed, an Indemnity Agreement (Old Age Security and Canada Pension Plan) (ISP-0425) form must be submitted with the completed option form. The option form must be accompanied by supporting documentation before retroactive benefits based on the option are approved and paid. This type of documentation may consist of: the income tax report of the deceased; a letter from the deceased individual's employer; a notice of acceptance from CPP or QPP; or any other document which supports the estimate of income. An option can be granted if a deceased applicant applied for the GIS/ ALW / ALWS benefit before their Date of Death (DOD), and the option form and supporting documents are submitted after the DOD.

topic_title: Time limit for submission of the statement of estimated income
text: The statement of estimated Income must be submitted within the legislated timeframes. The timeframes are calculated based on the date of the event. All requests must be date stamped to ensure the time limits are correctly applied. The following rules apply to time limits: If the event occurs in the current payment period, the statement of estimated income must be submitted no later than the end of the second payment period following the current payment period. If the event occurs in the previous payment period or in the 6-month period immediately before that payment period, the statement of estimated income must be submitted no later than the end of the payment period following the current payment period. If a statement of estimated income is received too late to grant a current year option, the individual may still exercise a previous year option, in the following payment period, as long as the Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form is received by the deadline.

topic_title: Types of income—employment and self-employment income Updated
text: Employment and self-employment income Individuals must report details of these payments including: the date the employment/self-employment stopped or will stop, if applicable; and the gross amounts expected before and after the event, if applicable. All employment/self-employment and pension income for the calendar year of the option is estimated. All other income is taken from the base calendar year. Any allowable deductions must be used when estimating employment or self-employment income. All other deductions allowed under the Income Tax Act will be taken from the base calendar year. An individual can retire from employment and derive an income from that employment in the calendar year of retirement, or in the calendar year following their retirement. This could include income derived from employment that is reported on line 101/10100 or 104/10400 of an individual's tax return, i.e.: vacation pay; sick leave benefits; retroactive salary adjustments (employment equity); commissions; and bonuses. It could also include income derived from employment or self-employment that is reported on line 130/13000 of an individual's tax return, i.e.: retiring allowances (severance pay); disposition of business assets; and profit sharing. This income must not be used in the calculation of an option. Further, the account will have to be reviewed the year after the year the option has ended, as the income may again be included in the base calendar year and will need to be manually removed at that time. If the individual receives subsequent employment or self-employment income from the retirement source that is beyond the calendar year following the retirement, it must be included in the calculation of income-tested benefits, and there is no legislative authority to grant a new option. Deductions allowed to reduce employment and self-employment income The following deductions are allowed to reduce employment and self-employment income and apply to each member of a couple when estimating income: CPP or QPP contributions (if known); Employment Insurance (EI) premiums (if known); Earnings deduction which is the lesser of $5,000.00 or the total earnings income; and A deduction of 50% on total earnings greater than $5,000.00 but not exceeding $15,000.00. Other income Individuals must report all other income as reported to the Canada Revenue Agency. This income includes but is not limited to: interest (from banks, bonds or mortgages); interest from estates and trusts; Canadian dividends; foreign dividends and capital gains; net income from rent; Repayment of their Registered Disability Savings Plan; Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) contributions; and RRSP withdrawals. All other income from the base calendar year, including allowable deductions, will be taken and added to the estimated income (employment, self-employment and pension income).

If the optionable event occurs during the current payment period or within the previous 6 months, the option is called a "current year option". If the optionable event occurs during the calendar year immediately preceding the payment period, it is called a "previous year option". The exception to this rule is when an option is effective in January. Current year option All employment, self-employment and pension income must be estimated for the option. The estimated income is added to the actual income from the base calendar year to calculate the total income. The total income is used to establish the benefit entitlement for the remaining months of the payment period after the event. Termination of employment or self-employment To calculate the estimated income in a current year option situation, any employment or self-employment income received from the source of retirement before or after the event took place is excluded from the calculation of estimated income. Any employment and self-employment income received from other sources in the calendar year of the event are included. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and included in the estimated income. All pension income received the month after the event to the end of that calendar year is prorated to a yearly amount and included in the calculation of estimated income. Termination or reduction of pension income To calculate the estimated income for a current year option where pension income terminates , the pension income received from that source is excluded from the calculation of estimated income. To calculate the estimated income for a current year option where a pension income reduces , any pension income received from that source will be prorated to a yearly amount beginning the month of the event using the reduced rate. All other pension income received the month of event to the end of that calendar year is prorated to a yearly amount and included in the calculation. If an option is granted due to the termination or reduction of pension income in the current payment period, all employment or self-employment income for the calendar year in which the loss or reduction of pension income took place will be included in the estimate. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and calculated for statements of estimated income in the same manner as indicated in the Employment and self-employment income section. Previous year option To calculate the estimated income for a previous year option where employment or self-employment income or pension income terminates , any income from the source of the event is excluded from the calculation. To calculate the estimated income for a previous year option where a pension income reduces , any pension income received from the source will be included in the calculation using the reduced rate. All other pension income that is not part of the event is also included in the calculation and estimated for the calendar year. All employment income or self-employment income and pension income which are not part of the event should be estimated for the calendar year. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and calculated for statements of estimated income. January effective dates Generally, when an option is processed for an event, 2 options or statements of estimated income are offered. A current year option that coincides with the calendar year in which the event occurs, followed by a previous year option for the payment period that follows the calendar year in which the event occurs. The exception to this is when an option is effective in January. When an option is effective in January, only one option is offered because the terminated income, or the higher income in the case of the reduction of pension income, no longer impacts the individual's base calendar year income. If the individual retired from employment or self-employment in the month of December, the event is considered to have occurred in December, but the option is effective January. As the event occurred in the calendar year immediately before the effective date, a previous year option calculation is performed for January to June and again for July to the following June, resulting in only 2 previous year option calculations. If the individual's pension income is reduced or terminated in January, the event is considered to have occurred in January and the option is effective January. Since the event occurred in the same calendar year as the effective date, a current year option calculation is performed for January to June and again for July to the following June, resulting in only 2 current year option calculations.

Previous to December 2021, a new payment (monthly, arrears, one-time payment) on an active account equal to or less than $2.00 was sent to the Standard Payment System (SPS) and subsequently returned via the cancelled payment reversal feed . Effective December 2021, payments issued from CPMS that are equal to or less than $2.00 will automatically be set to suspend monthly . Once the total amount of all the suspend monthly payables and the total amount of the monthly payments are equal to or greater than $2.01, the suspend monthly status will be set to pending and all payments will be issued at month end. Entitlement to an ALWS benefit is based on the net income of the applicant. An ALWS benefit application must be approved if the applicant has met the eligibility criteria. However, there will be situations where an application is approved with no entitlement. An application will be approved with no entitlement when: the applicant is a sponsored immigrant at the effective date; the applicant's income is in excess; or the applicant is incarcerated. An application will be approved but the entitlement cannot be determined in situations when: eligibility has been met; and required information or documentation has not been received to determine the entitlement amount (e.g. clarification of their income, documentation required to confirm foreign pension, documentation to confirm sponsorship agreement details).

topic_title: Applicant applying from outside of Canada
text: An applicant's residence status can affect their eligibility or entitlement if they submit an ALWS benefit application when they reside outside of Canada. The following table lists these situations and outcomes: Situation 1 Outcome The applicant left Canada more than 6 months before the ALWS benefit effective date. The application will be denied because there is no eligibility or entitlement to the ALWS benefit outside of Canada beyond the 6 months after the month of departure. If the applicant returns to Canada permanently, they must submit a new ALWS benefit application and statement of income. Situation 2 Outcome The applicant has at least 20 years of residence in Canada after age 18 and left Canada within 6 months of the ALWS benefit effective date. The application will be approved if all the eligibility criteria are met. The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period after the effective date. Situation 3 Outcome The applicant has at least 10 years but less than 20 years of residence in Canada after age 18 and left Canada within 6 months of the ALWS benefit effective date. The application will be approved if the applicant was residing in Canada on the day before the application's approval date. The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period after the effective date. Situation 4 Outcome At the effective date, the applicant has less than 10 years of residence in Canada after age 18, has lived or worked in a country with which Canada has an ISSA in force, and left Canada within 6 months of the ALWS benefit effective date. The application must be processed by staff in International Operations (IO) who will determine eligibility and communicate the approval or denial to the applicant. IO staff: The application will be approved if totalization is possible under the applicable ISSA and all eligibility criteria are met. The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period after the effective date. Situation 5 Outcome At the effective date, the applicant has less than 10 years of residence in Canada after age 18, has not lived or worked in a country with which Canada has an ISSA in force, and left Canada 6 months before the ALWS benefit effective date. The application will be denied. For more information, Eligibility Requirements— ALWS Benefit New Business (Policy)

topic_title: Determining eligibility under an International Social Security Agreement
text: Under an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA), an applicant's eligibility can be determined using foreign creditable periods (e.g. contributions and/or residence) in a country with which Canada has an ISSA in force. International Social Security Agreement Country List (Work Tool) An application will be considered under an ISSA when an applicant has lived or worked in a country with an ISSA with Canada and: does not meet the minimum residence requirement to qualify for an ALWS benefit and has completed creditable periods in an ISSA country; or meets the minimum eligibility requirements, however they could have an earlier effective date under an ISSA. The terms of most ISSAs allow for foreign creditable periods to be added to residence in Canada to meet the minimum residence requirements. This is known as totalization and is completed by International Operations (IO) staff. While totalization can assist an applicant to meet the minimum residence requirements, entitlement is still based on actual years of residence in Canada. For more information on when to transfer an ALWS benefit application to IO, Transfer a Client's File to International Operations (Action)

topic_title: How can an individual or their legal representative apply?
text: An individual can apply for the ALWS benefit online by accessing the client portal through their My Service Canada Account (MSCA) or by submitting an Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor - Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form. Income is required to determine initial and ongoing entitlement to the ALWS benefit. Entitlement is generally based on the income of the client from the calendar year preceding the payment period. This is referred to as the base calendar year income. Income is assessed using the information found on the: Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement with Statement of Income (ISP-3025B) form; Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form; CRA income feeds; or Liaison forms provided by International Social Security Agreement partners. You must reconcile any variances to ensure the initial income used to determine entitlement is accurate. In specific circumstances, a client's ALWS benefit entitlement may be calculated based on an estimate of their current year's income instead of their previous year income. topic_title: Income is received for the wrong income year
text: When a valid application for the ALWS benefit is submitted, it protects the date of the application (and possible retroactivity) based on the date the application was received. If the statement of income or the income information received from the CRA , is not for the correct base calendar year, the requirement for the statement of income is met. However, entitlement to the ALWS benefit cannot be determined until the required income for the applicable payment period is obtained from the CRA or the applicant. To determine which base calendar year income is required, you must consider the earliest possible effective date of the ALWS benefit. Refer to the examples below: Example: Situation 1 Direction An applicant submits an Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor – Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form on July 2, 2023. The ALWS benefit application is processed on July 24, 2023. The ALWS benefit application can be approved with an effective date of August 2022 (11 months before the application was received). To pay the full retroactive entitlement of August 2022 to July 2023, the following statements of income are required: 2021 (July 2022 to June 2023 payment period); and 2022 (July 2023 to June 2024 payment period). The CRA income feed has been received for 2022; however, the 2021 income is not available from the CRA . The requirement for the statement of income is met and payments for the client's ALWS benefit can begin effective July 2023. The period of August 2022 to June 2023 is date protected and can be considered once the 2021 income has been obtained from the client or the CRA . Example: Situation 2 Direction An Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor – Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form is received on October 2, 2023. The applicant's 60th birthday is at a future date of August 5, 2024. The application is processed on November 13, 2023, and the ALWS benefit is approved effective September 2024. Once an individual applies for the ALWS benefit, a request is made to the CRA for the applicant's income information. Since the application is being processed in the July 2023 to June 2024 payment period, the income for 2022 is received from the CRA feed. The requirement for the statement of income has been met; however, entitlement cannot be determined until the income that coincides with the payment period of the effective date (2023) is received. Since the 2023 income is not available at the time of processing, the application will have to be held until the 2023 income is available and entitlement can be determined. The payment period of the effective date is date protected. However, any subsequent payment year is reviewed individually and is subject to the conditions of the lifetime renewal designation.

When an ALWS benefit application is approved with 10 years of Canadian residence, the entitlement of the benefit does not increase with additional years of residence in Canada. However, if the applicant has resided in Canada for less than 10 years at the effective date and they are eligible under an International Social Security Agreement, the applicant may be entitled to a prorated ALWS benefit provided all eligibility and entitlement criteria have been met. Entitlement to prorated income-tested benefits is calculated at 1/10th of the benefit rate for each year of residence in Canada and increases with each additional year of residence in Canada after approval of the benefit, up to a maximum of 10 years. This is known as the special qualifying factor or proration of income-tested benefits. For more information, Special Qualifying Factor (Work Tool)

topic_title: When can an individual or their legal representative apply?
text: An individual or their legal representative can submit an application up to 12 months before their 60th birthday and up to 11 months after their 65th birthday. If an individual applies up to 12 months before becoming eligible, the application remains valid. However, in some cases, you may have to verify additional periods of residence at the time the application is approved (e.g. an additional year of residence is required and will be attained with continued residence up to age 60). If an individual applies more than one year before their 60th birthday or more than 11 months after their 65th birthday, deny the ALWS benefit application because the age requirement has not been met. The implementation of the updated policy for WA & SGO launched on December 13, 2021 and December 13, 2021 January 31, 2022 The policy direction provides revised guidance on how to assess applicants and beneficiaries who are engaged in paid work, as well as in volunteer activity and educational activity in the amount of 15 hours or more per week on a regular basis, for 4 months or more. It impacts all applicants participating in volunteer and/or educational activity and beneficiaries (including initial, reassessments, and reconsiderations). The CPP enhancement legislative changes are being phased-in over seven years, from 2019 to 2025. In January 2019, the Canada Revenue Agency began collecting enhanced contributions from working Canadians. System updates required to accommodate the CPP enhancement legislative changes are being implemented gradually through the CPP enhancement (CPPe) project. On November 23, 2019, system functionalities to split earnings and contributions in ITRDS (base CPP and first additional) were implemented. On May 21, 2022, system functionalities to pay the first additional portion of the CPP enhancement were implemented. The system release in May 2022 also included the introduction of system functionalities for 2 of the legislative changes stemming from the 2016-2018 CPP Triennial Review (flat-rate Death benefit and removal of the age-based reduction to the Survivor's pension). See System Updates for the Death benefit and Survivor’s Pension Triennial Review Reforms for additional details. System Updates for the Death benefit and Survivor’s Pension Triennial Review Reforms Additional system changes related to the calculation of the Child Rearing Drop-In and Disability Drop-In provisions, as well as calculation of the second additional portion of CPP enhancement will be implemented at a later date.

topic_title: Payment of the first Additional Portion of the CPP Enhancement
text: Effective Date: May 24, 2022 Amended Date: June 20, 2022

As the CPP enhancement impacts the way some CPP benefits and provisions are calculated, changes to systems are being introduced and knowledge products have been developed or updated. Changes to pension systems, application and tools ITRDS This system has been updated to determine entitlement and simulate the first additional portion of CPP benefits. CPMS This system has been updated to pay the first additional portion of CPP benefits. The CPP enhancement legislative changes are being phased-in over seven years (from 2019 to 2025), starting in January 2019. The enhancement components are not a separate benefit, but rather a top-up to the base CPP. The enhancement increases the CPP retirement (RTR) pension, post-retirement benefit (PRB), disability benefit and survivor’s (SVR) pension. Eligibility for CPP benefits is not affected. On May 21, 2022, updates were made to ITRDS and CPMS in order to process and pay the first additional component of CPP benefits. As part of the same system release, the Department has also introduced new system functionality to pay the $2,500 flat-rate Death (DTH) benefit and adjudicate an SVR pension for an applicant under the age of 45 (2016-2018 CPP Triennial Review). These legislative changes have required manual intervention and workarounds since they were implemented in January 2019.
Effective Date: May 24, 2022 Amended Date: July 27, 2022

CPP and QPP Apportioning of Dual Refund The CPP and QPP apportioning method for a dual refund of contributions for a dual year contributions has been modified in ITRDS. The apportioning method based on the CPP ratio of the CPP contributions on the total CPP and QPP contributions has been replaced by a CPP and QPP apportioning based on a ratio of CPP and QPP salary earnings similar to Canada Revenue Agency calculations. The CPP calculation guide has been amended to include the manual calculation in section 4.1.2. The new method applies for all dual years starting in 2012 with a dual refund. ITRDS now calculates and CPMS pays the first additional component for the CPP benefits and provisions, as well as a full rate DTH benefit and a full SVR pension to eligible beneficiaries under the age of 45 in accordance with the Triennial Review legislative changes. The original calculation of a benefit is now referred to as the base CPP component. The first additional component is calculated separately and added to the base resulting in an overall increase in payment. Because the enhanced component is considered a top-up to the base CPP, the base CPP and CPP enhancement components work together seamlessly. The client will receive one total amount. The first additional does not affect the eligibility requirements for benefits. Clients must be entitled and eligible to the base CPP benefit and have made enhanced contributions to be eligible for a first additional component of that benefit: ITRDS and CPMS will display the breakdown of the base CPP and first additional components on various screens. The navigation of screens has not changed. All systematic benefit adjudications and re-adjudications performed in ITRDS after May 21, 2022 will incorporate the first additional component. The re-adjudication of existing accounts with CPP benefits and enhanced contributions will begin in June 2022. When processing a SVR pension for a client under the age of 45, ITRDS will now calculate the full rate under 65, making existing workaround obsolete. ITRDS will adjudicate the DTH benefit with the flat rate of $2,500 for eligible contributors with a date of death after December 31, 2018. Applications are no longer required to be sent to the CPP Death Triennial team.

topic_title: Actions for the supervisor or supporting colleague
text: Stay calm. Acknowledge receipt of the message and offer support and guidance to the employee through MS Teams. Contact an additional supervisor or colleague to assist if needed. Monitor the call if able. Otherwise, continue communication with the employee through MS Teams. Obtain the client's name, phone number, location, details of the threat, if any weapons or other people are present and if the client has a relevant medical condition. If there is an imminent threat, call emergency services. If the client is within your community, dial 9-1-1. If the client is outside your community, obtain the 10-digit number of the client's local police service from the internet. If the voice message tells you to hang up and dial 9-1-1, do not hang up. Attempt to speak to the on-duty officer who will connect you to local emergency services. Obtain the officer's name and badge number, the name of the police service and the police report number. If the threat is towards the Department, contact the regional security office Internal link.. . regional security office Complete a security incident report Internal link , even if the client retracts their statement or a threat is determined not to be imminent. You will require: the client's name, phone number, location and any relevant medical condition; details of the threat, including if any weapons or other people were present; the name of the police service contacted, the officer's name and badge number, the police report number and what client information was released to them; and name, position and contact information of the employees involved in the situation. security incident report Ensure the employee adds a description of the call in the file and enters a note into ITRDS . Ask the client-specific questions about their intention to commit violence or self-harm. For helpful communication techniques, refer to the Conflict prevention section below. Threats of Self-Harm, Suicide or Violence - Examples of Questions for Agents to Ask the Caller A specific plan indicates a higher level of danger. It is better to be overcautious rather than underestimate the client's intent to harm themselves or others. To assess the level of danger, consider the following factors: Are there additional risk factors such as a recent major life event or lack of social support? What type of threat is present? Direct threat: I am going to kill myself. Indirect threat: I might as well end it all now. Conditional threat: If I do not get money soon, I cannot go on living. What is the tone, pitch and pace of the client's speech? At whom is the threat targeted? Has the client repeated the threat several times? Does the client convey a serious intent and plan to carry out the threat or are they demonstrating frustration? Does the client have access to a weapon or means available to commit violence or self-harm? Is the client alone? Where are they located? Is there a history of threatening or violent behaviour? Is there a medical condition that may contribute to threatening behaviour?

topic_title: Authority to release information to emergency services
text: If a client threatens to harm themselves or someone else, ection 37(1) of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act authorizes you to contact emergency services and provide a client's personal information. Only disclose information relevant to the situation: Your name, employer, and the type of work you do. The name, address, phone number, date of birth and location of the client. The person who is the subject of the threat. Factual details about the incident (e.g. mention of a weapon) and previous incidents. The medical condition if known and only if it is pertinent to the situation.

topic_title: Before making a potentially difficult call
text: Review the file and prepare questions. Identify if a supervisor or colleague is available. Notify them that you are making a potentially difficult call and may require assistance. Identify the phone number(s) for emergency and crisis services in the client's location. If the client is within your community, dial 9-1-1. If the client is outside your community, obtain the 10-digit number of the client's local police service from the internet.

Anger and aggressive behaviour by a client can be a reaction to the anxiety they are experiencing from personal stressors such as loss of income or illness. Providing timely information to clients in a supportive manner can allow them to maintain control of their lives and make appropriate decisions about their future. Guiding principles: Adopt a caring and compassionate approach by demonstrating respect and concern for every client and providing quality service. Communicate openly, honestly and implement better ways of explaining the program's eligibility criteria by using plain language, updating the client throughout the process and responding to their inquiries. Manage your own emotional reactions to cope with an angry, threatening or distressed client. If possible, prepare yourself ahead of a potentially difficult call. Table 1. Helpful communication techniques: Do Do not Remain calm, polite and professional. Do not take a client's anger personally or be defensive. Use active listening skills by giving your full attention, clarifying, paraphrasing and summarizing. Ask open-ended questions. Confirm that you understand the issue. Do not interrupt, argument, or tell a client to calm down. Do not assume anything or jump to conclusions about what is making the client angry or upset. Allow the client to explain their feelings. Allow them time to think. Do not be afraid of pauses in the conversation. Do not convey the impression that you are in a hurry or distracted. Show concern for their distress. Validate the client when you can. Do not relay pity or say everything will be all right. Explain the decision-making process. Do not feel that you have to make a hasty decision. Apologize for an error, delay or misunderstanding. Thank them for their patience and understanding. If you do not know the answer, say so and offer to help get the answer. Be honest. Do not feel that you have to solve problems alone. Do not make promises you cannot keep or say there is nothing you can do. Explore options to resolve the situation. Ask if there is other information the client can provide. Suggest actions the client can take and offer to help if you can. Do not give them personal advice or share your personal beliefs or values. Let the client save face and back down with dignity. Do not embarrass the client or minimize their distress or reaction to the situation. Be aware of some clients' cultural differences in relating and communicating with government officials, authorities or women. Do not allow the client to verbally abuse you. Warn them you will end the call if they continue.

A crisis incident may include: the client threatening to hurt or kill themselves or others; the client threatening to damage property; the client being verbally abusive or threatening to you; the client discloses they are in danger; or a threat coming from a third party such as a representative or family member.

topic_title: If the client becomes upset during the call
text: Remain calm. Do not place the client on hold. Listen and allow the client to express themself. Assess the seriousness of the situation. Go to Assess the level of danger section in the What you need to know section of the Overview tab. Tell the client that you want to help them. Help the client problem solve and plan a positive course of action such as contacting a family member, crisis centre Internal link or healthcare provider. Assist the client by looking up a crisis centre in their area. crisis centre If the incident escalates, go to the section If the client makes a threat during the call below. If the incident deescalates or a positive course of action is determined, offer to call the client back after a short period to determine if they are still okay or if they need further help to connect to a support system. Describe the incident in detail, including direct quotes, on a call record and place it in the client's file. Notify your supervisor of the incident. Create an Important note in ITRDS briefly stating what happened and what actions you took. Refer to ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete . ITRDS Notes—Review, Add and Delete

topic_title: If the client makes a threat during the call Updated
text: If the client makes a threat and hangs up, do not call them back. Inform your supervisor if there is a risk or threat. Remain calm. Do not place the client hold. Ask the client where they are. Ask the client not to harm anyone including themself. Tell the client that you want to help them. If you are in the office and there are colleagues close by, wave for assistance. Identify if the client threatens: self-harm or suicide, consider asking the following questions: Are you thinking about harming yourself or attempting suicide? Have you attempted suicide in the past? Have you thought of a plan? If yes, try to determine what the plan is. Do you have the means available to you for this plan? Would you be willing to make a no-suicide agreement and commit to it for a set period of time? Is there someone who can help keep you safe if you might harm yourself? If yes, can you speak to them when you feel the urge to harm yourself or attempt suicide? violence, consider asking the following questions: Are you thinking about harming someone? Have you harmed someone in the past? Have you thought of a plan? If yes, try to determine what the plan is. Do you have a weapon to hurt someone? Would you be willing to commit to a non-violence agreement for a set period of time before deciding to act on your decision? Is there someone who can help stop you from harming others? If yes, can you speak to them when you feel violent? Alert a supervisor or colleague through MS Teams. Under Type a new message select the exclamation mark then select Urgent . Ask them to call emergency services. Give the supervisor or colleague sufficient details so they can help you (client's name, phone number, location, details of the threat, if any weapons or other people are present and if the client has a relevant medical condition). Inform the client that you are taking their statements seriously and your supervisor is notifying emergency services. Stay on the line until a first responder is with the client or your supervisor tells you that emergency services has made contact with the client. Only call emergency services yourself if you do not have assistance from a supervisor or colleague: Only put the client on hold or hang up on them if you do not have another phone available. Tell the client that you are hanging up to call emergency services and you will call them back immediately. Tell them to answer the phone when it rings. If the client is within your community, dial 9-1-1. If the client is outside your community, obtain the 10-digit number of the client's local police service from the internet. If the voice message tells you to hang up and dial 9-1-1, do not hang up. Attempt to speak to the on-duty officer who will connect you to local emergency services. Obtain the officer's name and badge number, the name of the police service and the police report number. text: In a crisis incident, you have a specific set of roles: Assess the situation to determine the seriousness of the threat. Go to the Assess the level of danger section below. Foreign Direct Deposit currently exists as a work type only under the CPP program. Since the addition of work types, the Foreign Direct Deposit is now available under the CPPD, OAS and International Operations programs. Prior to July 1, 2022, processing sites identified PANs relating to Foreign Direct Deposits and set them to Halifax under the Location field. Currently, National Headquarters identifies original PANs relating to Foreign Direct Deposit and loads them directly in PWS under the Payment Advice Notice—FDD work type choosing Halifax in the Location field, providing the PAN has one of the following reasons: Account Closed; Invalid Account Number; Address; Invalid Financial Institution Number; Invalid Branch Transit Number; Branch Closed; Foreign Banking Info Missing; Enrolment Data Missing; or Enrolment Data is Invalid. For more information, Return Reason Code Table Furthermore, the Atlantic Foreign Direct Deposit unit will fully process the PAN once the work item is loaded in PWS. There may be occasions where regional input is sought. However, these cases are expected to be minimal. This will improve overall efficiency and improve service time to the client. In the event that a region receives a PAN that requires the Foreign Direct Deposit unit’s support, the work item can be adjusted to this work type and the Location field must be set to Halifax .

If additional guidance is required, send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool (BERT) and select Canada Pension Plan & Old Age Security (access is required). Business Expertise Request Tool

When the PRDB was first introduced in January 2019, a PRDB Statement Application (7044) was created and sent to potentially eligible clients. This work type did not capture the outcome of the PRDB once a decision had been made. Upcoming policy changes to the PRDB require a standalone PRDB application form. To capture the new PRDB application (1170) form in PWS, the PRDB – Statement Application (7044) work item has been updated to contain both variations. A decision field has been added so PRDB decisions can be captured when the benefit is adjudicated on its own (i.e., separate from the CPP Disability benefits application).
If additional guidance is required, send an enquiry via the Business Expertise Request Tool by following normal channels. Business Expertise Request Tool

When a standalone PRDB Statement Application (7044) or the new version PRDB Application (1170) is received, it will be captured in PWS using the updated work type: PRDB – Application (7044/1170) . Once a medical or non-medical decision has been made on the PRDB Application (7044/1170) , the decision will be reflected in PWS by selecting the appropriate decision in the new drop-down menu. Current PRDB procedures and policies continue to be in force. PRDB procedures and policies

Effective July 1, 2022, the PRDB – Statement Application (7044) PWS work type will be updated to PRDB – Application (7044/1170) . In addition, a drop-down menu will be added to this work type in order to capture the PRDB decision ( Grant , Deny , or Not Applicable ).
